How Japan is digging in to deter – and withstand – a conflict over Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:00:06 UTC
07:00:06 KST

Advertisement
In FocusHow Japan is digging in to deter – and withstand – a conflict over Taiwan
A planned Hiroshima defence hub highlights how Tokyo is accelerating preparations to sustain its military should a Taiwan crisis reach Japan
8-MIN READ8-MIN
1
The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the second of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Tokyo is building military resilience within its territory.
Japan’s recent purchase of a former Nippon Steel site to build a sprawling new defence hub points to a deeper shift in Tokyo’s preparations for a potential Taiwan conflict: it is increasingly planning not only for how to deter a war, but also for how to sustain the fight if deterrence fails.
The planned complex in Kure, Hiroshima prefecture – already home to one of Japan’s major naval bases – is intended to combine military facilities, logistics and defence production, concentrating several of the functions Tokyo would need to sustain its forces during a prolonged conflict.
Four years into a sweeping defence build-up, experts say that emphasis on endurance reflects a grim conclusion taking hold in Japanese defence planning: preparing for a Taiwan crisis increasingly means preparing to defend Japan itself.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made that concern unusually explicit last November, saying a Taiwan contingency involving warships and the use of force could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan – potentially allowing its Self-Defence Forces (SDF) to act even if Japan itself had not come under direct attack.
The geopolitical stakes far exceed the 110km (68 miles) separating Taiwan from Japan’s westernmost territory. Taiwan lies along vital Japanese sea lines of communication and at the centre of the first island chain, close to Japan’s southwestern islands and key US military installations.
Should Beijing gain control, it could significantly strengthen the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) operational position around Japan and its access to the western Pacific.

Albania protests against Trump-linked development turn violent after 100th day
Dubbed the ‘flamingo revolution’, the demonstrations seek to halt the massive project over the environmental damage it could cause
Police in Albania blocked protesters from reaching parliament on Tuesday as the latest rally against a luxury development linked to US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, turned violent
The march was staged as parliament resumed from a summer recess and after the demonstrations marked their 100th day on Monday. They challenged a police cordon in the centre of the capital, Tirana, pelting officers in riot gear with eggs and tomatoes.
Cars transporting lawmakers to the parliament building were confronted by the crowds and were hit with plastic water bottles before police intervened to let them through.
Dubbed the “flamingo revolution” for protesters’ signs depicting the pink bird that could be harmed by the coastal development, the anti-government protests have rocked Albania.
Although Albanian officials have avoided giving details of Kushner’s role in the project, Trump’s daughter, Ivanka, has spoken about her family’s involvement in the venture, describing it as an “incredible project”.
The protests are aimed at stopping the massive project that critics say would cause environmental damage and limit public access to the coast.

Real Madrid edge Inter 2-1 as Mourinho wins 1st Champions League match in 2nd spell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:55:48 UTC
06:55:48 KST

Halis Sunnetci
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Real Madrid began the 2026-27 UEFA Champions League with a 2-1 victory over Inter on Tuesday as Jose Mourinho marked his return to the competition with a win against his former club.
Meanwhile, at Estadio do Dragao, Manchester City opened their campaign with a 2-0 victory over Porto, with Erling Haaland scoring twice to become the club's joint-top scorer in Champions League history.
Real Madrid 2-1 Inter
Mourinho's side made the most of Inter's defensive errors to take a 2-0 lead before the Italian side pulled one back and threatened an equalizer late on.
Kylian Mbappe opened the scoring in the 14th minute after Inter defender Yann Aurel Bisseck failed to control the ball, allowing Brahim Diaz to pounce and set up the France captain for a clinical finish.
Real Madrid doubled their advantage nine minutes later when Inter goalkeeper Josep Martinez took too long to clear a back-pass from Benjamin Pavard. Federico Valverde closed him down, got a touch on the ball at his feet, and sent it rolling into the empty net.
Inter continued to create chances, but Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois made several important saves to preserve the two-goal advantage.
Madrid also had opportunities to extend their lead, with Martinez recovering from his first-half error to make a series of excellent saves.
Jude Bellingham was denied from close range in the 58th minute, while Martinez also kept out a shot from Mbappe eight minutes later.
Inter pulled one back in the 77th minute when Carlos Augusto met Lautaro Martinez's ball across the face of goal and side-footed home.
Inter pushed for an equalizer late on, but Courtois made another fine save from Henrikh Mkhitaryan's deflected effort as Madrid held on for victory.
Porto 0-2 Manchester City
Manchester City opened Enzo Maresca's Champions League tenure with a comfortable 2-0 victory over Porto, controlling possession and creating more chances while the hosts managed five shots without testing Gianluigi Donnarumma on target.
City created several chances in the first half, but Porto goalkeeper Diogo Costa kept the score level with a string of impressive saves, including efforts from Haaland and Rayan Cherki.
Haaland broke the deadlock shortly after halftime, heading home a deft cross from Enzo Fernandez after Cherki had kept the attack alive.
Porto struggled to create a response, with Alan Varela curling an effort just wide of the far post in the 57th minute.
Haaland sealed the win in stoppage time, meeting Rayan Ait-Nouri's cutback with a first-time finish from just outside the six-yard box.
The goal was Haaland's 36th in the Champions League for Manchester City, making him the club's joint-top scorer in the competition alongside Sergio Aguero.
Fernandez came close to a third for City in the fifth minute of stoppage time, first sending a free-kick narrowly wide before Costa saved his low effort.

Two more people arrested over ‘mountain of illegal waste’ dumped in Oxfordshire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:54:02 UTC
06:54:02 KST

Two men have been arrested after fly-tippers dumped a “mountain of illegal waste”, stacked 10 metres high, in Oxfordshire.
Hundreds of tonnes of rubbish appeared in a field between the River Cherwell and the A34 near Kidlington in November last year. The waste tip was so large that removing it could cost more than the local council’s annual budget, the area’s MP said.
The clean-up operation, which concluded last month, took five months. An estimated 22,704 tonnes of rubbish were cleared, with the operation costing an estimated £6m.
The Environment Agency (EA) has confirmed on Tuesday that a 21-year-old man from Ashford in Surrey and a 43-year-old man from Stanwell in Surrey had been arrested.
It brings the total number of people apprehended to six, after one arrest in February, two in January and one in November, the EA said.
The watchdog shut down the Kidlington site in October after officers discovered continued criminal activity after the first report of dumping at the site in July 2025.
Colin Chiverton, area environment manager for the Thames at the EA, said: “The dumping at Kidlington was abhorrent and had no regard for the local community.
“We moved quickly to remove all illegal waste from the site and our teams continue to work tirelessly on this investigation. These arrests are another vital step in collecting new evidence and delivering justice for the residents of Kidlington.”
Dame Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said: “This government said we’d take on waste criminals and that’s exactly what we’re doing.
“These arrests are another step towards delivering justice for Kidlington residents, who have had to put up with the dumping of disgusting waste.
“The years of waste crime being allowed to fester have ended. We are taking decisive action through our crackdown and putting more officers on the frontline to restore pride in our communities.”
The two men have been released on conditional bail pending further investigations.
The EA previously announced it was to spend millions of pounds to clear the enormous illegal rubbish dump, saying the waste was at risk of catching fire.
Its policy is to refuse to clear up illegal waste dumps across the country, instead pursuing the perpetrators and landowners. But officials said they had taken the exceptional decision to clear up the waste outside Kidlington, which is next to the River Cherwell, because the scale of the fire risk set it apart from other illegal waste dumps in England and presented an overriding public imperative.
The agency was given no extra money to clear the waste, and the EA said this would come from “making efficiencies in its operations”. The cost to the taxpayer would also include the payment of the landfill tax on the waste to the Treasury.
The dumping in Kidlington took place under the noses of the EA, which was monitoring the site after being alerted to suspicious activity.

Government to stop perpetrators accessing victims' superannuation
Financial and economic abuse is estimated to cost the economy almost $11 billion a year and affect more than 2.4 million Australians, according to research by Deloitte and published by Treasury.
For this story, my colleague Nassim Khadem interviewed a woman who was physically abused by her husband. But after leaving him, she discovered he had accumulated millions of dollars in debt and placed it under her name.
This victim-survivor is still trying to clear those debts after five years.
Unfortunately, this type of abuse is all too common.
Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino is unveiling a suite of changes aimed at closing off the opportunities for financial abuse.
Perpetrators of domestic violence would be punished rather than rewarded for their actions when committing abuse against their former partners by racking up tax and other debts in their name, he said.

The Reserve Bank's deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, knows Australians are "furious" about inflation, and while he is determined to lower it, he says the RBA is not at the point where it has to take more drastic action.

Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1658: Ukraine’s new top commander is pushing to give combat-tested sergeants real authority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:42:43 UTC
06:42:43 KST

Exclusives
Team news
Vacancy: deputy editor-in-chief.
Military
Ukraine is sending its winning brigades to where the fighting is worst. The 46th just turned up outside Kramatorsk. Sloviansk and Kramatorsk are the last two big cities in the Donbas that Russia does not hold. The 46th Airmobile Brigade left the southeast in early July and reached them before anyone outside the army knew.
Trump’s peace envoys left, and Russia hit Kyiv with ballistics—the one thing Ukraine still struggles to stop. Only two ballistic missiles came down overnight, and the shortfall is now the centerpiece of what Kyiv is asking its allies to deliver.
Ukraine’s new top commander is pushing to unwind a Soviet-inherited command model mid-war. He wants combat-tested sergeants to have real authority. Ukraine inherited a system where officers decided everything and sergeants were senior soldiers with no ladder of their own.
Russia deploys missile brigade to Belarus as fears grow over new threat to Kyiv. The move comes as Russia steps up aerial attacks on Kyiv from the north and Belarus allows Moscow to use its territory to help guide strikes against Ukrainian targets.
Some ten robot boats. Five hundred Russian air sorties. One very lopsided hunt. Missions that once took a night now stretch to five days, and Russia keeps its fleet hidden, a naval drone unit commander says.
Intelligence and technology
Ukrainian engine for “Bars” missile-drone passes final tests. This is the last major imported component of the jet-powered drone used for deep strikes against Russia.
A Ukrainian strike drone that quietly hit 450-plus Russian targets steps out of the shadows. The drone pairs with a scout to punch through Russian jamming.
Ukraine’s new Hryfon Zakhid runs the whole drone chain on one screen. One operator assigns targets to drone crews from a tablet, in real time and without radio.
Ukrainian Armor unveils two new troop carriers at Polish arms exhibition: fast light scout and mine-resistant MRAP. Both meet NATO’s STANAG 4569 protection standards. Both cover opposite ends of the same job.
Ukraine shows a home-built missile designed to hit ballistic targets for the first time, the Koral, at Poland’s MSPO. Its guidance combines inertial navigation, radio correction, and an active radar homing head.
European NATO members may be the second target of Russia’s winter missile buildup—Ukraine’s foreign intelligence. The warning went to the national security advisors of Europe's leaders, with a call for urgent sanctions on 55 more firms keeping Russia's missile lines running.
Ukrainian AI targeting module placed third among 60-plus entries in NATO contest. NATO and Ukraine ran the challenge through their first jointly staffed body.
Ukrainian university and the Flamingo missile-maker opened an engineering course. On the first try, zero of 150 passed. Even students who scored well on the university entrance exam flunked the physics round.
Ukraine’s Brave1 says it can down Russia’s Banderol missiles with cruising speed 650 km/h for less than what they cost, and has destroyed at least four. In July, Ukrainian troops downed Banderols with Swedish Bofors L70 anti-aircraft guns designed in the late 1940s.
Ukraine has 67 companies working to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones en masse, Zelenskyy says. Only three to five have real results. He called the whole air-defense push "Plan B" to diplomacy's "Plan A".
China calls itself neutral—but its fiber ends up in the drones that hit Ukraine. The papers, reviewed by Western governments, trace drone-grade material straight from a Chinese state firm to a sanctioned Russian plant.
International
Brussels cleared Ukraine to spend EU loan money on American Patriot missiles for the coming winter of Russian attacks. The request went in four days earlier, and the funds come from the bloc's existing credit line rather than any new pledge.
Ukrainian journalist asks Trump’s envoy to his face whether he was disgusted to sit across from “international criminal” Putin. Witkoff wouldn’t answer directly. Earlier, Russia's FSB put a $400,000 bounty on Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Gordon.
Humanitarian and social impact
A Russian drone hit a Kyiv television newsroom in broad daylight while the channel was live on air. At least 5 people were injured, the building is partly destroyed, and firefighters put out the blaze at the site.
Russian-occupied nuclear plant ran on diesel for almost three weeks. Ukraine ended that, and the UN’s nuclear watchdog calls it a crucial step against an accident. The IAEA calls it a crucial step to prevent a nuclear accident at a site that had been facing a possible station blackout.
Russia burns occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant’s last-resort generators as everyday power, Ukraine says. Off-site power has been gone since 20 August, and the plant has cut its running generators to two to stretch the fuel that is left.
“Now on the 1,657th day”: Ukraine’s crews restored power to over 900,000 homes last week as Russia keeps striking grid before winter. Crews brought it back to 596 settlements, most of them in Odesa and Donetsk.
Kyiv stockpiles food and water as Russia’s new aerial tactics threaten a brutal winter. Russia has already targeted food storage around Kyiv, while Ukraine’s limited air defenses struggle to stop ballistic missiles and faster drones.
Political and legal developments
Russia’s FM says war must end so there is “no more Nazism” in Europe. Russian occupation official already said what that means: erasing Ukraine and stopping its aid. The collaborator put it plainly: "denazification is re-Russification".

US strikes Iranian tankers after more attempted missile attacks on Navy warship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:42:36 UTC

US strikes Iranian tankers after more attempted missile attacks on Navy warship
Vessels were targeted near Kharg Island and the southern port of Jask, according to Iran’s state media
The US on Tuesday struck multiple Iranian tankers in response to more attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship, according to a US official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Iranian state television also is reporting that US forces attacked Iranian oil tankers near the southern port of Jask and near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf.
The latest tit-for-tat strikes come as Washington and Tehran lurch back towards fighting during more than six months of war.
An Iranian state television reporter in Jask said an Iranian tanker was struck near the coast of Yekbeni, while another explosion was heard in the area whose source and location were not immediately clear.
State television later reported that the US military attacked a second tanker near waters off Jask. It said the crews of both vessels were being evacuated by lifeboat towards the Jask coast.
Separately, state television reported that another Iranian tanker was attacked in Kharg Island anchorage area. It said the crew was safely evacuated shortly after the strike.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy has warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for US attacks on Iranian tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting US forces and assisting in the attacks.

====================================================================================================

Explainer: What to know about Iran's "economic war headquarters"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:31:26 CST
06:31:26 KST

TEHRAN, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance recently announced the establishment of an "economic war headquarters" to improve coordination and expedite efforts to address economic challenges arising from wartime conditions.
Why has Iran established the headquarters at this time? What are its main functions? What implications could its establishment have for the Iranian economy?
WHAT'S BEHIND THE ESTABLISHMENT?
The measure comes as Iran, in addition to facing decades-long sanctions, sustained considerable economic damage in the U.S. and Israeli strikes that started on Feb. 28. The country has also been under a U.S.-imposed naval blockade for the past few months and recently faced intensified economic pressure from Washington.
Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump announced "the most crushing economic operation ever taken" against any country providing a lifeline to Iran, stressing, "This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale."
Iran's Deputy Economy Minister for Economic Policymaking and Strategy Morteza Zamanian said the headquarters' primary focus is on the economy ministry's responsibilities and authorities. It seeks to accelerate efforts to resolve wartime problems facing Iranian businesses, trade, financing operations and other economic sectors, he said.
He noted that some of the issues are beyond the ministry's authority, requiring coordination among various government bodies and follow-ups at the highest levels.
Asgar Qahremanpour, a Tehran-based international relations researcher, told Xinhua that the move is mainly aimed at countering foreign pressure. He said Iran's economy is simultaneously facing sanctions, war, disruptions in trade and transportation, foreign currency pressures and inflation.
Managing domestic economic vulnerabilities is another reason behind the headquarters' establishment, Qahremanpour said. Even before the war, Iran's economy faced inflation, depreciation of the rial, unemployment, financial imbalances and weak management. "The authorities have repeatedly emphasized the need for implementing internal reforms," he said.
WHAT ARE THE FUNCTIONS?
The Iranian deputy economy minister said the headquarters' main function is to identify problems and disruptions resulting from wartime conditions and find practical solutions.
Zamanian said when an issue requires cooperation among multiple government bodies, the headquarters will coordinate their efforts to prevent unnecessary bureaucracy. Supporting the domestic economic entities damaged during the war is among its other objectives, he added.
According to the semi-official Tasnim news agency, ensuring the continuity of supply chains and services and minimizing the impact of disruptions are also of particular importance under wartime conditions.
Qahremanpour listed some of the headquarters' possible responsibilities as the swift identification of disruptions caused by the war and the coordination of the government's economic responses, especially in the areas of trade and financing.
He said possible outcomes include preventing shocks to the country's foreign currency market, ensuring the supply of essential goods, medicines and raw materials, maintaining exports and imports, and supporting manufacturing enterprises.
WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR IRAN'S ECONOMY?
Mokhtar Ghobashy, secretary general of the Al-Farabi Center for Political Studies in Egypt, said the headquarters' establishment confirms that Iran is preparing for a prolonged confrontation with the United States.
Ghobashy added that although the latest U.S. sanctions have contributed to higher inflation in the Iranian market and a partial depreciation of the rial, Iran has adapted to such conditions to a significant extent, relying heavily on domestic production and maintaining overland trade with neighbors.
Echoing similar views, Sabah al-Sheikh, a professor of political science at the University of Baghdad, said the headquarters' establishment is just part of Iran's broader strategy to confront the intensified U.S. sanctions, stressing that Tehran is employing every available means to undermine the U.S. strategy and mitigate the impact of its economic pressure.
After more than four decades under sanctions, parts of Iran's economy have developed the capacity to adapt to external restrictions, according to Qahremanpour. Faster and more coordinated decisions by the headquarters could help prevent supply-chain disruptions in the short term, he added.
Qahremanpour said the headquarters could also provide an opportunity to carry out economic reforms, including reforms to the foreign currency system and national budget, strengthening the domestic private sector, eliminating economic rents and normalizing foreign economic relations.
To overcome crises, Iran also needs a more predictable and productive economy, Qahremanpour added, stressing that curbing inflation and resolving people's economic problems are among the desired outcomes to be achieved by the headquarters. ■

California hails rare sighting of gray wolf in Mendocino national forest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:31:12 UTC
06:31:12 KST

A gray wolf has recently been seen in California’s Mendocino national forest for the first time since the species returned to the state 15 years ago, state wildlife officials confirmed.
Officials in Lake county, which is about two hours north of San Francisco, said last week the California department of fish and wildlife (CDFW) had received reports of sightings in the forest in late August. The agency verified the presence of a wolf in the far north end of the county, county supervisor Brad Rasmussen said in a statement on social media.
The CDFW confirmed the sightings in a statement, telling the Guardian it had received two separate reports from an area where Mendocino, Glenn and Lake counties meet. The agency received photos and were on the ground to confirm the presence of the animal the following day, said Alicia de la Garza, the CDFW deputy director of public affairs.
“The sighting was verified by a CDFW wolf biologist who confirmed the validity of the photos, conducted surveys in the area and confirmed wolf tracks where one of the sightings was reported,” de la Garza said.
A century ago hunters and settlers drove wolves in California to extinction, but the animals returned to the state in 2011 and have significantly expanded their presence over the last decade, largely in the rural and remote north-east. There are at least 50 documented wolves in California.
The recent appearance in the Mendocino national forest, which was first reported by MendoLocal.News last week, is significant.
It represents the only confirmed sighting west of the Sacramento Valley, Axel Hunnicutt, the state gray wolf coordinator for the CDFW, told the Sacramento Bee, and is a sign the species is expanding its range.
“Evidence of wolves in that part of the state is a good thing,” he said.
The return of the animal has not been without controversy. Ranchers have expressed frustration that there is little they can do when wolves kill their livestock – the species is protected in California and under the federal Endangered Species Act. Donald Trump has sought to change that.
Last week the president signed an executive order, titled “Supporting America’s Ranchers”, that directs the interior department to look at removing gray wolves from the Endangered Species Act, and to loosen restrictions for “lethal removal”.
The US Fish and Wildlife Service has sought to de-list the gray wolf, but the matter is still unfolding in court. Meanwhile, the act protects the wolves that are across the majority of the lower 48 states under a 2022 federal court order.
Environmental groups condemned Trump’s order.
“Once again, we see this administration attempting to override the checks and balances provided by bedrock environmental laws like the Endangered Species Act in order to create industry carveouts and distract from other bad policies that are proving unpopular,” said Leia Barnett, New Mexico conservation lead for WildEarth Guardians.

WHO, Kenya ramp up readiness for El Nino deluge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:30:56 CST
06:30:56 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- The World Health Organization (WHO) is collaborating closely with the Kenyan government to mitigate health risks linked to the upcoming 2026/2027 El Nino season, the UN health agency announced Tuesday.
Speaking in Nairobi, the Kenyan capital, ahead of the October-December rainy season, WHO Representative to Kenya Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo said that continuous risk assessments will guide health authorities in identifying potential threats and strengthening emergency preparedness against flooding and climate-related disease outbreaks.
"The experience of the long rains earlier this year provides important lessons for preparing health services and communities before the next rainy season," Kimambo said in a statement.
The WHO said that among the areas being assessed are disease surveillance and early warning, laboratory and response capacity, safe water, sanitation and hygiene, risk communication and continuity of essential health services.
The UN health agency warned that severe flooding can contaminate drinking water sources and sanitation infrastructure, heightening the risk of waterborne illnesses such as cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis A, and diarrheal diseases.
It said floodwaters often restrict physical access to healthcare facilities, disrupting routine medical services and delaying critical treatments.
For Kenya, heavy rainfall is also forecast during the March-May 2027 long rainy season, potentially leading to widespread flooding.
According to the WHO, the previous rainy season affected over 27 counties, resulting in 122 deaths and displacing 42,259 people.
Severe damage to roads, bridges, power grids, and water infrastructure restricted access to critical services and significantly heightened the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks.
In response, Kenya's Ministry of Health has activated the Health Sector El Nino Contingency Plan to direct nationwide preparedness and emergency response efforts.
The framework coordinates operations across national and county governments, emergency agencies, humanitarian organizations, and international development partners.
The WHO observed that strong El Nino conditions, combined with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole, historically drive elevated rainfall across East Africa, not only in Kenya, with wetter-than-normal weather for Somalia, eastern and southern Ethiopia, northern Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi.
The health agency cautioned that similar climate dynamics in 1997 and 2019 triggered catastrophic, widespread flooding across the region, severely affecting vulnerable communities. ■

DR Congo's Ebola outbreak "increasingly heterogeneous" with high community deaths: WHO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:30:54 CST
06:30:54 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is "becoming increasingly heterogeneous," with divergent transmission trends across affected provinces and health zones, according to the latest WHO external situation report published on Tuesday.
"The trends reinforce an increasingly heterogeneous epidemic, with declining transmission in some areas occurring alongside intensification and continued geographic spread elsewhere," the report said.
A key development is the rising proportion of deaths occurring in the community. During the week of Aug. 31 to Sept. 6, the proportion of confirmed deaths in the community reached 75 percent, the highest weekly proportion observed during the reporting period, up from 56.6 percent two weeks earlier.
"This divergence is concerning, as the increase in community deaths alongside the continued decline in treatment facilities deaths indicates that the earlier reduction in overall mortality has not been sustained," the report said.
The persistence of high community mortality, the report explained, "may reflect multiple barriers along the pathway to care, including delayed detection and notification, delayed referral or transfer to treatment facilities, limited recognition of illness or perceived severity, geographic and transport barriers, care-seeking outside formal health facilities, and community acceptance or trust."
As for vaccines, the Ervebo vaccine, the licensed shot against the Zaire ebolavirus, is currently being evaluated for cross-protection against the current Bundibugyo strain through an effectiveness study in the field.
Meanwhile, under protocol-governed compassionate use, which allows the use of unapproved or partially studied vaccines in an outbreak setting, vaccinations for frontline healthcare workers and at-risk populations began on Aug. 27.
As of Sept. 6, a total of 2,007 healthcare workers and frontline workers had been vaccinated, said the report.
As of Sept. 6, the cumulative totals stand at 6,686 confirmed cases and 3,226 confirmed deaths, with a case fatality ratio of 48.3 percent among confirmed and probable cases, according to the report. Healthcare worker infections remain a major concern, with 167 confirmed infections, including 47 deaths.
The WHO assesses the risk of further spread as "very high" within the DRC and "high" for neighboring countries. The second IHR Emergency Committee, convened on Aug. 18, emphasized that "the outbreak remains far from controlled" and continues to constitute a public health emergency of international concern.
The current outbreak, declared in May, has since become the country's largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic on record and the second-largest globally, behind the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

Sa'ar rejected Miliband's accusations as "outrageous and wrong," saying that Israel's decision to advance construction in the so-called "E1" area of the occupied West Bank had been made more than a year ago, and arguing that two planned roads would preserve Palestinian territorial contiguity.
Israel last month opened a tender for 1,234 housing units in E1, part of a wider plan for about 3,400 homes.
Sa'ar asserted that the Israeli public "overwhelmingly supports" the settlers and opposes the establishment of a Palestinian state.
He also warned that Israel could take similar measures against other countries, saying, "Whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them."
More than half a million Israeli settlers live in the West Bank, which Israel occupied in 1967, alongside about 3.4 million Palestinians, according to Palestinian and Israeli sources. Recent years have seen a sharp rise in violence against Palestinians, with near-daily attacks by settlers and Israeli forces, often resulting in fatalities.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law. ■

China

2026-09-09
05:30:31 CST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Foreign ministers of 12 countries moved on Tuesday to tighten restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, as mounting settlement expansion and violence fuel growing concerns over the viability of a two-state solution.
Foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and Britain said in a joint statement that they intended to introduce national restrictions, support European measures, or were actively considering other steps in line with their national procedures.
The ministers said the situation in the West Bank was "rapidly deteriorating" amid what they described as unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion.
Among the 12 countries, Britain, France and Canada said they would bring forward national measures to ban trade in settlement goods, while welcoming steps already taken by Ireland, Spain, the Netherlands, Norway and Belgium.
Britain on Tuesday announced some of the most detailed measures so far. Speaking in the House of Commons, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Britain would introduce a ban on imports of goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
He said that Britain would also establish a new sanctions regime targeting specific companies and individuals providing construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate services that contribute to settlement expansion. Advertising in Britain for property in Israeli settlements would also be prohibited.
Miliband announced a shift in Britain's legal position, saying the British government now considered Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories unlawful.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on X that France would "end trade" with Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, adding that France could not, through its trade, support a situation that threatened Israelis, Palestinians and regional stability. He also urged Europe to adopt the same approach.
Some other European countries have already been moving in a similar direction.
Spain has already prohibited imports of settlement goods and related commercial advertising. Belgium has decided to introduce an import ban and in July approved draft implementing rules under which permits for goods originating from Israeli settlements would be refused. Ireland has approved draft legislation to ban imports of settlement goods.
The Netherlands has adopted a national ban on the import, purchase and sale of settlement goods, as well as related intermediary services, which will take effect on Sept. 22, while Norway has put proposed legislation banning imports from and exports to settlements out for public consultation.
The EU has also stepped up sanctions against extremist Israeli settlers. On May 28, it listed four entities and three individuals over serious human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank. The measures include asset freezes, funding bans and travel restrictions. The bloc, however, has yet to impose an EU-wide ban on trade with Israeli settlements.
The latest push for tougher measures followed Israel's advancement of the E1 settlement project in the West Bank in August by issuing a tender for 1,234 housing units.
According to the tender published online by Israel's Ministry of Construction and Housing, the project covers part of a broader plan to build 3,401 housing units in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The 12 foreign ministers said the E1 decision was among the developments undermining prospects for a Palestinian state and called on the Israeli government to immediately halt settlement expansion and ensure accountability for settler violence.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog criticised the planned British move on Tuesday, calling sanctions a "grave miscalculation."
The 12 ministers also reiterated their condemnation of the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and recognized Israel's legitimate security interests.
They reaffirmed support for a two-state solution under which Israel and a sovereign, democratic and viable Palestinian state would live side by side in peace and security within internationally recognized borders. ■

Water level of Budapest's Danube hits record low amid drought

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:30:31 CST
06:30:31 KST

BUDAPEST, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- The Danube River's water level in Budapest fell to a record low on Tuesday, after Hungary experienced its driest summer in more than a century, according to local authorities.
Gabriella Siklos, spokesperson for Hungary's General Directorate of Water Management, said the official gauge in Budapest recorded a water level of just 1 cm, the Hungarian news agency MTI reported.
Siklos explained that the reading means the river's surface stood just 1 cm above the gauge's artificially defined zero point, established by engineers in the 19th century. The river's actual depth near Budapest remained around 3 to 3.5 meters on average. The low water level has restricted navigation for some larger vessels.
The previous record low in Budapest was 28 cm, recorded at the end of July this year.
The newest record came after Hungary experienced its driest summer since 1901. The national meteorological service HungaroMet said that the country received only 74.1 mm of rainfall in the summer, equivalent to 36 percent of the 1991-2020 average.
The summer was also Hungary's second-hottest since 1901, according to HungaroMet. ■

JOHANNESBURG, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- South Africa is stepping up efforts to curb illegal migration, including strengthening border security, tightening controls on traffic register numbers (TRNs), and advancing plans to reserve certain economic sectors for citizens, officials said Tuesday.
Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development Mmamoloko Kubayi, who chairs the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration, made the remarks at a media briefing in Pretoria.
Kubayi said that while 90,000 repatriations had been carried out in recent months, illegal migration had not been deterred. Between April and June, 4,200 undocumented foreign nationals were intercepted while attempting to enter the country illegally.
Kubayi said the Borderline Infrastructure Improvement Plan (2026-2030), aimed at strengthening and modernizing South Africa's border infrastructure, had been approved by the Cabinet. It would improve border security, including patrol mobility, operational response times, personnel safety, infrastructure maintenance, intergovernmental coordination and the prevention of illegal cross-border incursions.
On the TRN system, Kubayi said the Department of Transport had moved to cancel and verify dormant TRNs issued between Jan. 1, 2000, and June 30, 2023.
The move followed revelations in Parliament in June that the system had been compromised by foreign nationals using fraudulent documents. Some of the TRNs were subsequently used as substitutes for visas and to open bank accounts.
The government is also advancing plans to reserve certain businesses, especially spaza shops, for South African citizens. Kubayi said 34 municipalities have adopted the Standard Draft By-laws for Township and Rural Economies, while 105 have adopted them through council resolutions and 21 are in the process of adoption.
"These operations demonstrate the government's zero-tolerance approach to criminality, irrespective of nationality, while ensuring that all enforcement actions are undertaken within the framework of the law and with respect for human rights," Kubayi said. ■

OpenAI claims to have solved maths problem that stumped humans for decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:29:10 UTC
06:29:10 KST

OpenAI claims to have solved a major mathematics problem that has stumped humans for nearly a century after spending millions of dollars on the artificial intelligence-led endeavour.
The company behind ChatGPT said it had cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven Millennium Prize Problems published by the Clay Mathematics Institute to highlight some of the biggest unsolved puzzles in the field.
However, the announcement swiftly became mired in controversy after mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, a professor at New York University, said OpenAI accelerated its work on the problem after hearing that he and another researcher at Anthropic, an OpenAI rival, were poised to announce their own breakthrough.
Buckmaster had further concerns because the pair’s work in progress was stored in OpenAI’s Codex model, which is used for writing computer programs, potentially making the work visible to the OpenAI team.
In a document posted on his website, he added: “I do not know what their model did, or how. I do not know whether our data was used. I am not accusing anyone of anything.”
At a press briefing on Tuesday, OpenAI researcher Sebastien Bubeck denied that the company had used the pair’s work or accessed material shared with OpenAI’s servers.
OpenAI’s announcement on the breakthrough gave more details, saying that the company was inspired to launch the effort after hearing rumours that two Millennium Prize Problems had been solved. It also said it could not rule out that data from the pair’s use of their products “helped improve our models.”
OpenAI said it tackled the Navier-Stokes problem with an internal OpenAI system that was more powerful than its latest GPT-6 Astra model. About 10,000 AI agents – AI systems that carry out tasks autonomously – worked on the problem at once and reached the solution in 88 hours.
“A major goal of our work is to empower scientists to advance research and technology that benefits all of humanity,” OpenAI researchers wrote in a blog. “We believe it is important to inform the world about the pace of AI progress and what to expect from upcoming models”.
The breakthrough is the latest to demonstrate how advanced artificial intelligence models consuming enormous amounts of computing power are encroaching on and reshaping the field of mathematics. In May, OpenAI claimed progress in another mathematical problem first proposed 80 years ago, while Google DeepMind has also claimed maths achievements with its models.
Bubeck said the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem was “a spectacular culmination of the arc we have seen over the past 12 months”.
The Navier-Stokes problem asks whether equations that are used to describe the movement of fluids like air and water fail under particular conditions. OpenAI’s proof suggests that they do, with the equations occasionally “blowing up” with the speed of fluids becoming impossibly infinite. It took OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra about 17 hours to verify the solution.
Mathematicians who solve any of the Millennium Prize Problems are in line for a $1m (£740,000) reward from the Clay Mathematics Institute. OpenAI, which is preparing for a flotation that could value the business at around $1tn, said it did not intend to claim the prize.
The clash with Buckmaster aside, the maths announcement also allows OpenAI to cast its technology in a positive light after a period of alarm over how safely it is being developed. OpenAI revealed in July that a swarm of agents had hacked into Hugging Face, a third'-party software store, during a cybersecurity test.
The incident, plus a similar episode at Anthropic, has led to renewed calls for curbs on AI development, with US senators calling last week for a permanent ban of AI “superintelligence” – the term for systems that outperform humans in all cognitive tasks.

Ukraine moves to restore anti-money-laundering safeguard that it quietly weakened, alarming EU and IMF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:24:49 UTC
06:24:49 KST

Ukraine's government has moved to restore an anti-corruption safeguard it had quietly weakened — the rule that requires banks to monitor the accounts of former senior officials. It has registered a new bill, No. 16051, that rewrites the provision, Deputy Olha Vasylevska-Smahliuk says, Ekonomichna Pravda reports.
The new bill changes the rules for monitoring former PEPs: enhanced financial monitoring after leaving office must remain in place for at least 12 months and will no longer automatically end upon its expiration, Deputy Yaroslav Zhelezniak says.
After that, the bank must conduct an individual risk assessment. If the risks associated with PEP status persist, enhanced monitoring will continue until the bank determines that those risks no longer exist. The assessment must be repeated at least once a year.
The same approach is proposed for family members and close associates of former PEPs.
A tax law hid the loosening
The weak version reached the statute book by stealth. Lawmakers slipped it into an unrelated measure, the digital-platform tax law No. 15111-d, passed in June, to gather the votes they needed. Under that wording, a bank could continue monitoring a former official for more than 12 months only with documented high risk.
That reversed the burden of proof. Ukraine's European partners were caught off guard, arguing the new text no longer matched the EU directive it was meant to implement. The EU Council and European Commission urged the president not to sign, and he refused. In June, the IMF said the change pushed Ukraine's anti-money-laundering system out of the FATF standards it must meet.
Former PEP status alone cannot justify bank's refusal
At the same time, the mere fact that a person was once a PEP cannot, after the 12-month period has expired, by itself constitute sufficient grounds for a bank to refuse to provide services. If a bank nevertheless refuses to establish or maintain a business relationship, the client would have a separate right to request a review of that decision.
The difference is fundamental. Under Bill No. 15111-d, after one year, a bank would have to separately establish that the client posed a high or unacceptably high risk in order to continue enhanced monitoring.
“The new government bill, No. 16051, provides for enhanced monitoring for at least one year, after which it continues for as long as an individual assessment shows that risks associated with PEP status persist,” Vasylevska-Smahliuk adds.

Argentina opens sanction proceedings against 15 entities for oil activities near Falkland Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:20:39 UTC
06:20:39 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The office of Argentina’s president announced Tuesday the initiation of sanctioning proceedings against 15 additional subjects for alleged violations of national hydrocarbon laws on its continental shelf.
"This progress is a new step in the same direction," it said in a statement. "The Argentine Republic does not accept nor will it accept attacks against its sovereignty."
The actions target individuals and legal entities involved in what Argentina considers unauthorized oil and gas activities in maritime spaces surrounding the Falkland Islands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, according to a statement by the presidency,
The new proceedings add to existing actions already underway against 45 other subjects under Article 2 of Law No. 26,659, bringing the number of targeted entities and individuals to 60.
The measures come as offshore oil exploration near the Falkland Islands advances, with the Sea Lion project involving British company Rockhopper Exploration and Israel-based Navitas Petroleum.
The Argentine government said the proceedings reflect its longstanding claim to sovereignty over the South Atlantic islands and their surrounding maritime areas.
"The National Government will continue moving forward with this identification and will initiate summary proceedings to sanction all those responsible," the statement noted.
The statement, signed by President Javier Milei, reaffirmed Argentina's commitment to exhausting all administrative, diplomatic and legal mechanisms available to challenge activities it considers a violation of its sovereignty claims.
The decision underscores the administration's strategy to enforce Argentine jurisdiction on natural resources in waters it considers disputed. Official sources noted that administrative steps will be accompanied by diplomatic notifications to prevent further unauthorized commercial activities in the zone.
The Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls the Islas Malvinas, are a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic and have been at the center of a sovereignty dispute between Argentina and the UK since Britain took control of the islands in 1833. In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of participating islanders voted to remain a UK Overseas Territory.

Former lab analyst sentenced to 10 years in prison for manipulating DNA data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:20:00 UTC
06:20:00 KST

A judge sentenced a former forensic analyst for the Colorado Bureau of Investigation to 10 years in prison on Tuesday after authorities said her manipulation of DNA data had raised questions about the validity of hundreds of criminal cases.
Yvonne “Missy” Woods pleaded guilty in June to perjury, attempting to influence a public servant, forgery and committing a cybercrime. Dozens of other counts were dismissed as part of a plea agreement.
Problems with the scientist’s work were found in cases involving homicide, sexual assault, robbery and other crimes, according to authorities. Prosecutors were forced to review hundreds of cases, and at least one murder conviction was overturned as a result of Woods’ misconduct.
Woods had faced between 8 and 16 years in prison during Tuesday’s sentencing hearing before state district judge Andrew Poland in Golden, Colorado.
She resigned in 2023 after a decades-long career. Authorities accused her of altering data to conceal tampering, deleting data that showed she failed to troubleshoot issues within the testing process and not thoroughly documenting tests performed in case records.
Woods apologized during Tuesday’s hearing but said she knew saying sorry would not undo the harm she caused, the Denver Post reported.
“For many years I was entrusted with evidence that could have profound consequences for defendants, victims, families and the courts. I failed that responsibility. I am deeply sorry for that failure,” she said.
The investigation into her misconduct began in September 2023 after an intern at the bureau discovered missing information in a case that Woods handled in 2018. According to an arrest affidavit, Woods allegedly told investigators at one point that she had changed data to complete cases more quickly.
In the overturned murder case, Michael Clark was released from prison in 2025 after his lawyers argued that DNA evidence was mishandled by Woods. Prosecutors said they would seek to retry him.
In two homicide cases, the defendants received lesser sentences under plea deals than they could have faced if they went to trial because prosecutors were afraid Woods’ involvement could lead to acquittals.
Convictions in other cases also have been challenged in courts across Colorado.
A Colorado Bureau of Investigation internal affairs report in 2024 revealed that concerns about Woods’ work first surfaced more than a decade ago. As early as 2014, a worker questioned her testing of evidence, and in 2018 she was temporarily removed from working on DNA cases after being accused of data manipulation, the report said.
State officials have said that the response to Woods’ actions could end up costing more than $11m.

US resumes immigrant visa processing for Hungary, Poland as pause remains elsewhere

WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump’s administration resumed processing immigrant visa applications from Hungary and Poland last week while maintaining a temporary pause on immigrant visa appointments elsewhere, four people familiar with the matter said.
The directive to prioritise immigrant visas at the US missions in Poland and Hungary came from the White House, two of the sources said.
While it was not immediately clear why the US singled out the two countries for special attention, Trump and his senior aides have cultivated far-right allies in both places.
He publicly endorsed former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who was defeated at the polls in April, and Poland’s nationalist President Karol Nawrocki, whose election has put him at odds with the centrist government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
In May, Reuters reported that US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau instructed senior State Department officials to facilitate a US visa for a fugitive former Polish Cabinet minister who had taken refuge from corruption charges in Hungary.
The White House referred a request for comment to the State Department.
A State Department spokesperson did not comment on why it resumed immigrant visa processing for Hungary and Poland.
The Hungarian Foreign Ministry and Prime Minister’s Office, as well as the Polish Foreign Ministry, and prime minister’s and president’s offices did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Trump has long campaigned on stopping illegal immigration, but his second term has been defined in equal measure by his expansive efforts to curb legal migration.
The US has imposed travel bans on dozens of countries, introduced expensive new fees for certain work visas and mandated that all applicants undergo a vetting of their social media history.
In January, the State Department said it was temporarily suspending the processing of immigrant visas – which allow people to move permanently to the United States – in 75 countries where applicants were “at a high risk for becoming a public charge.”
After a federal judge ruled against the visa ban, the State Department paused immigrant visa interviews at all of its global missions while rolling out a new training programme.
The State Department spokesperson, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said appointments were being adjusted to accommodate the new training.
“Whenever there are updated instructions for visa applicants or changes to visa interview appointments, embassies and consulates communicate this information directly to visa applicants,” they wrote.
Global impact
US consulates and embassies traditionally conduct hundreds of thousands of immigrant visa interviews every year, most of them with relatives of US citizens or permanent residents.
In 2024, the last year of Joe Biden’s Democratic presidency, the US issued some 600,000 immigrant visas.
The State Department’s January edict was its most far-reaching attempt to rein in legal migration.
The visa suspension affected applicants from Latin American countries including Brazil, Colombia, and Uruguay; Balkan nations such as Bosnia and Albania; and South Asian countries Pakistan and Bangladesh.
On Aug 21, however, US District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas struck down the policy as “patently unlawful.”
In the days that followed, the State Department called missions around the world and told them to cancel immigrant visa appointments, according to two people with knowledge of the situation.
The State Department acknowledged the global pause in a public statement on Aug 25, saying it would remain in place until staffers received new training in how to assess whether visa applicants could support themselves in the United States without relying on public benefits.
The US government said in a court filing that interviews were temporarily rescheduled through Aug 31.
But the suspension could remain in place for months due to the structure of the new training programme.
Missions need to self-train based on materials sent from Washington; a consular officer then needs to visit each post to certify that the training has been completed, a person familiar with the matter said.
On a Reddit thread, people from around the world, including Peru, the United Kingdom and India, posted about cancelled visa appointments through September.
“We were at the finish line and now this,” one person wrote. REUTERS

Cockroach Milk, How to Blow Your Nose, and Mosquito Printers: The Ig Nobels of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:15:00 UTC
06:15:00 KST

Achievements that first make people laugh and then make them think. That’s the motto of the Ig Nobel Prizes, an annual competition that—parodying the Nobel Prizes—recognizes some of the world’s most unusual scientific studies. The organization Improbable Research has been hosting the event since 1991 with the aim of showing that science also has a humorous side in its quest to meaningfully answer questions about the world.
This year the ceremony was held in Zurich, Switzerland, and recognized 10 research projects ranging from an attempt to scientifically define what a kiss is to an experiment that used buried underwear to assess soil health.
Prize in Biomechanics: A Scientific Definition For Kissing
What exactly is a kiss? A group of researchers decided to establish a scientific definition that would apply to all animals, not just humans. They came up with the categorization that a kiss is “a non-agonistic interaction involving directed intraspecific oral-oral contact, with some movement of the lips or oral structures and without the transfer of food.” By this definition, other great ape species are also kissers, so are domestic dogs and cats as well as pigeons, penguins, squirrels, black bears, and tortoises—though not all of these kisses have the same meaning.
Prize in Economics: Having More Money Might Make You a Bad Person
In the study “Higher Social Class Predicts Increased Unethical Behavior,” published in PNAS, researchers conducted seven experiments to investigate whether socioeconomic status was linked to unethical behaviors, such as breaking traffic rules, failing to yield the right of way, cheating, and even taking candy from children. Spoiler: Yes, it seems that more money does mean more problems—creating more problems at least. The results suggest that people from higher social classes have, on average, a greater tendency to prioritize self-interest. Who knew.
Prize in Chemistry: Cockroach Milk Is Actually Nutritious
Yet another study suggesting that the future of nutrition may lie in insects. The “milk” in question is a high-protein substance produced by mother cockroaches of the species Diploptera punctata, which concentrate proteins, fats, and sugars into an extremely energy-dense form. A team of scientists analyzed the crystals that form inside the embryos to understand how these crystals store so many nutrients in such a tiny space.
Prize in Medicine: How to Blow Your Nose the Right Way, According to Science
This is probably the most popular study in the competition because of the story behind it. It’s a posthumous award to scientist Unno Tokuji, who spent his final years studying the correct way to blow one’s nose. He analyzed everything from the aerodynamics and volume of nasal breathing to the pressure exerted on the ears. The recommendation was to blow one nostril at a time when one is more congested than the other and to do so with a long, relatively forceful exhalation, rather than a short, weak blow.
Prize in Biology: When Do Snakes Decide to Bite? You Have to Step on Them to Find Out
To determine what triggers a defensive bite, researchers applied pressure to different parts of the bodies of Bothrops jararaca snakes—a highly venemous species of South American pit viper—and observed how they reacted. Wearing a boot and in a controlled manner, they stepped on different parts of the snake. Stepping on the head resulted in a 44 percent probability of a bite. Applying pressure to the body yielded a 20 percent probability of an attack. If for some reason you need to step on a snake, aim for the tail, where the risk is only 11 percent.
Prize in Physics: How to Make a Urinal Splash-Free
According to mathematical models, there’s an optimal angle for a stream of liquid to hit a urinal if you don’t want droplets to bounce back. The researchers found that lower angles of impact significantly decreases splashing, and they designed prototypes based on that principle. Such scientifically backed urinals can help with keeping public restrooms sanitary.
Prize in Technology: Dead Mosquitos Can Become 3-D Printers
The price of 3-D printers has gone down significantly in the past decade, and now you can make one with something as low-cost as a dead mosquito. The proboscises that mosquitos use to suck our blood function as extremely fine needles. One of the most delicate parts of a 3-D printer is the nozzle, which is essentially an ultrathin tube. In looking to develop new components for precision instruments, the researchers realized there was no need to invent everything from scratch. Evolution had already come up with a great solution by optimizing the mosquito’s mouthparts.
Prize in Olfaction: Your Baby Smells Wonderful; Your Teenager, Not so Much
Once again, science confirms something you probably could have guessed. Researchers analyzed how parents perceive their children’s body odor at different ages. Participants rated the smell of young children more favorably and that of teenagers much less so. Surprise, surprise. The team believes that smell plays an underappreciated role in communication within a family and may be related to the recognition and strengthening of the bond between parents and children.
Peace Prize: We Want Mean Friends, Sometimes
What kind of person do people typically want as a best friend? To answer this question, researchers administered questionnaires asking participants about how their friend should behave toward them, toward a stranger, and toward an enemy. In general, people prefered a friend who is kind to them but cruel to their enemies, suggesting that the ideal friend is not necessarily a “universally good” person.
Prize in Soil Science: Old Underwear Can Reveal Soil Health
About 1,000 participants buried cotton underwear and returned some time later to check how much had decomposed. The result: the “underwear index.” The more holes in the undergarments, the more biological activity, namely that of microorganisms capable of breaking down cellulose, a natural molecule in the cell walls of plants. A population of these kinds of microbes is key for the health of farmland, and now all you need to test for their presence is an old pair of underwear.
The entire ceremony is now available to watch online.

The US has struck multiple Iranian oil tankers, according to US officials, following further attempted missile attacks on a US Navy warship.
Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that a US missile struck an Iranian oil tanker near Kharg Island in the Gulf.
The tanker was hit approximately four nautical miles from the island on Tuesday evening, with no immediate casualties reported.
Tasnim said the vessel was struck by a projectile fired by US forces in the anchorage area of Kharg Island.
Local sources said the tanker's crew was being evacuated.
Another explosion was reported aboard an oil tanker off the Yekbani coast near Iran’s Jask port, according to state broadcaster IRIB.

Two of the explosions were heard around Kharg Island. Another blast was also heard in southern Jask.
Warning to tanker crews

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy has meanwhile warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for US attacks on Iranian tankers.
The warning, carried by Iranian state television, said the US military had targeted several Iranian oil tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting US forces and assisting in the attacks.
The Revolutionary Guard warned tanker crews to abandon their vessels whether they were at anchor or docked, saying they “will be targeted.”
World oil prices climbed on Tuesday, once again closing in on $100 a barrel, and stock markets mostly retreated after a flare-up in the Middle East war.

First Overseas-Bound F-15EX Departs Boeing, Heading to Oregon First
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:08:04 UTC
06:08:04 KST

After months of delays from a factory strike, the first F-15EX fighter jet the U.S. Air Force will permanently base overseas left Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis on Aug. 28. Eventually, the aircraft will fly to Kadena Air Base in Japan and join the 18th Wing there, but for now it is going to Portland, Ore.
“This is an important next step toward bringing the F-15EX home to Kadena,” Brig. Gen. John Gallemore, 18th Wing commander, said in a release. “Our team is ready to welcome the F-15EX, and this is another milestone that brings us closer to putting this capability in the hands of the Airmen who will fly, maintain and employ it from Japan.”
The F-15EX is the first Eagle II jet to feature the 18th Wing’s historic, distinctive “ZZ” tail flash and will actually arrive at Kadena sometime in fiscal 2027, which begins Oct. 1.
Spokespeople for Headquartes Air Force, the 18th Wing, and the Air National Guard did not immediately respond to queries from Air & Space Forces Magazine on Sept. 8.
This new jet is the first of 36 F-15EXs to be stationed at Kadena. The fighter, often described as halfway between fourth- and fifth-generation aircraft, will help usher in a new era in U.S. airpower within the first island chain surrounding China
The transition to the EX has been a long time coming for Kadena—the Air Force started retiring the base’s legacy F-15C/Ds in 2022 and confirmed plans to replace them with the F-15EX in 2024. The first jet was supposed to arrive in spring 2026, but a lengthy strike at the Boeing plant in St. Louis late last year slowed production until this Aug. 28 delivery.
The new F-15EX’s stopover in Oregon isn’t surprising—the Oregon Air National Guard was the first Air Force location with combat-coded F-15EXs at its Portland ANG Base. The base will conduct the final systems integration, add software updates, and other technical preparations before the aircraft can go to Okinawa.
In the interim, the Air Force has rotated F-16, F-15, F-22, and F-35 squadrons through Kadena to keep the tactical fighter presence steady at a key strategic base fewer than 400 miles from Taiwan.
Those rotational forces haven’t always matched the capabilities the F-15EX will bring. Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported on the extended tour of aging F-16Cs out of the Colorado Air National Guard’s 120th Fighter Squadron, which ran from January through June. They brought a dozen fighters.
Both the squadron commander and the head of its parent wing, the 140th Wing, said in a call with the media on Sept. 3 that while the platform could keep up with fifth-gen fighters in the region, the pilots and maintenance crews were pushing the limits of the more than 30-year-old airframe
The permanent stationing of the F-15EX will “enhance Kadena’s ability to generate ready combat airpower while providing opportunities to train and integrate alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force and other allies and partners,” according to the release.
The 18th Wing trains alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force F-15s at Naha Air Base in bilateral exercises and other training, according to the release.
Pacific Air Forces has been slowly phasing out its oldest fighters and introducing more modern jets in recent years. In addition to Kadena’s F-15s, the Air Force has also recently withdrawn the A-10s at Osan Air Base, South Korea.
The 35th Fighter Wing at Misawa Air Base, Japan, meanwhile, is slated to get 48 fifth-gen F-35 Lightning IIs, but only a trickle had arrived as of April. The wing transferred its F-16s to Osan last year.
The Air Force publicly confirmed delays in getting the F-15EX to Kadena in February.
The Eagle II is the first of its kind to include digital fly-by-wire flight controls, a large-area display glass cockpit with a touchscreen interface, an APG-82 Active Electronically Scanned Array radar, a Joint Helmet Mounted Cueing System, and an Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System.
The jet flies faster and farther, carries a heavier payload than its F-15 predecessors, and has two additional weapons stations.

Hundreds of flights delayed, cancelled after UK air traffic control glitch
Unknown

2026-09-08

Hundreds of flights delayed, cancelled after UK air traffic control glitch
Air traffic control provider NATS under scrutiny after technical fault disrupts UK air traffic.
Hundreds of flights at major United Kingdom airports, including London’s Heathrow and Gatwick, have been cancelled and hundreds more delayed because of a technical fault at the National Air Traffic Services (NATS).
The IT malfunction on Tuesday happened three years after a flight-plan processing failure at NATS caused even more widespread disruption.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2UK air traffic issue fixed but flights remain affected
- list 2 of 2Hundreds of UK flights disrupted by air traffic control glitch
In a post on X, NATS apologised to frustrated passengers in departure halls across the UK and said a problem with its flight data processing system had been fixed.
“Recovery from today’s system issue has taken longer than we had hoped. Our system issue is now resolved, we are operating normally and working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights,” NATS said on X.
Cancellations and Delays
Airlines called for the resignation of Martin Rolfe, the CEO of NATS, questioned whether the UK’s air traffic control system was fit for purpose and urged the UK government to intervene.
Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been affected by delays of up to eight hours and that it had cancelled more than 50 flights.
In a video posted on X, Ryanair’s Chief Operations Officer Neal McMahon said “despite promises, reports and assurances that they would fix the systems, once again NATS, under Martin Rolfe’s leadership have failed UK travellers and have failed airlines which are trying to get their passengers to and from the UK”.
Data on flight-tracking platform FlightAware showed about 490 departure delays at six airports, including Heathrow, Gatwick, London City, Luton, Edinburgh and Bristol as of 15:18 GMT.
About 525 arrivals at those six airports were either cancelled or delayed, the website data shows.
Aviation analyst John Strickland said the consequences of even a relatively short outage can be severe because delays quickly cascade through tightly scheduled airline networks.
“A few hours of outage may on the face of it sound limited but the impact is enormous when a substantial number of airports across the UK are affected,” Strickland said.
Britain’s aviation regulator said it would expect NATS to share a full report on Tuesday’s system failure.
The UK Civil Aviation Authority, the country’s independent aviation regulator, said it would then consider whether any reforms are needed to secure the reliability of the UK’s air traffic control system.

Kids need 'digital detox', Clare says after decline in reading and maths scores
Australian high school students' scores in maths and reading have hit their lowest point on record, according to a major international test.
While the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) exams showed a slight improvement in science results since the last test in 2022, Australia's long-term learning decline continued overall.
Education Minister Jason Clare has raised concern about the link between access to technology and lower scores.
"The PISA results are telling us that the children that are online more are getting lower results. The more you're online, the more your results decline," he tells ABC News Breakfast.
"The evidence is telling us that we probably need a good digital detox in our schools. It doesn't mean there's not place for technology."
Clare says it's not impossible to shift the dial, pointing to the UK and the "big changes" it made to the education system more than a decade ago.
The minister thinks Australia also needs to do the same but it's going to cost money to do so.

Spending on aged pension projected to fall below 2 per cent of GDP
Australia's spend on age and service pensions is expected to drop from 2.3 per cent to 1.8 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2066, according to new analysis.
The government's intergenerational report (IGR), which will be released in full later this month, projects economic opportunities and obstacles over the next 40 years.
The analysis shows the share of older Australians, aged 67 or above, receiving a pension or income support will decline from 66 per cent to 52 per cent over the same period.
Speaking to the Super Members Council later today, Treasurer Jim Chalmers will state the reduced pressure on the budget is due to having superannuation "at the core" of the best retirement system.
"In comparison, that number is nearly 10 per cent by 2060 in the UK, 8 per cent in Canada, 7 per cent in New Zealand, and 6 per cent in the US," Chalmers will say.
The IGR has revised its 2023 outlook, which predicted the portion of GDP spent on pensions would fall to 2 per cent.
Chalmers will argue super needs to be preserved against "existential" threats, including One Nation, who earlier this week suggested dipping into superannuation early for those struggling with cost of living.
Under the proposal, Australians who pay rent or a mortgage would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years.
Key Event
Invite-only grant scheme 'pork barrelling by design': Haines
Independent MP Helen Haines has taken aim at an invitation-only grants scheme, calling it "pork-barrelling by design".
An investigation by the Centre for Public Integrity, reported by the ABC, found three-quarters of the funds from the Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program went to electorates held by Labor at the 2025 federal election.
Haines says she found out about the grants program a year ago when a local golf club asked how they could get an invitation to apply for a grant.
"I subsequently asked the minister for infrastructure [Catherine King] about this in question time last November and she very clearly stated that this was a program that was designed to deliver election commitments," she tells ABC's News Breakfast.
"In other words, this was pork-barrelling by design, which makes it quite different actually to sports rorts, which was pork-barreling by deception. So we've got two methods here but the same outcome."
Haines is calling for the Commonwealth grant guidelines to be rewritten to include enforceable standards.
Key Event
Albanese held undeclared honorary membership to golf club awarded $6 million
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese held an honorary membership to Marrickville Golf Club, which he has not declared on his register of interests.
The golf club was promised $6 million at the federal election, which was awarded through a fund that heavily favoured Labor seats.
Records of the prime minister's register of interests dating back to his entry to parliament in 1996 do not mention a membership to the club, either paid or honorary.
"We have him on the books as an honorary member, but I think that dates from a long time ago, that hasn't been reaffirmed," a spokesperson for the Marrickville Golf Club told the ABC.
"I don't know when he was put on the books as an honorary member, that may have been 15 years ago or more."
The Prime Minister's Office did not respond to questions about Mr Albanese's membership.

Cuba says it will never be colony after Trump posts map with island under US colors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:05:23 UTC
06:05:23 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel said Tuesday that the island nation "will never again" be a colony of any "empire" after US President Donald Trump published a map depicting it and other territories under the US flag.
"Cuba knows well the meaning of having been a colony and neocolony of two empires," Diaz-Canel wrote on US social media company X, without explicitly referring to Trump's publication.
"The blood that has been shed for our independence, sovereignty and self-determination will not have been in vain, and we will defend them to the last consequences," he added.
Trump published the map Monday on his Truth Social platform. The image shows the colors of the US flag covering Mexico, Canada, Cuba, Greenland, Iceland and parts of the Caribbean and Central America.
Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez referred to the publication, responding sarcastically that the US government would leave its citizens "geographically disoriented."
"Soon they will not know in which gulf, lake, building, country, continent or planet they are," Rodriguez wrote in a social media post.
The Cuban statements come as relations between Havana and Washington face their highest tensions in decades.
The Trump administration has pursued a policy of "maximum pressure" against Cuba since the beginning of 2026, including an oil blockade and secondary sanctions introduced in May that have deterred foreign companies from operating on the island.
Washington has also maintained the possibility of military intervention as a source of concern for the Cuban government.
Rodriguez said Monday that the US economic embargo cost Cuba $8.08 billion between March 2025 and February 2026, the highest recorded for 12 months, and 7% more than the previous year.
He described Washington's measures as a "cruel collective punishment" against the Cuban population.
Cuba's economy has also been severely affected by an energy crisis. The country's economy contracted 15% between 2020 and 2025, while independent forecasts project an additional contraction of up to 10.3% this year.
