Putin reportedly also stressed that Russia had “no aggressive plans” toward Europe.
Neither the White House nor Trump had issued a readout of the call at the time of the report.
Diplomacy collides with renewed attacks
The call followed weekend discussions with government officials and senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who traveled to both Moscow and Kyiv in an effort to revive stalled diplomacy and broker an end to Russia’s war.
However, despite the three-day ceasefire that Putin announced on Saturday, Sept. 5, explosions have continued across Ukraine, including near Kyiv.
On Saturday afternoon, after Kyiv city authorities issued an air raid warning at 3:03 p.m., explosions were heard near the suburb of Boryspil. Several air raid warnings were issued on that same day, and were lasting for hours at a time.
Russian Strikes Kill 2 in Dnipropetrovsk, Wound Over a Dozen Across Kharkiv, Chernihiv Regions
A massive Russian barrage began on the evening of Monday, Sept. 7 and continued throughout Tuesday. Russia launched Oniks anti-ship missiles, Iskander-M, S-400 and North Korean-made KN-23 ballistic missiles, as well as 32 Kh-101 cruise missiles and 166 Shahed attack drones.
“Enemy shelling has continued nonstop since last night,” Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES) said.
Russian forces also struck a building of the “We Are Ukraine” TV channel in Kyiv while journalists were on air, partially destroying the facility and injuring at least five people.
“‘Shaheds’ against the media is a new page of Russian degradation, and there must definitely be a reaction from Europe and the world to this,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said, using the Ukrainian term for Russia’s Iranian designed attack drones.
Kremlin signals openness to talks with no signs of common ground
The attacks intensified even as Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that Russia expects trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US to resume, telling Indian media ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi that Moscow is “open to a peaceful resolution of the conflict.”
Peskov also claimed that Kyiv does not want the war to end, saying that “if it did, the war would have ended long ago.”
Separately, the Kremlin objected to involvement of E3 national security advisers – France, the United Kingdom and Germany – in the trilateral meetings.
“This is more likely to complicate the negotiation process,” Peskov said, according to Ukrainska Pravda. “Because, unlike the Americans, the Europeans are doing everything they can to prevent this war from ending.”
According to AFP, Zelensky said Russian, Ukrainian, and US negotiators could meet as early as this month for talks aimed at ending the war. “If all sides agree, we also want to hold it in the fall. If September works out, then it would be great. The earlier, the better.”
However, several previous rounds of negotiations have failed, and given Russia’s repeated strikes on Ukraine – trust remains critically low, with no tangible signs that Moscow has shifted its diplomatic position.
“The moment the US president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a statement on X.
“His [Putin’s] ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy. Strike after strike on residential buildings,” he continued.
Despite ongoing efforts to keep the momentum of peace negotiations going, Moscow continues demanding Ukraine cede territory in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, as well as renounce Western military support.
Kyiv has repeatedly stated such terms amount to capitulation and would only allow Russia to prepare a new attack in a bid to install a Moscow-friendly government.

UAE says it does not comment on reports about government leaders’ talks

Saber Ghaem Ibrahim Eid and Serdar Dincel
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
The United Arab Emirates said Tuesday that it does not comment on media reports or speculation about talks by government leaders, following an Israeli report alleging that the UAE warned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of the Oct. 7, 2023 attack.
"The UAE Government does not comment on media stories or speculation regarding conversations between government leaders," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement on the US social media company X.
Since Oct. 7, the UAE’s efforts have "consistently" focused on de-escalation, promoting regional stability and preventing violence, it noted.
"UAE and Israeli government entities have maintained open and direct lines of communication since the inception of the relationship more than five years ago," it stressed.
Relevant authorities have communicated and continue to communicate all pertinent intelligence "when necessary," the Emirates officials added.
The statement did not specify which media reports it was referencing.
Earlier Tuesday, however, the Haaretz newspaper in Israel alleged that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu during a call Sept. 23, 2023, of the intention of Palestinian resistance group, Hamas, to carry out an attack.
Netanyahu ignored the warning and did not pass the information on to senior officials in the security establishment, according to the newspaper.
Netanyahu’s office denied the report Tuesday, saying he did not speak with the UAE president that day and did not receive any warning from bin Zayed.
Former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett also said Tuesday that he had information indicating Netanyahu received warnings ahead of the attack, including one from the UAE president.
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid likewise spoke of warnings issued before the attack.
On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacked Israeli military bases and settlements along the Gaza border, killing and capturing Israelis, in response to daily crimes by the Israeli forces against the Palestinian people and their holy sites, particularly the Al-Aqsa Mosque.
Israel's deadly offensive in Gaza since Oct. 8, 2023, has killed more than 73,000 and wounded over 174,000. The military operation has caused massive damage, affecting around 90% of the enclave's civilian infrastructure.

Russia&#039;s Matryoshka bots target initiative to provide 5,000 drones for Ukraine, falsely claiming that Germany is embezzling the money
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:19:33 UTC
04:19:33 KST

The Russian "Matryoshka" bot network has launched a fresh disinformation campaign against a new German-Ukrainian initiative to produce 5,000 long-range drones. Researchers from the Antibot4Navalny project, which tracks the activity of pro-Russian bots on social media, provided The Insider with information about five fake videos, which are disguised as reports from reputable publications: the Financial Times, Handelsblatt, Bloomberg, Politico, and The Economist.
All five inauthentic videos follow a similar script and end with the claim that support for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU party has “neared a historic low” as a result of the drone program. The main false narratives put forward by the Russian operation are:
- Drone production will be located in a “residential area” in eastern Germany, posing a “direct threat to the population.” A video attributed to Handelsblatt claims that only a “small financial department, which would be of no military value in the event of an escalation,” will remain in central Munich, while the actual production facility, described as having a “low level of environmental safety,” will be concealed in a residential area, which is why its exact location is being withheld.
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz allegedly stole €700 million from the Ukraine aid program. According to the bots, of the €1.5 billion allocated in early 2026 to protect Ukrainian infrastructure, Kyiv received only €800 million, while the rest was diverted to Merz’s contracting companies in Sweden and Lithuania. Financial Times editor-in-chief Roula Khalaf is falsely quoted as saying: “We are used to hearing about corruption in Ukraine... However, in this case, the theft took place in Germany, and the mastermind behind this fraudulent scheme is Friedrich Merz.”
- A new draft of Germany’s national security strategy allegedly “does not envisage Ukraine existing beyond the end of 2027,” meaning the 5,000 drones will actually “remain in Germany.” Bloomberg editor-in-chief John Micklethwait is falsely quoted as concluding that Merz “knew this from the very beginning” and is using support for Ukraine as a pretext to rearm Germany’s own military with the aim of pursuing “revanchist ideas.”
- Sweden has allegedly become a “financial buffer” for Merz’s “fraudulent transactions.” The claim says Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson is conspiring with the chancellor, that “more than 90% of German military aid to Ukraine passes through Sweden,” and that €25 billion out of the €43 billion in civilian aid provided since 2022 has ended up in the accounts of Swedish companies “affiliated with Merz and Kristersson.”
- Merz allegedly “lives in a parallel reality,” believing that drones for Ukraine will boost his approval ratings. Politico editor-in-chief Jonathan Greenberger is falsely quoted as saying that Germans are “tired of militaristic statements and decisions.”
The Insider has obtained links to the original posts and materials from AntiBot4Navalny confirming that the accounts that posted them belong to the Matryoshka network. The newsroom is not publishing direct links to the posts to avoid helping spread the disinformation.
What the drone production program is
On Sept. 3, reports confirmed that Germany had begun serial production of more than 5,000 medium- and long-range attack drones for Ukraine. The German government contract, worth around €300 million, is due to be completed by mid-2027. The project is being carried out by a joint venture between multinational company Auterion and Ukrainian drone maker Airlogix, which was established in February 2026 at the Munich Security Conference.
The first drones have already been produced at a facility near Munich, while the company is setting up a second production line in eastern Germany. For security reasons, the drone maker's name, the exact locations of the facilities, and the names of the drones have not been disclosed. The bots are exploiting that secrecy, portraying it as the “concealment of dangerous production in a residential area.”
The kamikaze drones are being produced in medium- and long-range, with the latter capable of traveling up to 1,500 km. Airlogix is responsible for the airframes and mechanical components, while Auterion provides the software and operating system. The drones are equipped with artificial intelligence modules that allow them to reach their targets even in the face of active electronic warfare measures.
What is “Matryoshka”?
Researchers use the term “Matryoshka” to denote a Russian operation that spreads fake news on a mass scale through a coordinated network of bots, trolls, and anonymous platforms. Its aim is to generate artificial information noise and manipulate perceptions of events both in Russia and abroad. The Antibot4Navalny project named the operation after the eponymous Russian nesting doll, as its bots hide behind one another while fake stories are distributed in layers across different platforms, making their original source harder to identify.
The operation works in two ways. First, it creates large numbers of fake profiles posing as ordinary people, independent media outlets, or think tanks. These accounts publish dozens of posts a day while imitating local speech patterns. Second, the same content is deployed simultaneously across social media. To make the posts appear credible, the bots use the logos of well-known Western media outlets and human rights organizations.

This cosmic particle was never meant to reach Earth. Now scientists think they finally know why it did
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:15:59 UTC
04:15:59 KST

Pineapple on pizza and rain on weekends shouldn’t exist on Earth, yet somehow they do. And a mysterious cosmic particle that was detected in 2022 shouldn’t have made it to our planet either, but it did. Unlike the former two things, there may finally be an adequate explanation for how the particle got here.
The tiny particle originated in an enormous gamma-ray burst two billion light-years away from Earth. The burst was so bright that researchers nicknamed it “BOAT” (“brightest of all time”).
When light particles, known as photons, from BOAT reached Earth on October, 9, 2022, researchers realized that one of those photons was not like the others.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
It was detected by Russia’s Carpet, an ultra-high-energy-cosmic-ray detector, and carried about 300 tera-electron-volts (300 trillion electron volts) of energy—making it the most energy-dense photon ever observed from a gamma-ray burst and far more powerful than anything produced by high-energy particle accelerators on Earth, such as the Large Hadron Collider.
According to the rules of standard physics, a photon with that much energy should have hit other light particles from the universe’s microwave background and been destroyed in the process. So how did it survive? In a new paper in Physical Review Letters, a pair of physicists say they may have the answer.
They propose that hypothetical ultralight particles called axionlike particles, combined with the high energy of the photon, which allowed it to behave in previously unobserved ways. Essentially, they argue that tiny particles with enormous amounts of energy may gain access to the universe’s fast lane, allowing them to avoid other particles that should absorb and obliterate them.
Under this theory, the photon should have arrived at Earth around an hour later than its less energetic counterparts from the gamma-ray burst. And it turns out that a Chinese observatory did, in fact, detect less energetic photons an hour earlier than the one picked up in Russia.
“The most interesting aspect of our work is that, for the first time, it brings together two ideas that until now had been developed separately,” said Marco Roncadelli, an astronomer at Italy’s National Institute for Nuclear Physics and a co-author of the study, in a statement. “If future observations confirmed this scenario, the Universe would become a natural laboratory for studying quantum gravity at energies enormously higher than those achievable by any accelerator built on Earth.”

Jewish leaders in Sweden warn of antisemitism in the Left Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:13:52 UTC
04:13:52 KST

The Official Council of Swedish Jewish Communities has renewed its warnings regarding persistent antisemitism within the Left Party (Vänsterpartiet), following a fresh wave of expulsions involving local candidates.
The renewed scrutiny comes after the Left Party removed eight additional candidates from its electoral lists.
According to reporting by Expressen and regional media outlets, the candidates faced disciplinary action after internal investigations and journalistic exposés revealed they had shared antisemitic conspiracy theories, praised Russian President Vladimir Putin, and expressed support for Hamas.
According to public broadcasts by Sveriges Radio, these latest removals bring the total number of candidates ousted from the party over antisemitism, Holocaust denial, support for terrorism, homophobia, and praise for authoritarian regimes to 33.
Aron Verständig, chairman of the Official Council of Swedish Jewish Communities, stated on X/Twitter on Monday that the council previously criticized the Left Party in the autumn of 2024 because the party “had failed to distance itself from the antisemitism that leading representatives had spread during the summer.”
Problems with antisemitism in the party were structural
Verständig noted that when distances and expulsions were eventually enacted, they met with heavy resistance from large parts of the party.
“It became clear to me that the problems the party had with antisemitism were not limited to a few individuals but were structural,” he stated, adding that the council raised this directly in meetings with party leadership.
Verständig criticized the leadership’s ongoing approach, pointing out that media outlets have repeatedly uncovered representatives spreading explicit antisemitism.
While noting that the party has acted against these individuals, Verständig emphasized, “to my knowledge, it has never taken the initiative to investigate its own representatives.”
He added that apologetic explanations from party sympathizers surface with every new revelation. “It is simply frightening that this has been allowed to go this far,” Verständig stated, expressing deep alarm that “there are other parties that are considering cooperation with the Left Party.”
The Left Party did not respond to an emailed request for comment by the time of publication.

Far-right port protests: police told to improve intelligence gathering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:13:41 UTC
04:13:41 KST

Police have been told by the government they expect better intelligence gathering after masked far-right groups took to the streets at the weekend, the Guardian has learned, as the Kent force admitted mishandling warnings of potential trouble.
Police in Kent on Saturday and then Portsmouth, Hampshire, on Sunday said they were taken by surprise when hundreds massed to oppose what they say is illegal immigration via small boats.
Both protests are believed by police to have been far-right inspired, with evidence emerging that those behind them were determined to avoid detection.
Claims by Kent police since Saturday that they had no warning fell apart on Tuesday when the force admitted there were warning calls to police on Friday evening which were not acted upon.
Kent police said: “The force had received non-emergency information late on Friday evening that a protest could take place in the town the following day. This information was not fully assessed.”
The government’s view is that police actions once officers were faced by hundreds of men was reasonable.
But there is dismay at how Kent police explained their decision-making afterwards, for instance viewing the gathered masked men outside the port of Dover as peaceful protesters, with one source describing it as “fucking crackers”.
On Tuesday evening the prime minister, Andy Burnham, met police chiefs to discuss what had happened and preparedness for any further unrest.
In Dover on Saturday, where hundreds of masked men in black converged undetected, police believe those taking to the streets used walkie-talkies to coordinate their actions.
Police on the ground report the masked men had lawyers’ phone numbers and cited public order case law and were well briefed on how far they could go: “They toed the line perfectly to avoid arrest,” one source said.
In Hampshire police are investigating whether vehicles were deliberately left behind to block access roads.
Police said the Dover gathering passed peacefully, while in Hampshire there were clashes, with the local Police Federation saying anger and violence was directed at officers.
The Guardian understands that part of Hampshire police’s investigation will examine whether the gathering of 200 people was meant to harass or intimidate.
A spokesperson added they are also hunting for those behind the violence, conducting “a thorough review of the body-worn video” to look for offenders.
The protests are believed to have been coordinated on closed social media networks and not publicly advertised.
Police are considering whether the threshold for warrants for covert tactics has been met, with one source warning that police were wary of criticism of using “police state tactics” against people portraying themselves as peaceful protesters motivated by a legitimate issue.
The National Police Coordination Centre has intensified its monitoring.
The action in Kent was organised by Daniel Thomas, a long-term associate of the far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known as Tommy Robinson. Thomas, who has established an umbrella grouping called Patriot Platform, was also linked to the blockade in Portsmouth the following day.
Whitehall officials have asked police why tougher laws in place since last year meant to clamp down on the wearing of face masks at protests were not used.
The police view was that at Dover those gathered complied with requests from officers and dispersed after three hours. In Portsmouth, which was more heated, police prioritised a formal dispersal order which they think worked.
Both police and government sources say the “optics” of masked men in black thronging the streets looked “intimidating”.
Also on Tuesday it emerged that lifeboat staff who picked up 120 asylum seekers from a large dinghy in the Channel on Sunday were refused entry to two ports shortly before being harangued by right-wing protesters.
Crew on two RNLI vessels were also threatened with legal action if they approached Southampton Port and tried to bring the claimants ashore.
They were forced to take the migrants several miles away to Eastney, where police, firefighters, Border Force and other officials faced protests by up to 200 people, most of whom wore balaclavas and black clothing.
Peter Sparkes, the chief executive of the RNLI, said abuse of its volunteers is “wholly unacceptable in a civilised society”.
He said recent protests had “generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding” about the charity, and condemned threats by “those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard”.
Officials confirmed that a broadcast on an open marine VHF radio said Southampton Vessel Traffic Service and King’s Harbour Master Portsmouth denied the RNLI permission to enter their ports.
The two RNLI rescue boats from Bembridge and Yarmouth had intercepted a “mega-dinghy” that had left Utah beach near Cherbourg in Normandy.
A spokesperson for Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates the port of Southampton, said: “ABP did receive an enquiry about landing recovered migrants at the port of Southampton. We had to decline the enquiry as the port did not have suitable reception facilities available. If there had been a safety of life at sea issue where Southampton was the closest port or if we had received a formal direction from the relevant authority then we would have played a role. Neither was the case in this situation.”
On Tuesday, anti-migrant protesters attempted to identify RNLI volunteers involved in rescuing those onboard the dinghy. Demonstrators named and shared pictures on X of two people they said were volunteers, claiming they had tracked down an address for one of the men.
Sparkes’s words come after footage posted on social media showed volunteers labelled as “traitors”. In a statement issued on Tuesday, Sparkes said the misinformation led to “some of our volunteers and staff [being] the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse.
“The RNLI’s people represent the very best in our society. They selflessly give up their time to keep others safe.
“Yet they and their families are being threatened by those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard.
“Their action, in contrast, is wholly unacceptable in a civilised society.
“We will take whatever steps we can to care for and protect our people and their families.”

Serbia to hold parliamentary vote on October 25, president says
BELGRADE, Sept 8 - Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said on Tuesday he would set October 25 as the date for a snap vote, as he looks to tighten his grip on Serbian politics after nearly two years of student-led protests and be elected prime minister.
The government on Monday asked Vucic to dissolve the parliament and schedule a snap vote.
"The elections will be held on October 25," Vucic said in a state RTS central news programme, adding that he would officially announce the decision at noon on Wednesday.
This would allow Vucic, whose Serbian Progressive Party nominated him on Saturday to run for prime minister, to try to reassert his authority after the protests presented the biggest challenge to his rule.
The next parliamentary elections in Serbia were not due until December 2027. But following nearly two years of student-led protests, Vucic had said he would seek a snap vote.
Vucic, who has run the country as president or prime minister for 12 years, has faced anti-corruption demonstrations triggered by the collapse of a concrete canopy at a railway station in the northern city of Novi Sad in November 2024 that killed 16 people.
The opposition and demonstrators accuse Vucic and his allies of violence against political opponents, rampant corruption, ties with organised crime and stifling media freedoms, all of which Vucic and his allies deny. REUTERS

Ukraine to sign contracts for around 1,000 Patriot missiles with partner support and EU loan funding, defense minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ukraine to sign contracts for around 1,000 Patriot missiles with partner support and EU loan funding, defense minister says
Ukraine is preparing to sign contracts for the delivery of around 1,000 missiles for Patriot air defense systems with support from its partners and funding from an EU loan, Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on Sept. 8.
Khmara made the announcement during a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in the Ramstein format, which he attended for the first time alongside Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi.
The defense minister cautioned that the contracted missiles would take time to arrive. He urged Ukraine’s partners to supply interceptors from their existing stockpiles before winter, proposing that they be replenished with upgraded missiles delivered under Ukraine’s future contracts.
Strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses is an urgent priority as Russia continues large-scale attacks on Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure. A mass Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv overnight on Sept. 8 killed at least five people, injured 29 others, and resulted in massive fires that filled the morning air across the city with smoke.
Kyiv is also seeking additional air-to-air missiles and man-portable air defense systems to counter cruise missiles and jet-powered attack drones.
"Together with dozens of Ukrainian companies, we are already seeking affordable, scalable solutions, particularly for intercepting jet-powered Shahed drones. Some interceptors are already undergoing combat testing," according to the minister.
The European Commission is expected to approve the final 28.3-billion-euro ($33-billion) tranche of this year’s defense loans for Ukraine on Sept. 11, EU and national diplomats previously told the Kyiv Independent.
The financing package includes approval for Ukraine to purchase U.S.-made PAC-3 interceptors, which are used by Patriot systems to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
EU member states have already backed Ukraine’s request, though one procedural step remains before the bloc can grant formal approval, the Kyiv Independent learned from EU and national diplomats.

Will Spain finally evacuate its students from Gaza?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:10:33 UTC
04:10:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Will Spain finally evacuate its students from Gaza?
"I want to worry about an exam instead of whether there will be a tomorrow. I want to sit in a library and hear the quiet sound of people turning pages. I want to have a future that does not depend on whether a phone rings.
Instead, I'm still in Gaza. Still waiting. Still trapped between an acceptance letter and a departure date that is listed as: Unknown."
Hour by hour Lama*, a humanities student in Gaza, is watching her chance of a new life slip away.
She is one of 40 to 60 students in Gaza with places, including scholarships, at Spanish universities but who cannot evacuate their devastated region.
This summer, the situation became embarrassing for the Spanish government. Media articles highlighted the crisis. The Gazan students themselves started a petition to beg the government to unblock the corridors. They pointed out that their numbers were few. The logistics could not be that challenging.
To date, Spain has evacuated just 19 students since October 2023. This is in comparison with Italy, which evacuated nearly 270 students from Gaza. The United Kingdom, meanwhile, has facilitated the academic safe passage of 147, including students' family members.
Evacuating from Gaza is taxing no matter the destination. Before embarking on an arduous journey - usually through Israel and Jordan, often with just a few days’ notice and no more than a backpack - students must supply a host of documents such as passports, university admission letters, health insurance and financial guarantees.
Yet even when documentation was correct and Spain-based guarantors ensured students would not burden the country's public coffers, Spanish visa applications lay unprocessed in the country's Jerusalem consulate.
Agonising silence
Spain's cohorts are by no means the only students in Gaza to find themselves with guaranteed university places in Europe but no evacuation route.
What makes the Spanish situation especially frustrating is the lack of explanation. Both the Spanish consulate and the Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs - which supervise student evacuations - have not released information about the hold-up.
This silence has lent a particular sting to the students' agony.
"Opacity, condescension, arbitrariness and a lack of empathy and humanity bordering on cruelty" because "uncertainty tortures the students even more than they already are," is how the situation was described to Madrid newspaper El Diario by David Peñafuerte, a member of the RUxP (RED Universitaria for Palestina), a group of university staff from 43 Spanish universities who have pledged to support Palestine.
My questions to the Spanish consulate in Jerusalem went unanswered.
My request for information from the Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs elicited a generic statement - similar to that sent to El Diario - in which the ministry drew attention to the Spanish government's condemnation of Israel's behaviour, expressed itself as "not indifferent" to Gazan suffering and promised they were working to alleviate it through diplomatic channels.
Highlighting the €150 million the Spanish government allocated for humanitarian assistance to Gaza in 2026, the ministry drew attention to evacuations that had already occurred, mostly for medical reasons.
Such vagueness is no consolation to the stranded students. Some have lost their places entirely. Others have missed whole academic years.
Each visa application is punitively expensive for Gazans. One student stopped buying her medical treatment in order to cover her costs. Trapped in the twilight between old and new lives, she is struggling with suicidal thoughts.
In the face of ongoing scholasticide
The Spanish universities are not to blame for the crisis. Both the students and the Spanish organisations who support them, such as RUxP and Gaza 40 + – an international body devoted to student evacuations – testify that the academic institutions have created the necessary pathways once political documentation and permissions are in place.
Other Spanish ministries have successfully evacuated Gazans. Since 2024, medical evacuations have brought a total of 236 people, including patients' family members, to Spain thanks to the combined efforts of the Ministries of Health, Inclusion, Social Security and Defence.
Still, exhausted by uncertainty, some students have renounced their places. For a people for whom education is so precious, such choices are excruciating.
Palestine has an adult literacy rate of nearly 98%. The country's passion for learning saw over 28,000 Gazan students graduate high school this summer, having spent nearly three years battling through rubble-strewn streets, often studying in tents and writing on old papers and even food aid boxes because of paper shortages.
The Spanish Foreign Ministry's neglect of the Gazan students is particularly baffling given the government's steadfast defence of Palestine.
One of the first major European powers to recognise Palestinian statehood, left-wing premier Pedro Sanchez has pursued an agenda - via his commitment to international law and willingness to cancel trade and military links - that is potentially transformative for EU relations with Israel.
Israel, though it propagates a lie that Palestinians are "barbarians", is fully aware of the threat to Zionism posed by Palestine's superlative culture. That fear has provoked a scholasticide. Every university in Gaza has been struck by the Israeli military, making the opportunity to study abroad even more valuable.
It is possible that Netanyahu's regime, which must approve all evacuations, is singling out the students with Spanish offers for particular punishment because its terror of the highly educated nature of the Palestinian population is compounded by anger with Sanchez for his robust critique.
If this is the case, why has the Spanish Foreign Ministry not admitted that Israeli intransigence is causing the problem?
Nevertheless, media attention and the students' own efforts, such as the petition, may be having an effect. Sources say that a student evacuation might take place later this month.
But hopes have been raised and dashed before. Until those evacuation plans become concrete, the Gazan students remain on their rollercoaster of despair and expectation. Furthermore, the criteria for processing some visas, and not others, remain a mystery, making it impossible for students left behind to improve their chances.
As Lama navigates survival in Gaza, messages arrive from her Spanish university with details of courses including lectures, reading lists and extra-curricular student activities.
"I remember crying while reading some of those emails…[n]ot because I didn't want to see them, but because I wanted so badly to be there."
*Lama is a pseudonym used to protect the student’s identity.

Trump tells Putin he wants swift end to Ukraine war, Kremlin says
US President Donald Trump told Russian President Vladimir Putin he wanted a swift end to the Ukraine war, the Kremlin said, arguing that peace could pave the way for a broad restoration of US-Russia ties. The hour-long call Tuesday followed weekend talks by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow and Kyiv to try to revive stalled peace efforts.
Donald Trump told Russian President Vladimir Putin by phone on Tuesday that he wanted a swift end to the war in Ukraine, which would allow US-Russia ties to be fully restored, the Kremlin said, adding that Putin had supported the US president's view.
The call, which the Kremlin said lasted an hour, followed a weekend visit to Moscow and Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who are trying to revive stalled talks designed to find a way to end the fighting. Their weekend diplomacy did not appear to result in any immediate public breakthrough although they did raise the possibility that three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States could be resumed.
The Kremlin, which has said it does not rule that out, made no mention of the possibility in its readout of the Putin-Trump call. Instead, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that the two leaders had rated the US envoys' weekend diplomacy "with a plus sign" and that Putin had told Trump what he believed the United States could do to help end the conflict and given him an assessment of what the situation on the battlefield was.
Trump, Ushakov said, had made it clear he wanted the war quickly finished. "Donald Trump clearly emphasised the desirability of bringing the conflict to an end as soon as possible, which would immediately open up prospects – impressive and far-reaching ones at that – for the full restoration of relations between the US and Russia," said Ushakov.

"In his view, this would have a particular impact on trade and economic ties, promising enormous benefits for both countries. Donald Trump is keen to see a breakthrough achieved during his presidency. Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin supported this approach."
Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on how to end the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two, and both sides have escalated their attacks on each other in recent months.

Artist puts Kashmiri poet Lal Ded's mysticism on Pashmina
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:06:53 UTC
04:06:53 KST

SRINAGAR: MF Husain’s horses meant power. Flat, bold, Cubist, built for scale like the Bollywood billboards he once painted in Mumbai. Masood Hussain’s horse is painted on Pashmina and dyed in the wool — carrying the earliest Kashmiri poetry, passed down orally for 600 years before anyone wrote it down.This is a sharp turn from familiar ground for Srinagar-based Hussain, whose work for years has chronicled Kashmir’s conflict, grief and everyday life. For the first time, he has painted Lal Vakhs — mystical four-line verses of 14th-century Kashmiri poet Lal Ded — on Pashmina shawls.Twenty shawls. Two years. “These are painted shawls based on Lal Vakhs. I selected 20 Vakhs, then I conceived them and painted them,” Hussain said Monday at an exhibition in Srinagar.Lal Ded, also known as Lalleshwari, was born near Srinagar in a Kashmiri Pandit family. Abused at her marital home, she left at 26 to become an itinerant Shaiva mystic. Muslims called her Lal Arifa. Her Vakhs — from the Sanskrit vaak, meaning “speech” or “saying” — are among the earliest compositions in Kashmiri and a foundation of its literary tradition.Hussain’s shawls give those words a visual life. One features what Hussain calls a celestial horse — a rider moving beneath a sky stitched with constellations.
Other shawls turn towards Lal Ded’s references to death, spiritual passage and the unseen.The idea took root after Hussain’s collaborations with Irish poet Gabriel Rosenstock, who died of cancer in April this year. Their first project marked Mahatma Gandhi’s 150th birth anniversary. Rosenstock’s 150 minimalist haikus and tankas were paired with Hussain’s watercolours, bringing Irish culture, Kashmiri artistry and Gandhian philosophy of peace into one book.
“I mostly painted Kashmir and its conflict. Once I collaborated with Rosenstock, a lot changed,” Hussain said. “Why not work on Kashmir Sufism, Rishi culture, syncretic culture and convert them into paintings? Why not start on Lal Ded on Pashmina? I got the idea.”Lal Ded walked barefoot, wandered, spoke in riddles. Hussain began by reading extensively about her and her poetry. “A lot has been written, but no one has given it a visual shape. I tried,” Hussain said. The medium is the message. It is an old poetry in a new skin — mysticism that can be worn.

King Harald V of Norway has died28.08.26, 09:46 • 5183 views
As a reminder
Earlier, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced meetings with representatives of states and defense companies involved in the development of the joint antiballistic program Freyja.
What is Freyja
Freyja is a Ukraine-initiated project for a joint European antiballistic system, the first track of the Antiballistic Coalition, which includes 10 countries and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
The project is being built around the FP-7.x interceptor missile developed by Fire Point, while other components are supplied by European manufacturers. As UNN reported, Fire Point’s general and technical director Iryna Terekh said that development has reached the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem — radars, a launcher, a data transmission channel, and a command center — while tests are being conducted up to twice a week. The first interception of a ballistic target by the system is scheduled for 2027.

Does the UK have a legal obligation to redress the harms of slavery?

Inside Story
Does the UK have a legal obligation to redress the harms of slavery?
Jamaica petitions the British monarch over questions about the legality of the transatlantic slave trade.
Jamaica’s campaign for reparations from the United Kingdom is part of a broader push for countries to pay for their roles in the transatlantic slave trade and hundreds of years of slavery.
Momentum is building. In March, a United Nations resolution said the claims represent a step towards a remedy for the descendants of enslaved people. Most Western countries abstained from the vote, and the United States opposed it.
In June, African and Caribbean nations met in Ghana – where hundreds of thousands of people were forced onto slave ships. They put together a plan for reparatory justice, which would include debt relief and other support for African nations.
Last month, a UN committee said governments are obliged by law to consider paying damages.
So, will the legal argument boost the case for reparations?

Guests:
Hilary Beckles – vice-chancellor of the University of the West Indies and chairman of the Caribbean Community and Common Market (CARICOM) Reparations Commission

Patrick Vernon – British historian and social commentator knighted in 2026 for his services to racial equality and social justice

Programme GRIFFIN leads UK work on NATO medical readiness
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
20:01:03 BST
04:01:03 KST

The Ministry of Defence has established Programme GRIFFIN to coordinate the UK military contribution to NATO’s Medical Action Plan, with an initial assessment identifying relevant Defence activity across all five areas of the Alliance initiative.
The programme was confirmed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what assessment had been made of the extent to which Defence Medical Services are aligned with NATO’s Medical Action Plan. Veterans and People Minister Calvin Bailey said: “The Surgeon General formally agreed the NATO Medical Action Plan on behalf of UK Defence in January 2025.”
He said the plan is intended to strengthen medical readiness and interoperability across the Alliance, covering regulatory alignment, workforce shortages, mass casualty planning, patient evacuation and medical logistics. Bailey stated: “The NATO Medical Action Plan is a strategic initiative to enhance medical readiness and interoperability for collective defence and focuses on improving regulatory alignment, addressing healthcare workforce shortages, enhancing integrated mass casualty planning, streamlining patient evacuation, and strengthening medical logistics.”
Defence Medical Command, previously known as Headquarters Defence Medical Services, has been given responsibility for coordinating the UK military contribution.
Bailey said: “Defence Medical Command, previously Headquarters Defence Medical Services, has established Programme GRIFFIN to lead on the UK military contribution to the NATO Medical Action Plan.”
The MOD said Programme GRIFFIN has already completed a baseline assessment of activity across Defence relevant to the NATO plan. He added: “This has identified activity in all five themes as set out in the NATO Medical Action Plan and the assessment provides the basis for cohering and prioritising activity.”

I believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive | Andy Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:00:47 UTC
04:00:47 KST

In a difficult and dangerous world, a decade on from Brexit, there is a risk that Britain loses the confidence to lead and stand up for its values. I’m not prepared to let that happen. It is more important than ever that Britain stands for something.
We have called for years for a two-state solution in the Middle East, but we must recognise that those words are meaningless unless we back them up with action.
For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel. Today we are announcing carefully judged, targeted steps that are not aimed at the Israeli people, but at the unacceptable policies of the current Israeli government.
The suffering of the Palestinian people is a scar on the conscience of the world. Innocent Palestinians, including children, continue to be killed in Gaza. And there is still a humanitarian crisis, with far too little aid getting in.
The scale of destruction is hard to comprehend. More than 70,000 people lie dead – at least 20,000 of them children. Families and communities have been torn apart. Millions displaced. And the population of Gaza is now penned into just one third of the territory.
I know that people across the UK feel very deeply about this issue – and so do I.
Before I became prime minister, I said our country’s response had been too slow and simply not good enough. That’s why I committed to changing the government’s approach.
I will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two-state solution – the best hope for peace and stability in the region – comes under attack.
More settlements have been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years. The UN has reported more than 1,500 incidents of settler violence so far this year, aimed at driving out Palestinians. And the situation is growing worse, fast.
The Israeli government has now approved 104 new settlements since it took office in December 2022, and ahead of the October elections in Israel, it is allowing tenders for the construction of the E1 mega settlement to go ahead. This would cut a swathe through the heart of the West Bank – snuffing out the hope of realising a two-state solution. It cannot be allowed to happen.
That’s why we are announcing a new package of tough measures to put pressure on the Israeli government:
First, we will ban the trade in goods with illegal settlements in Palestine.
Second, we have formally changed the view of the British government to say for the first time that the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory is unlawful – independent of, but in line with, the conclusion of the international court of justice.
And third, we will sanction individuals and companies that support, facilitate or profit from illegal settlements. That includes any businesses or investors that take part in the construction of the E1 settlement.
In addition, we are announcing a new package of desperately needed humanitarian aid to Gaza.
We are taking these steps because it is the right thing to do.
I have condemned the monstrous terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 in the strongest possible terms – and continue to condemn Hamas. However, it does not justify the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza or the West Bank.
The measures we are taking are about targeting illegal settlements and increasing the pressure on the Israeli government to change course. We are not imposing sanctions on Israel as a whole, which would punish the Israeli people, many of whom disagree with their government’s position.
The Israeli people are not responsible for the actions of their government. And nor is the Jewish community in the UK. Blaming British Jews for the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is wrong, plain and simple. And it is antisemitism, plain and simple.
I met the representatives of the Jewish community just last week. I know the fear they live with day by day. My government will stop at nothing to ensure they are safe and to stamp out antisemitism in every part of our society.
The measures we are announcing today are about protecting the only solution that could see the Israeli and Palestinian people living side by side in peace and security – something that people up and down the UK desperately want to see. The government I lead will keep working with our partners around the world to keep that hope alive.
- 
  Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

Anthony Albanese held undeclared honorary membership to golf club awarded $6 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:00:09 UTC
04:00:09 KST

Anthony Albanese held undeclared honorary membership to golf club awarded $6 million
In short:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese held an honorary membership to Marrickville Golf Club, which he has not declared on his register of interests.
The golf club was promised $6 million at the federal election, which was awarded through a fund that heavily favoured Labor seats.
What's next?
The Coalition says the federal government must explain what process was used to construct the list of projects nominated for funding.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese held an honorary membership to the Marrickville Golf Club in his seat, which was promised $6 million at the 2025 election through an invite-only scheme, and which Mr Albanese has not declared.
Mr Albanese has previously spoken of his long association with the club, but records of his register of interests dating back to his entry to parliament in 1996 do not mention a membership to the club, either paid or honorary.
"We have him on the books as an honorary member, but I think that dates from a long time ago, that hasn't been reaffirmed," a spokesperson for the Marrickville Golf Club told the ABC.
"I don't know when he was put on the books as an honorary member, that may have been 15 years ago or more."
The Prime Minister's Office did not respond to questions about Mr Albanese's membership.
Speaking on ABC News Breakfast, Mr Albanese said he did not know he was an honorary member.
"Apparently that happened 15 years ago or something, I haven't been into the clubhouse for many many years, the ABC chose to do this, that is up to them," Mr Albanese said.
"I don't have a card, I don't go in there, I haven't been in there for years."
He said the three grants given in his electorate were appropriate, which also included funding to the Leichhardt Women's Health Centre and to St Vincent de Paul's for a shelter for women escaping family violence.
The register of interests requires MPs to declare membership of any organisation where a conflict of interest could foreseeably arise.
While it is generally expected that membership of a local community, sporting or charitable organisation would not pose or be seen to pose a potential conflict of interest, the prime minister has declared other honorary memberships over his time in parliament.
That includes an honorary membership to the Royal Sydney Golf Course, given in 2025, and an honorary membership of the Western Suburbs Lawn Tennis Association over multiple terms of parliament, as well as membership of the Marrickville Lawn Tennis Club.
The Marrickville Golf Club was one of 220 projects promised funding through an invitation-only grant program established to pay election commitments made by Labor.
A Centre for Public Integrity investigation found the $560 million program heavily favoured safe Labor seats, and marginal contests the party hoped to win.
Its chair, former justice Anthony Whealy, told the ABC on Tuesday that the government had a "heavy onus" to justify how projects were chosen for funding.
The federal government notes more than $1.7 billion in competitive grant funding was made available through other programs, and that its Major and Local Community Infrastructure (MLCI) program followed the grant rules and guidelines strengthened by Labor in 2024.
Club approached Albanese's electorate office with funding request
Marrickville Golf Club's management told the ABC that they had first approached Mr Albanese's electorate office after the club was brought back into the seat of Grayndler following a redistribution in October 2024.
The club says it did not speak with Mr Albanese directly, but rather with his office.
"That was an open-ended conversation, they were saying, well, PM would like — there is money available," a spokesperson said.
"They did say, look, what ideas do you have? What other needs may you have? Again an open-ended conversation. We came back with a presentation setting out our ideas, some of which we had on the boil already."
The club was awarded $6.05 million to fully renovate the clubhouse, including new outdoor dining, a fix to its sewage and stormwater systems, an accessibility ramp and landscaping.
That promise was announced by the prime minister in April last year while on the campaign trail.
It was the only golf club invited for funding under the MLCI program.
The MLCI fund was established after the election to manage Labor's election commitments, including undertaking a value-for-money assessment.
The federal government has not explained who identified projects for a grant invitation, or what process was used to determine projects for funding.
Shadow Infrastructure Minister Bridget McKenzie questioned what role Labor MPs or candidates played.
"I'd hate to see a situation where you would have to stock the beer of your local member in order to get a grant in this country," Senator McKenzie said.
Shadow Infrastructure Minister Catherine King said she gave the final sign off on grants under the program, and so Mr Albanese's membership was not relevant.
"The first thing is the prime minister is not the decision maker of this program, I am the decision maker of the program," Ms King told ABC Radio Newcastle.
"So nobody would declare anything, basically, because I am the decision maker and the only person who would need to declare something, who would have a conflict, would be me."
Albanese's long association with club
Mr Albanese has previously intervened to assist the Marrickville Golf Club.
In 2019, Mr Albanese and his Labor colleague and neighbouring MP Linda Burney joined a campaign against a local Greens proposal to cut the golf course in half to open up more space in the dense inner-west Sydney suburb.
A Daily Telegraph news article at the time noted Mr Albanese held a "non-golfing honorary membership" to the club, though his register of interests at that time does not include a membership declaration.
The proposal to shrink the 18-hole course to nine holes was defeated.
At a speech to the club's members arguing against the proposed course reduction, Mr Albanese spoke of his personal association to the club.
"I declare an interest, I live in Beauchamp Street … and I have been coming here for decades and using this club," Mr Albanese said.
Mr Albanese regularly walked his dog, Toto, at the course when he lived nearby. The clubhouse stocks Willie the Boatman's "Albo" beer, which is stocked in many places across his electorate and which the prime miinster has no financial interest in.
While the prime minister is not an avid golfer, he has received golf lessons there.
Mr Albanese also participated in Labor candidate launches at the Marrickville Golf Club.
In 2015, he joined the launch of state Labor candidate and now-member for Summer Hill Jo Haylen, which was hosted at the golf club.
And in 2012, Mr Albanese tweeted that he was at the Marrickville Golf Club for a "local Labor launch".
Membership not declared
The ministerial code of conduct separately requires ministers to declare and register "personal interests", including but not limited to pecuniary interests, where it could give rise to a conflict with their public duties.
Marrickville Golf Club is one of the more affordable courses in the country. A full membership costs $1,100 annually.
In 2020, Labor challenged then-sports minister Bridget McKenzie over a $36,000 grant she had awarded to a gun club after it was revealed the senator held an undisclosed honorary membership with that club.
The senator told the ABC she ultimately resigned over a perceived conflict of interest in awarding that grant, since she was the responsible minister who signed off on it.
The MLCI program sits under the Infrastructure Department, with Catherine King the approving minister except in her own seat, where grants are approved by another cabinet minister.
However, Senator McKenzie says the sports grants program was an open, competitive process with a departmental assessment process.
She said given the MLCI was invitation-only, and Ms King received a list of projects from the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, the government needed to explain its process.
"It's up for the ministers to explain who was the ultimate decision-maker, and how the project list was constructed," Senator McKenzie said.
The Greens have called on Mr Albanese to front the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters to explain how projects were chosen for funding.

We Must Defend the Refugee Convention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:57:12 UTC
03:57:12 KST

In 1941, as the Nazis swept through Greece and took Athens, my grandfather, Nicolas Taptiklis, fled for his life.
In the middle of the night, he boarded a tiny boat with twelve others and crossed the dangerous waters of the Aegean Sea to Turkey. Under Nazi occupation, his service with the British Navy made staying in Greece a risk he could not take. Greeks who helped the Allies risked arrest, imprisonment, or execution, and the punishment could reach their families and communities too. From Turkey, he made his way with thousands of others to Syria, where he finally found safety in Damascus.
That journey never left him. When the war ended, Europe was filled with people who had also lost their homes, their families and, in many cases, nearly their lives. Around 11 million people were displaced in Germany: Holocaust survivors, former prisoners of war, forced laborers, and others left in camps, waiting for the world to decide what came next.
My grandfather returned to Europe and put his medical training to work for people whose own lives had been broken by the same war he had fled. He joined the UN Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, one of the first humanitarian agencies and a precursor to UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency. In a camp in Göttingen, Germany, he treated tuberculosis, typhoid, and people whose bodies had survived the war but still bore its scars.
The world had learned, at unbearable human cost, what happens when people fleeing war have nowhere safe to go. Through WWII, Families were turned away from protection, people returned to countries where they feared for their lives, and millions were left in camps because home was no longer safe or even existed at all.
From that devastation came a simple lesson; people escaping war and conflict should be able to find safety. They should not be forced back to a place where they could be killed or tortured. When people flee for their lives, they need somewhere safe to go.
That principle became the heart of the 1951 Refugee Convention, adopted in the aftermath of the Second World War as countries tried to create a framework to prevent the atrocities of the war from ever occurring again. The Convention defined who is a refugee, set out the basic rights for refugees, and established the responsibilities of states toward people seeking protection. But more than a legal document, it was a promise of safety. A promise that, for the past 75 years, has saved millions of lives and stands as proof that even in our darkest hours, we can choose to protect one another.
Even the clearest lessons of history can fade. A world of indifference, even cruelty, is creeping back. Xenophobia is rising. Humanitarian aid is shrinking. International solidarity is weakening. And once again, the promise of safety is under strain.
As world leaders gather in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, we must reaffirm that promise. In times like these, we must hold fast to our promise and advocate for the continued need and lifesaving work of humanitarian agencies, like UNHCR, around the world. This is not only the morally right thing to do; it is also the practical one. When refugees are protected, communities are stronger, instability is reduced, and fewer people are forced to flee. A world that protects people in their greatest moment of need is a safer and more humane world for everyone.
My grandfather experienced the generosity and compassion of the Syrians who sheltered him, but he also knew what a world of chaos and violence was like, and what its consequences were if there was no safety net of international protection.
If my grandfather were alive today, he would be sounding a warning. He would be speaking up in defense of the Convention, of humanitarian action, of compassion. He knew all too well what it was like to flee in fear for your life. He saw how lives could be lost or shattered if there was no one to step in and protect them.
I think of my grandfather on that boat, making that journey. I sound the warning on his behalf. To remind people that becoming a refugee can happen to any of us at any time. The right to seek safety was a promise made for us all, and that promise needs protecting and defending.

What could your social media feeds look like without the algorithm?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:55:25 UTC
03:55:25 KST

What could your social media feeds look like without the algorithm?
Your social media feeds could soon look a little different.
The government is proposing new laws that allow it to require social media companies to send a notification to users, giving them the option of opting in or out of the algorithm on their feed.
But there are concerns social media companies could offer a substandard product, or engage in "protest design" by making non-algorithmic feeds less functional or more boring, to drive users back into the arms of the algorithm.
Several social media apps already have ways for you to exercise more control over what you see in your feeds, but these are often buried in the system settings, or have other limitations.
On Instagram, for example, you can limit your feed to just who you're following, although the app takes you back to the default every time you close and click back in.
Still, this could give us a hint of what an algorithm-free feed might look like.
Loading...
Firstly, what's the algorithm?
An algorithm is sometimes described as a recipe or step-by-step instructions for how to manage data.
But the term "the algorithm" has become shorthand for recommender systems fuelled by AI and machine learning which curate content in a hyper-personalised way based on user engagement.
The aim is to keep you on the platform for as long as possible, so tech companies can monetise that engagement, selling ads between bits of content.
That means users get served content that they linger over, which includes both things they want to see, but also content they engage with out of outrage or morbid curiosity.
"It's the stuff that we're most likely to react to, but not necessarily in a good way," said Tama Leaver, a professor of internet studies at Curtin University.
"It's the car accident principle, where none of us want to see a car accident, but if we see one, we'll slow down and look out the window."
Critics of the algorithm say it pushes increasingly extremist content, leading users down rabbit holes and creating echo chambers that can warp a user's view of reality.
One minute you're looking at puppy videos and fitness routines, the next you're being fed rabid conspiracy theories.
"The platforms want a layer of curated content in front of you that is addictive, that is created to make you spend more time on the platform," said Belinda Barnet, a media and communications expert at Swinburne University.
"TikTok's incredibly successful at that. Their algorithm is amazing. Teenagers can spend six hours on it if you don't interrupt them."
So what could your feeds look like?
One option is the reverse chronological feed — that is, showing you posts from accounts you follow in the order they were posted.
Proponents of this temporal model say it hails back to the "good old days" of the internet for early social media adopters, seeing posts from your family, friends and accounts you follow.
Daniel Angus, director of the Digital Media Research Centre at Queensland University of Technology, said that puts the burden back on the user to be the curator.
"You are perhaps getting bombarded by those who are frequent posters," he said.
One benefit is that it could stop the infinite scrolling — if you get the feeling that you're all caught up, you can leave the app.
"The mindlessness turns into endlessness and soon enough we're in this spiral," said Rashina Hoda, a professor of software engineering at the Faculty of IT at Monash University.
"By giving this opt-out feature for that algorithm, you're bringing intentionality back into how we interact with social media."
She said the current opt-out option for recommender algorithms might not always be accessible or easily implemented.
"For example, users may not even know they are in an echo chamber and therefore may not be able to help themselves,"
Professor Leaver said that since it's been so long since social media users have had a chronological feed as a default, it might feel pretty weird at first.
"I'm quite sure that there will be a whole lot of protest design," Professor Leaver said, explaining tech companies may react by poorly designing features that are compliant but not user-friendly.
"If this is forced on platforms, they will probably make things a bit worse and then blame the government and say that they're perfectly happy to roll it back if the legislation went away.
"So it may not in the short term lead to a better experience, but I do think Australia's politicians at least seem more willing to stare down big tech and see who blinks first."
Chanel Contos, founder of Teach Us Consent, told the Press Club last week the European Union's Digital Services Act pushed for mandatory "opt out" features, but it left room for social media platforms to "comply maliciously".
"Technically you can view a following-only feed in chronological order, but you can't access any other of the app's features and it resets back to an algorithm every time you close and re-open the app, punishing those who opt out of being force fed a diet of ads and polarised content," she said.
A hybrid approach
Professor Angus of QUT said another approach could be to move away from the algorithm vs non-algorithm binary.
Instead, he advocated for a hybrid approach that would give users more agency in how they curated their feeds.
He pointed to alternate social media spaces such as BlueSky and Mastodon, where people created lists to be able to discover like-minded creators.
"That's a really interesting space where you put the creativity back into the community and you allow them to kind of self-govern and come up with the ways that they want to experience that space," he said.
"You end up with a hybrid approach where it's not like there's one algorithm driving everyone's experience and everyone is locked into that choice.
"The agency is with the user and they're coming up with the tools they need to try and swim within that river."
What can you already do?
There are already steps you can take to control what you see on your feeds, but these steps are "typically buried a few levels deep inside of one's settings", David J Malan, a computer scientist at Harvard University, told ABC Radio National.
On Instagram, you can click on the logo to get a drop down, giving you the option of "following", which gives you a stream of posts from accounts you follow in reverse chronological order. But this will reset when you close and re-open the app.
In settings, you can also "snooze suggested posts" for 30 days, "reset" suggested, tweak "your algorithm" by clicking on what you want to see more and less of. You can also choose to see less political and sensitive content.
You can also flag content you don't like on several platforms by clicking "not interested", or unfollowing pages you don't wish to see.
TikTok and YouTube also have options for users to reset or delete history, telling the app to forget what it's learned about you and start fresh.
So will your social media feed be more boring under the proposed changes? It's possible.
But it's also part of the point to make platforms less addictive. Ultimately, we'll have to wait and see how companies react and what social media users choose.

Why Reading People's Confessions Online Feels So Good
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:52:59 UTC
03:52:59 KST

In January 2026, a new community popped up on Reddit, the online message board site. Called /r/GirlDinnerDiaries, it now has a sizable 6 million members and invites people to post a photo of a meal—whether it’s something you’re eating while you post or another meal that gets at your state of mind—along with an anonymous blurb venting or soliciting advice. "My partner only feels disgust at the idea of me as a mom," reads one. "I feel like it's never going to be OK," says another.
The point is to activate the feeling of sharing over food, but over the internet. The snapshots are messy, yet evocative: French fries consumed in a nightclub, a breakfast burrito in a diner, yesterday’s lunch eaten hastily over a keyboard with a plastic fork. The posts wax poetic about the fate of marriages and the bizarre serendipity of life. Reading these dishy dispatches feels like staying up late with friends you rarely see, working over all that's gone down in your life in search of some meaning.
Why are millions of people so captivated by these nameless confessionals served with a side of candid, unposed food photography? Scientists who study self-disclosure—the act of sharing personal, sensitive information with others—have some thoughts about why we share our deepest, darkest secrets on the internet.
Revealing ourselves builds trust
Talking about yourself feels pleasurable, and there’s science to back that up, says Leslie John, a professor of business administration at Harvard Business School and author of the book Revealing. She points to experiments conducted by psychologists Diana Tamir and Jason Mitchell, where people having their brains scanned in an fMRI machine answered either normal trivia questions or questions about themselves. “They found that in the ones that got to self-disclose, the pleasure centers of the brain were activated,” says John. “That's pretty powerful.”
Sharing feels good because it’s necessary for human social interaction, John speculates. “When you self-disclose, when you take the social risk—and it really is a social risk—of sharing something a little bit personal, a little sensitive, you're modeling that you trust the recipient. That gesture is implicitly saying, ‘Hey, I trust you not to make a fool out of me; otherwise, I wouldn't be sharing this.’ And when you do that, it causes the other person to trust you back. So trust begets trust,” she says.
In fact, John’s work has found that people are more interested in dating a hypothetical person who admits that they’ve done something terrible than someone who declines to answer the question. “It's better sometimes to admit the worst possible thing than to conspicuously abstain,” she says.
Posting a photo of a paper plate with yesterday’s messy BBQ and a brownie you ate while processing getting fired is, in the age of the perfectly lit Instagram plate, a similar kind of move. “It's super relatable,” says John. “Showing things that are unvarnished is kind of paradoxically attractive.”
How the internet changes the equation
Psychologists and sociologists used to think of self-disclosure mainly in the sense of sharing with people you know in real life, says sociologist Tamar Ashuri of Tel Aviv University. “The original studies back in the ’50s and ’60s on self-disclosure focus on face-to-face interactions,” she says. “In intimate relationships, people disclose, and it’s kind of an ultimate goal. You can't sustain an intimate relationship if you don't.” Another situation where people might self-disclose is the stranger-on-a-train context. It’s also face-to-face, but there is no lasting link, so the risks of disclosure are lower.
But the arrival of the internet, and social media especially, produced new forms of self-disclosure that scientists are still working to characterize and understand. In the case of /r/GirlDinnerDiaries, says Ashuri, posters are anonymously disclosing intimate thoughts in a public forum, stranger-on-a-train style, with no face-to-face interaction, and yet it is still somehow gratifying.
That combination emerged almost by accident, says the subreddit’s founder, a young woman named Taylor, who asked to be identified only by her first name. She had been posting frequently in another community, called Girl Dinner, and noticed a split: Some people wanted to know the slice-of-life stories behind the meals, while others only wanted to see the food. She created Girl Dinner Diaries as an overflow space for people who wanted both—and it took off almost immediately. “One of my favorite things is going out with the girls for some drinks and some appys and venting, getting it all off my chest,” Taylor says. Girl Dinner Diaries offered a place to do that without leaving the couch.
Not every diary is wrenching. Taylor’s favorite post is a happy one: A woman woke up to discover that her husband had created a scavenger hunt for her, then shared a photo of the pasta with burrata they ate that evening. “It looked quite fancy,” Taylor says. “It looked very delicious.”
Whether the story is heartwarming or devastating, the meal is an essential part of the formula. “Food provides a very positive, ordinary, culturally familiar medium,” Ashuri says. “But in this case, and this is what makes it so special, it allows people to express extraordinary issues…The food makes the extraordinary feel more ordinary.” She gives the example of one recent post, in which a woman posted a birthday cake and revealed that she and her son had celebrated his birthday in a domestic violence shelter. “I think this combination is extremely significant,” she says.
The setup allows posters to reveal what are sometimes extreme experiences to a community gathered around a shared sensibility—with the unifying force of a leftover chimichanga presiding over it all. Food helps make the extreme relatable. The subreddit also tightly controls who can enter the conversation: Only approved commenters are allowed to respond, adding a layer of protection to a forum built around unusually intimate disclosures.
Should we all be self-disclosing more?
There’s a happy medium to everything—don’t, perhaps, take to the web with every mental dip or life hiccup. And sharing online may not bring the same benefits as sharing in real life, cautions John. “Social media in so many ways facilitates self-disclosure,” she says. “But in many ways this medium doesn't give you the benefit you're looking for (e.g., real social bonding, connectedness).”
Indeed, research suggests that people who post to social media every day tend to score worse on measures of mental health. Posting online can give easy access to reassurance from others, but this behavior can sometimes become destructive—if we don’t get the reassurance we seek, that’s a big blow, and constant reassurance may not help in solving the larger problems.
But John thinks that in general, offline, we overestimate the harms of oversharing, while underestimating the costs of staying silent.
The impulse to put an experience into words may help even when no one else reads them. Some of social psychologist James Pennebaker’s research suggests that privately writing about traumatic events can provide significant psychological relief, and even boost the immune systems of some patients.
John never really applied her findings about disclosure to her own life, though, until she was working on her book about sharing. “Every time in my life that I could think of where I overshared, where I felt that cringe of TMI, it sucked in the moment. But every single time there was something amazing and redeeming in the long haul about it,” she says. “That made me think, ‘Oh wow, the decision we're making is systematically biased’…You get immediate negative social feedback, but there are benefits too. People trust you, people like you, people confide in you. Those come down the road.”
