EU, UK express dismay over Mladic funeral in Serbia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:52:00 UTC
01:52:00 KST

EU, UK express dismay over Mladic funeral in Serbia
September 8, 2026
Both the EU and UK on Tuesday expressed dismay over the funeral in Belgrade, Serbia of late war criminal Ratko Mladic a day prior.
Thousands of people, including at least six Serbian ministers, attended the event on Monday which was seen as glorifying Mladic. He received military honors at the funeral, with the head of Serbia's Orthodox Church presiding over the ceremony.
The Bosnian Serb commander died last month at The Hague, where he had been imprisoned for life. Mladic was convicted in 2017 of genocide, having orchestrated the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre, where 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.
Mladic, called the "Butcher of Bosnia" by some international press, is a revered as a war hero by many Serbian nationalists in both Serbia and Bosnia.
EU leader call Mladic state funeral 'deeply regrettable'
EU leaders condemned the funeral, with the bloc weighing an official response to the event.
"The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa said in statements posted on X.
"They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe's recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia's path towards the European Union," they added.
A European Commission spokeperson, in comments to German news agency DPA, said next steps were being evaluated.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas added: "Serbia's path into the European Union requires an unequivocal commitment in fundamental European values and historical truth."
Serbia first applied for EU membership in 2009. Serbia's EU candidacy was confirmed by the European Council in 2012.
UK summons Serbian envoy
The UK, meanwhile, summoned Serbia's charge d'affaires in response to the funeral.
"As a military commander, Mladic presided over crimes that are among the worst committed in Europe since the Second World War," the British Foreign Office said in a statement.
"The thoughts of the UK Government are with Mladic's victims and their families. They deserve respect, compassion and accountability, not efforts to rewrite proven history," the statement added.
The UK said that the "glorification of a convicted war criminal directly undermines trust, fuels division, and is incompatible with the process of reconciliation within Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region."
Bosnia expels Serbian diplomats, says Belgrade crossed 'red line'
In its reaction to the funeral, neighboring Bosnia expelled two Serbian diplomats, saying Serbia crossed a "red line" in its display of reverence for Mladic.
"They crossed every red line with what they did yesterday, the day before, and in the days leading up to the reception," Bosnian Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic told a Sarajevo press event.
Konakovic had also said he would withdraw most staff from the Bosnian Embassy in Belgrade in an effort to reduce ties to "the lowest possible level"
Serbian President Aleksander Vucic was not present at Mladic's funeral, although his son Danilo, did attend the event. Vucic rejected allegations that Mladic was being glorified at the funeral and said the event was put together by Mladic's family rather than the state.
The controversial funeral comes ahead of snap elections next month. Serbia has faced a political crisis in the past two years triggered by the collapse of a concrete canopy at a railway station in Novi Sad.

Separate strikes also hit the Kharkiv and Chernihiv regions.
Damage across Dnipropetrovsk districts
The Nikopol district bore the brunt of the attack, with the Nikopol, Marhanets, Pokrovsk, and Myriv communities coming under fire. Two men were killed there, while six other people were wounded, including a 33-year-old man hospitalized in moderate condition.

Kharkiv, Chernihiv also struck
The Dnipropetrovsk attack came amid a broader wave of Russian strikes across Ukraine on Tuesday.
In Kharkiv’s Kyivskyi district, a Russian drone struck a gas station, injuring two people and sparking a fire that set a fuel pump and a car ablaze, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES).

Emergency crews extinguished the blaze, and State Emergency Service units, medics, and police responded at the scene.

Rescue crews had to repeatedly retreat to safety amid the threat of follow-up strikes – a precaution against Russia’s so-called “double-tap” tactic, in which a second strike targets the same site it previously hit, aimed at rescue crews and emergency responders.

Russian drones were tracked heading toward Kyiv and its suburbs on Monday, Sept. 7, hours ahead of Moscow’s own stated deadline, while air raid sirens repeatedly sounded throughout the ceasefire period.
Although Witkoff said Monday that “substantive progress was made [during the envoys’ visit to Kyiv and Moscow over the weekend], including movement on scheduling additional trilateral talks,” Russia continued intensifying its attacks on Ukraine, casting further doubt on the possibility of reaching an agreement.

Neither political donations nor special interest groups should dictate policy | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:49:03 UTC
01:49:03 KST

George Monbiot condemns Andy Burnham for his alleged subservience to the interests of the wealthy (Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations, 2 September). If true, I agree. But the same could be said of any interest holding sway in our politics. Lobbying groups, activists, unions, thinktanks, people who obsess about this, that or the other. It is surely not OK for our democracy – at local or national level – to have its priorities dictated by those with the shrillest voices, as well as those with the deepest pockets.
Speaking from Scotland, I think that our public realm is a case in point. It seems special interest groups are, to all intents and purposes, the main driver of government policy now. And all too often, said influence is framed by an ideological mission that does not necessarily align with that boring, broad swathe of folks who don’t follow politics closely, and don’t see government as a means to progress personal hobbyhorses or single-issue causes.
The latter are, in their own insidious way, as injurious to democracy as the whispers of the wealthy in the ears of politicians. So too is turning a blind eye to such undue influence because its aims chime with your own beliefs. Leaders of any party must endeavour to serve not some, but all – without fear or favour – including those who didn’t vote for them. Not easy. No guarantee of success. But abandoning that principle makes our politics all the poorer.
Colin Montgomery
Edinburgh
I was surprised to see George Monbiot paying feasance to that liberal shibboleth, “the general interest”. If a society is fractured by inequalities of class, race, gender, sexuality, etc, then there can be no “general interest” until these are overcome. Ensuring trade union influence over Labour policy through the continuation of union donations acts as leverage against policy being captured by the likes of Lord Alli and Lord Sainsbury.
When Monbiot goes on to say that “Labour governments know they can safely bash benefit recipients, who aren’t unionised, while they tread very carefully – far too carefully in my view – around the interests of oil workers”, he misses the obvious point that the way, then, to protect benefit claimants is to organise them. Unite, for instance, already has a community membership for students, claimants and pensioners, and has organised days of action against benefit cuts and sanctions. Monbiot’s proposal would not strengthen the power of benefit claimants, it would simply weaken the power of trade unions.
Nick Moss
London
George Monbiot is right; Andy Burnham lacks the courage to take on vested interests, and nowhere is this more apparent than over climate breakdown. During an extensive Panorama interview with Laura Kuenssberg, the climate crisis was not mentioned once, despite record temperatures, drought affecting half the country and unprecedented wildfires raging throughout Europe. The cap on bus fares will be financed by abandoning international climate payments; and now Burnham wants to take a “pragmatic” approach to drilling in the North Sea.
Next year we will breach the 1.5C limit stipulated in the Paris agreement, and this will be followed by the disappearance of coral reefs and the eventual disintegration of the Western Antarctic ice sheet – irreversible events that will undermine the marine food chain and raise sea levels by six metres. Andy Burnham’s lukewarm approach won’t look so pragmatic to our descendants when coastal cities worldwide are under water.
Dr Robin Russell-Jones
Founder, Help Rescue the Planet

By dpa correspondents.
Berlin (dpa) – Thousands of people across Germany protested against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) on Monday following its landslide victory in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
In Berlin, police estimated a crowd of around 5,000 had gathered at Brandenburg Gate and said the demonstration passed without incident. Organizers put the number of participants at around 14,000.
The rally was called at short notice by campaign organization Campact and the Fridays for Future climate movement.
Among those taking part were prominent German climate activist Luisa Neubauer and the lead candidates of the Greens and The Left in Berlin’s state election on September 20.
Protesters carried banners with slogans including “Fascism is not an alternative” and “Stop AfD Nazis! End racism and social cuts,” while crowds chanted: “All together against fascism!”
The party won Sunday’s election by a wide margin but fell short of an absolute majority, leaving open the possibility of Germany’s first AfD-led state government.
The domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD’s state branch as “confirmed right-wing extremist.”
Protests were also called in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, where a new state parliament will be elected later this month and the AfD is leading in the polls.
In Schwerin, according to police reports, several hundred demonstrators gathered, while in Rostock, more than 500 people came together for a communal sing-along.
In Essen, about 1,200 people gathered, according to police. Carrying rainbow flags and cardboard signs with messages such as “Ban the AfD now” and “No place for Nazis,” the participants marched through the city centre.
Hundreds of people also gathered in Potsdam to protest against the AfD, as did others in Hesse. Around 80 people protested in Kassel.
Police said about 2,500 people demonstrated in Frankfurt on Sunday, calling for a review of the possibility of banning the AfD.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Tuesday pledged more Patriot interceptors, AIM-9 missiles and IRIS-T air defense systems for Ukraine.

“What is more, we are keeping up our continuous deliveries of IRST air defense systems, including guided missiles,” he said. ”I am pleased that Ukraine is going to order several thousand additional IRST-guided missiles that will be funded by the EU-Ukraine Defense Loan.”
Pistorius said Germany will keep up its continuous deliveries of drones and long-range ammunition to help stabilize the front. Beyond the ongoing support, he said Berlin will fund several tens of thousands of rounds of long-range artillery ammunition. OpenAI Just Claimed a Huge Math Discovery. Some Academics Are Crying Foul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:42:05 UTC
01:42:05 KST

OpenAI said today that it has found an AI-generated solution to one of the biggest problems in mathematics—a 200-year-old equation that describes the natural behavior of fluids like water and air.
The announcement appears to demonstrate the stunning power for AI to advance mathematics. But it has been marred by claims from another mathematician, Tristan Buckmaster, who says that OpenAI rushed ahead to solve the problem after learning of the work of Buckmaster and a colleague—Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge. Buckmaster claims OpenAI also tried to influence who got credit for the work.
The proof concerns the Navier-Stokes equation, one of the unsolved problems in the Clay Millennium prizes, which are each worth $1 million.
Sebastien Bubeck, a mathematician and AI researcher at OpenAI, said in a press briefing that the company began training a new AI model with advanced mathematical capabilities on August 28.
After reading rumors that Anthropic was making progress toward solving Navier-Stokes, Bubeck said the company decided to dedicate more resources to tackling the problem. The company had more than 1,000 agents tackle the problem over more than 50 hours; eventually, as many as 10,000 agents were hard at work before the company discovered that it had come up with a solution.
“I thought there must be a mistake somewhere,” Bubeck said. “And on Sunday morning we had the final solution, Lean-formalized and everything.” (Lean is a programming language that can be used to formalize mathematical proofs.)
OpenAI noted that solving this problem required using considerably more computing power than it had previously spent on solving mathematical problems. The amount required cost “in the millions of dollars,” said Mark Chen, head of research at OpenAI.
On Monday, Alpöge and Buckmaster, a mathematician at NYU, posted documents claiming key advances in an area relevant to the Navier-Stokes problem. The pair says they used several AI models, including Claude and Codex, to complete their work.
Buckmaster also posted a statement claiming that, last week, he learned that OpenAI had become aware of his and Alpöge’s work and had started putting significant resources toward the problem. Buckmaster claims that he asked OpenAI leaders about whether the company had accessed the pair’s Codex logs. He says he was told the model “didn’t look up user data” but claims the company didn’t respond to questions about training. He then says that OpenAI offered several “proposals,” including one in which Buckmaster could publish a paper announcing the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by an internal OpenAI model but without Alpöge’s name included.
In a post on social media, Bubeck pushed back on the idea that the company had suggested removing Alpöge’s name. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also stepped into the fight, and defended the team's work.
Buckmaster, Alpöge, and Anthropic did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
In the briefing, Bubeck and other OpenAI executives denied that the company had ever inspected the pair’s Codex prompts in order to inform their work. “We, whether it’s the researchers or the agents, did not see any of their work until it was released publicly last night,” he said.
In a blog post detailing the work, the company wrote, “while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.”
“I want to be extremely clear that we recognize the priority of Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster’s work on unforced Euler, and we have nothing but congratulations to them on this monumental achievement that they have made. To be clear, we did not use their prompt or proof to prompt our models or direct our agents,” said Bubeck.
Ven Chandrasekaran, a mathematician at the company, also emphasized that their solution was significantly different in nature from the one produced by OpenAI’s model.
The spat over who gets credit for solving one of the biggest problems in math may rumble on for a while. As AI takes on more of the work involved with finding proofs, such fights could perhaps become more common.

The arrival of the ‘ber months’ signals start of Christmas in the Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:50 UTC
01:41:50 KST

At a city block-sized market in the Philippine capital, a platoon of plastic Santa Claus figures parachute from the ceiling of a shop already stacked high with Christmas decor, despite the holiday being fully four months away.
The site is a familiar one in the Philippines, where Sept. 1 means radio stations playing Christmas carols, homeowners putting up lights, and the country’s giant shopping malls unleashing their most impressive displays.
Welcome to the “ber months” — September, October, November, December — a months-long countdown to the most anticipated holiday on the calendar in the deeply Catholic country.
Photo: AFP
“We can smell it coming,” sales clerk Cora Lansangan, 73, said during a reporter’s visit to a Christmas shop that began stacking its shelves on July 31.
The store was already packed with shoppers buzzing around displays of Christmas trees, ornaments, plastic reindeer, mangers and festive lanterns.
“Even though life is hard, the mere sight of a Christmas tree brings us relief,” Manila real-estate agent Kathlene Santidad, 33, said, as she hunted for tinsel and baubles for her own tree, armed with a 10,000-peso (US$160) budget.
She said she shopped for decorations early because “I hate crowds” and wanted to take her time picking specific items from shops crammed with everything from tiny 300-peso tinsel to an 8,000-peso Christmas tree.
Coming toward the end of a rainy season typically marred by destructive typhoons and floods, the Christmas countdown is a marker of better things ahead, said Mark Godwin Villareal, a sociologist at Manila’s University of Santo Tomas.
“It provides a kind of continuity and stability in our social life, despite these economic, political, or even personal challenges that we are facing as a community or society,” he said.
The “ber months” had a rhythm, Villareal said.
September was for decorating, while October was time to start saving money for gifts and food for reunions with friends and relatives and the all-important midnight meal on Christmas Eve.
More than 100,000 of the country’s crucial overseas workforce, dubbed OFWs (overseas Filipino workers), can typically be counted on to rush home in time for the main event.
The extended season drives foot traffic and sales for the country’s giant shopping malls, many of which AFP journalists saw were already heavily decked out.
“For Filipinos, Christmas symbolizes belonging, faith, hope and joy,” said Christian Mathay, senior assistant vice president for SM Supermalls, a chain of 90 shopping malls that began setting up Christmas ornaments in August.
“Starting early gives shoppers more time to enjoy that experience,” he said.
In Pampanga province, north of Manila, weeks of flooding that stranded thousands of commuters failed to dampen the enthusiasm of manufacturers of star-shaped holiday lanterns known as parol, the single must-have Christmas decoration in a Filipino home.
“Water seeped into the showroom, so we had to clean up instead of working ... the thing with lanterns is, they’re waterproof,” said fifth-generation lantern-maker Angelica David, 26.
“We all need to recover from the floods. After that, people should start buying lanterns,” she said.
The decorations will only come down on Jan. 6, marked in the Philippines as the day when the magi brought gifts for the infant Jesus.
School superintendent Ricky Angeles, on a Christmas shopping trip to Manila, said he preferred to leave his lantern hanging all year round in a window of his home in the northern city of Cabanatuan, along with blinking strings of lights in his garden.
“We need a lengthy display period” to justify their cost, the 51-year-old said with a smile.
Then he ducked into a store to buy some more.

A government taskforce has “activated haze response plans” for schools, workplaces and community centers, Singaporean Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu (傅海) said in a video message on Facebook. Server shipments to soar 15.1 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:50 UTC
01:41:50 KST

Global server shipments this year are expected to grow 15.1 percent year-on-year to 16.6 million units, while artificial intelligence (AI) server shipments are forecast to rise 20.7 percent to 4.6 million units, the Market Intelligence and Consulting Institute (MIC) said yesterday.
Next year, global server shipments are estimated to grow 12.4 percent year-on-year to 18.6 million units and AI server shipments are predicted to rise about 18 percent to 5.4 million units, MIC deputy director-general Edward Lin (林柏齊) told a news conference in Taipei.
Growth next year would be driven by AI infrastructure investment by major cloud service providers and AI model developers, as well as neocloud providers’ accelerated deployment of computing capacity to meet global inference demand, he said.
Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
Robust AI infrastructure momentum is expected to continue through 2028 and is unlikely to fade before 2030, Lin said.
Private-sector investment is continuing to grow as cloud service providers, technology companies and data center operators increase spending on servers, networking equipment, memory, power and cooling systems, he said.
Initiatives such as the Stargate Project in the US, the EU’s planned AI Gigafactories and China’s computing network strategy are moving toward the procurement and funding stage, creating new opportunities for Taiwanese and global AI supply chains, he said.
Taiwanese server makers — including Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海), Quanta Computer Inc (廣達), Inventec Corp (英業達), Wistron Corp (緯創), Wiwynn Corp (緯穎), Pegatron Corp (和碩) and Giga Computing Technology Corp (技鋼) — have accelerated their diversification of production to meet customer demand, Lin said.
Their production sites span Taiwan, China, the US, Southeast Asia and Mexico, he said.
Plants in Thailand and Malaysia are being tasked with higher-end system assembly, while those in Vietnam mainly focus on “Level 6 (L6)” compute-tray assembly, Lin said.
The companies also use Mexico and the US as interconnected manufacturing hubs, with Mexican plants mainly handling Level 10 (L10) assembly, while US plants, being closer to major cloud service providers, focus on Level 11 (L11) assembly, rack configuration and delivery, he said.
The diversification of Taiwanese server production to the US, Mexico and Southeast Asia would be a continuing trend, driven by customer demand for local manufacturing and geopolitical risk management, Lin told the Taipei Times on the sidelines of the forum.
“These manufacturers’ overseas capacity is expected to increase, but Taiwan would remain their main production base for AI servers,” he said.
Taiwan’s server industry would not be hollowed out, as global server demand is still expanding and the value of local production could continue to grow despite some capacity moving abroad, he said.
In the near term, Taiwan is likely to retain production of graphics processing units, next-generation server platform design, prototype development and validation, given its concentration of semiconductor and component suppliers, Lin said.
High-value, compact modules could be shipped overseas for further assembly, he said.
Large systems and rack-scale integration from L10 to L11 are more likely to move closer to overseas customers first, where local assembly can reduce transport and logistics costs, he said.
As manufacturing experience improves later, overseas plants could gradually take on more manufacturing stages, including L6 assembly, he said.
The extent of the shift would depend on whether upstream suppliers establish local operations alongside system makers, he added.

In the past, the company was able to build five or six factories a year, said Hou, who is also chairman of the Taiwan Semiconductor Industry

Decoding Bayeux Tapestry diplomacy between UK and France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:49 UTC
01:41:49 KST

Not since the treasures of the boy pharaoh Tutankhamun arrived in London more than 50 years ago has there been such excitement over a blockbuster exhibition.
The Bayeux Tapestry commemorating Duke William of Normandy’s victory over King Harold’s Anglo-Saxons at Hastings in 1066 is set to go on show at the British Museum this week. About 100,000 tickets were snapped up in minutes. The Times of London called it “the loan of the millennium.”
On Wednesday last week, Britain’s King Charles III, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and their spouses got a sneak preview. The king celebrated the display as a symbol of an “entente amicale” between France and Britain — one step up from the historical “entente cordiale” that led the two countries to fight as allies in World War I.
Contemporary symbolism was also on display. Sundered by Brexit, London and Paris are drawing closer together as they share the same fears: European security is threatened by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s revanchist nation and US President Donald Trump’s fickleness as an ally; last week the White House tacitly encouraged Argentine President Javier Milei to reclaim the Falklands, the South Atlantic islands that the UK fought to defend from an invasion by Argentina 44 years ago.
There is another European context, too. The year 1066 represented a turning point in history, marking Britain’s second political integration with the continent, after the Roman Empire and before the UK’s accession to the European Community in 1973. The tapestry was originally commissioned by William’s half-brother, Bishop Odo of Bayeux, as political propaganda. Today, the leaders of France and Britain promote the world’s most celebrated work of embroidery to make a point about the UK’s European destiny.
Not everyone is joining in the cordiality. John Redwood, a former Conservative leadership contender and arch-Brexiteer, tweeted sourly: “As we consider the Bayeux embroidery, we should remember the many killed by this French invasion. English men and women had their lands stolen. Many were put into serfdom by a new Norman governing class.”
That is a theme, not a quirk. Down the centuries, English nationalists and radicals have denounced “the Norman yoke” and praised semi-mythical Anglo-Saxon freedoms. History-obsessed Euroskeptics detect a line of descent from Norman feudalism to overlordship by the bureaucrats of Brussels.
The Battle of Hastings did indeed prise England out of the northern world dominated by the heirs of the Vikings, including King Canute, who legendarily ordered the incoming tide to stop. Today, some Brexiteers regret leaving the European Free Trade Association, the UK’s former trade agreement with mostly Scandinavian countries, which was relinquished when Britain joined the European Economic Community. They salute “plucky” Iceland, which has just rejected closer ties with Brussels in a referendum.
If Burnham is trying to send a message of readiness to reconnect through the tapestry, Macron has also defied nationalist opinion at home to bring the work across the English Channel — his critics on the far right said it was too sacred, too fragile a relic to hand over.
“The loan took longer to negotiate than Brexit,” Macron joked last year.
However, behind the flummery stands a cool calculation from a figure dubbed Jupiter for his ability to attract the limelight.
France and Britain are two nuclear-armed, former colonial powers with a muscle memory of operating independently from their great American ally. Unlike Germany, which is hobbled by its history, they have a distinct worldview. Macron would like to enhance that tradition.
A reanimated London-Paris relationship suits the “soft left” on both sides. Le Monde, the voice of French progressives, praises the UK’s new prime minister for his embrace of Gallic-style statism. Burnham, who has a Dutch-born wife and spends family time on the continent, is a vocal opponent of Brexit. The prime minister has made no secret of his ambition to rejoin the European single market.
Still, some caveats apply. In this scenario, the UK feels like a petitioner, while the French have taken a transactional view of their relationship with post-Brexit Britain and continue to extract a high price for cooperation. French demands for a huge financial contribution have prevented the UK from joining the 150 billion euro (US$174 billion) EU SAFE program, designed to scale up arms production across the continent.
Macron has also secured large sums from the British government to pay French police to stop migrants from sailing across the Channel. The day after the Bayeux Tapestry jamboree at the British Museum, the tabloid Sun newspaper alleged a “French stitch-up” on its front page — an excruciating pun, but one that makes a telling point in an article about French police officers failing to intervene in the crossings.
Moreover, rejoining the single market will be an uphill battle. Even Europhiles like former British prime minister Tony Blair warn against going too far, too fast.
Brussels regulation of the key industries of the future, where the UK has a comparative advantage, has become more restrictive since the Brexit referendum. Then, the concern was genome editing and clinical trials, today, it is artificial intelligence and low-carbon energy.
Duke William’s victory at Hastings was never inevitable; until his dying day, he feared that the Norse kings would steal his English prize. Although the EU exerts a powerful attraction on Britain, how London finally settles its relationship with Brussels remains to be seen.
Martin Ivens is the editor of the Times Literary Supplement. Previously, he was editor of the Sunday Times of London and its chief political commentator. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

12 countries including France, UK say will sanction trade with Israeli
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:47 UTC
01:41:47 KST

Twelve countries including Britain, Canada and France announced Tuesday they would sanction trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after increasing attacks by settlers against Palestinians in the occupied territory.
Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden also plan to issue restrictions on trade with the settlements, the nations’ foreign ministers said in a joint statement.
The action follows weeks of increasing attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the illegally occupied territory that has drawn widespread condemnation from the international community.
Photo: Reuters
Ireland and Spain have already taken measures against trade with Israeli settlements, and France has for weeks been pushing for a similar decision from the European Union, Israel’s leading trading partner, but has been blocked by some members.
The 12 ministers said actions by the Israeli government in the West Bank was "undermining the possibility of a two-state solution" referring to a plan under which two states -- one Israeli and one Palestinian -- would live peacefully side by side.
"The situation is rapidly deteriorating amid unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion," they warned.
The E1 settlement plan -- approved by Israel last year after decades of being frozen, notably due to pressure from successive US administrations -- would see 1,200 housing units built in the West Bank.
It would further isolate Israeli-annexed east Jerusalem from the rest of the occupied territory.
During an address to the UK parliament, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused the Israeli government of turning a "blind eye" to what he called "ethnic cleansing" by the Israeli settlers.
He announced Britain would introduce an "import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories".
"I do not believe the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets," he told the British parliament, flanked by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
"We will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion," he added.
In a statement posted on X, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said France "will end trade" with settlements located in the occupied territories.
Commenting on Britain’s move, America’s ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee told BBC Radio Tuesday: "I feel like it’s discrimination against the Israeli government. It’s a discrimination against the Jewish people."
Milibrand is the son of Jewish immigrant parents.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who leads a far-right party that advocates the annexation of the entire West Bank, called for the expulsion of Britain’s ambassador to Israel.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to continue establishing the illegal settlements despite mounting international pressure, promising a major wave of settler immigration into the West Bank.

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday highlighted expanded medical and rehabilitation services and increased support staffing for Taiwan’s athletes at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, saying the Ministry of Sports (MOS) is "making every effort" to support them.
Speaking at a flag-presentation ceremony at the Taiwan Sports Training Center in Kaohsiung, Lai said the delegation headquarters will be staffed by 53 support personnel this year, up from around 40 in the past, including medical staff, rehabilitation specialists and athletic therapists.
Staffing at the delegation’s support stations -- facilities separate from the headquarters that provide athletes with services such as training, recovery, medical care and meals -- has also increased from around 13 in the past to 42 this year, he said.
Photo: Lee Hui-chou, Taipei Times
The increases show that the MOS is "making every effort to provide the best possible support for our athletes," Lai said.
Set to open on Sept. 19, the 20th Asian Games will see a 740-member Taiwan delegation supported by the MOS, which was established in September 2025 and is headed by inaugural minister Lee Yang (李洋), a two-time Olympic gold medalist in badminton men’s doubles.
Lai also told athletes that he would not set a medal target for the quadrennial Games, Asia’s largest sporting event.
"I won’t set a target for how many gold, silver or bronze medals we should win," he said.
Instead, Lai urged them to focus on their own performances after earning the opportunity to compete on the international stage through years of training.
"This stage belongs to you," he said, adding that if athletes improve on their previous performances, "the country’s overall results will naturally be good."
Competing under the name Chinese Taipei, Taiwan’s 482 athletes will compete in 34 sports at venues across Japan, mostly in Aichi Prefecture and its capital Nagoya, with some events also being held in Tokyo and other parts of the country.
Among the most prominent athletes in the delegation are Olympic boxing gold medalist Lin Yu-ting (林郁婷), Olympic weightlifting gold medalist Kuo Hsing-chun (郭婞淳), Olympic judo silver medalist Yang Yung-wei (楊勇緯), and Olympic gymnastics silver medalist Lee Chih-kai (李智凱).
Taiwan’s best gold-medal haul at a single Asian Games is 19, achieved at both the 1998 Bangkok Asian Games and the 2022 Hangzhou Asian Games.
Taiwan finished sixth in the overall medal standings at both editions.

Semiconductor firms boost hiring, broaden talent search: 104 Job Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:44 UTC
01:41:44 KST

The semiconductor industry posted an average of 47,000 job openings per month this year, an increase of more than 20 percent from a year earlier, online job platform 104 Job Bank said yesterday.
The share of listings open to applicants from all majors also rose by 2-3 percent during the period, the platform said in a talent report.
Hiring demand in the industry is shifting from manufacturing operations toward factory construction support, machinery assembly and yield improvement as artificial intelligence (AI) continues to drive demand for greater production capacity, it said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
The top job categories were production; quality control and occupational hygiene; operations, technical and maintenance work; and research and development, the report said.
Workers capable of transferring technology between plants, sharing expertise and integrating systems will be key to improving the efficiency of capacity expansion, it said.
Companies are also increasingly seeking interdisciplinary talent with expertise in electronics, optics and materials science, making cross-departmental technological integration, communication and collaboration skills increasingly important, the report said.
Meanwhile, AI-related job openings in the industry averaged more than 10,000 per month, accounting for one in four openings and representing a 67 percent increase over the past five years, the platform said.
AI-related openings have increased rapidly since last year, while the skills sought have expanded from research and development to areas including production, equipment, quality control and supply chain management, 104 Job Bank manager Weber Chung (鍾文雄) said.
As geopolitical risks drive the industry to expand overseas, Asian markets excluding China, Hong Kong and Macau remain the main destinations for overseas job postings, the report said.
However, postings in the US and Canada have greatly increased since last year, indicating that while Taiwan’s semiconductor supply chain remains deeply rooted in Asia, companies are expanding their operations into key North American markets, it said.
Job postings in Europe have also increased slightly, while postings in China, Hong Kong and Macau remained low, it added.
The top three positions for overseas assignments are semiconductor engineers, field application engineers and occupational safety management specialists, according to the report.

Saxony-Anhalt election delivers a blow to Merz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:44 UTC
01:41:44 KST

The far-right Alternative for Germany’s (AfD) triumph in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt marks a defeat for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and sends a warning to other European leaders battling the same mixture of slow growth and disillusion with mainstream politics.
AfD, just short of an absolute majority in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament after Sunday’s vote, has become the face of opposition to the consensus-based political system that has governed Germany since World War II.
Thorsten Frei, the parliamentary leader for Merz’s conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), called it “a watershed for our country.”
In an increasingly polarized political system, Merz — whose personal approval ratings have sunk to record lows — was one of the main targets of voter ire over the cost of living, pensions and economic insecurity.
A survey by Infratest dimap for ARD public television found that 87 percent of voters in the state were unhappy with his government. A separate survey for ZDF television found that three-quarters of people, including almost half of CDU supporters, believed Merz had hurt the party’s result.
In his first reported comments on the election outcome, Merz on Monday told the CDU’s executive board that the result had shaken his party “to its very foundations,” but he also again ruled out cooperating with the AfD, according to the Bild newspaper.
The AfD has said it sees victory in Saxony-Anhalt as a first step toward winning federal elections due in 2029, but there was no immediate sign of any internal revolt against Merz in the party committees that met on Monday, CDU sources said.
One member who was present said that discussions had been “open and frank,” but added: “Everybody knows we have to continue with our policy.”
While far-right parties have governed in several European countries, the AfD’s best performance so far in a state election in Germany carries an urgent warning to other nations facing elections in coming months.
In France, where opinion polls suggest the far-right National Rally could win next year’s presidential election, French Minister of Finance Roland Lescure said the outcome of the election in Saxony-Anhalt was a “very, very worrying signal.”
“It shows we face a major challenge from a populist wave that is now global,” Lescure told RTL radio.
Saxony-Anhalt, a largely rural state of about 2.1 million inhabitants in the formerly communist east, is one of the smaller German states, which has lost about one-quarter of its population since Germany reunified in 1990. Sunday’s result can be partly explained by the unhealed divisions between east and west Germany.
And yet over the past 10 to 15 years it has staged a steady recovery from the shock of reunification in 1990, when its industry largely collapsed. Its unemployment rate is not far above the national average at 8 percent, and it has rebuilt its chemicals industry and developed new sectors including logistics and green energy.
However, voters disregarded warnings from business groups and economists, as well as Merz himself, that a vote for the anti-immigrant AfD would put much needed foreign investment at risk and discourage the skilled workers the state sorely needs.
Amid unusually heavy voter turnout, workers, male voters and young people all voted in large numbers for the party.
Under its 35-year-old candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, a TikTok adept who attracted thousands to election rallies and meetings, promising to bring back “our good, old, safe Germany,” the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt brushed off its classification by the domestic security service as “extremist” right-wing.
“The AfD is now a highly visible political force which is far more effective at getting its message across than other parties manage to do,” said Thorsten Faas, a political scientist at Berlin’s Free University. “And this is not set to change in the short term, which poses very significant challenges for the federal government in its attempts to paint a positive picture of the country and its future.”
For Merz, confronted with a deep-seated crisis in Germany’s industrial base and battling to push through pension reforms that have proved particularly unpopular in eastern Germany, there appear to be no easy answers.
Volkswagen AG’s announcement last week of a radical restructuring plan, which could see 50,000 job cuts worldwide and the closure of major factories in Germany, underlined the grim picture facing Europe’s largest economy, struggling to emerge from years of stagnation.
High energy costs, fueled in part by the wars in Ukraine and Iran, offered an easy attack point for the AfD, which found a ready audience for its argument that German support for Kyiv had needlessly antagonized Moscow and driven up oil and gas prices.
Merz came to power last year, pledging tough reforms to revive the economy. He abandoned decades of fiscal caution by promising to borrow hundreds of billions of euros to restore Germany’s withered military and rebuild infrastructure.
However, voters, particularly in eastern Germany, have given him no credit for the plans, which have so far produced few visible results.
By big majorities, voters favored the AfD to address their main concerns around social insecurity, peace in Europe and their own economic situation, the Infratest dimap poll showed.
Before the vote, Eva von Angern, the main candidate of the Left party, expressed some sympathy for Merz, saying: “He’s not responsible for everything.”
However, she added that on the campaign trail, he was “Hate figure No. 1” for voters.
“He’s the reason why people don’t want to vote for the CDU and all the other established parties,” Von Angern said.

Israeli opposition leaders yesterday called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unfit to serve after a report that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) had warned him before the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
Haaretz newspaper, in a report excerpted from a forthcoming book by its reporters, said UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan spoke to Netanyahu a week and a half before the attack and told him that Hamas was planning a major operation.
Netanyahu’s office called the report by the left-leaning newspaper “an absolute lie” and denied he spoke to the Emirati leader at that time.
Photo: AFP
Gadi Eisenkot, a former military commander who has emerged as Netanyahu’s top rival in upcoming Oct. 27 elections, accused the long-serving prime minister of evading responsibility for security lapses and resorting to “pathetic” excuses, such as saying he was not woken up soon enough on the morning of the attack.
“Netanyahu received dozens of warnings for October 7 and ignored them all. He is unfit,” Eisenkot wrote on X.
Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister also running in elections, said Netanyahu “bears personal and direct responsibility” for the deaths on Oct. 7.
“Netanyahu cannot continue to serve in his position for even one more minute,” Bennett said.
Haaretz said that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, later killed by Israel, had warned a former Palestinian official that the militants were preparing “a terrifying operation,” which he described as an “earthquake.”
The former Palestinian official relayed the message to an Emirati adviser, who passed it on to the Emirati leader, who then called Netanyahu, the newspaper said.
The UAE normalized ties with Israel in 2020 as part of the US-brokered Abraham Accords under US President Donald Trump’s first administration.
Netanyahu sees close ties with the UAE as a key achievement.
The newspaper, quoting mostly anonymous sources, said that Netanyahu replied calmly to the warning.
Netanyahu for years had sought to preserve the status quo with Hamas, which would receive funding via Qatar with an understanding the Islamist group was more interested in self-preservation than a devastating war with Israel.
Hamas on Oct. 7 stormed into Israel in a rampaage that included mass killing at a music festival.
The attack killed 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures. The militants also dragged into Gaza 251 hostages, 44 of them already dead.
The massive Israeli offensive in response has left most of Gaza in ruins and killed 73,658 people, according to the Gaza health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Australia’s web of Pacific alliances set to include Solomons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:43 UTC
01:41:43 KST

Australia is in the process of finalizing a treaty with another Pacific island nation, with the national broadcaster reporting that Canberra has struck an “in-principle” agreement with the Solomon Islands.
The two nations will work to sign the deal in the coming weeks, Australian Broadcasting Corp (ABC) reported, citing unidentified government officials.
The news comes after Solomons Prime Minister Matthew Wale saw off a challenge to his leadership from within his Cabinet, with the rival withdrawing over the weekend.
Photo: AFP
Australia has pledged A$980 million (US$706 million) in extra funding for the Solomon Islands’ government, according to a leaked text message from the Australian ambassador that was also reported by the ABC.
Once finalized, the deal would represent a significant diplomatic victory for Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s government. The Solomon Islands shot to geopolitical prominence in 2022 when then-prime minister Manasseh Sogavare signed a security pact with China, provoking alarm in Canberra and Washington.
Albanese was first elected prime minister just weeks after the Solomons-China agreement was revealed, and has worked over the past four years to reverse that deal and rebuild ties with the archipelago nation.
Since Wale came to power in May, he has shifted his government’s diplomatic focus back to Australia and the US, breaking with previous administrations’ tilt toward Beijing.
Wale’s first overseas trip was to Canberra in June, with Albanese then reciprocating in July, when he traveled to Honiara and announced the start of the negotiations for the treaty. That meeting came a day after Albanese signed two new deals with Fiji, including a military alliance, which New Zealand has also expressed an interest in joining.
Those talks are all part of a web of security and policing agreements that Australia has established with nations including Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu, Nauru, Indonesia and others as it seeks to limit Chinese influence in the region.
Canberra is also strengthening security ties with Japan, including plans to purchase Japanese-made naval vessels.
China’s test of a submarine-launched nuclear-capable ballistic missile in the Pacific region in early July also focused regional leaders’ attention on the risks of growing US-China strategic competition. Australia, Palau, New Zealand and others immediately condemned the test.
While Pacific nations were initially unable to agree on a joint response to China’s move, at the Pacific Islands Forum last week in Palau, all but one of the 18 member nations signed onto a statement calling out the firing of the missile and demanding proper advance notification and transparency.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:42 UTC

More than 80 percent of residents of Kaohsiung’s Linyuan (林園) and Daliao (大寮) districts did not know about a pending naphtha cracker expansion project in the region, a Greenpeace Taiwan poll released on Monday showed.
State-run CPC Corp, Taiwan launched the NT$106.2 billion (US$3.37 billion) project to replace the aging unit with a newly built naphtha cracker in Linyuan District.
However, environmental advocates said that describing the project as a replacement plan obscures that the new cracker would upgrade annual ethylene production capacity to 1 million tonnes from 350,000 tonnes.
Photo: Taipei Times
The poll showed that 90.3 percent of Kaohsiung residents were unaware of the project, while 82.9 percent of Linyuan residents and residents of neighboring Daliao did not know about it.
Asked whether they backed the project, 41.4 percent of respondents said yes, 25.8 percent objected and 32.7 percent had no opinion, it showed.
After respondents were given information about international plastic-reduction trends, petrochemical-industry air pollution and health risks associated with microplastics, 36.3 percent supported the plans, 47.6 percent objected and 15.9 percent had no opinion, it showed.
The poll showed 87.2 percent agreed that the project “requires a more prudent evaluation.”
Tseng Yi-ting (曾意婷), Greenpeace Taiwan’s director of public engagement and development, said that the project was approved by the Executive Yuan in May 2024 and is in the basic-design tendering stage.
However, there are shortcomings in the information-sharing of the government and CPC, as the poll results show, Tseng said.
Instead of this project, the government should invest resources in industrial transition and value-added upgrades, particularly as the domestic petrochemical industry is facing global overcapacity and shifting demand, she said.
Lee Chin-tsung (李進宗), a former Linyuan District borough warden, said that the communication of the central government to local residents might have been insufficient.
Lee said that he approves of replacing old equipment at the plant, but opposes increasing its production capacity.
CPC yesterday said that the new naphtha cracker is still being planned and undergoing environmental impact assessments.
More accessible explanations would be provided in terms of air pollution, health risks, carbon emissions, industrial necessity and the decommissioning of the more than 40-year-old naphtha cracker, it said.
The project aims to rebuild Taiwan’s essential raw material supply capacity with enhanced safety and reduced emissions, CPC said.
Production capacity is not equivalent to production amount, nor are plastics equivalent to pollution, it said.
The Kaohsiung City Government later on Monday said it has asked CPC to incorporate advanced green equipment into the project and propose a comprehensive carbon reduction plan.
Operations at the old cracker would be suspended once trial operations at the new plant begin, it said, adding that it would tighten pollution controls in line with its net zero targets.

Australia proposes ‘opt out’ legislation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

Australia has proposed legislation that would allow social media users to opt out of platforms’ algorithms, a potentially far-reaching step that deepens regulatory efforts worldwide to rein in Big Tech and limit online harm.
Under the Labor government’s draft Digital Duty of Care bill released yesterday, social media users would be able to block content suggested by algorithms, and instead choose the material they want in their feeds.
The proposal opens up a new domestic battleground with Instagram and Facebook-owner Meta Platforms Inc, TikTok and other platform operators. The country’s world-first social media ban for under-16s — which went into effect late last year — was quickly followed by governments around the world adopting similar restrictions.
Photo: EPA
Meta declined to comment on Australia’s proposal, while representatives for TikTok and Snap Inc did not immediately reply to e-mails.
Regulators are increasingly targeting what they perceive as the addictive design of the platforms. Last month, Meta agreed to pay up to US$18 billion in landmark settlements to resolve social media claims from US states.
Key parts of that deal require the company to put new guardrails on its platforms, including restricting how much time young people can scroll and preventing them from switching off certain safety settings without parental consent.
“There’s been some seismic cases in the past few weeks,” Australian Minister for Communications Anika Wells said at a press conference yesterday.
“This is our contribution,” she said.
The duty-of-care approach aims to force technology companies to make their products safe by design, imposing fresh burdens on the operating models of major platforms. Breaches of Australia’s proposed law could be penalized by up to A$109.2 million (US$79 million), the government said.
The EU has been investigating claims that Meta’s products are addictive to children, as the bloc increases regulatory pressure on the US social media company.
While details on implementation are still unclear and will be critical in assessing the potential impact, Australia’s move appears to be “a continuation of a trend rather than a completely novel innovation,” said Ewan Lusty, a Singapore-based partner at political and regulatory consultancy Flint Global.
“There is a global shift toward governments seeking to empower users and provide them with more control over how they interact with digital services, including the option to restrict personalization elements,” he said. “Digital services are also taking important steps and providing users with more granular controls over their experience.”
Australia’s draft legislation requires platform owners to send a notification to new and existing users offering them a choice over their default feed.
Other features of the Digital Duty of Care include: Digital services like online games, apps and AI chatbots would be required to protect under-18s from design features that have negative behavioral impacts, such as addictive features or those that can have an effect on a young person’s self-esteem
Such services will also be required to protect under-18s from: content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; content that promotes hostile ideas about women and gender equality; pornography; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that causes serious mental distress, including abuse and bullying

Too many options obscuring languages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

As the new school year begins, the number of students choosing Taiwan Sign Language (TSL) for their local-language classes has continued to rise. In some schools, more than 40 percent of students have reportedly chosen TSL. In elementary schools, students can choose to study other languages such as Vietnamese and Indonesian. The overall proportion of students choosing these languages remains low, but the growing number of options might risk obscuring the purpose of local-language education all in the name of respecting diversity.
Local-language classes are distinct from general language courses; they are intended to revitalize the languages of Taiwan that declined as a result of the Mandarin-only language policy implemented by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) regime. The current system seems to have lost sight of that goal.
Taiwan is linguistically diverse, but its languages have different roles and functions. Taiwanese served as a lingua franca across ethnic groups and regions, while Hakka and indigenous languages are associated with particular communities and geographic areas. They should not all be treated under the same system.
Today, sign language and the heritage languages of immigrant families have been placed in the same pool of language electives as local languages, from which students can choose. Does this really serve the revitalization of Taiwan’s local languages, or is it just creating a language buffet under the thinking that more options equals more progress?
Sign language and the languages spoken at home for children from immigrant families should be protected, but this should be planned independently and according to their respective communication needs and educational objectives.
More students are choosing to study sign language not out of a practical need, which is not the point of local language revitalization. The Southeast Asian languages offered as options are already official languages of their respective countries; they are not endangered, nor are they languages of Taiwan.
The need to offer them should be assessed in light of Taiwan’s broader needs and they should be incorporated as part of a foreign-language education distinct from local-language classes.
Local-language education originally sought to restore Taiwan’s multilingual environment, but the dominance of Mandarin remains unchanged. Those languages whose place in the education system is being “diversified” are precisely those that are most vulnerable.
Given that these languages are the only ones designated as “local,” would the Ministry of Education be willing to acknowledge Mandarin Chinese to be a foreign language? Or to answer why a foreign language enjoys such an advantage in teaching hours and assessment?
Taiwan’s language education system is in need of a comprehensive review.
Languages should be classified according to their status, geographic use and revitalization needs as common languages, regional languages, foreign languages or second foreign languages, with curricula then designed accordingly.
Otherwise, we might end up with an increasingly rich list of language choices, but with the Taiwanese languages in genuine need of being passed on disappearing even more rapidly under a system of “diversification.”
Khoo Hui-lu is a professor and chair of the Department of Taiwan Culture, Languages and Literature at National Taiwan Normal University.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader

It all comes back to Taiwan’s giant geopolitical issue: the multitude of countries cutting diplomatic ties with Taiwan

Ukraine’s new Hryfon Zakhid runs the whole drone chain on one screen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

Ukraine's Operational Command West has built an app that lets a single operator route drone strikes from a phone or tablet, in real time and without radio. The system, called Hryfon Zakhid, speeds the flow of tasks to drone crews and helps hide their positions from Russian reconnaissance, soldiers at the command's training center told Suspilne Rivne.
Drone war is won on the speed of the kill chain — the minutes between spotting a target and hitting it. The system compresses the decision and covers Ukrainian troops from Russian electronic reconnaissance. Hryfon Zakhid is a regional take on the digitization that Ukraine has pushed nationally with systems like DELTA, which has shortened the path from detection to strike from roughly 20 minutes to a few.
One operator runs the whole chain
The app replaces the manual scramble of calling crews up one by one.
"It is a very mobile program, and it speeds up decision-making," said Volodymyr Shvediuk, commander of the Operational Command West troops.
The military can share it with everyone who wants it — air-assault troops, marines, and army corps.
"You do not have to tell anyone, 'Petro, Vasyl, get ready.' One operator controls everything," he explained.
The program runs on a smartphone, tablet, or computer, and works in real time without radio, according to a training-platoon commander with the callsign Vegas.
The board turns recon into strikes
A soldier with the callsign Wolf described the system's workflow.
"A task comes to me from reconnaissance, and we send it to the striker's board. A target appears, and I choose the crew in the zone to work it," he said.
Then he chose which drone would carry out the strike and sent it.
"The board shows everything — where to fly, what to hit, and it even adds photos if we do not know which window to fly into," the Wolf adds.

Leaked docs allege a wide pattern of Chinese bribery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:40 UTC
01:41:40 KST

A national security official said yesterday that allegedly leaked Chinese documents indicated Beijing put a price on efforts to block Taiwan from the World Health Assembly (WHA).
National Security Council adviser Alex Huang (黃重諺) made the remarks in an interview with the Chinese-language Liberty Times (sister paper to the Taipei Times) when asked about suspected Chinese diplomatic documents leaked online that allegedly shows Beijing offered Micronesia 1 million yuan (US$149,002) to cover the cost of purchasing a vehicle in exchange for the Pacific island nation blocking Taiwan’s participation in the WHA.
The leaked documents allege to show a diplomatic note from the Chinese embassy in Micronesia in March asking the island nation to sign a letter supporting Beijing’s stance on Taiwan at the WHA. On April 8, Micronesia reportedly wrote to WHO Secretary-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, asking that Taiwan-related issues not be discussed. The WHA subsequently rejected Taiwan’s proposal in May. On June 10, China sent a 1 million yuan “grant” to Micronesia for the ostensible use of purchasing a vehicle for official receptions, and Micronesia replied on June 23 accepting the funding.
Photo: Reuters
The documents also show the African Union accepted a 200 million yuan “renovation grant” from China in April, then sought an additional US$50 million to build a new headquarters and recreation center.
Following Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs Wang Yi’s (王毅) visit to Africa earlier this year, Taiwan faced a number of complications, including the withdrawal of flight clearance for President William Lai’s (賴清德) chartered aircraft in April, Kenya blocking of Taiwan’s participation in a UN ocean conference in June, Morocco suspending visa issuance in July, and Uganda withholding passports last month.
Huang said in the interview that the allegedly leaked documents closely match intelligence held by Taiwan in terms of the officials’ titles, narrative and timeline, adding that they could “to some extent be considered highly credible.”
He said the documents focus on two major sets of activities. One involves Beijing’s efforts to rally Pacific island nations to sign a joint letter to the WHO calling for Taiwan to be excluded and for Taiwan-related issues not to be discussed. The arrangements appear to be “almost something that can be priced,” Huang said, with the number of signatories on the letter roughly corresponding to how much money would need to be spent.
The other set of allegedly leaked documents focuses on the African Union.
Huang said that “some of what we saw came as a shock.”
Lai was scheduled to visit Taiwan’s diplomatic ally Eswatini on April 22, but the trip was canceled after three African Union member states along the planned flight route withdrew overflight clearance. On the same day the Presidential Office announced the cancelation, the African Union wrote to China requesting another round of funding.
Huang said the strikingly coincidental timing reveals the pattern of Beijing’s operations.
China’s efforts to pressure Taiwan have never stopped, with Beijing constantly adopting new tactics, Huang said.
Stressing that friendships bought with money would not stand the test of time, Huang said that once recipient countries fall into Beijing’s trap and their overall national strength comes under its influence, China gains greater control over international resources that can be used to pressure other countries.
Huang said that China does not have unlimited resources to sustain an endless campaign of dollar diplomacy.
Moreover, if Beijing no longer respects the international order, he asked, “How can other countries expect [China] to honor its commitments to them?”

New Chinese sub missiles could hit the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:39 UTC
01:41:39 KST

Refits to Chinese nuclear submarines to carry JL-3 intercontinental ballistic missiles would put much of the US in striking distance, Taiwanese defense analysts said in a report commissioned by the Mainland Affairs Council.
Researchers from National Defense University’s Graduate Institute of China Military Affairs Studies said that the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) in July test-fired a missile with a training warhead.
Chinese state media reported without elaborating that a PLAN nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN) launched a missile with a training warhead, which accurately hit the designated target area in the Pacific, the report said.
Photo: AFP
The launch was a rare display of the PLAN’s nuclear might, despite the taciturn announcement from Beijing, it said.
Taiwan and the US tracked the ballistic missile’s trajectory during its descent and concluded that the weapon, a JL-2 intercontinental ballistic missile, splashed down in international waters near Nauru in the southern Pacific, the report said.
Several Pacific nations have protested China’s missile test, as the warhead fell close to their exclusive economic zones, it said.
Citing Ministry of National Defense officials and military officers’ remarks at a Legislative Yuan meeting, the report said Taiwan was able to confirm that the Chinese SSBN launched the missile from the surface and not underwater.
The launch, which was tracked jointly by the Taiwanese and US intelligence organs, took place in the waters off southern Guangdong, they added.
The JL-2, a sub-launched missile with an effective range of about 6,000km to 7,000km, is widely used in the PLAN’s SSBN fleet, the report said.
Chinese state-affiliated media withheld almost all technical information about the launch, declining to identify the submarine or missile involved, its location at the time of launch, or the coordinates of the target, it said.
The vagueness of Beijing’s release about the live-fire test was intended to strengthen its deterrence posture without giving away information about its capabilities, it said.
The report said that the PLAN is refitting its Type-094 SSBNs to carry the newer JL-3 ballistic missiles.
US Strategic Command former commander Anthony Cotton testified in the US Congress that Beijing is treating the JL-3 retrofit, with the missile’s 10,000km range, as a top priority, the report said.
A PLAN SSBN equipped with JL-3s would be able to launch nuclear strikes at most of the continental US from the relative safety of China’s littoral waters, it said, a feat the JL-2 cannot replicate.
Taiwanese intelligence analysis indicated that the launch’s purpose was to certify the submarine’s capability to deploy the JL-2, not to unveil a new capability to the world, it said.
This could indicate that the PLAN has not yet fully certified the use of JL-3, suggesting that it is not deemed a fully operational weapon, the report said.
The PLAN continues improvement of the seaborne leg of its nuclear triad, including construction of next-generation vessels, developing improved missiles and holding its established patrol perimeters, it said.
The Chinese SSBN fired the test missile from the northern part of the South China Sea, which is consistent with the PLAN’s established pattern of deploying SSBN patrols out of the Hainan naval base.
The PLAN test launch has ramifications for regional security, highlighting inadequacy in US-China communication mechanisms regarding nuclear weapon tests, it said.
Washington and its NATO allies have formally acknowledged that the lack of communication channels are a risk that could lead to dangerous misunderstandings, the report said.
In addition, Pacific nations and neighbors were alarmed by the southern drift of the PLAN’s missile tests, which crossed the boundaries of the region’s nuclear-test free area, it said.
Taipei should carefully monitor the changes in Beijing’s relationship with Pacific nations, the report said.

Taisun files suit over cooking oil case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:39 UTC
01:41:39 KST

Taisun Enterprise Co (泰山企業) yesterday filed a lawsuit against Central Union Oil Corp (中聯油脂) and three other companies, seeking NT$1 billion (US$31.71 million) in joint compensation over a food safety scandal involving Central Union-produced oil with excessive levels of the carcinogen benzo[a]pyrene (BaP).
The Taichung District Prosecutors’ Office on Aug. 18 indicted Central Union Oil, Taisun, Fwusow Industry Co (福壽實業) and Formosa Oilseed Processing Co (福懋油脂), as well as individuals, with the charges ranging from contraventions of the Act Governing Food Safety and Sanitation (食品安全衛生管理法) to forgery and fraud related to alleged distribution of tainted cooking oil.
The key issue to determine responsibility is when the information about abnormal BaP levels emerged and whether it was promptly passed on, Taisun lawyer Chen Cheng-hsi (陳政熙) said.
Photo courtesy of Taisun Enterprise Co
Namchow Oil and Fat Co (南僑油脂事業股份) received three test reports on May 13, May 22 and June 4 showing excessive BaP levels, but only privately notified Fwusow, Chen said, adding that neither company fulfilled its obligation to promptly report the findings to authorities.
Fwusow also failed to promptly notify authorities after learning of abnormal test results on May 18, he added.
Comparing the information in the indictment with Namchow’s public statements shows significant differences in when the companies obtained information, how much they knew and how they responded, he said.
The firms’ failure to report the problem meant the tainted oil was not identified and taken off shelves for two months, the lawyer said.
Companies, including Taisun, continued to use the oil without knowing there was a problem, later leading to major losses from product recalls, inventory disposal, consumer compensation, reduced profits and damage to their reputations, he said, adding that Taisun’s losses were about NT$1 billion.
Taisun initially believed that as long as a product bearing its name was on the market, it had a responsibility to consumers, Taisun marketing vice president Niu An-tse (鈕安澤) said.
However, while handling consumer complaints and during the confidential investigation, the firm did not know when other companies had discovered problems in their supply chains, Niu said.
After the indictment was released, Taisun compared it with statements from Fwusow and other companies and news reports, as well as its own test results from April and May, and filed a lawsuit against the companies to clarify responsibility, she said.
Taisun received the same Central Union Oil soybean oil as Namchow on April 8 and 9, had its own products tested by Switzerland-based SGS on April 10 and received passing results on April 21, giving it no reason to believe its products were unsafe, the company said.
If Namchow had disclosed the abnormal test results when they were first detected in the middle of May, Central Union Oil and other companies in the supply chain could have begun tracing the source, conducting additional tests and managing the risks, it said.
Mid-May to mid-June was a crucial period for containing the problem, but the delayed sharing of information postponed supply-chain tracing and risk controls, worsening the company’s loses, Taisun added.
The courts should determine the responsibility of Central Union Oil, Fwusow, Namchow and Formosa Oilseed based on when they learned of the problem and how promptly they reported it, Taisun said.
