Taiwan’s hiring outlook improves in Q4, poll shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

Taiwan’s hiring outlook for the fourth quarter of this year improved with the information sector reporting the strongest hiring prospects during the current artificial intelligence (AI) boom, a survey released yesterday by human resources advisory firm ManpowerGroup Inc showed.
Thirty-seven percent of 651 employers polled in Taiwan said they expected to hire more people in the fourth quarter, while 10 percent said they anticipated a decline in hiring and 52 percent said their hiring plans remain unchanged, the survey showed.
That translated to a fourth-quarter net employment outlook index of 27 percent before seasonal adjustments, and 26 percent after seasonal adjustments, ManpowerGroup said.
Photo courtesy of National Taiwan Normal University via CNA
The figure was up from 17 percent in the third quarter and 16 percent a year earlier, which the advisory firm said showed signs of improvement in hiring outlook.
Among major business sectors, the information sector had the highest hiring outlook for the fourth quarter with a net employment outlook of 42 percent, up 23 percentage points from the previous quarter.
Employers in the sector demonstrated a strong willingness to hire in a wide range of positions such as in development and operations, AI application development, communication systems and cybersecurity to meet demand for AI and digital transformation, ManpowerGroup Taiwan general manager Sandy Chang (張淑君) said.
The construction and real-estate sector was second with a net employment outlook of 41 percent, up sharply from 5 percent in the third quarter, the survey found.
The hiring outlook in the sector significantly improved as AI developers and high-end semiconductor suppliers seek to expand production, accelerating the pace of construction of new offices and plants, Chang said.
The trade and logistics sector reported the third highest net hiring outlook at 35 percent, up 19 percentage points from a quarter earlier.
Employers in the sector largely aimed to expand their talent pools to meet online business needs and enhance automation in logistics, Chang said.
Of the 11 Asia-Pacific economies in the ManpowerGroup survey, India had the highest net hiring outlook for the fourth quarter at 54 percent, ahead of the United Arab Emirates at 41 percent and Vietnam at 36 percent, the advisory firm said.
Taiwan was seventh at 26 percent, while Japan was at the bottom at 7 percent, it said.
All of the 42 economies surveyed reported positive hiring outlooks in the fourth quarter, while Taiwan’s score was slightly below the global average of 29 percent in the quarter, the survey found.

Taiwan students score among world’s best in 2025 PISA assessment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:40:58 UTC
01:40:58 KST

Taiwan’s 15-year-old students ranked fourth in the world in science and mathematics and achieved a record-high third place in reading literacy in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), the Ministry of Education and National Taiwan Normal University (NTNU) announced yesterday.
The results showed that Taiwan maintained its strong performance from the 2022 assessment despite a broader global decline in student achievement following the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the ministry and NTNU, which jointly released Taiwan’s PISA 2025 report Tuesday evening to coincide with the global release of the results.
PISA, organized by the Organisation for Economic Co- operation and Development (OECD), evaluates the knowledge and skills of 15-year-old students needed to participate effectively in society.
Photo: Yang Mien-chieh, Taipei Times
The 2025 assessment focused primarily on science, with reading and mathematics as secondary domains.
More than 760,000 15-year-old students from 91 countries and economic entities participated in the PISA 2025 study.
According to the report, Taiwanese students scored 540 points in science, maintaining the country’s fourth-place global ranking while matching its best-ever score in the subject, first achieved in 2022.
In reading literacy, Taiwan scored 508 points, improving from fifth place in 2022 to a record-high third.
Taiwan ranked fourth in mathematics with 546 points, slipping one place from third in the previous assessment.
In computational problem solving, which was included in the assessment for the first time, Taiwanese students ranked fifth, with a score of 551.
Tsai Chin-chung (蔡今中), chair professor of NTNU’s Program of Learning Sciences and Taiwan’s PISA project director, said he was surprised that student performance continued to decline globally after the pandemic, having expected scores to rebound from the previous assessment.
Among the 23 OECD countries that participated in both the 2022 and 2025 assessments, average science scores fell by five points, reading by 16 points and mathematics by 11 points, according to the report.
By comparison, Taiwan, Singapore and China showed greater resilience, with Taiwan’s science score rising by two points from 2022, while its reading and mathematics scores fell by seven and one point, respectively, outperforming the average trend among the 23 OECD participants.
Tsai said Taiwan’s ability to remain among the world’s top-performing education systems despite global declines demonstrates the resilience of its education system in the face of various challenges.
PISA has historically been conducted every three years by the OECD to assess students’ proficiency in science, reading and mathematics across participating countries and economies, but will transition to a four-year assessment cycle after the 2025 round.

Man faces murder charge over hit-and-run
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:40:57 UTC
01:40:57 KST

A man turned himself in to police in Taichung yesterday after allegedly hitting a woman with his car, making a U-turn and striking her again, before fleeing the scene, local authorities said.
The woman, a nurse, died.
The man, surnamed Lin (林), was handed over to prosecutors on homicide and hit-and-run charges, with recommendations that he be detained, the Taichung Police Bureau’s First Precinct said.
Photo copied by Chen Chien-chih, Taipei Times
The precinct said that it received a report of the incident at 1:10am.
The woman, surnamed Chen (陳), was taken to a hospital, where efforts to resuscitate her were unsuccessful and she was pronounced dead, police said.
Lin allegedly struck Chen as she was crossing at a crosswalk and did not stop, but instead made a U-turn and struck her again before driving off, police said.
Lin appeared disoriented when taken into custody, prompting police to conduct a breath alcohol test and a saliva drug test, they said.
He tested negative for alcohol and drugs, they said.
Police said they were questioning Lin to determine a motive for allegedly striking Chen a second time.
Prosecutors later asked the Taichung District Court to detain him, and prohibit communication and visits.
Lawyer Liu Chien-chih (劉建志), who is not involved in the case, said that a fatal traffic incident caused by negligence would ordinarily fall under negligent homicide, which carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison.
However, a deliberate second collision could amount to murder if homicidal intent and causation are established in court, Liu said, adding that the charge carries a sentence of death, life imprisonment or imprisonment of at least 10 years.
The victim’s family could also seek compensation, meaning the offender might not necessarily end up paying less if a vehicle-collision victim is dead, as some people believe, he said.

Taiwan telescope parts set to arrive in Mexico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:40:55 UTC
01:40:55 KST

The Trans-Pacific Two-Meter Telescope’s (TP2m) body and its first multicolor imaging system have been completed, and are scheduled to arrive in Mexico this month, while work on its control system is continuing, TP2m project leader Chen Wen-ping (陳文屏) said at the weekend.
The TP2m project — a public crowdfunding campaign for an astronomy initiative, which aims to raise NT$30 million (US$951,324) — would enable near-continuous tracking of changes in the universe across time zones by forming a trans-Pacific observation network with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile and NCU’s Lulin Observatory, said Chen, a professor in National Central University’s (NCU) Graduate Institute of Astronomy.
After the Rubin Observatory detects a newly appearing object or one that suddenly brightens, TP2m in Mexico would track it before observations are handed off to Lulin Observatory in Taiwan, creating a trans-Pacific relay system, Chen said.
Photo courtesy of National Central University professor Chen Wen-ping
While some astronomical events last only a few hours, under the planned allocation, 55 percent of observing time would be reserved for NCU and Taiwanese researchers, while Mexican and other international collaborators would share 45 percent, he said.
The TP2m has a 2m aperture and a light-collecting area about four times larger than that of the 1m telescope currently in use, he said.
The new telescope is expected to support observations of major astronomical phenomena, including gravitational-wave counterparts and supernovae, he said.
Participating institutions include NCU, Academia Sinica’s Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics, and the National Autonomous University of Mexico, with the San Pedro Martir Observatory the host observatory.
The telescope, which was initially funded from part of a NT$50 billion Ministry of Education plan more than a decade ago, was originally planned for installation at Lulin Observatory, but the project stalled due to environmental impact assessment issues, technical challenges and unsuccessful bidding processes, Chen said.
The telescope was later considered for deployment in Chile, but the COVID-19 pandemic prevented local partners from completing the required infrastructure, forcing the plan to be abandoned, he said.
Dry weather, a high proportion of clear nights and stable atmospheric conditions, as well as well-developed infrastructure — including water, electricity, Internet access, accommodation and transportation — in Mexico were considered good conditions for setting up the telescope, he said.
After more than three years of negotiations with the National Autonomous University of Mexico, the new site was finalized, he said.
The telescope was returned to its manufacturer for hardware and software upgrades, as well as the installation of a new focal platform, he added.
The project has encountered many unforeseen difficulties over the years, and the team has continued searching for ways to complete a project that has been nearly 20 years in the making, he said when asked about the need for crowdfunding.
“This is not just a research project or a piece of equipment — it is educational infrastructure,” Chen said, adding that Taiwan should also possess uninterrupted day-and-night observing capabilities.
Europe, the US and Japan all place major astronomical facilities at favorable sites around the world, while South Korea, China and Thailand are also expanding their global observation networks, he said.
Taiwanese researchers and students need access to advanced facilities to participate in international observation programs and help cultivate the next generation of astronomers, he added.
The fundraising campaign marks the first time a Taiwanese astronomy project has used a crowdfunding platform to solicit small donations from the public, he said.
The team hopes collective support would help complete the final stage of the project and allow the long-awaited telescope to achieve “first light” after nearly two decades of development, he added.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine’s anti-corruption bureau just took down a prosecutor general. That’s not the crisis—it’s the point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:40:54 UTC
01:40:54 KST

Ukraine's Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko resigned on 7 September, hours after publicly defending himself, as anti-corruption investigators closed in on an alleged criminal organization operating inside his own office.
"I do not want the position of prosecutor general to be used as an instrument of political confrontation," Kravchenko said, announcing his departure on Telegram. "My position regarding the charges remains unchanged"—a denial he has held throughout, including in a 6 September statement rejecting any role in protecting the call centers.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the resignation on the evening of 7 September. "I had a fairly long meeting with the prosecutor general; he submitted the relevant resignation letter, and the submission will be sent to the Verkhovna Rada," Zelenskyy said, adding that he had spent the day on personnel matters and had also met the heads of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO). The resignation is not final until parliament acts on it.
It reads as a scandal. It is closer to the opposite.
Kravchenko was appointed in June 2025, as the anti-corruption agencies were pressing toward figures close to the president—and his appointment came alongside the draft law, No. 12414, that would have put NABU and SAPO under his control. That law triggered the first street protests since Russia's invasion; within ten days, parliament reversed the part stripping the agencies' independence.
The provisions handing Kravchenko a personnel monopoly over the prosecution service were never repealed.
Since then, those agencies have forced out Andriy Yermak, the second-most-powerful man in the country. Now they have reached the prosecutor general—whose office kept, even after the capture law was reversed, a personnel monopoly over the prosecution service.
The corruption is not new. What is new is that it is being caught, and that being caught now costs the powerful their offices. The story of the past year is not that Ukraine is coming apart, but that its watchdogs have stopped being toothless.
What Operation Carthage found
On 5 September, NABU and SAPO announced they had uncovered a criminal organization run, investigators say, by a department head inside the Prosecutor General's Office. Its members allegedly took regular bribes from fraudulent call centers—operations that defraud victims in Ukraine and abroad—in exchange for shielding them from prosecution, then laundered the money through property, assets registered to other people, and associates' bank accounts.
The group was formed in mid-2025 and recruited serving prosecutors and associates, NABU and SAPO said. Over 20 million hryvnias (about $449,000) went on property, jewelry, and other high-value assets, according to NABU.
NABU described the organization as run by the head of a department inside the Prosecutor General's Office. Sources told Ukrainska Pravda that the official is Serhii Kropyva, deputy head of the office's International Legal Cooperation Department. He was remanded in custody on 6 September with bail set at 120 million hryvnias (about $2.7 million).
In recordings released by NABU, a figure using the codename "Chancellor," reported to be Kropyva, is described as protected by a "boss." Two details identify that boss: the patronymic "Andriiovych," and a previous job leading the State Tax Service. Ruslan Andriiovych Kravchenko ran the State Tax Service from December 2024 until he became prosecutor general in June 2025. The investigation understands the "boss" to be Kravchenko, the Kyiv Independent reported.
NABU has not publicly named Kravchenko as a suspect. He denies instructing anyone to protect illegal call centers or using his office to shield them. He resigned nonetheless.
Ukraine’s anti-corruption agencies target Prosecutor General’s Office official linked to fraudulent call centers
The searches, and the surveillance files
NABU searches also reached the offices of Kravchenko himself, his deputy Mariia Vdovychenko, and the head of the Odesa Regional Military Administration, Oleh Kiper. Kravchenko defended the handling of those searches at a 7 September press conference—the same day he resigned.
The investigation into the Prosecutor General's Office is the latest in a widening confrontation between Ukraine's anti-corruption bodies and the institutions around the presidency. When NABU announced the case, it described a senior official running a criminal ring from inside the office meant to prosecute exactly such crimes.
Why it matters
The Prosecutor General's Office is one of the institutions Kyiv relies on to supervise—and, critics say, to restrain—NABU's investigations into figures close to the president. That an investigation reached the prosecutor general himself is a measure of how far the anti-corruption bodies have pushed against that restraint, not a sign they have failed.
It caps a run of accountability cases since July 2025 that would have been unthinkable earlier in the war.
In June 2025, NABU charged Deputy Prime Minister Oleksiy Chernyshov—the only official at Zelenskyy's private birthday during lockdown—with a $24 million land scheme, the first case to reach the president's "family."
The attempt to capture the agencies came weeks later, and failed: in November, Operation Midas exposed a $100 million scheme that forced out Zelenskyy's chief of staff and two ministers, one of them later detained at the border. Other resonant cases include Operation Forest Gump, targeting officials inside the President's Office. Now Carthage has reached the prosecutor general himself.
The pattern that looks like a government in crisis is also a state where stealing at the top is no longer safe—and where the public has twice in a year come into the streets over how power is used: in July 2025 to defend NABU and SAPO, and in July 2026 for a sacked minister.
Kravchenko took office in June 2025. He is the second prosecutor general to leave under a cloud in three years, after Andriy Kostin.

The surprising ways to help save your brain from the cognitive cliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:40:53 UTC
01:40:53 KST

The Guardian: You write that instead of fearing cognitive decline, “changing the way you think about the brain cliff can literally change the way you think and remember.” How?
Norman Swan: There are three things you need to know which are not widely known.
Think cognitive change not cognitive decline: one way people think about our cognitive function is by comparing it to what it was like when we were in our 20s and it’s not a valid comparison. It leads to an assumption that we’ve declined into deficit. That’s not actually what’s happened, especially when we’re in midlife (40s and 50s).
Photo: AP
Our brains have changed, not deteriorated. Focusing on what that “change” looks like can make the task of maintaining cognitive function and perhaps even improving it, much clearer. Sure, our fluid intelligence — which is about speed and problem-solving — peaks in our 20s, but unless you’re a maths whiz or a gun lab researcher, that is less important than what’s called your crystallized intelligence, which can actually improve with age. It’s the wisdom of knowledge and experience.
Secondly, as the years pass, our thoughts move address.
This is about a phenomenon in the brain called scaffolding. To protect our cognitive abilities and perhaps even enhance them as the years pass, our brains build out networks of nerves which act pretty much like the scaffolding inside a skyscraper. It’s the infrastructure around which the brain works. The more successfully we scaffold, the further away we push the brain cliff. This scaffolding initially moves across the brain then into the frontal lobes — the all-important prefrontal cortex which brings our thoughts and memories together and is involved with judgment, decision-making and emotional control.
The third idea is that we should do as much as possible to encourage the scaffolding and as little as possible to get in its way.
For The Brain Cliff I interviewed seven cognitive super-agers, who are as different as you could imagine — from the illiterate 95-year-old shoemaker to the woman who taught Mick Jagger statistics and the 94-year-old woman who still works in McDonald’s in Kyushu, Japan. But underneath, they’re remarkably similar and they’re all protecting their scaffolding in several ways.
One example is how they respond to stress. They get over it. They problem-solve. They don’t ruminate. And where do you think we ruminate? Yes, in our prefrontal cortex. So you’re occupying valuable brain space for cognitive function with unproductive circular thoughts. As we move through life, the prefrontal cortex becomes more and more important and anything that distracts or damages it potentially brings the brain cliff closer. Depression affects the prefrontal cortex. Alcohol does too.
TG: You mention that the time to start helping our brains adapt is in our 40s and 50s. What should you be doing at that age and is it ever too late to start?
NS: It’s never too late to start.
Exercise enhances our brain plasticity, which in turn encourages brain scaffolding. An anti-inflammatory diet — with low amounts of red meat, high diversity of vegetables including leafy greens, fermented foods such as yogurt and fruits such as berries — can change the microbiome and aid direct absorption of bioactive compounds, both of which support brain scaffolding.
What’s also thought to be part of scaffold building is what’s called the default mode network — what our brain gets up to when it’s supposedly at rest. When the default mode network fires up, parts of the brain that don’t normally talk to each other make connections. How do you know if your default network is at work? Your mind wanders. Mind wandering looks as though it’s good for your brain.
An associated activity is mental time travel: reliving the past, being well anchored in the present and imagining the future. When you’re in midlife you’re in a good place when it comes to mental time travel. When you’re young, there’s not much past; when you’re much older, the past tends to dominate. Mental time travel and mind wandering seem to encourage our scaffolding.
TG: What was the thing about cognitive super-agers which most surprised you, having interviewed so many of them?
NS: One of the important findings from research has been that genes don’t play a large role in whether we’re on a journey to the brain cliff or when we might reach it. That means the environment and how we live matter hugely and that’s what the cognitive super-agers I interviewed illustrated.
There was only one of them where you could convince yourself that his family history mattered, and even he — a neuropsychiatrist from New Jersey aged 100 — was doing the things that maintain your brain. He had learned a new skill — pencil drawing — and through the classes had made new friends and was well connected with other people beyond his family.
TG: What have you changed in your own life or daily habits since going on this deep dive into cognitive decline?
NS: I’ve become much more aware of when I might be ruminating and how I respond to stress. I work hard at problem solving and “getting over it.” I’ve really cut back my alcohol intake — not that it was ever high. I’m much more assiduous about my coronary risk factors like cholesterol and blood pressure. Leafy greens, berries and yogurt are more prominent in my diet, and moderate to vigorous exercise is not an optional extra in my life. Oh … and I’ve no intention of retiring. Retirement is bad for your brain. So the ABC will have to sack me.
TG: You say that rumination and stress may accelerate cognitive change. How, and how can people best try to counteract this?
NS: For some people these are disabling and it’s hard to change by yourself. There are variations on cognitive behavioral therapy which can help in the hands of a well-trained clinical psychologist.
TG: You have a chapter titled “Don’t Retire”. Should we all be working until we drop?
NS: Work is mostly good for our brains. The evidence is strong that cognitive decline speeds up after retirement. Now some people with hard physical jobs simply can’t keep them up. The point here is what retirement means. If you move from your job to other work such as volunteering, new leisure activities, learning new and complex skills, then that’s actually not retirement. You’re still at work. Retirement to the couch and Netflix is a bad idea.
A decade ago, Taiwanese television had an image problem. When representatives of Taiwan’s Public Television Service (PTS) traveled to Singapore to meet Netflix, they brought two dramas: A Touch of Green (一把青, 2015), a sweeping story of war, displacement and military families, and Wake Up (麻醉風暴, 2015), a tightly constructed medical thriller. They were not simply trying to sell programs. They were trying to change an idea of Taiwan. International perceptions of Taiwanese television, PTS executives recalled in interviews conducted for my joint research with Chairman Hu Yuan-hui (胡元輝), were still strongly associated with the idol dramas that had enjoyed enormous regional popularity
No matter where one sits on the political spectrum and who one blames for the ongoing struggles between the executive and legislative branches or the latest food scandal, there has been noticeable frustration with the way democratic institutions are functioning. Attempts to circumvent political opposition and institutional checks can begin a slide toward authoritarianism, even when presented as short-term solutions to gridlock. While that might solve problems in the short term, it inevitably evolves into a system that serves the rulers and the powerfully connected at the expense of the rights of regular folks. A senior member of the Japan Innovation Party (JIP) yesterday called for closer Tokyo-Taipei cooperation, including on drone and space-based technologies, to meet modern defense needs and promote regional peace and stability.
Nobuyuki Baba, former JIP leader and head of the party’s Japan-Republic of China Friendship Study Group, met earlier yesterday with President William Lai (賴清德) at the Presidential Office in Taipei, and discussed bilateral relations, US-China ties and other issues.
Speaking at a press briefing, Baba thanked Taiwan for its generous donations to help people affected by a magnitude 7.1 earthquake that struck Japan’s Kumamoto Prefecture late last month, causing widespread infrastructure damage and transportation disruptions and killing at least 38 people.
Photo: Screen grab from the Presidential Office’s Flickr page
“True friendship reveals itself through adversity,” he said, adding that Japan and Taiwan have always been there for each other in times of crisis.
The Taiwanese government said that a dedicated bank account set up to accept private donations for the quake had reached more than NT$300 million (US$9.51 million).
The government also donated NT$5 million to support reconstruction efforts in Kumamoto, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.
Baba said his delegation and Lai agreed that both sides should continue to deepen bilateral cooperation and exchanges in areas such as the economy, culture, tourism and natural disaster preparedness.
On regional security, Baba said that Lai told him that Taiwan is strengthening its self-defense capabilities.
The Japanese government is also considering strengthening its self-defense capabilities amid rising regional and global tensions, he said.
The JIP, the junior coalition partner of Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), also hopes to harness drone and space-based technologies to revolutionize national defense and logistics and meet the challenges posed by modern warfare, Baba said.
Tokyo and Taipei should work together to complement each other’s capabilities and jointly develop cutting-edge technologies, including drones, he said.
At the meeting, Lai told the JIP delegation that Taiwan looks forward to an even stronger partnership between the two countries under the LDP-JIP coalition, to jointly build a “non-red” supply chain, thereby enhancing the resilience of global democratic supply chains and strengthening economic and trade cooperation, Lai said.
Separately yesterday, a delegation from the Japanese cross-party parliamentary group “Diet Members’ Association for Peace and Stability in the Taiwan Strait” arrived in Taipei for a three-day visit.
The delegation is led by Haruo Kitamura, a member of the House of Councilors from the Conservative Party of Japan.
Kitamura said Taiwan is Japan’s most important friend, adding that peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait are important not only to Taiwan, but also “vital to Japan’s very survival.”
He specifically cited two legislative goals, pointing to the US’ Taiwan Relations Act and Taiwan Travel Act.
He said Japan must, “by all means,” pass its own versions of the two laws to allow Japan to work with the US to continue conveying to the world the close ties between Japan and Taiwan and their peoples.
“Only by doing so can we take the most critical step toward safeguarding peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait,” he said.

Photo courtesy of Kadokawa
The ceremony brought together the six creators who won gold, silver and bronze in the Manga and Wordless Manga categories. The winners are from Taiwan, Vietnam, France and Switzerland.

Lin said in her acceptance speech that support from the Ministry of Culture enabled her to transition from an office worker to a professional manga creator just a few years ago.
Being in Tokyo to accept the award felt “incredible,” she said.
MurJi received the Bronze Prize in the same category for Hitokuji, which Segawa praised for its “overwhelming cuteness.”
MurJi said she hopes to create manga that can be a companion for readers in the same way manga has been for her, bringing comfort and a smile to those feeling exhausted or discouraged.
The winning works are available on Kadocomi, Kadokawa’s online manga platform.
Kadokawa is known for publishing iconic series such as Neon Genesis Evangelion and the manga adaptation of Your Name.

Mercury could fall to 17°C in northern Taiwan on seasonal winds: CWA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:40:51 UTC
01:40:51 KST

Temperatures in northern Taiwan are forecast to fall as low as 17 degrees Celsius in the coming days with the arrival of this autumn’s first northeasterly wind system, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said Tuesday.
CWA forecaster Tseng Chao-cheng (曾昭誠) said that the seasonal winds are expected to affect Taiwan from Wednesday through Friday, with northern Taiwan likely to feel the strongest impact.
Temperatures in the north from nighttime through early morning are forecast to fall to 17-20 degrees due to possible radiative cooling, which refers to the cooling of the ground under clear skies, light winds and dry conditions, Tseng said.
Photo: CNA
Elsewhere, nighttime and early morning temperatures from Wednesday through Friday could range from 21 to 24 degrees in central Taiwan and hover around 24-25 degrees in the south, Tseng said.
Daytime highs are expected to reach 30-32 degrees Wednesday to Thursday before falling by 1-2 degrees on Friday, Tseng added.
Tseng said the approaching seasonal winds are likely to bring moisture to windward areas north of Taoyuan and eastern Taiwan, with heavier rainfall forecast along the north coast and in the eastern counties of Yilan and Hualien on Friday.
The approaching seasonal winds are likely to weaken over the weekend, but Greater Taipei and eastern Taiwan could see brief showers, while sporadic showers are also possible in the south, Tseng said.
Cloudy skies are forecast elsewhere over the weekend, with afternoon showers possible, Tseng said.
From Monday to Tuesday, moisture is expected to decrease as rainfall eases, Tseng said.

Taiwan central bank governor gets ’A-’ grade from Global Finance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:40:51 UTC
01:40:51 KST

Central bank Governor Yang Chin-long (楊金龍) has received an "A-" grade from New York-based Global Finance magazine, according to the publication’s Central Banker Report Cards 2026 released yesterday.
It marked the second consecutive year that Yang received an "A-" grade from Global Finance.
Yang was among 25 top-tier central bankers worldwide who received an "A+", "A" or "A-" grade, according to the magazine.
Photo: Chen Mei-ying, Taipei Times
Commenting on the latest ranking in the annual report on central bankers, Yang was quoted by an aide as saying: "Thank you very much. My colleagues and I at the central bank will continue to work hard."
The magazine said its grading scale from "A" to "F" is based on "success in areas such as inflation control, economic growth goals, currency stability, interest rate management, and political independence." An "A" represents excellent performance, while an "F" signifies outright failure.
The magazine added that the Central Banker Report Cards, published annually since 1994, grade the performance of central bank governors in almost 100 countries, territories, and districts as well as the European Union, the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, the Bank of Central African States, and the Central Bank of West African States.
"Central bank governors face a complex balancing act, navigating persistent inflation pressures, uncertain growth, and rapidly changing economic conditions, while maintaining the confidence of markets and the public," Global Finance founder and editorial director Joseph Giarraputo said in a statement.
"Global Finance’s ’A’ Grade Central Bank Governors are leaders who have demonstrated the discipline, independence, and sound judgment needed to deliver stability while guiding their economies through an always unpredictable global environment," Giarraputo said.
According to Global Finance, only two central bankers — from Denmark and Peru — received an "A+" grade this year.
Eight central bankers — from Chile, Costa Rica, Guatemala, India, Jamaica, Paraguay, Singapore and South Africa — received an "A" grade from the magazine.
In addition to Yang, 14 other central bankers from Albania, Argentina, Cambodia, the Czech Republic, the Dominican Republic, Kenya, Kuwait, Morocco, the Philippines, Poland, Serbia, Switzerland, Tanzania and the United Arab Emirates earned an "A-" grade, Global Finance said.
Yang, who has worked at Taiwan’s central bank since 1989, has served as governor since February 2018.
Yang received an "A" grade in 2019, 2020, 2022 and 2023, an "A-" grade in 2021, a "B+" grade in 2024 and an "A-" grade in 2025 and last year.
His predecessor, Perng Fai-nan (彭懷南), has the distinction of being the only central banker in the world to have earned the top grade 14 times, receiving straight A’s from 2005 to 2017.

US consumers’ short-term inflation expectations unchanged in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:40:43 UTC
01:40:43 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
US consumers’ short-term inflation expectations remained unchanged in August, according to a survey released Tuesday by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Median inflation expectations for the next 12 months held steady at 3.6%, while five-year-ahead expectations remained at 3%, the bank’s Survey of Consumer Expectations showed.
Expectations for inflation three years ahead, meanwhile, declined 0.1 percentage points to 3.2%.
Median expectations for gasoline price growth for the next year rose 1.7 percentage points to 4.6%.
Expected price growth increased 0.3 percentage points to 5.3% for food and 0.2 percentage points to 9.1% for medical care.
Expectations for increases in college education costs climbed 0.3 percentage points to 6.1%, while those for rent rose 0.7 percentage points to 6.6%.
Labor market expectations were mixed, with the outlook for unemployment and finding a job deteriorating. Expectations on job losses and voluntary departures improved somewhat.
The probability assigned to the US unemployment rate being higher a year from now increased 1.6 percentage points to 44.4%, its highest since April 2020.
The perceived probability of losing a job in the next 12 months fell 0.4 percentage points to 13.8%, while the probability of finding a new job after losing one declined 0.8 percentage points to 45.4%.
Consumers also became more pessimistic about their current and future financial situations and access to credit.
Expected household income growth remained unchanged at 3%, while expected spending growth rose 0.3 percentage points to 5.2%.
The survey, conducted from Aug. 3 to Aug. 31, is based on a nationally representative panel of 1,300 US household heads.
US consumer inflation rose 0.1% month-on-month and 3.4% year-on-year in July. August inflation figures are scheduled to be released Thursday.

Germany is 'ready to provide' additional supplies of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 8.
"These are exactly the kinds of decisions that bring peace closer: when you reduce the aggressor’s ability to destroy lives," Zelensky said in a post on social media. No timescale was given for the arrival of the additional interceptors.
"Preparing Ukraine for winter is of the highest priority and it requires us to act resolutely and immediately," German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said in comments at the Sept. 8 meeting of the Ramstein Ukraine Defense Contact Group.
"In addition to PAC-2 interceptor missiles, Germany will further step up its continuous provision of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to provide greater quantities to Ukraine," Pistorius said, also committing to deliver additional IRIS-T air defense systems to Ukraine.
Ukraine relies on the American-made Patriot air defense system for its defense against Russian ballistic missiles, which Moscow has been increasingly using to pound Ukrainian cities.
Ukraine's stocks have dwindled as supplies have been diverted to the Persian Gulf due to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Ukraine's new Defense Minister Yevheniy Khmara urged Ukraine's foreign partners to secure funding for additional Patriot interceptors before winter at the meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group.
"To ensure Ukraine's resilience, we need solutions in the field of air defense," Khmara said. "We are concluding contracts for the supply of about 1,000 missiles for Patriot systems with our partners and through an EU loan," he said.
Khmara noted that long lead times for the manufacture of Patriot interceptors meant such missiles "will be supplied only in the coming years, so Ukraine is asking partners to provide missiles from their stocks today."
The announcement of the additional German support came after Kyiv suffered another overnight Russian drone and missile assault. Five people were killed in the Ukrainian capital and 25 were injured.
An additional £100 million package of British support was also announced on Sept. 8, with the funding also being directed toward additional Patriot interceptors.

====================================================================================================

’50 chairs at christie’s’ traces how designers keep reinventing the act of sitting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:38:52 UTC
01:38:52 KST

Christie’s Beverly Hills will fill with chairs later this month, though very few of them resemble the kind you would casually pull up to a table. Basic.Space has assembled 50 pieces for 50 Chairs at Christie’s, bringing together familiar names from 20th-century design with contemporary furniture that stretches the category into stranger territory. The exhibition opens by appointment from September 25th through 30th, and every chair will be available to buy.
The range becomes pretty clear from the first few works announced. Charles and Ray Eames’ LCW appears in a rare calfskin edition produced in 2002 for a Christie’s auction, contributed here by the Eames Foundation. A hammered-brass chair by Philippe Hiquily, made in the 1970s and coming from Kelly Wearstler’s collection, sits much closer to sculpture. Then there is Joe Colombo’s Elda Chair from 1963, with its huge molded-fiberglass shell wrapping around the body like a pod.
Vince Skelly for Basic.Space, 50 Chairs at Christie’s
from plywood to moose antler
Rick Owens takes the chair in a much heavier direction. His Stag Stool is made from black plywood with a natural moose antler rising from one side, an object that feels almost architectural in its bluntness. Sam Klemick’s Trumpet Dining Chair has a completely different energy. Its wooden legs widen toward the floor and the backrest seems to sag and bunch as if the timber had somehow softened under its own weight.
SeungJin Yang’s Lounge Chair 01 – Transparent Blue is probably the quickest piece to understand from a photograph. The chair begins with balloons, which Yang coats and fixes in resin until their temporary, inflated shapes become solid furniture. In transparent blue, the whole thing looks swollen and a little cartoonish, with every armrest and cushion still carrying the rounded pressure of air inside it. The Future Perfect is contributing the piece to the exhibition.
Trumpet Dining Chair by Sam Klemick, for Basic.Space, 50 Chairs at Christie’s
the owners are part of the story
The selection also says something about how these pieces circulate. Some arrive through galleries, while others come directly from people who have lived with or collected them. Eric Wareheim contributes the Elda Chair, Kelly Wearstler sends the Hiquily piece, and collectors Giampiero Tagliaferri and Adrien Dewulf contribute the CL9 ribbon chair. Basic.Space is building the exhibition through its own network, so the room will reflect personal collecting habits alongside the usual design-history names.
Jesse Lee, founder and CEO of Basic.Space, describes discovery as central to the company’s approach: ‘Discovery has always been at the heart of Basic.Space and our ecosystem of designers, artists and creatives.‘ The Christie’s takeover follows other physical events organized by the platform and comes after its acquisitions of Design Miami and Platform, which gives Basic.Space a growing presence across both the collectible design market and the events built around it.
Chairs make an unusually good subject for this kind of exhibition because everyone already knows the basic assignment. A seat needs somewhere for the body to land and some way of holding it off the floor. Beyond that, designers have spent decades seeing how far they can push the object. In this group alone, plywood becomes a sculptural block, balloons become resin, and molded fiberglass grows into a shell large enough to surround its sitter.
Putting all 50 together should make those differences immediate. A 1940s Eames design can sit a few steps from a contemporary chair whose form began as an inflated balloon, with the distance between them visible before anyone reads a label. Christie’s Beverly Hills gives that comparison a suitably formal setting, though the premise itself is pleasantly simple: one room, one furniture type, and 50 very different answers.
Lounge Chair 01 – Transparent Blue by SeungJin Yang, The Future Perfect for Basic.Space, 50 Chairs at Christie’s
NH DePass, Autobody Autobody for Basic.Space, 50 Chairs at Christie’s

NATO chief urges allies to step up Ukraine support, warning delays cost lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:37:49 UTC
01:37:49 KST

Melike Pala
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
The Ukraine Defense Contact Group met Tuesday to address Kyiv's urgent defense needs, with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte urging countries to increase support for Ukraine.
He also warned that delays in delivering military assistance were costing lives.
"As we work on modernizing the alliance and building a stronger Europe and a stronger NATO, we must continue to support Ukraine's security and help them defend from Russia's brutal attacks," Rutte said at the virtual meeting.
"Delays simply cost human lives," he said, adding that the number of civilians killed in Russian attacks was at its highest since May 2022.
He said allies pledged €70 billion ($81 billion) in support for Ukraine at the Ankara Summit and stressed that additional bilateral assistance would be needed to meet the commitment.
"Nations must dig deeper. We do not have a choice, I believe," Rutte stressed.
 
UK commits $135M
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said the UK's commitment to Ukraine remained "strong" and "unwavering," stressing that military support would continue alongside diplomatic efforts to achieve a negotiated peace.
He announced a £100 million ($135 million) British contribution to the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism to support the rapid delivery of air defense interceptors to Ukraine ahead of the winter.
Streeting said Britain delivered more than 25,000 drones as part of a commitment to provide 120,000 drones to Ukraine this year, with thousands more expected before winter.
Britain has also continued supplying large-caliber artillery ammunition to Ukraine, he said, adding that the country delivered its 1 millionth round in July, with tens of thousands more expected.
 
US warns about prolonged war
US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby said Europe's greater responsibility for its defense was compatible with maintaining a strong Ukrainian defense, provided European countries continued to act with "seriousness and urgency."
He warned that Russia was rebuilding its forces and defense industrial capacity, saying the US could not predict when the war would end and that allies should be prepared for a protracted conflict.
"We must be prepared for a protracted conflict and for Ukraine's requirements to persist in the months and years ahead. And we must also be prepared for other plausible contingencies as well," said Colby.
He also urged long-term procurement planning to support Ukraine's force reconstruction and Europe’s defense requirements, saying European investments should be integrated with and complementary to US capabilities.
Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara said Ukraine had received €62 billion of the €70 billion in security assistance pledged in Ankara, including bilateral assistance and an EU loan.
He said, however, that Ukraine's overall defense funding gap stood at €23 billion.
Khmara urged partners to make the necessary financial decisions by November so that their effect could be felt on the battlefield during the winter.
The Ukraine Defense Contact Group brings together Ukraine and its international supporters to coordinate military assistance and address Kyiv's battlefield requirements

The Italian Ambassador to Algeria, Alessandra Schiavo, visited the Italian Navy ship “Raimondo Montecuccoli” today, which is docked in the port of Oran, in the western part of the country, where she was received by the ship’s commander, Commander Sebastiano Maruca. This was reported by the Italian Embassy in Algiers.
                                    
                                       
				   The Montecuccoli, a ship of the Multipurpose Offshore Patrol Class, is in the western Algerian city from September 6 to 9 as part of a cooperation initiative between NATO and Algeria. Since July 2026, it has been operating as part of NATO Standing Maritime Group 2, one of the Alliance’s permanent, high-readiness naval forces, deployed primarily in the Mediterranean for maritime security, surveillance, and integrated training missions.
                                    
                                       
				   Addressing the crew, Schiavo recalled the ship’s motto, “Centum oculi,” “a hundred eyes,” emphasizing that the ability to quickly assess any situation is now even more essential in the face of “hybrid and multifaceted” threats, the unprecedented evolution of technology and artificial intelligence—including its application to defense—as well as an increasingly fragile and fragmented multilateral system.
                                    
                                       
				   According to the Italian diplomat, these factors increase vulnerability, make deterrence increasingly necessary, and require operations in complex, changing, and multidimensional scenarios.   The head of the diplomatic mission in the North African capital then described Algeria as a “fundamental and irreplaceable partner” for Italy, not only for energy supplies but also for the stability, security, and development of the region.
                                    
                                       
				   Cooperation between the Italian Navy and the Algerian Naval Forces, she added, constitutes a “solid pillar” based on mutual respect, established trust, and joint training.
                                    
                                       
				   The ambassador emphasized that the presence of the Montecuccoli in Oran reaffirms both Italy’s commitment to NATO and the value of naval diplomacy as a tool to further strengthen bilateral relations and promote peace and stability in the region.
                                    
                                       
				   Ambassador Schiavo concluded by noting that Italy is a maritime nation and that freedom and security of navigation are essential for trade and the economy, thanking the crew for the spirit of service and sense of patriotism with which they carry out their mission in the waters of the Mediterranean.

Ceuta President urges the EU to take firm action against Morocco, as the city is 'on the brink of collapse'

Juan Jesús Vivas accused Rabat of pursuing a “harassment policy” aimed at suffocating the exclave, while the Spanish government and the EU continue to regard Morocco as a trusted partner in addressing irregular migration.
Ceuta’s president, Juan Jesús Vivas, has accused Morocco of a “policy of harassment” towards the city and urged the EU to take a tougher stance and fund border security after some 80,000 migrants entered the exclave on 30 July, distancing himself from Spain’s cooperative approach to Rabat.
Vivas met three EU commissioners and several lawmakers in Brussels on Tuesday, urging help to return irregular migrants and restore normality in the exclave, where thousands of third-country nationals, including unaccompanied minors, remain. "Ceuta is on the brink of collapse," he said.
The Ceuta leader broke with the national government, accusing Pedro Sánchez’s administration of failing to respond adequately before, during and after the July incident, which left more than 150 people dead at sea.
“The EU should tell Morocco that any fruitful and mutually beneficial cooperation begins by respecting our borders,” he said at a press conference at the European Parliament, where EPP lawmakers and staff greeted him with applause.
Spain has not blamed Morocco for the Ceuta incident, despite calling it a violation of its territorial integrity.
Instead, Madrid has pointed to false claims on social media and human traffickers as the main drivers of the mass influx, while continuing to describe Rabat as a “trusted partner” in tackling irregular migration — a position echoed by the European Commission.
“The government should explain why it refuses to hold Morocco responsible, whether directly or through inaction, for the invasion,” Vivas said, after being asked about a leaked police report suggesting Moroccan forces played a role in the crisis.
He claimed that Rabat maintains a “policy of harassment” towards the city and that his fellow citizens now live in fear that a sudden major influx could happen again.
Vivas stopped short of calling for the suspension of EU funds to Morocco, a request made in recent days by Spain’s far-right party Vox. The EU is currently financing Rabat’s migration management strategy with €160 million until 2027.
In his talks with the Commissioners, he also asked for financial support to build border infrastructure and manage the humanitarian crisis that erupted after the mass influx.
According to Vivas, EU Commissioners Andrius Kubilius, Magnus Brunner, and Dubravka Šuica expressed support for Ceuta, but the Commission made no specific commitments.
Brussels is now set to send a technical mission to Ceuta this week to "assess the situation", a Commission spokesperson said on Tuesday.
As Europe’s only land border with Africa, Ceuta, along with Melilla, should have a “special status," within the EU and migration rules adapted to their circumstances, Vivas said.
Another request is for a “permanent presence” in Ceuta of the EU asylum agency (EUAA) and Frontex, the agency responsible for the bloc’s external borders.
“The situation is untenable. We need EU support to restore normality. If Ceuta falls, Europe falls,” Vivas said.

====================================================================================================

Something unique seems to be happening to the brain in menopause
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:36:10 UTC
01:36:10 KST

Scientists have long known that women’s brains undergo substantial remodeling during puberty and pregnancy. These moments of hormonal upheaval are linked to a rewiring of neural networks and reductions in the volume of the brain’s outer, wrinkly layer—called cortical gray matter—which plays a role in memory, reasoning and movement. But far less is known about what happens to the brain in another major hormonal shift: menopause.
Now a new study published in Nature Communications sheds some light on how the brain changes in menopause. Unlike during puberty and pregnancy, the menopausal transition—the moment the body is going through menopause—doesn’t appear linked to an overall decrease in cortical gray matter volume. The finding suggests the female brain responds in different ways to points of hormonal flux throughout the lifespan.
“No one had looked at the changes in the whole brain matter in this menopause transition before,” said Sophie van ’t Hof, a Ph.D. student at the Amsterdam University Medical Center in the Netherlands, at a press conference discussing the results. Van ’t Hof is first author of the new study.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Gray matter declines as people age, no matter their biological sex. But by comparing the brains of individuals who were transitioning through menopause with those of women who were premenopausal and postmenopausal, the researchers found little change in gray matter volume during menopause. The results suggest that sex hormone levels affect the brain in different ways at different times during the lifespan.
“This is really fundamental research, and it’s really understanding the basic brain mechanisms of the female brain. It’s long been overlooked,” van ’t Hof said.
The study has some limitations, the authors write. For one, the individuals in the study self-reported their stage of menopause, which the researchers didn’t confirm with hormone or other diagnostic tests. It also doesn’t entirely jibe with previous research that found distinct reductions in gray matter volume in the hippocampus during the menopausal transition.
Van ’t Hof said that it is too soon to say whether any specific structural brain changes or effects are linked to cognitive function in menopause. The results beg for further research, she added.
“The exact implications are very difficult at this stage,” Van ’t Hof said.

Yemen had been under a relative lull since 2022 after nearly 12 years of war between government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, and the Iranian-backed Houthis, who seized control of the capital Sana and large parts of the country in 2014.
Since late 2023, after the Gaza war began, the Houthis have become increasingly involved in regional hostilities, launching attacks on Israel and commercial shipping in the Red Sea, while recent renewed fighting has raised fears of a return to full-scale conflict in Yemen.

IMF report groups Moldova with EU applicants ahead of Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:28:42 UTC
01:28:42 KST

Ukraine's and Moldova's EU membership bids have so far moved in tandem, but an International Monetary Fund (IMF) report released on Sept. 8 has separated Kyiv from Chisinau and grouped the latter with the Western Balkans, where several countries are further ahead in the process.
Moldova and Ukraine had their membership applications joined together when they opened the six so-called enlargement clusters: to-do lists of reforms that the countries have to do in order to align with the EU.
They have each opened only two clusters so far, on rule of law and external relations, respectively, but there are signs that Moldova is starting to advance at a faster pace.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said the decision to group Moldova with the Western Balkans was because they "share very similar features."
The IMF report itself mentions Ukraine's "much larger size and ongoing military conflict" as reasons for its exclusion.
The report is meant to answer questions about the potential gains to EU candidate countries from membership, as well as to the bloc as a whole.
"We recognize the importance of continuing engagement with other countries seeking to join, especially with Ukraine," Georgieva said at a launch event for the report organized by the Center for European Policy Studies (CEPS), a Brussels think tank.
The EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos already singled out Moldova in July as the "best performer" in accession talks.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's parliament has struggled to advance reforms required by the EU and the IMF.
The EU's Economy Commissioner, Valdis Dombrovskis, held a call with Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi on Sept. 7, during which Dombrovskis insisted that Ukraine adhere to the agreed-upon timetable for reforms.
The commissioner is also set to discuss the topic with Georgieva later on Sept. 8.
Several of the countries in the Western Balkans are significantly ahead of Moldova and Ukraine in their EU accession processes.
In Montenegro, work is already underway to draft an accession treaty for it to join the EU as the 28th member state.
Albania is working to close negotiation chapters rather than open them.
Serbia remains ahead of Ukraine and Moldova in the number of negotiating chapters opened, even as the gap closes.
But North Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo all lag behind.
The IMF report nevertheless underscored that EU membership would be a major economic boon for countries joining, including Ukraine.
Georgieva presented data showing that after 10 years of membership, the countries in the study saw their GDP per capita increase by roughly 35%, mostly due to productivity gains (~20%) and partially to capital investment (~12%).
Those increases would be driven by three roughly equally important factors, Georgieva explained: participation in the EU single market, the inflow of EU funds, and domestic reforms.
The latter refers to adopting the EU's to-do list for fully aligning with the bloc.
Kos said she has "no doubt" that Ukraine could enjoy similar economic prosperity, "if it delivers on EU accession reforms."
Ukraine could "become one of the most dynamic investment markets in the world" upon EU accession, the enlargement commissioner said.
"Another Wirtschaftswunder ('economic miracle') in Europe."
read also
Geopolitics threatens integration
Kos also emphasized that "for the first time in history, we have adversaries in the enlargement process."
"Clearly, Russia is one of them," Kos said, accusing Moscow of seeking to prevent candidates from joining the bloc.
The full-scale war in Ukraine and the Russian occupation of Moldova's Transnistria region are both issues that complicate accepting them as members of the EU.
Countries are generally required to have sovereign control over all their territory, though Cyprus shows there are exceptions: its government does not exercise control over the northern part of the island, which is de facto governed by a Turkey-aligned, internationally unrecognized authority.
"We also feel pressure from the West, from the MAGA ideologists who try to persuade us that our European civilization is in decline, that our economy is in decline."
Kos also pointed to China as a potential challenge for EU enlargement.
Beijing is "somehow nestling in our candidates," Kos explained, so that once the countries join the EU, these Chinese companies will have infiltrated the bloc's single market.
Kos warned that if candidates are left outside the EU for years or decades, these adversaries will "jump in and turn them against us."
"We have to be clever enough to jump in first, in the sense that they (candidate countries) will be able to get some fruits of the membership before they become members."

Court approves tender for new homes to be built in E1, legal challenge remains open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:27:12 UTC
01:27:12 KST

The Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday allowed a tender for 1,234 homes in the E1 area to move forward, but did not decide whether the underlying construction plans are legal.
That means the government may continue looking for developers, but the ruling is not final approval for construction. Three petitions challenging the E1 plans remain before the court, which could still cancel or change them.
E1 is a largely undeveloped area between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim. Its location has made it one of the most disputed construction projects in the West Bank.
Supporters say building there will strengthen the connection between Ma’aleh Adumim and Jerusalem. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who holds authority over civilian affairs in the West Bank, has also presented the project as a way to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Opponents say Israeli construction in the area would interrupt Palestinian territorial continuity between the northern and southern West Bank and further separate east Jerusalem from surrounding Palestinian communities.
Judge rejected request to freeze the tender
Judge Nimrod Flax rejected a request by Palestinian residents and Israeli rights groups to freeze the tender until those
Judge Nimrod Flax rejected a request by Palestinian residents and Israeli rights groups to freeze the tender until those petitions are decided.
A temporary freeze is intended to prevent something irreversible from happening before a court can rule on the main case. Flax found that no such danger existed at this stage because construction is still far away.
Contractors have until October 19 to bid for the project. Their proposals must then be examined, winners selected, and building permits obtained before work can begin.
Flax said the court was likely to decide the petitions before any physical change took place at the site.
The state has also promised that it will not later argue that the tender has progressed too far for the court to intervene. Prospective contractors have been warned that the project is under legal challenge and that any rights they receive will depend on the final ruling.
In other words, a company may win the tender but cannot rely on that victory if the court later cancels the plans.
Palestinian residents file a request to freeze the tender from proceeding
The request for a freeze was filed by Palestinian residents and the organizations Ir Amim, Bimkom - Planners for Planning Rights, and Peace Now.
They argued that allowing the tender to advance would draw private developers into the project and make it increasingly difficult to stop. If contracts were signed before the petitions were decided, they said, the court might be left with fewer practical ways to remedy any problems it found.
The petitioners also accused the government of rushing to advance the project before the October 27 election.
The tender was published on August 18 without advance notice, despite an earlier undertaking by state attorneys to alert the petitioners before it was issued. The petitioners described the move as an attempt to create facts on the ground before the election and before the court could intervene.
The state acknowledged that its lawyers had not been informed before the tender was published because of an internal error. It argued, however, that the promise to provide notice was informal and that the mistake did not justify stopping the tender.
It also maintained that the danger described by the petitioners was still theoretical, as no bids had yet been submitted, no developers had been selected, and no construction was imminent.
Ma’aleh Adumim Municipality, which also opposed a freeze, submitted aerial images that it said showed that the area covered by the tender was empty of buildings. It agreed to notify the court seven days before physical development begins if the petitions have not been decided by then.
Petitioners say the project would force Palestinian communities from surrounding area
The petitioners argue that the harm cannot be measured only by whether buildings currently stand on the specific construction plots. They say the wider E1 project would eventually force Palestinian and Bedouin communities from the surrounding area and lead to home demolitions.
Tuesday’s ruling addressed only whether the tender had to be paused while those claims are examined.
The three main petitions challenge two plans for approximately 3,400 homes in E1. They allege that the plans were approved through a defective and discriminatory process that failed to properly consider their effect on nearby Palestinian communities.
The state and Ma’aleh Adumim reject those allegations and argue that the plans were lawfully approved. They say stopping the project would delay housing and development intended to meet the needs of the area’s growing population.
The court previously refused to freeze the plans in October and November 2025. In June, however, it declined to dismiss the petitions and ordered the state to answer them in detail.
The petitioners argued that the June order showed that their case had gained strength. Flax rejected that interpretation, explaining that asking the state for a full response was a procedural step and nothing more.
Those larger questions remain unresolved. The tender may continue for now, but the project remains subject to the court’s final decision.
Separately on Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused settlers of carrying out ethnic cleansing in parts of the West Bank, saying the Israeli government had too often turned a blind eye and that some of its members had supported forced displacement. He separately cited E1 as a project that would cut across land sought for a future Palestinian state and put a two-state solution at risk.
Reuters and Tovah Lazaroff contributed to this report.

Portuguese comedy duo Cebola Mol, made up of Eduardo Madeira and Filipe Homem Fonseca, have also withdrawn.
"We will celebrate justice, freedom and joy with you on another occasion," the pair wrote on social media.
Their announcement featured an illustration of the comedians alongside a watermelon, a widely recognised symbol of Palestinian identity and solidarity.

The inaugural Lisbon International Humour Festival is scheduled to run from 29 October to 1 November, with Seinfeld due to close the event at Lisbon's MEO Arena on 1 November.
His performance remained on the programme as of Monday despite the mounting withdrawals, while calls for further artists to boycott the festival have circulated on social media.

How Israel's election has stalled Trump's Gaza Peace Plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:26:56 UTC
01:26:56 KST

Breadcrumb
How Israel's election has stalled Trump's Gaza Peace Plan
Donald Trump's plan for Gaza was supposed to move the territory towards a new post-war order.
Instead, it is increasingly becoming a test of how far the US president is willing to push Benjamin Netanyahu.
At the centre of the dispute are some of the most consequential parts of the plan: Israeli military withdrawal, the deployment of an international force, and the transfer of civilian administration to a Palestinian body.
While Netanyahu has not rejected the plan outright, analysts say he is instead seeking to slow it down, balancing pressure from Washington against an Israeli right that opposes relinquishing military control over Gaza.
Palestinian specialist on Israeli affairs Firas Yaghi told The New Arab that there was a "real struggle" over who would hold political and security decision-making power in Gaza after the war.
He said Netanyahu was working to "delay and reshape" Trump's plan to fit the Israeli position.
Israel's elections
A roadmap announced by Trump and the US-led Peace Council at the end of July calls for a new Palestinian administration in Gaza, the withdrawal of Israeli forces, the disarmament of Hamas and other armed factions, and the deployment of an International Stabilisation Force.
Hamas, the Palestinian armed and political movement that governed Gaza before the war, has accepted the roadmap in principle, while saying the second phase depends on Israel first fulfilling obligations including opening crossings and allowing aid to flow.
Netanyahu rejected the Peace Council's 15-point plan last month.
Haaretz has since reported that Israeli officials, with his backing, are obstructing its implementation and refusing to cooperate fully with the Peace Council.
One example is the Erez crossing in northern Gaza.
Germany supplied Israel with an advanced scanning system intended to facilitate its reopening for aid deliveries. But Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz later said there were no instructions to open the crossing to goods, and the project stalled.
Israel is due to hold parliamentary elections on 27 October.
Ahmed al-Tanani, a Palestinian political affairs specialist, told The New Arab that Netanyahu is seeking to avoid concessions that his rivals could use against him.
Allowing an international force into Gaza or withdrawing Israeli troops could reopen arguments about what the war actually achieved, he said, and put renewed scrutiny on Netanyahu's promise of "total victory".
Al-Tanani said Israel did not want the international force to enter Gaza because its presence could restrict the Israeli military's freedom of movement and mark a step towards an Israeli withdrawal from areas of the territory.
He argued that the United States had the ability to apply greater pressure, but had not yet reached the point of using "overwhelming pressure".
The disagreement, in his assessment, remains tactical rather than strategic.
Washington wants to preserve the ceasefire and move towards a new political framework, while Israel wants to retain as much security freedom as possible.
Who controls Gaza?
The most important dispute may be over security authority. The US plan envisages international forces playing a role alongside a Palestinian administration and police force. Netanyahu's right-wing coalition, by contrast, has opposed giving up Israeli security control in Gaza.
That puts some of the plan's central elements in direct conflict with the political position of his government.
Yaghi said the US administration was seeking to move towards the second phase, including disarmament, Palestinian administration, reconstruction, security arrangements and the management of crossings.
The Israeli government, he said, is trying to modify how those measures would work.
One proposal is a system of Lebanese-style "pilot zones".
Yedioth Ahronoth reported that Israel was considering designated areas inside Gaza, agreed with the United States, where international forces would enter and "clear" weapons and armed infrastructure before a new civilian administration was established.
Hamas members would be prevented from returning to those areas.
The idea resembles arrangements being discussed in southern Lebanon, where international involvement would be introduced gradually rather than through an immediate transfer of control across an entire territory.
But even that model would require the presence of the International Stabilisation Force, a Palestinian administrative committee and Palestinian police.
Those are precisely the arrangements Netanyahu is currently reluctant to implement.
Both al-Tanani and Yaghi argue that the dispute does not amount to a fundamental break between Trump and Netanyahu.
Instead, it reflects different priorities. Trump wants to show that the ceasefire can be converted into a broader political achievement. Netanyahu wants to preserve Israeli military freedom and avoid steps that could damage his standing with the right before elections.
The Israeli prime minister is therefore trying to avoid two risks at once: appearing to defy a supportive US administration, while also appearing to surrender control over Gaza.
That balancing act may explain why implementation has slowed rather than collapsed. But it also means the future of the plan could depend heavily on Israeli politics and the fate of Benjamin Netanyahu.

Iran's 'last man standing': Will weakening Houthis put Iran's Middle East plans to bed? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:26:52 UTC
01:26:52 KST

Reports from Yemen that express optimism and portray a new offensive against the Houthis as potentially successful may be part of a path to reshape the Middle East.
Some had assumed that the US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February would lead to a new Middle East. Under this concept, the Iranian regime would either collapse or be so weakened that the whole region would change.
The Iranian regime has withstood the blows so far. It’s possible that the regime won’t collapse and that it will continue, in much the same way Saddam’s regime continued throughout the 1990s.
If the Iranian regime doesn’t collapse, that doesn’t mean that change may be stymied. In fact, a blockaded and weakened Iran may not be able to support its proxies as much.
The Houthis have, to some extent, become the “last man standing” among the Iranian proxies. This is because they have not faced the pressure or the fighting that the other proxies have faced. Hezbollah has seen its rocket arsenal badly degraded.
Iranian proxy forces heavily degraded
Hamas has lost half of Gaza and many of its fighters. It can be argued that Hamas and Hezbollah are now weakened back to their 2002-2006 levels. They are still dangerous. However, they are different. Israel’s defense technology has also improved exponentially since the 2002-2006 era.
The area that is controlled by Hamas and Hezbollah is today quite small, considering the size of the Middle East. Iran, for instance, is around 150 times larger than Lebanon. Hezbollah only controls several areas in Lebanon today. The strength of Hezbollah lies in its support among the Shi’ite minority in Lebanon.
The Shi’ites also support Amal, another party. Amal generally runs interference for Hezbollah, tacitly supporting it in some ways, or at least excusing its activity. Amal’s leader, Nabih Berri, was born in 1938 and has been Speaker of Parliament in Lebanon since 1992. With Hezbollah weakened and a potential leadership crisis in Amal, it’s plausible that change may come to Lebanon over time.
Another pro-Iranian axis in the region is the Shi’ite militias in Iraq. They have some 100,000 fighters. They are divided into numerous brigades of various militias. These militias also come under the government-backed Popular Mobilization Forces.
The US is pressuring Iraq to rein in the militias. Some militias might agree to place their arms under state control. Others are saying they will not. They want the US to fully leave Iraq by September 30. Then they say they may consider changes in their armament. If they do agree to some changes, this could fundamentally reshape Iraq.
THE SPOTLIGHT now focuses on the Houthis. Cut off from Iranian funding and supplies of Iranian know-how for missiles and also some components, they may be weaker than before. Iran used to smuggle weapons to them using various types of ships.
Now the US has a blockade off the coast of Iran. Perhaps the ships have stopped. Saudi Arabia and its allies in the Yemen government forces may sense an opportunity. There is optimism in the Yemen government ranks and in supporters of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.
Houthis poor at city, coastal defense, but hard to dislodge from highlands
Michael Knights, an adjunct fellow at The Washington Institute for Near East Policy and an expert on Yemen and battles there, wrote on X/Twitter this week about the challenges facing the Yemeni forces who are fighting the Houthis.
He noted, discussing the Houthis, that they are “serially poor at defending cities and coastal areas; but they would be harder to dislodge from highlands, and no Yemeni offensive has ever successfully developed a ‘second echelon’ of forces to exploit an initial break-in onto the central massif. The Houthis only still hold terrain because of the weakness of Yemeni/int’l forces, not intrinsic Houthi strength.”
Knights has written two important books on the war in Yemen, including 25 Days to Aden: The Unknown Story of Arabian Elite Forces at War and The Race For Mukalla: Arabian Elite Forces and the War Against Al-Qaeda.
He also noted that “the winning formula against the Houthis is a concentric attack on [more than] six fronts with air power intervening as needed. The Houthis have never successfully defended terrain, even plateau, under such conditions.”
The Houthis are now facing pressure. The question is whether they will begin to lose ground or if this offensive will stall. Even if it does stall, lessons may be learned. Iran is having a harder time backing its proxies.
This is a far cry from where Iran was a decade ago. It used to feel that it controlled much of the region. IRGC Quds Force commander Qasem Soleimani had encouraged Moscow to intervene in Syria in 2015. The Houthis were on the march toward Aden. Hamas felt confident in Gaza. Hezbollah was able to threaten Israel in Lebanon and Syria.
Now, much of that map of Iranian expansion in the region has changed. Iran has still seen successes. It didn’t collapse under US and Israeli airstrikes. It has lashed out around the region and threatened US bases in the Gulf. It has launched 1,000 missile and drone attacks on Iraq and appeared to pre-empt a Kurdish uprising.
Iran is still hollowing out countries in the region. However, it’s possible that some more of its dominoes may fall. Decades of Iranian investment in proxies is no longer paying off.
Soleimani was killed in 2000 alongside Iraqi militia leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis. Iranian proxies have shot their bolt in some cases. Recovery for them will take time. Pressure on them could lead to a lasting defeat for the proxies.
