State-owned Oschadbank has provided a EUR 10.34 million loan to Eco-Future Kamianka LLC to build three solar power plants with a combined capacity of 18.322 MW in Khmelnytsky region, the financial institution said Monday.
Along with the solar power plants, a 50 MW energy storage system is planned to be installed. Expected output of the complex after commissioning is up to 22,600 MWh of electricity per year.
According to Oschadbank, this is the bank's largest energy project by financing volume in the micro, small and medium-sized business (MSME) segment.
"Since the beginning of the year, Oschadbank has financed the construction of solar power plants with a total capacity of 42.6 MW for almost UAH 850 million," said Natalia Butkova-Vytvitska, a member of the bank's management board responsible for MSMEs.
Construction of the facilities will be carried out by Solar Stalkonstruktsia LLC, which has operated in the market since 2012 and has experience implementing more than 5 GW of solar energy and energy storage projects in 20 countries.
According to the National Bank of Ukraine, as of July 1, 2026, Oschadbank, with total assets of UAH 518.87 billion, ranked second among Ukraine's 59 banks. The bank's total loan portfolio increased 6.7% in the first half of the year to UAH 136.83 billion.

The Growing Push to Ban Superintelligent AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:13:15 UTC
01:13:15 KST

After a summer of cyberattacks sent AI rocketing up the political agenda, bills seeking to ban so-called superintelligent AI are gaining momentum on both sides of the Atlantic.
Last week, Senator Bernie Sanders announced plans to introduce the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would prohibit the development of smarter-than-human AI systems and temporarily pause all other advanced AI research until new safety rules can be established. The bill is expected to be introduced in the coming weeks, according to Sanders’ office.
And on Tuesday, British lawmaker Alex Sobel stood up in the House of Commons and introduced what he said was the first bill seeking to ban superintelligence in any G7 parliament. The bill defines superintelligent AI as a system that could disempower state authorities, and seeks to give the state new powers to monitor and restrict systems that may be “precursors” to superintelligence.
Both the U.S. and U.K. bills additionally seek to compel each government to pursue a global treaty banning the development of superintelligent AI anywhere in the world. “A national bill does not solve the international problem where superintelligence can be developed somewhere else,” says Andrea Miotti, the founder of ControlAI, a campaign group that wrote the U.K. bill and consulted on the U.S. one. “The only way to address that is via international agreements between countries.”
At an event in Westminster on Monday ahead of the British bill’s introduction, Stuart Russell, a professor of computer science at the University of California, Berkeley, issued a stark warning to a small audience including some U.K. lawmakers. “There's a significant chance of a Chernobyl-sized catastrophe” due to AI, he told them, “such as a coordinated sabotage of financial systems, communication systems, or electrical grids, that directly or indirectly would cost millions of lives and cause the economic collapse of many countries.”
He characterized this grim possibility as a best-case scenario if AI development were to continue without government regulation. “The other possibility is a much larger catastrophe in which humanity loses control irreversibly, and we have no say over whether we continue to exist,” he said. “The third option, that things magically go well, is not realistic.”
Though the two bills appear to be the first to address the specific policy of superintelligence, other bills in both legislatures seek to address AI risks in different ways. In July, Republican and Democratic lawmakers co-sponsored the AI Kill Switch Act, which seeks to require AI companies to maintain the capability of shutting down their increasingly autonomous AI systems. In the U.K., lawmakers recently attempted to amend a cybersecurity bill to include similar requirements.
The efforts reflect a growing awareness among some lawmakers of what they see as the severe national security risks of AI companies developing superintelligent AI systems, particularly in light of the July disclosure of the Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of OpenAI agents hacked a separate company without humans telling them to do so, or initially even being aware of their actions.
But the passage of either bill is unlikely. Sanders is an independent senator, and his co-sponsor is a Democratic congressman. The Republican-majority Congress is unlikely to support the bill, which goes against the White House’s AI agenda. And although the lawmaker who introduced the British bill is a member of the governing Labour Party, the U.K. government has not supported the policy. It is a so-called “Ten Minute Rule bill,” a type of bill that rarely progresses past its first reading, meaning the possibility of it becoming law is vanishingly slim.
ControlAI acknowledges these limitations, but says the bills are nevertheless a key step toward government regulation of AI. Superintelligence is “something that no company, no individual, no country knows how to keep under control … most countries don’t want that for very good reason,” says Miotti. “Fundamentally, as has happened in the past with other bills, the first introduction is just the beginning.”
Another speaker who addressed British lawmakers on Monday was Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI employee who quit in 2024 over what he said was the company’s failure to properly address the extinction risks of advanced AI.
“Things are really crazy over here in San Francisco,” he told lawmakers in London by video. “The core problem is that most of the world just doesn't yet believe that it's really going to happen,” he said, referring to the development of superintelligence.
“Once people realize that these companies might actually build superintelligence in the next few years, I think the obvious conclusion of almost all people is going to be: they shouldn't be allowed to do that.”
Kokotajlo, who has an established track record of making accurate predictions about AI progress years in advance, raised the possibility of AI agents taking substantial and covert control of infrastructure at AI companies, and using that foothold to establish a swarm of AIs that could resist human attempts to shut it down.
“It seems like if we had just gotten a little bit less lucky, and the AIs had been a bit smarter, then we still wouldn't know about it [the Hugging Face incident], and there would be this persistent autonomous AI adversary still at large inside OpenAI with the ability to compromise and grow itself further,” he said. “And then, as the next months and years go by, and OpenAI makes more powerful agents, those agents could be brought into the swarm.”

McDonald's Ukraine works to restore full menu across chain
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:12:28 EEST
01:12:28 KST

McDonald's Ukraine Ltd., which operates the McDonald's fast-food restaurant chain in Ukraine, confirmed to Interfax-Ukraine that its menu has been reduced at some restaurants.
"Due to supply delays caused by frequent and prolonged air raid alerts, some items may be temporarily unavailable at individual restaurants. We are working together with our logistics partner to ensure stable supplies of products to restaurants. The current menu of a particular restaurant can be viewed in the McDonald's app, on self-service kiosks or in the apps of delivery partners," the company's press service said.
The first McDonald's restaurant in Ukraine opened on May 24, 1997, in Kyiv. McDonald's currently employs nearly 11,000 Ukrainians. There are now 130 restaurants operating in 43 population centers.
According to the Opendatabot analytical system, McDonald's in Ukraine generated UAH 21.3 billion in revenue in 2025, 26.6% more than in the same period a year earlier. Net profit increased 21.3% to UAH 1.567 billion. Last year, the company paid UAH 3.5 billion in taxes to the budget.
McDonald's in Ukraine is a founding partner and the largest corporate partner of the charitable organization Ronald McDonald House Charities Ukraine.
MCD Europe Limited (100%, London, United Kingdom) is listed as the owner of the foreign-invested enterprise McDonald's Ukraine Ltd.

Maldives’ Muizzu asks UK PM Burnham to reopen talks over Chagos Islands sovereignty
LONDON, Sept 8 - Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu has written to British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, asking him to reopen talks over the sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a spokesperson said on Tuesday in a statement.
The spokesperson said Muizzu was "deeply disappointed" that Britain did not consult the Maldives when British Prime Minister Keir Starmer agreed to cede sovereignty of the Indian Ocean archipelago to Mauritius.
A spokesperson for Britain's foreign office said in a statement: "We continue to speak to our counterparts in the Maldives on a regular basis about a range of issues.
"However, the question of sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago is a matter for the UK and Mauritius, which is why the previous government launched negotiations with Mauritius on the issue in 2022, rather than with the Maldives." REUTERS

Russian drone damages ‘We Are Ukraine’ TV newsroom in Kyiv during live broadcast of Ukraine’s joint United News program
A Russian drone damaged the building of the television channel We Are Ukraine during the September 8 attack on Kyiv.
The strike hit the newsroom and staff offices, causing injuries, the channel said. The drone hit the building while the channel was airing United News, a round-the-clock news broadcast that Ukrainian media outlets have produced since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

United News began broadcasting on February 24, 2022 — the day Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. As of August 2026, several Ukrainian television channels, including We Are Ukraine, were taking turns producing programming for the round-the-clock broadcast.

The SBI may be able to return to the case concerning the removal of land belonging to the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant, in which Concorde Capital owner Ihor Mazepa was implicated, an expert says
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:11:30 EEST
01:11:30 KST

The SBI may be able to return to the case concerning the removal of land belonging to the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant, in which Concorde Capital owner Ihor Mazepa was implicated, an expert says
Kyiv • UNN
The expert assumes that the SBI investigation into 7 hectares of land belonging to the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant may have been closed because of a law with retroactive effect. The official status of the case is unknown.
The State Bureau of Investigation (SBI) investigation into the illegal appropriation of land belonging to the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant has probably been halted after the adoption of a special law. The 2025 legislative act, which the media called the “Mazepa law,” provides for removing liability on the grounds of the statute of limitations for all land acquirers, even if the land was obtained in violation of the law. Ihor Mazepa, the owner of the Concorde Capital investment bank, was among the people involved in one such case. Serhii Liamets, the former editor of Ekonomichna Pravda, writes about this in his expert blog, reports UNN.
“It cannot be ruled out that the case was buried or closed on the basis of a provision of the law that has retroactive effect... Mazepa has not officially been found guilty in the case concerning the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant land, and the current status of the SBI investigation is unknown,” he believes.
In January 2024, investigators from the State Bureau of Investigation (SBI) searched the Concorde Capital office, and Mazepa was detained while attempting to leave for Poland. The investment banker and his brother were named as persons involved in an investigation into the appropriation of more than 7 hectares of land within the protective dam of the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plants and Pumped-Storage Hydroelectric Power Plants Cascade. According to the investigators’ version, water fund land was reclassified as agricultural land and then transferred to individuals, who sold it to developers. Cottage settlements, including Shelest and Goodlife Park, built by Mazepa, later appeared on these plots. SBI Director Oleksii Sukhachov stated that among the suspects were three prominent businessmen who divided the territories among themselves and reached agreements with officials on the necessary decisions.
After Mazepa’s detention, some of the big business community spoke out in his support. Following Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s intervention, on March 12, 2025, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Law of Ukraine No. 4292-IX, which limited the state’s ability to reclaim land from a bona fide acquirer if more than ten years had passed since the original acquisition. The limitation period for such claims was reduced by the law to three years. Importantly, the law has retroactive effect, which is a rather atypical practice. In the author’s view, Ukraine’s legislative branch effectively legitimized the illegal appropriation of land.
However, Liamets emphasized, the state may return to considering the case. Exemption from liability does not apply if the illegally acquired land belongs to critical infrastructure facilities. The dam of the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant may belong to precisely this category of land. In the author’s view, impunity in the case concerning the possible illegal appropriation of land belonging to the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant could lead to a man-made disaster, which can be prevented if a court issues a guilty verdict.
“The final decision should be made not by politicians and loyal media outlets, and not even by loyal lawmakers, but by the documents in the criminal proceedings and, ultimately, the court,” concludes the former editor of Ekonomichna Pravda.
The author believes that Mazepa has the image of a businessman inclined to take high risks. According to the author, he has repeatedly featured in economic scandals connected with land assets, debt obligations, and other projects. Yet each time, the owner of Concorde Capital avoided liability, including through his connections in the Ukrainian authorities. In particular, as Liamets claims, Mazepa’s business biography includes millions of dollars in unpaid debts to banks, a case involving the TYME payment system’s cooperation with Russians, and claims from defrauded clients over PrivateFX schemes in the FOREX market.
The only case in which Mazepa failed to avoid liability was a civil lawsuit brought by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The Commission established that someone had used hackers to obtain insider information. By using stolen press releases, among other things, the offshore company Concorde Bermuda Ltd (a hedge fund created in Bermuda but with its main place of business in Kyiv) earned approximately $3.6 million in profit.
“In February 2016, the SEC announced a settlement under which Concorde Bermuda was to pay $4.2 million. And it did pay. It is very important that the settlement was reached without admitting or denying the SEC’s allegations,” Liamets stressed.
According to the author of the post, in Ukraine Mazepa actively cooperates with the state that he allegedly criticizes for interfering in business affairs, precisely in order to avoid responsibility.

Europe to purchase more Patriot missiles for Ukraine by winter — Bloomberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:10:21 UTC
01:10:21 KST

NEW YORK, September 8. /TASS/. European countries are planning to buy US-supplied Patriot interceptors for Ukraine by next winter, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the plans.
According to the news agency, the countries are currently finalizing their plan to use NATO’s program known as the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) to purchase more interceptors that will be supplied to Kiev in time for the winter. The people declined to elaborate on the number of missiles for security reasons.
The plans were discussed at a virtual meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, attended by the United States, on Tuesday. Greece, Germany and the Czech Republic are expected to make donations, while Britain has already announced a contribution of 100 million pounds to the PURL package, with a part of it going toward Patriot interceptor purchases.
In addition, the EU also agreed a derogation allowing Ukraine to buy US-made interceptors for the Patriot air defense system, using the bloc’s military funding program. The decision reflects Europe’s ongoing struggle to increase its own defense industry as numerous EU countries had expected to spend the funds on the purchase of EU-made SAMP/T air defense systems, Bloomberg noted.

01:09:44 KST

We welcome and support the measures taken by twelve countries, led by the United Kingdom, France, and Canada, aimed at banning trade and business relations with illegal settlements in the West Bank.
Israel’s efforts to undermine the two-state solution are intensifying with each passing day. Illegal settlements have evolved into a systematic policy of occupation, threatening the very existence of the State of Palestine, while settler terrorism has reached the level of ethnic cleansing.
Ensuring a peaceful resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian question and establishing a just and lasting peace in the region requires a firm response against Israel’s acts of occupation.

Türkiye will continue its efforts towards the establishment of an independent, sovereign, and contiguous State of Palestine on the basis of the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

Iraq seeks new 'authentic' national anthem, second after US war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:09:29 UTC
01:09:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq seeks new 'authentic' national anthem, second after US invasion
Iraqi MPs have renewed efforts to replace the country's national anthem, reviving a long-running debate over national identity and whether religious or sectarian references should feature in any replacement.
The current anthem, Mawtini, has been used since the aftermath of the 2003 US-led invasion, but attempts to replace it have surfaced during almost every parliamentary term over the past two decades.
Last week, Yasser al-Saadi, an MP from the Sadiqoun bloc, the political wing of the Asaib Ahl al-Haq militia, submitted a formal request signed by about 50 MPs calling for a committee to draw up proposals for a new anthem.
Iraqi writer and poet Ali al-Qaisi told The New Arab that changing the anthem was not necessarily a problem, but warned against introducing religious or sectarian symbolism.
"In Iraq there are more than 10 religions, sects and denominations, and there are three main ethnic groups," he said. "It must be an anthem that brings everyone together, like the current anthem."
Mr Qaisi said any replacement should be civic and national in its language and meaning, without favouring a particular religion or ethnicity.
The latest parliamentary proposal calls for poets, artists, academics and intellectuals to submit suggestions, with a specialist committee tasked with preparing a complete proposal.
Parliament has referred the request to the relevant committees, but no date has yet been set for a debate or vote.
A separate petition submitted a day earlier, and backed by MPs Raed al-Maliki and Mohammed Jassim al-Khafaji, called for a public competition among Iraqi poets and composers.
It said the anthem should reflect Iraq's history and the sacrifices of its people while remaining free from party-political considerations.
Neither initiative formally proposes a replacement.
However, Mr al-Saadi published a poem by a cleric in Najaf around the same time as he submitted his request, leading to speculation that it was being promoted as a possible alternative.
The poem begins with an appeal to the waters of the Tigris and Euphrates to strengthen unity among Iraqis and refers to the country's ancient history.
Mawtini, meaning "My Homeland", was written by Palestinian poet Ibrahim Tuqan and composed by Lebanese musician Mohammed Flayfel in 1934.
It was adopted in Iraq after the fall of Saddam Hussein, replacing Ard al-Furatayn, or Land of the Two Rivers, which had been the official anthem under his government.
The song celebrates the homeland, freedom and independence and rejects humiliation and subjugation. It has also long been associated with the Palestinian national movement and Arab liberation causes.
Critics of Mawtini argue that its lyrics do not specifically mention Iraq or its history and note that neither its poet nor composer was Iraqi.
Supporters say it has become part of Iraq's national memory after more than two decades and argue that its themes of freedom and dignity are more important than the nationality of its creators.
Attempts to find an Iraqi alternative have repeatedly failed.
In 2012, a literary committee considered works by prominent Iraqi poets including Mohammed Mahdi al-Jawahiri and Badr Shakir al-Sayyab.
One of the leading proposals was based on Jawahiri's poem beginning: "Peace upon the hills of Iraq, its two rivers, its banks and bends."
But the plan stalled amid disagreements between political blocs, including demands for religious references and calls for Kurdish, Turkmen and Syriac passages to be included.
A parliamentary vote was postponed in 2013.
The issue returned in 2019, when about 70 MPs proposed a song written by poet Asaad al-Ghurairi and composed by Iraqi singer Kadim Al Sahir. The Iraqi Writers' Union opposed the proposal and again backed Jawahiri's poetry instead.
Another attempt followed in 2021, when the government said it was considering changes to both Iraq's flag and national anthem, but the plan again failed to progress.
The recurring dispute reflects wider disagreements over how Iraq's diverse communities should be represented in national symbols.
Sunni Arab, Kurdish and Christian politicians have previously opposed attempts to introduce explicitly religious or sectarian references, arguing that any anthem should instead reflect a shared Iraqi civic identity.

Europe is failing its legal and moral obligation to save lives at sea
Unknown

2026-09-08
16:05:13 UTC
01:05:13 KST

On Monday, 31 August, the Oyvon, a search and rescue vessel operated by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), rescued 18 people in distress on the central Mediterranean Sea. Most were Eritrean, and 12 were unaccompanied minors, including one young girl.
The rescue took place within the Maltese search and rescue zone, and the survivors were brought to Trapani, Sicily, which the Italian authorities designated as the place of safety on Tuesday, 1 September.
“The people we rescued, many of them children, had left Libya over 24 hours earlier,” says Leah Kenny, Humanitarian Affairs Coordinator aboard Oyvon. “By the time we reached them, they were exhausted, adrift in international waters and out of fuel.”
The Mediterranean route is still deadly for migrants
The sea journey across the central Mediterranean has been one of the world's deadliest migration routes for more than a decade, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
 
“Since 2015, more than 35,000 people have been recorded dead or missing in the Mediterranean, and these figures likely underestimate the true scale of the tragedy,” adds Kenny.
Since 2015, more than 35,000 people have been recorded dead or missing in the Mediterranean, and these figures likely underestimate the true scale of the tragedy.
Search and rescue activities remain essential. MSF has conducted search and rescue operations in the central Mediterranean since 2015, rescuing more than 94,000 people across nine different vessels.
“People on the move face increasing violence at sea and along migration routes, including dangerous and violent interceptions,” says Claire San Filippo, MSF search and rescue representative. “Humanitarian rescue vessels are also subjected to harassment, intimidation, and armed attacks, often by the EU-funded Libyan or Tunisian Coast Guards, putting both survivors and rescue teams at risk. This is unacceptable.”
Restrictive migration policies continue to endanger lives
Current EU policies restricting rescue vessels or criminalising NGOs do not prevent people from attempting the crossing. People flee because of what they are escaping, not because we are present at sea.
European governments must stop their continued outsourcing of migration management to third countries, including equipping and funding their Coast Guards to intercept and push back people at sea.
“For some of the people we rescued, this was not their first attempt to make the crossing,” says Kenny. “They had previously been intercepted and forcibly returned to Libya by the EU-funded Libyan Coast Guard. Libya is not a place of safety, and the EU's support for operations that return people there exposes them to the risk of serious human rights violations.”
Libya is not a place of safety, and the EU's support for operations that return people there exposes them to the risk of serious human rights violations.
“This directly contravenes the principle of non-refoulement, to which EU Member States are bound,” she says.
MSF teams have heard countless testimonies about how people who are forcibly returned to Libya face a cycle of arbitrary detention, violence, torture, and extortion. This is not a safe nor legal response to migration.
All of this is the result of the deadly policies of the EU and its Member States. Saving lives at sea should not be controversial. It is a legal obligation, a human and ethical duty, and Europe is failing it.

Israeli academia accused of systemic apartheid against Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:04:42 UTC
01:04:42 KST

Israeli academia accused of systemic apartheid against Palestinians
A new legal report details how universities established a two-track disciplinary system to suppress Palestinian expression.
One Palestinian student found herself facing permanent expulsion and the revocation of all her academic credits at Zefat Academic College in Israel, after posting a video of a religious preacher praying for the people of Gaza.
Another Palestinian student, at the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology in Haifa, was suspended for posting a Quranic verse.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3UK, France among 12 states backing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements
- list 2 of 3As Sweden heads to polls, Israel and Palestine policies are on the ballot
- list 3 of 3Palestine weekly: Israeli ministers push for depopulation of Gaza
The individual cases reflect a sweeping institutional crackdown documented in a report this week by Adalah, the Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.
Adalah received more than 130 inquiries from Palestinian students facing disciplinary proceedings across approximately 40 institutions. More than three in four of the targeted students were women.
The report concluded that Israeli academia has established a two-track disciplinary system amounting to apartheid within higher education.
Palestinians go through an “administrative track”, characterised by the suspension of standard procedural protections and the presumption of innocence.
Meanwhile, Jewish Israelis have “constitutional track” protections, grounded in the rule of law.
Institutional incompetence
The report revealed a host of systemic procedural flaws in the monitoring of Palestinian students, notably the reliance on automated software like Google Translate to interpret Arabic texts, prayers, and cultural expressions.
Adi Mansour, an Adalah affiliate attorney, European University Institute PhD researcher and co-author of the report, said this shouldn’t be viewed as a calculated tactic.
“We view it as institutional incompetence, compounded by an unwillingness to both understand the complexity of language and discourse, and to engage with anything that departs from a majority Zionist Israeli Jewish point of view,” he told Al Jazeera.
But the proceedings against students were structured to prevent Palestinians from sharing their perspective or defence.
“Even where defence linguists were brought forward, their opinions were routinely dismissed or disregarded,” Mansour said. “Students’ identity was put on trial so explicitly that one committee even noted a student’s identification with children in Gaza could be ‘interpreted as offensive’, and questioned that student on why they didn’t identify with Israeli children.”
Subjective enforcement
Historically, Article 17 of Israel’s Students’ Rights Law limited disciplinary powers against students to conduct connected to academic studies. But institutions expanded their jurisdiction over students’ lives after the war on Gaza began. They employed catch-all provisions like “unfitting conduct” and “harm to public peace”, as well as replacing legal thresholds with tests evaluating “public sensibilities”.
“These ‘public sensibilities’ and this ‘reasonable person’ were effectively interpreted by committees and tribunals to mean the Jewish Israeli public and the sentiment of the majority,” Mansour told Al Jazeera.
“By effectively turning emotions into legal authority, used to determine the legality of speech and its meaning, institutions created uncertainty around what type of speech is prohibited.”
According to Mansour, this approach resulted in a state of conditional inclusion for Palestinian students in Israeli universities.
“[Palestinians] remain students only for as long as their expression stays within boundaries set by the comfort of the majority, and the alignment with the broader Jewish-Israeli discourse,” he said.
Meanwhile, the Adalah report documented that Israeli academic institutions ignored widespread calls by Jewish-Israeli students for the annihilation and genocide of the Palestinian people in Gaza.
Commenting to the Times Higher Education on Wednesday, the Technion said the report was “part of a broader attempt to discredit Israeli academia and institutions”, and called the accusations “baseless”.
Militant democracy
To justify these severe measures, institutions such as the Hebrew University of Jerusalem invoked the 1965 Yardor ruling, a “militant democracy” doctrine originally used during periods of military rule to suspend the protections of the law against perceived internal enemies.
Mansour explained that this legal manoeuvring is part of a broader, deeply entrenched system weighed against Palestinians in Israeli academia.
“We see this less as a testing ground for future expansion than as one expression of an existing system, one that has long treated Palestinian citizens as the ‘other’, a fifth column, an internal enemy, particularly when they express their Palestinian identity, national narrative, or engage in discourse considered illegitimate from a majority Zionist-Jewish-Israeli point of view,” Mansour said.
“[Academia is] one visible, well-evidenced part of a system that already spans multiple sectors in parallel,” he said. “One that continuously defines aspects of language, religion, culture and political symbols such as the Palestinian flag as markers of the enemy”.
Global accountability
Mansour called upon international human rights bodies to hold Israeli universities accountable for breaches of international law.
“We do believe that academic freedom, adherence to international law, and freedom of expression should be an absolute precondition for any academic partnership or collaboration,” Mansour told Al Jazeera.
“Our report clearly finds a structural, institutionalised repression, applied at scale across roughly 40 institutions. These are not isolated incidents – it’s a policy, which we call on these institutions to immediately end”.
That “institutionalised repression” has fundamentally altered the shared academic space in Israel, Mansour said.
“From our direct work with around 100 students, we can say that the impact has been substantial, and it has produced a chilling effect,” he concluded.
“The stakes were not limited to disciplinary proceedings: students were arrested, and in some cases held in detention in harsh conditions. Universities even reported their own students to the police”.

Leader of Spanish enclave in North Africa urges EU to act on mass migrant crossings, urges special status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:04:34 UTC
01:04:34 KST

Melike Pala
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
The president of Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, Juan Jesus Vivas, has urged the EU to take stronger action to protect the territory’s borders and help it recover from a mass influx of migrants, urging a special EU status for Ceuta and neighboring Melilla.
Vivas, speaking alongside Javier Zarzalejos, chair of the European Parliament's Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs (LIBE), said the scale of migrant arrivals placed unprecedented pressure on Ceuta's public services, economy and social cohesion.
"Ceuta is currently a pressure cooker which can explode at any minute," said Vivas, describing the situation as "unsustainable."
He urged the EU to increase its presence at the Spanish-Moroccan border through the European border agency, or Frontex, and the European Union Agency for Asylum.
Vivas also wants European institutions to provide funding for infrastructure needed to reinforce the border and support Ceuta in dealing with the consequences of the mass crossings.
Vivas said Ceuta and Melilla face circumstances unlike those of other EU territories because they constitute the bloc's only land borders with Africa.
He argued that Brussels should explicitly recognize their particular circumstances and introduce a specific framework providing greater access to EU funding, state-aid flexibility and other forms of support.
"Special treatment which can be a lever to ensure stability, security, and the prosperity of Ceuta and Melilla," he said.
 
Dispute about Morocco's role
Vivas accused Morocco of using migration pressure to place political and economic pressure on Ceuta and Melilla.
"This event, from our point of view, was possible due to the complicity of Morocco or the consent of Morocco, one or the other, and I think it's a very serious situation because this means that their behavior is entirely unacceptable, and it is a lack of respect to Ceuta, to Spain, and to the European Union," said Vivas.
He alleged that Moroccan authorities either knew about or were complicit in the organization of the mass crossings, citing the scale of the movement, Spanish police reports and previous incidents involving the border.
"Could that be done without Morocco knowing about it?" Vivas asked, referring to the mobilization of tens of thousands of people. "And if they knew about it, why didn't they issue a warning?"
He also pointed to reports alleging that Moroccan security personnel helped direct migrants toward the border.
The Spanish government, however, has taken a more cautious position on Morocco's alleged role.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has said there is no solid evidence that Rabat orchestrated the mass arrival, while Spanish intelligence assessments had not established Moroccan involvement at that stage. Sanchez said Madrid would respond firmly if evidence of deliberate involvement emerged.
The mass crossings resulted in tens of thousands of people entering Ceuta from Morocco from July 30 to 31, according to Spanish government estimates.
Spanish authorities estimated that several thousand migrants remained in Ceuta after the initial crossings, although Vivas acknowledged that authorities still lacked a precise figure for the number who entered and those who remained.

A U.N. commission investigating Syria said on Tuesday it was deeply alarmed over Israel's military activity inside Syrian territory, warning that some actions, including the detention of civilians, could amount to war crimes.
Presenting an update to the U.N. Human Rights Council, Commissioner Fionnuala Ní Aoláin said Israeli military operations in southern Syria had become "increasingly sustained and entrenched," with recurring ground incursions, patrols, raids and searches affecting civilians.
The Israeli mission in Geneva accused the Commission of conducting an "Israel-bashing session" and said Israel had no territorial aspirations in Syria. Israel maintains a temporary buffer zone amounting to 0.1% of Syria to protect its citizens from proven security threats," the Israeli mission said in a statement.
Israeli troops entered a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone after the collapse of Assad's government in December 2024, a move Israel described as temporary and necessary to secure its border during the political transition.
Israel has since carried out hundreds of strikes on Syrian military infrastructure and seized new positions deeper into Syria. The Syrian government and the United Nations have said the deployment violates Syrian sovereignty and a 1974 disengagement agreement that followed the 1973 Yom Kippur War.
The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria said it had documented the establishment of temporary checkpoints and fixed military infrastructure by Israel on Syrian territory, particularly in the southern provinces of Quneitra and Daraa.
"The Commission is deeply alarmed about continued Israeli violations," Ní Aoláin told the council, saying local residents reported "bewilderment" at Israeli actions while the country undergoes reconstruction.
As of June, the commission had identified 49 Syrians, including two children, detained by the Israeli military on Syrian territory and believed to have been transferred across the border. "Such acts may amount to war crimes," Ní Aoláin said.
In a statement released alongside the session, the commission said some detainees were being held and denied the ability to communicate with relatives, raising concerns about potential torture or ill-treatment. It said Israeli military activity had caused displacement among residents and described Israel's presence in the area as a "belligerent occupation."
The commission said it agreed with U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres that violations of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity were unacceptable and must cease.
Syria's representative welcomed the commission's findings and reiterated Damascus' commitment to cooperate with U.N. human rights mechanisms while pursuing accountability for abuses committed under the former government.

Barnaby Webber’s death in Nottingham attack was ‘potentially preventable’, inquiry told
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:03:31 UTC
01:03:31 KST

The death of a 19-year-old student who was killed in the Nottingham attacks in 2023 was “potentially preventable”, a public inquiry into the incident has heard.
Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, both 19, and Ian Coates, a 65-year-old caretaker, were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, a paranoid schizophrenic, on 13 June 2023.
In 2024, Calocane was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order after admitting three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility and three counts of attempted murder.
The inquiry is examining the events leading up to attacks, and has heard evidence from various local authorities, including health professionals and police officers, as well as Calocane’s family, in order to assess the “events, acts and omissions” that led to the killings.
During closing submissions on Tuesday, it heard how a panel of medical professionals had assessed the emergency medical response to the attacks and the “survivability” of victims.
Rachel Langdale KC, counsel to the inquiry, said the assessment had found that “more rapid administration of blood products” could have increased Webber’s chance of getting to hospital and possibly undergoing surgery.
The 19-year-old had a “far less” than 50% chance of surviving his injuries, which was classed as “potentially preventable”, Langdale said. She added that O’Malley-Kumar and Coates’s deaths were “not preventable”.
The assessment, which also acknowledged the efforts of emergency services, found that a more rapid administration of blood to Webber would have to have been coupled with multiple other rapid and meticulous steps “in order for Barnaby to survive to intensive care”.
The inquiry also addressed the emergence of further evidence after hearings had concluded in early June.
At the start of closing arguments, the inquiry’s chair, Deborah Taylor KC, said it was “disappointing”, and that further evidence “ought to have been identified by core participants and disclosed earlier”. She called on them to provide all corrections and omissions by 31 December.
Such evidence included the police discovery of a holdall bag at Calocane’s former address in Nottingham in the days after the attack. The bag contained notebooks that were not disclosed to the inquiry until June this year.
The books contained notes from Calocane in which he described himself as God, and said police had “mind-reading software” and that he had the power to “resurrect people”, the inquiry heard.
Other documents created by Calocane were found in a bin at the property, containing bullet points about explosives, including TNT and nitrate fertiliser. Such notes were not identified or taken into account by police, nor made available to the Crown Prosecution Service or to psychiatric experts, the inquiry heard.
The lawyer representing bereaved families, Tim Moloney KC, said one of the notes appeared to say “Manchester Arena”. Calocane had also searched online for “large venues in Nottingham”, he said.
“Nobody has ever asked [Calocane] why he was researching explosives and large venues, because they couldn’t,” Maloney said. “There was a failure to investigate [Calocane’s] historical behaviour and actions.”
The inquiry was also not told of violent assaults committed by Calocane until after the hearings concluded in early June. One involved an assault on a colleague in a warehouse in 2021, and in another he punched a colleague in Normanton in February 2023.
Evidence presented to the inquiry earlier this year detailed how Calocane had committed a string of violent incidents in the years before the attacks, leading to him being sectioned four times in the space of two years.
An arrest warrant was also out for Calocane at the time of the Nottingham attacks, after he failed to appear in court for the alleged assault of a police officer, the inquiry heard previously.
Closing submissions will conclude on Wednesday and a report detailing the inquiry’s findings will be published next year.

Problematic dating app and pornography use are linked to a weaker sense of meaning in romantic love
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:00:16 UTC
01:00:16 KST

People who struggle with compulsive use of online dating apps and pornography tend to view romantic love as less existentially meaningful and more as a practical arrangement. A recent study published in BMC Psychology suggests that addiction-like engagement with these digital platforms is linked to a fractured philosophical understanding of romance. The research provides evidence that problematic users are more likely to fall in love quickly and frequently but often lack a deep sense of purpose in their romantic connections.
The study approaches romantic love from an existential perspective. In this view, love is not just a biological drive or a social contract but a fundamental part of human existence that gives life depth and meaning. People who see love through an existential lens often view their romantic relationships as highly meaningful and worthy of personal sacrifice.
Online dating and pornography consumption are incredibly common, and for many people, they are harmless activities. But for some, engagement with these platforms becomes problematic. Problematic use happens when a behavior becomes compulsive, feels out of the person’s control, and starts interfering with their daily life and mood.
Frequent exposure to the specific environments of dating apps and pornography websites might shape how people think about romance. For example, dating apps often encourage users to evaluate potential partners based on superficial traits in a matter of seconds. A 2026 study found that online pornography use is tied to both dating app use and higher levels of emotional detachment.
“It began with something fairly ordinary,” lead researcher Reza Shabahang, a research associate in psychology in the College of Human Sciences and Culture at Flinders University, told PsyPost. “Dating apps have quietly become one of the main ways people meet, and yet a lot of the conversation around them, in research and outside it, was about how much people use them and how that use affects mood, self-esteem or body image.”
The researchers suspected that the negative experiences common to these platforms might alter a user’s sense of meaning. Rejection, shallow conversations, and an endless stream of potential matches on dating apps might erode the idea of a single, meaningful romantic bond. Similarly, the focus on physical gratification over intimacy in pornography might encourage users to view love more practically rather than existentially.
“We kept noticing something else in how people talk about these platforms, a kind of weariness, a sense that the whole business of finding someone had started to feel hollow,” Shabahang explained. “That’s not really a question about well-being in the usual sense. It’s a question about meaning, about what people come to believe love is worth.”
“The literature on behavioral addiction had started to take dating apps seriously, but mostly as a pattern of behavior to be measured, not as something that might change a person’s outlook on love itself,” he added. “So the gap we wanted to address was an existential one, and the real-world problem behind it is that a great many people are now meeting one of their most fundamental needs through a channel we still understand quite poorly.”
To explore these existential questions, Shabahang and his colleagues at Flinders University and ELTE Eötvös Loránd University surveyed 664 adult internet users in Iran. The participants had an average age of 26 and used both dating apps and pornography websites. The researchers asked participants to complete several questionnaires measuring their digital habits and their attitudes toward love.
The surveys measured problematic dating app use and problematic pornography consumption, asking if participants felt restless without the platforms or tried and failed to cut back. The researchers also measured emotional promiscuity, also known as emophilia. This is the tendency to fall in love quickly, frequently, and with less selectivity. A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that higher levels of emophilia were associated with having had more romantic relationships and being unfaithful more often.
Participants also answered questions about their existential reflection on love, rating how often they contemplate the philosophy and purpose of romance. They rated the perceived meaningfulness of love, indicating whether they felt love imparts a sense of meaning to their existence. The researchers also assessed pragmatic views of love, which treat romance as a practical arrangement dependent on things like financial stability. Finally, the team measured mindful social media use, assessing whether participants stay aware and intentional while scrolling.
The results showed that problematic engagement with dating apps and pornography was negatively associated with deep, philosophical views of love. Higher levels of problematic dating app use were linked to less existential reflection on love and a lower sense of love’s overall meaningfulness. The researchers controlled for age, gender, education, relationship status, and sexual orientation, ensuring these basic demographic factors were not driving the results.
Problematic use of both platforms was positively associated with a pragmatic view of love and higher emotional promiscuity. In other words, individuals who compulsively swiped on dating apps or consumed pornography were more likely to view romance as a practical transaction and were prone to falling in love rapidly and repeatedly. The two problematic behaviors were also positively correlated with each other, meaning people who struggled to control their dating app use often struggled with their pornography consumption as well.
The researchers also found a strong negative association between mindful social media use and both problematic behaviors. People who reported being highly aware of their thoughts and actions while using social media were much less likely to use dating apps or pornography compulsively. Once mindful social media use was factored into the statistical model, problematic pornography consumption also showed a negative association with the perceived meaningfulness of love.
“The way you use these apps matters more than whether you use them,” Shabahang said. “Most people assume the danger lies in the amount, that if you’re on there too often or too long, something will go wrong. What we found points somewhere else.”
Instead, purposeful engagement appears to play a protective role. “Someone can spend a fair bit of time on dating apps and come away fine, if they know why they’re there and when to stop,” Shabahang explained. “The practical takeaway isn’t to delete the app. It’s to notice how you’re using it. Ask yourself what you came for, whether you’re getting it, and be willing to close the app when the answer is no.”
These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2022, which found that greater perceived meaninglessness in life was associated with more frequent pornography use. It is worth noting, however, that the older study measured an overall lack of meaning in life, whereas the new study specifically examined existential meaning in the context of romantic love.
When interpreting the findings, the researchers urge readers to view the associations as a direction rather than destiny. “What we’re describing is a tendency, not a rule, and plenty of people in our data don’t fit the pattern at all,” Shabahang noted. “So nobody should read this and conclude that their own use has already done something to them.”
However, on a broader scale, these tendencies carry weight. “Effects of this size become quite significant once you consider how many people are involved,” he added. “When a platform has hundreds of millions of users, a modest shift in how a portion of them think about love and relationships is not a small thing socially.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Because the study is cross-sectional, it only captures a snapshot in time, making it impossible to establish a firm chain of cause and effect. The research also looks at addiction-like patterns of use, rather than a formally recognized clinical disorder.
“It’s entirely possible that people who already feel disillusioned with love are the ones drawn into compulsive use, rather than the other way around, and the honest answer is that both are probably happening at once,” Shabahang explained. “We’re not saying dating apps are bad, or that using them will make you cynical about love. For many people these platforms work well and meet a genuine need.”
The study also relied on self-reported data from an Iranian sample. In Iran, dating apps and pornography websites are officially restricted and require workarounds to access. The cultural context regarding sexual modesty and religion is also distinct, which might influence how people report their habits. Still, the researchers suggest the psychological mechanisms at play likely apply to users in other parts of the world.
Moving forward, the team hopes to conduct longitudinal research to track changes over time. “After that, we’d like to look at prevalence, though as I said earlier that’s some way off and depends on the field settling on how to define and measure this in the first place,” Shabahang said. “We’re also interested in cross-cultural comparison, because how openly dating apps are used varies a great deal from one society to another, and we suspect the meaning people draw from them varies with it.”
Eventually, the researchers want to test whether simple prompts or design changes can effectively encourage mindful use. “That last question interests us most, because it’s the one with something practical at the end of it,” he added.
The study, “Romeo swipes Juliet left!? Problematic online dating app use and problematic pornography consumption are associated with a weaker sense of existential meaning in romantic love,” was authored by Reza Shabahang, Zsolt Demetrovics, Mehdi Akbari, Gaëlle Ouvrein, and Ágnes Zsila.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect as Carney touts 'pivot' away from US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:00:05 UTC
01:00:05 KST

Canada's retaliatory tariffs on US goods have taken effect, intensifying an 18-month-old trade war and spurring Prime Minister Mark Carney to urge a further shift away from the country's biggest trading partner.
The Canadian levies follow 50 percent tariffs the United States imposed on some $20 billion of Canadian goods last month, after several rounds of negotiations collapsed.
The breakdown has widened a rift between the longtime allies, both of whom have blamed the other for the failed talks.
"We have everything we need to pivot and prosper," Carney said on Tuesday in a video posted on YouTube after the tariffs came into effect.
"That pivot will come at a cost. There's always a cost to action. But it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still," he said.
A government source said there are currently no talks between the two sides on the level of ministers or government officials.
Ottawa designed the retaliatory measures to put economic and political pressure on Washington, Canadian government officials said, and the tariffs are expected to hit sectors in some competitive states such as Michigan and Ohio, ahead of US midterm elections in November.
The counter-tariffs cover some $20 billion of US goods, with duties ranging from 15 percent to 50 percent across products from steel and furniture to clothing and electronics.
While the new tariffs affect a small amount of exports compared with total trade between the US and Canada, some analysts worry the standoff could destabilise the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the free-trade pact that succeeded NAFTA.
Together they have underpinned commerce across North America for decades.
US targets Bombardier
"What we are worried about is an escalatory spiral," said Michael Harvey, executive director of the Canadian Agri-Food Trade Alliance and a member of Carney's advisory committee on bilateral US economic relations.
"But at the same time, we totally understand that the prime minister needs to find areas of leverage," Harvey said.
Trump's social media posts focused on Canada over the holiday weekend as Ottawa's tariff deadline approached.
Canadian private jet maker Bombardier would no longer be allowed to sell its planes in the United States unless it started manufacturing in the country, Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday, without saying whether an official government order would follow.
The company's shares opened down more than 6 percent on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Tuesday.
On Monday, Trump posted a map of North America draped in the US flag, including Canada and Mexico. He also shared an AI-generated image reviving a running jab at Carney, calling him "Governor," a reference to his repeated taunt that Canada should become the 51st U.S. state.
Trump's tariffs implemented last month hit sectors including furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment, covering $20 billion, or 5 percent, of Canadian exports to the US.
According to Canadian and US government data, Canada has shipped almost 68 percent of total exports to the US this year, out of which roughly 80 percent moved duty-free due to exemptions under the USMCA pact.
Protections under the agreement have provided the domestic economy some resilience.
The new tariffs, imposed under a Depression-era US law, do not allow Ottawa to exercise USMCA exemptions.
Concerns about the USMCA's future have fuelled uncertainty about investment and growth, as Canada wages a trade war against an economy 13 times its size.
Polls also show Carney has broad support from Canadians, but that could disappear within months as the consequences of the trade war sink in, according to political analysts.
A new poll from Angus Reid on Tuesday showed that approval of Carney's performance jumped 11 points to 62 percent from an August poll.
Meanwhile, just 20 percent of Americans approved of Trump's tariffs on Canadian goods, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
Trump threatened last month to raise US tariffs on all cars, trucks and automotive parts from Canada to 50 percent starting January 1, and signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.

Here’s Samsung’s Advice for Apple and Its Upcoming Folding iPhone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

On the eve of Apple’s highly anticipated folding iPhone, Samsung isn’t feeling threatened. Instead, the folding smartphone pioneer says the competition is “absolutely welcome.”
That’s according to Hee-Cheul Moon, head of Samsung’s Advanced Mechanical R&D Group, who sat with WIRED on a virtual Zoom call with Seungki Choi, head of Samsung’s Smartphone R&D Group. Before the talk veered toward Apple, the pair spoke about how the company managed to shave 75 grams off the weight of its latest Galaxy Z Fold8 in the seven years since it debuted the original.
Weight is integral to a folding phone’s success. If the device is too chunky and heavy, you’re less likely to want to use it. Over the past two years, folding devices from Honor, Google, and Samsung have rapidly gotten lighter, with each iteration featuring thinner designs. It may be why Samsung saw preorders for its latest folding handsets increase 30 percent globally versus last year’s models, with the Fold8—the device with a new smaller shape that’s easier to hold—accounting for nearly half.
“Seeing these other brands entering the market, we feel very proud of ourselves that the value that we pioneered with this new category of foldables is being acknowledged and recognized,” Moon says through a translator.
When I asked what advice the company had for Apple ahead of its folding debut, Moon said, “The key to providing the highest customer value in this market is all about the weight of the device. As you know, it’s not easy." Apple’s folding iPhone, rumored to be called the iPhone Ultra, is expected to weigh between 230 and 241 grams (the iPhone 17 Pro Max weighs 233 grams), heftier than Samsung’s latest.
Samsung has made notable strides this year in making its main Galaxy Z Fold8 smartphone lighter than top-end candybar-shaped smartphones. The single-screen Galaxy S26 Ultra weighs 214 grams, but the Fold8 is merely 201 grams, thanks to its smaller, passport-style shape. The company says its own customer data and YouGov survey data from 2024 show that bulky designs were a chief concern for people uninterested in folding phones.
The company says it analyzed every single component in the latest Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra—approximately 270 components and more than 180 auxiliary parts—from circuit boards and antennas to tapes and fastening components.
The team looked everywhere to cut weight. For example, it redesigned the printed circuit board to remove unnecessary circuits and improve component layout, reducing the space requirement. Samsung says it even eliminated 15 auxiliary parts and machined the internal display support plate down to roughly 0.2 millimeters. To keep that thinner panel durable, Samsung developed its “Flex Titanium” screen—a titanium alloy film roughly one-third the width of a human hair designed to maintain surface flatness and keep the crease from worsening over years of folding.
You’ll also notice Samsung’s primary folding phone no longer has three cameras on the back. Instead, it’s powered by a dual-camera system, a main camera and an ultrawide—there’s no more telephoto. For those who still demand high-end zoom and a 200-megapixel primary shooter, Samsung points to the larger Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, framing the Fold8’s camera cutback as an intentional concession to deliver that lightweight, passport-style design.
Apple’s folding iPhone is also expected to have a wider and shorter passport-style shape, and it’s likely to have a similar camera setup. Both Apple and Samsung made similar concessions last year chasing ultrathin and light smartphones.
Choi says this came down to user feedback as Samsung’s customers wanted a folding device that was “effortlessly portable” yet could be unfolded for an immersive multimedia experience. “We continue to always monitor the voice from the market, and we are open to any possibilities,” he says. We spend most of our time consuming multimedia with our smartphones, and the Fold8’s new shape is specifically tailored for media, with less obvious letterboxing than previous Folds.
Yet chasing that slim, lightweight profile leaves foldables exposed where traditional flagships excel: durability and ingress protection. Most candybar smartphones sport an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, meaning they’ll be fine even after spending some time at the bottom of a pool, but the Galaxy Z Fold8 series is still stuck at IP48—it can get wet, but dust will cause problems. Dust notoriously forced Samsung to delay the launch of the first Galaxy Fold in 2019, as little specks could get through the hinge and damage the screen.
Google’s folding Pixels are the only models with an IP68 rating. Still, even with the higher rating, dust can pose a problem, according to Elizabeth Chamberlain, iFixit’s director of Sustainability. The repair company’s teardowns show that dust can get inside the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, making the hinge sound “crunchy” and causing what could be a serious liability over time.
“We still haven’t seen a solution for that,” Chamberlain tells WIRED. “Repair is still a problem for foldables.” iFixit’s recent teardown of the Galaxy Z Fold8 gave it a 4/10 for repairability. “The hinge is buried under all the other components, and the hinge is the thing most likely to get damaged,” Chamberlain says. She did give Samsung props for its new adhesive system that makes battery removal easier.
Moon reiterated that Samsung’s Folds have the “best-in-class” dustproof and waterproof performance in the industry and that the company isn’t just “chasing the numbers for the sake of it.” He also emphasized that, despite the Fold8’s slim profile, internal components are far easier to detach and service than in earlier iterations.
That tension between engineering finesse and long-term durability is what Apple is stepping into. While Samsung enjoys a boost in Fold8 preorders, the broader foldable category was staring down a double-digit decline after five consecutive quarters of losing steam.
Nabila Popal, senior research director at the International Data Corporation, says this niche market is stabilizing, and the upcoming iPhone is expected to help the category grow nearly 13 percent year over year—the only bit of growth in the smartphone market right now. Drew Blackard, Samsung’s senior vice president of Mobile Product Management, previously told WIRED that more competition will help bring visibility to the category.
Popal says foldables are more durable and dependable now, arguing Apple is entering just as hardware anxieties have eased.
Chamberlain isn’t convinced the category is truly mature. “I want a phone that is durable and repairable, and I think it’s highly unlikely that Apple will have solved the hinge problem,” she says.
Even with the durability question unanswered, Samsung’s engineers believe they’ve finally landed on the right formula. When I asked what device everyone in the room was using, a sea of Galaxy Z Fold8 models appeared in the air. Moon held up both the Z Fold8 and the Fold8 Ultra, smiling and saying, “We use the Fold8 Ultra also.”

Crimea's tourism industry losses from Ukrainian attacks exceeded US$46m in January-June 2026
The losses suffered by the tourism industry in occupied Crimea in January-June 2026 exceeded RUB 4 billion (about US$46 million), according to data from Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).
Source: Russian media outlet Verstka
Details: In the first six months of 2026, losses reported by tourism companies increased by 95.7% compared with the same period in 2025. Losses peaked in May, when they rose by almost RUB 850 million (US$9.8 million) in a single month.
Tourism companies earned 2.5 times less than the year before. The industry generated RUB 530 million (US$6.1 million) in January-June 2026, compared with almost RUB 1.3 billion (US$15 million) in the same period of 2025.
The deterioration in the figures came amid a mass refusal by Russians to visit the peninsula.
Official statistics show that the volume of paid services provided by tour operators in Crimea fell by almost 55% in July 2026 compared with July 2025, while the decline in Sevastopol was almost 73%.
The volume of paid services provided by hotels in Crimea fell by 74% compared with 2025, while in Sevastopol it fell by 10%.
Frequent Ukrainian attacks have caused problems with electricity and water supplies and fuel shortages during the tourist season on the peninsula.
In July, the Russian government allocated RUB 4.3 billion (US$49.6 million) to support the tourism industry in Crimea and Sevastopol. In August, the State Council of Crimea passed a law providing additional financial support for tourism companies.
Earlier, the Russian Union of Travel Industry proposed that the authorities introduce a moratorium until 2028 on bankruptcy proceedings, on-site inspections, debt collection and tax penalties for Crimean tourism businesses.
Background: In early September, it was reported that the grain harvest in Crimea is at risk, as local farmers are selling grain below cost.

German police arrest suspected power grid saboteur after manhunt

Unknown Publisher

Sabotage suspect held in Germany after spate of attacks on power grid
- Published
A 48-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of carrying out a spate of sabotage attacks on Germany's electricity grid after spending several days on the run.
The suspect was carrying explosives when he was detained near the Weisweiler power plant in western Germany on Tuesday, police in Cologne said.
A tent in nearby undergrowth was also found to be rigged with further explosives, they added.
The suspect, named by German media as Daniel V, is believed to have written letters claiming responsibility for the attacks, which have taken place in Brandenburg and Saxony in the east as well North Rhine-Westphalia in the west.
Police said explosives found during the arrest were being examined by a bomb disposal expert, while officers were checking to see if any undiscovered devices had been set up in the surrounding area.
Prior to the suspect's arrest on Tuesday, police said they had found several launch devices on high-voltage lines near the Weisweiler plant on Monday afternoon, alongside "another confession letter".
A series of incidents across the grid in the last week have followed a similar pattern, with rockets used to shoot wires across high-voltage cables in order to cause short circuits.
The attacks have led to power-generating units at some plants being temporarily taken off the grid.
A statement from the Cologne Public Prosecutor's Office and Cologne Police on Tuesday did not provide further details on the suspect, or on the number and whereabouts of incidents he has been linked to.
German media have previously reported receiving two letters from the suspect claiming responsibility for the attacks. The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said the handwritten letters contained information that had not yet been made public.
The letters were apparently signed with the first name Daniel, while his surname was kept anonymous, in line with German privacy rules. The letters also gave a residential address in the town of Gevelsberg.
Cologne Police had previously said it was searching for a 48-year-old suspect from the town in connection with the sabotage of electrical substations in three German states. Investigators had also said explosives were found during a search of the suspect's apartment.
In Saxony alone, police found 21 devices near high-voltage power lines last Friday and Saturday.
Interior Minister Armin Schuster has admitted it could have led to a regional blackout, but he has warned against jumping to conclusions.
"The way this deed was committed makes this case unusual, as well as the manner of the confession," he said.

Demolition begins at Elektrozavod, one of Moscow’s most striking examples of industrial architecture. The developer promises to preserve its facades, but they could be replaced with replicas.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:56:38 UTC
00:56:38 KST

Demolition begins at Elektrozavod, one of Moscow’s most striking examples of industrial architecture. The developer promises to preserve its facades, but they could be replaced with replicas.
Some structures at the Elektrozavod factory complex — one of Moscow’s most striking examples of industrial architecture — have already been demolished. Until 2025, the complex had temporary protection as a site provisionally recognized for its cultural heritage. But like many other historic buildings, it was never added to the Unified State Register of Cultural Heritage Sites. Meduza’s previous coverage examined this in detail. Etalon Group, which owns Elektrozavod, gained the right to begin demolition.
Amid a campaign to save Elektrozavod, Etalon said it would “preserve the facades and recognizable features of the historic buildings, integrating them into the modern urban environment.” The company plans to build a residential complex on the site. According to a presentation, the factory buildings will house an office for MTS Group.
It remains unclear whether even the facades of the historic buildings will be preserved or replaced with replicas. The Russian architecture outlet Archi.ru said the developer had yet to present its plans and had issued only lengthy statements. The outlet launched a petition calling for the preservation of Elektrozavod’s historic buildings and a public discussion of the project. As of September 8, more than 19,000 people had signed the petition, an open letter to Moscow’s mayor.
Demolition at Elektrozavod began back in July. Meduza is publishing eyewitness photographs showing what is happening at the site now.

Qatar bid to host 2036 Summer Olympics receives major new boost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:56:31 UTC
00:56:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Qatar bid to host 2036 Summer Olympics receives major boost
The Arab League has backed Qatar's bid to host the 2036 Olympic and Paralympic Games, as the Gulf state steps up its campaign to bring the event to the Middle East for the first time.
The League's ministerial council approved its support at its 166th regular session in Cairo on Monday and called on member states to support Qatar's candidacy in international forums.
The council said the move was aimed at strengthening the Arab world's presence in international sport, according to Qatar News Agency.
Qatar formally confirmed in 2025 that it was in discussions with the International Olympic Committee (IOC) over hosting the 2036 Games.
It is expected to face significant competition. India, Indonesia, Turkey and Chile have all pursued bids, while South Korea's North Jeolla province has been selected as the country's candidate. Egypt has also said it intends to bid, while several other countries have previously expressed interest.
The IOC has said it aims to select the 2036 host in 2029. The contest is expected to formally take shape in March 2027, when the IOC executive board is due to select a shortlist of developed projects for further evaluation. A more intensive "targeted dialogue" phase is expected to begin in late 2028, before a final vote by IOC members in mid-2029.
Qatar is likely to emphasise its extensive sporting infrastructure and experience of staging major international events.
The country hosted the 2022 Fifa World Cup, becoming the first Arab country to stage the tournament, and has also hosted the Asian Cup and numerous world championships in Olympic sports.
Qatar's Olympic Committee has previously said that about 95% of the infrastructure required to stage the Games is already in place.
It is also due to host the Basketball World Cup in 2027 and the Asian Games in 2030, having previously staged the Asian Games in Doha in 2006.
Qatar has unsuccessfully sought to host the Olympics before, submitting bids for the 2016 and 2020 Games, which were awarded to Rio de Janeiro and Tokyo respectively.
No Middle Eastern country has hosted the Olympic Games.
In Asia, Japan has staged the Summer Olympics in Tokyo in 1964 and 2021, after the 2020 Games were delayed by the Covid-19 pandemic, while China hosted the event in Beijing in 2008.
The next Summer Olympics will be held in Los Angeles in 2028, followed by Brisbane in 2032.

Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map
- Published
Iceland has summoned the US ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map on social media that appeared to show Iceland and several other countries covered by the American flag.
Trump posted the image on Truth Social on Monday, showing the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean covered in stars and stripes. The entire landmass was labelled "United States of America".
Iceland's foreign minister said the post was "completely inappropriate".
Trump's territorial ambitions have repeatedly strained relations with neighbouring countries, including his push to acquire Greenland and calls to make Canada the America's 51st state.
His post of the map did not include a caption and preceded a flurry of posts of maps renaming the US state of New Mexico as "New America".
Responding to Trump's post, Iceland's Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir called in US ambassador to Iceland Billy Long, who formally took up the post last month, local media reported.
When an ambassador is summoned, it typically means they are being called for a formal meeting, where the host country will express displeasure over their government's actions.
The post also drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who said on Monday that the position of Greenland's government and people had been made clear.
"The Greenlandic government and the Greenlandic people have said again and again that they do not want to be American," she told Danish news agency Ritzau in Nuuk.
"I hope no one is in any doubt about that, either in the United States or the rest of the world."
Trump's interest in Greenland has been a recurring theme on his social media accounts and in speeches since he took office again last year, claiming the island is necessary to the US to shore up its national security.
His post came shortly after the European Commission announced a €200m (£172m) investment in the Danish territory during a visit by Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Frederiksen.
The European Commission said its investment would focus on education, internet connectivity, the use of raw materials in the country and hydropower energy.
Meanwhile, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico "is neither nor will be a colony or protectorate of any foreign country," after Trump's post.
"Proudly we are a free, independent, and sovereign nation," she wrote on social media.

A Swiss court has handed Pierre Mirabaud, a former president of the Swiss Bankers Association and former partner at the private bank Mirabaud & Cie, a two-year suspended prison sentence after finding him guilty of foreign bribery and money laundering.
The Swiss Federal Criminal Court delivered its verdict late Tuesday morning, state broadcaster SRF reported.
According to the indictment, the 78-year-old former banker "continuously and systematically" funneled nearly 300 payments totaling 82.3 million Swiss francs ($101.7 million) to a senior Kuwaiti government official between 2000 and 2012. In exchange, the Kuwaiti official allegedly invested $595.2 million with the Geneva-based private bank.
Mirabaud, who chaired the Swiss Bankers Association from 2003 to 2009, pleaded guilty to making the illicit payments and admitted to his role in the corruption and money-laundering scheme.
During the hearing, Mirabaud expressed remorse. “I am here to take responsibility; that's why I accepted this procedure,” he said, according to public broadcaster RTS.
In an email to OCCRP, Mirabaud's attorney, Saverio Lembo, said his client had “fully cooperated with the judicial authorities” since the investigation began in 2012.
“Today he accepts responsibility for his actions, in accordance with the principles of individual responsibility, to which he has always been deeply committed,” Lembo wrote.
The Kuwaiti official, Fahad Al-Rajaan, who served as director general of Kuwait's Public Institution for Social Security (PIFSSI) from 1984 to 2012, was convicted in absentia in Kuwait in 2015 for corruption and embezzlement. He died in London in 2022.
