‘Fighting for our life’: Canadian businesses reel from US tariff shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:50:25 UTC
23:50:25 KST

‘Fighting for our life’: Canadian businesses reel from US tariff shock
- Canada’s small businesses face severe challenges due to US tariffs, losing orders and considering job cuts, as trade talks collapse and tariffs hit US$20 billion (S$25 billion) worth of goods.
- Tariffs disproportionately affect small and mid-sized firms, vital to Canada's economy, prompting government financial support that may be too slow to save some businesses.
- Businesses like Fine Cotton Factory and Jerico fear closure and supply chain collapse, while others lose US sales. Some see local support rise, but stress and uncertainty remain high.
AI generated
ONTARIO – The economic pain that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned would come from a trade war is now a harsh reality for some small businesses that export to the United States.
Across Canada, companies are losing orders, contemplating job cuts and paying higher costs. For some, the threat is existential.
Toronto-based Fine Cotton Factory exports 30 per cent to 50 per cent of its products to the US. Since the tariffs kicked in, some US orders have been cancelled or postponed, and new ones from both sides of the border have slowed, according to executive vice-president Skip Kann.
He fears he will need to let go of a small number of his 250 employees as soon as this September.
“We’re fighting for our life right now,” Kann said.
Talks between the two countries collapsed on Aug 21, triggering 50 per cent US tariffs the next day on US$20 billion (S$25 billion) worth of Canadian goods such as textiles, paint, apparel, alcohol and honey.
Canada announced retaliatory duties on imports from the US worth roughly the same amount, which came into effect on Sept 8. The risk is that the trade war will spiral further.
Many small Canadian manufacturers were shielded from earlier US tariffs because of exemptions under the North American trade pact. But the latest levies imposed by President Donald Trump in August ignore that deal.
While the US$20 billion accounts for only about 5 per cent of Canada’s annual goods exports to the US, the new tariffs appear to disproportionately affect small and medium-sized businesses.
In turn, those firms account for about half of Canada’s gross domestic product. The Canadian government bolstered loans and other financial support for such firms as part of a broader C$7.5 billion (S$6.9 billion) package for businesses and workers hit by the latest round of tariffs.
Those measures will not put out the fire, Kann said.
Like many entrepreneurs whose growth potential lies beyond Canada, he says he has already exhausted domestic opportunities. Plus, some federal support, such as funding for market research and new technology, are longer-term fixes.
It could be too late by the time the government solutions come through, Kann said.
Fine Cotton’s survival is not just important for its workers. As owner of one of Canada’s only large-scale dye houses, the manufacturer is also crucial to Jerico, an Ontario clothing maker that prides itself on a fully domestic supply chain.
If that dye facility closes, Jerico will not be able to dye and finish knitted fabrics at scale in Canada, said Salmaan Andani, managing director at Jerico.
In Andani’s telling, manufacturers like his would be forced to source products overseas, and the country’s knitting and apparel manufacturing industry could unravel, link by link.
Andani said the tariffs mean the company will likely lose all of its US exports, which account for up to 10 per cent of sales.
He has C$22,000 worth of products ready to ship to the University of San Francisco, which ordered from Jerico because the institution wanted to support ethical, organic manufacturing, he said. It will now cost the school an extra C$8,600 to receive the shipment, so the two parties agreed to put it on hold instead of cancelling.
Redwood Classics Apparel is another Canadian manufacturer expecting a complete loss of US sales, currently about 25 per cent of production.
Kathy Cheng, an immigrant from Hong Kong, co-owns the business with her dad. A clothing wholesaler, Redwood has supplied brands such as Roots Canada and Holt Renfrew from its Toronto factory, which employs about 80 people.
Cheng describes her operation as a “love story to Canada”: giving back to the community that embraced her family by insisting on manufacturing domestically.
She wants Canadian corporations to choose Canadian partners, which can move the needle for a small business like hers. She said she does not need to cut staff for now, thanks in part to more inquiries for corporate apparel orders from local firms.
Cheng has also received order requests from longtime American customers since the tariffs kicked in. But because neither side can absorb the 50 per cent surcharge, she, like Andani, has put these orders on hold.
Devastating blow
Kevin Nixon runs a honey farm in southern Alberta and sells as much as half his production across the US border. He shipped a few loads in early August to beat the tariff deadline.
He does not know if his US buyers can absorb a 50 per cent increase in price, but said he cannot take the hit because his margins are already thin. Meanwhile, he’s trying to wrap up the harvest season and market this year’s crop.
“We’re in limbo,” Nixon said. “It’s stressful.”
For others, Canada’s counter-tariffs hurt more than the initial tariff blow.
Cloverdale Paint makes industrial paint in British Columbia, but its steel cans are made in the US. As of Sept 8, those containers are subject to a 50 per cent levy, up from 25 per cent.
Altogether, Cloverdale president Darrin Noble expects tariffs from both sides of the border to shrink profitability by 20 per cent, which will likely come out of the bonuses of the firm’s more than 1,100 Canadian employees.
“It’s devastating,” he said.
Noble is asking the Canadian government for relief from the levy on imports of steel cans. Cloverdale benefitted from a similar programme instituted in March 2025, during the first round of the trade war. That time, the support came through in a matter of weeks.
Henry of Pelham Family Estate Winery expects the duties to kill all of its exports to the US.
But Paul Speck, who owns and runs the business with his two brothers in St Catharines, Ontario, counts himself as a winner of the trade war.
Less than 1 per cent of his sales go to the US, and business jumped 25 per cent after the province banned US alcohol, including wine, from government-controlled stores. In turn, Speck is switching to European providers for farm equipment that he used to buy from the US.
Grassroots support is a familiar sentiment to Nixon, the honey farmer. Days after the tariffs went into effect, people from all over Canada began asking to buy a few jars to help out a Canadian business caught in the trade war.
“I had people from Vancouver Island to Ontario emailing,” Nixon said. “We’ll work through it.” BLOOMBERG

Beyond the flight: Why community can make or break aliyah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:48:31 UTC
23:48:31 KST

Making aliyah is only the beginning. For many new immigrants, the harder question comes afterward: where in Israel can they build a life in which they genuinely feel they belong?
That question was at the center of a panel at ynet Global’s Aliyah Live Summit, where Attorney Itzhak Lax, chairman of Ofek Israeli; Edna Weinstock-Gabay, CEO and director general of Keren Hayesod; Yosef Bergman of the Aliyah and Integration Ministry; and Rabbi Avi Berman, executive director of OU Israel, argued that successful absorption should be measured not simply by how many people arrive, but by whether they find the right community and build a sustainable life in Israel.
Lax said Israeli communities themselves need to be prepared to receive newcomers.
He described three elements as critical: strong local leadership, Israeli families willing to mentor new immigrants and what he called a “culture of invitation.”
“We have to let the olim feel that we really want them,” Lax said.
For Weinstock-Gabay, that sense of belonging can start even before aliyah.
She highlighted programs supported by Keren Hayesod that connect Jewish communities abroad with communities in Israel, as well as group aliyah initiatives that allow families to make the move alongside others rather than begin their lives in Israel alone.
“When you come with a group, it helps a lot,” she said. “You have a strong relationship that connects you, and it makes everything much, much easier.”
Finding the right place — not simply reaching Israel
Bergman said one of the biggest changes in the way Israel thinks about immigration is the recognition that simply getting an oleh onto a plane is not enough.
He compared earlier waves of aliyah to a paratrooper whose primary goal was simply to land safely. Today, he said, the ambition should be much greater.
“We want that oleh to land on his feet, shake off the dust and be able to run ahead,” he said.
That means helping prospective immigrants determine which Israeli city and community best suit their profession, family structure and lifestyle.
“It’s not only making aliyah,” Bergman said. “It’s finding the right place for you.”
The Aliyah and Integration Ministry, he said, works with municipalities and organizations serving different immigrant communities and also sends advisers abroad to meet prospective olim and understand their individual needs before they move.
If immigrants arrive in Israel, fail to find their place and eventually leave, Bergman warned, the consequences can extend beyond one family.
“They’re a bad ambassador,” he said, explaining that friends and relatives considering aliyah may then hear that the move did not work out.
The social side of absorption
Berman said one of the most overlooked challenges is recreating the community structure many Jews had abroad.
In Diaspora communities, a synagogue can function not only as a place of worship but as the center of a family’s social and communal life. In Israel, that structure does not always exist in the same way.
Berman said this can be especially significant for women who spend their first year focused on helping children settle into schools and activities and may not immediately enter the workforce.
“When women are not finding their social community, it makes no difference how successful the man is going to be and how well his job is going to be,” he said. “A happy family is what stays in Israel.”
OU Israel has therefore invested in English-language religious, educational and social frameworks designed to give newcomers a familiar base while they gradually integrate into Israeli society.
The organization has also spent more than two years mapping where English-speaking immigrants are settling across Israel.
Berman said it has identified 475 communities with either a significant Anglo population or at least 20 English-speaking residents. The information is intended to eventually help prospective olim identify communities that better match their needs.
A different way to measure success
Lax argued that Israel should also rethink how it evaluates aliyah.
“We measure all the time how many olim arrived in Israel,” he said. “I think that we have to measure how they integrate into Israeli society.”
That means asking whether immigrants have suitable jobs, whether their children are thriving in school and whether they have friends and a meaningful place in their communities.
For the panelists, those questions ultimately determine whether aliyah becomes more than relocation.
As Berman put it, Israelis also have a role to play: recognizing what newcomers bring to the country and helping them turn the decision to move into a lasting sense of belonging.
“We’re a country of immigrants,” Bergman said.

Germany sending ‘urgently needed’ Patriot air-defence missiles to Ukraine

- The UK announced £100 million to supply interceptors, ammunition, and drones to support Ukraine's air defence.
- Ukraine seeks about 1,000 Patriot missiles but most deliveries will only start in coming years, urging allies to provide current stockpile missiles now.
AI generated
BERLIN – Germany is sending Ukraine further “urgently needed” interceptor missiles for Patriot air-defence systems from its own military stockpiles, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said on Sept 8.
“I have decided... to deliver urgently needed PAK-2 interceptor missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to Ukraine,” Pistorius said, during an online meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group.
He also appealed to other supporters of Ukraine “to look into their own stocks and make similar deliveries”.
However, Pistorius did not specify the number of interceptors or mention a timeline.
Faced with Moscow’s intensified ballistic missile strikes on the capital, Ukraine has warned of its urgent need for US-made Patriots amid dwindling supplies.
Patriot interceptors are among the few air-defence weapons in Kyiv’s arsenal that are capable of shooting down ballistic missiles, which fly at high speeds on steep trajectories.
However, the United States is conserving its stocks after having used a large number of Patriot interceptors during the war with Iran.
US deliveries of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine have been drastically reduced, and other countries are also clamouring for the weapons.
“I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
“But please, if in doubt, decide in favour for Ukraine.”
The United Kingdom announced earlier on Sept 8 that it was releasing £100 million (S$170 million) for interceptors, large-calibre ammunition, and drones for Kyiv.
Ukraine’s new acting defence minister, Yevgeniy Khmara, underscored the importance of air-defence weaponry as the country tries to fend off increased Russian drone and missile strikes.
“Just last night, the enemy has resorted to another mass air attack,” Khmara said at the meeting.
Ukraine is currently placing orders for roughly 1,000 Patriot interceptors with help from supporters and a loan from the European Union, Khmara said.
“However, the majority of these missiles will only start to be shipped in the coming years, which is why we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today,” Khmara told Pistorius and other officials from countries supporting Ukraine. AFP

German students post worst PISA scores since testing began
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:46:34 UTC
23:46:34 KST

Ayhan Simsek
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Fifteen-year-old German students recorded their weakest results since the OECD launched its PISA tests 25 years ago, with about one in three students failing to reach basic levels in reading and mathematics, according to findings released on Tuesday.
Students scored 486 points in science, 465 in reading and 464 in mathematics. Average 2025 results in Germany were lower than in 2022 in mathematics and reading, and about the same as in 2022 in science. About one in four 15-year-olds lacked basic science skills.
“What we are seeing today is, without any doubt, an alarming finding,” Education Minister Karin Prien told reporters in Berlin. “Too many young people are failing to achieve the basic competencies required for their future educational paths,” she said, adding that social media, artificial intelligence, and the difficult circumstances of students from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds were major challenges.
The Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) checks whether 15-year-olds can use knowledge in everyday tasks, such as understanding a longer email, comparing prices or reading a chart. About 6,700 students at some 250 German schools took part in spring 2025. Worldwide, some 760,000 students in 91 countries and economies sat the 2025 tests.
Despite the historic slump at home, Germany stayed close to the OECD average of 482 in science, 461 in reading and 463 in mathematics. Fourteen OECD countries, including Estonia, Canada, Switzerland and Austria, scored higher overall. The Netherlands and France were close to Germany.

Ukraine shows a home-built missile designed to hit ballistic targets for the first time, the Koral, at Poland’s MSPO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:44:04 UTC
23:44:04 KST

Ukraine has shown off, for the first time, a home-built missile designed to shoot down ballistic targets. The Koral surface-to-air missile appeared at the MSPO defense expo in Poland, in an Ukroboronprom image showing a launch from a self-propelled launcher on a Czech Tatra truck chassis, Militarnyi reports.
It is unclear what is meant by “ballistic targets.” Russia has a wide range of ballistic weapons, from Iskander ballistic missiles to Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles.
More broadly, the term “ballistic target” can refer to an object following a ballistic trajectory after the powered phase of its flight has ended, with its subsequent motion governed primarily by gravity and aerodynamic drag. This category can also include rockets fired by multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), such as the Grad and Smerch.
Evolution of the Koral
The missile weighs 450 kg, including a 36-kg warhead. Its guidance system combines inertial navigation, radio correction, and an active radar homing seeker. The missile is 4.8 meters long and has a diameter of 230/300 mm.
At the initial stage, the “Koral” was advertised with significantly more modest specifications: an engagement range of up to 30 km, an engagement altitude of up to 10 km, a weight of around 300 kg, and a 25-kg warhead. The missile was 4.33 meters long and had a diameter of 230/260 mm. At the same time, the designers emphasized that the specific specifications could vary depending on the customer’s requirements.
History of the developement
Development of the “Koral” began as early as 2016. Initially, the project was conceived as part of a ship-based surface-to-air missile system. In 2021, the Luch State Design Bureau unveiled a full-scale mock-up of the missile for the first time at the “Arms and Security” exhibition.
At the time, the “Koral” was presented as a unified, modular missile for both land-based and shipborne SAM systems, with potential applications as an air-to-air missile as well.

Swiss soldiers increasingly unfit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:44:00 UTC
23:44:00 KST

Swiss soldiers increasingly unfit
The physical fitness of Swiss soldiers has declined since 2006, according to a study. Yet the soldiers say they are fitter than ever.
Since the mid-2000s, the average number of points achieved by recruits in the army’s fitness test has fallen from 74.2 to 70.4, the Federal Office of Sport said in a press release on Tuesday.
However, the proportion of soldiers who consider themselves to be fit has increased. It rose from 40% to 56% between 2006 and 2024.
This percentage has also risen among female recruits, from 50% to 64%. This is understandable, as fitness test results have improved for female soldiers. The number of points scored has risen from 45.4 to 49.9.
More
Swiss militia facing shortage of recruits
“Everyone tends to overestimate their own performance when self-assessing,” said the Federal Office of Sport. And the most popular sporting activities at present are often not sufficiently targeted to develop the specific skills required for the army’s fitness test, it said.
The federal office has analysed data from some 700,000 military personnel over a period of nearly 20 years. The Swiss Federal Institute of Sport in Magglingen, the Swiss Armed Forces and the University of Zurich took part in the study. It is described as one of the largest long-term studies in Europe on the objectively measured physical fitness of young adults.

====================================================================================================

50 years after his death, Mao still shapes China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:44:00 UTC
23:44:00 KST

50 years on, Mao still matters in China
September 8, 2026
On September 9, 1976, Mao Zedong died. The revolutionary leader who led the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to power and founded the People's Republic of China left behind a profoundly contradictory historical legacy.
He shaped the narratives of revolution, nation-building and national independence, but also left behind immense social trauma as a result of successive political campaigns and persecutions.
50 years of transformation: How far has China moved away from Mao?
Over the past five decades, China has undergone radical changes.
When Mao died, China was still a poor and relatively isolated communist state. Today, it is the world's second-largest economy, deeply embedded in the supply and value chains of global capitalism, with a vast private sector, a large urban middle class and a highly digitalized society.
Zhang Lun, a professor at Cergy-Paris University, said Mao left behind four major political legacies: the authoritarian and highly centralized political system; a model of governance that relies on revolution and political campaigns to solve social problems; populist tendencies marked by anti-elitism and anti-rationalism; and utopian visions of egalitarianism and moralism.
From the perspective of political legacies, Zhang told DW, the most fundamental change in China over the past five decades has been "de-Maoization" — while its greatest challenge has been that this process was never fully completed.
The legacy that never left: the party's supremacy
Mao's name remains written into the CCP's constitution, while his thought remains part of China's official ideology and his portrait still hangs in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Mao helped forge the Chinese Communist Party, and his insistence on the party's supremacy over the state and society has remained a fundamental principle throughout the decades, said Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt, professor at the University of Zurich.
Veteran journalist and political commentator Chang Ping agrees, adding that what has truly endured is the institutional core of the principle that "the party leads everything," serving a state vision of being able to "concentrate resources to accomplish major tasks."
The CCP, he said, can pursue such objectives "at all costs" — meaning the interests of ordinary people can be sacrificed to the maximum extent necessary to preserve the regime.
A return to the 'Mao era?'
Under current leader Xi Jinping, a number of political concepts and methods of governance associated with the Mao era — such as ideological unity and the spirit of "struggle" — have again attracted attention.
Xi's actions such as abolishing the presidential term limits, strengthening his personal authority and the incorporation of his political thought into the party and state constitutions have invited comparisons between him and Mao.
Chang argues that the very term "return" is misleading, since elements of the Mao era have never fully disappeared.
Zhang holds a similar view.
Authoritarian rule, political rigidity, weak rule of law and the lack of effective guarantees for citizens' rights, he argues, are not only important elements of Mao's political legacy but also among the most significant continuities between the Mao era and China's current political system, he underscored.
And Xi, who personally suffered during the Cultural Revolution, seems even move closer to Mao-era policies.
"What Xi learned from the Cultural Revolution was not the lesson of a victim, but the lesson of power," Chang told DW.
The lesson was not that "such a system must never exist again," but rather that "whoever loses power is at the mercy of others," he added.
Felix Wemheuer, professor of modern China studies at the University of Cologne, echoed this view.
"The conclusion Xi appears to have drawn from his own experience of the Cultural Revolution was clearly not that Mao should be completely abandoned," he told DW, "but rather that, for political reasons, Mao's historical status as the founder of the state, the military and the party must be upheld."
Wemheuer views the current CCP leadership's approach to Mao as "fundamentally Machiavellian and pragmatic."
In economic policy, for instance, there is no sign of a return to the Mao era, he said. Today's China operates a highly dynamic model of state capitalism, with a mix of ownership forms coexisting and maintaining a strong private sector. Nor is there any indication that China intends to return to the Mao-era model of a communist welfare state.
The same applies to the idea of "self-reliance." Today's China could hardly afford to withdraw from the global economy and international supply chains.
Xi remains a product of the system Mao created
Experts say similarities between Mao and Xi can be seen in areas such as the emphasis on the CCP's supremacy, the elevation of a core leader, and populist elements that stress a close connection between the people and the leadership.
Wemheuer argues that Xi possesses neither Mao's historical authority nor his personal charisma.
The two also exercise power in fundamentally different ways. Mao could bypass party institutions, go for years without convening a party congress and mobilize the masses against the party and state apparatus.
Mao himself was a populist with certain anarchic tendencies, Wemheuer said, and even tolerated the temporary collapse of the party-state system at the grassroots level in 1966-67.
Xi, by contrast, would never allow such a situation to occur, the expert stressed. Xi places greater emphasis than Mao on control and top-down governance, consolidating power by strengthening institutions and the party apparatus.
Mittelstaedt likewise cautions against equating Xi with Mao.
First, Mao was a revolutionary who destroyed existing institutions during the Cultural Revolution and was fundamentally anti-bureaucratic in his political orientation. Xi, Mittelstaedt argues, does the opposite.
Second, Mao stood above the party. His power came from "being Mao himself" rather than from the party's institutional structures.
Xi, by contrast, is "a party man through and through." His authority derives from party institutions, and he governs through those institutions, Mittelstaedt pointed out.
"At the end of the day," he told DW, "Xi Jinping remains a product of the system Mao created."
Mao nostalgia among younger generations?
China has also seen recurring waves of Mao nostalgia, with some Chinese citizens invoking Mao online and expressing longing for what they describe as an era without social inequality, when everyone supposedly had enough to eat.
Chang argues that what they are longing for is neither Mao himself nor the real Mao era.
The actual Mao era, Mittelstaedt said, was marked by rigid hierarchies, pointing to the urban-rural household registration divide, different levels of privileges and supplies for officials, and a system in which one's family background could determine one's fate. It was, in many respects, more unequal than China today — and voicing grievances could be fatal.
The imagined vision of a more equal world, he underlined, is therefore actually an indictment of the present situation, with widening inequality, soaring housing prices and persistently limited social mobility.
Still, many express the dissatisfaction with contemporary reality through Mao's image and language.
In Chang's view, this is connected to the continuing contraction of space for public criticism in China. When forms of political expression such as independent trade unions, street protests, free media and opposition parties are tightly restricted, Mao remains a historical symbol that official ideology cannot entirely exclude.
The result is a striking irony, he said, pointing to some people invoking Mao's language of anti-bureaucracy, resistance to oppression and even "rebellion" to criticize what they see as corruption, inequality and abuses of power in Xi's China today.
Mittelstaedt said this makes Mao a double-edged sword. He remains an important symbol of the CCP's political legitimacy — but parts of the revolutionary language he left behind can also be turned into standards by which contemporary reality is measured and criticized.
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

Hong Kong students drop in global rankings for maths, science and literacy
City’s students drop out of global 10 in Pisa’s science section – the first time since Hong Kong joined international assessment
Hong Kong secondary school students’ performance has fallen in an international assessment focused on three core subjects, with their science score dropping out of the global top 10 for the first time in the study’s history.
Experts said on Tuesday that the decline in Hong Kong scores in the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) was partly due to the post-Covid impact on study habits and learning motivation.
Held every three years, Pisa is a worldwide study by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) that tests 15-year-old students on reading, mathematics and science.
The latest study, which ranked 91 countries and economies, was conducted from May to July 2025.
Each cycle since 2012 has also featured an “innovative domain”, which refers to a rotating test topic that measures real-world skills.

Russian singer Larisa Dolina awarded large payout from defendants convicted in fraud case over her apartment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:42:40 UTC
23:42:40 KST

Russian singer Larisa Dolina awarded large payout from defendants convicted in fraud case over her apartment
Moscow’s Lefortovo District Court has ordered the defendants convicted in the fraud case over singer Larisa Dolina’s apartment to pay more than 114 million rubles, the press service of the city’s courts reported.
Under the ruling, Angela Tsyrulnikova and Andrei Osnova — a courier and a money mule, respectively — must compensate Dolina for her losses and pay more than 335,000 rubles in state fees.
Dolina had initially sought 176 million rubles in damages, but her claim was later reduced to 114 million rubles after another court awarded her a separate 61-million-ruble claim.
Dolina had originally filed suit against four defendants in the case: Tsyrulnikova, Osnova, Dmitry Leontyev, and Artur Kamenetsky.
The case against Leontyev and Kamenetsky was separated into its own case after Leontyev signed a contract with the Defense Ministry and left for the war in Ukraine, while Kamenetsky was never notified of the hearing. According to reports by the Russian business daily Kommersant, the court was unable to determine where Kamenetsky is serving his sentence.
More on the case and each defendant's role
The case involves the sale of Larisa Dolina’s apartment in Moscow’s Khamovniki district.
According to investigators, fraudsters called Dolina in 2024 and convinced the singer that criminals were trying to steal her money and take out a loan against her apartment.
Posing as employees of Russia’s Federal Financial Monitoring Service and Federal Security Service, the fraudsters persuaded Dolina to transfer her savings to \“safe accounts\” and sell her central Moscow apartment for 112 million rubles.
Investigators said Kamenetsky, Osnova, and Leontyev opened bank cards that Dolina used to transfer the money and later cashed out part of the funds, while Tsyrulnikova collected cash from Dolina in person. The defendants claimed they had been used \“in the dark\” and did not know they were taking part in a fraud scheme.
A court convicted them of large-scale fraud in November 2025, sentencing Osnova to four years in prison, Kamenetsky to seven years in prison, Leontyev to seven years in prison, and Tsyrulnikova to seven years and three months in prison.
The case gained even more attention after Moscow resident Polina Lurye, unaware of the fraud, bought the apartment. Dolina, who had already handed over the sale proceeds to the fraudsters after being deceived, then went to court in an attempt to reclaim the property.
Lower courts initially upheld Dolina’s ownership of the apartment and ruled that she owed Lurye nothing, leaving Lurye with neither the property nor her money. The case eventually reached Russia’s Supreme Court, which ruled in December 2025 that the apartment belonged to Lurye.

Bosnia expels two Serbian embassy diplomats in protest over Mladic funeral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

Bosnia expels two Serbian embassy diplomats in protest over Mladic funeral
SARAJEVO, Sept 8 - Bosnia expelled two Serbian diplomats on Tuesday and suspended plans to sign a regional cooperation accord in protest over Belgrade's decision to hold a lavish public funeral for former Bosnian Serb General Ratko Mladic.
Mladic died on August 27 in The Hague, where he had been serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity for his role in the siege of Sarajevo and the 1995 massacre of at least 8,000 Muslims at Srebrenica.
Thousands of people attended his funeral in Belgrade on Monday, in a demonstration of how Mladic remains revered among many in Serbia and Bosnia's autonomous Serb Republic. Government officials were among the mourners at the funeral, which was presided over by the head of Serbia's Orthodox Church.
Bosnia's Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic said two people at Serbia's embassy in Sarajevo, military attache Milan Dulanovic and intelligence adviser Danko Maksimovic, had 48 hours to leave the country. He did not elaborate.
Konakovic said Bosnia would also abstain from signing a memorandum on good neighbourly relations and cooperation of the Western Balkan countries, which is due to be signed in Montenegro on October 1.
"With such a Serbia we will not sign documents on good neighbourly relations," he told a press conference, adding that Serbia had "crossed all red lines" with its handling of Mladic's death and funeral.
Konakovic said on Monday that Bosnia would withdraw most staff from its embassy in Belgrade in protest at Serbia's handling of Mladic's funeral.
On Tuesday, Konakovic criticised a lack of response from the Serbian government after supporters displayed a gigantic picture of Mladic at a soccer match in Belgrade at the weekend, with his finger pointing "Direction Potocari," the site of the 1995 massacre near the town of Srebrenica.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described on Tuesday the images of Mladic's funeral as "shocking" and said the presence of some senior Serbian officials there "demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe's recent history" and could undermine Belgrade's plans to join the EU.
In New York, U.N. Under-Secretary-General and Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide Chaloka Beyani said he was "following with concern the public expressions of genocide denial and glorification of convicted war criminal, the deceased Ratko Mladic, in Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina."
"The large-scale public commemoration of Mladić, including the participation of political figures and official ceremonial elements, is both deeply inappropriate and profoundly disturbing," he said in a statement.
Beyani said the U.N.'s International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and the International Court of Justice had "determined conclusively that a genocide was committed in Srebrenica in 1995."
He noted that Mladic was convicted by the ICTY in 2017 of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes and sentenced to life imprisonment, a sentence upheld on appeal in 2021. REUTERS

UK wargames defence supply chains for crisis resilience
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:41:59 BST
23:41:59 KST

The Ministry of Defence is using industry wargaming and scenario planning to test weaknesses in defence supply chains, including their ability to cope with disruption and increase production during periods of greater demand, Defence Minister Luke Pollard has said.
The work was disclosed in a written parliamentary answer to Labour MP Callum Anderson, who asked what discussions the Defence Secretary had held with industry on strengthening supply chain resilience.
Pollard said: “The Ministry of Defence engages regularly with industry to strengthen supply chain resilience through the Defence Industrial Joint Council (DIJC) Readiness and Resilience Working Group and the Industrial Resilience Programme (IRP).”
Those forums bring government and defence companies together to examine vulnerabilities within the industrial base, including strategic dependencies and the availability of materials needed to sustain defence production. The MOD is also using the Defence Supply Chain Capability Programme alongside exercises intended to test how industrial networks would perform under different pressures.
Pollard stated: “The Department also works closely with industry through the Defence Supply Chain Capability Programme (DSCCP) and a programme of industry wargaming and scenario planning activities.”
The exercises are being used to examine how supply chains respond to stress, where vulnerabilities could restrict the availability of equipment or components, and what measures could improve the ability of industry to increase output when required.
Pollard said: “These engagements help improve understanding of supply chain vulnerabilities, test resilience under a range of stress scenarios, and inform measures to strengthen supply chain visibility, surge capacity and support to Defence operations.”
The reference to surge capacity concerns the ability of the defence industrial base and its suppliers to increase production or support activity above normal peacetime levels when operational demand rises. Critical minerals are also being considered as part of the resilience work. Defence equipment can depend on specialised materials sourced through complex international supply chains, making security of supply one of the issues being examined between the MOD and industry.

According to him, these funds would make it possible to finance drones and ensure their stable supply through the end of this year and into early next year.
“Up to 90% of our success on the battlefield is driven by drones,” he added.
The minister asked partners to make the necessary financial decisions by November so that their impact could be felt on the battlefield as early as winter. He also emphasized the need to maintain an adequate level of defense support for Ukraine in 2027.

Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats as relations worsen
- Published
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán says 10 Russian diplomats have been ordered to leave Budapest for taking part in "unacceptable" activities.
"This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote on social media, without giving details.
Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the European Union under Viktor Orbán for years, but since his election defeat in April the new government has pivoted away from his pro-Kremlin stance.
The Hungarian foreign minister said the decision to expel the diplomats "does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia", but the foreign ministry spokeswoman in Moscow said "the response to the Russophobic lobby will be harsh and painful".
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow from the moment his Tisza party was elected in April. He and the foreign minister have both called on Russia to bring an end to the war in Ukraine.
In May Anita Orbán summoned the Russian ambassador to protest against a big drone attack on the Transcarpathia region of Ukraine that is home to a large Hungarian minority. Commentators have pointed out that her predecessor had not summoned the ambassador since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion in 2022.
Then last month Magyar formally broke with the previous Fidesz government's policies, with new guidelines spelling out that Russia's conduct in Ukraine "poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, and also puts the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia in serious danger".
Russia's Ambassador to Budapest, Evgeny Stanislavov, reacted bitterly to Anita Orbán's intention to continue "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules".
Budapest's promise of pragmatic co-operation was worth absolutely nothing, he complained, adding that Hungary's "extremely unfriendly step constitutes an unprecedented and ungrounded escalation".
Before Magyar was voted into office, Hungary had for years insisted on maintaining close relations with Moscow, partly citing cheap Russian oil imports. Viktor Orbán objected to the EU's supply of aid to Ukraine and repeatedly delayed packages of sanctions on Russia.
Ahead of the April elections, independent Russian investigative website Agentsvo reported that 15 of the 47 Russian embassy staff in Budapest were linked to Russian intelligence agencies and six more might be linked.
Former Hungarian foreign intelligence deputy head András Telkes told the BBC that even though "Russian spying activity" had been investigated before the election, the Fidesz government had prevented any action being taken.
The Russian embassy in Budapest had also rejected as false a report alleging that three Russian military intelligence officers had travelled to Budapest to influence the Hungarian vote.
Russia has routinely denied its embassies are used for espionage. However, hundreds of Russian diplomats have been expelled across Europe since 2022, and Russia has responded in kind.
Telkes told the BBC that the big question now was how Moscow would respond: "If 10 Hungarian diplomats were to be expelled from Moscow, in a tit-for-tat move, that would effectively close the Hungarian embassy there."

AI generated
LONDON – Flights at major British airports were disrupted on Sept 8 by a technical fault at air traffic control provider NATS, the latest in a series of failures that renewed questions about the resilience of Britain’s aviation infrastructure.
The cancellation of hundreds of flights and delays to hundreds more renews scrutiny on NATS three years after a flight-plan processing failure caused even more widespread disruption.
As passengers waited for information in departure halls across the country on Sept 8, airlines questioned whether the country’s air traffic control system was fit for purpose.
NATS said at 1934 BST (2.34am Singapore time on Sept 9) that the issue, which had impacted its flight data processing system, has been resolved.
It had earlier said that “safety was not compromised.”
“Recovery from today’s system issue has taken longer than we had hoped. Our system issue is now resolved, we are operating normally and working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights,” NATS said on X.
Hundreds of flights delayed and many cancelled
Close to a thousand flights were disrupted on Sept 8, including to and from the largest UK airport, Heathrow.
Data on flight-tracking platform FlightAware said some 490 departures were delayed at six airports, including Heathrow, Gatwick, London City, Luton, Edinburgh and Bristol as of 1518 GMT (11.18pm in Singapore).
Some 525 arrivals at those six airports were either cancelled or delayed, the website data shows.
At Heathrow, 38 of 661 scheduled arrivals had been cancelled or were unable to operate, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.
British Airways was the most affected carrier at the airport, cancelling 16 of 333 scheduled departures.
Europe’s traffic-filled skies
Air traffic control is a tightly timed system in Europe’s extremely busy skies.
Aviation analyst John Strickland said the consequences of even a relatively short outage can be severe because delays quickly cascade through tightly scheduled airline networks.
“A few hours of outage may on the face of it sound limited but the impact is enormous when a substantial number of airports across the UK are affected,” Strickland said.
Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been affected by delays of up to eight hours and that it had cancelled more than 50 flights, calling on NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe to resign.
“How many more failures do passengers have to suffer before overpaid failure NATS CEO, Martin Rolfe, accepts responsibility for his repeated mismanagement and resigns?” Ryanair chief operating officer Neal McMahon said.
NATS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on McMahon’s comments.
Wizz Air also called for urgent reform of the air traffic controller, saying airlines, passengers and airports should not continue to bear the consequences of recurring system failures.
“A critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill. NATS is simply not fit for purpose in its current form,” Wizz Air said.
Britain’s aviation regulator said it would expect NATS to share a full report of the Sept 8 incident.
The Civil Aviation Authority said it would then consider whether any further steps need to be taken to secure the reliability of the UK’s air traffic control system.
In 2024, the CAA said NATS needed to review its contingency plans for outages after the automatic processing of flight plans had malfunctioned a year earlier, causing chaos across Britain’s airports.
Airline bosses said that outage had cost them over £100 million (S$170 million) in refunds and compensation.

Israel’s opposition could secure a parliamentary majority if a new party led by Yoaz Hendel joins its bloc, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies would win just 47 seats, according to a new poll published Tuesday.
The survey, conducted by the private Lazar Research Institute and published by Israeli daily Maariv, projects 57 seats for the opposition parties and four for a new party led by Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha.
If the Hendel-Zelekha party joins the opposition, the bloc would reach 61 seats, the minimum threshold needed to form a government in Israel’s 120-member Knesset.

The Joint List would take seven seats and the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, five.
The Hendel- Zelekha alliance’s projected four seats could therefore determine whether the opposition reaches a governing majority.
The poll surveyed a random sample of 600 Israelis and had a margin of error of 4 percentage points.
The results come ahead of Israel’s general election scheduled for Oct. 27. Political parties submitted their candidate lists Monday, ahead of Tuesday’s deadline.

Army associations told to review private club links
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:35:33 BST
23:35:33 KST

Army Corps and Regimental Associations have been directed to review their links with private members’ clubs and consider cutting ties where club rules or practices may conflict with Army values of equality and respect, the Ministry of Defence has said.
The position was set out in two written parliamentary answers to Conservative MP Mike Wood, who sought details of a previously disclosed review of Armed Forces links with private clubs, including whether it covered single-sex clubs.
Veterans and People Minister Calvin Bailey said: “The then Deputy Chief of the General Staff directed Corps and Regimental Associations to conduct their own reviews of their affiliations with private members’ clubs, including whether any associated clubs have rules, policies or practices that may not align with Army values of equality and respect.”
The MOD stressed that the exercise is not being run as a single Army-wide review. Instead, individual Corps and Regimental Associations have been left to examine their own relationships with private clubs.
Bailey said: “This was not a centrally coordinated Army review. Rather, Corps and Regimental Associations were asked to consider their own arrangements, reflecting the fact that such affiliations are informal, privately funded and managed at Association level.”
Where an association identifies concerns over a club’s rules, policies or practices, it has been asked to consider either pressing the club to change or ending the affiliation. Bailey stated: “Where concerns were identified, Associations were requested to consider engaging with the relevant club to advocate for change, or to disassociate where appropriate.”
Wood also asked whether the review was considering single-sex private members’ clubs. The MOD did not give a separate yes-or-no answer on that point, instead repeating that associations had been asked to examine whether the rules, policies or practices of clubs with which they are affiliated align with Army values of equality and respect.
The decentralised nature of the exercise means there will be no single set of terms of reference or Army-wide deadline for completing the reviews. Bailey added: “Ministers were not asked to approve a central review, and there is no plan to make a statement to Parliament on this matter.”

SC sets condition for Rajpal Yadav’s surrender relief
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday directed actor Rajpal Yadav to deposit Rs 5 crore with its Registry by Wednesday as a condition for exempting him from surrendering to serve his sentence in a cheque-bounce case involving film producer-financier Murli Projects Pvt Ltd.A bench headed by the Chief Justice, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, passed the order after Yadav’s plea was orally mentioned before it, as cited by ANI.The court issued a conditional notice on Yadav’s plea challenging the Delhi High Court’s July 10 judgment upholding his conviction and three-month imprisonment in seven cases under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.The matter will next be heard on September 15.The Delhi high court had earlier directed Yadav to surrender and serve his sentence by September 10 after dismissing his criminal revision petitions challenging his conviction and sentence.The case stems from seven complaints filed by Murli Projects against Yadav, his wife Radha Rajpal Yadav and their film production company over the dishonour of seven cheques issued in connection with financing for the film Ata Pata Lapata.
According to the case records, Murli Projects advanced Rs 5 crore in 2010 for completion of the film. As the film’s release was delayed, the parties subsequently entered into a series of agreements, with the repayment amount revised at different stages.Yadav’s petition states that the original transaction was an investment in the film rather than a loan, and that the cheques were issued as security. Under a third supplementary agreement signed in August 2012, eight post-dated cheques were issued, with the repayment obligation linked to the film’s release.The dispute escalated after Murli Projects approached the Delhi High Court in 2012 over the film and obtained an order restraining the petitioners from creating third-party interests in its rights. Subsequently, seven complaints under Section 138 of the NI Act were filed over the dishonour of seven cheques.
The petitioners, however, rely on a subsequent consent agreement dated April 21, 2013, under which the parties agreed to a full and final settlement of Rs 10.40 crore, including Rs 40 lakh already paid through RTGS.Four fresh post-dated cheques were issued to secure the settlement. Yadav’s plea says the agreement required the earlier eight security cheques to be returned, but Murli Projects instead proceeded with the dishonoured-cheque cases.The trial court convicted Yadav and the other accused in April 2018 in all seven complaints. Yadav was initially sentenced to six months’ imprisonment and fined Rs 1.60 crore in each case.The sentence was later reduced. On May 22, 2019, he was sentenced to three months’ simple imprisonment and fined Rs 1.35 crore in each of the seven cases, with the sentences to run concurrently.

BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Tuesday that Taiwan has never been a country and will never be a country, adding that the Lai Ching-te authorities' deliberate distortion of UNGA Resolution 2758 once again revealed their separatist nature for "Taiwan independence."

From political, legal and procedural aspects, the resolution resolved once and for all the question of the representation of the whole of China, including Taiwan, in the UN, she said, adding that it made clear that there is only one seat of China in the United Nations, and there is no such thing as "two Chinas" or "one China, one Taiwan." ■

Feature: Bumper fishing season beckons, but Turkish fishermen feel the squeeze
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:35:00 CST
23:35:00 KST

ISTANBUL, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- As the clock struck midnight on Sept. 1, ending Türkiye's four-and-a-half-month seasonal fishing ban, Ahmet Kurt, a veteran captain at Istanbul's Kirecburnu docks, gazed across the Black Sea with renewed optimism.
"This will be the best fishing season of the last 20 years," Kurt said confidently as he prepared his crew for the first catch of the new season.
He attributed the expected boom to favorable weather conditions during the spawning season. Early signs in the water suggest a strong run of bonito and anchovies this year, raising hopes of a catch unlike any seen in decades.
Fishing in Türkiye is about far more than putting more seafood on the table. Bordered by seas on three sides, the country depends heavily on its fishing industry, which employs around 250,000 people, according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry.
At the same time, with food prices up 37.5 percent year on year in July, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute, a plentiful catch could provide consumers with a relatively affordable source of protein.
"People should prepare to fill their deep freezers," Kurt said, predicting that bonito prices, now at 200 Turkish liras (about 4.13 U.S. dollars), would halve within a week.
Yet beneath the surface of this apparent windfall lies a more precarious reality. For every consumer welcoming lower prices, a fisherman is grappling with soaring costs.
On a neighboring vessel, veteran fisherman Ozgur Inci leads a 30-member crew paid under a share system, with their earnings tied directly to the size of each catch.
As his crew geared up for what they hoped would be a bumper season, one shadow loomed over Inci: soaring diesel prices. At around 80 liras per liter, fuel costs are now roughly twice as high as they were in previous seasons.
"My boat burns about a ton of diesel in a single night," Inci said, adding that daily operating costs can reach 100,000 liras, with fuel driving expenses at every stage, from casting the nets to getting the catch to market.
The challenge of balancing affordable prices for consumers with the economic sustainability of the fishing industry emerged as a central theme at the season's official opening.
Recep Duzgit, vice chairman of the Chamber of Shipping, warned that protecting fishermen's margins is not a sectoral concern but a national one.
"Behind this labor lies a massive economy," Duzgit cautioned. "When a fisherman goes to sea, multiple sectors are activated, from port workers to transporters, from wholesalers to restaurants."
To help stabilize fishermen's incomes, Duzgit called for a nationwide campaign to increase domestic seafood consumption, arguing that it would both support the fishing industry and encourage healthier eating.
Speaking at a parallel season-opening ceremony in the Aegean province of Izmir, Agriculture and Forestry Minister Ibrahim Yumakli announced concrete state support: investment financing limits for the fisheries sector have been raised from 15 million to 40 million liras, part of a broader effort that has injected billions into the industry over the past 24 years.
Yumakli stressed that the government's goal is to strike a balance between keeping seafood affordable for consumers and protecting fishermen's livelihoods.
Yet for Inci and his crew, as they steam into the dark waters, those measures offer little immediate relief from the high costs they face.
"We want to provide the public with affordable fish, but we also have to survive without operating at a loss," he said. "We are trying to find that balance." ■

====================================================================================================

News Analysis: Europe's drive for competitiveness gets tougher two years after Draghi report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:34:51 CST
23:34:51 KST

WARSAW, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Two years after former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi presented his report on the future of European competitiveness on Sept. 9, 2024, implementation of its recommendations has slowed.
The European Policy Innovation Council's July index showed that 15.7 percent of the 383 recommendations have been fully implemented, while 41.3 percent have been fully or partially implemented. These figures rose by 3.9 and 7.5 percentage points respectively between September 2025 and January 2026, but by only 0.6 and 2.4 points in the following six months.
Europe now faces new challenges on three fronts: energy costs, strategic financing and industrial scale-up.
ENERGY SHOCK RETURNS
The latest Middle East conflict has once again exposed Europe's vulnerability to high energy costs.
Euro area annual inflation is expected to be 3.3 percent in August, up from 2.9 percent in July, according to a flash estimate from Eurostat. In June, the European Central Bank raised its key interest rates by 25 basis points, citing inflationary pressures from the war.
Energy costs are also weighing on trade. The European Union (EU) recorded a 21.8-billion-euro (about 25.2 billion U.S. dollars) goods trade deficit in the second quarter of 2026, its first since the second quarter of 2023. The deficit in energy products widened from 71.3 billion euros (about 82.9 billion dollars) to 101.1 billion euros (about 117.6 billion dollars) and was the main reason the overall balance turned negative.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimated that higher energy prices will reduce euro area growth by 0.5 percentage points in 2026 and 0.2 percentage points in 2027. Private investment was also projected to decelerate because of higher input costs and protracted uncertainty.
MORE CLAIMS ON LIMITED CAPITAL
The Draghi report estimated that meeting its objectives would require an additional 750 billion to 800 billion euros (about 872 billion to 930 billion dollars) in investment each year.
Two years on, that financing challenge has grown, as defense spending rises sharply across the continent.
The European Defense Agency expects defense spending by the EU's 27 members to reach 454 billion euros (about 528 billion dollars) in 2026, or 2.4 percent of GDP, up 36 billion euros (about 41.9 billion dollars) from last year.
The European Central Bank (ECB) estimated annual public funding requirements for defense, and the green and digital transitions, at around 510 billion euros (about 593 billion dollars), at a time when fiscal space is limited in many member states.
The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said the economic effects of higher defense spending are uncertain. Resource competition can push up prices and crowd out private activity, while maintaining debt sustainability may require higher taxes or cuts to other public spending.
The challenge is therefore no longer simply to invest more, but to finance security, energy, digitalization and infrastructure simultaneously without weakening growth elsewhere.
THE SCALE-UP CHALLENGE
Europe's third challenge is turning innovation into scale. In emerging industries such as artificial intelligence (AI), success increasingly depends not only on technology, but also on capital, infrastructure and access to a large market.
ECB research published in August put the total size of U.S. venture capital funds at about 930 billion euros (about 1081 billion dollars), around six times the EU's 150 billion euros (about 174 billion dollars). The ECB also pointed out that Europe's venture capital challenge goes beyond aggregate scale.
Market fragmentation makes scaling harder. The European Commission said firms still face 27 national legal systems and more than 60 company legal forms in place, which can make setting up and expanding businesses slower and more costly.
The Center for European Policy Studies (CEPS) argued that regulatory simplification alone is not enough, with market fragmentation and lack of scale posing more fundamental barriers to global competition.
The infrastructure demands of emerging industries such as AI are also growing. The European Commission says Europe faces a critical deficit in large-scale computing infrastructure. Therefore, the EU is mobilizing 20 billion euros (about 23 billion dollars) for AI gigafactories to expand computing capacity.
Two years after the Draghi report, Europe's competitiveness agenda faces a tougher setting: energy costs have returned as an immediate constraint, strategic demands on capital have multiplied, and technological competition increasingly rewards complete industrial ecosystems. The reforms remain relevant, but the conditions for delivering them have become more demanding. ■

Xi holds phone talks with British PM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:34:48 CST
23:34:48 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday held phone talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Congratulating Burnham on assuming office as British prime minister, Xi said that China and Britain are comprehensive strategic partners.
Despite differences in their social systems and national conditions, the two countries share more common interests than differences, Xi said, urging the two sides to respect and trust each other, transcend differences, seek common ground while reserving differences, and expand mutually beneficial cooperation.
Both governments are committed to developing their economies and improving people's well-being, and the two countries can complement each other's strengths and assist each other, Xi said.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China will further expand opening up in such areas as education, healthcare and finance, all of which offer great potential for bilateral cooperation, Xi said.
Pointing out that China and Britain are both major countries in science and technology with rich resources in education, culture, sports and other fields, Xi called on the two sides to maintain an open and forward-looking mentality and strengthen exchanges and cooperation in various fields.
Xi expressed the hope that the British side will fully protect the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese investors.
Xi noted that China and Britain, as permanent members of the UN Security Council and major economies in the world, both support multilateralism and open trade, and uphold the central role of the United Nations.
The two sides should strengthen communication and coordination within frameworks such as the United Nations, the Group of 20 and the World Trade Organization, and promote an equal and orderly multipolar world and a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization, Xi said. ■

US closes $1.9B loan to restart Iowa nuclear plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:32:47 UTC
23:32:47 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
The US Energy Department announced Tuesday that it had closed a loan of up to $1.9 billion to help NextEra Energy restart the Duane Arnold nuclear power plant in the state of Iowa.
The financing, provided through the department’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing, will support efforts to return Iowa’s only nuclear power plant to service after it ceased operations in 2020.
The 615-megawatt facility in Linn County will provide enough electricity to power nearly 500,000 homes and help meet growing demand in Iowa and across the US Midwest, the department said.
The project is expected to create nearly 1,500 jobs during construction and support more than 450 positions once the plant is operational.
“Returning 615 megawatts of reliable baseload generation will drive down electricity costs, while supporting thousands of American jobs,” Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly said.
NextEra said it plans to restart the facility no later than the first quarter of 2029, subject to approvals from the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission and other authorities.
The company said a study estimated that the restart could generate more than $9 billion in economic benefits for Iowa over 25 years and approximately $75 million in tax revenue during the project’s lifetime.
The restart is also backed by a 25-year agreement under which Google will purchase electricity from the plant.
NextEra Chairman and CEO John Ketchum said bringing new generation online would strengthen the power grid and help prevent the costs of rising electricity demand from being passed on to Iowa families and businesses.
The Duane Arnold plant operated for more than four decades before shutting down. The Iowa Utilities Commission issued NextEra a certificate in June authorizing the facility’s construction and operation.
The financing forms part of the Trump administration’s effort to revive the US nuclear industry as electricity consumption rises, driven partly by artificial intelligence data centers and broader electrification.
The administration has called for 10 large conventional nuclear reactors to be under construction by 2030 and for federal financing to support the restart of shuttered plants.

Air traffic control issue causes flight delays and disruption across UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:32:31 UTC
23:32:31 KST

Hundreds of thousands of air passengers had flights delayed or cancelled after another UK air traffic control technical glitch kept planes grounded for hours on Tuesday.
Airlines demanded action after a “technical issue” at the air traffic control services provider Nats caused the third large-scale stoppage in just over three years.
Flight monitoring website Flightradar24 said more than 1,000 flights had been cancelled at UK airports by about 8pm in an incident that started at about 1pm and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports, including Heathrow and Gatwick.
Nats said on Tuesday evening that work was continuing to assist airlines and airports recover from the disruption, adding: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.”
By the time Nats said it had identified and implemented a fix to restart its flight processing system almost four hours later, most flights scheduled to depart from the London airports and others were yet to take off. The disruption had spread to include incoming flights to much of southern England.
Cancellations and delays were continuing well into Tuesday evening, and British Airways said disruption would affect operations through Wednesday at least, with passengers offered free rebooking until Friday.
Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed and 50 flights cancelled. The knock-on effects hit flights across Europe, according to easyJet. Eurocontrol said some inbound flights were being held at airports abroad, with disruption likely until the evening.
All London airports, as well as Manchester and Birmingham, were among the most directly affected. Flights to and from other airports around the UK, including Edinburgh and Belfast, were also disrupted.
According to the flight monitoring website FlightRadar24, easyJet had 137 flights cancelled, British Airways 111, KLM 26, Eurowings 22 and Ryanair 21 by 5pm.
Nats initially announced at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”. It later identified the problem in its flight processing system, and announced at 4.40pm that it had implemented a fix.
A spokesperson said the fault was not the same as the ones that caused previous outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025.
They said the system was only “starting to recover”.
“We are continuing to work closely with our airline and airport customers on recovery,” they said. “We apologise sincerely for the disruption to people’s journeys today and they should continue to check with their airline.”
The chief executive of Nats, Martin Rolfe, expressed his “huge sympathies to everyone who has been caught up in today’s disruption”.
“We absolutely take responsibility for this,” he told Sky News.
“We never want this sort of thing to happen. I completely understand how frustrating it is for passengers.”
He claims, however, “these things are relatively rare”.
“We resolved it to get back to our systems operating normally,” he added. “But of course, there’s a huge amount of disruption that’s now built up in the system.
“We’re working very closely now with airlines and airports to try to work through the night to make sure that we can get as many people travelling as possible.”
The air traffic control problems follow an “isolated event” a year ago that caused widespread disruption, although it so far appears less severe than the full grounding of flights in August 2023, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry.
However, British Airways said that “the severity of the issue means there will be a significant knock-on impact for customers and colleagues”.
“We were forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights on Tuesday afternoon, inconveniencing tens of thousands of customers,” a spokesperson said.
“This incident was entirely out of our control and incredibly frustrating for our customers and colleagues, with aircraft and crews ending up out of place.”
Heathrow said late on Tuesday that departures had resumed with disruptions but arrivals had been suspended for the rest of the night.
Airlines renewed calls for Nats to be overhauled after the third incident ascribed to its systems in as many years.
Ryanair repeated its calls for Rolfe to resign. The Irish airline’s chief operating officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Families travelling on holiday, people travelling for work and thousands of visitors to the UK have once again paid the price for Nats’ abhorrent failure.”
He said the government should “stop making excuses for repeated Nats failures and appoint a new leader capable of running the UK ATC system”.
Wizz Air said: “A critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill. Nats is simply not fit for purpose in its current form.”
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “I’m aware of a technical issue impacting flights at airports including Heathrow and Gatwick. Technicians have identified the issue and are fixing it as we speak. I know this will be frustrating for passengers and I’m sorry.
“I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job.”

Japan’s foreign reserves fall $79.6B after record yen intervention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:31:09 UTC
23:31:09 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Japan’s foreign reserves fell by $79.6 billion in August following the government’s record intervention to support the yen, official data showed.
The country’s reserve assets declined 6.2% from the previous month to $1.208 trillion as of Aug. 31, according to Japan’s Finance Ministry.
Foreign-currency reserves totaled $994.98 billion, including $839.56 billion in securities and $155.42 billion in deposits.
Japan also held $124.10 billion in gold, $61.17 billion in International Monetary Fund special drawing rights and an $11.42 billion reserve position at the IMF.
The decline followed Japan’s intervention in foreign-exchange markets between July 30 and Aug. 26, during which authorities spent 15.399 trillion yuan ($99 billion) to support the national currency.
The operation was the largest monthly currency intervention ever undertaken by Japan.
Authorities generally finance yen-buying operations by using their foreign-currency assets. However, the monthly reserve figures do not provide a complete breakdown of how much of the decline resulted directly from intervention, security sales or valuation changes.
The sharp reduction highlights the financial cost of defending the yen and could draw attention to Japan’s holdings of foreign government debt, including US Treasury securities.
Markets will next focus on the Bank of Japan’s Sept. 17–18 monetary-policy meeting. Higher Japanese interest rates could provide more lasting support for the yen by narrowing its yield disadvantage relative to other major currencies.

From Toronto to Tel Aviv: New olim share the realities behind starting over in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:30:40 UTC
23:30:40 KST

Making aliyah can involve months of planning, but even careful preparation does not eliminate the surprises that come with building an everyday life in Israel.
At ynet Global’s Aliyah Live Summit, three recent immigrants — Danielle Adessky, Arielle Sabol and Daniel Bielak — spoke about the practical and emotional realities behind the move, from finding an apartment and navigating Hebrew to adjusting to Shabbat and discovering just how different familiar routines can feel in a new country.
All three made Aliyah with the help of Nefesh B’Nefesh, in partnership with Israel’s Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, The Jewish Agency for Israel, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael and Jewish National Fund-USA. They have also been documenting their Aliyah journeys on social media, giving prospective immigrants a glimpse of the experiences that do not always appear in official guides.
For Adessky, who moved from Toronto to Tel Aviv, one of the biggest surprises was the cost of living.
“I come from Toronto, which is already a big, expensive city, and I had been told that Tel Aviv was expensive,” she said. “But I didn’t really understand the extent of it.”
Apartment hunting became another crash course in Israeli life. Adessky searched largely through Facebook Marketplace and quickly learned that rental expectations differ from those in North America, including which appliances come with an apartment.
“I really had to learn how to change those expectations and understand what I can get for my budget here versus what I would have expected back home,” she said.
‘You can prepare — but living it is different’
For Arielle Sabol, who made aliyah with her husband and two young daughters, even speaking Hebrew did not eliminate the adjustment.
“You can prepare for making aliyah,” she said, comparing it to becoming a parent. “You can do everything ahead, but when you get here and live it, it’s a totally different experience.”
Her latest culture-shock moment came at her daughter’s parent-teacher conference, where she found herself struggling to follow the Hebrew despite already knowing the language.
The small moments, she said, can be the most revealing — filling out a school form, arranging medical appointments or finding the products her children were used to at home.
Sabol did much of her apartment search before arriving and hired someone locally to view properties on her behalf. After weeks of moving with her daughters while their belongings were in transit, she said finding the right home made a major difference.
“We literally live in our dream apartment,” she said.
Her four-year-old daughter, meanwhile, appears to be adjusting even faster.
“She made a best friend already,” Sabol said. “They’re like soul sisters, and she did it in five minutes.”
One week into aliyah
Daniel Bielak was only one week into his own aliyah experience when he joined the panel.
Originally from Canada, he said family in Israel helped provide a “soft landing,” though adjusting to the climate while volunteering on a farm in northern Israel came as a shock.
“As a Canadian that really loves winter, I find it sometimes unbearably hot,” he said.
Other surprises have been more positive. After missing a bus, Bielak said people around him simply told him to put out his hand and find a ride — and someone soon stopped and drove him to Afula.
“People here are really nice,” he said.
Bielak described himself as an “aliyah amateur,” a label he sees as an advantage.
“One of the best things about being an amateur is that you’re always able to learn,” he said. “If you want to make something happen, you can go make it happen.”
He plans to begin an MBA at Tel Aviv University and said the move is also part of a broader spiritual journey.
“This is the best place on earth for you to live out your dreams,” he said.
Sharing the parts nobody tells you about
For all three, social media has become a way to document the details prospective olim may not otherwise hear about.
Adessky said she began leaning more heavily into aliyah-related content after deciding to move because she wanted to share her connection to Israel with an audience interested in following the experience.
Sabol said her posts often generate messages from people experiencing the same frustrations or uncertainties.
After sharing how overwhelmed she felt at her daughter’s parent-teacher conference, she said, she received numerous messages from other immigrants who immediately understood.
“It feels really good to be able to share and be part of this new olim community,” she said.
Their experiences also illustrate how integration is built through small adjustments: learning Hebrew, finding the right apartment, adapting family routines and accepting that even ordinary errands may work differently.
Asked what had surprised him most during his first week, Bielak pointed not to bureaucracy or the weather but to the reception he had received.
“How passionately in love the people are with Israel,” he said, “and with the fact that we’re coming home.”
