Everyone knows the F-35 has problems. So why is everyone buying it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:53:31 UTC
22:53:31 KST

The F-35 was supposed to rule the skies. It can barely outrun its problems
The F-35 multi-role fifth-generation fighter has made headlines for various reasons: its deployment in the conflict with Iran, deliveries to nations participating in the F-35 program, new missiles designed for the aircraft, and staggering operational costs. Even though production of the F-35 has surpassed 1,000 units, doubts persist regarding the program’s overall effectiveness and the aircraft’s compliance with all the standards of a fifth-generation fighter. Let’s take a closer look.
In June 2015, a report by an American test pilot appeared online under the title “F-35A High Angle of Attack Operational Maneuvers.” It revealed that the latest F-35 was outperformed in a mock dogfight by the fourth-generation F-16D aircraft. Despite the F-35’s advertised advantages, it struggled to get behind the F-16D and lagged in energy maneuverability and pitch rate. What the media overlooked was that the test involved an experimental prototype of the F-35 that lacked operational combat software. Additionally, this prototype was restricted to a 5.5 G overload limit compared to the F-16’s ability to withstand up to 9 G. Once the F-35 received a full software update (starting with Block 3F), the upgraded versions decisively outperformed F-16s and other fourth-generation aircraft during Red Flag exercises – not through maneuverability, but by leveraging their stealth capabilities at long ranges without entering close combat.
Therefore, the main advantage of the F-35 fifth-generation fighter is its stealth capabilities. For the US, stealth is the defining characteristic of fifth-generation aircraft. This refers to the low radar cross-section achieved through the aircraft’s design and specialized coatings that disrupt radar wave reflection. The American strategy hinges on the belief that stealth aircraft can employ long-range missile systems while remaining undetected by enemy aircraft, effectively avoiding dogfights by striking the enemy from a distance.
The second major advantage of fifth-generation fighters is their capability for network-centric warfare, utilizing information systems that enable not only data sharing but also directing other aircraft and managing drones. An ‘invisible’ aircraft can detect adversaries either directly or through its wingmen and is capable of orchestrating attacks independently or by coordinating strikes with other planes and drones. Technically, the F-35 is already equipped for such operations.
Other characteristics of the F-35 are more problematic. For example, fifth-generation fighters have a powerful engine capable of sustained supersonic flight without using an afterburner. While the F-35 formally meets these criteria, the F-35B and F-35C variants are restricted from flying above Mach 1.2 for extended periods due to risks of thermal damage to their stealth coatings and tail surfaces. How can a supersonic jet not fly at supersonic speeds? Moreover, the F-35A appears to struggle with sustained supersonic cruising. Compounding these concerns are reports in the media regarding the P&W F135 engine. Reportedly, it faces issues like turbine blade wear, overheating, and a shortage of components for timely repairs.
On top of that, the operational cost of the F-35 is historically high. The total cost of the development and lifecycle of the F-35 has soared to nearly $2 trillion and continues to rise, making it the most expensive weapons system in history. For end users, however, the hourly flight cost is what truly matters. Operating an F-35 runs between $35,000 and $42,000 per hour, while standard F-16s operate at around $22,000 per hour. Overall, this is extremely expensive for a mass-produced fighter.
Another area where the F-35 falls short compared to its competitors, including Russia’s Su-57 and likely others, is maneuverability. Of course, if the ‘invisible’ fighter manages to hit its target undetected, it may never have to engage in a dogfight. But should close combat occur, the F-35 will face significant disadvantages against highly agile fifth- and even fourth-generation aircraft.
Those are some of the most obvious issues in the “generation conflict” between different aircraft iterations. However, there are deeper implications tied to the reliance on software and the high costs associated with the aircraft. The software for the F-35 is arguably the most complex in modern weaponry, encompassing over 24 million lines of code. Media outlets frequently report on coding errors and recall the 800+ “unresolved bugs” identified by Pentagon auditors. Yet, a sophisticated aircraft cannot function without powerful software, and this raises the question: How can one make such a complex software system secure?
Given that the F-35 clearly has its share of issues, it leads to another important question, namely: Why is it being produced in such massive quantities? Today, it stands as the only fifth-generation fighter jet in the Western world, with over 1,300 units already built and plans for another 2,000 on the way. In the next decade, more than 20 countries will incorporate these jets into their arsenals. So what’s behind this global trend?
The answer seems to lie not in the aircraft’s capabilities or technological advancements, but strictly in the political arena. The F-35 isn’t just a fighter; it is a symbol of close alignment with the US. Countries that purchase the F-35 gain certain privileges from Washington. For example, Israel possesses carte blanche for combat operations and unrestricted access to US weapons arsenals. As for Germany, it may be acquiring the F-35 because it’s currently the only aircraft on the market certified to carry US nuclear weapons within NATO’s nuclear sharing program. This factor may have played a decisive role in Germany’s decision.
Some countries – potentially South Korea, Japan, and Türkiye – are counting on the F-35’s network-centric warfare and a broad range of munitions while they develop their own viable alternatives to the ‘golden’ F-35. These nations are actively developing their own fifth-generation fighters and are even looking ahead to sixth-generation designs. However, they need a modern aircraft today, and therefore may be willing to overlook certain flaws of the “Battle Penguin” (the unofficial nickname for the F-35 due to its stout appearance). Maintaining strong ties with Washington is crucial for these countries as well. So political commitments and the urgency of having a contemporary fighter jet go hand in hand. After all, they aren’t going to buy Russian Su-57s, are they? Washington and Brussels wouldn’t like that. Though perhaps it wouldn’t be such a bad idea.

New York releases 170,000 pages on 9/11 air quality concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:53:26 UTC
22:53:26 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
New York City has released more than 170,000 pages of previously undisclosed records Tuesday concerning air quality in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.
The documents reveal that officials were aware of serious contamination concerns around Ground Zero while publicly assuring New Yorkers that the air was safe.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the release at City Hall, ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks. The documents, drawn from 68 boxes discovered in a city government office, contain contamination data, air-quality reports and communications between officials that show concerns about toxic exposure and potential legal liability.
Mamdani said the records were being released to provide survivors, first responders and the public with answers that had been withheld for years.
“The suffering did not end once the smoke cleared and the dust settled,” said Mamdani. He added that thousands who worked, lived or studied near Ground Zero faced years of illness.
“As the years pass and the human toll grows, we reckon with the cost of Sept. 11 whenever another New Yorker is stolen from us too soon,” he said.
Mamdani acknowledged the painful reality that officials failed survivors. “People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air,” he said.
The city has committed more than $34 million to establish a public portal where hundreds of thousands of pages will eventually be available free of charge. The first release includes records detailing asbestos contamination and the city’s response to the disaster.

Announcing the summoning of Serbia’s charge d’affaires, the UK Foreign Office said in a statement that Mladic presided over crimes that are "among the worst committed in Europe since the Second World War. "
"The denial and whitewashing of his crimes is an affront to international law and directly undermines regional stability and trust," said a Foreign Office spokesperson.

He was convicted of crimes committed during the 1992-1995 Bosnian War, including genocide for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.

Tunisian journalists protest over media crackdown after colleague’s arrest
TUNIS, Sept 8 - Tunisian journalists protested on Tuesday to demand the release of prominent journalist Mohamed Yousfi, whose arrest has become a new flashpoint amid accusations that President Kais Saied is cracking down on the country's remaining independent voices.
The protesters, who also included activists, gathered outside a court where a judge was questioning Yousfi over illicit enrichment and money laundering charges, which critics say were fabricated to punish him for his outspoken journalism.
Yousfi, a fierce critic of Saied and the editor-in-chief of investigative news website Al-Qatiba, was arrested last Friday as he was preparing to enter Express FM Radio to take part in a radio programme.
His arrest prompted widespread condemnation of Saied’s government, with rights groups saying the case was aimed at increasing a climate of fear among journalists.
"The situation is dark and difficult. Journalists who disturb the authorities are facing legal persecution and fabricated charges," Zied Dabbar, the head of journalists' syndicate SNJT, told Reuters.
"Today journalists either end up in exile or in prison... But we will resist."
Several media figures have been jailed this year, including Zied Heni, Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies, while Khaoula Boukrim was sentenced in absentia in June to four years.
Free speech initially flourished following the 2011 uprising that toppled Zine El Abidine Ben Ali and ignited pro-democracy protests known as the "Arab Spring".
But critics say Saied's accumulation of power in 2021 and decrees he has issued since then have dismantled democratic safeguards and enabled the authorities to pursue many journalists.
The leaders of Tunisia's main opposition parties have been jailed in the last three years, along with dozens of politicians, activists, journalists and businessmen, on charges of conspiring against state security, of money laundering and corruption.
Saied says he will not be a dictator and that freedoms are guaranteed in Tunisia. REUTERS

Some Israeli actions in Syria may amount to war crimes: UN probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:51:22 UTC
22:51:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Some Israeli actions in Syria may amount to war crimes, UN probe says
A UN commission investigating Syria said on Tuesday it was deeply alarmed over Israel's military attacks and actions inside Syrian territory, warning that some actions including the detention of civilians could amount to war crimes.
Presenting an update to the UN Human Rights Council, Commissioner Fionnuala Ní Aoláin said Israeli military operations in southern Syria had become "increasingly sustained and entrenched", with recurring ground incursions, patrols, raids and searches affecting Syrian civilians.
Syria is seeking to rebuild nearly two years after the fall of former President Bashar al-Assad.
Israeli troops invaded a UN-patrolled buffer zone after the collapse of Assad's government in December 2024, a move Israel described as temporary and necessary to secure its border during the political transition.
Israel has since carried out hundreds of strikes on Syrian military infrastructure and invaded and occupied positions deeper into Syria. The Syrian government and the United Nations have said the deployment violates Syrian sovereignty and a 1974 disengagement agreement that followed the 1973 war.
The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria said it had documented the establishment of temporary checkpoints and fixed military infrastructure by Israel on Syrian territory, particularly in the southern provinces of Quneitra and Daraa.
"The Commission is deeply alarmed about continued Israeli violations," Ní Aoláin told the council, saying local residents reported "bewilderment" at Israeli actions while the country undergoes reconstruction.
As of June, the commission had identified 49 Syrians, including two children, detained by the Israeli military on Syrian territory and believed to have been transferred across the border, she said.
"Such acts may amount to war crimes," Ní Aoláin said.
In a statement released alongside the session, the commission said some detainees were being held incommunicado, raising concerns about potential torture or ill-treatment. It said Israeli military activity had caused displacement among residents and described Israel's presence in the area as a "belligerent occupation".
The commission said it agreed with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres that violations of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity were unacceptable and must cease.
Syria's representative welcomed the commission's findings and reiterated Damascus' commitment to cooperate with UN human rights mechanisms while pursuing accountability for abuses committed under the former government.
The Syrian delegate also condemned Israeli military operations, accusing Israel of violating international law and the 1974 disengagement agreement.

EU welcomes derogation allowing Ukraine to purchase key Patriot air defense products
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:51:07 UTC
22:51:07 KST

Melike Pala
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Tuesday welcomed EU member states' agreement to grant Ukraine a derogation allowing it to purchase crucial products needed for Patriot air defense systems.
"Together with NATO Secretary General Rutte, I welcome the agreement by member states on the derogation for Ukraine to purchase crucial products for Patriot air defense systems," von der Leyen said in a statement.
She said the next disbursement of €3.2 billion ($3.7 billion) under the Ukraine Support Loan would enable Kyiv to better protect its airspace against Russian attacks.
"This comes on top of €8.4 billion already disbursed under the Ukraine Support Loan, including for air defense," she added.
Von der Leyen said the European Union would continue working closely with NATO and its allies to support Ukraine and strengthen Europe's defense posture.
EU’s Support Loan terms include a European preference, and Ukraine is expected to buy from European manufacturers first. Derogation is a relaxation or suspension of law to secure foreign-made equipment if no European equivalent exists or cannot be produced at the scale and pace needed.

Police are investigating whether the holes discovered on Sunday in the façade of the joint ministry building in Tallinn may be bullet holes.
On Monday, police received a report that the exterior façade of the joint ministry on Suur‑Ameerika tänav has several holes at different heights that resemble bullet impacts.
Both police and rescue services responded to the scene, and criminalists took samples on site.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on Sept. 8 received letters of credentials of new ambassadors from Thailand, Sweden, the United Kingdom, Azerbaijan and Canada.
Erdoğan welcomed Thailand’s Ambassador to Türkiye Chaturont Chaiyakam, Sweden’s Ambassador Ulrika Funered, Azerbaijan’s Ambassador Rashad Aslanov, UK’s Ambassador Jennifer Elizabeth Anderson and Canada’s Ambassador Marcel Lebleu on Sept. 8.
Souvenir photos were also taken with the new envoys.
Türkiye has enjoyed good relations with all of these countries, particularly Azerbaijan, sharing the motto of “two states one nation.” Türkiye and Azerbaijan have advanced their relationships to the level of strategic partnership that involves economy, trade, energy and transportation as well as security and defense industry.
Türkiye supports the ongoing efforts for the full normalization of ties between Azerbaijan and Armenia with the prospect of boosting stability and welfare in the South Caucasus.
Before being appointed to Ankara, Aslanov was serving as Azerbaijan’s Ambassador to Italy since 2022.
The new U.K. ambassador arrived in Ankara on Aug. 26, announcing the start of her tenure.
Anderson, who previously served as deputy head of mission in Ankara, announced that she had begun her new posting in the Turkish capital in a video shared on social media.
Describing her journey from London to Ankara, Anderson said she had flown to Türkiye many times before, but that this trip was different for her.
Recalling her previous posting in Ankara, Anderson said: “Over the years, I have flown from London to Türkiye many times, including during my time as deputy head of mission in Ankara between 2017 and 2020. But this flight is different. My return to Ankara as the United Kingdom’s ambassador-designate to Türkiye is very special and symbolic for me.”
Noting that seven years had passed since her last posting in Ankara, Anderson said many things had changed in Türkiye during that time.

Child rights body had sought Meta's explanation after taking suo motu cognisance of a BBC Eye report.
NEW DELHI: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) has summoned Meta India's managing director and head of public policy for a hearing on Wednesday, September 9, over allegations concerning advertisements linked to Child Sexual Exploitative and Abuse Material (CSEAM) on Meta's platforms.The summons follows an inquiry initiated by the child rights body after it took suo motu cognisance of a BBC Eye report alleging the presence of advertisements related to CSEAM.The NCPCR had issued a notice to Meta Platforms Inc. on July 3, seeking an explanation from the company over the allegations. Meta submitted its response a week later.
After examining the company's response, the NCPCR has now decided to institute an inquiry to ascertain the facts and circumstances of the matter.As part of the inquiry, the commission has summoned Meta India's Managing Director and Head of Meta India to appear before it on September 9.The proceedings are aimed at determining the facts surrounding the allegations and examining Meta's response to the concerns raised by the child rights body.

Ukraine's Luch presents surface-to-air missile based on Stuhna anti-tank missile
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:48:00 EEST
22:48:00 KST

Ukraine's Luch presents surface-to-air missile based on Stuhna anti-tank missile
Luch, a Ukrainian armaments design office, has presented the RK-2PZ surface-to-air missile, developed based on the Stuhna anti-tank guided missile (ATGM).
Source: Ukrainska Pravda at the MSPO-2026 exhibition in Poland
Details: The RK-2PZ surface-to-air missile is actively used on the battlefield. It is designed for use with the Desna surface-to-air missile system or, after modernisation, the Soviet-era Strela-10 system.
The missile retains the Stuhna ATGM's dimensions and guidance principle: a laser beam transmits commands to a receiver in the missile's rear section.
Once the target is visually detected, the operator locks it for automatic tracking and commands the launch. The system then guides the surface-to-air missile to the target.
The proximity sensor activates when the missile approaches the target. If the missile hits the target directly, the contact sensor activates, triggering the warhead.
The missile weighs 29 kg and carries a 6.1kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead. It is detonated by proximity using onboard sensors or upon direct impact with the target.
The manufacturer has not disclosed detailed specifications for the missile or its typical targets. However, the anti-tank version had a subsonic speed of 200-220 m/s. This makes the missile difficult to use against cruise missiles but suitable for engaging slower-moving drones.
The missile's design also points to its intended use against UAVs. The RK-2PZ has a series of laser proximity sensors around its nose that trigger the warhead when the missile approaches a target. This differs from conventional radio-fuze systems.
Suspilne Kherson, a local branch of the Ukrainian public broadcaster, previously reported on the use of the Ryf, a surface-to-air missile system based on the Soviet-era Strela-10, by the 30th Marine Corps.
The Ryf systems were equipped with surface-to-air missiles that visually resemble the RK-2 and intercepted aerial targets at a range of 4-5 km.

State appeals 17-year sentence for man who posed as woman to direct child sex crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:47:19 UTC
22:47:19 KST

The prosecution on Tuesday appealed the 17-year prison sentence imposed on Uri Alfi, who posed as a woman online and persuaded fathers to sexually abuse their young children, sometimes watching and directing the acts through live video calls.
Alfi spent about a year approaching dozens of men through fictitious accounts and false identities, using technological tools to make the woman he portrayed appear and sound real. He gained their trust through sexual conversations and induced them to perform and record sexual acts.
In several cases, Alfi contacted fathers of young children and instructed them to abuse their children while sending him live or recorded footage. In others, he attempted to persuade fathers to commit further offenses. He also threatened one father with exposure to force him to continue.
Alfi was convicted on 11 counts containing numerous offenses, including causing and attempting to cause rape and indecent acts against minors within their families, extortion by threats, possession of child sexual abuse material, and using minors to produce such material.
The Central District Court in Lod sentenced him on July 12 to 17 years in prison, suspended sentences, and NIS 200,000 in compensation, to be divided among 10 identified victims.
The prosecution is now asking the Supreme Court to increase that sentence substantially, arguing that even the lengthy prison term does not reflect the extreme severity of the conduct, the number of offenses and victims, or the danger Alfi continues to pose.
Conviction remains unchanged under appeal
The appeal concerns only his punishment. It does not challenge his conviction, which followed his admission to the allegations in an amended indictment under a plea agreement.
The District Court found that the online nature of the offenses did not reduce their severity. It said Alfi was the driving force behind the abuse, although the fathers physically committed the acts and bore their own responsibility.
The prosecution’s appeal focuses partly on how the court combined the punishment for the different counts.
The District Court set a separate sentencing range for each, reflecting the appropriate punishment for each criminal episode but then establishing an overall range of 17 to 22 years and imposing the lowest sentence within it.
Prosecutors argue that this created excessive overlap between the punishments. The minimum terms set for the individual counts would total 27 years if added together.
The state is not arguing that all the terms must be served consecutively.
It says, however, that the final sentence failed to give sufficient weight to the fact that the offenses occurred separately and involved different victims.
The appeal also challenges the weight given to Alfi’s personal circumstances and rehabilitation prospects.
At sentencing, the defense emphasized his young age, lack of a previous criminal record, guilty plea, military service, difficult personal history, and participation in treatment while in custody. A private expert retained by the defense said Alfi had rehabilitation potential and recommended treatment.
The defense also argued that Alfi did not physically touch the children himself and that a distinction should be drawn between physical and online offenses.
Court says personal circumstances warrant limited consideration
The District Court accepted that Alfi’s personal history had affected his conduct and found that he had some rehabilitation potential. It nevertheless said the private opinion should receive limited weight and that the circumstances described did not significantly reduce his responsibility.
Prosecutors argue that the court ultimately relied too heavily on that opinion when it placed Alfi at the bottom of the sentencing range.
Alfi declined to undergo an assessment by the state probation service, and the defense accepted for sentencing purposes that he posed a high level of sexual danger.
The state further argues that the combination of online deception and sexual abuse within families made the case exceptionally serious and difficult to detect.
Alfi’s use of technology, the systematic nature of the offenses, the material he retained, and his attempts to escalate the abuse required a stronger punishment to protect the public and deter similar crimes, prosecutors said.

Saudi energy group signs landmark oil, gas agreements with Afghanistan

2026-09-08
13:47:15 UTC

Saudi Arabia’s Delta Energy Group on Monday signed landmark agreements with Afghanistan’s Ministry of Mines and Petroleum covering oil and gas exploration across approximately 9,000 square miles in western Afghanistan.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The agreements also include a natural gas utilization study in Herat and plans for a proposed 435-mile gas pipeline, in a deal that could pave the way for billions of dollars in future investment.
The agreements were signed in Kabul on Monday in the presence of former US Special Representative for Afghanistan Zalmay Khalilzad, whose participation added a notable geopolitical dimension to the investment deal with Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities.
Delta Energy is a Saudi-based independent energy group involved in oil and gas exploration, natural gas, pipelines, and energy infrastructure.
Delta Energy to explore area of 9,000 square miles
According to Afghan media reports, under the main agreement, Delta Energy will explore the Kushk-Tirpul contract area in western Herat province, covering approximately 9,000 square miles.
The company plans to carry out geological and geophysical studies, seismic surveys, exploratory drilling, and reservoir evaluations to determine the scale and commercial viability of hydrocarbon resources in the area.
The company will also finance a study examining the use of natural gas in Herat, including supplies for the Herat Industrial Park, Herat city, and other approved areas. The study will assess possible applications in industry, electricity generation, and other energy requirements.
A separate agreement establishes a framework for studying a proposed 435-mile gas pipeline, which Delta describes as the “CentGas–Corridor of Prosperity.”
The proposed route would connect a gas receipt point near Guzara district in Herat with a delivery point near Spin Boldak in Kandahar, potentially creating a new domestic and regional energy corridor.
Delta estimates that the proposed pipeline alone could require about $10 billion in investment over a decade.
An important step to developing Afghanistan’s hydrocarbon resources
Afghanistan’s acting Minister of Mines and Petroleum Hedayatullah Badri described the agreement as an important step toward developing the country’s hydrocarbon resources, saying cooperation with Delta could help improve energy security and support economic activity.
Khalilzad, who served as the US special envoy for Afghanistan and later as the US special representative for Afghan peace negotiations, welcomed the agreement during the signing ceremony.
He said Afghanistan had significant natural resources and a strategic geographic position that could help connect Central and South Asia, describing the agreement as a significant development for the country.
His presence at the ceremony is particularly notable because Khalilzad has remained engaged with Afghanistan’s political and economic affairs since leaving official US government service.
His appearance alongside senior Taliban officials and executives of the Saudi energy group highlights the increasingly business-oriented engagement taking place around Afghanistan’s natural resources, even as the Taliban government remains diplomatically isolated from much of the international community.
Multiple outlets reported that Khalilzad, now a private citizen with no official US government role, attended high-level meetings with Taliban Deputy Prime Minister Abdul Ghani Baradar and Delta executives, as well as the signing ceremony.
His presence has raised questions about his role, including whether he helped arrange or influence the agreements and why a former senior US envoy attended deals covering about 9,000 square miles of Afghanistan.

Halis Sunnetci
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha was nominated Tuesday for the Men’s Goalkeeper of the Year award at the 2026 Ballon d’Or following his standout performances at the World Cup.
The 40-year-old played a key role in Cape Verde’s historic World Cup campaign, producing several impressive performances as the African nation reached the knockout stage on its tournament debut.
In their opening match against Spain, Vozinha made seven saves as Cape Verde held the eventual champions to a goalless draw despite Spain having 74% possession.
The result made Cape Verde the first African team to keep a clean sheet against the eventual champions in a World Cup match.
Vozinha produced another strong display in the knockout stage against Argentina, making eight saves, including one on a close-range effort from Lionel Messi.
His performance, however, was not enough to prevent Cape Verde from suffering a 3-2 defeat after extra time and elimination from the tournament.
Vozinha finished the World Cup with 18 saves in four matches.
Only two goalkeepers aged 40 or older have made more saves at a single World Cup: Italy’s Dino Zoff, who recorded 27 in 1982, and England’s Peter Shilton, who made 28 in 1990.
Following the World Cup, Vozinha moved to Chilean club Colo-Colo and has since amassed more than 29 million followers on Instagram.
The 10-man shortlist does not include reigning goalkeeper award winner Gianluigi Donnarumma, while Liverpool’s Alisson Becker also missed out.
France’s Mike Maignan and England’s Jordan Pickford, who both started for their countries at the World Cup, were also left off the list.
The other nominees are Morocco’s Yassine Bounou, Belgium’s Thibaut Courtois, Spain’s Joan Garcia, Switzerland’s Gregor Kobel, Argentina’s Emiliano Martinez, Senegal’s Edouard Mendy, Spain’s David Raya and Unai Simon, and Russia’s Matvey Safonov.
The winner will be announced at the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London on Oct. 26.

Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats on Tuesday, saying they had acted in ways incompatible with their status, in a clear signal that the pro-Russian era of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban is over.
Russia said it would retaliate against what it called an "extremely unfriendly step."
"(Those expelled) were engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention," Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban, who is not related to the former prime minister, said in an emailed statement.
"This decision... does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialog," the statement added.

Viktor Orban kept close ties with Putin

Under him, Hungary continued buying Russian oil and gas, defied European Union sanctions on Russia, and blocked a €90 billion ($97 billion) EU loan to Ukraine.
After Russia invaded Ukraine, many European countries expelled dozens of Russian diplomats, while Hungary expelled none. Until Tuesday, it had not sent any home publicly since 2018.
New Prime Minister Peter Magyar and his center-right government have repeatedly said that Hungary's main alliances are the European Union and NATO and that the government aims to rebuild trust eroded under Orban's rule.
In a parliamentary hearing in May, Anita Orban said Russia would "remain a partner" but the relationship could not be based on "one-sided dependency," adding that Moscow's policies pose a security challenge to Hungary and Europe.

Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, speaks at a national conference on textbook work in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 8, 2026. (Xinhua/Liu Weibing)
BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang on Tuesday called for accelerating the development of a high-quality textbook system with Chinese characteristics, as schools across the country started a new academic semester.
Ding, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, made the remarks at a national conference on textbook work held in Beijing.
He emphasized the need to fully understand the political, people-centered and strategic nature of education, and to strengthen and improve textbook development with a strong sense of political responsibility and historical mission.
Efforts should be made to speed up the establishment of a high-quality textbook system with Chinese characteristics to provide strong support for building China into a leading country in education, Ding said.
He highlighted the correct political direction and value orientation concerning textbooks and called for efforts to ensure that the Party's educational policies are implemented throughout all aspects of textbook development.
Efforts should focus on fostering virtue through education and further incorporating the Party's innovative theories into courses and teaching materials.
China should better adapt its textbook development to the requirements of the times and accelerate efforts to establish a Chinese intellectual system and an original textbook system in philosophy and social sciences, he noted.
He also stressed stricter management of the compilation, review, publication and distribution of textbooks, as well as standardized procedures for their selection and use.
The conference came as a new school year got underway across China. Primary and secondary schools and universities in many parts of the country welcomed students back to campuses in early September following the summer vacation.
In 2025, China had 440,700 schools at all levels and of all types, with over 280.4 million students enrolled in education programs of various types, underscoring the scale of the country's textbook development and management endeavors.
Ding's remarks also came amid a years-long national push to strengthen textbook work. The State Council established a national textbook committee in 2017, and all 31 provincial-level regions on the Chinese mainland subsequently set up provincial-level leading bodies for textbook work.
Strengthening the creation and management of teaching materials was included in the report to the 20th CPC National Congress in 2022.
The push was further highlighted in China's long-term education planning in 2026, when the State Council issued the 15th Five-Year Plan for education development. The plan called for implementing the state's responsibility for textbook development and comprehensively advancing the development of a high-quality textbook system with Chinese characteristics. ■

Feature: In Gaza, journalists document a war that has reshaped their own lives
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:46:17 CST
22:46:17 KST

GAZA, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Every time Nisreen Thabet leaves her tent to cover the war in Gaza, she carries two fears: one for the people she is going to report on and another for the children waiting for her to return.
For Thabet, a 40-year-old journalist and mother of two, journalism and motherhood have become inseparable since the latest round of the Palestinian-Israeli conflict began in October 2023.
Her children, Majd and Ahmed, lost their father during the conflict and now depend entirely on her.
"I don't have the luxury of choosing between my role as a mother and my duty as a journalist," Thabet said. "Many times, I had to take my children with me to the field. Other times, I left them with my mother and walked long distances to work amid bombardment and a lack of transportation."
"I worked with a double burden: fear for them and fear for myself, because I know they have no one else in this world but me after their father's death," she added.
Her husband, Haider al-Masdar, a writer and researcher in political and media affairs, was killed in July 2024 in an Israeli airstrike targeting a tent housing journalists inside a hospital in central Gaza.
After her husband's death, Thabet considered abandoning journalism. She watched colleagues leave their homes, change their phone numbers or withdraw from the field.
Yet she chose to continue, describing journalism as "the last line of defense for the truth."
Today, she and her children live in a tent. Repeated displacement has left her constantly prepared to flee, keeping essential belongings nearby and monitoring reports of strikes and evacuation orders.
At the tent, she tries to create fragments of normal life for her children, supporting their education and speaking to them about school, home and the future she hopes awaits them when the war ends.
For Amer Sultan, the war also transformed journalism into a painful separation from family.
Sultan, 32, has worked as a photojournalist since 2014, driven by a desire to document events in Gaza, particularly nighttime incidents that often received little coverage.
"From the beginning of my career, I saw the camera as a means to document what happens to people," he said. "I wanted there to be a picture, a testimony to what is happening."
On Oct. 7, 2023, Sultan left his home in Jabalia refugee camp for Gaza City to cover the escalating events. His family remained in the north as he was later displaced in the southern Gaza Strip. Since then, he had never seen them.
"I was waiting for a ceasefire, counting the hours and days, not only because I wanted the bombing to stop, but because I wanted to return north and see my family," he recalled.
On Jan. 16, 2025, that hope was shattered. At around 10 p.m., Sultan learned that 13 members of his family had been killed inside their home, including his mother.
"The shock was immense," he said. "Throughout the war, I photographed the victims and thought about my family, asking myself: Could the same thing happen to them? Then came the day when my family became the victims."
The following day, he returned to work. "I made it a point to never put down my camera, my pen, or my phone," he said.
Fuel shortages, destroyed roads and a lack of transportation have forced Sultan to walk long distances to cover events. Amid the hardships, he chose to stay despite offers to leave Gaza.
"For me, journalism isn't just a job," Sultan said. "It's a responsibility toward the people living through this war. I want to convey their lives and suffering to the world, not just show them as numbers."
Thabet and Sultan are among more than 1,500 Palestinian journalists whose lives have been transformed by the war, according to Tahseen al-Astal, deputy head of the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate in Gaza.
"With restrictions on the entry of foreign journalists into Gaza, Palestinian journalists have found themselves on the front lines of coverage," al-Astal said. "They work amid bombardment, displacement, shortages of fuel, electricity and internet access, and difficulties reaching events and sources."
He said more than 250 journalists had been killed during the war, while dozens were injured, some more than once.
More than 150 local, Arab and international media outlets and production offices have also been destroyed or damaged, he added. ■

‘I’m Not Soviet Armenia’s Communist Party Chief’ – Pashinyan Pushes Back on Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:45:39 UTC
22:45:39 KST

At a Sept. 3 government briefing, a journalist suggested that Pashinyan’s recent meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin had involved “harsh ultimatums” and described the Armenian leader as having been “summoned” by Moscow.
“You say that I was ‘summoned to Russia,’” Pashinyan replied. “This year, I was invited to many places.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He said the phrasing made him sound like the first secretary of Soviet Armenia’s Communist Party, an official expected to answer to Moscow.
“How can Armenia be forced to hold a referendum?” Pashinyan asked. “I want to understand how that is possible.”
His sarcasm carried a clear political message: Armenia may eventually have to choose between European integration and continued membership in Russia’s economic bloc, but the Kremlin will not dictate the question, timing or answer.
Putin demands a choice
The disagreement spilled into public view during a Sept. 1 meeting between Putin and Pashinyan on the sidelines of a regional summit in Bishkek.
Putin acknowledged Armenia’s sovereign right to pursue EU membership but warned that simultaneous membership in the EU and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) would be incompatible.
Armenia’s 2025 legislation launching a process of European integration “essentially amounts to an announcement of withdrawal” from the EAEU, Putin argued. He demanded clarity from Yerevan “as soon as possible” and proposed putting the choice directly to Armenian voters.
Zelensky Reveals Possible Venues for Trilateral Talks
Pashinyan rejected that premise.
Armenia has not formally applied to join the EU, received candidate status, agreed on an accession roadmap or opened membership negotiations. It has also not issued the six months’ notice required to leave the EAEU.
Pashinyan said Armenia would hold a referendum only when a concrete proposal existed and voters had an actual question to answer.
“We are not going to take people to polling stations for the sake of it when there is neither a question nor an answer,” he said.
Break from Moscow over Nagorno-Karabakh
Armenia was once among Russia’s closest formal allies. It hosts a Russian military base, remains a member of the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), and is deeply connected to Russian trade, energy and transport networks.
The relationship began to fracture after Azerbaijan regained control of Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023. Russian peacekeepers failed to prevent the takeover, leaving many Armenians feeling abandoned by the country that was supposed to guarantee their security.
“Many Armenians concluded that Russia was either unwilling or unable to protect its closest regional ally,” Russian opposition activist Daniil Chebykin, who lives in Yerevan, previously told Kyiv Post.
Armenia subsequently froze its participation in the CSTO, strengthened relations with the EU and the US and expanded contacts with Ukraine through humanitarian assistance. In 2026, Yerevan hosted the European Political Community summit attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders.
As Kyiv Post previously reported, Armenia represents the clearest example of Russia’s declining influence across its former sphere. Unlike countries that had always maintained greater distance from Moscow, Armenia began its pivot as a treaty ally deeply embedded in Russian-led institutions. Especially in light of the Russia-Ukraine war, which showed Yerevan the limits of Moscow’s real military power.
The shift received electoral approval.
In Armenia’s June parliamentary election, Pashinyan’s Civil Contract party won nearly half the vote and secured a parliamentary majority. Its two principal Russia-aligned rivals together received approximately one-third.
The result weakened Moscow’s claim that Armenia’s turn away from Russia was merely Pashinyan’s personal project.
Moscow still has leverage
Armenia has not severed ties because Russia still accounts for roughly one-third of its foreign trade, or approximately one dollar in every three. Putin said bilateral trade reached $2.5 billion during the first half of 2026.
Moscow has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to disrupt that trade. Russia has restricted imports of Armenian fruit, vegetables, flowers, fish and alcohol, forcing Pashinyan to raise the issue directly with Putin.
Russian officials have also threatened Armenia’s access to subsidized gas and other EAEU benefits if Yerevan continues moving toward Europe.
These dependencies explain why Pashinyan is building alternatives before making a final choice. His government is deepening Western ties, pursuing new transport routes and challenging Russian control over critical Armenian infrastructure.
A railway dispute discussed in Bishkek illustrates this approach.
Armenia’s railway network has been operated since 2008 under a 30-year concession by South Caucasus Railway, a company wholly owned by Russian Railways. Pashinyan said freight traffic had fallen by half, some routes had stopped operating and promised investments had not materialized.
He told reporters that he had pressed Putin to resolve the concession and asked why coverage of the meeting did not describe Yerevan as presenting Moscow with a “tough choice.”
Pashinyan has suggested transferring the concession to another friendly country. He also said Armenia would not object if Moscow decided to withdraw its 102nd military base, although Yerevan is not currently demanding its departure.
He continued to describe relations with Russia as important, with Armenia remaining in the EAEU, having frozen rather than formally ended its CSTO participation, and not having applied for EU membership. But it also firmly rejects Moscow’s ill-disguised ambitions to govern its internal affairs.

Unions to organise national protest against austerity on 9 October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:44:18 UTC
22:44:18 KST

The socialist trade union ABVV and the Christian trade union ACV are set to take action against the federal government’s austerity measures on 9 October. The ABVV refers to it as a demonstration; the ACV calls it a day of action. This will mark the fourth national demonstration in the space of a year.
“For 19 months now, the De Wever I government has been chipping away at the pillars of our social model: pensions, wages, working conditions and working hours, protection in the event of illness, unemployment insurance, social security and public services,” says the ABVV. “In the process, social dialogue has repeatedly been presented with a fait accompli, undermined or simply ignored.”
According to the ABVV, the strongest shoulders should bear the heaviest burdens, which, the trade union argues, is not currently the case. “Other choices are possible. This requires political courage,” it adds.
The ABVV expects the De Wever government to adjust its policies: no further erosion of the wage and benefit indexation mechanism, no VAT increase and no annualisation of working hours, whereby the average working hours are calculated over a whole year rather than per week.
“It is becoming increasingly clear that government measures are causing great hardship for many people and are doing nothing to shore up the budget,” says the ACV. The Christian trade union does not yet want to speak explicitly of a “national demonstration” but refers to a “National Day of Action”.
If the government stands its ground, the ABVV is threatening a national strike in the week of 23 November. The ACV has not yet put it quite so bluntly.
The demo will be the fourth national demonstration in the space of a year. According to the police, 80,000 people took part in last October’s demonstration, 80,000 in March this year, and 40,000 in May. The independent trade union Synova will decide next week whether to join next month’s action.

UK, France among 12 countries to sanction trade with illegal Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:43:50 UTC
22:43:50 KST

Twelve countries, including Britain, Canada and France, have said they would slap sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, after increasing attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the occupied territory.
Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden also plan to limit trade with the settlements, the nations' foreign ministers said in a joint statement on Tuesday.
Ireland and Spain have already taken measures against trade with Israeli settlements, and France has for weeks been pushing for a similar decision from the European Union, Israel's leading trading partner, but has been blocked by some members.
"The government of Israel's actions in the West Bank are undermining the possibility of a two-state solution," the 12 ministers said, referring to a plan under which two states - one Israeli and one Palestinian - would live peacefully side by side.
"The situation is rapidly deteriorating amid unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion," they warned.
"The government of Israel must immediately halt the expansion of settlements and civilian administrative powers, ensure accountability for settler violence, and investigate allegations against Israeli forces," the ministers added.
‘Ethnic cleansing’
The ministers said the 12 countries "confirm their intention to introduce national and/or support European restrictions on trade in goods with settlements which are illegal under international law, or that they are actively considering these and other measures, in accordance with their national procedures."
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused the Israeli government of turning a "blind eye" to what he called "ethnic cleansing" by illegal settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Today's measures "represent a clear message" to both the Israeli government and Palestinians that "we will not acquiesce in destruction of the two-state solution," he said in a statement to lawmakers in the House of Commons.
On top of Israel's official state policy, "settler terrorism is rampant," he noted, adding that the UK will sanction a further set of extremist settlers in the occupied West Bank "who have supported or incited acts of violence" against Palestinians.
Miliband stressed that those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements in the West Bank "will face the full force of UK sanctions."
He went on to say that the UK will take action against "specific companies and individuals" who provide services and financing for the expansion of illegal Israeli settlements.
Miliband said the British government agrees that there is "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians" in the occupied West Bank perpetrated by Israeli "settler terrorists."
During his address, he also confirmed that the existing British suspension of 30 arms export licences to Israel will remain "fully in place."

Invictus Games Ukraine founder Frolova: need to stop treating veterans like 'wedding generals'
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:43:31 EEST
22:43:31 KST

Ukraine is a country still learning how to work with veterans, and veterans themselves understand this, according to Alina Frolova, founder of the Invictus Games in Ukraine and the StratComUA Center for Strategic Communications.
"You have to understand that a veteran is, first and foremost, a person with a certain kind of experience. Simply inviting a veteran or a person with a disability isn't always the solution... When it comes to testing services, that definitely needs to be done with the people who actually use them, and in fact it should be done constantly. But I think we need to stop treating veterans a little like 'wedding generals,'" Frolova said at the third annual "My Barrier-Free Life. Lessons Learned" forum in Kyiv on Tuesday.
Every veteran has their own experience, she said, and barrier-free access isn't only about people with an official diagnosis, but also about many people suffering from what might be called invisible injuries.
"You just need to, first, try to bring in specialists; second, of course, test the solution with the people who will actually use it; and third, simply have empathy. Because the ability to talk normally — especially for staff working in service roles — the ability to talk normally, to see, and to ask what's comfortable or uncomfortable right now, resolves most of the problem," Frolova said.
At the same time, she said, "we're a country that's learning, and veterans understand that too."
The third annual "My Barrier-Free Life. Lessons Learned" forum was initiated and organized by Oschadbank with support from Visa, as part of first lady Olena Zelenska's "Without Barriers" initiative. Oschadbank, together with its partners, is working to make barrier-free access an established social norm.
Interfax-Ukraine is the event's general media partner.

Spain dismantles 'narcobank' tied to cocaine trafficking ring
Unknown

Spain dismantles 'narcobank' tied to cocaine trafficking ring
MADRID, Sept 8 - Spanish police said on Tuesday they had dismantled an illegal banking network that served some of Europe's biggest cocaine traffickers, arresting 21 people in several countries including in the Middle East and uncovering assets worth €20 million ($23.2 million).
The network, dubbed the "narcobank", is suspected of having financed cocaine shipments, moved money internationally outside the banking system, used cryptocurrency to settle transactions and provided money laundering services.
"Without this financing, these shipments could not be moved from one country to another. Drug trafficking on this scale would not be possible," chief anti-money laundering inspector Encarna Ortega told reporters.
Authorities said 14 suspects were arrested in Spain and seven others in the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, the Netherlands and Sweden. Twelve more suspects remain at large. Europol, which supported the investigation, said that among those arrested was an underground banker it identifies as a high-value target.
The investigation stemmed from the 2021 seizure of 1.84 metric tons of cocaine aboard the vessel Nehir, which police said was later deliberately sunk in the northern Spanish port of Gijon to conceal a further shipment of 1.65 tons.
Investigators seized 121 bank accounts holding €2.3 million, 48 properties valued at more than €14 million and luxury vehicles worth more than €1.6 million as well as other items. REUTERS

Barca star Lamine Yamal says will not beg for Ballon d'Or

'Never been happier': Barca star Lamine Yamal says will not beg for Ballon d'Or
Barcelona star Lamine Yamal said Tuesday he will not beg for the Ballon d'Or trophy after winning the World Cup with Spain and La Liga with the Catalan giants.
On Monday Real Madrid star Kylian Mbappe made his case to win the trophy, highlighting his World Cup Golden Boot win, which also saw him become the competition's all-time top goalscorer.
Yamal, 19, thought he had played very well while winning trophies for club and country but said he was happy to let others decide whether he deserved the prize.
The teenager, Mbappe, Harry Kane, Ousmane Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are the main candidates to win the award at the ceremony in London on October 26.
"I don't think I need to (make a campaign for it), I'm not thinking about what I deserve, everyone can think what they like," Yamal told reporters. "I'm proud of everything I've done this year with my club and with the national team. We've become world champions, we've won the league again. I can't ask for anything more. I think... I've shown an incredible level, it's (the media's) job and I will not beg for anything."
Yamal came second in last year's Ballon d'Or voting behind PSG star Dembele.
France forward Dembele recently told France Football that Kvaratskhelia, Kane and Mbappe would be in his top three to win the award.
"He's a friend of Kylian, right?" joked Yamal of the French winger, formerly of Barcelona. "The truth is I don't care, I'm very happy with the year I had, when I played against both of them together I must have annoyed them."
Spain knocked out France in the World Cup semi-finals with a convincing 2-0 victory.
Yamal suffered a hamstring injury in April and has only just returned to his best level.
The winger appeared unhappy at the start of the season but seemed far more cheerful as he netted two goals against Rayo Vallecano and Valencia in his last two outings.
"In the end, I'm 19, coming off winning a World Cup, having had the best holidays of my life," said Yamal. "I've never been happier at any point in my life than I am now."
Champions League dream
The teenager said a key ambition this season was to aim for the "very special" Champions League trophy, with Barcelona beginning their campaign on Wednesday at home against Dutch side Feyenoord.
Barca last won the trophy in 2015, led by the Lionel Messi, Luis Suarez and Neymar attacking trident.
Under coach Hansi Flick they reached the semi-finals in 2025 and then the quarter-finals last season.
"Every big club is dreaming about this because this is the best competition," said the German. "We have the quality to win this, but there's a long way (to go)."
Flick hailed Yamal and said the most important thing was that the Spaniard is enjoying himself on the pitch.
"Lamine is a player who can decide games on his own, fantastic quality," added Flick. "It's great, you can see it every day how he is enjoying playing football. For me the best thing is that he enjoys this game and then he's on a top level."
Yamal will be the favourite to win a third consecutive best young player award at the Ballon d'Or ceremony.
He was one of 10 players nominated on Tuesday, including Johan Manzambi, Yan Diomande and Ayyoub Bouaddi, who all impressed at the World Cup and were then the subject of big-money summer transfers.

America: the gulf, the lake and now the state – what’s next on Trump’s huge renaming spree? | Marina Hyde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:41:13 UTC
22:41:13 KST

Busy times for crayon-wielding US president Donald Trump, Earth’s most tireless freelance cartographer, who at the weekend celebrated the US labouring under the highest diesel prices in its history while his “two-week” Iran war edges into its seventh month with a social media spree in which he pushed renaming New Mexico as New America.
In some ways, it was a surprise to see Trump go for merely rebranding a state at this point, given that it was only so recently that he declared: “If you think about it, we have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean.” This is believed to be a reference to the Gulf of America, formerly – and indeed currently, in every meaningful sense – the Gulf of Mexico. It was also a nod to Lake America, as precisely no one calls Lake Ontario despite Trump supposedly retitling it by executive order last month, in another fit of pique over his trade war with Canada. Candidates for this heavily trailed American Ocean clearly include the Pacific and the Atlantic – though why the other oceans should be locationally ineligible increasingly feels unclear. At this rate, geography exams in the US are also about to get a whole lot easier.
In the end, you sense, most of the places in the US will go to the chop shop, and either have “America” bolted on the back, or have the Trump name fused on to them as a prefix. See the Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, or the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington DC. Or, indeed, the President Donald J Trump International Airport in Palm Beach, Florida. A new class of warship may also be procured for naming privileges.
As for potential rebrand candidates/victims, how your area votes clearly affects the order in which its landmarks – or itself in its entirety – will be slapped with a fun new identity. When proposing the New Mexico renaming, Trump casually noted that it was “one of the great vote-cheating states of all time”. I wouldn’t be feeling all that confident if I were the Georgia state capitol, or the Trump America capitol as it may imminently be known.
Meanwhile, it must be said that all this frenetic activity does feel born of Trump’s conviction that it should surely be possible to shitpost his way out of anything, even a war. After all, the Iran war, which I seem to remember was won on day one, has now been going on for more than six months. This feels confusing. First it was going to be two weeks, then four to five weeks. Four days into Operation Epic Fury, Trump explained that the US was “already substantially ahead of our time projections”, while the secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth, added: “It could move up, it could move back.” Having said that, evidence suggests it could only move up, although Trump wrapped up his first week of the conflict back in March by assuring the American people that his campaign continued “to totally demolish the enemy far ahead of schedule and at levels that people have never seen before”. Two days after that, the conflict was downgraded to “a short excursion”, with non-committal historical allies dismissed with a triumphant: “We don’t need people that join Wars after we’ve already won!” The war was “complete, pretty much”, he said two days later.
And yet, was it? A couple of weeks in, Trump was explaining he’d know when the war should be over because he’d “feel it in my bones”. Alas, he seems to have failed to get the arthritic signal to pull out as late as three weeks in, despite assuring everyone that – contrary to appearances such as still bombing the shit out of things – the war had in fact been over “in two or three days”. Flash forward to a month in, and they were still “way ahead of schedule”, although once the five-week mark was hit Trump was dropping casual asides like “a whole civilization will die tonight”. Six weeks in, things were going “swimmingly”. Although, not to nitpick, but were they?
That was April. In May, a deal with the Iranians could apparently “happen any day”. By the end of the month, it could have potentially happened “over the weekend”. Same thing a weekend later. A whole two months after that, unfortunately, Trump shifted from the war being over to declaring that his notional/imaginary agreements to end the war were in fact the thing that was “over”. He no longer wished to negotiate with Tehran. Jump ahead to the present day, in fact, and he has spent quite a lot of the past week bombing the shit out of things again. Which is very much the behaviour of any state that won a war back in the first days of March. Unhelpfully, the former US defence secretary Leon Panetta estimated at the weekend that the war would drag on for another six months.
All of which suggests there has really never been a better time to rename New Mexico. Those eternal searchers for a so-called Trump doctrine are surely beginning to see that it essentially boils down to wimping out of the big, painful calls that could literally move the dial – for example, boots on the ground – and existing in an eternally figurative zone where you can simply post the problem away. Here, there is no better way to signal that the war is over than to unilaterally rename the strait of Hormuz either the strait of Trump, or the strait of America. As some psychologists like to say: you have to name it to tame it.
- 
  Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist

Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:40:34 UTC
22:40:34 KST

Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized
- Date:
- September 8, 2026
- Source:
- Michigan State University
- Summary:
- More than 1,200 genetic variants have been linked to the Big Five personality traits, and many of the same variants are also associated with health, longevity, careers, income, and everyday habits. The findings reveal a surprisingly wide genetic connection between personality and life outcomes while showing that environment still plays a powerful role.
- Share:
An international team of scientists has identified more than 1,200 genetic variants associated with the Big Five personality traits. The findings also suggest that many of the same genetic patterns connected to personality are related to a wide range of life outcomes, including health, longevity, education, careers, and income.
The study, led by the Revived Genomics of Personality Consortium, brought together data from 46 research cohorts around the world. Participants provided DNA samples and completed questionnaires designed to measure the Big Five personality traits: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism.
These traits describe relatively stable patterns in how people tend to think, feel, and behave. Researchers compared participants' genetic data with differences in their personality scores to identify genetic variants associated with each trait.
No Single Gene Determines Personality
"There is no single 'personality gene,'" said Ted Schwaba, lead author of this study and faculty at MSU's Department of Psychology. "Personality traits are associated with many genetic variants, but even the largest effects of individual genetic variants are still very small. However, even though any individual genetic variant makes very little difference in personality, the effects of many variants together can be more sizeable."
Although the influence of any one genetic variant was tiny, the researchers found that their combined effects were more substantial and consistent. The genetic patterns also appeared to hold across very different groups of people.
For instance, variants associated with extraversion in a young adult living in the Netherlands could also help predict extraversion in an older retired adult in the United States. By using methods that compared relatives with one another, the team found evidence that these genetic associations could not simply be explained by growing up in the same environment.
Even so, genetics is only part of the picture. The findings also reinforced the important role that a person's environment plays in shaping personality.
Personality Genetics Reach Across Daily Life
The researchers found that genetic variants associated with personality overlap with genetic patterns connected to many other areas of life. These include mental and physical health, longevity, education, career choices and outcomes, as well as the way people are viewed by those close to them.
Some of the links involved everyday habits. Genetic variants associated with conscientiousness were also related to being more active during the daytime. Meanwhile, variants associated with openness to experience and extraversion were connected with a greater tendency to be a night owl.
The results also highlight how genetics and environment can interact with one another rather than operating independently.
For example, common genetic variants associated with openness to experience were linked to a greater likelihood that someone would move to a more cosmopolitan neighborhood. Living in that type of environment could then reinforce or further shape the same personality trait.
Genetics, Environment and Life Outcomes
"Personality seems to be relevant nearly everywhere you look. We hope this study will encourage many other scientists to incorporate personality traits into their fields of study," said Schwaba. "For example, genetic variants associated with neuroticism predict more time spent in the hospital, which is relevant to physicians and health researchers, and variants associated with openness to experience are linked to income and switching jobs, which is relevant to vocational researchers."
The findings suggest that studying the genetics of personality could have implications well beyond psychology, potentially informing research in medicine, health, education and the workplace.
Funding was supported in part by grants from the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute on Aging.

India, China hold first high-level military flag meeting in Arunachal sector
NEW DELHI: India and China have held their first Senior Highest Military Commander-Level Flag Meeting in the Arunachal Pradesh sector, with talks taking place on both sides of the frontier earlier this week.The meeting followed understandings reached during the Special Representatives dialogue between National Security Advisor (NSA) Ajit Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi. The talks are part of efforts by the two countries to maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and gradually improve bilateral ties.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the meeting was held at Wacha on the Indian side on September 6 and at Damai on the Chinese side on September 7.
New military mechanism along eastern frontier
Jaiswal said the meeting followed agreements reached during the Special Representatives talks in August 2025 and August 2026, along with subsequent discussions under the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination."Pursuant to the understandings reached between the Special Representatives of India and China in August 2025 and August 2026, and subsequent discussions at the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination meetings held in Beijing and New Delhi in May and August 2026 respectively, the first Senior Highest Military Commander-Level Flag Meeting was held at Wacha on the Indian side in Arunachal Pradesh on September 6 and Damai on the Chinese side on September 7," Jaiswal said at his weekly media briefing.
"A similar mechanism also exists in the Western Sector," he said.The talks took place amid reports of aggressive military posturing by Chinese troops along the LAC in the Upper Subansiri region of Arunachal Pradesh.Jaiswal also said that India-China relations are gradually moving in a "positive direction".
Border peace remains key to improving ties
Doval and Wang, who are the designated Special Representatives for the India-China boundary talks, held their latest dialogue in Beijing last month.During the meeting, the two sides discussed the delimitation of the boundary, trans-boundary cooperation and the need to maintain peace along the LAC.The Indian side stressed that peace and tranquillity along the border are important for the continued development of bilateral relations.
The Special Representatives mechanism was established in 2003 to address the India-China boundary dispute, which covers a 3,488-km frontier.
Military engagement ahead of Xi visit
India and China have taken several steps in recent months to rebuild relations that deteriorated sharply after the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020. The latest military engagement comes days before Chinese president Xi Jinping is expected to visit India for the BRICS summit. Xi is likely to arrive in New Delhi on Saturday.

Hungarian foreign minister’s statement

Drone strikes killed 1,120 civilians in Sudan in first half of 2026: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:38:34 UTC
22:38:34 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
At least 1,120 civilians were killed in drone strikes in Sudan in the first six months of 2026, accounting for 80% of all civilian deaths documented by the UN human rights office during the period, a senior UN official said Tuesday.
Addressing the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights Awa Dabo said the Kordofan region remains the “current epicenter” of Sudan’s conflict, with the majority of civilian deaths documented by the office this year recorded there.
While drone strikes in El Obeid, North Kordofan, decreased sharply in July, civilians continue to face “dire conditions and grave risks,” she said.
Repeated strikes on gas stations and water and electricity infrastructure have left families struggling to obtain safe water, food and medical care as prices rise, Dabo added.
She also raised alarm about attacks on humanitarian personnel and assets, including the detention of aid workers, looting of a warehouse in Kauda and an aerial strike outside Dilling that destroyed World Food Program trucks carrying aid.
“This horrific war has been fueled by interests, both inside and outside the country,” said Dabo.
She urged the international community to end arms transfers to parties where weapons are used in “manifest disregard” of obligations to protect civilians. She also demanded accountability and sustained efforts toward a permanent ceasefire and inclusive civilian rule.

Qualcomm, Amazon partner on customized chips for AI data centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:38:27 UTC
22:38:27 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
US chipmaker Qualcomm announced Tuesday a multi-generation product collaboration with Amazon to develop customized silicon and advanced connectivity solutions for artificial intelligence data centers.
The companies will work together on chips designed for AI inference, the process through which trained AI models generate responses or predictions, Qualcomm said in a statement.
The collaboration is aimed at supporting the expansion of Amazon Web Services’ (AWS) AI infrastructure as growing workloads increase demand for computing capacity, networking, storage, and memory bandwidth.
Qualcomm and Amazon will also develop optical connectivity solutions capable of reaching speeds of up to 1.6 terabits per second, as well as future-generation technologies.
The connectivity systems will use Qualcomm’s serializer-deserializer and optical digital signal processor technologies to support high-bandwidth connections within Amazon’s data center networks.
Qualcomm also plans to expand its use of AWS infrastructure, including the Amazon Bedrock generative AI platform, for electronic design automation workloads, with the goal of shortening chip design cycles.
“As AI demand accelerates, data center infrastructure will require advances in both computing and connectivity to deliver greater performance with more efficiency,” said Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon.
Prasad Kalyanaraman, vice president at AWS, said the partnership would help deliver “more performant, efficient, and cost-effective infrastructure” to customers.
Financial details and a timetable for the deployment of the jointly developed technologies were not disclosed.

'Family of the woods' get a new social worker
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:37:51 CEST
22:37:51 KST

The so-called 'Family in the Woods' made up of a British-Australian couple and their three children who were taken into care last year because of the family's allegedly detrimental off-the-grid lifestyle in an Abruzzo forest is reportedly being given a new social worker after the current one was put under disciplinary proceedings. 
    The case has been assigned to Giuseppina Tittaferrante after the Abruzzo Order of Social Workers opened a procedure against Veruska D'Angelo for alleged breaches of its code of ethics over statements made in the press and over an allegedly hostile attitude towards the couple, according to the reports. 
    Luca Bauccio, the lawyer representing D'Angelo, told ANSA that the fact a new social worker has been assigned to the case does not mean his client has been "replaced", stressing she was still on it and new members had been added to the team. 
    Bauccio also said D'Angelo welcomed the disciplinary procedure as an opportunity to clarify matters, saying the documentation shows she acted correctly at every stage. 
    Last week a court for minors in L'Aquila ruled that Birmingham and Trevallion could be reunited with the children, but said the process must be gradual, in stages and under strict supervision by social services. 
    The couple have been fighting to get their kids back since last November. 
    At the end of April the same court court in L'Aquila ruled that the couple's appeal against a juvenile court's decision to eject the mother from the foster home where their three children have been living was inadmissible. 
    The couple had been raising the children, an eight-year-old girl and two six-year-old twin boys, in a house without electricity or running water in woods near the town of Palmoli in central Abruzzo. 
    They were put into care after being poisoned by mushrooms and amid concerns about their safety, their education and their ability to socialize with other children. 
    The case has caused widespread dismay in Italy and Premier Giorgia Meloni and other members of her government have expressed concern about the way the social services have handled it. 
    Many ordinary folk have also voiced solidarity and deep sympathy with the parents.
