This year’s program, initiated by the China Public Diplomacy Association under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ guidance, brings together journalists from Africa, Asia-Pacific, Latin America, Eurasia, the Arab world, and Central and Eastern Europe.
Distinctively, the journalists themselves delivered some of the most compelling remarks.
Mark Longyen from Nigeria and Mahendra Subedi from Nepal delivered speeches as the representatives of the attending journalists.
Immersive Experience at Renmin University
Participants are accommodated on the Renmin University campus, offering a unique opportunity to experience student life at one of China’s premier journalism institutions. The program combines journalism training, diplomatic briefings, cultural activities, and field visits to many provinces and regions across China.
Participants will also undertake internships at major Chinese media organizations including CGTN, Xinhua News Agency, and People’s Daily, gaining practical exposure to China’s media landscape. The program runs through mid-December, building bridges between China and the developing world through independent journalism and cross-cultural understanding.

The Security Service of Ukraine and the National Police have blocked five new schemes to evade military service and mobilization and detained 11 organizers of the schemes in various regions of Ukraine. The SBU reports this, UNN reports.
Details
The suspects were detained in the Lviv, Rivne, Donetsk, Cherkasy, and Kirovohrad regions. It is reported that, for amounts ranging from $5,000 to $22,000, the individuals involved helped persons liable for military service to "dodge" conscription and illegally leave the country.
Among the organizers of the scheme were representatives of the criminal underworld who involved members of the Military Medical Commissions, officials of hospitals and military units, as well as employees of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers, in the illegal activities. For amounts of up to $20,000, the suspects provided clients with a full "package of services"—from obtaining medical certificates declaring them unfit for service, with the assignment of the second disability group, to "striking" conscripts off the military register on health grounds
All those detained were notified of suspicion, in accordance with the crimes committed, under several articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine:
-  Part 3 of Article 332 (illegal transfer of persons across the
state border of Ukraine); 
-  Part 3 of Article 369-2 (abuse of influence combined with
demanding an undue advantage); 
-  Parts 1 and 2 of Article 255 (establishment and leadership of a
criminal organization, as well as participation in it); 
-  Part 1 of Article 114-1 (obstruction of the lawful activities of
the Armed Forces of Ukraine and other military formations during a special period). 
The suspects face up to 12 years in prison with confiscation of property.
Recall
In the Kyiv and Chernihiv regions, military personnel of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers were notified of suspicion of beating civilians during mobilization activities. The head of one of the district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center departments was also notified of suspicion.

Netanyahu orders demolition of West Bank settler outposts – Reuters

Netanyahu orders demolition of West Bank settler outposts – Reuters
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the removal of illegal settler outposts in the occupied West Bank, Reuters has reported, citing two people familiar with the matter.
Netanyahu made the demand under pressure from Israel’s main ally, the US, which recently expressed concerns over the rise in attacks on Palestinian homes by the Jewish settlers, the agency said in an article on Sunday. It was not immediately clear when the demolitions would start, it added.
The Israeli outlet Ynet claimed earlier that the prime minister had instructed that some 100 outposts, built without permission from the Israeli government, be brought down.
According to data from the Israeli NGO Peace Now, there are some 340 outposts erected on Palestinian land in the West Bank, along with 146 settlements formally recognized by the authorities in Israel and receiving funding from West Jerusalem.
The outposts usually consist of light prefabricated houses, in which small groups of settlers reside. The Israeli government has demolished some of the unauthorized settlements over the years, but they are being rebuilt quickly by radicalized Jews.
The UN and most other countries consider all of the Israeli settlements to be illegal under international law due to them being erected on occupied Palestinian territory.
The UN relief agency, OCHA, said in August that there were an average of six settler violence incidents every day in the West Bank during the first six months of 2026. The attacks by radicalized Jews have led to the displacement of more than 2,300 Palestinians, including over 1,000 children, it added.
On Saturday, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, a strong supporter of the Jewish State and self-professed Christian Zionist, said that the settlers behind the attacks were not just criminals, but “terrorists.”
 Huckabee insisted that he Israeli government must provide security to Palestinians in the West Bank and make sure that those who assault their homes are aware that they will face “severe consequences.”
The ambassador’s stance was echoed by Netanyahu’s main rival in the Israeli parliamentary election in late October, former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who said on Sunday that “if someone comes to burn down the home of innocent Arabs with the people inside it, then of course that is Jewish terrorism.”
“If it is done for nationalist reasons, that is the definition. I don’t understand how this serves the settlement movement,” he stressed.

Georgy Matyukhin, Russia’s First Central Bank Chief, Dies at 91
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:23:07 UTC
22:23:07 KST

The first governor of Russia’s Central Bank after the fall of the Soviet Union, Georgy Matyukhin, has died at the age of 91.
Russia’s Central Bank announced Tuesday that Matyukhin passed away on Saturday, one day ahead of his 92nd birthday.
The regulator praised Matyukhin as an “active and responsible leader” who was appointed to lead the State Bank of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic “during a critical turning point” in 1990.
“He oversaw the formation of the Bank of Russia under new conditions, leading it until 1992,” the Central Bank said in a statement.
Matyukhin played a key role in the development of modern Russia’s financial sector during severe currency shortages and soaring inflation.
Russian business media described one of his main achievements as the establishment of Russia’s two-tiered banking system, with separated central monetary authority from commercial banking operations.
Matyukhin is also remembered for personally signing the 5,000-ruble banknote, a gesture that no subsequent Central Bank governor has since repeated.
Born in the Altai region city of Barnaul on Sept. 6, 1934, Matyukhin initially trained as a geologist before graduating from the Moscow State Institute of International Relations in 1961.
He then worked within the KGB’s foreign intelligence division before being stationed under diplomatic cover in Uruguay, from where he was eventually expelled alongside a group of Soviet spies.

Israeli attacks on southern Syria may amount to war crimes: UN commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:21:33 UTC
22:21:33 KST

The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria on Tuesday expressed “deep concern” over Israeli attacks on southern Syria, saying they violate the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and “may amount to war crimes.”
The commission made the call during a briefing to the UN Human Rights Council, whose 63rd regular session began in Geneva on Monday and runs through October 7.
“We are deeply concerned about the Israeli attacks on southern Syria and affirm that they constitute a violation of its sovereignty and territorial integrity,” the commission said, according to Syria’s SANA news agency.
“This is unacceptable and must stop,” it added.
Fionnuala Ni Aolain, a commissioner with the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria, warned that such acts “may amount to war crimes.”
Areas of southern Syria, particularly Quneitra and Daraa provinces, have witnessed repeated Israeli military incursions, including raids on homes, the establishment of checkpoints and arrests, as well as shelling.
Israel has occupied most of the Syrian Golan Heights since 1967.
Following the fall of the Bashar al Assad regime on December 8 2024, Israel declared the 1974 Separation of Forces Agreement collapsed and occupied the demilitarised buffer zone and other positions, including the Syrian side of Mount Hermon (Jabal al-Sheikh).
On developments inside Syria, the commission said it was witnessing an acceleration in reconstruction and progress in efforts to build accountability institutions.
It stressed that “accountability is an essential element for the success of the transitional justice process in Syria.”
The commission also welcomed the renewal of its mandate and thanked the Syrian government for enabling it to carry out its work.
The UN Human Rights Council established the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria in August 2011 to investigate alleged violations of international human rights law since March that year and identify those responsible where possible.
For years, the commission conducted its investigations from outside Syria because it lacked access to the country, relying on interviews with victims and witnesses as well as documents, photographs, videos and satellite imagery.

Channi vs Warring: Why Sachin Pilot may be Congress's best bet in Punjab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:21:02 UTC
22:21:02 KST

Congress has handed Sachin Pilot a familiar problem and a bigger opportunity.
NEW DELHI: The Congress leadership last week finally responded to 'Mayday' calls from Punjab rebels and brought in Sachin Pilot, replacing Bhupesh Baghel, to prevent a crash landing of the deeply fractured state unit ahead of the assembly elections early next year.Months of open infighting between Charanjit Singh Channi, the former chief minister leading the rebel camp, and Raja Warring, the state unit chief, not just embarrassed the Congress but also threatened to derail its 2027 campaign.Before being put in the driver's seat in Punjab, Pilot was in charge of Chhattisgarh, where Baghel remains a key Congress leader and former chief minister.
Why Congress was forced to budge
The Congress had sent former Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhagel to Punjab in February this year to defuse the brewing Channi vs Warring crisis in the state unit. Ironically, as things turned out, Baghel faced resistance and became part of the crisis, with the Channi camp openly accusing him of siding with Warring. More so, since July, after the party’s central leadership decided to ignore Channi’s claim for the top post in the state and announced that it would continue with Warring as state Congress president.
Bhupesh Baghel had asserted that it is not a 'child's play' and the decision of the high command will not change.
With several senior state leaders backing Channi, the fight turned ugly and Baghel became ineffective.
Congress meetings in the districts saw open “Go back Baghel” chants from Channi supporters, taking the infighting to the streets and embarrassing the top leadership.So, while the ruling Aam Aadmi Party was already in full election mode with chief minister Bhagwant Mann at the centre of its campaign, the Congress was still struggling to get its senior leadership to sit across the table.Not just the AAP, even the BJP and the Akalis had their house in order and were planning their electoral moves on the ground. With the party's 2027 campaign failing to take off under Baghel, the Congress was forced to budge and turn to Pilot.
Why Sachin Pilot
The Congress decision to send Pilot to Punjab, while ironic, may still be the best bet for the leadership. Sachin Pilot, during his years in the Congress, has seen enough internal wars to know how quickly a fight over one post can turn into a larger battle over leadership, political space and, of course, eventually the chief minister's chair.Throwback to Rajasthan, where he spent years at the centre of a similar leadership tussle with senior leader Ashok Gehlot. Pilot brings something the Congress needs badly right now: the experience of being at the centre of a difficult internal power struggle.
Punjab Congress working president welcomed Sachin Pilot’s appointment, saying it will help iron out differences within the state unit.
Pilot has led the Rajasthan unit, worked closely with the high command, weathered the bitter internal battle, survived the fallout and then rebuilt his position within the Congress.He was appointed Rajasthan Congress chief in 2014, after the party's abysmal performance in the 2013 assembly election. Over the next four years, he emerged as one of the key faces of the party's rebuilding effort before Congress returned to power in 2018. That victory, however, did not give him the chief minister's chair.Ashok Gehlot became chief minister, while Pilot was made deputy chief minister and continued as PCC president. While both sides got something, the arrangement never really settled the rivalry between Gehlot and Pilot.By 2020, those differences exploded into an open rebellion.Pilot left Jaipur with a group of MLAs and challenged the Gehlot government. Congress responded by removing him as deputy chief minister and state president. The Gehlot camp even accused him of working with the BJP. A truce was eventually worked out, and Pilot stayed with Congress.But he never quite returned to the position he had occupied before and has been on the sidelines ever since. He remained a prominent face in the party and was later given charge of Chhattisgarh, but his role in Rajasthan remained limited.It is interesting how, in Rajasthan, Pilot was the leader asking the Congress high command to listen to a dissatisfied camp. In Punjab, he now has to convince dissatisfied leaders to accept the high command's decisions and work together.That may be why Congress believes he is best suited for the job.
Baghel gone. Will Warring be next?
But will Pilot’s appointment end the crisis in the Punjab unit?Channi's supporters had demanded Warring be removed as Punjab Congress chief, and the Jalandhar MP be declared Congress’s chief ministerial face for the 2027 assembly polls. The Congress has not accepted either of the two demands. So, while Channi has not made any significant gains, Warring has been left wondering if he will be the next to be axed.Warring was picked up to lead and rebuild the Punjab unit after the Congress was decimated in the 2022 assembly polls. Channi, who was the chief minister then, led the Congress to its worst-ever performance in the state. The Congress not just lost its government to AAP but was also reduced to 18 seats in the 117-member assembly.The leadership tussle between the two had been brewing for quite some time. But as is the Congress’s wont, the party kept dilly-dallying on the issue for nearly 4 years. Finally, when the Congress did take a decision, it ended up opening deep faultlines.For now, both camps have welcomed his appointment. Warring said Pilot's energy and dynamism would "for sure" add to the vigour of the party ahead of the crucial polls, while Gurdaspur MP Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa, a close associate of Channi, said Pilot's experience, leadership and connect with the people would give new strength and momentum to the Congress in Punjab.Punjab Congress working president Raj Kumar Verka hopes that under Pilot’s leadership all state leaders would come together. "Pilot knows all leaders of Punjab, and they also have confidence in him," said Verka.For Pilot, this may be his first real test. If party leadership decides to keep Warring, he has to get Channi, Randhawa and other leaders to fall in line. If Warring goes, he has to make sure one problem is not replaced by the other.
Congress has a lot at stake
The Congress, which remains the main challenger for now, cannot afford this infighting because Punjab is one of the states where it still has a real chance. There is anti-incumbency against the Bhagwant Mann-led AAP government.In 2022, AAP swept 92 of the 117 assembly seats, while Congress was reduced to 18. But the 2024 Lok Sabha election brought some relief for the grand old party. The Congress won seven of Punjab's 13 seats, compared with AAP's three, showing that the party still has enough ground to be a serious challenger.AAP is perhaps no longer riding the wave that brought it to power in 2022 and is now defending its record under Bhagwant Mann. Raghav Chadha's exit has also added to the churn in the party.The BJP and the Akalis are still on the margins of the state’s politics. But the scenario could change very fast. The BJP is going all out to broaden its organisational base and rope in leaders from other parties. There are also reports of talks between the BJP and the Akalis to revive their old alliance. The Congress needs to remember that the BJP is coming off a massive victory in West Bengal and is looking to expand its footprint in Punjab as well.
Punjab could shape Pilot's Rajasthan future
Pilot has already made it clear that he sees Punjab as a comeback opportunity for the Congress. On Monday, he said he was confident that with a strong organisation, collective effort and the energy of party workers, Congress could return to power in the state.
Pilot has the experience of being a part of successful strategising in Himachal Pradesh in the previous assembly polls and has also been a senior observer for the Kerala polls, where Congress returned to power after a decade.If Pilot can manage to bring the rival Punjab camps together and help the Congress put up a strong show in 2027, it will add to his standing within the party at a time when Rajasthan is already looking ahead to the 2028 assembly election.There has long been speculation over a bigger role for Pilot in Rajasthan. He may not have got it yet, but a successful Punjab stint could considerably strengthen his case.For a leader who has had to rebuild his own position in the party before, Punjab could well become the next big step in that comeback.

UK announces sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:21:02 UTC
22:21:02 KST

Citing the existence of "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians," Britain will impose a trade ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, the country's foreign secretary announced Tuesday.
 
In a statement to lawmakers in the House of Commons, Ed Miliband said today marks the "beginning of a new approach" on Israel, announcing that the UK will introduce an import ban on goods from illegal settlements.
 
"The legislation I have announced today will be in place within six to nine months and we will also take more immediate steps," he noted.
 
Tuesday’s measures "represent a clear message" to the government of Israel, to the Palestinians in the Occupied Territories, and to the world that "we will not acquiesce in destruction of the two-state solution," he said.
 
However, he noted that the sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel itself, adding that for this reason, he "wholeheartedly" opposes the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement.
 
On top of Israel's official state policy, "settler terrorism is rampant," he said, adding that the UK will sanction a further set of extremist settlers in the West Bank "who have supported or incited acts of violence" against Palestinians.
 
Miliband stressed that those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements in the West Bank "will face the full force of UK sanctions."
 
He went on to say that the UK will take action against "specific companies and individuals" who provide services and financing for the expansion of illegal Israeli settlement.
 
"I can also announce that we are extending the existing global human rights regime such that it will enable swifter action to deter settlement expansion, including crucially seeking to present the development of E1," said the foreign secretary
 
Ban will remain 'as long as occupation persists'
 
Miliband said the British government agrees that there is "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians" in the occupied West Bank perpetrated by Israeli "settler terrorists."
 
In his address, he also confirmed that the existing British suspension of 30 arms export licenses to Israel will remain "fully in place," adding that the UK will refuse all license applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation, in effect a double lock against arms sales.
 
"This means the ban on such exports will now remain as long as the occupation persists," Miliband underlined.
 
The foreign secretary also urged Israel to lift its withholding of revenues, saying the measure is financially "crippling the provision of essential services in the West Bank."
 
On Gaza, he cited "increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed" in Gaza Strip, adding that the UK supports legal processes to determine this.
 
He said that the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks "cannot justify what has happened in Gaza,” noting that over 70,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks since then, including "at least 20,000 … children."
 
Miliband also said the UK has already designated Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and said the government "will do more today on Iran’s proxy groups."
 
"So today I can also announce we are sanctioning Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard Al-Hassan," he added.
 
Miliband also said he is "proud of my Jewishness and unwavering" in his support for the state of Israel.
 
He added: "There is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state of Palestine. Indeed quite the opposite."
 
Miliband said that they should be proud that it was a Labour government that took the "historic step" of recognizing the state of Palestine.
 
He added: "But the Prime Minister (Andy Burnham) is right to say that the Labour government has not done enough in the face of what is happening."
 
Palestinian ambassador welcomes 'historic' announcement
 
Palestinian Ambassador to the UK Husam Zomlot welcomed Miliband's announcement, calling the new measures "historic."
 
"Today marks a turning point in UK–Palestine relations — from recognition to action, from condemnation to consequence," he said in a statement.
 
Saying the announcement comes a year after Britain's recognition of the state of Palestine, Zomlot said that it represents continuity of purpose, not an end in itself.
 
"Recognition cannot be meaningful if the territory of the recognised state is simultaneously being taken from its people in Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem," he added.
 
Britain’s new measures follow Israeli plans to develop 1,200 new homes in the occupied territory, a move that sparked widespread condemnation from the international community. as all settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.
 
The prime minister recently vowed "comprehensive measures" in response to the expansion of illegal settlements.
 
UN data indicate that violence by Israeli occupiers has reached "unprecedented levels," with more than 1,400 attacks resulting in casualties or property damage documented in 2026 alone.
 
Approximately 750,000 Israeli occupiers currently reside in 516 illegal settlements and outposts across the occupied territory, carrying out near-daily efforts to displace Palestinians from their land.
 
'Suffering of Palestinian people is scar on conscience of world'
 
Later, the British government released a statement giving details on how the UK will use its power to enable sanction regime.
 
The statement noted that with the immediate sanctions against perpetrators of settler violence, the number of those currently sanctioned by the UK as a result of settler activity has risen to 38.
 
Also explaining the UK's legal opinion, the statement reiterated that the occupation is unlawful in line with the central finding of the International Court of Justice in its advisory opinion.
 
"Our view is based on the nature and totality of the Government of Israel’s actions in Palestine over many decades: the length of the occupation, Government of Israel’s entrenchment of its control and expansionist agenda via illegal settlements," it noted.
 
The statement noted that the current Israeli government has approved 104 new settlements and permitted tenders for the construction of the E1 mega settlement to go ahead, which as planned would cut through the heart of the West Bank.
 
In the statement, Burnham said that he is determined his government "will continue to act in defence of our values."
 
He noted that Tuesday’s measures aimed not at the Israeli people, but in support of the two-state solution, and the prospect of Israelis and Palestinians living side by side in peace.
 
"The suffering of the Palestinian people is a scar on the conscience of the world. Innocent Palestinians, including children, continue to be killed in Gaza. And there is still a humanitarian crisis, with far too little aid getting in," he added.

Russia’s readiness for talks on Ukraine and EU’s attempts to derail them: Lavrov’s remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:20:40 UTC
22:20:40 KST

MOSCOW, September 8. /TASS/. Russia is always ready for talks on Ukraine so long as it is rooted in the causes of the crisis and aimed at reaching agreements to address them, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told a news conference after talks with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud.
According to the top Russian diplomat, the European Union continues to do all it can to prevent the situation around Ukraine from moving toward a long-term settlement by addressing those very root causes of the conflict.
TASS has summed up the Russian foreign minister’s key statements.
Ukrainian settlement
Russia values Saudi Arabia’s efforts toward ensuring a lasting settlement of the Ukrainian crisis: "We are thankful to our Saudi friends for their principled, responsible, and well-balanced position on Ukraine, for their aspiration to make a contribution to the settlement of humanitarian problems that emerged amid this situation, and for their overall role in the common efforts toward ensuring a lasting political settlement on the basis of removing the well-known root causes of this crisis."
Russia is always ready for talks on Ukraine based on an understanding of the root causes of the crisis and aimed at reaching agreements to address them: "If we focus on the main point, first and foremost, talks must be held - and we are always ready for them - based on an understanding of the root causes and on reaching agreements to address the root causes of the current Ukrainian crisis, which was created by the West, primarily by the previous US administration and by the European Union and NATO members, who are still trying, as they put it, to inflict a defeat on Russia and support Ukraine in everything."
The US President Donald Trump administration seems as if it is open to entertaining the root causes of the Ukrainian conflict: "From the very beginning, the Trump administration has displayed both the wish and the ability to see the root causes of the conflict, and this is precisely what allows us to expect that conversations, negotiations, and contacts with the relevant envoys will be beneficial for both sides."
The European Union continues to do everything to prevent the situation around Ukraine from moving toward a long-term settlement by addressing the root causes of the conflict: "It is the European Union that continues to do everything to prevent the situation from moving toward an examination of the root causes and an examination of paths toward a reliable, long-term settlement based on the elimination of these root causes."
Intervision song contest
The date of the next Intervision international song contest to be held in Saudi Arabia will be announced later due to the situation in the region: "Naturally, we have to take into account the situation in the region. That is why we have agreed to discuss the date at a later stage."
Middle East
Reasonable compromises are needed to implement the Islamabad memorandum between the United States and Iran, which is now not being followed: "Together with our Saudi colleagues, we call for looking for reasonable compromises to resolve all the differences in order to ensure the implementation of this agreement."
Russia and Saudi Arabia insist that the Palestinian-Israeli conflict cannot be resolved by force methods: "Both Moscow and Riyadh are convinced that only a comprehensive, all-embracing settlement of the Palestinian issue - and there is a well-known basis of international law materialized in US resolutions for that - will guarantee durable peace for all nations in the region, including Israel, whose security must be guaranteed too, of course, as well as the security of all other countries of the region. But this should be done only through agreements rather than using military force."
There is no progress toward settling the situation in the Gaza Strip, despite Trump’s peace plan: "Regrettably, despite the existing agreement that was presented as US President Donald Trump’s plan, there is no progress on this track either."
Russia slams Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s infrastructure as counterproductive: "We believe that it is unacceptable to try to resolve these issues militarily, by military means that not only pose risks to the civilian population but also negatively impact the global economy, bearing in mind the Arabian Peninsula and its waterways’ importance for the routine operation of global trade routes."
Relations with Saudi Arabia
Russia and Saudi Arabia reaffirmed their commitment to continuing close coordination within OPEC+, which is particularly important in the current environment: "In the context of economic cooperation, we reaffirmed our commitment to continuing close coordination within OPEC+ to ensure a balance between supply and demand on the global energy market. This is particularly important under current conditions. Russia and Saudi Arabia, as co-chairs of this group of countries, will consistently pursue the approaches they have agreed upon."
Tourist exchanges between Russia and Saudi Arabia are growing fast in both directions: "We have good opportunities in the travel sector. Saudi tourists visit Russia quite willingly. Last year, we welcomed 35% more of them compared to the previous year. The number of Russian tourists visiting Saudi Arabia is growing at a similar pace. This is facilitated by the visa-free travel agreement that came into force this May."
Both countries demonstrate "mutual interest in expanding cultural and humanitarian ties."

From sacred spring to stone museum: the long journey of Khusro II's bust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:19:01 UTC
22:19:01 KST

From sacred spring to stone museum: the long journey of Khusro II's bust
Located north of Kermanshah, the Taq-e Bostan archaeological complex is renowned for its magnificent Sasanian rock reliefs and royal grottoes.
Among these celebrated carvings stands a lesser-known but equally significant artifact: a heavily damaged freestanding bust locally called Kol-e Jubor. This Kurdish toponym translates to "the short one who cuts the water stream" and is deeply rooted in regional agrarian folklore.
Local farmers traditionally attributed supernatural powers to the statue, blaming it for magically interrupting irrigation channels from the Kulehkehu River (Cham-e Bashir) whenever their fields ran dry, cementing its folkloric identity as an aquatic saboteur.
The bust is one of the few surviving examples of freestanding Sasanian sculpture, offering exceptional insight into the artistic and ideological expressions of the late empire. The most prominent parallel is the Colossal Statue of Shapur I, which stands in a limestone cave near Bishapur in southern Iran. Together, these two monuments constitute the only known major examples of Sasanian freestanding stone statuary.
The Kol-e Jubor's historical trajectory has been marked by severe instability and displacement. After being recorded by the 10th-century Arab historian Mis'ar bin al-Muhalhil (Abu Dolaf) in 341 AH, the statue toppled and remained submerged in the large karst spring before the grottoes for centuries. Western travelers Eugene Flandin (1840) and Annee Holt (1867) documented it lying in the water. By 1878, it had been extracted and propped up on dry ground, where it suffered extensive degradation from prolonged submersion and human vandalism, including gunfire that obliterated its facial features.
The statue's turbulent history is further illuminated by photographic and archaeological records. A modern image reveals a pockmarked, cracked, and heavily eroded stone torso, stripped of all facial features, currently secured within a gray metal frame and wooden clamps at the Taq-e Bostan Stone Museum. This condition is contextualized by early 20th-century documentation.
The renowned archaeologist Ernst Herzfeld photographed and recorded the statue, categorizing it within the "Sasanian Monuments" subseries of his papers. His handwritten notes explicitly identify it as a "Statue in round, Khusro II" (Taq-i Bustan: Carved in the Round Statue of Khusro II). This archival record, part of the Ernst Herzfeld Papers at the National Museum of Asian Art Archives, Smithsonian Institution, provides crucial evidence of the statue's early 20th-century state.
Despite the severe damage, the surviving torso preserves critical iconographic details. It highlights imposing, bulky shoulders and arms resting across the chest, along with a distinct vertical line of erosion indicating the placement of a sword vertically between the legs, against which the figure heavily leans. This configuration is interpreted as a deliberate symbolic allusion to military power and martial authority. The posture echoes the central investiture scene, while the attire matches Khusro's hunting reliefs. Facial reconstruction studies further indicate the king's characteristic short neck and broad visage, firmly aligning the bust with the monumental imperial effigy of Khusro II (Khosrow Parviz) and corroborating Herzfeld's identification.
Beyond royal portraiture, scholars have proposed a ritualistic interpretation, suggesting the grotto and statue collectively functioned as a tomb-sanctuary. In this framework, the lateral hunting and musical reliefs symbolize the preparation of sacred food and joyful entertainment meant to appease the Fravashi (royal guardian spirits) during the Zoroastrian Hamaspathmaedaya festival. The statue may therefore have embodied the sovereign's physical presence on earth, complementing the celestial representation of his investiture in the grotto.
In September 1818, Sir Robert Ker Porter recorded carved pairs of feet attached at the ankle on the flat plateau above the large arches.
Subsequent field surveys confirmed these remnants at the end of the sculpted staircases on the eastern side, indicating this elevated platform as the statue's original pedestal. Likely toppled from this height due to iconoclastic violence, the statue fractured severely. Consequently, recent research proposes that the fragmented torso undergo careful restoration and be re-erected at its original location atop the arches, allowing the Kol-e Jubor to once again preside over the sacred springs of Taq-e Bostan.

Swiss electricity prices set to fall by around 4% next year

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

Swiss electricity prices set to fall by around 4% next year
Electricity prices will fall slightly in 2027. Tariffs will fall by an average of 4%, according to the Electricity Commission (Elcom). For a typical household, the annual electricity bill will be CHF53 ($65) lower. However, there are regional differences.
On average, a household consuming 4,500 kilowatt-hours a year will pay CHF0.26 per kilowatt-hour next year. That is around CHF0.012 less than in 2026, amounting to a total of CHF1,194. This was announced by the Federal Electricity Commission (Elcom) on Tuesday.
The energy tariff will fall, while grid costs and the metering tariff will rise. A similar picture emerges for medium-sized businesses, Elcom wrote. Electricity tariffs have stabilised at a high level. The fact that they are falling slightly overall is mainly due to lower energy prices.
More
Switzerland among world’s most expensive for household electricity
However, these figures are median values. In reality, tariffs vary considerably depending on the network operator. This is primarily due to the significant differences in energy procurement. These costs depend on the proportion of electricity generated in-house and the procurement strategy.
The 2027 tariffs for individual municipalities and distribution network operators are available online on Elcom’s electricity price website. By the end of August, the roughly 580 electricity network operators were required to disclose their tariffs to their customers and to Elcom.
Electricity tariffs for the current year have already fallen by around 4% compared with the previous year. In 2025, however, the decline was 10%, following some significant price rises in 2023 and 2024.

Ukraine is sending its winning brigades to where the fighting is worst. The 46th just turned up outside Kramatorsk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:18:50 UTC
22:18:50 KST

- Free to redeploy from the stabilized southeastern front, a key Ukrainian brigade has moved north to help defend Kramatorsk and Sloviansk
- It took two months, and almost nobody outside the Ukrainian army knew it was happening
- The 46th Airmobile Brigade's first task may be to cover a short retreat by an adjacent brigade
Kramatorsk and Sloviansk are the last two big cities in the Donbas that Russia does not hold, and taking them has been the main Russian objective in eastern Ukraine since 2022. Ukraine is now moving forces north from the southeast to defend them.
The 46th Airmobile Brigade began that move in July. The first outside confirmation came this week.
Shifting north to plug a gap between two Ukrainian corps, the brigade could protect adjacent units as they retreat a short distance from what's left of Chasiv Yar—a battleground since the spring of 2024—and straighten the Ukrainian line where the 11th and 19th Corps meet. Both corps now sit under Biletskyi's new force grouping, according to Unit Observer—a command relationship no Ukrainian outlet has reported and which open sources cannot independently confirm.
Zooming out, the reshuffle around Kostiantynivka runs alongside a wider effort to redistribute Ukrainian troops along the 1,200-km gray zone threading through southern, eastern, and northern Ukraine. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi took over as commander-in-chief on 22 July, arriving with a mandate to unwind the Soviet-inherited command model Ukraine has fought this war with, and a reputation for favoring decentralized command. The 46th began moving before he did, in early July, according to Unit Observer, so this redeployment is not his. But the 33rd Assault Regiment was partially reassigned to Biletskyi's corps after the handover.
The best-case scenario is that the redeployment helps stabilize the front 16 km south of Kramatorsk, delaying the Russian siege of that city and Sloviansk to the north. In the worst case, the 46th Airmobile Brigade and its thousands of troops are too few and too late to make much of a difference as the Center Group of Forces and its tens of thousands of troops grind through Ukrainian defenses on their slow march toward Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
The 46th Airmobile Brigade spent years fighting in southeastern Ukraine. But it's arguably no longer needed along the southern end of the gray zone after a Ukrainian counteroffensive that kicked off in February halted and then rolled back Russian forces, stabilizing what was once Ukraine's most vulnerable flank.
Free to fight elsewhere, the brigade began its move north toward Kostiantynivka and Chasiv Yar two months ago. The move happened almost entirely in secret. "Strict OPSEC measures have become the standard for the Ukrainian armed forces in 2026," mapper Unit Observer noted, "with units delaying posts up to several months to avoid giving away their relocation along the front line."
That discipline is now visible across the whole Ukrainian effort. The southeastern counteroffensive that freed up this brigade ran for six months with very few videos and small teams. Ukraine's Swedish radar planes flew combat sorties for half a year before the defense ministry said so. A brigade crossing the front unremarked for two months is the same practice, applied to ground forces.
Confirmed moves
Recent videos confirmed the deployment. The 46th Airmobile is now in position just north of the ruins of Kostiantynivka and just west of the ruins of Chasiv Yar, which lie 11 km northeast of Kostiantynivka. Sitting astride the juncture between two Ukrainian corps, the 11th and 19th, the brigade is set to play a crucial role in the ongoing Ukrainian defense of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
According to Unit Observer, the 46th Airmobile Brigade's move "will likely support the gradual retreat of elements of the 24th Mechanized Brigade remaining between Chasiv Yar and the village of Stinky," 6 km west of Chasiv Yar. The 24th Mechanized Brigade has fought long and hard in and around Chasiv Yar to hold back a much larger Russian force. But incremental Russian advances north and south of the 24th Mechanized Brigade's positions have put the brigade at risk of partial encirclement.
It's a dangerous position for the weary brigade. If it could fall back to the west a few kilometers, it could eliminate the risk to its flanks—and straighten and shorten the overall Ukrainian line. It's possible the 46th Airmobile Brigade's job is to safeguard the short retreat.
Desperate to save Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Ukrainian forces counterattack and reinforce
The command and control process is deceptively complex, and the confusion is exactly the kind Drapatyi is trying to engineer out. Ukraine's new corps are supposed to be its highest front-line commands, coordinating the brigades, regiments, and battalions fighting in the same sectors. But in the areas where two corps meet, it may be unclear which corps is in charge.
Ukraine's answer has been to add a layer above the corps. On 26 August, Zelenskyy announced that two reinforced groupings would take over the defense of Donetsk Oblast, commanded by Denys Prokopenko of the 1st National Guard "Azov" Corps and Andrii Biletskyi of the 3rd Army Corps, both named Heroes of Ukraine.
The 3rd Corps' zone of responsibility has grown daily since the start of the year, its deputy commander Lt. Col. Rodion Kudriashov told NV, and he framed the new groupings as Ukraine scaling up what already works.
The grouping formalizes an arrangement that had already grown up in practice. The 46th Airmobile Brigade fits the same logic. It belongs to neither the 11th nor the 19th Corps—it is an 8th Air Assault Corps unit—but it is a brigade that works, freed by an offensive that worked, arriving in the sector that matters most. It is also arriving into a corps run by its own former commander: Brig. Gen. Valeriy Skred, recently given the 19th, led the 46th through 2022 and 2023.
Only time will tell whether the reshuffling of Ukrainian forces will bolster the defense of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. And even if the redeployments do stiffen the Ukrainian line south of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, they do nothing to stiffen the line north of the twin cities.
Russian troops are closing in from that direction, too. Fortunately for the Ukrainians, there's a separate plan for that northern sector. A carefully planned series of Ukrainian counterattacks has quietly cut across a salient of Russian troops marching on Sloviansk.
The Ukrainian attacks may compel the Russians to pull back a short distance. That could give the defenders of Sloviansk more space and time to prepare for the coming siege.

Pakistan Takes SCO Presidency at a Crucial Time: What to Expect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:17:00 UTC
22:17:00 KST

The annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) held in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, from August 31 to September 1, brought together leaders from across Central Asia as well as Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
The meeting took place amid significant geopolitical shifts in West Asia. It was the first major Eurasian multilateral gathering after the 2026 Israel-U.S. war on Iran and the subsequent Islamabad Memorandum ceasefire negotiations.
Over more than 25 years, the SCO has evolved into a platform spanning Asia, the Middle East, and Eurasia. While member states often pursue divergent priorities, the grouping has still delivered measurable benefits.
For members of developing countries, including this year’s host Kyrgyzstan, the SCO has offered a practical framework for advancing transit connectivity, improving access to larger markets, particularly China, and coordinating regional security efforts. One example is the summit’s approval for the establishment of a permanent Bishkek Center, which is expected to begin operating with a practical role in coordinating law enforcement cooperation, facilitating the exchange of operational information, and conducting joint activities. For Kyrgyzstan, this represents the creation of a lasting SCO mechanism on its territory even after the end of its presidency.
This year’s summit carried particular diplomatic weight for Iran. In the Bishkek Declaration, SCO leaders condemned military strikes on Iranian territory as violations of international law and the U.N. Charter that create serious risks to international peace and security. They also reaffirmed Iran’s right to develop and use nuclear technology for peaceful purposes without discrimination.
While the declaration refrained from explicitly naming the attackers, securing consensus among member states was itself significant. This outcome arguably represents a continuation of the SCO’s main stance on the conflict. The moderate phrasing of the Bishkek Declaration on the war on Iran likely reflected strategic restraint by key players seeking to forge common ground.
Pakistan reportedly sought to protect the stability of the Islamabad Memorandum ceasefire negotiations between Iran and the United States by avoiding explicitly naming the attackers. On the other hand, India likely aimed to protect its balanced posture toward Western partners by agreeing to a joint declaration that avoided singling out the U.S. and Israel. Similarly, Central Asian member states, which also maintain diplomatic relations with major powers, benefited from this moderated language. In this context, by focusing on core principles of sovereignty and non-aggression rather than naming specific actors, the SCO arguably demonstrated its capacity to build a functional consensus amid complex geopolitical fault lines.
For Pakistan, this consensus arrives at a crucial time. The country has assumed the rotating chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026–27. The presidency is the organization’s highest rotating leadership role, which lasts one year and culminates in the host country organizing the next Heads of State summit. This means Pakistan is going to steer the forum’s agenda at a time when its international profile has grown markedly.
There are three main developments likely to shape the SCO under Pakistan’s presidency of the forum.
First, Pakistan’s policymakers now likely view their role through the lens of a country that has already made a tangible impact in West Asia, particularly through its mediatory efforts between Iran and the United States in recent months. Moreover, they increasingly see Pakistan as a responsible player and key stakeholder in regional conflict resolution. This is a perspective that is likely to shape the SCO presidency under Pakistan and bring sharper focus to practical priorities such as regional connectivity, trade facilitation, energy cooperation, and counterterrorism-related issues.
Pakistan has announced that it will host the 2027 SCO summit under the theme “Turning Vision into Action: Connectivity, Innovation and Shared Prosperity.” This suggests the country’s intention to leverage its chairmanship to prioritize shared development issues among member states.
Second, Pakistan’s assumption of the presidency is going to elevate its role from coordinating economic or ministerial agendas to chairing the SCO’s primary strategic and security discussions. In this important position, Islamabad is unlikely to use the forum to confront or vilify India, as doing so would risk making the presidency appear divisive and could undermine the organization’s credibility at a delicate time.
Instead, Pakistan is expected to prioritize developing consensus in an effort to ensure that bilateral tensions do not spill over into the SCO’s formal agenda or disrupt its proceedings. By keeping the focus on shared regional concerns rather than contentious bilateral issues, Islamabad would likely aim to protect the overall standing of the forum and avoid perceptions that the organization stalled or fractured under its leadership. That said, Pakistan is likely to use the opportunity to build consensus on issues such as river water sharing to ensure that water is not weaponized, as that would threaten regional stability.
Third, Pakistan is likely to use its presidency to advance its connectivity-hub narrative. Islamabad has already repeatedly presented the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) as a flagship project aligned with SCO goals. Under Pakistan’s chairmanship, it can be expected to expand this framing by highlighting new routes via Iran and Central Asia that link the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) to the Arabian Sea. This can allow Pakistan to showcase tangible regional benefits of SCO cooperation while reinforcing its strategic position as a key transit and logistics hub ahead of the 2027 summit in Islamabad.
A key challenge for Pakistan’s incoming presidency will be fostering institutional alignment on major regional transport routes like CPEC. India has repeatedly expressed its reservations, even opposition, to the corridor’s path through Pakistan-administered Kashmir, which may complicate Islamabad’s efforts in the coming year to reach unanimous agreement within the forum.
Moreover, persistent instability in Afghanistan and heightened Afghanistan-Pakistan border tensions could pose significant challenges to Islamabad’s chair agenda. This has the potential to derail Pakistan’s agenda on transit corridors and complicate the idea of integration of Central Asian economic routes with South Asia. At the same time, regional volatility surrounding the Iran-U.S. conflict could create additional friction.
If, against all odds, Islamabad can take this agenda forward, it would enhance Pakistan’s diplomatic standing.

Manipur musician killed in Indian capital, reviving racism concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

Manipur musician killed in Indian capital, reviving racism concerns
The guitarist’s killing leads to an outcry, again exposing the decades of racial discrimination faced by people from India’s northeastern states.
New Delhi, India — Late on Sunday night, Chongtham Vikram Singh was troubled by loud noises outside his home in the Indian capital, where he lived with his son and wife. He climbed down the stairs, but an argument ensued with nearly a dozen men, who chased him back to the third floor of his apartment.
The chase ended with 54-year-old Singh, a renowned guitarist from India’s northeastern state of Manipur, left unconscious on the stairs by the mob. Within hours, he had died from his wounds at a nearby hospital.
Singh’s killing has revived anxieties over entrenched racial discrimination and marginalisation that people from the northeastern states have long faced in the rest of India.
For his friends and fans, the tragedy comes as Manipur enters a fourth year of a deadly civil war that has displaced tens of thousands in the state.
“Vikram is an icon and legendary guitar player for us,” said Akhu Chingangbam, a popular Manipuri lyricist and singer. “That’s his heritage. He inspired generations to pick up guitar in the land where the arms and lives are so cheap.”
Singh’s tragic end, after teaching music for 20 years in the capital, is a reminder, Chingangbam said, that racism is a stark reality for thousands of domestic migrants from India’s northeast.
‘Best person you can come across’
In New Delhi, Singh gave private music classes and helped young musicians to gain a foothold. Back in Manipur, he was a rock star, the guitarist of a popular, socially conscious rock band – Eastern Dark.
The 54-year-old was among the region’s rock pioneers in the early 1980s.
The Eastern Dark band’s name is also a nod to the political marginalisation of people in northeastern states, including Manipur.
“We living in the east are living in this dark; in every aspect it’s dark socially, politically and anywhere you look. Our lifestyle and, geographically, every aspect of our life is dark,” Eastern Dark vocalist Heishnam Malemngangba Lokeshwar told a researcher in 2020.
Manipur has seen decades of armed rebellion, involving ethnic groups fighting Indian rule and, at times, each other.
Two decades back, Singh moved to New Delhi “to make something out of life”, said Chingangbam, Singh’s friend, “to expand the horizon and opportunities as a musician”.
Chingangbam remembers him as “the finest guitarist” he knew, but also as the person with the widest smile in the room, who would exchange stories during their jamming sessions. “He would always shake my body when he burst into a laugh,” Chingangbam said, recalling their days together in New Delhi. “Vikram was the best person you can come across in the world.”
Chingangbam also grew up listening to Singh’s music. When he was lined up to play at the music festival NH7 Weekender in 2016, Singh took him to a friend to get him a new acoustic guitar.
“But look at what it came down to — how he succumbed in Delhi,” Chingangbam told Al Jazeera. “It is a tragedy for people like us, who don’t feel safe anywhere. With war at home, we just don’t have a place where we feel secure, protected.”
The Delhi police have arrested eight accused, including a minor, on charges of murder, but have not commented on the motive behind the murder yet.
India’s ‘long history of racism’
Singh’s killing led to a wider outcry against years of marginalisation of people from the northeast in mainland India, where casual racism has become commonplace.
In 2014, the killing of Nido Taniam, a 19-year-old from India’s far northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, triggered by racial slurs over his appearance, led to protests in the capital. It also pushed the government, then led by the Congress party, which is now in opposition, to set up an independent committee to examine the larger concerns among the communities.
The committee found that about 86 percent of more than 200,000 northeastern migrants had experienced some form of racial discrimination in New Delhi, followed by metros including Mumbai, Hyderabad and Chennai.
The committee recommended an antiracism law, with non-bailable charges and investigation within 60 days, followed by fast-tracked trials. The new incoming government, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, did not adopt the suggestions.
The roots of the racism that people from northeast India face go back to colonial times, said Deepak Kumar, an assistant professor at the University of Hyderabad, with a focus on the northeastern states.
“It has a very long history. Under colonial rule, the British characterised the people from the northeastern regions as Mongoloid,” an offensive racial category to identify Indigenous communities in parts of Asia, he added.
“They developed policies that dealt with northeastern provinces differently than what was the idea of mainland India back then,” Kumar said.
In postcolonial India, with power centralised in New Delhi, several issues of regional identities and autonomy erupted. And with increased liberalisation of India’s economy and the migration of more people from northeastern India, the cultural differences became apparent and “created more conditions to complement existing racism”, Kumar told Al Jazeera.
Singh’s killing is headline racism, argued Kumar, but the rot lies in what he calls footnote racism. “They are charged extra to buy vegetables on the streets. People stare at them in a packed room. It is a daily reality,” he added.
‘Our legend’
Following Singh’s killing, India’s opposition leader Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday hit out at Modi and his close confidante, Home Minister Amit Shah, for “growing lawlessness, especially against people from the northeast”.
Gandhi wrote in a post on X: “After many such incidents, every Northeast family in Delhi is asking the same question today – are we safe here?”
Laishram Kangleinganba, the president of the Manipur Students’ Association Delhi, told Al Jazeera that despite the swift arrest of the accused men, the community is not hopeful of justice.
“The attack on him was vicious and unprovoked,” he said. “And I felt like: ‘Here we go again’. It has been decades of racial discrimination; all of us have worked for years to create awareness, but nothing changes.”
“This attack might happen to my friends or me one day — but it is happening to one person or another daily,” the 24-year-old said.
Kangleinganba said he had grown up listening to Singh’s music. “I don’t remember how I discovered Vikram. He was just around, always, since my childhood,” he said. “He was our first exposure to rock.”
Singh’s friend, Chingangbam, said these memories that the late guitarist left behind will ultimately define his legacy — not the violence that ended his life. “And we need to preserve his memory. He is our legend,” Chingangbam said.

Fitburg defendants deny sabotage as second anchor-dragging trial begins
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:15:35 EEST
22:15:35 KST

Helsinki District Court on Tuesday began hearing the case against two crew members of the cargo ship Fitburg, which is suspected of damaging cables in the Gulf of Finland last New Year's Eve.
The preliminary investigation uncovered evidence that the Fitburg dragged a broken anchor along the seabed for at least 130 kilometers until Finnish authorities stopped the vessel.
The two defendants in the case are the Russian captain, Andrei Maksimenko, and an Azerbaijani bosun. A bosun is a senior petty officer in charge of a ship's deck crew and rigging.
They face at least two and a half years in prison if found guilty on the charges of aggravated sabotage and aggravated interference with communications networks. Both men have denied the charges.
According to prosecutors, the Fitburg damaged two telecommunications cables in Estonia's exclusive economic zone, with some of the damage also occurring in Finnish territorial waters.
This could have had serious consequences for the functioning of telecommunications, electricity, and gas networks in Finland, the prosecutor told the court.
Finnish authorities took control of the ship in the immediate aftermath of the incident on New Year's Eve. The vessel was en route from Russia to Israel, according to the ship-tracking website MarineTraffic.
At the time, it was sailing under the flag of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — a commonly-used so-called "flag of convenience", which allows a shipowner from one country to fly under the flag of another.
The case has striking similarities with the Eagle S, which is also suspected of damaging undersea cables in the Gulf of Finland — a year earlier, over Christmas 2024. In October 2025, the district court ruled that Finland does not have jurisdiction and dismissed that case, but the Appeal Court overturned that decision at the end of last month and returned it to the district court.
Henrik Ringbom, a Professor of Maritime Law at Åbo Akademi in Turku, told Yle that the district court's decision in the Eagle S case was "surprising" as it could set a precedent for any potential similar incidents in international waters.
"In practice, it would mean free game – come on in, as long as you're outside the territorial waters boundary, we won't do anything," Ringbom explained.
The issue of jurisdiction is likely to be a key factor in the Fitburg case as well, with the legal counsel for the Azerbaijani bosun telling Yle just before the hearing that this case should not be heard in a Finnish court.

Australia unveils landmark Bill to let social media users opt out of algorithms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:15:00 UTC
22:15:00 KST

Australia unveils landmark Bill to let social media users opt out of algorithms
- Australia introduced a bill allowing social media users to opt out of content algorithms, aiming to improve online safety and reduce exposure to harmful content.
- The bill requires platforms to offer an opt-out pop-up and imposes fines up to A$109 million for non-compliance, empowering users to see content only from friends and followers.
- Experts warn of challenges in user uptake and platform resistance but see the law as a crucial step toward reducing social media harms and limiting tech giants' control.
AI generated
SYDNEY – Australia unveiled a landmark Bill on Sept 8 to let social media users opt out of the algorithms that control content, a move experts hailed as “profound” – and overdue – in improving online safety.
Warning that technology giants face a “global reckoning”, the government said that platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and TikTok would need to offer users the choice to opt out in a pop-up message and will face fines of up to A$109 million (S$99.6 million) if they fail to comply. Users who opt out will see content from friends and people they follow.
Analysts said the draft laws marked a significant milestone in global efforts to limit the exposure of social media users to misinformation, extremist and sexually explicit content, scams, deepfakes, grooming, and content that affects people’s body image. Most experts said an opt-in approach – in which algorithm-generated content was not the default – would have been a better way to tackle the problem but would have been more divisive and led to a fierce backlash from social media giants.
Rashina Hoda, professor of software engineering at Monash University, told The Straits Times that the new laws were “much required” and “if anything, a little late, given the types of harms we have seen on social media for years”. But she expressed concern about how many people will choose to opt out of the algorithm, especially as social media encourages an “inertia” that leaves many users as passive consumers of endless feeds.
“This could have a profound effect and change how we deal with social media and how social media doles this (content) out to us,” she said.
“Social media has made us used to the default settings for decades. If and when we have the control back to opt out, it will be fascinating to know whether people know what to do with that control and how they use it.”
The new opt-out measure is part of a draft Digital Duty of Care Bill that also requires technology firms that operate AI chatbots, search engines, apps and social media platforms to protect children under 18 from harms such as eating disorders, bullying and content that is misogynistic or glorifies crime. Examples cited by the Minister for Communications, Anika Wells, on Sept 8 included a chatbot that advises girls on how to survive on 600 calories a day and platforms with content likening women to “beasts or animals”.
The draft Bill, set to undergo a consultation period, follows Australia’s world-first move in December 2025 to ban children under 16 from having accounts on social media – a move that has been followed by countries around the world, including Indonesia and Malaysia.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who plans to address the United Nations in New York on the changes later in September, told reporters on Sept 8 that the opt-out measure was designed to “empower people” to choose the content they see.
“If people want to doomscroll… that’s up to them,” he said. “But if people want to have a change, then this will provide them with the opportunity.”
Australia’s opt-out plan goes further than a policy the European Union introduced in 2023 that required technology giants to provide an opt-out feature. Analysts say social media platforms found ways around the law, such as making the option difficult to find.
Ellese Ferdinands, a Social Media Specialist at the University of Sydney, told ST that platforms will inevitably try to circumvent Australia’s opt-out measure but supported the new legislation because “we have to start somewhere”. She said the opt-out option could result in a heavy hit on the revenues of technology giants, whose algorithms aim to keep users on platforms for as long as possible to maximise advertising revenue.
Despite her preference for an opt-in measure, Ferdinands said she was confident many people would opt out, citing trends such as “scroll-free Sundays,” when people voluntarily avoid social media on Sundays.
“People who opt out will be less addicted to social media and will spend less time on the app,” she said.
“Over the long term, we could see drops in revenue for the platforms. This has huge implications for their bottom line.”
Asked about the risk that the new laws could cause a rift with Donald Trump over the potential hit to the profits of American technology firms, Albanese said he had a good relationship with the United States President, whom he plans to meet in New York in several weeks, but he believed the curbs on the technology giants were in Australia’s interest.
Albanese acknowledged the move could prompt a backlash from technology firms, saying: “We’re taking power from big global tech companies and giving it to ordinary Australians... It’s the right thing to do.”
Hoda said the government should create an independent body to oversee the opt-out option and introduce an education campaign to promote awareness and encourage users to take control of their content feeds. She said algorithms had led to “relentless” flows of content that were based on users’ personal data and frequently targeted people’s vulnerabilities.
“We can’t rely on social media to self-monitor and self-regulate,” she said. “The algorithm works on profiling and hyper-personalisation of content that is geared to playing with our vulnerabilities… You might start off looking for recipes to make lasagne and end up in some weird corner of the net and wonder, ‘How am I seeing this?’”

Baltic states discuss joint response to Russian, Belarusian grain transit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:15:00 UTC
22:15:00 KST

Lithuania is discussing a joint response with Latvia and Estonia to efforts to transit Russian and Belarusian grain through the Baltic states, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Tuesday.
Sinkevičius said he discussed the issue by phone with his Latvian counterpart Monday, amid reports that grain allegedly stolen from Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories could be transported through the Baltic countries.
The shipments will not be allowed to pass through Lithuania’s Klaipėda port “unchecked”, Sinkevičius told reporters in Klaipėda.
“The issue concerns not just Lithuania as a state; in this case, we are talking about three states – Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania,” he said. “We will, of course, carry out checks, monitor the situation and will not allow such cargo to pass unchecked.”
Lithuania supports Ukraine and does not want its port and rail infrastructure used to facilitate Russian grain shipments, Sinkevičius said.
“We will certainly not allow our port infrastructure and railways to be used in such a way that doubts might arise later, as our partners in Ukraine are watching to see how we behave,” he said.
The Lithuanian Agriculture Ministry on Monday asked the State Food and Veterinary Service to immediately investigate the origin of all grain transiting from Russia and Belarus, including both feed and food-grade grain.
The service last week took samples from one grain shipment at the port of Klaipėda and plans to have their origin determined at a foreign laboratory. It confirmed Monday that no additional samples had been taken.
Sinkevičius said authorities want shipments to undergo genetic testing to establish their origin, although the volumes involved are relatively small by Lithuanian standards.
Agriculture Minister Kęstutis Mažeika said the three Baltic states should verify the origin of both feed and food-grade grain arriving from Russia and Belarus.
Mažeika said Lithuania was considering requiring inspections at the border with Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region rather than at the Klaipėda port. That would allow the port to prioritise exports of Lithuanian grain, he said.
“Our priority is to free up the port for Lithuanian grain from Lithuanian farmers so that as much of it as possible can be exported,” Mažeika said.
Authorities are also considering extending mandatory origin testing to other food products, including edible oil, he said.
Mažeika said Lithuania would seek a European Union consensus on applying such checks to food products, which currently benefit from an EU exception covering both raw and processed food.
The issue has gained attention following reports that grain allegedly stolen from Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia could be entering European markets through the Baltic states.
The Lithuanian president’s chief foreign policy adviser Asta Skaisgirytė on Tuesday called for measures to prevent Russia from exploiting ports in Lithuania and other EU countries to export grain.

Ukrainian woman designing a ballistic missile to put Moscow in reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:13:28 UTC
22:13:28 KST

Millennial woman designing Ukraine's own ballistic missile says it will soon put Moscow in reach
Kyiv — Ukraine's most important weapons manufacturer wears mismatched earrings and a black knit dress.
"The good thing about being the boss is that you get to set the dress code," Iryna Terekh, the 34-year-old CEO of Fire Point, one of Ukraine's largest drone makers, told CBS News, grinning as she took a seat next to a model of one of the company's latest designs.
With her high heels, bright smile, and entourage of millennial assistants and executives, Terekh stands out in her factory, where throngs of middle-aged men lug drone parts, wield power tools and chain-smoke cigarettes. But she is hardly an exception in a country forced to reinvent itself since Russia launched its invasion in February 2022.
"When the full-scale invasion started, a lot of people had to review what could be their personal impact," she said. "You never really know what kind of knowledge and what kind of experience could be transformed and pivoted into something new."
Terekh's experience was in design and management.
Trained as an architect in the northern Ukrainian city of Irpin, she started building patios and outdoor furniture while also developing a successful high-performance concrete company.
In the early months of 2022, Russian forces occupied Irpin, destroying roughly 70% of the city.
"I understood how vulnerable we are to the complete barbarian behavior of our enemy," Terekh told CBS News. "And if there are any competences that I could put on the table for the sake of fighting this war, then I have to do this."
After escaping Russian occupation, Terekh began looking for a way to help. In the fall of 2022, Russia started attacking Ukrainian cities with Iranian-made, long-range Shahed exploding drones. It also started manufacturing its own versions, known as Gerans.
Terekh and Ukrainian businessman Denys Shtilerman, whom she had worked with designing outdoor urban spaces before the war, decided to build their own long-range attack drones to help Ukraine strike back.
Shtilerman had a background in defense engineering, but most other initial members of the team, including Terekh, came from civilian backgrounds. Yehor Skalyha, their third co-founder, was a film producer.
At first, the company aimed to build 20 of its FP-1 drones per month. By 2024, they were regularly being used to strike Russian airfields, ammunition depots and oil refineries. But over the last two years, the company's ambitions, and its arsenal, have grown.
Fire Point now makes 300 to 400 long-range attack drones per day, and it has added more advanced weapons to its production lines.
In June, a Fire Point cruise missile completed a mission of over 1,000 miles, which she claimed as the longest-range strike ever carried out by a cruise missile in combat history.
Terekh also made the bold claim that Ukraine has launched twice as many deep strikes into Russia as Russia has into Ukraine in 2026 — with 60% of the Ukrainian attacks using Fire Point weapons.
She said her company is now just months away from deploying Ukraine's first domestically designed and manufactured ballistic missile. Unlike cruise missiles, which stay lower to the ground, ballistic missiles follow an arc trajectory that takes them much higher, making them harder to intercept.
Fire Point is among many Ukrainian startups that have helped to shift the country from being solely a recipient of military aid to an engine of defense technology innovation.
Many other companies have similar, unlikely stories of their beginnings. The founder of Sine Engineering, which has attracted American investment in its communications and navigation technology, ran a business making standing desks before the war. Yaroslav Azhnyuk, founder of the Fourth Law, which makes autonomous guidance systems for drones, previously founded Petcube, a pet tech startup backed by the American business accelerator Y Combinator.
Terekh believes these companies, with their founders' diverse backgrounds outside the defense sector and their shared ability to pivot to new endeavors, have been key to their successes.
"This works in Ukraine because we have very low bureaucracy, because we have direct communication with the army, and because we have companies that react," she said.
The country's innovative approach to defense manufacturing and procurement has also attracted the attention of its allies.
In 2025, the U.S. military announced its own program to copy Iran's Shahed drones, known as "LUCAS," which deployed its first relatively cheap long-range drones in the Middle East in February.
The U.S. and Ukrainian governments are expected to sign a new defense agreement soon that would expand Ukrainian military technology exports to the U.S. and joint ventures with American companies.
Terekh said Fire Point's primary focus remains on Ukraine's defense, but she welcomed the idea of one day playing a role in a new, wider Western security architecture.
"We need to ensure that Ukraine will stop just being a breadbasket for the world," she said, referring to the country's longtime primary export of grains. "Now we have something to offer which is much more valuable, and the defense industry is a huge driver for this."
