====================================================================================================

Trump’s approval rating is plummeting – as his fortune grows and grows | Arwa Mahdawi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:12:18 UTC
22:12:18 KST

If I had a dollar for every time Donald Trump said something inane, I would be a very rich woman. But even with an income that steady, I could never hope to be as flush as the president. A Forbes calculation from March puts his net worth at about $6.5bn – and it’s growing rapidly. Trump made $2.2bn in 2025 via business interests that ranged from selling cryptocurrency and Trump Bibles to offering early access to his (often market-moving) Truth Social posts.
To be fair, Trump isn’t making all this money just so he can buy golf clubs and gold toilets. No, he’s amassing these billions for the good of the little people; it’s altruism, not avarice! “I do this for our Country, not myself,” the president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday night alongside an AI-generated picture of him trading Intel stock. “I’ve made Hundreds of Billions of Dollars on Stocks, and many other type Holdings, for the U.S.A., not myself, and all I do is get criticized by the Radical Left Dumocrats. Very unfair, but what can you do!”
Oh, I have some ideas about what you can do, Mr President. Unfortunately, I can’t print most of them. I also can’t explain why Trump said he’s made hundreds of billions, apart from pointing to his propensity for exaggeration. It seems his post was referring to the fact that the US government took a 9.9% stake in Intel last year. That stake was worth $8.9bn at the time and as of Friday is worth nearly five times as much.
According to the Trump administration, this is a win for everyone. In May, the White House released a statement calling Intel’s surging stock price “a direct windfall for American taxpayers”. Weirdly, I seem to have missed my portion of that windfall. Intel’s stock price has had little impact on my life. What is having an impact is the soaring cost of necessities such as electricity and groceries.
But I shouldn’t be grumpy, should I? I should be grateful that our intrepid president is balancing the demands of the day job with stock trading for the good of the country. According to Trump’s latest government disclosure, he made more than 1,000 equity trades in June. And his picks are doing very well: a report published in August by Democrats on Congress’s joint economic committee argued that Trump’s holdings in oil and gas stocks had risen by nearly $16m because of the war with Iran. “Experts on government ethics have flagged how rare it is for presidents to hold and trade stocks in individual companies, especially since Trump’s war in Iran and his other favors to the oil industry have all pushed up the value of Big Oil stocks,” the report read.
Trump’s shamelessness may be rare, but he isn’t the only politician with serious conflicts of interest issues apropos stock market dealings. A 2022 New York Times investigation found that, from 2019 to 2021, 97 lawmakers or their family members traded financial assets in industries that could be affected by their legislative committee work. In 2020, for example, the wife of the now retired Democratic congressman Alan Lowenthal sold her Boeing shares a day before a House committee on which Lowenthal sat released a damning report about the company. Lowenthal told the Times that he was not involved in this trade at all, so I imagine it was just a funny coincidence.
Still, these sorts of funny coincidences don’t do much to build up trust in the US government, do they? A majority of Americans support commonsense legislation to stop lawmakers and their family members from trading individual stocks. After a lot of resistance, a bill to this effect is winding its way through Congress. The bill does not affect the president or the vice-president, however.
Money can’t buy you everything, of course: while the president’s stock portfolio is rising, his personal stock is plummeting. According to an FT poll this week, Trump’s approval rating has hit a record low, with only 33% of registered voters saying they approve of his performance.
But don’t take that as a sign that the US is coming to its senses or that Republicans are cognisant that dear leader’s war is bleeding the country dry: the same poll found that 72% of Republicans still approve of the president. That figure is down from 82% in May, but it’s still an awful lot of people. Either these Trump loyalists are bigoted fools or they are getting the Intel windfall checks that I’m missing.
Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Hunter Biden turns laptop scandal into memecoin
Hunter Biden is launching a memecoin called $LAPTOP, named after the infamous notebook that became the center of a political scandal during the 2020 US presidential campaign, his X post has indicated. The post features a video montage of media reports referencing the laptop and promotes a September 9 launch.
The device contained emails and financial records tied to the former US president’s son’s overseas business dealings, alongside explicit images and videos documenting his drug and alcohol use.
The token will launch on Coinbase’s Base network with a total supply of one billion coins, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday. Biden and his fellow founders will control 30% of the supply, while another 20% has been earmarked for airdrops – free token distributions used by crypto projects to promote new coins.
Among those in line for free $LAPTOP tokens are subscribers to Biden’s Substack and video journalist Andrew Callaghan’s mailing list – as well as investors who lost money on US President Donald Trump’s $TRUMP memecoin. Unclaimed airdrop tokens will be permanently burned.
Memecoins are highly speculative assets and can lose value rapidly. The $LAPTOP project itself says the token has no utility or ownership rights and warns that digital-asset prices “can fall to zero.”
A further 30% of the total supply is tied to 30 political, crypto, and cultural predictions. Tokens will be burned if specified outcomes occur – including a Democrat winning the 2028 presidential election, Bitcoin reaching another record high or $LAPTOP overtaking $TRUMP in value – while tokens tied to outcomes that do not materialize will go to charity.
$LAPTOP
September 9 pic.twitter.com/QokgWLNxgL
The offer to $TRUMP investors comes after Trump and his wife Melania launched their own memecoins shortly before his return to the White House in January 2025. Trump reported about $635 million in income from $TRUMP in 2025, while most investors lost money – nearly one million wallets were down a combined $3.8 billion by the end of June, according to crypto analytics firm Nansen.
Biden’s laptop became the center of a political scandal just weeks before the 2020 US presidential election, after the New York Post published emails purportedly taken from the device. The newspaper and Trump’s Republican allies alleged that Joe Biden had used his position as vice president to help his son’s business interests in Ukraine, where Hunter served on the board of energy company Burisma. Joe Biden denied involvement in his son’s business dealings.
The laptop’s authenticity itself soon became part of the story. Democrats and more than 50 former US intelligence officials claimed at the time that the laptop story had the “classic earmarks” of a Russian information operation, although the officials acknowledged they had no evidence of such involvement. Subsequent forensic reviews found no evidence of Russian interference and authenticated thousands of emails from the laptop data.
The laptop also contained explicit images and videos documenting Biden’s drug and alcohol use, some of which later featured in his federal gun trial. He was convicted on three felony gun charges in 2024 and pleaded guilty to separate tax offenses before his father granted him a sweeping federal pardon shortly before leaving office.

AI may have just solved a million-dollar math problem. The field will never be the same
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:10:20 UTC
22:10:20 KST

Today may go down as the biggest day in math in at least two decades, if not far longer.
In a development that crystallizes an existential shift in humankind’s oldest intellectual discipline, artificial intelligence has reportedly solved one of the six open “million-dollar” problems in mathematics. The achievement proves that the equations that govern the motion of fluids are fundamentally flawed.
“This is a Deep Blue–Kasparov moment,” wrote mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, referring to the sea change in thinking about machine intelligence that occurred when a supercomputer beat world champion Garry Kasparov at chess in the 1990s, in a statement released late on Monday. “The community needs to have serious and unhurried discussion about where to go from here.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But according to Buckmaster, the proof’s origins may be murkier than they seem. In the same statement, he wrote that he and Levent Alpöge, a mathematician and an Anthropic employee, made significant progress toward the problem last month. But before the pair could publish, Buckmaster alleged in the statement, rumors of their method reached OpenAI, where researchers used the company’s large language model (LLM) to finish the job with a single prompt. The prompt “had been sent in the past few days, after information about our work had reached OpenAI,” Buckmaster alleged.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment; in a press conference later on Tuesday, the firm denied the allegations.
The mathematical problem concerns the Navier-Stokes equations, which govern the flow of fluids—from the whirlpool circling your bathtub’s drain to the turbulent winds El Niño hurls across the North American continent. After two centuries of study, mathematicians haven’t been able to figure out whether these equations perfectly describe reality in every situation or if they sometimes admit aberrant mathematical blips that could never happen in a real fluid. Answering this quandary has been viewed as so beyond the reach of existing mathematics that the Clay Mathematics Institute has offered $1 million to anyone who does it.
Over the past few years, two mathematicians, Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa, worked out a potential trick to break the equations—or “blow them up,” as such an achievement is described in math. They called the method “forcing.” It focuses on a part of the equations, as written in the Clay problem, that mathematicians previously deemed inconsequential. In fact, most experts typically write the problem without this term, assuming that any blowup should be the same with or without it. But Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa realized there might be a way to break the equations solely by using this often overlooked piece.
About a year ago, Buckmaster took up Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa’s approach, working with Alpöge and using LLMs from OpenAI’s rival company Anthropic to parse through the mathematical possibilities. Progress was slow, according to Buckmaster’s statement, until August 15, when he and Alpöge used the method to prove that the Navier-Stokes equations’ simpler, frictionless cousins, the Euler equations, did in fact blow up.
This finding, on its own, is a monumental mathematical achievement that is worthy of any award in math and a key step toward solving the Navier-Stokes problem. Buckmaster and Alpöge were able to verify that the proof was correct using the programming language Lean, but the English-language explanation the LLMs produced was barely readable, according to Buckmaster. The pair started trying to make sense of the mathematical steps one by one and wrote them in a way other researchers would be able to digest.
According to Buckmaster, rumors of their work reached OpenAI at some point in the past week, and the company apparently had a team that was already working on the problem. But after becoming aware of the pair’s work, he alleged, OpenAI focused its attention on “forcing”—the often-ignored piece of the Clay problem. In a major effort over last weekend, the OpenAI team apparently used an internal model to take the result further, blowing up the full Navier-Stokes equations, according to Buckmaster.
Buckmaster wrote in his statement that he spoke on the phone on Sunday with Sébastien Bubeck, who leads OpenAI’s math team, and another unnamed OpenAI employee. Buckmaster alleged that the call became contentious, with OpenAI offering him sole authorship for the Navier-Stokes result in a paper that would acknowledge that the company’s internal model had solved it. Bubeck allegedly wanted to exclude Alpöge, an employee of OpenAI’s competitor, according to Buckmaster. He asserted that he threatened to inform the media and alleged that “the reply was ‘Why would you ruin your career?’” according to the statement.
At 11:58 P.M. EDT on Monday, Buckmaster posted his and Alpöge’s results, along with the statement laying out his account of events. According to the statement, he does not know how the OpenAI team so quickly reconstructed the details of its approach. Buckmaster wrote that he asked Bubeck if the OpenAI LLM was given access to his personal prompts to the company’s model Codex, which he and Alpöge were using throughout the process and thought were private. Bubeck told him no but wouldn’t answer whether the model’s training involved user data, which might have included Buckmaster and Alpöge’s private prompts, Buckmaster alleged.
Beyond the jockeying for credit among the AI vanguard and the implications for the future of mathematics as a human vocation, there’s a mathematical issue. The Clay problem, as written, is solved. But the Clay problem, as many experts imagine it, lacks the piece that the forcing method relies on. Moreover, because this element is so crucial to the method, it’s not clear whether there’s any way to extend the proof to blow up the Navier-Stokes equations without it. Some in the community may say that the problem hasn’t really been solved or that this has only been achieved through a loophole. That leaves the Clay Institute, and the field of mathematics, in a bit of a quandary. In any case, Buckmaster is emphatic that the key ideas be credited to Martínez-Zoroa and Córdoba. “I believe Luis Martínez-Zoroa deserves a Fields Medal,” he wrote in his statement.
Ultimately, math may never be the same. AI companies have fixated on using their technology to solve math problems for more than a year. Because the field’s focus on objectivity aligns with these companies’ goal of developing superhuman intelligence, they’ve been pushing their models to do math that no human can faster than any human can. It appears they’ve succeeded.
“There is a far bigger story here than the one in my statement: the sheer magnitude of what frontier models can now do, and what that means for us all,” Buckmaster wrote on Mastodon a little before 6 A.M. EDT on Tuesday. “I hope the labs can see this and set the petty posturing aside.”
Editor’s Note (9/8/26): This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

Ukraine Unveils Coral Air Defense System Launcher for the First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:09:52 UTC
22:09:52 KST

During the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland, Ukraine presented the Coral anti-aircraft missile launcher for the first time.
A correspondent for Militarnyi reported this.
An image released by Ukroboronprom shows a missile being launched from a self-propelled launcher mounted on a Czech Tatra truck chassis. The missile is intended to intercept aerial and ballistic targets. It is planned to be used as part of an air defense system.
As the developer notes, in exceptional cases, it can also engage ground-based or surface-based radar-contrast targets.
The missile weighs 450 kg, of which 36 kg is the warhead. Its guidance system combines an inertial navigation system, radio correction, and an active radar homing seeker.
The missile has a diameter of 230/300 mm and a length of 4.8 m. Its wingspan is 835 mm, and its control surface span is 685 mm. Research and development work on the Coral project began in 2016. At that time, the missile project was referred to in documents as a component of a ship-based anti-aircraft missile system.
Coral became a topic of widespread public discussion in 2021, when the Luch Design Bureau unveiled a full-scale mock-up of the missile at the Arms and Security-2021 exhibition.
At that time, it was positioned as a standardized modular missile intended for use in both land-based and ship-based air defense systems, and potentially also as an air-to-air missile.
In the initial phase, Coral had significantly more modest stated specifications: a range of up to 30 km, an altitude of up to 10 km, a weight of about 300 kg, and a 25-kg warhead. The missile was 4.33 m long with a diameter of 230/260 mm. At the same time, the designers emphasized that specific characteristics could vary depending on the customer’s requirements.
One of the project’s key features was the maximum standardization of components.
In 2021, Oleg Korostelov, chief designer of the Luch Design Bureau, estimated the system’s readiness at approximately 70%. At the time, Luch was considering creating an entire line of Ukrainian air defense systems with engagement ranges of about 10 km, 30–40 km, and up to 100 km. Coral was intended to take the middle range in this system.

Cluster bomb casualties near record, driven by war in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:07:09 UTC
22:07:09 KST

Cluster bomb casualties near record, driven by war in Ukraine
GENEVA, Sept 8 - Cluster munitions killed or wounded at least 1,063 people in 2025 — most of them in Ukraine — in the third-highest annual toll on record, according to a report released ahead of a conference reviewing a treaty banning the weapons.
The vast majority of the casualties — 87% — were civilians, and around two-fifths were children, the Cluster Munition Coalition's annual report said on Tuesday.
The treaty was helping affected communities, "yet the rising human toll, continued and new use, production, and transfers by states not party are stark warnings that these gains cannot be taken for granted," coalition director Tamar Gabelnick said.
The highest annual toll, 1,172, was recorded by the coalition in 2022, the year that Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Cluster munitions, fired from the ground or by aircraft, explode midair, spraying smaller bomblets over a wide area.
Survivors often suffer major injuries from blasts and burns that can result in lifelong medical needs. Unexploded bombs can remain on the battlefield long after a conflict ends.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine has signed up to the Convention on Cluster Munitions, under which 112 states parties have agreed to prohibit the use of the weapons.
Russia has long argued that cluster munitions are lawful weapons and says humanitarian problems arise from their improper use.
Ukraine has also used cluster munitions, the report found. Ukraine's military says it adheres to the norms of international humanitarian law in using such weaponry, the report added.
Iran, Myanmar, Russia, Thailand and Ukraine, none of them parties to the convention, used cluster munitions during the reporting period, said the report, which has been recording casualties since 2010.
It also found evidence of new production in nine countries, including China, Israel, North Korea, Russia and South Korea.
The Red Cross has called for more states to join the Convention ahead of a conference reviewing the treaty in Vientiane, Laos in mid-September.
"We need a larger group of states and most big military powers to join this convention," Fahad Ahmed, Legal Adviser at the Red Cross, said.
The Red Cross said funding cuts have forced it to reduce physical rehabilitation support for victims. REUTERS

BSW and AfD – a political love-hate relationship in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:07:00 UTC
22:07:00 KST

BSW and AfD – a political love-hate relationship in Germany
September 8, 2026
Following the election in Saxony-Anhalt, there is no clear governing coalition because the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) with its 44% share of the vote has fallen just short of securing an absolute majority. That means the formation of a new government in one of Germany's 16 federal states is more difficult than ever. This is also partly due to the success that the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which was founded only in 2024, has managed to achieve. Wagenknecht, a trained economist, was a longtime member of the socialist Left Party, formerly a communist who over time has distanced herself further from her political roots. Her party does not conform to traditional labels. Many people can no longer relate much to labels like "left" or "right," she says.
From the very beginning, Wagenknecht also showed no reluctance to engage with the AfD. Her long-held credo has been that the party includes people who are treated unfairly if labeled as Nazis.
Now, Sahra Wagenknecht and her followers are working towards seeking common ground with the AfD and can even imagine helping the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund into the role of state premier by abstaining from the vote. Wagenknecht mentioned this scenario before the September 6 election.
Both AfD and BSW oppose 'uncontrolled migration'
A few days before the vote, Sahra Wagenknecht spoke on TV broadcaster ntv about overlapping policy preferences of BSW and AfD voters: "These are people who have similar concerns: They want controlled migration, they do not want this uncontrolled migration and they want above all that politics is again conducted in their interests, that their lives are the focus."
However, there is also a significant degree of agreement on issues other than German immigration policy: both parties call for an end to German arms deliveries to Ukraine, which has been attacked by Russia in violation of international law. Or they claim that freedom of speech no longer exists in Germany.
Whether the BSW will actually team up with the AfD remains completely open. AfD lead candidate Siegmund emphasized even before the election that he intended to govern only with an absolute majority of his own.
When the BSW was founded in January 2024, it had a spectacular start: Formed as a splinter party from the socialist Left Party, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) was swiftly elected to the European Parliament and in the same year received double-digit results in three state parliament elections. In the eastern German states of Brandenburg and Thuringia, the party entered straight into government coalitions. That would also have been possible in Saxony, but coalition negotiations with the CDU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) failed.
The BSW favors a tough approach to refugees. It opposes any form of military support, whether for Ukraine or for Israel.
The party's leader, Sahra Wagenknecht, is an economist who grew up in communist East Germany. She has had no reservations about contact with the AfD from the beginning. As early as 2023, she stated that some people within the party were being labeled Nazis unfairly.
From rising star to struggling party
However, the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt has ruled out a classic coalition. Following elections in Brandenburg and Thuringia in 2024, the branches in those states went against the stated will of their founder and joined governments alongside established parties. The permanent conflict between the federal leadership of the party and its state branches led to the breakdown of the coalition with the Social Democrats in Brandenburg, starting in 2025.
In Thuringia, led by a coalition of the CDU, SPD and BSW, most of the BSW lawmakers declared that they were leaving the party two days before the election in Saxony-Anhalt. However, they wanted to remain a part of the CDU-led state government.
"We have not been elected to tolerate flirts with right-wing radicals," is how Finance Minister Katja Wolf explained this decision, referring to the rapprochement with the AfD initiated by Wagenknecht.
The BSW's success in Saxony-Anhalt and accompanying key role in the formation of the government has given the party, at least for the moment, a largely unexpected significance. During the Bundestag federal election of 2025 the BSW narrowly failed to reach the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament and, also due to its many internal conflicts, it seemed to have little credibility among the population.
Furthermore, its figurehead Sahra Wagenknecht has stepped back from the leadership of her party and is no longer running for its chairmanship. She continues to exert her influence in the background, though, and is a drawcard at BSW rallies, especially during election campaigns.
Boost for upcoming state elections?
Following their successful entry into Saxony-Anhalt's parliament, which according to pre-election polls was by no means guaranteed, Wagenknecht responded confidently.
"The BSW's comeback has begun," she told German news agency dpa.
How sustainable this upswing is will be revealed on September 20, when parliamentary elections will be held in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the city-state of Berlin.

INTERVIEW - Palestinian Christian town Taybeh seeks justice in US courts over occupier ‘terrorism’: Mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:06:02 UTC
22:06:02 KST

- The lawsuits would target American Jews and American associations that support settlements, Suleiman Khourieh says 
The Christian-majority town of Taybeh, northeast of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, is preparing to pursue legal action in the US against Israeli occupiers over attacks on Palestinian residents, homes, land and livelihoods, the town’s mayor said.
In an interview with Anadolu, Taybeh Mayor Suleiman Khourieh said the municipality has begun contacts with a specialized rights group in the US to file civil lawsuits before American courts against occupiers.
The town is seeking to use the fact that many affected residents hold US citizenship or permanent residency, known as green cards, he said.
“We are always trying, day and night, to curb these occupiers by all means,” Khourieh said.
“That is why we intend to file lawsuits in the US, because most of our lands are owned by people who hold American citizenship or green cards. Therefore, in the US, we have the right to file cases against those occupiers,” he added.
“In recent days, we contacted an association in the US to file civil cases in American courts against the occupiers,” he said.
Taybeh is one of the most prominent Christian-majority towns in the occupied West Bank. It includes churches, religious and archaeological sites, while agriculture and tourism are sources of income for many residents.
In recent months, the town has seen a rise in occupier attacks on homes, land and livelihoods, amid local and church warnings that the continued attacks could push more families and young people to consider emigration.
Israeli legal path ‘failed’
Khourieh said several Taybeh residents had previously turned to Israeli courts over attacks or damage they suffered, but did not see deterrent results or restoration of their rights.
“That failure pushed the municipality to search for an alternative legal track outside Israel, particularly in the US, where many Taybeh residents or landowners live or hold citizenship,” he said.
The mayor said the attacks include arson, theft, killings, and racist slogans and threats written on homes, as well as attacks on livestock pens and horse stables and the takeover of facilities in the town.
“All of this has been taken over by occupiers, in addition to preventing us from entering 16,000 dunams of our land,” he said.
Taybeh is surrounded by illegal settlements and settlement outposts, while residents say the attacks are no longer isolated incidents but part of a daily reality that increasingly restricts access to agricultural and grazing land.
“The goal of the expected legal action is to press for an end to the attacks and hold those involved accountable, rather than settling for political condemnations that residents say have not changed the situation on the ground,” Khourieh said.
The mayor said the municipality is currently preparing documents and evidence of the occupier attacks to support the lawsuits, in coordination with a US rights group whose name was not disclosed.
The move raises legal questions over the jurisdiction of US courts regarding acts committed outside the US, and whether the status of plaintiffs as US citizens or permanent residents could provide grounds for such lawsuits.
It also raises the possibility of pursuing institutions or bodies believed to provide funding or support to occupiers.
“The lawsuits would target American Jews and American associations that support settlements,” Khourieh said.
“The US-based group coordinating with the municipality had told us that there was a strong possibility the lawsuits would be accepted,” he said, adding that the town is now preparing the needed documents and evidence.
Legal attempt to curb occupiers
Khourieh placed the new legal move within a broader context of international contacts conducted by the Taybeh municipality over the past years, which he said also brought no concrete results.
“Almost all ambassadors of the world visited us, along with ministers from different countries,” he said.
“They all promised us, but until now we have not seen any benefit from them, and until now they have not curbed any occupier,” he added.
The move comes amid escalating occupier violence in the West Bank and growing international criticism of the Israeli government over its failure to take sufficient measures to prosecute attackers.
“Taybeh will continue searching for ways to curb occupiers,” the mayor said, adding that turning to US courts came after previous tracks failed to protect Palestinians or stop the attacks.
The move comes days after US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee visited the town of Turmus Ayya near Ramallah, where he met Palestinians holding US citizenship and relatives of American citizens killed in occupier attacks.
During Saturday’s visit, Huckabee described occupier attacks on Palestinians, including burning cars and mosques and storming and vandalizing homes, as “an act of terrorism,” and called for the perpetrators to be prosecuted.
Huckabee said the US Embassy does not have the authority to investigate crimes, but can inform the Israeli government of the need to address specific cases and crimes, stressing that such acts cannot continue without investigation and accountability.
His visit coincided with occupiers entering the eastern part of Turmus Ayya, about 100 meters from where the ambassador was present, according to municipal council member Awad Abu Samra.
The envoy’s visit adds further weight to efforts by Palestinian-Americans to pursue legal action in US courts against those involved in attacks against Palestinians.

Ilayda Cakirtekin

The European Commission president on Tuesday denounced the funeral ceremony held for convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, known as the “Butcher of Bosnia."
"The images from Ratko Mladic’s funeral yesterday in Belgrade were shocking. Ratko Mladic was a convicted war criminal. He was responsible for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity," Ursula von der Leyen wrote on US social media company X.
She called the apparent official support and presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral "deeply regrettable."
"They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe’s recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia’s path towards the European Union," von der Leyen added.

Confidence in imminent victory, Putin’s visit to India: statements by Kremlin spokesman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:03:45 UTC
22:03:45 KST

MOSCOW/NEW DELHI, September 8. /TASS/. Moscow is confident in an imminent victory, and combat operations are progressing very successfully for Russia, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov stated during a briefing for Indian media ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi.
He also noted that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India, which will take place in a few days, will be significant for both countries.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the Kremlin spokesman.
Conflict in Ukraine
Russia did not want and did not start the war in Ukraine but it is trying to stop it: "We actually never wanted this war. What we’re trying to do, we’re trying to stop the war that was launched before, and it was not launched by us. It was not started by us."
Russia remains open to the peaceful settlement of the Ukrainian conflict: "We do want the solution of the Ukrainian conflict by peaceful means, and Russia is open for this process."
India’s position regarding the Ukrainian conflict largely coincides with Russia’s: "We know the position of India on the Ukrainian conflict, and to great extent it corresponds with our own position".
Russia has to achieve its goals regarding Ukraine through a special military operation, although it would prefer to do so by peaceful means: "We have to reach our goals during the special military operation, but we would prefer to do it in a peaceful way."
Russian troops are advancing in the special military operation zone: ""The dynamics on the front is known to all the experts. We’re moving forward."
Russia is confident in an imminent victory: "We are sure that the victory is very near. We are very confident in our military potential, in our military. Our military actions are going on very successfully."
Russia welcomes any efforts by other countries to achieve a peaceful settlement of the conflict in Ukraine: "We welcome all the attempts to make any contribution in the sphere of the Ukraine settlement. We welcome the willingness of the Indian side to contribute. We welcome the efforts of American President President Trump."
Moscow expects the resumption of trilateral negotiations with Washington and Kiev to resolve the Ukrainian crisis: "We hope that there will be some movement in this respect. We hope to restart negotiations between three parties: Russian, Ukrainian, and American."
The conflict in Ukraine could have ended long ago, but Kiev, being incited by Europeans, does not want an end to it: "I wouldn’t say that Kiev is that flexible, and I wouldn’t say that Kiev is really willing to stop this war. Should they be willing to do that, the war [would have] been over for a long time, but they’re being provoked to great extent by some European countries."
Europeans are inciting Kiev to go to war and deluding themselves with the hope of achieving a "strategic defeat" of Russia: "They [the Kiev authorities] are still being provoked to a great extent by some European countries that cannot get rid of the idea of strategically defeating Russia. We will not let that happen, and we’re not letting that happen."
Indian citizens participating in the special military operation will be returned home as soon as their identities are established and a list of names is compiled: "Now the work is being done to make a list of those Indian citizens, who are now on the battlefield, and they will be sent back home as soon as they are determined. We are in very deep contact, profound contact with the Indian side on this issue."
Dangers of trying to preserve a unipolar world
Attempts to preserve a unipolar system in the world are very dangerous: "Unipolar system is actually collapsing, it is losing losing its competitiveness, and then at the same time, the unipolar system is trying to regain power, taking sometimes very harsh steps, injuring the global system, the global economy, the global environment and politics, the global system of international law. So this is a very dangerous process."
The global majority, represented by BRICS, is striving for a different world order: "Where every country is equal to another, where every country has a right to a say, where every country has the right to fair competition and trade, where every country is secured from any illegal sanctions or illegal pressure, where every country can secure its national interests without without experiencing somebody’s pressure and demands to do otherwise."
Sanctions and de-dollarization
Russia is not seeking de-dollarization: "It’s not because we are aiming for de-dollarization <…>. To the contrary, we’re open to every acceptable method of payment. But you know that certain countries are using some national currencies as a tool for political pressure."
Since some countries do not allow Russia to use their currency for trade, Russia must use rubles: "So, if they don’t let us use their money, we use our own money."
The United States itself is undermining confidence in the dollar as a reserve currency: "The more trust is ruined, the more trust goes in favor of national currencies. This is the process, and this is the nature of the process."
Russia considers Western sanctions unacceptable: "Of course, we do not accept, and we consider it to be definitely illegal in terms of international law, any attempts to introduce limitations on international trade and to threaten other countries' third parties for doing trade with others."
Russia intends to discuss this issue as part of settling the Ukrainian crisis, but the settlement itself is of paramount importance to Moscow: "[The] issue of sanctions is on the agenda. It is not in the front row because the settlement itself is the issue number one, but it’s an untakable part of the whole agenda of the peaceful settlement around Ukraine."
Putin’s visit to India and bilateral relations
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India, which will take place in a few days, will be significant for both countries: "In a couple of days he [Putin] will start his visit to India. <...> Jointly our two leaders are going to visit some forums."
Putin and Modi are also going to hold a mutually important bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 11.
Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi have a close yet pragmatic relationship: [They are] able to discuss in a very open and constructive way the most sensitive issues of the global agenda and our bilateral relations."
They will be discussing economic cooperation, although the specifics will remain confidential so that unfriendly countries cannot interfere: the conversation will proceed "discreetly, but in a very very constructive manner."
During the meeting, Putin will tell Modi about the current situation in the special military operation zone: "It will be another opportunity for President Putin to inform his Indian friend on the current situation on the fronts, on the war with Ukraine."
The leaders will also discuss the impact of US aggression against Iran on the global economy: "Negative consequences of all that are inevitable, unfortunately. And our two countries, they are also subject to those consequences."
India is Russia's strategic partner, and Moscow expects to develop relations with New Delhi across a wide range of issues: "We really consider it of extreme importance for our two countries that we continue to develop our cooperation in a very very wide scope of fields, we're quite successful in that."
Russia has excellent military equipment and is ready to continue supplying it to its Indian partners: "We have very good military equipment. Some of the equipment items are the best in the world, and we're ready to share them with our Indian partners."
Middle East
Russia believes that the situation around Iran is having a negative effect on the global economy: "The situation [surrounding Iran], unfortunately, is still very tense, and every day brings new turbulences. This is definitely not doing well for the global economy."
Russia would prefer that the United States and Iran return to the previously signed memorandum of understanding: "We prefer that countries involved return to the memorandum of understanding that was signed between Iran and the United States, or turn to something else that would bring peace to this region."
Trump's statement about the Moon
Space should be a space for interaction, not confrontation between countries, and cannot be subject to any "privatization": "I don't think that we can support the idea of privatization in space. It should be free of that. Space should be a ground for mutual cooperation and for mutual dialogue, not a ground for confrontation."
As for US President Donald Trump's publication, he hardly "declared" the Moon as belonging to the United States: "When [US] President [Donald] Trump said that 'the Moon is ours,' I think he meant that it wasn't their property, but he meant that very soon, hopefully, American astronauts will stand on the moon."

Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers.
Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations.
The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS
— Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026
Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”.
The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment.
“Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”.
Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events.
However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people.
Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company.
However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”.
“We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned.
Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska.
The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska.
Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation.

The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour.
However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”.
A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company.

When is it really worth changing a child’s school, and how can this transition be made without unnecessary stress?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:02:41 EEST
22:02:41 KST

When is it really worth changing a child’s school, and how can this transition be made without unnecessary stress?
Kyiv • UNN
A first-grader’s adaptation may take up to three months. A transfer should be discussed with the child and decided upon after clarifying the reasons.
The start of the school year does not go smoothly for all children. It can be especially difficult for first-graders, teenagers, and students transferring to a new school. Psychologist Olha Holubytska, who has 16 years of experience working with children and adults, told UNN journalist in more detail how to distinguish normal adaptation from a situation in which it would truly be better for a child to change schools, and how to properly discuss such a step with them.
Details
According to the psychologist, after entering first grade, a child needs time to get used to the new conditions, so adaptation can take up to three months, and certain changes in behavior during this period do not necessarily indicate problems at school.
In first grade, children adapt to learning. Adaptation of up to three months is considered normal. That is, during this period, a child may be getting used to a new stage. This does not mean that absolutely every child needs exactly three months. But during this time, we will consider it normal if a child behaves differently than usual. They may not want to go to school, and it may be difficult for them — all of this may be part of the adaptation process
The psychologist advises parents of younger children to pay particular attention to the child's relationship with the teacher. In her view, in the early grades, the teacher has a major influence on how a student perceives learning and school in general.
With first-graders, we should probably talk in advance about the fact that, first and foremost, the child should like not the school but the teacher. This is because in the early grades and preschool education, a great deal depends specifically on the teacher. The school may be wonderful, but the child's adaptation will depend to a significant extent on the teacher
At the same time, conflict between parents and a teacher can also affect the child. Therefore, the psychologist advises adults to assess not only the student's behavior but also how the teacher communicates with the family, whether they provide information about the child, and how they respond when problems arise.
If the parents do not like the teacher or, for example, the teacher does not like the parents, the child will suffer in the end regardless. If the parents and the teacher have been unable to agree on something and conflicts have begun, this will primarily be evident in their communication: how the teacher contacts the parents, what she tells them, whether she provides information or not, whether she is satisfied with the cooperation or, on the contrary, dissatisfied
It is also important to consider situations in which a child talks about conflicts at school. Olha Holubytska emphasizes that it is important to trust the child, but conclusions should not be drawn solely from their first account.
I have always supported trusting children, but we must not forget that they have an imagination. When they do not know how to tell you about their discomfort or their lack of understanding of why they have to attend this school, they may begin to exaggerate certain stories
For teenagers, the question of changing schools can be even more complicated. According to the expert, if a child has been bullied for a long time, transferring to another school may indeed be a good idea.
For example, when there has been bullying, but it was not possible to stand up for the child, and stereotypes about them have already spread throughout the school, while the school does not give the child a chance for a new reality. In such a case, it is indeed safer to transfer the child to another school. They will be able to start communicating with a clean slate — without the prejudices and labels that may have been attached to them
At the same time, the decision to transfer should not be made based on just one isolated signal, the expert says. First, it is necessary to speak with the child, the homeroom teacher, other teachers, and, if necessary, other parents in order to form a complete picture of the situation.
First, we need to obtain answers from the child, the homeroom teacher, other teachers, parents, and other children. Only after we have formed this complete picture can we draw conclusions, because drawing conclusions based on just one factor means risking making things even worse for the child
She also pays attention to the student's behavior. Changes in a child's mood and behavior do not necessarily indicate problems specifically at school, so, once again, it is important to find out the reason.
If I mention some signs now, they may not be related to problems at school. We cannot know whether the child has actually encountered difficulties at school or, for example, is having problems in a friendship, especially in the case of teenagers. A child may behave in the same way in any stressful situation: either withdrawing into themselves or becoming overly explosive—that is, displaying intense reactions or taking actions that are not usually characteristic of them
Olha Holubytska names trusting relationships as one of the main ways to understand what is happening with a child. This is not only about asking direct questions about school, but also about spending time together without phones, when the child can relax and bring up what is troubling them on their own.
The best way to understand that something is wrong with your child is to build a trusting relationship. A trusting relationship, time together, necessarily without phones. We go for a walk somewhere, we go somewhere together, we do things together, and then there is a chance that at some point the child will relax, see the connection and trust, and may suddenly tell you something they have wanted to say for a long time but did not dare to
However, if the change of school was caused by a move or other circumstances, the psychologist advises first explaining the situation to the child calmly and honestly, at a moment when there is already contact between the parents and the child and a calm atmosphere.
The conversation should take place after everyone has had a good walk and eaten. This is actually very important: not before eating, but when you have already eaten—you have relaxed, and you all feel good. The situation is like this, the atmosphere is pleasant and trusting, you are all lying around talking about something or watching a movie, and then you can pause the movie and say: I have wanted to talk to you about something for a very long time
Olha Holubytska also emphasized that during such a conversation, the child's emotions should not be invalidated, because even a forced transfer to another school may be perceived as the loss of a familiar environment, friends, and important relationships.
Everything should be said honestly and gently, with your own feelings, and the child should be allowed to express any feelings they have. You should not try to reassure them by saying: "Don't worry, everything will be fine." Do not use these invalidating phrases: "Don't cry, everything will be fine, what's wrong with you, you'll find friends." These are all invalidating phrases
Instead, if parents believe that the school is having a negative impact on the teenager, the decision should also be discussed with them. The child needs to be told why the adults see a problem, have their position heard, and discuss possible options.
It can never be an ultimatum about transferring the child; in other words, there must be an honest conversation with them. For example: "I want to talk to you about your school. I have been observing the environment there for a year now, where many children your age smoke, drink, or use drugs, and we can see this. And this is not the environment you need, but I understand that it may seem different to you; let's talk about it"
According to the expert, after the transfer, the child will still have to adapt to the new environment. Therefore, the psychologist advises not to leave the student alone to cope with this period and, if necessary, to involve the school psychologist.
If you transfer your child to another school, you need to understand that they will have to go through another adjustment period, which may also last a long time, while the problems that caused the difficulties at the previous school will most likely not disappear—which means that support will most likely be needed, and perhaps even a psychologist
The main thing, says Olha Holubytska, is not to pull the child out of one school and immediately place them in another without explanations or a conversation. Parents should gather information from various sources, listen to the child, and show them that their opinion is respected, even if the final decision remains with the adults.
It is very important not to pressure or humiliate them, and not to become a tyrant who simply puts this child in a situation where there is no choice. You are saying, "Even though you are my child and I am responsible for you, I make the decisions, but I leave you room for your human rights—to be respected, to have space, to talk, and to be heard and accepted"

Mind the gap: how 30% ruling changes may affect your paycheck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:02:20 UTC
22:02:20 KST

Partner content
Mind the gap: how 30% ruling changes may affect your paycheck
If you are one of those clever people who spent years studying abroad and is now contributing skills to the Dutch economy, there’s good and bad news.
Some economists in the Netherlands have raised alarm bells at the drop in highly-skilled migrants since the failed “hard right” government in 2023. The first international scientists have landed in the Netherlands as the result of a new “tulip” fund to support top thinkers.
But at the same time, the country is winding back a ruling to compensate some temporary highly-skilled workers for their costs, and it will in future be restricted to people with even higher salaries.
From next year, for new highly-skilled migrants and everyone who arrived after January 1, 2024, the 30% ruling for people with rare skills will be cut to 27%. This means that for five years, the first 27% of their salary will be paid untaxed – an incentive to make this high-tax country more attractive and compensate top international talent for costs such as expensive housing.
“This will make a difference of between €50 and €100 a month for most of the people we help,” said a tax adviser for Blue Umbrella. “One more dinner at home each month, perhaps, but it is still money.”
The tax break, which has strict conditions and must be applied for by the employer, will also only be valid for salaries from just over €50,000 from 2027, or for masters students under 30, earning from around € 38,000. This is a slight rise from the current levels.
It is also limited at the top end to what is known as the Balkenendenorm, the top salary for civil servants and quango employees – €262,000 this year. There are around 100,000 people nationally with the “expat” ruling for skills that cannot be found locally and most Blue Umbrella clients and internationals, of course, earn nothing like this amount.
“Typically, it’s around €60,000 to €80,000,” says the Blue Umbrella adviser, who points out that this may be a family’s single salary after an international move. “Every month, the expat ruling might save €500 on the usual tax rate. And they will lose an extra 3%.”
While there is sometimes criticism of highly-skilled migrants in Dutch media for living in local housing, Blue Umbrella points out that these people are vital for the economy.
“Fewer of them are coming to the Netherlands in general because the mood is one where we say: no migrants,” he said. “But we need highly-skilled migrants. Companies are closing in the games industry and IT specialists are going to other countries that try to attract them, like Portugal.”
The tax climate is less conducive to starting a business too, he added, meaning that entrepreneurs may be less likely to choose the Netherlands. But Blue Umbrella is hopeful that there will be a greater realisation that this small country is competing for global talent.
“We are a knowledge economy, we are known for technology and trading, and you need smart people,” he said. “There’s a battle going on around the world because other countries want them too. We are known for our schools and education, the cyber war is coming, and this should be a moment of change.”
Find out more about your personal tax situation and the 27% ruling by contacting Blue Umbrella.

Free menstrual pad dispensers installed across University of Tartu

Free menstrual pad dispensers installed across University of Tartu
Free pads are now available at University of Tartu (TÜ) buildings across the city, with 39 dispensers installed to make menstrual products easier to access when needed.
The initiative was launched this academic year after the university's Faculty of Science and Technology student council raised concerns about access to menstrual products. The dispensers are located in academic buildings across Tartu and are regularly restocked by cleaning staff, the university said Tuesday.
Research suggests that easier access to menstrual products can support students' well-being and participation in school.
A 2024 TÜ bachelor's thesis, based on 2022 data from more than 1,000 students at 19 schools across Estonia, found that 64 percent of students had missed school, practices or other activities due to menstruation, 26 percent had difficulties obtaining menstrual products and 73 percent had used alternatives when such products were unavailable.
Nearly all respondents, or 94 percent, said menstrual pads should be available for free at Estonian schools.
TÜ equality officer Eveliis Padar said these findings show that practical menstruation-related barriers affect a considerable number of learners.
The new initiative will help make menstruation less of an obstacle to participating in university life, Padar noted, supporting a learning and working environment at TÜ "where menstrual pads are regarded as an everyday necessity, just like toilet paper, soap or hand dryers."
No more leaving mid-class
Astrid Jõerand, a student under the Faculty of Science and Technology and one of the leaders of the initiative, said the basic premise is simple: menstruation should not interfere with anyone attending university.
"Students shouldn't have to panic when they get their period unexpectedly, or worry about where they can quickly find a pad," Jõerand said.
Having pads available in university bathrooms, she added, means more students can get what they need and return to class rather than having to leave or go home.
Jõerand also welcomed the fact that a student council proposal was accepted and turned into positive change at the university.
"Sometimes a small and practical change like this can make someone's school day considerably easier," she said.
The dispensers are installed at more than a dozen university buildings, stocked with thin menstrual pads with flexible wings for regular flow.

Basra to Baniyas: Iraq expands energy exports through Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:01:17 UTC
22:01:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Basra to Baniyas: Iraq expands energy exports through Syria
Steps to rebuild economic relations between Iraq and Syria are accelerating, with Syrian territory becoming an effective route for Iraqi energy exports to the Mediterranean.
The volume of Iraqi fuel oil transported through Syria reached about 21.4 million barrels between March and the end of August, alongside efforts to expand cooperation to include the future transport of crude oil and develop a pipeline linking Iraq to the port of Baniyas.
According to data from the Washington-based Energy Research Unit, Iraqi fuel oil exports via the Syrian route rose from 254,000 barrels in March to 686,000 in April. Then they jumped to 3.86 million barrels in May, followed by five million in June and 5.65 million in July, reaching about 5.91 million barrels during August.
The quantities are transported by tanker trucks through land crossings between the two countries, particularly the Al-Waleed-Tanf and Rabia-Yarubiyah crossings. They travel through Syria's road network to storage tanks at the port of Baniyas on the Mediterranean, where they are loaded onto tankers for re-export to foreign markets.
The expansion of fuel oil traffic through Syrian territory gives a new economic dimension to relations between the two countries.
Syria began receiving convoys of Iraqi tankers heading to Baniyas in April, amid disruptions to shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and Baghdad's efforts to find additional outlets for its exports.
Expanding export routes
Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair said on Saturday that "Iraq is working to build a more flexible export system by diversifying outlets and not concentrating most oil exports through a single route".
In an interview, Khudair explained that the move towards Syria and the port of Baniyas is part of this strategy, alongside existing outlets and other projects being developed by the ministry.
He said that Iraq's export capacity had exceeded 3 million barrels per day, and that the ministry aims to raise this to 5 million barrels per day after completing strategic infrastructure and export pipeline projects, including the route extending towards Baniyas on the Mediterranean.
He added that the importance of this route was not limited to adding new export capacity and would provide an alternative outlet that could be used when disruptions affect traditional export routes.
Khudair further stressed that diversifying outlets had become a key part of Iraq's policy to ensure the continued flow of oil to global markets and reduce risks that could affect exports.
As part of efforts to expand export outlets and increase volumes transported through Syrian territory, Ali Nizar Al-Shatri, director-general of the Iraqi Oil Marketing Company (SOMO), confirmed that talks are under way with the Syrian Petroleum Company to conclude an agreement allowing Basra crude to be transported by tanker trucks to the port of Baniyas.
Al-Shatri told local media that Iraq does not yet have contracts to export crude oil through Syria.
However, the anticipated agreement would allow quantities of Basra crude to be transported from the Zubair 1 and Zubair 2 facilities to Baniyas storage tanks.
The tanks' currently available capacity ranges between 1.5 million and 2 million barrels, in preparation for loading the crude onto tankers and selling it in foreign markets.
He said quantities would be limited during the first phase because Baniyas storage tanks require maintenance.
Road transport would serve as a secondary route to increase export flexibility until the completion of the pipeline project between the two countries.
Viability of the Syrian route
Oil expert Kovan Sherwani said using Syrian territory and the port of Baniyas provides Iraq with an important option for diversifying its export routes and reducing risks resulting from heavy reliance on southern outlets and the Strait of Hormuz.
He said the experience of transporting fuel oil had demonstrated that the route could operate in practice.
Sherwani told The New Arab that "transporting Iraqi crude oil by tanker trucks overland through Syrian territory provides a quick and flexible solution in emergencies, but it is more expensive and has less capacity than pipelines, so it cannot permanently replace the maritime export system".
He added that "the strategic importance of the Syrian route will increase significantly with the operation of a pipeline to Baniyas, giving Iraq direct access to the Mediterranean and increasing its ability to deal with geopolitical crises and disruptions to shipping routes".
Sherwani said the long-term success of this option would remain linked to the storage and loading capacity of facilities in Baniyas.
It would also depend on the efficiency of Syria's transport network, as well as insurance and security costs and stability along the route.
Economic gains
Economic expert Karim Al-Hilo said the Syrian route could go beyond its role in oil to become a basis for expanding economic interests between the two countries.
Syria would benefit from transport, storage, ports, logistics services and transit fees, while Iraq would gain an additional outlet towards the Mediterranean and European markets.
Al-Hilo told The New Arab that growing transit traffic could open the way for expanding trade and investments linked to transport, energy and infrastructure.
This could extend to agriculture, food industries, pharmaceuticals, construction materials and reconstruction.
He said transforming the route from a solution imposed by regional circumstances into a long-term economic partnership would require developing border crossings, transport and storage networks.
It would also require facilitating payments and the movement of companies and traders, allowing for the creation of a sustainable economic corridor linking Iraq with the Syrian coast and foreign markets.
Al-Hilo noted that the economic impact could emerge if energy cooperation becomes an entry point for rebuilding supply chains.
Transport would then not be limited to oil exports, but the same trucks and logistics infrastructure could also benefit from increased movement of goods and investment.
This could reduce transport costs, increase the viability of border crossings and expand economic interests.

Becerra, Hilton to debate in governor’s race days before voters receive mail-in ballots

- Days before mail-in ballots arrive statewide, Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton will face off Sept. 30 in California’s high-stakes governor’s race.
- Voters will see sharply contrasting views on taxes, spending and California’s clashes with the Trump administration as the state prepares to choose a successor to termed-out Gov. Gavin Newsom.
- After weeks of Hilton accusing Becerra of ducking debates, the nationally televised, hourlong CNN event — without a studio audience — will give millions of Californians a side-by-side comparison.
Days before California voters receive their mail-in ballots, gubernatorial candidates Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, and Steve Hilton, a Republican, will debate in a nationally televised face-off.
On Sept. 30 at CNN’s Burbank studio, the two candidates hoping to succeed termed-out Gov. Gavin Newson are expected to spar over sharply divergent visions for the future of the state. California’s next leader is expected to face pressing fiscal issues, as well as a continued battle with the Trump administration.
Given California’s deep Democratic tilt, there was a question whether the two men would debate.
On Aug. 19, Becerra promised multiple debates with Hilton ahead of the general election.
“We will have debates, and between now and Nov. 3, we will continue to go out there and meet with folks to make sure they have an opportunity to see the candidates,” Becerra told reporters after greeting business owners, community leaders and voters during a walking tour of Little Tokyo in downtown Los Angeles. “Voters need to have good information. We’ll make sure they have it, and there will be debates.”
The following day, Hilton said he was skeptical of Becerra’s promise.
“I don’t believe him unless he commits to an actual debate. Invitations are on the table for dates and places,” Hilton said. “Why can’t he just accept them? I think he’s lying. I don’t think he wants to do debates because he doesn’t want to debate his record.”
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton are competing in the race for California governor. Here’s what you need to know about the candidates.
September’s hourlong debate, taking place shortly before county elections officials begin mailing ballots to all the state’s registered voters, will be moderated by the cable network’s anchors Dana Bash and Jake Tapper.
It is the most attention a California gubernatorial contest has drawn since 2010, when “Today” show host Matt Lauer and NBC News Political Director Chuck Todd moderated nationally televised clashes.
That is perhaps unsurprising given how sharply the California electorate has swung left, with no Republican winning a statewide contest since 2006. Two did that year.
While there will not be a studio audience, the debate will air on CNN, CNN International, CNN en Español, CNN.com and related TV and mobile apps for subscribers.

Made in Uzbekistan: Local brands look to new markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:00:59 UTC
22:00:59 KST

From fashion and traditional crafts to electronics and manufactured goods, Uzbek companies are increasingly looking beyond production to build brands that can compete at home and reach consumers abroad.
The “Made in Uzbekistan” label is appearing across an increasingly diverse range of products, as local companies expand production and entrepreneurs look to turn locally made goods into recognisable brands.
The shift can be seen across industries, from textiles, clothing and traditional crafts to electronics, home appliances, food and other manufactured products. It comes amid broader growth in Uzbekistan's manufacturing and exports: industrial production increased by 6.8% in 2025, while exports rose by 24% to about €29 billion, according to the National Statistics Committee.
Changing attitudes towards local products
That change has been particularly visible in Uzbekistan's creative sector.
Teplo Store started organising markets for local designers in 2018 before expanding into a permanent store, festivals and, more recently, an online platform. Today, its store represents around 100 designers, while its festivals can bring together up to 150 participants. Overall, more than 200 designers have worked through the platform.
Co-founder Charos Kamalova says attitudes towards locally made products have changed considerably during that time.
When the project began, she said, products made in Uzbekistan were often associated either with traditional crafts or affordable mass-market goods. Independent designers have since helped create another category based around distinctive ideas, presentation and quality.
“Today it became kind of cool to support local brands,” Kamalova said. “People are coming here, buying this stuff and showing others that, look, I'm supporting local brands.”
Traditional craftsmanship remains an important part of that identity, but designers are increasingly adapting it to contemporary products.
Designer Gulnoza Jo‘rayeva has worked with traditional Uzbek adras, a silk-and-cotton textile, and natural silk for more than 12 years. Her business started at home before gradually expanding and is now represented in seven locations across Uzbekistan.
The production involves young designers, seamstresses and artists, while much of the process remains based on manual work and traditional techniques. Demand has also extended beyond Uzbekistan: the company ships worldwide and has received requests from customers to expand into other cities.
For Teplo co-founder Timur Kamolov, this heritage gives Uzbek designers an advantage — but only if it can be adapted to the needs of modern consumers.
“The key competitive advantage for our brands would be the craftsmanship that we have,” he said.
Kamolov argues that traditional techniques need to be reinterpreted in contemporary and practical products if designers want to compete internationally. At the same time, companies need stronger business processes to turn creative projects into scalable businesses.
Moving beyond the domestic market
Some local brands are already testing demand abroad.
Teplo operated a six-month pop-up store in London's Soho and participated in the London Design Biennale, taking products from Uzbek independent designers directly to international consumers.
Kamalova said the project attracted visitors from different countries and demonstrated interest in Uzbek design beyond the domestic market.
“We saw people from around the world, not only locals in London, that showed huge interest,” she said. “We think that our designers have great potential there.”
Digital sales are providing another route. Teplo has since developed an online platform allowing customers outside Uzbekistan to buy products from local designers, while e-commerce marketplaces are creating additional channels for producers across different sectors to reach consumers abroad.
But moving from local production to international sales brings practical challenges.
For Teplo's London project, the company handled logistics, customs procedures and documentation for participating designers. Kamolov said these processes can be particularly difficult for independent creators, whose expertise often lies in design and production rather than international trade.
The challenge extends beyond the creative industries. According to figures presented by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev following a recent study of exporters, 40% reported difficulties finding foreign customers, while 36% struggled to adapt products to international standards and certification requirements. Another 37% pointed to insufficient financial instruments for exports, and 33% reported gaps in market information, marketing and branding skills.
Building brands for export
New measures announced in August during President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s open dialogue with entrepreneurs aim to address some of those barriers as Uzbekistan seeks to increase exports and develop national brands.
An “Export Navigator” system is planned to support companies entering foreign markets. Authorities also intend to identify 100 products with export potential and provide guidance on overseas competitors, tariffs, certification requirements and logistics.
The measures specifically target branding and market access. Businesses will be eligible for subsidies of up to €43,000 to promote national brands abroad and adapt them to international requirements. Half the cost of bringing in foreign branding specialists is expected to be covered, as well as half of certain warehousing and sales expenses associated with marketplaces.
The government has also announced support covering 80% of consulting costs for participation in international tenders as part of a wider €860 million export-support system.
For Uzbekistan's businesses, these measures come as the idea of what constitutes a locally made product is broadening. Traditional materials and craftsmanship increasingly sit alongside modern manufacturing, independent design and new consumer businesses.
The next test is whether more producers can turn those locally made products into brands that consumers recognise beyond Uzbekistan.
