South Sudan, Uganda agree to ease cross-border activities during health emergencies
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
20:55:36 CST
21:55:36 KST

JUBA, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- South Sudan and Uganda have agreed to remove administrative barriers to facilitate the rapid movement of health personnel, medical vehicles, and emergency supplies across their shared border.
The commitment was formalized Monday evening in Juba, the capital of South Sudan, when the two countries' health ministers signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at strengthening cross-border disease surveillance, joint outbreak response, and regional health security.
South Sudan's Vice President for the Service Cluster Hussein Abdelbagi Akol stated that the government will expedite temporary visa and work permit waivers to allow emergency personnel to move unhindered across the border to support joint surveillance activities.
"The Republic of South Sudan and the Republic of Uganda stand united in our resolve of strengthening cross-border collaboration, seamless information sharing, and preparedness and coordinated response to the public health threat," Akol said during the signing of the MoU.
South Sudan Health Minister Luke Thompson Thoan Teny said the MoU elevates bilateral cooperation from informal goodwill to an institutionalized rapid-response framework, and he cautioned that localized disease outbreaks can quickly escalate into regional emergencies.
Under the pact, the two nations will exchange real-time epidemiological data, issue mutual outbreak alerts, execute joint contact tracing, standardize border entry screening, and coordinate mobile health unit deployments.
Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi emphasized that the agreement is critical given the frequent cross-border movement and lessons learned from past epidemics.
Baryomunsi noted that Uganda contained its recent Ebola outbreak within about 73 days, recording 20 confirmed cases, 18 recoveries, and two fatalities, and reaffirmed the country's readiness to share its containment experience with South Sudan.
Baryomunsi urged both nations to move swiftly from signing to implementation, emphasizing that the agreement requires a structured roadmap outlining clear priorities, responsibilities, timelines, and resources.
He also called for broader regional cooperation, proposing the creation of a standby health workforce, similar to regional security arrangements that could be rapidly deployed to countries facing disease outbreaks.
Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention South Sudan Country Director Tolbert Geewleh Nyenswah said that South Sudan has identified 15 high-risk counties and 22 priority entry points as key components of its preparedness strategy.
Nyenswah noted that the country's updated six-month preparedness plan requires over 30 million U.S. dollars to bolster laboratory infrastructure, medical supplies, logistics, disease surveillance, and healthcare worker safety. ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

21:55:24 KST

GUANGZHOU, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng on Tuesday launched a production line for humanoid robots. The company aims to begin sales and deliveries of these robots in both China and overseas markets by 2027.
Its advanced general-purpose humanoid robot IRON completed automated final assembly and walked off the production line on its own at the launch, marking XPeng's shift from R&D and trial production to line-based manufacturing.
Mass production has been a major challenge for the humanoid-robot industry, which has traditionally depended on small-batch manufacturing and labor-intensive semi-manual assembly.
The company said the production line was designed specifically for large-scale robot manufacturing, drawing on quality-control practices used in the auto industry. More than 80 percent of the production line's core manufacturing processes are automated, XPeng said.
XPeng Chairman He Xiaopeng said the company had built the robot production line from scratch and would continue working to shorten production cycles and expand manufacturing capacity.
After entering mass production, IRON robots will initially be deployed at XPeng stores and internal industrial parks. They are expected to handle tasks including customer reception, vehicle introductions, visitor guidance, inspections and small-item handling.
XPeng said the robots will be tested first in its own commercial and industrial settings, allowing the company to refine their algorithms through real-world use before a broader market rollout in 2027.
China's humanoid robot industry is entering a critical stage of large-scale commercialization and deployment, as embodied intelligence products move from small-batch trials to broader adoption, Xu Xiaolan, chairwoman of the Chinese Institute of Electronics, said at the 2026 World Robot Conference held last month in Beijing. ■

How could Iran’s proposed maritime zone shape US-Iran tensions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:54:36 UTC
21:54:36 KST

While the Trump administration repeatedly suggested that the US war on Iran would end “pretty soon”, rising tensions between the two adversaries and recent tit-for-tat declarations from Washington and Tehran suggest they remain in a war of attrition.
Most recently, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, announced that Tehran would declare a maritime exclusion zone stretching from the US blockade line in the Arabian Sea to Gulf waters near the Strait of Hormuz, prohibiting foreign vessels from entering.
“Any ship entering this new zone will be placed on the sanctions list of Iran,” Rezaei said in a recent interview with Iranian state TV.
In another statement, he warned that US economic warfare on Iran “will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to the blockade perimeter”.
Oral Toga, an Iran expert at the Ankara-based Center for Iranian Studies, sees Tehran’s description of the proposed zone as an attempt to formalise what Iran has sought to operate as “a permission-based transit regime throughout the war” by restricting access to the Strait for its adversaries.
“The zone as described begins at the US Navy's blockade line and extends into parts of the Gulf, which means Tehran is answering a naval blockade with a mirror image of one,” he tells TRT World.
“The stated penalty is not a strike but placement on an Iranian sanctions list, with consequences for a vessel's insurance and its future passage. That is Washington's own tool turned around, and it tells you Iran is trying to move the contest from the military domain, where it is losing, to the administrative and commercial one, where it still has a say,” he says.
Iran’s proposed maritime zone also signals an attempt to widen the perceived scope of the confrontation beyond the Strait of Hormuz.
By threatening restrictions on vessels across waters stretching from the Gulf to the US blockade line in the Arabian Sea, Tehran is creating uncertainty over how far the maritime confrontation could extend, even as questions remain over its ability to enforce such a zone.
In the short term, however, Iran’s proposed zone “hardens the central dispute rather than creating a new one,” Toga says, referring to tensions over Hormuz.
“The question of who administers the strait is precisely what caused the 60-day deadline of the Islamabad agreement to expire on 17 August,” as both sides failed to reach common ground on how to manage traffic through Hormuz, according to Toga.
Iran’s proposed zone also restates Tehran’s “maximal position” on the Strait of Hormuz, while signalling that the country is moving “from a rhetoric of retaliation to one of offence”, Toga says. Tehran appears to be acting on the belief that it holds leverage over the Strait, he adds.
But Toga says Washington will not accept “an arrangement that legitimises an Iranian permission regime” for one of the world’s most important maritime arteries. As a result, Tehran’s proposed zone makes the prospect of a US-Iran settlement even “harder to finesse”, he adds.
‘More escalation than settlement’
The current deadlock, increasing attacks and competing claims over the Strait of Hormuz suggest that the conflict could enter a more escalatory phase, as both sides seek greater leverage before any potential settlement, according to experts.
By new exclusive zone declaration, Iran signals a hardening stance aiming to increase the costs of US naval blockade over the Trump administration, says Ali Akbar Dareini, a Tehran-based political analyst. This decision means Iran would do everything to stop vessel traffic across the Strait of Hormuz, Dareini tells TRT World.
Iran has “political will and means to do so,” he says, seeing an escalatory curve “in the days, weeks and months to come” aiming to persuade Trump that continuing war is much less advantageous for the US than bringing an end to it.
Iran’s “prohibited zone” should be seen “less as a tactical measure than as one of the conceptual expressions of Iran's new war strategy”, which focuses on pushing the US out of the region through further escalation, according to Theo Nencini, an expert on Iranian politics.
According to a recent CNN analysis, American military and intelligence officials are discussing reducing Washington’s military presence in the Middle East as the US seeks to recalibrate its post-9/11 regional strategy.
At its peak, the US presence reached an estimated 250,000 troops during the invasion of Iraq. Currently, the US has around 50,000 troops in the region.
By attacking American bases across the Middle East, Iran is seeking to create the perception among regional states that the US military presence cannot protect them and could instead expose them to greater instability and insecurity.
Its proposed “prohibited zone”, attacks on US bases across the region and targeting of commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz form part of a broader Iranian strategy aimed at widening the costs and perceived risks of the conflict while ensuring the survival of its political system, Nencini says.
“Iranian leaders see that, weakened as the country is, the system is holding. That changes their calculation,” he says.
“They want an agreement with Washington, but they think they can play for time. They can afford to hold a hard line. And they can read the US calendar: the midterms are a test of strength for Trump, and Iran will want to make it an expensive one. So I would expect a harder phase of the conflict in the months ahead rather than a settlement.”
Other experts also see the conflict moving toward more escalation than a settlement.
“I don't see this ending anytime soon. Iran still has enough leverage to escalate tensions if it chooses to do so,” Fatemeh Karimkhan, an Iranian journalist, tells TRT World, referring to Tehran’s potential to widen regional tensions.
“Iran is unlikely to surrender under any circumstances. Iranian officials have repeatedly stated that if Iran is prevented from selling its oil, it will seek to ensure that others cannot do so freely either,” she says.
Toga also sees further escalation rather than resolution, but in the form of “managed instability”, with transits gradually increasing under a de facto toll system while negotiations remain frozen and both sides test each other’s endurance through periodic violent flare-ups.
How the conflict can de-escalate
Under current circumstances, with both sides claiming to be winning the war and asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz, experts see little prospect of an immediate settlement. But growing domestic pressure in both the US and Iran could eventually change political calculations on either side.
In the US, the war with Iran is proving unpopular, while tensions around Hormuz have contributed to higher fuel prices. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that only a quarter of Americans believe the war with Iran has been “worthwhile”.
The war is polling badly ahead of November’s mid-term elections, while disruption around Hormuz has raised fuel costs for American consumers, adding to the political pressure on Washington, Toga says.
As the mid-terms approach, US top officials have sought to downplay the scale of the conflict as the president’s approval rating has fallen to a record low. In a recent statement, Trump called the war “small potatoes”.
Despite Trump’s efforts to downplay the Iran war, Tehran wants to maximise damage to Republicans in the mid-terms by escalating Hormuz tensions, according to Dareini.
Iran, meanwhile, is also under mounting pressure. Its navy, ports, oil installations and parts of its civilian infrastructure have been heavily damaged during the war, compounding economic pressure on ordinary Iranians already struggling under decades of sanctions.
“The unresolved question of the leadership in Tehran remains the single variable capable of invalidating every current calculation,” says Toga, referring to differences between supporters of reformist President Masoud Pezeshkian, who favour an agreement, and hardliners who oppose concessions to the US.
But a former senior Iranian diplomat, who asked to remain anonymous, sees those internal tensions differently.
He describes Rezaei, whom many Western analysts regard as a hardliner, as someone whose position combines pragmatism with what he calls the dignity of “not yielding to pressure”.
“If a little wisdom prevailed in Washington, they would announce full compliance with the Islamabad Agreement and stop repeating boring, provocative, contradictory statements every day,” the Iranian diplomat tells TRT World.
“They have to stop being under the illusion that Iranian people yield to pressure. Iran’s thousands-year-old civilisation will not disappear with US bombardment.”

Anti-AfD protests sweep Germany as far right closes in on two more states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:54:24 UTC
21:54:24 KST

Thousands of Germans have staged protests against the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) after the party’s watershed victory in a state election, warning it posed a danger in two more polls this month.
Demonstrators at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate held a peaceful pro-democracy rally denouncing the anti-immigrant, pro-Russian AfD, which has called for mass deportations of asylum seekers and a rollback of state support for renewable energy and public broadcasting.
The party captured its best-ever state result in the former communist eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, with clear momentum heading into regional elections in the capital and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Baltic coast, on 20 September.
Police reported 5,000 protesters, while organisers said they drew more than 14,000 people in a campaign to mobilise voters against the AfD. Posters in the crowd read: “Fascism is no alternative”, “Stop the Nazi AfD: end racism and cuts to social services” and “History has its eyes on us”.
With less than two weeks to election day, demonstrators at the Berlin rally cautioned against resignation and cynicism after Sunday’s shock result.
The AfD’s nearly 44% vote in Saxony-Anhalt, the best for a nativist party since the Nazi period, is a “disgrace that makes you furious and stunned”, Jens-Christian Wagner, the director of the memorial at the former Nazi concentration camp Buchenwald, said from the stage.
Wagner sounded the alarm that the AfD, although it fell just short of an absolute majority, was on the brink of taking power in Saxony-Anhalt, a first for the far right since the second world war. That “should not be accepted in silence”, he said.
Max Schneller, 17, a member of the far-left Linke, from Saxony-Anhalt, said activists in the state would fight any attempts by an AfD government to target minorities. “We will not start categorising our neighbours according to their origin, religion or skin colour – we are too humane to hate,” he said to loud applause.
The AfD is three votes short of the support necessary to form a government under its candidate, the media-savvy firebrand Ulrich Siegmund, who hopes to peel off dissenters from the remaining parties willing to play kingmaker.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has since 2023 listed the state chapter of the party as rightwing extremist, saying it poses a threat to democratic norms.
Hundreds of anti-AfD protesters also gathered in Potsdam, near Berlin, with rallies also organised in Münster, Göttingen, Dresden, Aachen, Bamberg, Darmstadt, and Halberstadt, in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD captured nearly half the votes, local media reported.
In Halle, the region’s second largest city, leftist groups and civil society organisations have been staging a protest camp since election day.
The AfD is leading in voter intent polls in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, with about 35%. However, the centre-left Social Democratic party (SPD) of the state premier, Manuela Schwesig, mounted a remarkable comeback over the summer and is now scoring above 30%.
In Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the picture is more mixed, with several parties jockeying for first place. It is governed by a coalition of conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the SPD.
The CDU, the party of chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose record unpopularity is reported to have weighed heavily with voters in Saxony-Anhalt, holds a wafer-thin lead in the capital, with about 20%.
Hot on its heels is the Linke, which has focused on soaring housing costs in its campaign, and the AfD, followed by the SPD and the ecologist Greens, both polling in the mid-teens.
Merz has vowed to stay in office and fight for a signature package of painful reforms, arguing the only way to defeat the AfD is to get Europe’s top economy moving again and repair its creaking social welfare system.
However, the SPD, his junior coalition partner, has indicated its willingness to backtrack on some of the most unpopular measures to shore up support for the embattled government.
Analysts say the dispute could further destabilise the shaky coalition.

A Chinese court sentenced former Governor of Shanxi province Jin Xiangjun to death with a two-year reprieve for accepting more than 148 million yuan ($20 million) in bribes, state media reported Tuesday. 
The Xinyang Intermediate People's Court in Henan province also deprived Jin of his political rights for life and ordered the confiscation of all his personal property, Beijing-based Xinhua News reported.
The court also ordered that the proceeds from Jin's bribery and any interest earned be turned over to the national treasury.
The court, which held a public hearing in the case in June, ruled that Jin was guilty of bribery involving an exceptionally large amount and that his actions caused serious losses to the interests of the state and the people, warranting the death penalty.
It granted him a two-year reprieve, however, citing mitigating factors, including his confession after being apprehended, disclosure of previously unknown bribery offenses, guilty plea and expression of remorse.
The court also noted that some of the illicit gains had been recovered.
Jin was expelled from the ruling Communist Party of China (CPC) and dismissed from public office for serious violations of party discipline and laws in October last year.
Also a former deputy chief of the CPC Shanxi Provincial Committee, Jin was found to have taken advantage of his position to seek profits for others in matters such as business operations and project contracting, illegally accepting huge amounts of money and gifts in return.
Separately, Wang Xiangxi, a former emergency management minister, was expelled from the CPC and dismissed from public office over serious violations of discipline and laws, China's top anti-graft agency announced Tuesday.
The investigation found that Wang violated the party's organizational rules by improperly seeking benefits for others in the promotion of officials.

EU court rules against Belgian far-right party in IKEA case
September 8, 2026
A top European Union court ruled in favor of Ikea on Tuesday in a challenge brought by the company against Belgian far-right and Flemish separatist party Vlaams Belang.
The popular Swedish brand may prevent the Belgian party from using its signature illustrations. Vlaams Belang launched the "Ikea Plan" in 2022, a proposal to reform the country's migration and asylum laws.
The plan included images similar to Ikea's furniture assembly instructions. Ikea filed a legal complaint in 2023, accusing the far-right party of unlawfully using its branding.
What did the court rule?
"A proprietor of a trademark with a reputation may prevent that mark from being used by a political party where the latter has not demonstrated that its freedom of expression takes precedence over the rights and interests of that proprietor," the ECJ court said in a statement.
Vlaams Belang argued that the campaign was protected under freedom of expression. However, the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice found this argument insufficient, ruling that the use of Ikea's branding could harm the company's name and reputation.
The Luxembourg judges urged the Belgian court to issue a ruling on the matter in light of the decision by the European Court of Justice.
What did Vlaams Belang and IKEA say about the ruling?
In a statement, Vlaams Belang said it had taken note of the judgement, adding that it "will thoroughly study its scope in the context of the further legal proceedings."
Meanwhile, IKEA representatives welcomed the judgement.
"Inter IKEA strongly believes in and has great respect for freedom of expression. At the same time, the company cannot accept the use of IKEA’s trademarks in a way that harms their reputation or distinctiveness", Inter IKEA, a Netherlands-based holding company that handles the Swedish firm's intellectual property, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.
Besides its anti-immigration stances, Vlaams Belang also advocates for the independence of Flanders — the northern, Dutch-speaking part of Belgium.
While it made considerable gains in 2024 elections, other parties refuse to cooperate with it.

France posts some of its lowest-ever results in PISA student assessment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:53:53 UTC
21:53:53 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
French students recorded some of their lowest-ever results in mathematics, science, and reading comprehension, according to the OECD’s PISA 2025 survey published Tuesday.
Despite remaining close to the OECD average overall, France saw a sharp deterioration in student performance over the past decade, French broadcaster BFMTV reported.
“When we look at student performance, there has really been a significant drop in 10 years,” said Eric Charbonnier, an analyst at the OECD’s Directorate for Education and Skills.
Between 2015 and 2025, French students’ scores fell by 40 points in both mathematics and reading comprehension.
“Forty points represents the equivalent of two years of learning,” Charbonnier said. “We have a real problem with student performance, which has deteriorated in France as in many European countries.”
The decline also affected students from the most privileged families, whose scores fell by 50 points in reading comprehension and 28 points in mathematics over the same period.
Only 5% of French students achieved the highest performance levels in mathematics, compared with the OECD average of 8%.
The proportion of struggling students increased by four percentage points in science, 11 points in reading comprehension, and 12 points in mathematics compared with 2015.
The survey also revealed a widening gender gap in reading. Girls scored 32 points higher than boys, while boys continued to perform better in mathematics, although the gap narrowed.
Socioeconomic background remained a strong predictor of performance. The most advantaged French students scored 100 points higher in science than disadvantaged students, exceeding the average OECD gap of 85 points.
The report also highlighted declining parental involvement. Only 34% of French parents regularly asked their children whether they had experienced problems at school, while 60% showed interest in their school day once or several times a week.
“All the PISA results show that when families get involved in their children's schooling, the results and performance are significantly better,” Charbonnier said.
Teacher shortages and classroom disruption were also identified as concerns.
In 2025, 45% of French students attended schools where principals said teaching was hampered by staff shortages, compared with an OECD average of 39%.
Nearly half of French students said noise and disorder disrupted most or all of their science classes, against an OECD average of 31%.

INTERVIEW - Germany’s AfD surge driven by economic fear rather than migration, pollster says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:53:47 UTC
21:53:47 KST

- Company closures, auto-industry trouble and higher prices are driving anxiety, he tells Anadolu, as confidence in Germany’s economic future slides
- CDU has lost its historic reputation for economic competence, he warns, while the AfD benefits from middle-class pessimism and status anxiety
Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is riding a surge driven by economic fear rather than migration alone, a prominent expert said after the party’s record win in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Peter Matuschek, director of research for pollster Forsa, said surveys indicate Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) must rebuild its reputation for delivering prosperity rather than shifting its rhetoric on immigration to lure voters from the AfD.
“It would be a very clear strategy to win over voters on the main issues that people are most concerned about, which is the economy,” he told Anadolu.
“When we ask about the major problems people see in the country, it’s not migration … Migration comes in fourth or fifth place.”
It is the economy, company closures, auto-industry troubles and higher prices that are driving anxiety, he said.
Declining confidence and a CDU that lost its edge
Weekly Forsa tracking shows most Germans are worried about the worsening economic conditions.
AfD supporters are consistently the “most pessimistic” about future prospects even though many are middle class, Matuschek said.
For decades, he noted, the CDU was seen as the party most competent to handle the country’s problems and deliver economic prosperity, with 30%, 40% or even 50% of voters saying so, followed by its coalition partner, the Social Democrats.
“Now we have the CDU at 13%, 14%,” he said.
That confidence, he stressed, will return only through “sound economic policy” that gives people the impression the government can still act on their problems – and through credible figures who can “win over the hearts of voters again.”
‘Saxony-Anhalt is not representative of Germany’
The AfD won a record 43.8% on Sunday and moved closer than ever to taking power in a state for the first time, while CDU slumped to a historic low of 17.2%.
Matuschek called the surge a significant development, but cautioned against reading Saxony-Anhalt as a national trend – or as proof the party could match that level of support in a federal election.
“I think Saxony-Anhalt is not representative of the whole country,” he said, adding that the medium-sized eastern state accounts for only a small share of Germany’s national electorate.
“It is an eastern state with a very special history, a special legacy where the AfD had very good results in the past already.”
AfD scores are generally much higher in the former communist east — often roughly double those in the west — even though the party has also increased its vote share in western Germany in recent elections.
“We have to wait for the upcoming regional elections this month to see whether the Saxony-Anhalt election will have repercussions” on voting behavior, Matuschek said.
“There are many possibilities that might strengthen the AfD in other states, or it might strengthen the other parties, because there might be a backlash.”
Another eastern state, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and the city-state of Berlin will elect state parliaments on Sept. 20.
‘Radicalized’ middle class
Surveys show the AfD mobilized both its base and former non-voters in Saxony-Anhalt, helping the party more than double its score.
About 170,000 people who stayed home in 2021 went to the polls this time and voted for the AfD, according to a survey by public broadcaster ARD.
Matuschek said Forsa polls show that concerns about the economy and migration were key themes for AfD voters. That fear, he stressed, is about losing what they already have.
“So there are different factors at play, but I think what combines all those issues is this fear and this anger of losing something and of wanting something back, that's to say, going back to the past,” he said, adding that this mood was especially strong in eastern Germany.
“It’s not the poorest who vote for the AfD. We’ve seen this in many, many analyses. It’s a radicalized middle class with fears of losing their status,” Matuschek said.
The Saxony-Anhalt election also highlighted AfD voters’ more favorable view of Russia and their opposition to economic and military support for Ukraine, Matuschek said.
“They believe that if we sought an agreement with Russia and did not support Ukraine, we might get cheaper gas and return to prices as they were before the war,” he said.
Anger at Merz and his coalition
Surveys after the vote highlighted how far anger at Merz’s federal record shaped the result.
Public broadcaster ZDF found that 75% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt believe Merz damaged the CDU’s regional performance. Some 88% said if Merz’s government had pursued better policies, the AfD would not have grown so strong in Saxony-Anhalt.
Matuschek said that in several state elections in recent years, regional lead candidates managed to distance themselves from federal politics and their party’s leadership in Berlin.
Saxony-Anhalt’s CDU premier Sven Schulze, he said, failed to persuade voters that the party was addressing economic and regional issues.
Merz on Monday called the outcome his party’s heaviest defeat in years or even decades.
“We are all deeply shocked,” he told reporters in Berlin.
Ruling out a resignation, he said: “Giving up is not an option for me.”
The result fueled media speculation that pressure could grow inside the CDU for Merz to step down, given his historically low approval ratings.
Matuschek said Merz’s personal approval score has already fallen to about 13%, with little sign of a rebound after Sunday.
“This is a loss of confidence we haven’t seen with any chancellor in such a short time,” he said.
No snap federal election expected
Matuschek said Sunday’s result could fuel further infighting among the governing parties in Berlin over the right policy course.
However, he saw little appetite on either side of the coalition for early elections.
That path, he argued, would not help either the CDU or the Social Democrats, given the AfD’s strength in national polls.
Snap elections are “not really an alternative” for either the CDU or the Social Democrats at this moment, he said.
“Because they would lose the majority right away and we would have the AfD as the strongest party in the German parliament. So I assume that neither of them is interested in snap elections.”
With about three years left in the federal term, he said Merz’s coalition wants to remain in office and step up efforts to improve its ratings, while demonstrating that its policies are delivering concrete results and addressing people’s concerns.
However, he noted that the result of upcoming regional elections could further ignite the leadership debate within the Christian Democrats.

LONDON — France and Canada will join the U.K. in imposing new trade sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in a major diplomatic boost for Britain as it toughens its stance on Israel.
In the House of Commons Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband confirmed Britain, France and Canada will impose a ban on the trade of goods and some services from Israeli settlements, having last month condemned Israel’s plans for 1,200 new homes in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.
In response, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said the British consulate in Jerusalem will be closed, and warned “countermeasures” could be taken against other countries acting “against Israel.”
Advertisement
The U.K., France and Canada are among 12 countries which issued a joint statement Tuesday warning the Israeli government’s actions in the West Bank are threatening the two-state solution.
Miliband told MPs the British government “agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank,” adding that “all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this.”
He said the U.K. will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion.
U.K. sanctions legislation will take between six and nine months to implement, meaning the effects will not be felt immediately.
Britain will “act in concert with others in a broad international coalition,” he said, adding that France and Canada will also ban the import of goods from illegal settlements.
Confirming France’s involvement in a post on X, the country’s foreign affairs minister Jean-Noël Barrot said: “France cannot, through its trade, support a situation that threatens the security of both Israelis and Palestinians.”
Advertisement
Anita Anand, the Canadian foreign affairs minister, said her country will introduce restrictions “in the coming months.”
The coordinated announcement follows a major diplomatic effort by the British government over the summer, which culminated in a visit to Downing Street by French President Emmanuel Macron last week.
Writing on X, EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas noted the announcement and said: “All EU Member States agree that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law. The Israeli Government’s settlement expansions in the West Bank are undermining the prospects for a viable two-State solution.”
Change of tone
Miliband’s announcement marks a sharp shift in Britain’s stance on Israeli settlements under new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
The U.K. foreign secretary told MPs Britain “should have acted earlier,” and it had taken a change of prime minister “to come in and recognize the gravity of the situation.”
In a press statement to camera, Sa’ar accused Miliband of telling “outrageous lies” in the British parliament and acting for “domestic political reasons” ahead of the ruling Labour Party’s annual conference this month.
Advertisement
Israel also said will deny 12 MPs and British nationals entry to Israel, including veteran Labour MP Diane Abbott and the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, who has since been expelled from the party.
The relationship between Israel and France — historically one of its close allies and home to more Jews than any other country in Europe — has also become strained in light of the war in Gaza.
Macron last year said Europe must “harden” its collective position on Israel given the dire humanitarian situation in the coastal enclave, and he found some success in convincing other Western democracies to join France in recognizing a Palestinian state last year.
Barrot said last week that the recent effort to sanction EU-wide trade with illegal West Bank settlements has been met resistance in Brussels.
Jean-Noël Barrot leaves the Elysée Palace in Paris after a meeting on Aug. 31, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images
Although several EU countries have pledged to ban trade with the settlements, the move is legally murky under EU law, because trade is an exclusive EU competence. Member countries can do it on the grounds of either national security or violation of human rights and democracy, but any measures at national level are assessed for compatibility with EU law.
UNGA looming
It comes just two weeks before world leaders meet in New York for the U.N. General Assembly — and ahead of Burnham’s expected first in-person meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump since becoming British prime minister.
Advertisement
Miliband said the U.K. will use the gathering to “shine the clearest and harshest spotlight on what is happening and what must change.”
In advance of the sanctions statement Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee suggested the U.S. could retaliate against the U.K. over the move.
Huckabee, who over the weekend condemned the government’s “Jew hate” despite Miliband being Jewish, told the BBC that the decision would be a “discrimination against the Jewish people.” He also suggested that individual U.S. states — specifically Florida — might take trade action against the U.K.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. was made aware of the decision, but are “not going to do what the U.K. did.”
While Trump has yet to respond to the sanctions, political differences have previously influenced his decisions on trade.
In January, the president threatened to impose 10 percent tariffs on eight countries, including the U.K., for opposing his demands to use military force to take control of Greenland.

Israel: The great and powerful vs the isolated pariah - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:52:13 UTC
21:52:13 KST

In his August 29, 2026 article for The Wall Street Journal, “The ICC Tried to Take On the World’s Big Powers. Now It’s Fighting for Survival,” Matthew Dalton framed Israel as a global power alongside Russia and the United States.
Conversely, an alternative media narrative swings to the opposite extreme. NPR and the Associated Press have framed Israel as “diplomatically isolated,” implying severe weakness in its ability to build international coalitions.
These framings, which malign the Jewish state through two different extremes, mirror the anti-Jewish tropes that societies have popularized through the ages, portraying Jews as either all-powerful manipulators or weak, stateless wanderers. Neither is accurate.
Dalton’s central thesis stated, “When the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued arrest warrants for [Russian President] Vladimir Putin and [Prime Minister] Benjamin Netanyahu, human rights groups applauded the decision to go after the leaders of major powers...”
Dalton argued that the ICC’s decision to target Netanyahu opened the door for Washington to dismantle the court.
While it is reasonable to argue that the charges against Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant accelerated US opposition to the tribunal, describing Israel as one of the world’s “great powers” misrepresents reality.
Quantifying power and influence is inherently difficult (and academics hotly debate methodology), as the metrics of national strength evolve alongside shifting global values. Nevertheless, tangible indicators like economic output and military projection can provide some vital clarity.
In measurable terms, Israel ranks far below the US and Russia. Media outlets could classify Israel as a dominant regional power (even that claim is debatable), but grouping it with the US and Russia is factually inaccurate.
Economically, Israel’s 2025 nominal GDP reached $611 billion, whereas the US and Russian nominal GDPs reach into the trillions ($32 trillion and $2.6 trillion, respectively). Adjusted for Purchasing Power Parity (PPP), Israel’s economy hovers just above half a trillion dollars, while the US and Russian PPP economies comfortably reach tens of trillions.
Military force projection reveals an even wider divide. The US maintains global force projection capability, while Russia can project military power across Europe and Asia. Israel’s conventional military reach, by contrast, is primarily regional, with neither the naval nor air-force capacity to sustain large-scale deployments far beyond the Middle East.
The Global Firepower Index, which evaluates conventional military capabilities, ranked Israel 15th in the world in 2026, whereas the US and Russia ranked first and second. Furthermore, differences in population size and strategic partnerships compound these disparities.
The US and Russia draw from populations of roughly 342 million and nearly 144 million, respectively, compared with Israel’s roughly 10 million. The US maintains more than 1.3 million active-duty service members, while Russia has sought to expand its armed forces to roughly 1.5 million personnel. Even the US active-duty force alone amounts to more than one-eighth of Israel’s entire population.
Beyond manpower, the US anchors its security posture in collective-defense arrangements such as the 32-member NATO, alongside a network of bilateral agreements that allow it to maintain military bases and station forces around the world.
Russia similarly maintains military forces and bases outside its borders, including in several countries that belong to the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO). Israel, by contrast, has no comparable alliance or overseas-basing network and therefore must project military power primarily from its own territory.
Crucially, alliances do not imply equal footing. In the US-Israel security relationship, Washington has substantial diplomatic and economic leverage through its military assistance and broader security relationship with Israel, which can shape and, at times, constrain Israeli military actions.
Notably, perception-based surveys, such as the annual US News & World Report Power Rankings (developed with the Wharton School), frequently place Israel among the top 10 most powerful nations globally, often ranking it as high as eighth or 10th based on surveyed global public opinion. But perception is not synonymous with reality.
These surveys measure visibility, news presence, and perceived military leverage, so the media’s outsized reporting on Israel has an outsized influence on their results.
While Israel cannot be claimed as a world power, news outlets cannot accurately describe it as impotent either.
Media whiplash
Regarding the AP’s mischaracterization of Israel as diplomatically isolated on February 5, 2026, CAMERA’s Tamar Sternthal pointed out that Israel maintains active diplomatic relations with over 166 countries.
At the time of the article, Israel had recently signed major agreements with Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and Germany worth $35 billion, $2.3 b., and $3.5 b., respectively. More recently, as of August 31, Israel and Greece signed a defense export deal worth nearly $3.5 b.
Sternthal argued that the AP’s framing echoed the strategic objective articulated by Hamas leader Khaled Mashaal at a February Al Jazeera forum: “We must pursue Israel and entrench the idea that it is an outcast entity that has lost its international legitimacy.”
This media whiplash – framing Israel as an omnipotent global orchestrator on one hand or an isolated, powerless pariah on the other – channels two long-standing historical fabrications.
The medieval legend of the “Wandering Jew,” originating in 13th-century Europe, depicted Jews as cursed, stateless, and permanently isolated wanderers.
Conversely, The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a 19th-century fabrication, alleged a secret Jewish conspiracy controlling global banks, media, governments, and international conflicts.
Modern reporting that alternates between calling Israel an outcast or a superpower echoes these exact archetypes.
Rather than reducing the Jewish state to extreme platitudes, journalists must report on Israel as it exists: neither a global superpower on par with the US and Russia, nor a helpless, isolated pariah.
Distorting these facts undermines fair reporting on a complex region where actual military capacity and the perception of strength carry profound, real-world consequences.
The writer is a US media researcher at the Committee for Accuracy in Middle East Reporting and Analysis (CAMERA) in Israel. She was previously a Breaking News desk manager at The Jerusalem Post.

Breakfast at noon? Turns out weekend meals at random times can hurt men’s hearts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:52:12 UTC
21:52:12 KST

A new study suggests that eating at inconsistent times on weekends compared to weekdays could increase the risk of heart disease.
Do you eat breakfast at lunchtime and dinner at a time when you’d normally be sleeping during weekends? This inconsistency is what researchers call “eating jet lag” and it might be hurting men’s – you read it right, only men’s – hearts.
Early work or school starts often force people to adjust their eating schedules during the week, which differs from meal times on weekends and days off.
Such a shift in eating patterns may disrupt the body’s biological rhythms and could have implications for cardiovascular health, according to a new French study. Each additional hour of “eating jet lag” increased the risk of cardiovascular disease by 14% and the risk of coronary heart disease by 21% among men, researchers found.
“This study suggests the importance of regular meal-timing patterns, beyond sleep and diet quality, in cardiovascular disease prevention,” the authors wrote.
The research, published in Communications Medicine, analysed the timing of more than 100,000 participants' first and last meals on working days and on weekends over a 14-year follow-up period between 2009 and 2023.
Men are more affected
Participants were classified by their eating schedules: the first group ate meals earlier on the weekends than during the week, the second group kept similar schedules across both and the last group had their meals later at weekends.
Both groups that ate either later or earlier than usual faced a higher cardiovascular risk than the regular group, regardless of overall diet quality.
Surprisingly, this pattern was only found among men, and women did not appear to be affected by schedule changes.
Why?
One reason could be that men generally have a higher absolute risk of cardiovascular disease. The authors also noted that women tend to be more inclined towards morning routines than men, a difference linked to variations in anatomy and hormones, which may influence how their bodies respond to shifts in meal timing.
What’s behind the irregular meal timings?
The authors’ leading theory for why this happens is that eating jet lag increases the risk of cardiovascular events through circadian disruption.
Circadian rhythms are the body’s internal clocks, running on a 24-hour cycle that help regulate its functioning. They are mainly regulated by light, but eating patterns can also act as a synchroniser for peripheral clocks, such as those in the liver and heart. Aligning eating patterns with these internal rhythms boosts metabolic health, while inconsistency can disrupt the body’s internal balance.
The authors noted that if the results are confirmed by further large-scale studies, meal timing regularity could become a key focus for interventions to reduce chronic disease risk and ease public health burdens.

Mecca Defense Alliance puts India’s regional strategy to the test - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:51:58 UTC
21:51:58 KST

The newly established Mecca defense pact has put a strategic question before India: Will the collective-defense pact linking Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey remain mainly political, or develop into an operational military arrangement?
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on Aug. 7 and met in Istanbul on Aug. 31 to establish a secretariat in Saudi Arabia, to be led by a Pakistani secretary-general for three years. Reuters reported that the agreement treats an armed attack on one signatory as an attack on all three, but the governments have not released a detailed public text setting out the commitments that would follow.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said after the Istanbul meeting that the alliance was designed to expand and that officials had begun work on an accession roadmap. The talks addressed counterterrorism, defense production and interoperability, including possible joint land, sea and air exercises, air defense, drones, autonomous systems, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence.
The alliance is taking shape as Gulf states confront renewed Iranian attacks. On Sept. 3, Kuwait said its air defenses intercepted Iranian missiles and drones targeting the country. Reuters reported that Tehran had struck a US base there after a major escalation in the US-Iran conflict.
India can measure the Mecca pact against Kuwait’s limited arrangement with Pakistan. The newer alliance uses broader mutual-defense language, but its practical military obligations have yet to be publicly defined.
American and Indian troops are training together this month in the Rajasthan desert, where India faces Pakistan, and in the Himalayas, where Auli is about 60 miles from the disputed frontier with China.
The US Embassy in New Delhi announced the exercise Tuesday, a day after the Istanbul meeting. Since 2004, the embassy said, Yudh Abhyas has strengthened the US-India Major Defense Partnership in support of a free and open Indo-Pacific.
'Training for war'
Yudh Abhyas, Hindi for “training for war,” is in its 22nd edition. The three-week exercise involves 350 soldiers from each army, starting at the Mahajan Field Firing Range near Bikaner and moving to Auli. Mahajan focuses on live fire and mechanized maneuver, while Auli tests high-altitude logistics.
Dr. Arzan Tarapore, a research scholar at Stanford University, said the public record provides scant evidence that the pact is a binding mutual-defense treaty in the operational sense. He told The Media Line that he does not expect the three to conduct military operations together, whether against Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia or in coordination against India.
He expects flows of money, arms and technologies, including drones, among the members and across the region. Pakistan already used Turkish drones against India in May last year, Tarapore said, and that is the kind of defense-industrial cooperation he expects to deepen.
Brig. Anil Raman, a retired Indian officer at the Takshashila Institution in Bangalore, reached a similar conclusion. India has asked Washington for nothing so far, he told The Media Line. It should seek tighter controls on American-origin weapons that could reach Pakistan through Turkey and urge Saudi Arabia and Turkey to limit the cooperation, he said.
“Any expectation that Saudi fighter jets, Pakistani F-16s and Turkish F-16s are going to be running joint raids somewhere in the Middle East is Hollywood fiction,” Kabir Taneja, who directs the Observer Research Foundation’s Middle East office in Dubai, told The Media Line. “It is never going to happen.”
Taneja also cautioned against comparisons with NATO. Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty has been invoked only once in the alliance’s history, he said.
The alliance does not eliminate or replace Turkey’s obligations under NATO or its other agreements, Fidan said in Istanbul. It complements them.
Asked at the same news conference about Israeli statements calling Turkey a strategic threat, Fidan said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should be stopped and called him “an enemy of humanity.” He said hostility toward Turkey from Netanyahu’s government had grown since Israel’s election campaign began.
The three countries do not agree on the adversary either, Taneja said. Each has its own view of what the arrangement is for and a different neighbor in mind.
“Ankara and Riyadh were not on good terms until 2022 or 2023,” he added. “That can happen again.”
Islamabad has reportedly sent 8,000 troops, a squadron of JF-17 fighters and an air defense system to Saudi Arabia under the bilateral agreement the two countries signed in September 2025. Neither government has publicly provided a full account of the deployment. Pakistan has sent soldiers to the kingdom for decades. More than 20,000 served under the 1982 Joint Defense Protocol, and a Pakistani general commanded the Saudi-led Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition beginning in 2015.
Pakistan raised $3 billion on the international bond market on Sept. 3, its largest single issuance, with orders near $6 billion. The proceeds will repay a $3 billion Saudi loan made in April, which Islamabad had used to repay the United Arab Emirates and which Riyadh had already extended once.
Saudi Arabia committed another $3 billion in support in April and extended an existing $5 billion deposit as Islamabad faced repayment obligations to the United Arab Emirates. The assistance ties Riyadh to Pakistan’s financial stability as well as its defense planning.
Pakistan spent decades treating the Gulf as its own ground, Taneja said. It lobbied hard to keep India out of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation when the bloc of Muslim-majority states was founded in the 1960s.
India’s economic rise shifting the playing field
India’s economic rise changed the picture. Dubai was built by Indian hands in the 1990s, Taneja said, and Indians now come as engineers, managers and chief executives rather than as construction workers, while it has become more difficult for Pakistani laborers to obtain Emirati visas.
“What we are seeing now with the Mecca agreement, with the mediation with Iran, with the—dare I say—good relationship with President Trump, is Pakistan finding a very good wedge to re-enter,” Taneja said. “And to be fair to them, they seem to be doing a decent job of it.”
“If you are going to build an architecture that will require mobilization at some level, you cannot mobilize if you are not trained, and you cannot mobilize if you are not experienced,” he said. “Pakistan brings all those things together.”
India’s national security adviser has visited Saudi Arabia four times in the past six months, Taneja said, and Riyadh kept New Delhi informed before signing its bilateral agreement with Islamabad so India would not read the arrangement as a coalition against it.
Asked at a New Delhi forum on Aug. 22 whether the pact worried him, S. Jaishankar said: “There are live military situations which each of the signatories face, what has the Mecca pact done in response to that?”
He said India would not ignore it either. “In my calculus, everything counts, everything will have a weight,” he said, “and sometimes things need to play out.” India factors in developments involving countries whose policies are not favorable toward it, he added.
India’s quarrel with Turkey predates the pact. Days after the May 2025 fighting, New Delhi revoked the security clearance of Celebi Aviation, a Turkish ground-handling company operating at nine Indian airports. Indian officials said drones Pakistan launched at Indian towns came from Turkey.
The deeper irritant is Kashmir, Taneja said. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan raises it at the UN General Assembly almost every year, which India treats as a red line and an endorsement of Pakistan’s position. New Delhi has told Ankara so repeatedly.
For India, he added, the larger concern is Saudi Arabia’s membership. The relationship with Turkey was already contentious.
Indian commentators have also asked whether the pact responds to India’s closer ties with Israel. India and Israel upgraded their relationship in February to what the two governments call a special strategic partnership for peace, innovation and prosperity. Their bilateral investment agreement took effect in July; the three countries signed in Mecca on Aug. 7.
The Hindi-language outlet Webdunia asked whether the alliance was a direct response to India-Israel ties and to mechanisms such as I2U2 and the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor. Netanyahu telephoned Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Aug. 6, the day before the signing, and Modi posted about the call in English and Hebrew.
India’s Foreign Ministry has rejected reports that New Delhi approached Israel seeking a new defense treaty in response to the pact.
The Qatari Foreign Ministry welcomed the pact as a positive step but declined to discuss joining it. Doha is already present in more than one platform, the ministry said.
Qatar has a US security assurance that Washington did not extend to Saudi Arabia. After the Israeli strike on Doha in September 2025, President Trump issued an executive pledge that the United States would treat an attack on Qatar as a direct threat to itself. The US-Saudi defense agreement two months later provided Riyadh with F-35s, tanks, civil nuclear cooperation and major non-NATO ally status, but did not include the same formula.
Turkey has maintained about 3,000 troops in Qatar for almost a decade under several defense agreements. Their presence did not prevent Iranian strikes on Qatar in 2025 and 2026 or the Israeli attack on Hamas leaders in Doha.
Saudi Arabia building a regional security architecture in the Middle East
The United Arab Emirates has kept its distance. Abu Dhabi has the Abraham Accords, ties to Israel, expanding relationships with India and China, and a defense industry of its own. It has less urgency than Riyadh to accept automatically triggered obligations.
Col. (res.) Dr. Hanan Shai wrote for the Misgav Institute for National Security and Zionist Strategy on Aug. 18 that “Israel cannot assume that the Mecca pact will also remain an empty declaration.” He proposed not a rival military alliance but an economic-security organization built around the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, with India, Israel, Greece, Cyprus and the United Arab Emirates at its core, Jordan providing land continuity and Saudi Arabia welcomed even while Riyadh remains in the Mecca pact.
Saudi Arabia has invited Bangladesh, a Bangladeshi official told Reuters, and Dhaka says it is interested. Turkish officials said after Istanbul that they had begun building a mechanism for other countries to join. Taneja is untroubled by the prospect. Bringing in countries from outside the region would dilute the agreement, he said, and he does not know what Bangladesh would add to it.
The idea is to build a regional security architecture in the Middle East, he said. Expand geographically before it has any depth, and other organizations offer the warning: the core mandate becomes diluted, and symmetry replaces purpose.
“There is very little unity in the Gulf right now,” Taneja said. “They have a lot of their own stuff to figure out first. It is going to be chaotic. It may be violent.”

UK Foreign Secretary accuses some Israeli settlers of ethnic cleansing

Since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, hundreds of Russian diplomats have been expelled from EU member states. Hungary, however, whose government was previously led by the Kremlin-friendly Viktor Orbán, did not participate in these measures. The last time a Russian diplomatic mission employee was officially declared persona non grata in Hungary was in 2018.
Current foreign minister Orbán said she had instructed a subordinate to inform Russian Ambassador to Hungary Yevgeny Stanislavov that “10 members of the Russian mission had engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention.” As she stressed:
“The Hungarian side has therefore called on the individuals in question to leave Hungary. This decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty. It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules.”
As reported by the independent news outlet Vot Tak, between February 2022 and October 2025, nearly 700 Russian diplomats were expelled from European countries (those of the EU, plus Montenegro, Norway, North Macedonia, and the UK). Hungary was the only EU member that did not join such measures. Before today, the last time Budapest had declared a Russian diplomat to be persona non grata was in March 2018, when Hungary joined a mass expulsion of Russian diplomats by Western countries over the poisoning of former GRU Colonel Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia in the city of Salisbury, England.
Earlier this year, the Hungarian government also expelled an undercover Russian agent. On May 8, 2026, investigative outlet VSquare reported on the expulsion of Russian spy Artur Sushkov, who had been working in Hungary under diplomatic cover. He was forced to leave the country with his wife on May 4, five days before the government officially changed hands following Viktor Orbán's electoral defeat.
VSquare noted that Hungarian counterintelligence had been pushing for Sushkov’s expulsion since February 2026, but the Orbán government had blocked the proposal. According to the outlet, the authorities did not want to risk worsening relations with Moscow ahead of Hungary’s elections. Sushkov’s ultimate expulsion took place quietly, without any official announcements.
Budapest’s rhetoric changed after Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party lost the April elections and Péter Magyar became prime minister. The new Hungarian government said it viewed Russia’s actions as a threat to Hungary itself, as well as to Europe and the to the wider “global order.”

Placement & AOS
Which areas of specialization have been correlated with higher placement into “permanent” (typically tenure-track or tenured) positions over the past few years?
“The broad finding is that those in Value Theory and History & Traditions (n=1125) have a higher proportion in permanent academic placement… than those in LEMM or Science, Logic, & Math (n=864),” according to Carolyn Dicey Jennings (UC Merced), who analyzed data gathered by Academic Philosophy Data and Analysis (APDA) on graduates from 2021 through 2026 and shared the results in a post at the APDA Blog.
Jennings breaks down the areas of specialization into “big” (more than 100 graduates over the past five years), “mid-sized” (between 20 and 100 graduates), and “small” (fewer than 20 graduates). Within each of those size categorizations, she lists the percentage of graduates with particular AOS’s who have found permanent placement.
Her findings are below. AOS’s listed in bold have a higher than average placement rate (the average across all areas is 32%).
Big
- Social/Political (37%; n=254)
- Ancient (37%; n=101)
- Ethics (36%; n=274)
- Epistemology (33%; n=165)
- Philosophy of Science (29%; n=102)
- Metaphysics (28%; n=112)
- Philosophy of Mind (25%; n=151)
Mid-Sized
- Law (60%; n=25)
- Medieval/Renaissance (52%; n=23)
- Gender/Race/Sexuality/Disability Studies (48%; n=56)
- Philosophy of Physics (40%; n=25)
- Logic (33%; n=39)
- German Philosophy/Kant (31%; n=68)
- Applied Ethics (31%; n=85)
- Modern Philosophy (31%; n=36)
- Historical Philosophy (29%; n=28)
- Continental Philosophy/Phenomenology (29%; n=56)
- Metaethics (26%; n=34)
- Philosophy of Religion (25%; n=20)
- Philosophy of Language (24%; n=70)
- Value Theory (22%; n=27)
- Cognitive Science/Psychology/Neuroscience/Linguistics (22%; n=73)
- Philosophy of Technology (20%, n=40)
Small
- Education (100%; n=2)
- American/Latin American Philosophy (100%; n=2)
- African Philosophy (67%; n=3)
- Philosophy of Action (67%; n=3)
- Philosophy of Biology/Environmental Philosophy (45%; n=11)
- 19th/20th Century Philosophy (44%; n=16)
- Metaphilosophy/Experimental (40%; n=5)
- Asian Philosophy (38%, n=8)
- Decision Theory (31%; n=16)
- Philosophy of Economics (23%; n=13)
- History of Analytic Philosophy (22%; n=9)
- Aesthetics (18%; n=11)
- Philosophy of Math (17%; n=18)
- Comparative Philosophy (15%; n=7)
- Other (0%; n=2)
Jennings adds: “A final point worth considering is that hiring trends come and go, and this analysis is not future-facing/predictive. Yet, the headline success of those in Value Theory and History & Traditions appears to be consistent across past analyses.”

LONDON — France and Canada will join the U.K. in imposing new trade sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in a major diplomatic boost for Britain as it toughens its stance on Israel.
In the House of Commons Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband confirmed Britain, France and Canada will impose a ban on the trade of goods and some services from Israeli settlements, having last month condemned Israel’s plans for 1,200 new homes in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.
In response, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said the British consulate in Jerusalem will be closed, and warned “countermeasures” could be taken against other countries acting “against Israel.”

The U.K., France and Canada are among 12 countries which issued a joint statement Tuesday warning the Israeli government’s actions in the West Bank are threatening the two-state solution.
Miliband told MPs the British government “agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank,” adding that “all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this.”
He said the U.K. will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion.
U.K. sanctions legislation will take between six and nine months to implement, meaning the effects will not be felt immediately.
Britain will “act in concert with others in a broad international coalition,” he said, adding that France and Canada will also ban the import of goods from illegal settlements.

Advertisement

Writing on X, EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas noted the announcement and said: “All EU Member States agree that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law. The Israeli Government’s settlement expansions in the West Bank are undermining the prospects for a viable two-State solution.”

The U.K. foreign secretary told MPs Britain “should have acted earlier,” and it had taken a change of prime minister “to come in and recognize the gravity of the situation.”

Advertisement
Israel also said will deny 12 MPs and British nationals entry to Israel, including veteran Labour MP Diane Abbott and the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, who has since been expelled from the party.
The relationship between Israel and France — historically one of its close allies and home to more Jews than any other country in Europe — has also become strained in light of the war in Gaza.
Macron last year said Europe must “harden” its collective position on Israel given the dire humanitarian situation in the coastal enclave, and he found some success in convincing other Western democracies to join France in recognizing a Palestinian state last year.
Barrot said last week that the recent effort to sanction EU-wide trade with illegal West Bank settlements has been met resistance in Brussels.
Jean-Noël Barrot leaves the Elysée Palace in Paris after a meeting on Aug. 31, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images
Although several EU countries have pledged to ban trade with the settlements, the move is legally murky under EU law, because trade is an exclusive EU competence. Why is Israel rallying behind Argentina in disputing Britain’s claims over Falkland Islands?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:49:18 UTC
21:49:18 KST

Far-right Israeli ministers are using the Falkland Islands dispute to hit back at the UK by framing the South Atlantic archipelago as “occupied Argentine territory”.
The latest barrage of criticism follows expected restrictions by the British government on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir posted on X in Spanish that it was time for Israel to “publicly recognise that the Malvinas Islands (otherwise known as Falkland Islands) are Argentine territory under occupation, which the British violently steal from the Argentine people”.
He accused Britain of oil drilling that “steals money from the Argentine people” and called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to recognise Argentine sovereignty and impose sanctions “as long as the occupation continues”.
Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich also demanded the British ambassador’s expulsion, declaring the British Mandate over “the Land of Israel is over”.
The sharply critical remarks by top ministers further weaken Tel Aviv’s already deteriorating relationship with London as far-right politicians look for maximum domestic political mileage in the run-up to the general election next month.
Why is Falkland suddenly in the news?
Argentina recently demanded that Britain hand over the islands to the Latin American country, a similar move to London transferring Hong Kong to China in 1997.
But what triggered the critical statements by the Israeli ministers was the prospect of a ban by Britain on trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The planned restrictions will be in line with a 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion, which requires that governments worldwide must not help Israel with its occupation of Palestinian territories.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is also expected to “reassert” support for a two-state solution, which has ruffled feathers among right-wing Israeli politicians.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have already been sanctioned by the UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway in 2025 for repeated incitement of violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and elsewhere.
The same ministers have aimed their guns at Britain on the so-called occupation of the Falkland Islands, even though Israel keeps expanding its own settlements in the occupied West Bank in clear violation of international law.
Analysts say that far-right politicians in Israel are competing for electoral support from voters who want to shift the international focus away from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
There is also a commercial angle. An Israeli-linked company, Navitas Petroleum, holds 65 percent shares in the Sea Lion oil project north of the islands. Argentine President Javier Milei has announced sanctions targeting firms, shareholders and suppliers involved in the project.
What is at stake?
Falklands consist of two main islands: East Falkland and West Falkland, apart from the archipelago of more than 700 smaller islands.
These are located about 480 kilometres east of the Argentine mainland.
Britain has administered them since 1833. Argentina says it inherited the islands from Spain after independence and that Britain occupied them by force.
But Britain insists that the islanders have the right to self-determination.
In 1982, Argentina moved into the islands. A fight ensued when Britain intervened, resulting in the deaths of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three islanders in the next 74 days.
Even though Argentina surrendered, it never dropped its claim to the territory.
A 2013 referendum showed 99.8 percent of islanders wanted the archipelago to remain a British Overseas Territory.
Argentina dismissed the vote, arguing the population was implanted after 1833, the year Britain assumed control of the area.
The islands are important for many reasons. For example, the Sea Lion oilfield is estimated to hold 1.7 billion barrels of oil, with first production targeted for 2028.
Is Israel diplomatically alone on this issue?
Most governments around the world either stay silent or recognise the islands as British-administered while calling for negotiations.
The UN lists the Falklands as a non-self-governing territory and does not recognise either claim as definitive.
But Latin American states usually back Argentina’s claim at the UN.
The US, however, has traditionally recognised British administration of the islands. But that neutrality is now in question.
According to a leaked Pentagon email, the US may be reviewing its support for Britain’s claim to the Falkland Islands. The possible change in the US stance is apparently in reaction to Britain’s lack of support for Trump’s war against Iran.
Analysts say any change in the US stance on the Falkland Islands will be a psychological blow to Britain’s sovereignty claim over the territories.
Britain midwifed Israel’s birth
The irony in Israel calling out Britain for “occupying” the Falkland Islands is sharp. After all, it was Britain that issued the 1917 Balfour Declaration that called for a “national home for the Jewish people” in Palestine.
The League of Nations later granted Britain the Mandate for Palestine. Afterwards, Jewish immigration increased to Palestine despite Palestinian Arab opposition.
Britain eventually withdrew in 1948 when Israel declared independence, amid an ongoing Arab-Israeli war and the mass displacement of Palestinians from their ancestral lands.
For decades, Britain has remained one of Israel’s most consistent Western supporters. But that relationship has somewhat frayed over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, illegal settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank and the recognition of a Palestinian state.
How Britain, others have reacted
London’s position on the Falkland Islands remains “unwavering”.
So far, there has been no direct official rebuke of Ben-Gvir’s latest post. However, the two ministers are already persona non grata in Britain for their involvement in incitement of violence towards Palestinians.
US President Donald Trump has said he is reviewing “every position”, reflecting his dissatisfaction with Britain’s hesitation to join the recent US-led war against Iran.
Foreign policy analysts view the statements by the Israeli ministers as transactional rather than principled. They say that sovereignty disputes offer politicians an easy “rally-around-the-flag” opportunity.

Here in Liverpool, buses are back under public control – and that’s great for the only people who really matter | Steve Rotheram
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:48:35 UTC
21:48:35 KST

One of the best-known scenes from the TV series The Inbetweeners is the four angst-ridden teenage characters shouting abuse at people queueing at a bus stop. Only losers take the bus, is the point – except they use a much ruder word. There’s also a statement, misattributed to Margaret Thatcher, that any man over the age of 26 using a bus was a loser. This idea is deeply ingrained.
But when I was an MP it became obvious that there wasn’t the same stigma attached to jumping on the bus in London as there often was in other big cities. It often wound me up that the rest of the country was expected to accept a suboptimal public transport system – so much so that it could be joked that only losers would use it – while London retained its excellent bus service, which it ran under public control.
And I remember thinking: why can’t we have something like this at home in Liverpool? Well, last weekend Liverpool city region combined authority began to roll back the Thatcherite belief that private was all good, while public was all bad. For the first time in four decades, buses in the Liverpool city region have begun to be brought back under public control, starting in St Helens in Merseyside before spreading across the rest of the region.
What does this mean? Instead of private operators deciding where and when buses run, we will set the routes, fares and standards. Our franchised buses will still be operated by third parties. But we will set the rules, decide what kind of network our communities need and hold operators accountable for delivering it. It is the biggest change to public transport in our region for generations. Nobody standing at a bus stop at six in the morning cares about the finer points of franchising legislation. But they do care whether the bus turns up; whether they can get to work on time, get their kids to school or college, or make it to a hospital appointment.
Public control means we can start putting passengers first, with more frequent services, more evening and weekend buses, better connections to hospitals and railway stations and simpler fares. And we have kept single bus fares capped at £2, the price they have been for the past four years.
Change will be immediate. A new express service now connects St Helens directly with Liverpool John Lennon airport. For a family heading on holiday, that may mean avoiding airport parking charges. For somebody looking to work at the airport, it could open up a job. These changes will make a massive difference to people’s lives.
And, for me, that gets to the heart of the argument for public control. A bus route that helps somebody take a job, gets a student to college or allows an older person to remain independent has a value that won’t always show up on an operator’s balance sheet. Markets have their place. But public control allows us to ask not simply, “does this route make money?” but “do our people need it?”
That principle doesn’t stop with buses. We have bought a £500m fleet of new trains and are working towards bringing Merseyrail services into public ownership in 2028. In the coming weeks, the Royal Daffodil – our first new ferry ’cross the Mersey in 60 years, built by a loyal local workforce – will make its maiden voyage.
For decades we were told that privatisation and deregulation would inevitably deliver better services and that the government’s job was to get out of the way. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story.
When he was mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham and I spent years working together to make that case and show what can be achieved when local leaders have the power to shape the services their communities rely on. Now we have a Labour government bringing our railways back into public ownership and giving local leaders more power over the essentials that ordinary people depend on.
After decades in which the state steadily retreated from people’s lives, we have an opportunity to prove that active government can be a force for good again. That is what started in St Helens last weekend.
I want the Liverpool city region to have the best public transport system in the country. I want people to come here, get on one of our buses, trains or ferries, see what we have built and go home asking the same question I used to ask in London: why can’t we have this at home?
- 
  Steve Rotheram is mayor of the Liverpool city region

12 South Koreans arrested in Thailand scam centre crackdown
Police say the alleged scammers entered Thailand from a neighbouring country and rented a luxury house south of Bangkok
Thai authorities arrested 12 South Koreans and a Chinese national accused of running a scam call centre from a high-end rented house south of Bangkok, police said on Tuesday.
The alleged scammers “entered Thailand from a neighbouring country and were hiding in Samut Prakan province, renting a luxury house”, Thai police said in a statement, without naming the country.
Cambodia and Myanmar, which border Thailand, have become hubs for criminal groups operating fake romance, investment and other schemes that defraud victims around the world of billions of dollars each year.
But authorities in both nations have also raided scam compounds in recent months, pushing some scammers to set up elsewhere in the region.
Inside the house in Thailand, authorities found a call centre set-up with 13 workstations equipped with Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) phones and other equipment, including dozens of computers, mobile phones and scripts allegedly used in online scams.
Police also discovered a list of South Korean victims and forged documents falsely claiming to be official letters from the South Korean prosecutor’s office.
