Iran proposes regional action plan to preserve Caspian seal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:43:22 UTC
20:43:22 KST

Iran proposes regional action plan to preserve Caspian seal
TEHRAN – The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has submitted a draft regional action plan aimed at preserving the Caspian seal to the Secretariat of the Tehran Convention for consideration at the ministerial meeting of the Caspian littoral states.
Effective conservation of the Caspian seal is impossible without regional cooperation; the proposed regional action plan aims to require all littoral states to participate in the protection of this valuable species, as the measures implemented by a single country cannot guarantee the success of preservation efforts, ISNA quoted Shahram Fadakar, director general for the protection of marine ecosystems and coasts at the Department of Environment (DOE), as saying.
The Caspian seal is the only marine mammal native to the Caspian Sea, which is listed as an endangered species facing numerous threats. The depletion of food sources, particularly Kilka, which is a key food source for the Caspian seal, sea pollution, chemical contamination, hunting, accidental capture in fishing nets, viral and parasite infections, and climate change are among other major threats to the species, the official noted.
Reducing mortality rates within the species requires the implementation of a set of simultaneous measures such as monitoring, conservation, rescue operations, and personnel training. The expansion of rescue centers in coastal provinces, the enhancement of coastal monitoring efforts, the training of fishermen and local communities, and the prompt examination of fresh carcasses can facilitate the identification of threats and mitigation of potential harm, Fadakar highlighted.
The movement of the species across the shared waters of the Caspian Sea and the potential drifting of carcasses between the coastlines of littoral states indicate that a transboundary approach is needed to address this crisis. Pursuing a regional action plan for the conservation of the Caspian seal can facilitate the enhancement of coordination among the coastal nations and the adoption of joint measures to preserve the species’ population, Fadakar further noted.
Over the past few years, the Department of Environment has adopted various measures to protect the species and mitigate these threats, he added.
The DOE, in cooperation with related executive agencies, universities, and other stakeholders, has developed the regional action plan to safeguard the endangered species, Fadakar highlighted.
Currently, the DOE is implementing the following measures to protect the Caspian seal; these include launching a secretariat for the Caspian seal conservation, establishing executive working groups in the northern provinces, setting up and equipping rescue centers, installing information signs in sensitive areas, and preparing educational and informational materials to train target groups regarding this species.
Conservation action plan to save Caspian seal
In recent years, the increasing discovery of seal carcasses on the southern coast of the Caspian Sea has raised concerns among environmentalists that the Caspian seal is at a greater risk of extinction than ever before.
The species is now listed as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, with its population declining due to various reasons, from one million in the past to 70,000 currently.
In 2025, the first specialized center in the country for the conservation, treatment, and dissection of Caspian seals opened in Bojaq National Park in the Caspian Sea province of Gilan.
The center aims to revive and care for the seals, the only marine mammal in the Caspian Sea; the inauguration of the center will serve as a milestone in the implementation of national and regional programs for the protection of this endangered animal, IRIB quoted Ahmad-Reza Lahijanzadeh, the deputy head of the Department of Environment for Marine and Wetlands Affairs, as saying.
The center has the capacity to become a specialized veterinary and research complex to study the causes of death in seals, he added.
Training fishermen to report incidents and transport injured seals quickly (to the center), and using drones to monitor seals will play a key role in lowering losses, Lahijanzadeh added.
The official went on to say that the coastal community can also contribute to the preservation program through reporting seal sightings or carcasses.
In November 2024, DOE started implementing a national action plan that focuses on the conservation of the Caspian seal.
The main objective of the plan is to conserve the Caspian seal, a rare, valuable, endemic, and endangered species of the Caspian Sea, as the priority of marine environmental activities. IRNA quoted Mohammad Talebi-Matin, an official with the DOE, as saying.
The establishment of a center for the Caspian seal conservation in Tarbiat Modarres University’s branch in Noor County is among the important measures taken in this regard.
It has fostered positive interactions between the university and the executive units, which is expected to bring about positive results in the protection of Caspian seals in the near future, the official noted.
Executive working groups have been formed in cooperation with governors and other beneficiaries under the management of provincial departments of environment in Gilan, Mazandaran, and Golestan provinces.
Also, the rescue centers for seals in these three provinces are well-equipped, and a specialized training workshop has already been held for the beneficiaries and rangers, Talebi-Matin said.
The training included basic methods of rescue, release, carcass disposal, and correct sample gathering.
In addition, examining the seals’ carcasses on the beaches to identify the cause of their loss is being pursued in cooperation with neighboring countries and related organizations.

Saudi-Houthi fighting in Yemen escalates: What happened, and what’s next?

Saudi-Houthi fighting in Yemen escalates: What happened, and what’s next?
Saudi Arabia promises firm retaliation after Houthi attacks allegedly injure 73 and disrupt energy facilities in southern cities.
Yemen’s Houthi group has carried out attacks in southern Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh saying that dozens of people have been wounded, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and pro-Saudi forces in Yemen sharply escalates.
The Houthis on Tuesday said they targeted Saudi energy sites belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco in southern areas, with the group’s military spokesperson calling it “a broad operation”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Breaks my heart’: Yemen jab shortages spark fears for millions of children
- list 2 of 3How significant are the Yemeni government’s military gains against Houthis?
- list 3 of 3Yemen gov’t forces launch air strikes on Houthi targets
Saudi authorities confirmed attacks on several facilities and installations related to the energy sector in the south of the country, vowing a firm response. Riyadh also accused the Houthis of wounding at least 73 people in the attacks.
The conflict between the Yemeni armed group and Saudi Arabia is unfolding as the Houthis are currently fighting Yemen’s Riyadh-backed internationally recognised government, which announced that it was launching counteroffensives against Houthi-held positions across several provinces on Monday.
The renewed hostilities are the most serious since a United Nations-brokered truce halted large-scale fighting in 2022, after eight years of a full-blown conflict that killed tens of thousands of people in one of the world’s poorest countries.
The escalation also comes as the strategic importance of Yemen’s Bab al-Mandeb Strait grows amid Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key passageway for global oil and gas supplies.
The Houthis have sought to advance towards the vital Red Sea shipping route, while government forces say their campaign ultimately aims to retake the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa.
So what do we know about the latest fighting, and what comes next?
How did the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis unfold?
The Houthis on Monday said Saudi Arabia launched multiple attacks on Houthi-held areas.
The group said Saudi attacks using aircraft and cruise missiles struck al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Marib and Taiz provinces.
Moreover, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out an air strike on a prison in al-Hazm, the capital of al-Jawf, killing seven people and injuring seven others. Riyadh did not immediately comment on the attacks.
At the same time, the Houthis claimed to have shot down Saudi reconnaissance drones over al-Jawf and al-Bayda.
Meanwhile, on Tuesday, Major-General Turki al-Malki, the Saudi spokesman for the Riyadh-led coalition in Yemen, said the Houthis carried out attacks on the Saudi cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran, injuring at least 73 people, among them women and children.
According to a statement from Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry, the strikes also triggered fires at multiple oil installations and utility sites across the kingdom’s southern provinces.
Southern Saudi Arabia is home to key oil infrastructure, including the Jizan refinery, one of the kingdom’s largest, with the capacity to process 400,000 barrels of crude per day.
Shortly after, the Houthis announced that they had targeted Saudi energy infrastructure operated by oil giant Aramco in the south using drones and ballistic missiles.
The group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the attacks were retaliation for recent Saudi attacks on Houthi-controlled areas across Yemen. Later on Tuesday, Houthi-affiliated media Al Maisrah said Saudi forces had targeted the Al-Jubah district in Marib in the Houthi-controlled part of Yemen.
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan al Saud said the kingdom “strongly condemns” the Houthis’ attacks.
“The Houthis choose to prioritise their narrow interests over the interests of Yemen and resort to violence,” Prince Faisal said in a joint press conference with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Moscow.
However, Prince Faisal said diplomacy is still possible with the Houthis to end the fighting after heavy strikes on the country.
“The road to diplomacy is not closed,” he said. “Saudi Arabia will always support diplomatic solutions, but the kingdom will never hesitate to defend itself and its interests. We will use every tool to do our job and our duties.”
Why is this escalation taking place now?
A key focus of the fighting is the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The Houthis declared a blockade against Saudi shipping in July. The Houthis have also pushed towards government-held areas near al-Makha (Mocha) and territory bordering the Bab al-Mandeb Strait amid reinforcements and counteroffensives from government forces.
The strait’s strategic importance has increased dramatically because Iran’s restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz have forced Saudi Arabia to rely more heavily on its Red Sea export route. Between March and mid-July, Saudi seaborne crude exports through Bab al-Mandeb were eight times higher than during the same period in 2025.
In 2024, about 4.1 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products passed through the strait daily on average – about 5 percent of the global total.
Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said the strait holds importance “when we look at the Houthis’ broader strategy”.
“The move towards the western coast is not only about gaining territory on the ground. It also has a maritime dimension,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The Houthis have already linked their military campaign to the Red Sea and the shipping routes around Bab al-Mandeb. So gaining more control over the … western coast could give them greater depth and allow them to sustain pressure on maritime traffic in the Red Sea. In that sense, the ground offensive and their maritime campaign are closely connected.”
The latest escalation also follows fighting that resumed in July after an Iranian aircraft attempted to land in Sanaa without Saudi authorisation, followed by strikes on Sanaa airport and Houthi retaliation.
What has been the international reaction?
- Qatar: The Foreign Ministry said the attacks represent a “reprehensible act of aggression and an unacceptable disregard for the lives of civilians”.
- Bahrain: The latest attacks “represent a dangerous escalation [and] a flagrant violation of the rules of international law”, the country’s Foreign Ministry said.
- United Arab Emirates: Abu Dhabi, in addition to condemning the attacks, also decried the continued targeting of commercial vessels in the Red Sea.
- Russia: Foreign Minister Lavrov said Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia were “counterproductive” and were damaging the global economy.
- Pakistan: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called the attack “cowardly”, adding that such “treacherous attacks threaten the lives of innocent people as well as regional peace and security”.
What is happening between government forces and the Houthis?
On Sunday, Yemen’s internationally recognised government said its warplanes had struck Houthi positions in Hodeidah, Marib and al-Jawf, as fighting spread across several fronts.
On Monday, government-aligned forces stepped up their counteroffensive. They announced a ground push towards the al-Labanat mountains in al-Jawf, while also reporting rocket attacks on Yatma and “intensive battles” with Houthi fighters in the province. Government forces also claimed advances towards Dhi Na’im district in al-Bayda.
The Houthis said they had repelled the advance towards al-Labanat and inflicted casualties on government-aligned forces. Houthi official Mohammed al-Farah also claimed the group fired ballistic missiles at reinforcements in al-Jawf.
By late Monday, government-aligned forces reported carrying out further air attacks against Houthi positions west of Taiz.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the battlefield claims by the Houthis or the Yemeni government.
Rashad al-Alimi, who heads Yemen’s Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, meanwhile said on Monday that government forces had made significant gains against the Houthis, pointing to advances in al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Taiz and Hodeidah.
“Our armed forces will continue to carry out their constitutional duty until state institutions are restored and their authority extends over the entire territory of Yemen,” al-Alimi said in a statement.
Yemen’s deputy defence minister, Major-General Samir al-Sabri, said in comments aired on state television that the government had resolved to “retake Sanaa”.
Majid al-Nuzaili, a spokesperson for government-aligned forces, said the goal of the offensive was to “liberate Yemen from the grip” of the Houthis “and restore Sanaa as a capital for all Yemenis”.
What is the humanitarian situation on the ground?
The World Health Organization said on Monday that at least 728 people have been killed or wounded in Yemen since August 23, with the majority in Taiz and along the western coast.
It said an estimated 21,000 people, roughly 3,000 families, have been displaced from Taiz alone since Thursday.
“Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it’s safe to go back,” said Abdusattor Esoev, head of the International Organization for Migration’s mission in Yemen. “Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before.”
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said the casualty count is expected to rise.
“These casualties are said to be in the hundreds from both sides, especially as we have reports of air strikes being conducted in the governorate of al-Jawf,” he said.
The Crisis Group’s Nagi said the world was witnessing “significant deterioration in what is already a catastrophic situation”.
“We saw in the past few days a lot of displacement from areas where there has been fighting between the two sides, especially in Taiz,” he noted.
“Those are the direct impacts, but there are also indirect ones. The economic situation is likely to get worse, which will put even more pressure on the humanitarian situation. Ultimately, I think it will depend on how long this round of fighting lasts. The longer the conflict continues, the greater the humanitarian impact will be.”
What’s next?
Analyst Hisham al-Omeisy said the fighting in the war-torn country was no longer simply a domestic issue.
“We are way beyond the concept [of it] being domestic. It all started with the Houthis pushing to control Bab al-Mandeb and the western coast, to control the chokehold on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, with the Iranians controlling the Strait of Hormuz,” al-Omeisy, a senior Yemen adviser at the European Institute of Peace, told Al Jazeera.
“This is definitely not domestic, especially when the Houthis have started attacking Saudi Arabia as well for the better part of the last month, and now escalating since today [Tuesday].”
Domestically, the Crisis Group’s Nagi said it was “unclear” what the outcome of this round of fighting will be, describing the situation on the ground as “very fluid”.
“But what we are seeing is that the government seems to be in a stronger position than at any time before, and it sees this round of fighting as an opportunity to consolidate its position and gain more territory from the Houthis,” he said, while warning that this did not mean the Houthis were weak.
“It’s true that the Houthis are fighting in Taiz, and they were the ones who launched the offensive against government forces there and made some gains. But on other fronts, in al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Marib and elsewhere, government forces have advanced and gained several key areas, while the Houthis have been on the defensive.”
On whether there will be a winner in this conflict, al-Omeisy said that in the long term, he expects a negotiated settlement.
“Look at the history of Yemen … we always inevitably reach some sort of a deal, so it’s not going to be a winner-takes-all,” he said.
“I don’t imagine there’s going to be a push to regain the capital [Sanaa], for instance. It’s going to be a bloodbath if they [government-aligned forces] do that.”
“There’s going to be a humbling of the Houthi forces. There’s going to be losses. But eventually, you will need a political deal,” al-Omeisy added.
According to Saudi political analyst Khaled Batarfi, the Houthi strikes will trigger a response, but not a prolonged war.
“This is an escalation, of course,” Batarfi told Al Jazeera. In past attacks, Saudi Arabia tried “to not get engaged in a civil war, keep its distance, and to not respond to attacks. But now this is too much [of an escalation],” he said.
“The coalition will have a say on that,” Batarfi noted. “This is a civil war inside Yemen, and it affects us as one of the parties. And so any response … in the same way [will be] an eye for an eye. But I don’t see a prolonged war – not with Iran, and not with the Houthis.”

Dutch children’s literacy falls further behind European average
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:39:44 UTC
20:39:44 KST

Dutch children’s literacy falls further behind European average
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Nearly four in 10 Dutch children are at risk of leaving school with a low level of literacy, according to an international study that shows a steep decline in educational performance across Europe.
The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), carried out every three years in more than 90 countries, shows the Netherlands has fallen behind the European average over the past decade.
Dutch children still outperform their peers in most European countries in maths and science, where the figures show a less pronounced downward trend. In science they have dropped to the average level for the 23 nations in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) used for long-term comparisons.
The figures, which compare educational performance in 91 countries altogether, show a general worldwide decline in literacy standards since 2015, but the picture is especially stark in the Netherlands.
Some 39% of 15-year-olds had a reading level deemed inadequate to function in society, up from 33% the last time the report was compiled in 2022.
The points score used to grade performance has fallen from 503 in 2015 to 441 last year, including an 18-point drop between 2022 and 2025.
Three years behind
A drop of 20 points is seen as the equivalent of falling a year behind in educational development, meaning today’s 15-year-olds are learning at the same level as 12-year-olds a decade ago.
The 14 European countries which took part in the study – 13 EU nations plus the UK – had an average score of 464, with Ireland and Latvia topping the table. Singapore topped the global rankings with 535, followed by China.
Researchers speculated last time that school closures during the pandemic might be responsible for the decline in performance, but the continuing trend since the end of lockdown has forced them to consider that they may have overestimated the impact.
The growing use of digital technology such as smartphones, social media and AI may also be holding back the development of children’s reading skills, the researchers say.
Digital media
In a paper published last year they said children’s performance in maths, sense of belonging at school and overall life satisfaction were lower if they spent more time on their smartphones and called for more support for families to manage digital leisure time out of school.
The figures for science show Dutch students’ performance fell by three points to 485, one point lower than the OECD average, while in maths the Netherlands is still above the average despite dropping 10 points to 483.
Junior education minister Judith Thielen promised earlier this year to come up with an action plan in the autumn to tackle low literacy.
“It is my ambition to stop the downward trend and turn it around,” she said. “I want to see better results in three years’ time.”

Investigation after female staff at Eiffel Tower replaced by men for religious visit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:38:07 BST
20:38:07 KST

Investigation after female staff at Eiffel Tower replaced by men for religious visit
- Published
An investigation has been launched in France after female staff at the Eiffel Tower were replaced by male colleagues for the visit of a Hindu religious group.
A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the iconic landmark in Paris on Saturday.
"Women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated", staff union representative Diane Davoine said. The tower closed on Monday as staff went on strike to show their outrage.
BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances.
Ariel Weil, who is the president of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower, blamed its managers for being "a bit overzealous" in complying with the request without considering whether it was "inappropriate".
Weil, who is also mayor of Paris Centre, told French broadcaster Franceinfo on Tuesday that the incident was "totally shocking and unacceptable".
An internal investigation will determine who was responsible for putting the conditions in place, Weil said, and ensure it "never happens again".
In a statement reported by AFP news agency, staff at the monument said that during Saturday's visit, female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present".
"Tensions mounted over the weekend, so [on Monday morning], the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again," Davoine said.
Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), which runs the Eiffel Tower, had previously said the conditions imposed on female staff were not in line with its values "nor with the principles of equality between men and women".
BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in a Parisian suburb.
In a statement on X, BAPS said the trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".
It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".
On its website, the group describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.
It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.
It draws its beliefs from the teachings of Lord Swaminarayan, a late 18th-Century celibate ascetic who is regarded by his followers as an incarnation of Vishnu, the revered Hindu god of preservation.
BAPS says the segregation of men and women was introduced for the benefit of women, but critics say 18th-Century beliefs have no place in today's world, and keeping women out in the name of religious practices is discriminatory.
Politicians in France have condemned Saturday's incident.
Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."
French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."
Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."

Bill on privatizing damaged housing registered
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:37:58 EEST
20:37:58 KST

The government has registered bill No. 16012 in the Verkhovna Rada, meant to regulate the privatization of state and municipal housing damaged or destroyed by Russian aggression, the Ministry of Communities and Territories Development press service said.
The Cabinet of Ministers had earlier supported the ministry's proposal to allow the privatization of such housing and amend the law on the privatization of the state housing fund, as previously reported.
People currently living in non-privatized apartments or homes are tenants rather than owners, and are therefore unable to receive compensation for damaged or destroyed property as owners would. The bill proposes an exception to the general rule, allowing the privatization of unsafe housing if it was damaged or destroyed after February 24, 2022, and has a corresponding damage assessment report. This would allow tenants eligible for privatization to obtain ownership and apply for assistance under the eVidnovlennia program.

Ayhan Simsek
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Police have arrested a man in western Germany in connection with a week of sabotage attempts on electricity substations, local media reported on Tuesday.
Der Spiegel said that the man, identified as Daniel V., 48, was arrested at a traffic stop near Weisweiler, close to the city of Aachen in northwestern Germany.
Investigators had been hunting him for days after homemade devices were used against substations that serve brown coal power plants.
On Monday evening, police found several of those homemade launch devices near the Weisweiler power plant — the same type used in earlier sabotage attempts. The devices were built to fire thin wire over high-voltage lines and trigger short circuits.
Similar ramps appeared last week in the states of Brandenburg, North Rhine-Westphalia, and Saxony. The first confirmed attacks came on Sept. 1 at substations serving the Jaenschwalde lignite plant in eastern Germany and facilities near Bergheim, west of Cologne.
Letters claiming responsibility reached German media last week. They were signed with the suspect’s full name. The writer said he acted alone and that left-wing groups and activists “had nothing to do with it.”
“Electricity generation from fossil fuels is a crime that brings unspeakable suffering,” one letter said. “Because the media don’t do a damn thing to convey the urgency of the situation and the state does not intervene to avert this suffering, I have to do it now.”
In another passage, he wrote: “I am not attacking the country but the fossil fuel industry, even if for some politicians that is the same thing.” He said he was “pleased that there were no power outages and yet coal-fired power plant units went offline.”
He also wrote that he would “not be sad” if Germany’s arms industry were hit by outages, “particularly as long as Germany supports the genocide in Palestine.”

Ukraine is seeking a new trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, potentially as early as this fall, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday, Sept. 8, as the Kremlin claimed that a resolution to Russia’s war was “very close.”

“If everyone agrees, the meeting could take place in September. The sooner, the better,” Zelensky said.
No date or venue for such a meeting has been formally agreed, and neither Washington nor Moscow has publicly confirmed that preparations are underway.
UAE, Switzerland, and Turkey considered as venues
The UAE, Switzerland, and Turkey are among the possible venues for the next round of trilateral negotiations, Zelensky said.
Ukraine has received invitations from several countries and is also considering other potential locations, according to his reports.

Kremlin claims peace is “very close”

“Russia is confident that a resolution to the conflict in Ukraine is very close,” Peskov said, according to Russian state-run news agency TASS.
Peskov provided no evidence of an imminent agreement and announced neither a date nor a venue for negotiations. A day earlier, however, he said it was too soon to discuss specific arrangements for a meeting.
Russia has repeatedly claimed to support diplomacy while continuing its attacks on Ukrainian cities and demanding that Kyiv surrender territory that Moscow’s forces have failed to occupy.
Zelensky said Ukraine would continue presenting constructive proposals but stressed that negotiations must deliver tangible humanitarian and security results.
“We need to continue working actively and jointly so that diplomacy exists,” he said.

The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and the National Police have blocked five new schemes for evading military service and mobilization, detaining 11 organizers of the operations across various regions of Ukraine, the SBU reported.
"For amounts ranging from $5,000 to $22,000, the suspects helped draft evaders dodge conscription and illegally travel abroad," the agency stated on Telegram on Tuesday.
In Lviv region, seven members of a criminal organization were detained for facilitating the illegal discharge of mobilized personnel from service and helping conscripts evade draft.
"Among the scheme's organizers are representatives of the criminal environment who involved members of the Military Medical Commission, hospital officials, military unit personnel, as well as TRC employees in illegal activities," the statement specifies.
According to the Ukrainian special service, for sums up to $20,000, the perpetrators provided clients with a full "service package"—ranging from issuing fake medical certificates of unfitness for service with Group 2 disability status to "striking" conscripts off the military register on health grounds.
In Rivne region, a local lawyer was exposed for organizing the production of fictitious medical documentation on "severe" illnesses for draft dodgers.
"To achieve this, the lawyer involved acquaintance officials from expert teams evaluating individual daily functioning, who falsified medical histories with subsequent establishment of disability groups. The cost of such 'services' amounted to $9,000," the report notes.
Additionally, in Donetsk region, a former employee of the Pokrovsk TRC received a notice of suspicion for offering draft evaders removal from the wanted list and military register based on forged medical conclusions. In Cherkasy region, a resident of Smila district was detained for promising draft-eligible men "reserved" status from mobilization based on fictitious diagnoses for $10,000.
Currently, the suspects have been served with notices of suspicion corresponding to the committed crimes.
Comprehensive operations were conducted under the procedural guidance of the Rivne, Lviv, Donetsk, Kirovohrad, and Cherkasy regional prosecutor's offices.

Number of job openings remains modest in Estonia
In the second quarter of 2026, there were 8,363 job vacancies in Estonia. This is nearly 2,000 job vacancies fewer than in the second quarter last year, Statistics Estonia data reveals.
In the second quarter, there were a total of 590,408 vacant and occupied positions, 0.9 percent fewer than in the same period a year earlier.
The largest numbers of job vacancies in the second quarter were in education (1,558), public administration and defense (1,274, including compulsory social security), wholesale and retail trade (1,029, including the repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles) and manufacturing (968).
"Looking at the labor market as a whole, employment did not increase in the second quarter. Labor force survey data published in August showed that while the unemployment rate fell, this was not accompanied by a comparable increase in employment. We are seeing the same trend in job vacancy statistics," said Krista Vaikmets, a lead analyst at Statistics Estonia.
A job vacancy is a newly created or unoccupied position or a position that will become vacant when an employee leaves for which an employer is actively seeking a new employee and intends to fill the position either immediately or within a specified period. The number of job vacancies therefore directly reflects employers' demand for additional labor. If companies do not need additional workers, there is also no reason to create new positions or quickly fill existing vacancies.
"The current data points more toward a situation in which companies are cautiously adapting to the improving economic situation. As a result, the number of job vacancies may remain modest even if some labor market indicators, such as the unemployment rate and wages, are moving in a positive direction," the lead analyst explained.
Job vacancies accounted for 1.4 percent of all positions in the second quarter of this year, compared with 1.7 percent in the same period last year.
The largest increases in job vacancies were recorded in administrative and support service activities, arts, entertainment and recreation and accommodation and food service activities. However, there were fewer vacancies than last year in professional, scientific and technical activities and in the energy sector.
There were a total of 582,045 occupied positions in the second quarter, 3,371 fewer than a year earlier but 431 more than in the first quarter of this year.
The largest numbers of occupied positions in Estonia were in manufacturing (98,025), trade (81,968) and education (62,827).
Compared with the second quarter of 2025, the number of occupied positions fell the most in trade, by nearly 2,000.
A total of 51,313 people were hired in the second quarter, more than 600 more than in the same period last year.
By county, Harju County had the largest share of job vacancies in the second quarter of this year, at 80.2 percent. "For the most part, this still means the city of Tallinn, which accounts for 69 percent of job vacancies. Tartu County accounted for 6.6 percent of vacancies, Pärnu County for 2.6 percent and Ida-Viru County for 2 percent," Vaikmets said.
Harju County also had the largest share of occupied positions in the second quarter of this year, at 55.2 percent, followed by Tartu County at 10.5 percent.
"Estonia's labor market is therefore becoming increasingly concentrated in Tallinn and Harju County and most new job opportunities are also more likely to emerge near the capital," the lead analyst added.

Do birds enjoy flying? Scientists asked cockatoos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:30:30 UTC
20:30:30 KST

As a kid, Jorg Massen would watch birds swoop and swirl overhead and wonder whether they were doing it for enjoyment. Massen is now a behavioral biologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, and thanks to a special setup at a nearby bird park, he was finally able to put that question to the test.
For several months each year the birds at Avifauna Bird Park are free to leave their aviaries at certain times every day. When the gates open, each bird decides for itself: fly out into the open sky or stay home. They get no penalty or reward either way.
Among these birds at the time of Massen’s study were 17 pink-and-gray Galah Cockatoos that, in the wild, fly long distances to find seeds. The Galahs chose to fly for almost every 20-minute period offered, Massen and his colleagues reported in a paper published in Behaviour.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Their consistent choice to fly is “in line with the notion that the birds found flight rewarding,” says Michael Mendl, an animal behavior researcher at the University of Bristol in England, who was not involved in the study. The only exception was a pair of birds that skipped flying once, on a day when they had just been given new nest boxes, Massen says: “they had other activities to attend to”—such as courtship and mating—“which are also considered joyful.”
After flight sessions, the Galahs foraged, scratched and raised their crests more—behaviors the researchers interpreted as signs of “positive excitement resulting from free flight.” And in a test designed to measure optimism, the Galahs grew more hopeful of finding their favorite treat (a walnut) when they’d had several days of free flight and more pessimistic about their walnut prospects after several days of being grounded.
The birds’ hormones did not change after flight as predicted, however; an expected dip in the stress hormone cortisol might have been masked by a rise caused by physical exertion, Massen says.
We can’t be certain about whether wanting to fly and liking the experience add up to feeling happy, Mendl notes. Animal-cognition scientists have typically been extremely hesitant to ascribe feelings or desires based on animals’ behavior, but researchers have become increasingly open to attributing such conscious experiences to animals when the data support it. If birds are capable of conscious experience, Mendl says, “the findings would indeed suggest that the birds enjoyed flying.”
For Galahs, Massen says, flight appears to be “an ethological need”: a behavior they’re naturally driven to perform. Massen sees his study as part of a broader shift in animal-welfare science away from simply preventing suffering and toward designing environments that let animals express the natural behaviors that seem to make them feel good.

====================================================================================================

Bosses are using AI to spy on employees' productivity—does it work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:30:06 UTC
20:30:06 KST

Ready for a Whopper with a side of Orwell? Earlier this year, Burger King announced the rollout of Patty, an AI chatbot imbedded in headsets that tracks if cashiers neglect to say please and thank you and chimes in when a soda fountain is running low.
Advances in AI, cameras, sensors and tracking software have given employers unprecedented power to monitor employees. They now observe the physical location of workers, the length and content of phone calls, keystrokes per minute, and even the tone and pitch of conversations with customers.
Now, as companies search for new ways to watch their workforce, researchers are taking a close look at the consequences of constant surveillance.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Employee monitoring has become standard practice in multiple industries and workplaces. Drivers delivering packages or pizzas are increasingly being watched by AI-powered surveillance systems. Many employees in Amazon warehouses are continuously tracked through handheld scanners, badge swipes and workstation software.
Technologies that keep tabs on employees hold a strong appeal for corporate leadership, says Cornelius König, a psychology researcher at Saarland University in Germany. Leaders may believe that close surveillance can help identify top performers, increase efficiency or improve safety, he says.
In practice, though, such benefits are elusive. When König reviewed studies on employee monitoring in the 2025 issue of the Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, he found little to suggest that electronic surveillance improved performance. “My general take is that [monitoring] isn’t going to matter as much as employers assume,” he says.
Despite the lack of evidence, the global market for employee-monitoring technology is expected to exceed $4 billion in 2026, largely due to major companies in North America. A New York Times investigation in 2022 found that eight out of the 10 largest private US employers, including United Parcel Service, Amazon and UnitedHealth Group, tracked productivity metrics of individual workers, often in real time.
US postal workers are also closely watched. Delivering mail “feels less like public service and more like working inside a quiet surveillance state,” said a Reddit user in 2025. “We’re tracked down to the second. Every scan. Every step. Every stop. They monitor our GPS in real time. They can pull up on us unannounced. We get questioned for things as human as needing the restroom or checking a package twice.”
Any employer of any size can get into the monitoring business. Amazon Web Services sells thousands and thousands of software programs for employee monitoring, says Michele Molè, an employment law researcher at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands. Adding a monitoring app to the workplace can be as easy as downloading Spotify, he says. But instead of music, employers get a stream of data about how each employee is behaving every minute of their day.
Companies that hope to increase their workforce’s performance through monitoring face a basic obstacle in human nature, König says. Workers might briefly up their game, but they tend to revert to their normal routines. “They become habituated,” he says. In his review, he pointed to growing evidence that even body cameras worn by police — an especially high-profile, high-stakes example of surveillance — don’t significantly change the behavior of either the police or the public over the long term.
When workers do respond to monitoring, there can be unintended consequences. A 2020 study found that electronically monitored truck drivers were less likely to exceed daily limits for driving hours, but they also were more likely to crash.
König is far from the only skeptic. “There’s really very little evidence that the mere implementation of monitoring employees is, in itself, going to increase productivity or performance,” says Daniel Ravid, a management researcher at the University of New Mexico.
Ravid conducted a 2022 meta-analysis that combined the results of studies involving more than 23,000 subjects in laboratory experiments and workplace settings, including workers in call centers and offices and police on patrol. Taken together, the studies found no correlation between levels of monitoring and employee performance.
That’s partly because some employees find workarounds to monitoring, even if that means tapping their keyboard periodically while they’re reading a book at lunch. “People are incredibly creative and adaptable, and they’ll find ways to reassert their freedom when it’s threatened or taken away,” Ravid says.
Ravid’s meta-analysis found that any type of monitoring — subtle or obvious, incidental or invasive — tended to increase workplace stress. “I think anything that undermines a sense of dignity is also going to undermine employee attitudes,” he says.
A 2024 study of more than 3,500 workers in Canada underscored the potential downsides of monitoring: Employees who perceived that they were being surveilled on the job reported that they felt more pressure and stress and less autonomy and privacy at work.
In an age of “datafication,” it’s not surprising that companies would look for new metrics to evaluate employees, says Kirstie Ball, a management researcher at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. “The systematic gathering of data about people and what they’re doing is part and parcel of modernity,” she says. “Surveillance becomes a means of getting things done.”
But not every company knows how to make good use of all those data points, Ball says. “There are many pitfalls along the way. Are you measuring what you think you’re measuring? Are you interpreting the data correctly according to the purpose that you gathered it, or are you looking at it just because you can?”
Employee surveillance without any coherent plan to use the data has become a commonplace scenario in modern companies, König says. Many workplaces end up collecting data simply because they have the technology, not because surveillance supports the company’s overall business strategy. “They end up with terabytes of data on a drive somewhere but don’t know what to do with it.”
“There’s really very little evidence that the mere implementation of monitoring employees is, in itself, going to increase productivity or performance.” —Daniel Ravid, University of New Mexico
Modern surveillance is an inherently electronic exercise, but companies can’t just install an app and expect results, Ravid says. “If managers think that they have a perfect way to measure performance because they have advanced technologies, they’re wrong,” he says. “They still need human insight and conversations to contextualize that data.”
Laws protecting employees from overly invasive surveillance generally haven’t kept pace with technology, says Molè, who wrote the 2026 book Monitored at Work. While the European Union has strong employee privacy laws, with additional legal protections in nations like Italy, Spain, France and Germany, workers in the US have far fewer safeguards and are more likely to be placed under a microscope.
In 2023, three current or former Amazon delivery drivers in Colorado filed a class action lawsuit against Amazon claiming that they were under excessive AI-assisted surveillance and that delivery quotas made it difficult to take necessary breaks. “The drivers were forced to pee in bottles,” Molè says. “This is not happening in Europe.” Amazon called for arbitration, noting that drivers work directly for outside delivery service providers who have contracts with the multitrillion-dollar company, not Amazon itself. The case is ongoing.
Other legal issues can lurk in the fine print that comes with monitoring software. Bosses who download monitoring apps they can’t customize are essentially letting outside companies take control of their employees’ data with little oversight or knowledge of how the data could be used. “We need more labor laws that target providers of technologies,” Molè says. Surveillance companies should be required to work directly with companies and their employees to clearly explain the technologies and tailor each product to meet specific needs and reach specific goals, he says.
Theoretically, monitoring could be a part of a healthy company culture that encourages success, Molè says. “People under monitoring should have a sense of being valued, and the monitoring should be truly meaningful for improving everyone’s working conditions and methods,” he says. “Good monitoring is based on mutual trust.” Companies that thoughtfully build their own system for tracking employee outputs instead of superimposing some “creepy and odd” tool found online are more likely to see actual benefits, he adds.
Success is certainly possible. Headbands that track brainwaves may seem invasive, but an Australian mining company found that such technology helped reduce fatigue-related accidents to almost zero. A 2024 study of remote workers on Upwork found that the productivity of top-performing workers dropped nearly 20 percent after they were allowed to turn off monitoring software without explanation, suggesting that the software had some benefits.
But productivity didn’t fall when that high-performing group was told they had the opportunity to go without supervision because of their impressive output, underscoring the importance of good management — leading the researchers to conclude that spending money on good managers could yield better results than spending it on monitoring software.
Transparency can go a long way to improving workplace culture, Ravid says. His meta-analysis found that, compared with workers who are surveilled without much explanation or consent, workers who have a clear understanding of how they are being monitored and how the data will be used also have a greater sense of fairness and job satisfaction.
New technologies will continue to join the ranks of Burger King’s Patty and other monitoring devices in the modern workforce. But if companies don’t change their basic approach, the results will likely be the be the same: suspicion and confusion for employees and few tangible benefits for employers.

Moscow vows ‘harsh and painful’ response to Hungarian expulsions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Moscow vows ‘harsh and painful’ response to Hungarian expulsions
Moscow will deliver a “harsh and painful” response to Hungary’s expulsion of ten Russian diplomats, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has warned.
The remarks were in response to Budapest’s decision to expel ten members of Russia’s diplomatic mission over alleged activities deemed “unacceptable for diplomats” under the Vienna Convention.
“The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful,” Zakharova said on Tuesday.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban announced the decision on Tuesday. She said the Russian ambassador had been informed that, “according to the assessment of the Hungarian authorities,” the diplomats had engaged in activities incompatible with their status.
Orban did not specify the alleged activities or say how long the diplomats had been given to leave. She said the decision was intended to protect Hungary’s “security and sovereignty,” while stressing that Budapest was not severing diplomatic ties with Moscow and intended to maintain dialogue.
The expulsions come as Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s government has sharply reversed Hungary’s policy toward Russia since taking office in May. In a new foreign policy directive, Budapest designated Russia a “threat to Hungary, Europe, and the global order,” marking a dramatic break with the pragmatic relations pursued under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Hungary had not formally designated Russia as a “threat” at any point since 1945. Under Orban, Budapest repeatedly opposed what the former prime minister called the West’s “war policies,” refused to supply weapons to Kiev, and argued that the conflict could not be settled through a Ukrainian military victory.
Orban also repeatedly delayed or watered down EU sanctions on Moscow and resisted major financial packages for Kiev, while seeking exemptions that allowed Hungary to continue importing Russian oil, gas, and nuclear fuel. He maintained that cutting Europe off from comparatively cheap Russian energy would damage the bloc’s industrial competitiveness.
Magyar’s new position closely mirrors that of the EU, which also advocates “sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees,” but only on terms that recognize Kiev’s maximalist demands – a return to Ukraine’s 1991 borders, freedom to pursue NATO and EU membership, and NATO-like security guarantees provided by European and American forces.
His government has also backed new sanctions on Russia and dropped Budapest’s objections to a €90 billion ($105 billion) EU package for Kiev, reversing policies that had previously set Hungary apart from most other EU members.

Putin spends nearly 25 million euros an hour on war in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:28:35 UTC
20:28:35 KST

Russia’s federal budget spending on the war in Ukraine reached a historic high between January and June 2026. The aggressor state spent 10.687 trillion rubles (106.28 billion euros) on military needs and weapons production, Dialog.ua reports.
The figures were published by Janis Kluge, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, following a review of data from the Russian Ministry of Finance.
Compared with the first half of 2025, Russia’s military spending increased by 30%, with an additional 2.46 trillion rubles (24.5 billion euros) spent.
Compared with January–June 2024, expenditure increased by 65%, or 4.211 trillion rubles (42.1 billion euros). Compared with 2023, the increase amounted to 145%, while spending was 285% higher than in the first year of the full-scale war.
Compared with the pre-war year of 2021, Russia’s military spending has increased more than fivefold. On average, Russia’s military machine cost the state budget 1.78 trillion rubles (17.7 billion euros) per month.
That amounts to approximately 59 billion rubles (587 million euros) per day,
or around 2.5 billion rubles (24.9 million euros) per hour.
Almost half of all Russian state budget expenditure is now devoted to military needs. During the first six months of the year, 43.8% of all budget expenditure was spent on the military and weapons production, marking a new all-time high.
Most of Russia’s current military spending is hidden from the public. Around two-thirds of the military budget is classified. In the first six months of 2026, Russia spent 3.546 trillion rubles (35.25 billion euros) on publicly disclosed defence items, while another 7.141 trillion rubles (71 billion euros) was spent under classified budget items.
Classified expenditure is growing particularly rapidly. Compared with last year, such spending has increased by 42% and is now more than seven times higher than before the war.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Russian authorities have allocated 57.144 trillion rubles (567.6 billion euros) to military spending and weapons procurement.

20:28:33 KST

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were “surprised” at being given little notice of a formal letter sent to government departments and the military on behalf of King Charles reiterating their status as non-working royals.
Harry and Meghan, who returned to the UK from the US two weeks ago, had insufficient time to clarify any points before details were issued to the media, it is understood.
The letter, the first official public clarification of the couple’s status since their return, was issued by Buckingham Palace’s most senior officer, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon.
It was revealed to the media at 3.06pm on Monday. It is understood the contents were shared with Harry and Meghan’s team almost an hour before at 1.59pm, who sent a response back to Buckingham Palace at 2.19pm asking whether the guidance had already gone out, in the hope of letting the couple know before the media, and for the team to have the chance to clarify one or two points.
Harry was in a meeting and could not be contacted until 3.09pm. The Sussexes’ team received confirmation at 3.11pm it had already been sent to the media.
The letter was revealed before a reported meeting this week of the executive committee for the protection of royalty and public figures (Ravec), which is responsible for making decisions about royal security.
Harry is waiting to hear the conclusion of the risk management board’s threat assessment and Ravec is expected to decide at the meeting whether the Sussexes are entitled to taxpayer-funded security now they live in the UK. The Home Office does not comment on such decision making and would be unlikely to reveal the outcome of such a meeting.
Lord Benyon’s letter reiterates the couple’s “current” status as non-working royals. “This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working royal family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected.
“Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and are not used.
It says their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity”.
“In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests.”
The letter says questions from official and state organisations about the courtesies extended to the couple, “and particularly where recourse to public funds may be required”, should be directed to Buckingham Palace, adding: “Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities.”
The couple’s children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, are expected to be starting school in the UK near to the family’s reported countryside retreat.
The palace’s clarification came on the day Harry was revealed to have visited Tower Bridge Studios, a London filming and podcast studio, where shows such as the podcasts Diary of a CEO and Jimmy Carr’s The Big Pitch are recorded.

Mamdani Expected to Announce Release of 9/11-Related Documents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:26:35 UTC
20:26:35 KST

As the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in New York City approaches, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has launched a portal giving the public access to about 170,000 pages of documents concerning air quality, health hazards, and the government’s response following 9/11.
Its long-sought documents, which had previously been kept out of the public eye, show that New York City leaders were aware of the dangers posed by toxic contamination around Ground Zero following the attacks, even while they continued to tell New Yorkers that the air was safe to breathe.
Some of the pages were reportedly found in 68 boxes stashed in a city office, which advocates argue had been kept away from the public for years. According to a press release from the Mayor's Office, the records "were not located until 2025 despite multiple Freedom of Information Law (FOIL) requests."
Another document included in the records is the so-called Harding memo, an October 2001 document showing that city officials had in the weeks after the attacks already anticipated approximately 10,000 legal claims arising from exposure to toxic air.
The new portal was announced Tuesday morning at a press conference that was also attended by longtime advocate Jon Stewart and others involved in the yearslong legal effort to obtain the records. In June, the mayor allocated $34.2 million from the city’s $125.8 billion fiscal year 2027 budget to create and maintain the portal.
"Now, close to 25 years later, more people have died from 9/11-related illnesses than were killed on the day itself," Mamdani said at the conference announcing the portal. The World Trade Center Health Program, which provides no-cost monitoring and treatment for covered 9/11-related health conditions, said thousands continue to be diagnosed with ailments resulting from their exposure to dust, smoke, debris, and the traumatic events.
The city’s Fire Department released a report on Sept. 1 detailing the lasting effects of the 9/11 tragedy on first responders. More than 12,000 FDNY members have been diagnosed and certified with at least one related physical or mental health condition, including cancers, according to the report.
The mayor’s office has said that additional documents will be added on a rolling basis. "The City expects substantially more documents will be released in the coming year as they are reviewed, and personally identifiable information is removed," the press release said.
“For too long, New Yorkers have had to fight for access to records that should have been available to them in the first place," Mamdani said in the press release. "This portal is part of our administration’s enduring commitment to honor those we lost, care for those living with lasting health consequences and give thousands of New Yorkers the answer they’ve been asking for.”
Mamdani also announced Tuesday that the city had settled two lawsuits brought by 9/11 Health Watch, ending a multiyear legal battle over records concerning post-9/11 air quality and health risks.
What do we know about the content of the documents?
The New York Times obtained early access to the documents and reported that they contain information relating to 15 John Street, near the collapsed World Trade Center, which purportedly detected asbestos—at times exceeding acceptable limits—about a year after the attack.
Among the pages was also an audit from November 2001, submitted to the federal Environmental Protection Agency, which reportedly showed high concentrations of benzene, a cancer-causing substance, in the air near the towers, according to the Times.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has said that exposure to these contaminants increases the risk of developing health conditions, such as illnesses concerning the airways and digestive systems. The CDC added that after the attacks, around 400,000 people were exposed to these contaminants and other factors that increased their risk for such conditions.
Taking questions at the conference on Tuesday, Mamdani addressed what people can expect to learn from the documents that they might not have already known. "I think that there is going to be a lot to learn from these documents," he said, adding that it's important that "those who faced such sustained pushback for years are finally told by the city of New York: 'You were right.'"
Why Mamdani is under pressure
The release of the documents coincides with Mamdani drawing calls from families of victims of the tragedy and some Republican politicians not to attend the 9/11 remembrance event in New York City on Friday.
In July, 9/11 widower Giovanni Galante began a petition against Mamdani’s attendance, citing concerns over “Mamdani's public positions, associations, and responses to rhetoric that many perceive as hostile.” The petition cites Mamdani’s refusal to condemn those who say “globalize the intifada” as one of the issues. The petition also references Mamdani’s appointment of Ramzi Kassem, who worked for the Biden Administration, as chief counsel to the mayor. Kassem served as legal counsel for Ahmed al-Darbi, who plead guilty to charges stemming from a 2002 al-Qaeda tanker bombing plot and who is the brother-in-law of one of the hijackers in the plane that crashed into the Pentagon.
Former New York Gov. George Pataki told a local CBS affiliate on Thursday that Mamdani should first reject Hasan Piker, who previously earned public ire over a comment that the U.S. “deserved” the attack. Mamdani has already denounced Piker’s comment.
Rudy Giuliani, who was the mayor of New York in 2001, told right-leaning news organization Newsmax that Mamdani should skip the event. “Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he's coming,” Giuliani said. The former mayor also attacked Mamdani’s religion, Islam, and baselessly suggested the mayor was supportive of Muslim extremist ideology.
Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor who was nine years old when the attack happened, has long faced Islamophobic comments. Speaking to the Times last year, Mamdani lamented how the 2001 attacks had made anti-Muslim prejudice “a fact of life” for Muslim-Americans, claiming: “It was this horrific day that was also, for many New Yorkers, the moment at which they were marked an ‘other.’”
Before Giuliani’s comments, Mamdani signed city executive orders designating Sept. 11 a New York-wide "Day of Remembrance and Service" and updating emergency preparedness procedures. But the signing caught the ire of some critics after Mamdani handed the 9/11 ceremonial pen to Kassem.
Despite the pushback, Mamdani still plans to attend the commemoration on Friday.
“I’m proud to be the mayor of this city,” Mamdani said. “I love this city. I love this country. And what I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11th, and a focus also on the first responders who gave everything they could to this city and to the people who came together to try and help their fellow New Yorkers.”

Russia looking forward to revival of trilateral Ukraine talks – Kremlin
Moscow appreciates efforts to resume direct negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine, and the US as Washington has stepped up efforts to settle the conflict, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
Speaking to Indian media on Tuesday, ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi, Peskov said intensive diplomatic work is underway, with American negotiators carrying messages between Moscow and Kiev.
“We hope for a restart of negotiations between three parties – Russia, Ukraine, and America. We do hope for the best. We do hope that sooner or later we will pursue a peaceful solution,” he said.
Peskov added that Russia welcomes mediation efforts by both Washington and New Delhi, and emphasized that Moscow never wanted the Ukraine conflict to happen and launched its offensive in order to end the war started by Kiev in 2014 following the Western-backed Maidan coup.
The spokesman also said Kiev does not appear to be “flexible” or “really willing” to actually end the hostilities, adding that it appears to be “provoked to a great extent by some European countries who cannot get rid of the idea of strategically defeating Russia.”
His comments follow a fresh round of shuttle diplomacy by US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The pair met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday for more than three hours before traveling to Kiev for talks with Vladimir Zelensky the following day.
The Kremlin described the Moscow meeting as constructive and “extremely candid,” saying the Americans presented several ideas for ending the conflict while Putin reiterated Russia’s conditions for a lasting settlement.
Witkoff later said progress had been made toward scheduling another three-way meeting, while expressing optimism that diplomacy could produce an agreement.
Zelensky suggested on Tuesday that the next trilateral talks could be held in the UAE, Türkiye, Switzerland, or another country as early as September or October. Moscow and Washington have yet to comment on specific venues or time frames.
The trilateral format was last used in Geneva in February, following two earlier rounds in Abu Dhabi. However, the talks ended without any significant breakthroughs, although Washington said there had been “meaningful progress.”
The negotiations have since stalled as the US shifted its focus to its war against Iran while hostilities between Russia and Ukraine have continued.
Moscow has repeatedly said it remains open to diplomacy but insists any final agreement must address the root causes of the conflict and respect the new realities on the ground. Kiev, however, has resisted Russian demands on territorial and security issues.

Gaza's tents are withering away after three years of genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:25:11 UTC
20:25:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's tents are withering away after three years of heat, rain and endless displacement
Displaced Palestinian people in the war-torn coastal enclave of the Gaza Strip are find it exceedingly hard to afford new tents or maintain their old ones after nearly three years of an Israeli genocide.
Thousands of displaced families remain in tents and makeshift shelters, many of which were intended to provide temporary refuge but have become their only homes.
When Israel's genocidal war began in 2023, Hanaa al-Soltan, 44, left northern Gaza carrying clothes, documents and a few belongings for her children, believing the family would return home within days or weeks. Nearly three years later, she remains displaced in a tent in central Gaza.
"At first, we said it would only be a few days or weeks. Then the first winter came, followed by summer, then another winter, and we're still here," she told The New Arab.
The summer heat is particularly difficult for the family. Under direct sunlight, the tarpaulin heats rapidly, turning the tent into an oven, while limited ventilation offers little relief.
"At midday, the children can't stay inside. We go out looking for shade and return when the sun becomes weaker. Sometimes I feel like we're living in an oven," she said.
But when summer ends, the damage it leaves behind becomes a threat. Months of exposure to heat and wind weaken the tarpaulin, leaving holes and cracks through which rainwater and cold air enter.
"When it rains, we put pots and pans under the holes and lift the mattresses off the ground. We sleep watching the water instead of sleeping," she said.
Unable to afford a new shelter, Hanaa buys used plastic sheets and attaches them to the damaged sections.
"We're no longer looking for a house. We just want a tarpaulin that will last us," she added.
Little protection
Hanaa's experience is shared by thousands of displaced families who have spent years moving from one location to another in search of safety, only to find themselves trapped in increasingly fragile shelters.
Mahmoud al-Arja, 39, moved several times with his wife and six children before settling in a tent in the al-Mawasi area in Khan Younis City in southern Gaza. Since the beginning of the war, he has bought three tents and repaired each of them repeatedly.
"The tarpaulin traps the heat. We open the sides and lift the cover, but the sun comes in from everywhere. The children sweat all the time and can't sleep," he told TNA.
The prolonged exposure to sunlight has weakened the material.
"The sun eats away at the tent. You buy one thinking it will protect you, but after a while, you discover its edges are starting to tear," he said.
When winter arrives, those damaged sections become entry points for rain and wind. Al-Arja uses plastic sheets, blankets and old clothes to seal the gaps before storms arrive.
"In winter, we fear the rain and wind. When water gets into the tent, there's nowhere else to take the children," he said.
The cost of keeping the shelter standing has also become a burden. Families need poles, ropes, plastic sheets and other materials, many of which have become increasingly expensive.
"We're not buying a tent; we're buying extra time," al-Arja added. "Work has stopped, income has stopped, but the expenses for the tent haven't."
Three years of trying to stay dry
Rasha Salama, a 36-year-old mother of three from Gaza City, could not afford a new tent for her four children, so she bought one that had been used by another family.
"I wasn't looking for a nice or new tent. I just wanted anything to give us a roof over our heads," she said.
During the summer, her children sleep drenched in sweat. Opening the tent from both sides provides some ventilation but exposes the family to dust, insects and direct sunlight.
"Some nights, the children want to sleep outside because it's too hot inside," she said.
Winter, however, brings greater anxiety.
"When it rains, the sand under the tent turns to mud, and water seeps in from several places. We lift the mattresses and pile things on top of each other, then wait for the rain to stop," she said.
Rasha keeps scraps of plastic and old fabric inside the tent for emergencies.
"Every piece has a purpose. This one's for patching a hole, this one's for under the mattresses, and this one's for when it rains," she said.
"We've been living like this for three years. The summer suffocates us, the winter terrifies us, and in between, we just try to keep the tent standing," she added.
Market built around survival
The prolonged displacement has created persistent demand for tarpaulins, ropes, wood and other shelter materials. But as families' incomes have collapsed, many can afford only the cheapest or second-hand options.
Abu Salah, a Gaza-based shelter-supplies vendor, told TNA that the market has changed dramatically during the war.
"At first, people would buy complete tents. Now, many just want a tarpaulin because they can't afford a whole set," he said.
Used tarpaulins have become increasingly common, while poles, wood and ropes are salvaged from damaged or abandoned shelters.
"There are families who ask for the cheapest thing available. Even if the tent has a hole, they say they will repair it themselves," he added.
Political analyst Akram Atallah believes the continued reliance on tents nearly three years into the war cannot be separated from the broader political and reconstruction crisis.
"The transformation of the tent from a temporary solution into a dwelling for years reflects the absence of any real prospect for reconstruction and places residents before a new form of daily depletion," Atallah told TNA.
Restrictions on building materials and shelter supplies, he said, delay reconstruction while leaving hundreds of thousands of Palestinians vulnerable to weather, poverty and disease.
"The continuation of these conditions deepens the disintegration of life," he added.

Most Poles use social media but seniors show higher trust, poll finds
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:24:45 CEST
20:24:45 KST

Most Poles use social media but seniors show higher trust, poll finds
Nearly three-quarters of Poles (73 percent) use social media networks, driven by a 95 percent adoption rate among young adults, though older generations are far more likely to trust online information and share personal content, a new survey has shown.
The study by the Market and Social Research Institute (IBRiS), commissioned by PAP, found that Facebook remains Poland's most popular service (53 percent), followed by Instagram (31 percent), TikTok (25 percent), and X at 18 percent.
Despite younger generations dominating overall numbers, IBRiS report author Marcin Duma told PAP that older users are far more likely to share their daily lives online and believe the information they find there, whereas younger users exhibit a strong "digital detachment".
Social media adoption stands at 95 percent among adults aged 18–29 but drops to 39 percent for those over 70. Generation Z heavily distrusts online content, viewing it as commercial self-promotion. They form a "silent majority" that rarely posts and strongly guards privacy, Duma said. Older users willingly share personal everyday updates, making them more vulnerable to scams by mistaking commercial content for credible news.
Furthermore, digital confidence shapes threat perceptions. While 85 percent of all Poles have encountered online scams, only 65 percent of young adults view artificial intelligence (AI) fraud as "very dangerous", compared to around 89 percent of older users.
Social media usage also varies sharply by political electorate. Left-wing Razem voters (88 percent) and ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) supporters (85 percent) boast the highest presence. The high digital presence of Grzegorz Braun's party is surprising because his voters are mostly lower-income, less-educated, and live in rural areas - groups that usually use the internet less. However, Braun's exclusion from mainstream media forced highly effective, targeted online campaigns.
Supporters of the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) and centre-right Development Plus sit at the bottom with just 56 percent usage due to older voter profiles. Meanwhile, the ruling Civic Coalition (KO) maintains high usage despite an older demographic, driven by higher education and urban residency.
A sweeping 81 percent of all respondents demand stricter state cybersecurity regulations, viewing it as a priority or vital issue. Only 4 percent believe current laws are sufficient. This legislative push is highest among Development Plus (97 percent) and KO (94 percent) loyalists, while far-right Confederation voters remain the most sceptical of state intervention (62 percent).
The data is based on an IBRiS survey conducted between August 29 and 30, 2026, across a representative sample of over 1,000 adult Polish residents. (PAP)

Polish presidential couple join National Reading campaign
Poland's President Karol Nawrocki and First Lady Marta Nawrocka joined this year's National Reading, an initiative promoting Polish literature, held at the Adam Mickiewicz monument on Krakowskie Przedmiescie Street, in Warsaw, at noon on Saturday.
This year's chosen text is Forefathers' Eve (Dziady), a landmark work by Mickiewicz, considered Poland's national poet and a leading figure of European Romanticism whose work transformed Polish literary language.
Inaugurating the annual event, Nawrocki said that literature possesses the power to preserve and transmit Polish national identity across generations, to carry it despite the 19th-century partitions or the 20th-century occupations.
"Literature has the power to carry Polishness across the borders of all Europe and the entire world," Nawrocki stated.
Referring to the importance of this year's chosen text, Nawrocki said that there is no Polish literature without Adam Mickiewicz's legacy.
"He remains a fundamental, pivotal figure for understanding the Polish soul and Polish national identity," Nawrocki said.
He also announced that Joseph Conrad's novel Lord Jim had been selected as next year's National Reading featured text.
Forefathers' Eve is a four-part dramatic work composed between 1820 and 1832. The drama's title refers to an ancient Slavic and Lithuanian ritual commemorating the dead. This is a major work of Polish literature, and it is one that elevates Mickiewicz to a position among the "great Europeans" such as Dante and Goethe.
The National Reading campaign was launched in 2012 with a joint reading of Pan Tadeusz by Mickiewicz. Past editions featured pieces by other major Polish writers, including Nobel laureate Henryk Sienkiewicz, novelist Boleslaw Prus and playwright Stanislaw Wyspianski. (PAP)
