'Catastrophic event on historic scale': Israel plunges in PISA rankings with worst-ever test scores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:27:29 UTC
19:27:29 KST

Israeli students recorded their worst-ever results in all three subjects measured by the international Program for International Student Assessment (PISA), with Education Ministry officials describing the findings as a "catastrophic event on a historic scale," according to results published by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Tuesday.
No improvement was made in any of the three skills tested. Compared with the previous PISA tests in 2022, Israeli students fell eight places in science, seven in reading, and six in mathematics.
In science, Israeli students ranked 44th. While science performance was measured in no fewer than 90 countries, 20 countries ranked ahead of Israel while still scoring below the developed-country average, including the United Arab Emirates, Vietnam, Uruguay, and Chile.
Students from China, Singapore, Taiwan, Japan, Estonia, South Korea, the UK, Canada, New Zealand, and Australia led the science rankings, far ahead of Israel.
In reading and mathematics, students from the 44 OECD member countries were assessed, and with developing countries excluded from the comparison, Israeli students found themselves alarmingly close to the bottom of the table.
Israel ranked 37th in reading, with 12 countries below the developed-world average still ranking ahead of it. And that was the good news.
In a comparison of mathematics skills among students from the 44 developed countries, Israel "won" 43rd place, with only Albania ranking below it.
For comparison, East Asian countries led the mathematics rankings, while the UK, for example, placed 10th, well above the average. Even the US, which scored below the average, ranked 27th.
Israel hits lowest recorded PISA scores in 2025
Across all three subjects, Israel's 2025 PISA results were the lowest ever recorded for the country and were significantly lower than those recorded in 2018, 2015 and 2012.
Compared with 2015, the proportion of Israeli students classified as low performers, with scores below proficiency Level 2, rose by 14 percentage points in mathematics, 14 percentage points in reading and nine percentage points in science.
Social disparities in Israel do not explain the strikingly poor results, the report says. Between 2022 and 2025, the gap in Israel between the highest-scoring students, the top 10%, and the weakest students, the bottom 10%, did not change significantly in mathematics or science, while it narrowed in reading.
Every three years, the National Authority for Measurement and Evaluation in Education and the Education Ministry publish a detailed national analysis simultaneously with, or close to, the OECD's official publication.
But long after the organization had granted media representatives full access to the data, and despite the publication being known about and scheduled years in advance, representatives of Education Minister Yoav Kisch and officials from the measurement authority still had not managed to "complete the necessary coordination regarding the format of publication."
In other words, while Kisch could not prevent the publication of the embarrassing report, which casts his tenure in the stark colors of failure, he tried to delay it until the last moment and chose to hold a media "briefing" at the exact time the report was released.
This came after the publication of the nationwide Meitzav assessment results was postponed, by agreement between the sides, until the end of the month despite the bad blood between Kisch and the authority, in an effort to soften the blow that the PISA report was expected to deal the Education Ministry.
PISA tests skills and knowledge of 15-year-old students
PISA tests are conducted once every three years and measure the skills and knowledge of 15-year-old students in education systems around the world, not only in OECD member states. For Israel's education system, however, the main benchmark is the average performance among developed countries.
The assessment focuses on three main areas: reading, mathematics, and science. In practice, it measures how prepared teenagers are to cope with the challenges of modern society and integrate into the future labor market.
The tests examine students' ability to solve complex problems, think critically, and communicate effectively. Israel first participated in PISA in 2002.
"In Israel, all data met the quality standards established by PISA and were considered suitable for reporting," the OECD stressed.
The organization added that a smaller share of students in Israel than the OECD average were top performers, reaching Level 5 or 6, in at least one subject. At the same time, fewer Israeli students than the OECD average reached the minimum proficiency level, Level 2 or higher, in all three subjects.
Israeli students' average score in computational problem-solving was also below the OECD average.
Only about 5% of students in Israel were top performers in mathematics, meaning they reached Level 5 or 6 on the PISA mathematics assessment, compared with an OECD average of 8%.
At these levels, students can interpret complex situations mathematically and can select, compare and evaluate appropriate problem-solving strategies for dealing with them.
Only 54% of Israeli students reached at least Level 2 in mathematics, compared with 65% on average across the OECD.
At a minimum, students at this level can interpret and identify, without direct instructions, how a simple situation can be represented mathematically, such as comparing the total distance across two alternative routes or converting prices into another currency.
Only 4% of students tested in Israel were top performers in science, compared with an OECD average of 7%, meaning they demonstrated proficiency at Level 5 or 6.
Students at these levels can apply their scientific knowledge creatively and independently in a wide range of situations, including unfamiliar ones.
About 60% of students in Israel reached Level 2 or higher in science, compared with 74% on average across the OECD.
At a minimum, these students can identify the correct explanation for familiar scientific phenomena and can use that knowledge to determine, in simple cases, whether a conclusion is valid based on the data provided.
More than 85% of students in the highest-performing countries, China, Singapore, Estonia, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, reached this level or higher.
Five percent of students scored at Level 5 or above in reading, compared with an OECD average of 6%.
Students at this level can understand lengthy texts, deal with abstract or counterintuitive concepts and distinguish between fact and opinion based on implicit clues relating to the content or the source of the information.
About 59% of students in Israel reached Level 2 or higher in reading, compared with 69% on average across the OECD.
At a minimum, these students can identify the main idea in a moderate-length text, locate information based on explicit (though sometimes complex) criteria, and reflect on the purpose and form of texts when explicitly instructed to do so.

August in the financial markets: fed signals, a global rise in bond yields, and new records in the semiconductor market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:26:34 UTC
19:26:34 KST

By Kārlis Martiņš Gulbis, Investment Analyst at Signet Bank.
Six months into the Hormuz war, August added borrowing costs at multi decade highs and a Fed preparing to hike. The 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest since 2007 mid-month before the Treasury doubled buybacks of 10- to 30-year debt, steadying the long end of the curve but stoking debasement talk and carrying gold to a three-month high near USD 4,700/oz. Then came Jackson Hole. Kevin Warsh, in his first symposium as Chair, warned that better summer CPI and PCE prints “do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved” and that the Fed still has work to do, language that lifted September hike odds from 36% to roughly 60% in a session.
The S&P 500 gained roughly 2.6% and the Nasdaq Composite 3.9%, both snapping two month losing streaks, while the Dow’s 1.3% secured a fifth consecutive winning month. Seoul, the epicenter of July’s rout, delivered the mirror image – KOSPI rebounded some 22% in ten trading days off its 30 July low, helped by SK hynix’s KRW 40t buyback.
STOXX 600 added 0.3% for a fifth straight positive month, while Bitcoin rallied 25% to about BTC/USD 78k. Brent dipped below USD 80/bbl early in the month before closing near USD 90.50/bbl, up only ~3% after July’s surge, as Washington and Tehran exchanged fire on the final weekend of August for the first time in a month and Trump threatened Iran’s Kharg Island export hub.
Everyone’s a bond vigilante now
July’s long-end selloff was largely American, but in August it stopped being so. The August 18 session that carried the 30-year Treasury to 5.34% also lifted 10- and 30-year Bunds to their highest since 2011, Canada’s 30-year to a 2010 high and the UK’s 50-year gilt to a record 5.39%. Japan moved furthest, the 10-year JGB reaching 2.945%, its highest since 1996.
The response came from issuers rather than central banks as Washington doubled long-end buybacks, Japan’s Ministry of Finance cut super-long issuance to a 17-year low, and the UK Debt Management Office shifted its GBP 252b remit shorter. France remains the most exposed in the EU, the 10-year OAT above 4.1% for the first time since November 2008 and the Bund spread near 83bp against a deficit of 5.1% of GDP.
Two summits for two global orders
The last 48 hours of August produced two competing views of the global order. In Asheville, the G20 finance track, 85% of global GDP met under the US presidency against an IMF briefing showing five-year growth projections near their weakest since 2009. Bessent’s message was that “the world is awash in debt and only growth gets it out”, though the joint statement set no targets. The more consequential item was “Economic D-Day”: secondary sanctions on enablers of Iranian oil exports, with EU backing secured, and “all options on the table” on China’s Iranian crude purchases. The bloc on the receiving end marked its own 25-year anniversary in Bishkek.
The SCO’s ten members, part of a 27-country grouping with combined GDP near USD 30t, signed a declaration condemning unilateral sanctions and demanding more developing country weight in the IMF, alongside 27 documents, a 2026-2030 ports roadmap and progress on the USD 4.7b China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway. Putin cited USD 400b of trade and 98% local currency settlement with the rest of the SCO. Yet the proposed creation of a Development Bank agreed a year ago still has no charter, capital or timetable, and the chair passed to Pakistan with the financial architecture no further along.
Memory chips now cost more than gold
Nvidia’s 26 August result was the beat the market wanted: revenue of USD 96.2b against USD 92.1b expected, a next quarter guide of USD 108b against consensus near USD 104b, and an 8.7% move in the shares. Management put CapEx at the five largest hyperscalers at USD 1.3t next year, up from roughly USD 800b in 2026, and AWS committed to 2m GPUs. The more consequential number came from Korea.
DRAM export prices averaged USD 92,183/kg over the first twenty days of August, up 401% YoY, with export values up 505%. Since January 2023 memory has risen twelve and a half times against gold’s two and a half, and Germany’s DDR5 retail index reached 486% of its mid-2025 level. Analysts now expect higher memory costs to cut global PC and smartphone shipments this year on physical constraint, with fabs years away and the DRAM deficit projected to widen into 2027.
Nothing from the greenback, but plenty from commodities
The Dollar Index failed to hold above 100 mark and has moved back into its established range, while EUR/USD briefly traded above 1.1700 before the dollar found buyers late in the month. We see 1.1400-1.1800 as the key range and a decisive break either way could mark the start of a more durable trend. Our dollar outlook remains neutral to modestly negative.
With inflation expectations rebuilding, precious metals have recovered from their recent correction. We continue to favor silver and platinum over gold, while our newer idea, agricultural commodities, was one of the standout performers of the month.

Ukraine's vehicle fleet gained a total of 110,200 electric vehicles in 2025, twice as many as the previous year. New vehicles accounted for 20% of registrations, down from 24% in 2024.

Taipei ranked 3rd-safest major city in world

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei ranked third among the world’s safest major cities in Visual Capitalist’s latest city safety ranking.
In the latest rankings, Taipei scored 83.4, slightly lower than 83.8 last year. It ranked ahead of Hong Kong, Singapore, Tokyo, Shenzhen, and Seoul.
In July, the city government said Time Out named Taipei the world’s safest city for female digital nomads in 2025. It also cited Taipei’s Special Mention in the Lee Kuan Yew World City Prize 2026 and its reputation for public transportation, tourism, and safety.
Qatar’s capital Doha topped the list with a score of 84.6, followed by Dubai at 83.8. The ranking was based on Numbeo’s Safety Index, which uses user-reported data from the past five years.
Numbeo considers perceptions of crime and personal safety, including how safe people feel walking alone during the day or at night and concerns about robbery, theft, assault, harassment, and other crimes. It also factors in property crimes such as burglary and vandalism and violent crimes including assault, murder, and sexual offenses.
Asian and Middle Eastern cities dominated the top 10, with Hong Kong ranking fourth at 78.2, followed by Singapore at 77.7, Tokyo at 75.9, Shenzhen at 75.5, Riyadh at 75.4, Jeddah at 75.1, and Seoul at 74.6. No European city made the top 10, despite strong performance in global livability rankings.
The lowest-ranked cities were concentrated in Latin America and Africa, led by Caracas at 18.5, Johannesburg at 19.2, and Durban at 19.5. Other cities in the bottom 10 were Salvador, Fortaleza, Rio de Janeiro, Recife, Guayaquil, Cape Town, and Cali.
Brazil accounted for four cities in the bottom 10, while South Africa had three.

Experts say Taiwan must take urgent action to bolster defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:23:37 UTC
19:23:37 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan needs to prioritize national security and strengthen asymmetric warfare capabilities, Oriana Skylar Mastro, a fellow at Stanford University’s Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, and Alessio Patalano, professor of war and strategy in East Asia at King’s College in London, said Tuesday.
Mastro and Patalano made recommendations on how Taiwan can better strengthen its defense against a Chinese invasion during a Taiwan Foreign Correspondents' Club panel discussion Tuesday.
Mastro urged Taiwan to begin conscripting women into its military to improve whole-of-society defense. “You cannot be really serious about a whole-of-society defense if your conscription is only of men,” she said. “You have half of the population who are completely incapable of defending (themselves). Not great,” she added.
On Jan. 1, 2024, Taiwan began implementing one-year conscription for all males born in 2005 or later. Mastro suggested Taiwan learn from Israel’s approach and “actually train everyone to resist and to fight.”
Taiwan introduced a dual-track reservist training system in 2022. Reservists can either take the standard option of five to seven days of training, done four times over eight years, or choose 14 days of training, done twice within the same period.
Mastro also urged Taiwan to continue increasing defense spending and investing in asymmetric capabilities. She noted that the military has begun to do so but “there has to be a little bit more honesty about the quality of the capabilities that are developing.”
Taiwan has proposed a defense budget of NT$1.1225 trillion (US$35.3 billion) for 2027, which Mastro noted is approximately 29% of the central government’s approved NT$3.93 trillion budget.
Mastro said Taiwan must decide what its priorities are. “Everything has to be about the defense and resilience and security of Taiwan, and that means making some tough decisions and making some sacrifices,” she said, pointing out that the opposition KMT still maintains close interactions with the Chinese Communist Party.
Taiwan has not made those sacrifices yet, which sparks doubt among the international community, she said. People are going to wonder, “Is Taiwan really going to put up the resistance necessary (to counter China)?”
“If Beijing is wondering that, that's not good. And if the American people are wondering that, that's not good.”
She acknowledged that Taiwan has already made significant strides in decoupling from China economically. “No one thought that that was possible,” she said.
Patalano emphasized that Taiwan should “invest like there's no tomorrow in undersea domain capability.” “It's the one place where you can develop (an) absolute kill zone,” he said, which is an advantage for Taiwan.
The country is already developing an undersea unmanned vessel, dubbed the Huilong. It is a joint project between the National Chung Shan Institute of Technology and Lungteh Shipbuilding, per Radio Taiwan International. It underwent sea trials in 2024.
The Taiwan Navy is also conducting tests for its first domestically produced submarine, the Narwhal, which is expected to remain on track for delivery later this year. The Navy plans to acquire eight submarines to patrol the nation’s waters.
Last month, NCSIST signed an MOU with US defense startup VATN Systems to establish a technical partnership on unmanned underwater vehicles and promote innovation and system integration for autonomous underwater vehicles. The institute said the deal would accelerate related technological development, improve underwater reconnaissance capabilities, and bolster the nation’s asymmetric warfare capacity and maritime defense resilience.
Patalano also said Taiwan should bolster resilience by developing an integrated communication system. He warned that reliance on a foreign system meant that if a Taiwan Strait conflict broke out, “whatever contract you might have … the contract is no longer valued as it was.”
NCSIST has already developed an ICS, which “provides wired and wireless connections in a communication control center,” according to its website. “It is suitable to support those communication mission systems which require long-range and mobile capabilities,” the institute added.
Additionally, the Taiwan Space Agency plans to expand development of CubeSats, next-generation communications satellites, and secure satellite networks. It also seeks to launch eight Formosat-8 optical satellites and two Formosat-9 synthetic aperture radar satellites by 2030, TASA Director-General Wu Jong-shinn (吳宗信) said in July.
Patalano said developing a national security strategy is also a priority. Having one provides “clear guidance to everybody” on how to integrate different government agencies during wartime, he said, adding that this makes deterrence more manageable and preparation for war more realistic.
Taiwan first distributed the “National Public Safety Guide” to all citizens and residents in 2022, which contains detailed information on how to respond to crises, such as natural disasters. It also includes instructions for how to handle military aggression, warning the public that “in the event of a military invasion of Taiwan, any claim that the government has surrendered or that the nation has been defeated is false.”

Taiwan’s TSMC, ASML target 12-inch reticle pilot line by 2031
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:23:02 UTC
19:23:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TSMC is working with ASML to develop 12-inch reticles for High-NA EUV lithography, with the companies targeting a pilot production line by 2031 and full system readiness by 2033.
TSMC said Tuesday that the collaboration aims to help the semiconductor industry transition to larger EUV lithography reticles. A reticle, or photomask, is a template containing a chip’s circuit patterns that is used to transfer those patterns onto a silicon wafer during the lithography process.
The move would eliminate the need to stitch together images from two 6-inch reticles during High-NA EUV exposure, improving fab productivity and lowering chip manufacturing costs, per CNA.
TSMC Chair and CEO C.C. Wei (魏哲家) said the industry can unlock new possibilities only by working together to solve complex problems. “By bringing together expertise from across the industry’s value chain, we hope to keep providing the benefits of cutting-edge technology through continuous innovation that lowers barriers and puts advanced solutions accessible at scale,” he said.
TSMC plans to begin introducing ASML’s High-NA technology into advanced process production in 2030, per UDN. As process technology advances, particularly as AI drives increasingly complex transistor architectures, TSMC expects the number of mask layers requiring High-NA EUV exposure to increase.
ASML President and CEO Christophe Fouquet said High-NA EUV adoption is expected to grow as the industry advances its device-scaling roadmap. “We are pleased by the strong initial support of semiconductor manufacturers, mask suppliers and partners for this initiative,” he added.

Lithuanian 15-year-olds performed above the average of OECD countries in mathematics, reading, science and information problem-solving in the latest PISA assessment, ranking ahead of more than two-thirds of participating countries, officials said Tuesday.
The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment, or PISA, covered about 700,000 students in 91 countries, including 38 OECD countries or parts of countries and 53 partner countries. Science literacy was the main focus of the assessment.
Lithuanian students ranked above 64 countries in mathematics, 63 in reading, 62 in science and 63 in information problem-solving.
“Average Lithuanian scores in all four assessment areas are higher than the OECD average,” said Rita Dukynaitė, a member of the OECD PISA governing board. She added that Lithuania’s results were stable or had declined less than the OECD average, which she described as encouraging.
Lithuania’s science results were statistically similar to those of the Czech Republic, Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Slovenia, France, Italy and Portugal. Lithuanian students also performed similarly to their peers in Denmark, Slovakia, Finland, Italy, Germany and the United States in mathematics.
Estonian and Polish students outperformed Lithuanians in mathematics, while Latvian students scored lower.
In reading, Lithuania ranked above 63 countries and below 18. Its results were statistically similar to those of Switzerland, the Czech Republic, Austria, Sweden, Belgium, Germany, Portugal and Denmark.
Information problem-solving was another strong area for Lithuania, with students outperforming those in 63 countries and scoring below 13. Their results were statistically similar to those of the Czech Republic, the United States, Ireland, Austria, Belgium, Poland, Finland and the Netherlands.
Students from four Chinese regions recorded the highest results in mathematics, reading and science, while students in Macao, China, performed best in information problem-solving. Rwanda recorded the lowest science, mathematics and reading results, while Kenya ranked last in information problem-solving.
Within Lithuania, students in the capital and other major cities achieved the highest average results across all four areas. Students in small towns and rural areas recorded the lowest scores.
Students attending schools where Lithuanian is the language of instruction performed best, followed by those in Russian-language schools, while students in Polish-language schools had the lowest results.
Girls performed better in science and reading, while boys had higher mathematics scores.
The assessment also found a link between school attendance and achievement. Students who skipped classes without a valid reason tended to have lower results. Attendance in Lithuania has improved since 2018, although the rate of students arriving late to school has remained unchanged.
More than 90% of Lithuanian students said they felt safe at school, although corridors, cafeterias and restrooms were identified as places where students felt least safe.
Education, Science and Sports Vice Minister Jonas Petkevičius said improving reading skills would be a priority following the results.
“We need to improve students' reading skills,” he said, adding that the ministry was considering new programs and school initiatives to encourage reading.
The ministry also plans to expand support for high-achieving students, including through information technology and artificial intelligence-based programs, while continuing efforts to help students who fall below required achievement levels.
Lithuania has participated in PISA since 2006. About 7,700 Lithuanian students from 295 schools took part in the 2025 assessment. Starting in 2025, the PISA study is conducted every four years.

Belgium’s largest airport is back on Europe’s high-speed rail map after more than a decade, with a new Deutsche Bahn service connecting Brussels Airport with Cologne and Antwerp.
After more than 10 years, international high-speed rail has returned to Belgium’s largest airport.
At around 8:30 am on 7 September, a Deutsche Bahn high-speed train arrived at Brussels Airport for the first time. The service began at Cologne station in Germany, with stops including Aachen, Liège, Leuven and Antwerpen-Centraal being the final destination.
This new service follows after a deal was inked between Brussels Airlines and Deutsche Bahn in February, opening the airport’s network of more than 180 destinations worldwide to travellers from western Germany. At the same time, travellers arriving at the airport can now connect directly with destinations in Germany via rail.
As part of the agreement, Brussels Airlines travellers departing from and arriving in western Germany can book their rail and flight journeys on a single ticket.
“The arrival of this high-speed rail service marks an important step in the further development of Brussels Airport as an intermodal hub,” Arnaud Feist, Chief Executive Officer at Brussels Airport, said.
“We want to offer travellers a range of sustainable options to travel efficiently to and from the airport, across national borders.”
Feist also hopes that this move will be the catalyst for even more high-speed train connections in the future.
Two return services will operate daily between Cologne and Antwerp, with Brussels Airport’s train station being directly located below its terminal.
According to the airline, more than 1,000 tickets have already been sold since the partnership was announced in February. For the single-ticket rail and flight journeys, New York, Accra and Alicante have proved to be the top destinations so far among travellers for this intermodal offering.
Brussels Airlines added that travellers will also benefit from a guaranteed connection should there ever be a delay, and they can also earn miles through Lufthansa’s Miles & More programme.
“Direct to Antwerp, direct to Brussels Airport, and all on our state-of-the-art trains: this is how we’re making international rail travel even easier and more appealing for passengers,” Dr. Michael Peterson, DB board member for long distance passenger transport at Deutsche Bahn, said.
“We’re connecting two key transport hubs via the ICE service: Cologne, as a hub for cross-border long-distance travel, and Brussels Airport, as an international hub for onward journeys by air.”

Huawei heads to trial in US over its business dealings in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:21:26 UTC
19:21:26 KST

Breadcrumb
Huawei heads to trial in US over its business dealings in Iran
Eight years after US prosecutors secretly charged China's Huawei Technologies with defrauding HSBC and other banks over its business with Iran, the case is finally heading for trial.
Huawei also faces charges for conspiring to steal trade secrets from five US technology companies, and is accused of lying about its dealings in North Korea and supplying surveillance equipment to Iran to track protesters during 2009 anti-government demonstrations in Tehran. Jury selection is expected to begin on Tuesday in federal court in Brooklyn, New York.
The trial will bring to a close one of the US government's earliest and most closely watched battles against a Chinese company, and will play out as tech competition heats up between the two countries and Washington seeks to prevent American technology from aiding Beijing's military. The US-China tech war has now spread across multiple technology sectors, including artificial intelligence.
The saga began in 2018 with the arrest of Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou in Vancouver, which sparked a diplomatic crisis involving the United States, China and Canada.
Convictions on the Iran-related charges would bolster Washington's case for having placed Huawei, one of China's leading technology companies, on a US trade blacklist in 2019, citing alleged criminal conduct that threatened national security.
The trial before US District Judge Ann Donnelly is expected to last about three months and overlap with Chinese President Xi Jinping's September 24 meeting with President Donald Trump in Washington. Potential jurors have filled out 27-page questionnaires, including about their views on China's and Iran's governments.
Other charges include violating US sanctions against Iran, money laundering, racketeering, wire fraud and obstruction. Huawei has pleaded not guilty on all charges and denied any wrongdoing.
The criminal case is based in part on reporting by Reuters in 2012 and 2013 about close ties between Huawei and Skycom, a firm that operated in Iran.
Reuters reported that Skycom had offered to sell at least €1.3 million ($1.5 million) worth of embargoed Hewlett-Packard computer equipment to Iran's largest mobile-phone operator in 2010. Reuters also reported that Meng had served on Skycom's board of directors between February 2008 and April 2009. The coverage can be read here and here.
Beijing has long criticized the case, saying it was part of a bigger campaign against China's technological rise. A Huawei spokesperson said in a statement on Saturday, "The government's overarching narrative is demonstrably false."
Today Huawei is a centerpiece of China's AI chip ambitions, and has diversified beyond network gear and smartphones. It has described the criminal case as an effort to undermine its competitiveness and the theft accusations as a repackaging of long-resolved commercial disputes.
If Huawei is convicted, prosecutors will seek the forfeiture of property or proceeds obtained from its illegal activity.
The case against the company was brought during the first Trump administration, which also took actions to curb the use of Huawei equipment in the US and pressed other countries to drop Huawei from their telecommunications networks, saying China could use its equipment for espionage.
The indictment covers alleged wrongdoing between about 1999 and 2020.
It accuses Huawei of using Skycom to obtain embargoed US goods, technology and services for Huawei's Iran-based business, and to move money out of that country through the international banking system.
The US said one bank, which was not named in the indictment but which sources and documents reviewed by Reuters identified as HSBC, cleared more than $100 million worth of US-dollar transactions related to Skycom.
Prosecutors accused Meng of misrepresenting Huawei's ownership and control of Skycom in a presentation to an HSBC executive. She later admitted the statements were false, as part of an agreement with prosecutors to drop the charges against her.

Last year, the trust signed an MOU with Cambodia’s Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport to bring the programme to the country’s primary schools. It was officially rolled out earlier this year.

Investors pour record US$1.3 trillion into Hong Kong investment products

Record US$1.3 trillion pours into Hong Kong investment products
Record investor numbers drive 63 per cent surge in sales of non-traded products, led by collective investment schemes, FICC offerings
Sales of non-exchange-traded investment products in Hong Kong surged to a record HK$9.9 trillion (US$1.3 trillion) in 2025, marking a 63 per cent year-on-year increase, according to the latest joint survey by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).
A significant expansion in market participation drove the record-breaking performance. The number of investors completing at least one transaction rose 33 per cent to a record at more than 1.6 million, while the number of licensed corporations and registered institutions engaged in product sales grew 9 per cent to 452. Reflecting this broader industry scale, the number of large firms – categorised as those recording significant transaction volumes – increased 27 per cent to 128.
“The strong growth captured in this year’s survey is a clear testament to investor confidence in Hong Kong’s asset and wealth management industry,” said Kenneth Hui, the HKMA’s executive director for banking conduct.
Collective investment schemes emerged as the top-selling product category, with sales surging 85 per cent to overtake structured products for the first time since 2020. Within this segment, money market funds accounted for 88 per cent of the top five sales reported by large firms, up 80 per cent in 2024, according to the survey results released on Tuesday.
Fixed-income, currency and commodity (FICC)-related offerings remained central to investor asset allocations, as market participants prioritised liquidity and income-generating assets.
Notably, currency-linked product sales increased by 50 per cent year on year to HK$698 billion. Debt securities continued on a solid growth trajectory, driven by a 138 per cent jump in sovereign bonds and strong interest in corporate bonds from mainland Chinese issuers, illustrating Hong Kong’s vital role as an offshore fundraising hub.

The families still searching after Nepal's deadly flood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:17:12 UTC
19:17:12 KST

Breadcrumb
In Kathmandu's wards, survivors of Nepal's deadly flood wait for news of the missing
Half-mast flags hung over Singha Durbar, the seat of Nepal's government, on Monday as the country observed the 13th day since the glacier collapse that sent floodwaters tearing down the Bhotekoshi River on August 26, killing more than 1,300 people.
For many Nepalese families, the 13th day carries particular significance in Hindu mourning practices, when rites are traditionally performed for the dead.
But with about 5,000 people still unaccounted for, including roughly 900 hydropower workers, 500 of whom are still believed to be trapped in tunnels, thousands of families are still waiting to learn of their loved ones' fates.
Kishan Adhikari, a civil engineer on the Upper Trishuli 3B project in Nuwakot, was conducting a routine inspection on the morning the flood hit. Then someone told him a flood was moving downstream.
Kishan called a senior officer at the project and asked him to check. The call lasted only moments. Between 9:22 and 9:24 that morning, the flood wave reached the site – just two minutes after he made the call and roughly seven minutes after an alert had been issued for his district.
"Until then, we had absolutely no information about the flood," Kishan tells The New Arab. "I don't know what my mind thought or what decision I made, but I turned right. Maybe I survived because I turned right, but I couldn't save my other colleagues. I took off my boots and climbed straight up through the bushes."
From higher ground, he could see mudslides moving toward the project site and a handful of people who had escaped. The powerhouse, offices, staff quarters, and workers’ camp had disappeared beneath the floods.
"My daughter and mother were at the project quarters. I had brought them only a month earlier," he continues, breaking into tears. "I never thought something like this would happen."
To this day, neither his mother nor his daughter has been found, and Kishan has not left Kathmandu since.
He is still at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, where relatives of people who disappeared in Rasuwa and Nuwakot move between wards, lists, posters, and officials, looking for information.
Names on a list
The Ministry of Health said on September 1 that only about 4 percent of the roughly 900 bodies recovered by then had been named.
One of the people still looking is Rakesh Prasad. He has spent several days at the hospital looking for his younger brother, Umesh Prasad, who was working as a builder at Sherpa Hydropower in Rasuwa. The brothers are from Motihari, across the border in India.
Umesh last spoke to his wife at about 7:30 on the morning of the flood. He has four children: girls aged 12 and 10, and boys aged 7 and 5.
"I only have a list forwarded to me by a relative with my brother's name on it," Rakesh tells The New Arab. "I have no idea who prepared the list, what it represents or whether being on it means my brother is missing or dead."
Hospital officials say there are no details of Umesh in their records.
Sapana Sherpa, another concerned family member at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, travelled 260 kilometres from Khotang to Kathmandu in search of her uncle and his wife, who had lived in Rasuwa, where they ran a small hotel.
Her uncle, Dorchi Sherpa, had lived in Rasuwa for decades. Sapana had never met his wife, Sobita Tamang, and the family knew little about her. When she reached Rasuwa, villagers told her that her uncle and his children had been swept away. But there was still a possibility that Sobita had survived.
"We had never met her, so we contacted people in Rasuwa and asked them to send us photographs so we could identify her," she says.
"They said her name was also on a list, but nobody could tell us what kind of list it was."
At the hospital, however, her uncle’s wife's name did not appear on any of the official lists. With no other way to search for her, Sherpa pasted photographs of her uncle and aunt on the hospital walls.
"Thousands of photographs are pasted here by families looking for their loved ones," she adds. "I could only put up their photographs and hope that someone might recognise them or tell us what happened."
The trauma that follows
Four days after the flood, Aalok Mishra, a medical officer, travelled from Methinkot Hospital in Kavre to a temporary holding centre at Devighat in Nuwakot, one of several set up in the area.
The centre, operating from the Ayurvedic and Alternative Hospital, was treating 200 to 300 patients a day. Most had cuts, bruises and what appeared to be simple fractures. Others had suffered severe limb injuries or amputations. Those patients were stabilised at the centre before being taken by ambulance to Kathmandu, says Aalok.
"Wherever roads remained accessible to vehicles, the facilities were adequate," Aalok tells The New Arab. "From food and drinking water to medicines, the necessary supplies were available."
But across the Trishuli River from the centre, there were no roads. Supplies and patients on that side had to be moved by drone or helicopter, in operations jointly run by the Armed Police Force, the army and Nepal Police.
Patients were brought to Devighat for treatment and referred to Kathmandu if they needed care beyond what the centre could provide.
Medical teams rotated every three or four days. Aalok's team of four stayed for three days before another team took over, while an Armed Police Force medical team had been there since day one.
For Aalok, however, the flood's most difficult injuries were not always physical.
"Facing something we already know is one thing, but facing something sudden and shocking, which takes away a lifetime's earnings, the house and the entire family in a single moment, carried away by that flood," he shares.
He saw patients slip into depressive states, lose their appetites and withdraw from others, spending much of the day in profound sadness. His team and the Armed Police Force medical team provided counselling, while separate psychiatry teams rotated between the holding centres.
No early-warning systems
There was no early warning system when the glacier fell, according to glaciologist Rijan Bhakta Kayastha of Kathmandu University's Himalayan Cryosphere, Climate and Disaster Research Centre.
The terrain is extremely steep and uninhabited on both the Nepali and Chinese sides, with no trekking routes or trails, which is why the government did not install any systems there, Rijan tells The New Arab.
He estimated that the danger of further flooding has not completely subsided, as temporary ponds and lakes have formed in the affected area, raising the risk of sudden releases, debris flows, and secondary flooding. One of the ponds that has since formed at the collapse site. It has already burst twice.
"Nepal needs stronger monitoring and early-warning systems across its glaciated river basins, including round-the-clock monitoring during the monsoon," he explains.
The expert says the safest option would be to monitor Nepal's glaciated river basins from east to west, with personnel deployed around the clock during the monsoon months from June to September.
"The government has begun doing this, and the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology now has a camera-equipped system in place at the site," he adds.
But downstream, Nepal's existing flood-warning system did work. According to an NDRRMA report, the ice-rock avalanche struck at around 8:40 a.m., and the Bhotekoshi-Syafrubesi monitoring station stopped transmitting shortly afterwards.
By about 9:15 a.m., the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology had confirmed a major flood wave and issued warnings downstream.
NDRRMA said about 679,295 SMS alerts were sent. In Bidur, Nuwakot, the warning arrived early enough to help about 900 students escape uphill. But for some, the window was far narrower.
Kush Kumar Shrestha thought it was an ordinary flood. He walked toward the river to see what was happening, as his mother and others called after him: "The flood is coming. Don’t go over there!"
He heard a roar and then saw a section of the jungle-covered hillside give way, sweeping away the people standing on it.
"A sister was crying out, pull me, pull me, but I couldn't pull her, and when I looked back, she was gone," Kush tells The New Arab.
His uncle, just a step behind him, was swept away; his mother and sisters too. He is at the hospital now, looking for any news on any of his family members.
"I can't sleep, I can't eat, and whenever I close my eyes, that massive flood flashes right back," he shares.
He is at the hospital, still searching for any information about his family members.
Like other families, he has added their photographs to the walls, hoping that someone will recognise them or provide news of what happened.
The search has become increasingly difficult as the recovery of bodies has far outpaced their identification.
Meanwhile, the search for those still missing continues at 12 hydropower sites along the corridor, where the army and other rescue teams are digging through mud and debris in tunnels and damaged facilities.
Pratik Ghimire is a journalist based in Kathmandu, Nepal

Hungary has expelled 10 Russian diplomats over activities deemed incompatible with their diplomatic status, Foreign Minister Anita Orban has announced.

China

19:15:13 KST

HANOI, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Nguyen Mau Xuan Kieu, a Vietnamese student studying in China, and her elder sister in Vietnam were both surprised and excited when they learned that China's new visa-free transit policy could make their year-end reunion and overseas travel plan much easier to arrange.
Under the new arrangement, Kieu's sister can travel from Vietnam to China to visit her, spend time together in Shanghai's Xintiandi entertainment area and the iconic Bund, and then continue with Kieu to a third country, turning a transit stop into part of their holiday.
Effective from Aug. 20, Vietnamese citizens holding ordinary passports and interline passenger tickets with confirmed dates and itineraries bound for a third country or region may enter China through any of the 65 ports across the country and stay up to 240 hours, or 10 days, without a visa.
Vietnamese ordinary passport holders are also eligible for the 30-day visa-free entry policy for Hainan Province in south China starting the same day.
Kieu said the policy could save her sister both time and money, as she would no longer need to apply for an additional transit visa, which she estimated would otherwise cost around 3 million Vietnamese dong (about 117 U.S. dollars).
"Airfares are also quite reasonable, with tickets from Ho Chi Minh City to Shanghai and from Shanghai to Seoul allowing us to save another 1 million to 2 million Vietnamese dong (about 39 to 78 dollars)," she said.
For Vietnam's tourism industry, the expanded policies are expected to open up more room for travel products combining China with onward destinations.
Huynh My Yen, general director of a travel company in Vietnam, said transit tours through China currently account for around 10 percent of the company's total outbound international business.
"The 240-hour visa-free transit program allows Vietnamese tourists to simplify paperwork, cut transit visa fees and processing time, and seamlessly enjoy a 'one journey, two countries' travel experience," Yen told Xinhua.
The company is also stepping up promotion and consultation, expanding routes and offering China's capital Beijing stopover tours for passengers on long-haul flights to destinations such as Russia, Yen told Xinhua.
"We expect 30 to 40 percent of customers booking transit and multi-destination tours in the second half of 2026," she said.
The company's push comes as visa-free travel accounts for a growing share of foreign arrivals in China.
In the first half of 2026, China recorded 17.82 million visa-free entries by foreign nationals, up 30.6 percent year on year and accounting for 77.7 percent of all foreign entries, according to the National Immigration Administration (NIA).
Vietnam ranked as China's fourth-largest source of inbound foreign travelers during the period, after South Korea, Russia and Malaysia, the NIA said.
Vietnam welcomes China's decision to include Vietnamese citizens in the 240-hour visa-free transit program and the 30-day visa-free entry policy for Hainan Province, Pham Thu Hang, spokesperson for the Vietnamese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, has said. ■

====================================================================================================

Column: Arrogance in excess -- The West's double standards on China's "overcapacity"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:14:49 CST
19:14:49 KST

by Ma Kangduo
A recent article in The Economist bluntly declared "China won't apologize for overcapacity." The subtitle is even more direct: "Its industrial policy rests on a simple principle: might makes right."
The real problem with this narrative is not about capacity pressures; it is about turning economic competition into a moral judgment. When a country expands its manufacturing, lowers costs, and achieves efficiency across its supply chains, it is nevertheless asked to "apologize" -- as if success itself were a sin.
MORE PRODUCTION THAN DEMAND IS NOT OVERCAPACITY
To be sure, China has substantial production capacity and strong exports in electric vehicles, photovoltaic products, batteries, and steel. But that does not automatically amount to "overcapacity." Defining production capacity that exceeds domestic demand as overcapacity is an overly simplistic way of understanding the concept.
By that logic, most of the aircraft manufactured by the United States, such as Boeing airplanes, are exported because the domestic market cannot absorb the entire output. German automobiles, Japanese machine tools, South Korean chips, French luxury goods and Swiss watches -- almost all highly specialized industries with comparative advantages -- produce far more than their domestic markets consume. If all of these were deemed "overcapacity," then international trade and the international division of labor themselves would become a problem, and the theory of comparative advantage would be turned on its head.
A country specializing in the products it can produce most efficiently and then trading them for other goods is precisely the foundation of modern economic efficiency. To single out China's advantages in certain sectors and simply label them "overcapacity" is, in essence, a selective double standard.
DOUBLE STANDARD IN INDUSTRIAL POLICY
China's industrial policy is portrayed as a "whole industry chain model" and cited as evidence of "market distortion" and "overcapacity generation." In contrast, the massive, targeted, and exclusionary industrial subsidies of the United States and Europe are largely ignored, or treated as if they were not even worth mentioning.
The U.S. Inflation Reduction Act provides an estimated 369 billion dollars in clean-energy and climate-related incentives, including tax credits for clean energy and electric vehicles, while incorporating domestic-content and North American sourcing requirements. The CHIPS and Science Act likewise provides substantial incentives to support semiconductor manufacturing in the United States. The EU's Clean Industrial Deal goes even further, planning to mobilize more than 100 billion euros (116 billion dollars) to support EU-made clean manufacturing.
The underlying logic of these policies is remarkably similar to that of the Chinese industrial policies they criticize: using fiscal subsidies, tax incentives, and domestic content requirements to actively shape the industrial landscape. The only difference lies in the labeling. When China does it, it is called "market distortion," "overcapacity," and "might makes right." When the United States and Europe do it, it is called "strategic autonomy," "industrial security," and "responding to the climate crisis."
"I CAN HIT YOU, BUT IF YOU HIT ME BACK, THAT'S AGGRESSION"
This double standard becomes even more apparent in the narrative surrounding "actions" and "counteractions."
When the United States raises tariffs and promotes manufacturing reshoring, or when Europe advances "Made in Europe," the Clean Industrial Deal, or the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, these measures are framed as "defending the remaining industrial base," "safeguarding strategic autonomy," or "responding to unfair competition." The language is defensive, legitimate, and even tinged with a sense of victimhood.
Yet when China takes reciprocal countermeasures -- whether tariffs, export controls, or equivalent restrictions -- they are immediately labelled "geopolitical weapons," "economic coercion," or "weaponizing interdependence." At its core, this is the logic of "I am defending myself when I hit you, but you are committing aggression when you hit me back."
The West is presumed to have a unilateral monopoly on defining what constitutes "legitimate industrial policy" and "illegal countermeasures." They can use subsidies, domestic-content rules, and tariff barriers to restructure supply chains, while China is expected simply to accept the outcome and refrain from responding in kind. Once China does respond, economic competition is immediately escalated into a "threat to the international order."
THE REAL EXCESS
A developing country is asked to apologize for "being too successful," while the West remains silent about its own massive subsidies and subjects equivalent responses by others to moral judgment. This is a real double standard. It reveals not economic rigor, but anxiety and arrogance in the face of the erosion of its own comparative advantages.
A genuinely fair debate should acknowledge that virtually all major economies use industrial policy. The real question is not whether industrial policy exists, but whether it is transparent, whether it complies with the rules, and whether it creates unsustainable distortions. Singling out China for moral condemnation while remaining silent about one's own massive subsidies and protectionist measures will only strip the concept of "overcapacity" of its credibility and reduce it to nothing more than a rhetorical weapon.
What the West's "overcapacity of China" narrative really reveals is not economic reality, but arrogance and a glaring double standard.
What the West has in excess is arrogance and double standards -- spinning competitiveness into a sin, efficiency into a threat, achievement into a blunder to be repented, and reciprocal responses into aggression -- it is this narrative itself that needs to be scrutinized the most.
Editor's note: The author is a researcher and commentator specializing in international affairs.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

Turkey's Kılıçdaroğlu opens door to İmamoğlu presidential bid in Euronews interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:13:22 UTC
19:13:22 KST

In an exclusive interview with Euronews, Kılıçdaroğlu defended his court-ordered return to the CHP leadership, said İmamoğlu is not a political prisoner but should not have been detained, and left the door open to backing İmamoğlu in a presidential bid.
Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu returned as interim leader of Turkey's main opposition Republican People's Party (CHP) earlier this year after a court annulled the 2023 leadership election that had removed him — and he says jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu is not a political prisoner, while leaving the door open to supporting an İmamoğlu presidential bid.
In an exclusive interview with Euronews at CHP headquarters in Ankara, Kılıçdaroğlu defended his court-ordered return, acknowledged the party split would cost the CHP votes and called for Turkey to lead a new regional peace organisation.
İmamoğlu was arrested in March 2025 on corruption charges, triggering Turkey's largest street protests in more than a decade.
His supporters say the charges are politically motivated, noting his status as Erdoğan's most credible electoral rival.
His 2019 victory ended 25 years of AKP and other rule in Istanbul and his re-election in 2024 reinforced that standing. The government has rejected accusations of political interference.
Kılıçdaroğlu said İmamoğlu's potential candidacy for the presidency did not make the corruption case political.
"Being a presidential candidate is one thing. These cases are another," he said, noting that he had voted for İmamoğlu in the CHP's own presidential primary.
But Kılıçdaroğlu said İmamoğlu should not have been detained while awaiting trial. "He can stand trial, but I did not think it was right to detain him. I still hold that view today."
A separate legal complication arose when Istanbul University annulled İmamoğlu's degree in March 2025, raising questions about his presidential eligibility — Turkey's constitution requires candidates to have completed higher education.
İmamoğlu has since joined Yeni Parti, the breakaway political group led by his ally Özgür Özel.
Asked whether he would back an İmamoğlu presidential bid if those legal obstacles were resolved, Kılıçdaroğlu did not give an unconditional endorsement but said talks would be needed and stressed that opposition unity was a mathematical necessity.
"How will you get 51%? By working together. How can you get it without working together?" he said. "There is no place for grudges, anger or hostility in politics."
The CHP was founded by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1923 as the party of the Turkish republic and its founding secular ideology, known as Kemalism.
It governed Turkey without interruption until 1950 and remains the main vehicle for secular, centre-left politics. It draws its core support from western Turkey's urban and coastal populations, civil servants, professionals and voters who prioritise secularism and EU integration.
A court-ordered return
Kılıçdaroğlu, who led the CHP for 13 years, came closer to defeating Erdoğan than any opposition candidate in two decades when he ran against him in the May 2023 presidential election.
The race went to a second round — the first runoff in Turkish history — where Erdoğan won 52.2% to Kılıçdaroğlu's 47.8%.
The result ended the most serious electoral challenge to Erdoğan's rule and directly triggered the CHP leadership contest that replaced Kılıçdaroğlu with Özel. İmamoğlu backed Özel in the party contest.
A court ruling on 21 May annulled that congress and restored the previous leadership on an interim basis. Özel's leadership team denied the vote-buying allegations and accused the government of using the judiciary against the party.
Özel has appealed the ruling, leaving Kılıçdaroğlu's interim leadership subject to further judicial review.
Kılıçdaroğlu denied any involvement in the case. "I am not a party to this case. I did not file it. I did not testify. I have no involvement in this case," he said.
Asked whether returning through a court ruling rather than a delegate vote bothered him, he said the ruling had restored the full previous leadership, not just him personally.
Asked whether accepting the ruling implied trust in the judiciary, he replied: "Who said I trust the judiciary?"
The cost of CHP's split
The CHP came first in Turkey's 2024 local elections under Özel, retaining Istanbul and Ankara and dealing a major setback to Erdoğan's ruling AKP.
Turkey's parliament has 600 seats. With 91 MPs, Yeni Parti is now the second-largest parliamentary group after the ruling AKP and the largest opposition bloc, while the CHP has 44 MPs.
Kılıçdaroğlu insisted that his party's core voters remained loyal, but acknowledged that the division would come at a cost.
"Will it lose strength? Of course it will. But we will recover over time. No one should be concerned," he said.
Citing his own unsuccessful presidential bid in 2023, he argued that political success could no longer be measured solely by parliamentary seat totals.
"A party's success now depends on its presidential candidate winning," he said.
He also said he had instructed provincial party leaders not to criticise or quarrel with Yeni Parti, and remained willing to meet Özel.
"It is the government we should be criticising," he said.
Erdoğan's current presidential term runs until 2028. Whether he is constitutionally eligible to stand again is disputed: Turkey's constitution limits presidents to two terms, but the AKP argues the clock reset when the new presidential system took effect in 2018, making 2028 effectively his first term under the new rules.
The Constitutional Court has not definitively ruled on the question. If he does stand, he would face an opposition that is currently divided.
Turkey 'a leading force for peace'
Asked about Turkey's role in the conflict between Israel and Iran, Kılıçdaroğlu called for closer cooperation among regional countries.
"Turkey should not want war in its region. It should be a leading force for peace," he said.
He pointed to the CHP's proposal for a Middle East Peace and Cooperation Organisation, initially led by Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Syria, which he said could later expand.
Regional countries should work together to secure peace, economic integration and stability, he argued.
Relations between Turkey and Israel deteriorated over the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, with Ankara suspending bilateral trade in May 2024. Their rivalry also extended into Syria after Bashar al-Assad's fall.
Kılıçdaroğlu also condemned what he described as Israel's threatening stance towards Turkey.
"It is absolutely unacceptable for Israel to threaten Turkey," he said. "Israel does not even have the right to criticise Turkey."

AfD victory clouds Merz's reform agenda as ally seeks changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

AfD victory clouds Merz's reform agenda as ally seeks changes
BERLIN, Sept 8 - The far-right's historic election victory in a German state election has reopened divisions in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government, with calls by his Social Democrat coalition partners for planned economic and social reforms to be softened.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) surged into first place in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, reflecting frustration with the federal government over bureaucracy, the rising cost of living, uncertainty over pensions and economic insecurity.
Merz – whose personal approval ratings are at a historic low – insisted that a package of planned reforms including a raising of the pension age and a clampdown on sick pay must go ahead, while admitting he needed to better explain them to voters.
But his centre-left SPD partners insist he must go further, demanding talks on possible changes to the proposals on pension and care reform, plus a new discussion of the 2027 budget and a reopening of debate over inheritance and wealth tax.
"The SPD ... must make it clear where we are heading,” SPD Secretary-General Tim Kluessendorf said on Monday in a TV interview with Phoenix.
COALITION TENSIONS
The rise of the AfD – which came second in the 2025 federal election - has forced Germany's mainstream parties of the centre-left and centre-right to work together in coalition to exclude the far-right from power.
But analysts said the calls from the SPD could, at the very least, delay the reforms, and might derail them altogether if coalition tensions rose.
"The main question will be whether both coalition partners will move closer together to push through with reforms or whether a survival instinct leads to the coalition’s self-destruction," said Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING.
Commerzbank senior economist Ralph Solveen agreed that the election would likely trigger calls by politicians for change that would inevitably raise tensions within the government.
"As is often the case after defeats, calls for the individual parties to take a stronger stance will surely be heard soon," Solveen said.
SPD sources said the current reform agenda should not be abandoned altogether, but that further measures should be considered, particularly to strengthen its social dimension.
"The government must convey the message that the reforms will improve people's lives," said party co-leader Baerbel Bas. "That message just isn’t getting through right now."
ECONOMIC PACKAGE FAILS TO WIN OVER VOTERS
Merz came to power in 2025 pledging tough reforms to revive the economy but an initial package of economic measures unveiled in July failed to restore voters' confidence.
An investment surge made possible by a special €500 billion ($580 billion) infrastructure fund and an exemption from debt rules for defence spending is taking longer than expected to feed into the economy.
The economy is finally gaining momentum and economic institutes have revised up their economic forecasts, but the improvement came too little, too late to convince voters in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, Germany's poorest by GDP per capita.
The anti-immigrant AfD, which fell just short of an overall majority in the state parliament in Sunday's vote leaving it unclear whether it can form a government, has become the face of opposition to the consensus-based political system that has governed Germany since World War Two.
The coalition parties differ over how to interpret the election defeat. The SPD points to excessive spending cuts, while the CDU blames high taxes and debt, party sources said of internal discussions.
Saxony-Anhalt represents only 1.8% of German GDP, and key levers such as taxes, the structure of the labour market and social security systems are beyond the scope of a state government, so the AfD victory will not materially alter national fiscal or economic policy.
However, economists fear the AfD win could deter foreign investment and discourage skilled workers.
The further concern is that the election result shows a wider waning of public support for European integration, open markets and free movement of workers that once drove Germany's economic success.
Pro-reform voices argue that politicians should, however, pursue the difficult structural changes to an economic model that has been thrown into question by the rise of Chinese manufacturing and the removal of cheap Russian energy sources since the Ukraine war.
"We urgently need change reforms that go far beyond the Agenda 2010 reforms of 25 years ago," said Marcel Fratzscher, president of the Berlin-based DIW research institute.
"Failure to do so will make it more likely that the AfD will win an absolute majority in 2029." REUTERS

Drone activity at US-Mexico border dropped 75% after US started using laser weapon system: Report

Berk Kutay Gokmen
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Less than two weeks after the US military first used a laser weapon system to down suspicious drones, there has been a roughly 75% decrease in the number of drones probing the country's southern border with Mexico, CBS News reported Monday, citing US officials.
The system was first used to take down three drones on Aug. 25 and 26 after months of training, including an episode that caused the Federal Aviation Administration to briefly shut down the airport earlier this year in the border city of El Paso, Texas.
The US military already uses jamming to send some drones back to where they came from, but the laser weapon system offers the option to destroy a suspected threat.
Since the beginning of the year, the military has stopped 300 drones that officials say are linked to drug cartels, including 11 that the laser weapon system took down over 10 days.
"When you just send it back and then it comes back up or is defeated temporarily, but the game changer is ensuring that that tool can't be used again against you," said Army Col. Robert Felicio, commander of the 130th Maneuver Enhancement Brigade.
Officials said cartels use drones to survey US service members and law enforcement, helping them identify areas to avoid when smuggling people or drugs.
Army Lt. Col. Ray Richards said disrupting drones has a financial impact on cartels.
"When you think of 75% reduction of that capability and how that spreads based on X amount of dollars are tied to that — I think when you talk about disruption to the cartels, that is a huge part of that story," Richards said.
Cartels also use armed drones in Mexico to attack rival groups. The report said that military officials are weighing the threat to roughly 8,000 US service members and law enforcement personnel along the border.

Netanyahu’s office denied that he had spoken with the UAE president during the relevant period or received a warning, according to the Jerusalem Post.
Accusing Netanyahu of ignoring repeated warnings

He accused Netanyahu of ignoring repeated warnings from both the security establishment and anti-government protesters who said his policies were endangering Israel.
“He was warned again and again. The security establishment warned,” Golan wrote.
“We warned — hundreds of thousands of democrats who stood in squares, on bridges, and in streets and cried out: You are endangering Israel and leading us to disaster.”
Golan said Netanyahu had responded by calling them “anarchists and Kaplanists”, while prioritising his own political survival and backing “the draft dodgers and the extremists”.

Israeli firm lands first order for its new drone defense turret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:10:58 UTC
19:10:58 KST

- Axon Vision received its first order for ForceField, an AI-powered counter-drone system, worth up to 15 million shekels ($5.0 million) from an unnamed Israeli defense organization.
- The system is designed to counter fiber-optic-controlled FPV drones that traditional radio jammers cannot stop, with deliveries expected over the next 12 months.
Axon Vision has received its first order for ForceField, an AI-powered counter-drone system it launched in July, with an Israeli defense organization placing a deal worth up to roughly 15 million shekels ($5.0 million), the company announced September 7.
The order includes an initial payment of about 6 million shekels ($2.0 million), with the customer holding options to expand it by another 9 million shekels ($3.0 million). Axon Vision expects to deliver the systems over the next 12 months. The company did not name the Israeli defense organization placing the order.
The Defence Blog first reported on ForceField in July, when Axon Vision unveiled the system as a way to shield tanks, armored vehicles and troops on the move from first-person-view drones, including a newer variant that trails a thin fiber-optic cable back to its operator instead of a radio signal. That design makes fiber-optic FPV drones immune to the radio jammers most militaries already use, since there’s no wireless signal to disrupt in the first place.
ForceField compresses an engagement into three steps the company calls detect, understand and respond. It starts with passive sensors that watch for incoming drones without emitting signals that could reveal a protected unit’s position, then uses onboard artificial intelligence to classify the threat before handing the engagement decision to a human operator under what Axon Vision calls Man-on-the-Loop control, meaning software flags the threat but a person retains authority over whether to fire. The system engages threats using standard weapons and ammunition already common in military inventories, rather than a specialized interceptor munition units would need to stock separately, and it’s built to integrate onto existing vehicles without requiring deep changes to their electronics.
This latest order followed a series of live-fire trials in which ForceField intercepted FPV drone targets and other low-altitude threats under conditions the company designed to mirror real combat, according to Axon Vision.
“Receiving this first order shortly after the launch of ForceField is a significant milestone for us and reflects our transition from development and live-fire validation to initial commercial adoption by defense organizations,” said Neri Zin, CEO of Axon Vision. “We are seeing growing demand for solutions that combine AI and autonomy to address the evolving drone threat, and are advancing additional opportunities with customers and strategic partners in Israel and international markets.”
Axon Vision, founded in 2017 by veterans of Israeli military technology units, went public on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange in a listing that raised roughly $26 million. The company has separately built a strategic cooperation agreement with Leonardo DRS, the U.S. subsidiary of Italy’s Leonardo, signed in late 2025 to pursue AI-enhanced counter-drone systems for American customers. That partnership produced a roughly $350,000 order from Leonardo DRS in January for demonstrator systems now under evaluation with U.S. defense and homeland security customers.
Axon Vision has said it expects ForceField to help drive its expansion into European and U.S. markets, building on this first confirmed sale in its home market.

Six months into Hormuz blockade, Qatar and UAE test ways to keep LNG moving
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:10:12 UTC
19:10:12 KST

LNG exporters are looking for ways around the disruption in Hormuz, with three Gulf cargoes recently moved using ship-to-ship transfers (STS) as Qatar and UAE exports remain far below pre-war levels.
Qatar and the UAE are rerouting damaged LNG tankers via ship-to-ship transfers to keep gas flowing to buyers worldwide, in emergency operations that add more than $1 million per transfer and up to 35 hours of additional sailing time as the ongoing war continues to affect traffic through the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.
Three LNG cargoes loaded in Qatar and the UAE were transferred between vessels off Oman and the UAE in August before continuing to buyers in Asia, according to ship-tracking data from Kpler and Vortexa.
Two of the three transfers involved vessels that had previously been damaged or involved in incidents.
The QatarEnergy-run Al Rekayyat, which was struck by a projectile near Hormuz in July, transferred its cargo to the Qatari tanker Tembek off the UAE coast. Tembek later delivered the LNG to India.
GasLog Shanghai, which was involved in an incident while leaving Hormuz in late July, later transferred its cargo to GasLog Savannah off Oman.
A third operation involved ADNOC-controlled Mraweh, which transferred LNG loaded at Das Island to LNG Enugu off Oman. The cargo then continued towards Japan.
A costly way around the disruption
Ship-to-ship LNG transfers are technically complex and rarely used outside emergencies.
Unlike crude oil, which can be transferred between vessels relatively quickly, LNG must be kept at minus 162 degrees Celsius to remain liquid.
The transfer requires specialist cryogenic equipment, fenders, tugboats and trained personnel on both ships.
For these reasons, STS transfers are standard practice in the crude oil industry but remain exceptional in the LNG trade, where they are typically reserved for situations where a vessel cannot complete its voyage.
Bogdan Ratiu, commercial and shipping director at LNG Synergy, said most of the recent operations were emergency transfers rather than routine commercial transfers.
“This is a constraint, they have no choice in certain situations,” Ratiu told Euronews.
Ratiu said an LNG ship-to-ship transfer can take around 30 to 35 hours and requires specialist equipment, tugboats, fenders and specialist personnel.
“It will easily add over $1 million (€860,600) if STS is involved,” he said.
Once LNG is loaded onto a tanker at Ras Laffan, the vessel is normally sent to the customer as quickly as possible. Keeping LNG on board for long periods ties up ships and can lead to losses through boil-off, when some of the gas naturally evaporates.
Newer vessels can turn some of that gas back into liquid LNG, while older ships have fewer options to recover it.
Ratiu said QatarEnergy has traditionally tried to minimise the time LNG remains on board after loading, while Ras Laffan was designed for rapid ship turnaround.
“Desperate times require desperate solutions,” he said.
Qatar's Ras Laffan Industrial City, the loading terminal for Qatargas and QatarEnergy LNG exports, is the world's largest LNG production and export complex.
Before the war it loaded between 140 and 150 LNG cargoes per month, making it the single most important point of origin for global LNG supply.
All of its output must transit the Strait of Hormuz to reach international markets. No pipeline or alternative route exists.
Gulf LNG shortfall remains severe
Between March and June, LNG loadings from Qatar and the UAE fell by 35 billion cubic metres compared with the same period a year earlier, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
Qatar exported just 18 LNG cargoes during the first six months of the Iran war, compared with 509 during the same period a year earlier, a decline of around 96%.
Qatar is estimated to have lost around $24 billion (€20.7 billion) in gas sales over the period, while QatarEnergy remains under force majeure on some deliveries, with cancellations extending into early November.
Much of the missing Gulf supply, however, has been replaced elsewhere.
The IEA said non-Gulf LNG production rose by almost 18%, or around 27 bcm, between March and June, offsetting around three-quarters of the fall in Qatar and UAE deliveries. Overall global LNG production fell by around 4% during the period.
North America and Africa were among the regions adding supply, supported by new LNG projects and improved gas availability for existing plants.
The additional supply has offset part of the shortfall, while gas prices remain well above pre-war levels.
Hormuz remains the main problem
The UAE can bypass Hormuz for some oil exports through a pipeline to Fujairah, but no similar large-scale route exists for LNG.
Diplomatic efforts are also under way to restore some shipping through the strait. Qatar and Iran discussed a proposed temporary shipping corridor through Hormuz and a joint project to clear mines from the waterway during talks in Tehran in late August.
Qatar has said the proposal is part of wider efforts to restore freedom of navigation through the strait.
Fitch Ratings removed Qatar from Rating Watch Negative on Friday and affirmed its AA sovereign rating, saying the immediate risks to the country’s LNG facilities had eased.
It maintained a negative outlook because of continued uncertainty over LNG exports through the key waterway, which usually sees one-fifth of the world's oil and gas travel through.

Hong Kong seizes HK$1.4b suspected drugs over summer as traffickers target students
Customs says 150 people aged between 18 and 68 arrested and 6.1 tonnes of suspected drugs seized between May and August
Hong Kong customs has smashed an international drug trafficking network over the summer, seizing 6.1 tonnes of suspected narcotics worth more than HK$1.4 billion (US$178.5 million) and arresting 150 people as syndicates actively recruited students during the holiday period.
Acting head of the Customs and Excise Department’s drug investigation bureau Wong Ngar-lun said on Tuesday that real-time intelligence exchanges with overseas law enforcement agencies helped dismantle complex, multilayered smuggling routes before the narcotics could reach local or global markets.
“During the summer break, many students travel abroad after sitting for public exams or during their school holidays. Criminal syndicates take advantage of this period to exploit and mislead young people, particularly students, into cross-border drug trafficking,” Wong said.
“In response, Hong Kong customs launched a joint operation with various mainland and overseas law enforcement agencies between May and August this year, targeting syndicates that attempt to smuggle drugs in and out of Hong Kong via air passenger and cargo channels.”
Wong said the operation uncovered 424 cases – 118 involving passengers and 306 through cargo – and led to the seizure of 6.1 tonnes of suspected drugs.
Cannabis accounted for almost 60 per cent of the haul, or 3.6 tonnes, followed by 2.2 tonnes of ketamine, which made up 36 per cent. The remainder included cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and Ecstasy.
