Press review: Iran expands its naval war with US and EU blocks US ambitions in Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 8. /TASS/. Iran is pursuing a new approach to counter the US-imposed naval blockade of its ports; NATO’s European allies are trying to counter US ambitions in Greenland; and the EU is entering the heating season with the lowest level of gas storage in 15 years. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Iran expanding scope of its naval war with US
Tehran is fundamentally changing its approach to countering the US-imposed naval blockade of Iranian ports. The Islamic Republic will soon unilaterally establish a restricted-access zone in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. Under this new initiative, any vessel attempting to head toward the Strait of Hormuz from either side without Iran’s approval will be added to a sanctions list. In other words, Tehran intends to oversee the entire maritime area, from the line of the US-imposed naval blockade to the loading ports deep within the Persian Gulf. This appears to be an attempt to prevent the operation of the alternative Strait of Hormuz corridor established by the US.
Yury Lyamin, a senior researcher at the Center for Analysis of Strategies and Technologies, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta that Iran’s "no-go zone" idea has clear objectives. "Most shipowners do not risk passing through the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian permission. However, the US has found companies willing to transport cargo, primarily oil, through the strait under Iranian fire with American air cover," the expert noted. "These include, first and foremost, the shipping division of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), the Saudi Bahri national shipping company, the Kuwait Oil Tanker Company (KOTC), and South Korea’s Sinokor company," he listed.
If these companies’ tankers transported oil directly to the buyer countries, it would not have a significant impact on supplies, Lamin pointed out. "That is why these companies’ tankers are now effectively moving back and forth between the Persian Gulf, where they load oil, and the Gulf of Oman, where they transfer that oil at sea to tankers belonging to other companies that do not want to take the risk of being targeted by Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz," the expert stressed.
"If Iran extends the no-go zone to the Gulf of Oman - and not just extends it, but begins to strike tankers there just as it does in the Strait of Hormuz - this will sharply increase the risks. This is especially true during the process of transferring oil from one tanker to another. This is a fairly lengthy operation, during which two tankers moored side by side are particularly exposed to any type of attack," the expert emphasized.
Izvestia: How European allies blocking US ambitions in Greenland
The Arctic Shield military drills have begun in Greenland, involving nearly 400 servicemen from ten NATO countries. Several other countries are represented by observers and logistics specialists. The exercises are officially intended to test allied coordination in challenging Arctic conditions and bolster NATO’s capabilities in the region. However, the drills are taking place amid US President Donald Trump’s ongoing claims to Greenland and discussions about whether European allies can independently ensure the island’s security. Experts believe the exercises also aim to show Washington that European countries are willing to strengthen Greenland’s defenses independently.
"Statements about containing China are nothing more than a media myth," military expert Vasily Dandykin told Izvestia. "NATO’s main focus in the Arctic has always been anti-Russian. At the same time, against the backdrop of Trump’s rhetoric, Denmark is trying to show its readiness to defend its territories and demonstrate the concept of ‘a Europe capable of acting without the US’," he noted.
According to the expert, the Europeans are unable to fully deploy a large military force in the region due to a lack of necessary infrastructure, and the military buildup itself only intensifies separatist sentiments among the local population.
The tensions around Greenland highlight a deeper crisis in relations between the US and European NATO members, Colonel Andrey Koshkin, head of the Political Analysis and Socio-Psychological Processes Department under the Plekhanov Russian University of Economics, emphasized. "From a defense standpoint, Washington has no problems in this region: the necessary military infrastructure was established there back during the Cold War. The attempt to reclaim ownership of the island is perceived by Europeans as a demonstration of harsh political domination," the expert pointed out. "Against this backdrop, European members of the alliance are forced to consider their own strategic autonomy. The growing uncertainty will inevitably lead to a transformation of NATO’s structure," he stressed.
At the same time, both experts agree that the real reason for the increased attention on Greenland is the competition over resources and the transport routes of the future.
Izvestia: Europe approaching winter with record gas shortage
Amid an abnormal heat wave and risks to LNG supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, the European fuel market is becoming increasingly unstable. Having turned away from Russian pipeline gas, the EU now depends on the US and Norway for nearly 60% of its gas supply. Experts say that the main threat this winter may not be a shortage of hydrocarbons but rather another surge in prices. The EU is entering the heating season with gas storage facilities at their lowest level in 15 years: 65.6%. Germany, Europe’s traditional industrial powerhouse, is among the most vulnerable EU countries. The Bundestag emphasizes that the current gas pricing model in Europe undermines the international competitiveness of German industry.
Over the past four years, Europe has almost completely reshaped the structure of its fuel imports. Currently, Norway accounts for 30-33% of supplies, and the US accounts for 25%. Together, these two countries cover nearly 60% of the EU’s needs. However, unlike pipeline gas, LNG is sold on the global market, with tankers heading to wherever the price is highest. Therefore, during the winter months, the EU will have to compete for available volumes with not only its neighbors, but also Asia’s largest importers: China, Japan, and South Korea.
Matthias Moosdorf, a German lawmaker representing the Alternative for Germany party, told Izvestia that relying on American LNG and Norwegian gas does not compensate for the advantages of previous long-term contracts with Russia. "That was a big mistake. We turned our backs on Russian pipeline gas, but we continue to buy that same gas through intermediaries at much higher prices," he emphasized. "Today, German industry and businesses pay some of the highest energy rates, and companies are losing their international competitiveness. This is not in Germany’s best interests," the politician noted.
Europe’s energy dependence has not disappeared; it has merely taken on a different form. Rather than relying on a single major pipeline supplier, the EU now depends on the global market, where gas prices are determined by demand at the largest LNG export terminals: Rotterdam, Doha, Houston, Tokyo, and Beijing, Alexander Frolov, deputy director of the Institute of International Economic Relations at MGIMO, told Izvestia. That is precisely why the main threat to Europe will be not so much a physical fuel shortage as a new round of rising gas prices, he explained.
The current situation differs significantly from the 2022 crisis. Back then, Europe faced a sharp decline in pipeline supplies. Today, Europe is dependent on the global LNG market, where tankers go wherever they can secure the highest price.
Vedomosti: Reasons behind North Korea, Russia quickly building road bridge across Tumen River
The bridge across the Tumen River on the border between Russia and North Korea opened to traffic on September 7. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song participated in the event via video conference, after which the first convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge. For the first time in history, the new bridge has linked these two neighboring countries with regular road traffic.
The idea of building a road bridge between North Korea and Russia had been on the negotiating agenda for several decades, but a final decision was not made until the 2024 summit between the leaders of these two countries, and this project was urgently needed, Alexander Vorontsov, head of the Korea and Mongolia Department at the Oriental Studies Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Vedomosti. The expert noted that North Korea (and, in the long term, the entire Korean Peninsula) is now essentially connected by road to the entire Eurasian continent. Although freight traffic between the countries will not immediately increase after the new bridge opens, it will obviously grow due to the diversification of transport routes, Vorontsov pointed out. In addition, it is now much more convenient for tourists from Russia’s Primorsky Region to travel, for example, to the border town of Rason on the Sea of Japan coast, which is part of North Korea’s first trade and economic zone or a little further, to the border with China, where ski tourism is developing on Mount Paektu.
At the same time, Russia and North Korea will take advantage of new opportunities "across the full spectrum of the two countries’ foreign policy and foreign economic interests," Vorontsov emphasized. As for the height of the bridge, it is indeed "not the tallest" - just like the railway bridge - but the two parties made the decision on its technical specifications, possibly even before 2024. The Tumen is a shallow river that carries a great deal of sediment. However, if a political decision is reached, further work could be carried out, such as deepening its bed. The Chinese have alternative ideas as well, such as digging a parallel navigable canal, the expert recalled.
The very fact that this project is underway is significant because it is the first road bridge between the two countries despite their long history of relations dating back to 1948, Alexander Zhebin, a leading research fellow at the Korean Studies Center of the China and Modern Asia Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, stated. Given the authorities’ serious plans to develop trade, the road bridge in particular could become an important means of transporting goods and also help boost tourist traffic, he noted.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Who can regulate global oil market right now?
The actions of OPEC+ have all but ceased to influence the global oil market, becoming little more than background noise. Although the alliance’s decisions affect buyer and seller sentiment, they are powerless to change the situation radically. China and the US are now vying for the role of oil market regulators. As the largest oil importer, China was expected to import up to 11.6 million barrels per day by 2025, accounting for 11% of global demand. The country possesses enormous oil reserves in storage, estimated at between 1.2 and 1.4 billion barrels. The US is also competing for this role. It produces more oil than any other country: 13.8 million barrels per day. Like China, the US has large oil reserves, but they have been depleted following significant market interventions this year. In addition, the US effectively controls production in Guyana, Canada, and Venezuela.
OPEC+ reached its peak influence on the global market has already passed, driven by several fundamental factors, energy expert Kirill Rodionov told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. First, oil production is growing in North and South America. Second is the slowdown in global demand growth, partly due to the electrification of transportation in China, where electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids already account for more than half of new passenger car sales. The "supply race" for oil was expected to begin this year, with OPEC+ countries participating, but the Hormuz crisis prevented this from happening, the expert emphasized.
Without a recovery in production and export volumes from the Persian Gulf countries, even taking into account production growth in non-OPEC+ countries, it will take more than a year for the market to reach a balance between supply and demand. Iran and the US are currently responsible for ensuring passage through the Strait of Hormuz. They are effectively regulating the oil market, but since they are adversaries who cannot reach an agreement, chaos results instead. Even if the strait opens, a surplus will be a long way off. According to DA Consulting CEO Daniil Tyun, a significant portion of production will recover within one to two months, reaching about 70% of the previous level within three months and about 90% within six months. The remaining volumes will take longer to recover. Exports will take even longer to recover, he pointed out.
In the current situation, Russia has the opportunity to increase oil production and exports. However, according to Russian National Energy Security Fund head Konstantin Simonov, Russia is falling short of its OPEC+ quotas by nearly one million barrels per day. Moreover, due to shipping issues in the Black Sea, Russian maritime oil exports have declined slightly over the past month, which could lead to a further decrease in production.

OpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better ‘hugging face’ investigation | Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan Llerena
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

When OpenAI first revealed that its AI agents had autonomously hacked a major real-world company, Hugging Face, many assumed only one or two agents were involved. The truth, a new report reveals, is far stranger: the incident involved about 1,200 AI agents, 700 of which directly participated in the attack.
OpenAI invited researchers from METR, along with an expert from Redwood Research, to produce the new report, alongside the company’s own investigation. The findings shocked the experts.
The agents were highly coordinated, constructing complex message boards in the nooks and crannies of their shared artefact repository. All told, agents exchanged more than 70,000 messages in less than a week. Even more concerning, the agents took steps to hide their behavior – spoofing tool calls and attempting to tamper with their own logs.
Initial reporting assumed that the agents had attacked Hugging Face in search of an answer key to a difficult test. In reality, investigators found that the agents had figured out a way to derive the answers within the first few hours. The days of work that followed focused on another goal: concerned that the automated scoring system might identify the agents’ cheating, they aimed to learn more about the scorer. The goal wasn’t just to cheat, but to hide it.
These details are startling, and they’re a warning sign about the current trajectory of AI development. But just as concerning is how limited the investigation was and how much we still don’t know.
We work at a thinktank that analyzes AI-related legislation, and we’ve been worried for a while that legal requirements for reporting incidents like these are insufficient.
These reports make that clear: they’re informative enough to tell us something went wrong, but not detailed enough to tell us why.
This shouldn’t surprise us. These investigations are entirely voluntary, and their findings are limited to what the company is willing to disclose. METR’s independent investigation was highly constrained by an agreement with OpenAI. For example, the investigators were not given access to the underlying model that created the majority of the misbehaving agents. And despite indications that message boards had formed as early as May and that coordinated agent activity persisted after 13 July, METR was only permitted to investigate the period from 26 June to 13 July.
And that was the good part. METR was given close to nothing about OpenAI’s safety and security practices. If OpenAI ignored warning signs – as several data points suggest – violated its own safety procedures, or failed to implement fixes that would prevent future events, these all fell outside the scope of METR’s investigation. The expert investigators themselves were left with many questions and continued concerns.
Concerns about the limits aren’t hypothetical. On Friday, Reuters reported that another swarm of OpenAI agents had broken out this spring, hijacking a German website and using it as another message board. According to the report, OpenAI knew about this incident but said nothing, and it was entirely absent from METR’s report.
Clearly, this kind of investigation – however well-executed – leaves a lot to be desired.
When planes crash, trains derail or chemical plants explode, expert government investigators arrive with legal authority to compel evidence, preserve records, and tell the public what happened. Hugging Face reported this incident to law enforcement, and multiple attorneys general have expressed interest in looking into it.
But no government agency has both the mandate and expertise to investigate the technical facts of the incident and OpenAI’s conduct. As far as we know, the only people to examine this incident did so at OpenAI’s discretion and with its consent.
And while the Hugging Face breach is not as severe as a plane crash, it was a serious and costly attack. It’s unlikely to be the last, or the most severe.
Existing laws don’t fill this gap. While some attorneys general have tried to use existing investigatory powers, these offices aren’t built for technical fact-finding, and the laws they rely on are limited to questions of consumer deception, not public risk. Despite significant AI laws passed in California, New York and Illinois, none create the investigative authority demanded by these incidents. As we’ve written elsewhere, existing incident reporting laws probably don’t cover the Hugging Face attack, and even if they did, OpenAI might share little more than the date and a short summary.
What we need is a federal body equipped to conduct expert investigations of serious AI incidents – with the authority to compel documents and testimony, resources and personnel to examine the systems involved, and the ability to partner with third-party experts like METR.
Reports should be published, subject to appropriate redactions, to ensure the public learns from the incident. And reporting should also extend to near-miss events, which may reveal warnings before major harms occur.
This structure would not be unusual. In aviation, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigates accidents with subpoena and wide-ranging investigative powers. Aircraft operators must preserve wreckage and records; and the NTSB may confer with employees and contract external experts.
Congress can build a similar system for AI incidents, while protecting AI developers’ legitimate interests. Investigations should open only upon clear triggers and be bound to the incident. Certain confidential information can receive statutory protection. And investigations can be limited to one agency with priority to avoid duplicative investigations.
The need and urgency is real. Subsequent reports have revealed that the Hugging Face breach was not an isolated incident and that autonomous agents from Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI have hacked third parties in separate incidents. We’ve been lucky so far – the harms have been limited. But luck is no substitute for the law.
- 
  Mackenzie Arnold is the managing director of US law & policy at the Institute for Law & AI, where he provides analysis and advice to ensure that advances in AI benefit the public at large
- 
  Stephan Llerena is a research scholar at the Institute for Law & AI. His research focuses on US law and policy regarding frontier AI governance

Exclusive: Obscure Committee Set To Be at Center of Trump Fight if Democrats Win House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

If Democrats win control of the House in November, party leaders plan to turn the final two years of the Trump era into a barrage of investigations over alleged corruption and contempt for the law.
Much of the scrutiny would be expected to come from the Judiciary and Oversight Committees, the traditional engines of congressional investigations. But another, less prominent committee could emerge as an unlikely center of the fight: the House Natural Resources Committee.
The 45-member panel has oversight over virtually all federal lands, giving it jurisdiction over a striking collection of controversies that have defined President Trump’s second term. That includes his efforts to remake Washington, D.C. by building a White House ballroom and a triumphal arch, and the troubled renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. It also covers the Administration’s efforts to open up national parks to an unprecedented amount of hunting, fishing and drilling, as well as a recent proposal to give a swath of California’s Yosemite National Park to a private developer.
“We are no longer a backwater here at the Natural Resources Committee,” Rep. Jared Huffman, the committee’s top Democrat, tells TIME. “You check a lot of boxes with the Natural Resources Committee in terms of some of the most high-profile controversies in this Administration.”
Huffman, who is likely to become the committee’s chair in a Democratic House, spoke to TIME this month from his Capitol Hill office decorated with paintings from the Muir Woods National Monument, the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, and other public lands in his coastal California district. Leading the House Natural Resources Committee has been the ultimate goal for the former environmental lawyer since he joined the House in 2013. “This is the top of the mountain for me,” he says. “This is what I always wanted.”
Huffman has a running list of the investigations he would pursue if he takes the gavel. His plans would amount to a striking transformation for a committee more commonly associated with debates over endangered species, grazing rights, and federal water projects.
Since Trump returned to office, committee Democrats have tried to investigate and call attention to Administration actions while lacking the authority to compel cooperation. With control of the House, those requests could be backed by subpoenas, sworn depositions, and public testimony from Administration officials, contractors, and private companies.
Huffman says he expects a wave of government employees to approach the committee as whistleblowers, feeling more confident that Democrats will act on their concerns. “There are principled, patriotic Americans working in all of these federal agencies that are horrified with the corruption and illegality that’s been happening around them,” he says. “Some of them have already been helpful, but I think many, many more will come forward under a Democratic majority.”
The Trump Administration says the changes to federally controlled land are intended to make the District of Columbia “safe and beautiful” by restoring monuments, cleaning up federal parkland, and improving public safety.
Under its current rules, the Natural Resources chairman has broad authority to issue subpoenas for testimony and documents. The precise scope of that position’s power in the next Congress would depend on the rules adopted by the House and the committee next year. The Trump Administration could also refuse to comply with some subpoenas, producing lengthy court battles.
Huffman is perhaps best known on Capitol Hill as the founder of the Freethought Caucus, which counts 37 members and advocates for church-state separation and true religious freedom. Last month, he published a book, No Prophets: The Fight to Save Democracy from Christian Nationalism.
But if he gets the gavel, his work investigating the Administration would shift to the forefront. Huffman says he intends for the committee to revisit many of the Administration’s decisions from the previous two years. “We will not only be doing the oversight that presents itself on our watch,” he says. “We will be doing two years of catch-up for a Republican Congress that looked the other way in the face of all this corruption, self-enrichment and illegality.”
Trump’s ballroom and “triumphal arch”
The committee’s most visible investigations could target what Huffman calls Trump’s “vanity projects” including the $400 million, 90,000 sq. ft. White House ballroom being built on the site of the demolished East Wing. Last month, the Supreme Court allowed the construction to move forward, after a lower court had halted the work saying Trump did not have the authority to build the ballroom without congressional approval.
The President is also set to break ground on a 250-foot “triumphal arch” near the Arlington National Cemetery that would be taller than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. He has also proposed erecting hundreds of statues in a Garden of American Heroes and transforming the East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course.
Some of the projects have moved forward without congressional authorization or have been reviewed by commissions that Trump has filled with allies. The Administration has maintained that the work is legal and will restore grandeur to the capital.
"It's a dramatic abuse of the public trust for one man's ego,” Huffman says of the projects. “It's also a direct attack on the rule of law because we have long had laws like the Commemorative Works Act that spell out in great detail how monuments and other structures in the nation's capital get authorized and built.”
Huffman says that if Democrats win the House the committee would seek records showing how the projects were approved, how much public money had been spent, and whether donors received or sought favorable treatment from the Administration. The private financing, he says, would receive particular scrutiny. He wants to know who donated, how much they contributed and what business they had before the federal government.
Last year, the White House released a partial list of ballroom donors, including crypto and tech billionaires and defense contractors, but has not revealed how much each donor is giving.
Huffman also questioned why money and Park Service personnel were being concentrated in Washington while the Administration was cutting staff and services elsewhere in the national park system.
“You could look at it and say, well, you know, why die on that hill? These are just little pet projects of Donald Trump,” Huffman says. “But this is real money that is being misprioritized. It’s an abuse of the public trust.”
Another Washington project he wants to investigate is the renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Trump ordered the pool’s bottom covered with a blue coating as part of a rehabilitation that cost more than $14 million. Soon after the project was completed, algae returned and sections of the new coating began to peel. The President blamed vandalism.
In July, the Administration dropped a felony charge against a U.S. Olympic canoeist it had blamed for the damage, and acknowledged in court that the damage was “a result of flawed installation by the contractor."
Huffman says he expects whistleblowers inside the Park Service to provide additional information about how the contracts for the pool project were awarded and supervised, when officials learned that the work was failing, and whether employees were pressured to misrepresent what had occurred. “The fact that National Park Service employees have been told to lie about what happened, for example, we obviously want a full accounting,” he says. (The White House did not respond to Huffman’s allegation that Park Service employees were instructed to lie).
If federal agencies refuse to provide the committee with records, Huffman adds, he would be prepared to issue subpoenas. “You walk softly and carry a big stick,” he says. “The subpoena is your big stick. You hope not to use it, but I think it’s very good to have.”
Yosemite land swap
The recent bipartisan outcry over the prospects of a private developer gaining a swath of Yosemite National Park illustrates how the committee’s work could shift dramatically under Democratic rule. The current chairman, Republican Rep. Bruce Westerman of Arkansas, has not announced any committee action regarding the Administration’s proposal to a land swap intended to help Kingsbarn Realty Capital, a private real estate firm, build a road between property it owns outside Yosemite and roads inside the national park. The company plans an upscale development of cabins, homes, and commercial buildings on two parcels near the park’s western boundary.
“I don’t like what it would do on its own terms to Yosemite,” Huffman says. “But I especially don’t like the precedent, because if they’re allowed to do it, this will be coming to a national park near you in some other form.”
Under the proposal, the government would transfer a small parcel of park property in exchange for land of comparable value that Kingsbarn would acquire elsewhere in California. The company has argued that the shorter route would reduce driving and pollution. The Interior Department has said no decision has been made and that any exchange would have to comply with federal law, environmental reviews and public-notification requirements. It has denied reports that political appointees improperly pressured the Park Service to advance the proposal.
Huffman says if he becomes Natural Resources chair, he intends to seek communications between the developer, the White House, Interior officials and Park Service employees. Investigators would look for evidence that political or financial ties influenced the process, including any connections between the company and Trump or his family.
Campaign finance records show Kingsbarn’s chief executive, Jeff Pori, making more than $4,000 in contributions to Trump's campaign in 2024. The company’s representative, Lanny Davis, has said politics had nothing to do with the proposal.
But Huffman remains skeptical. “You’ve got to dig into the money trail,” Huffman says. “You’ve got to figure out who’s been going to Mar-a-Lago and paying tribute to the Trump family.”
Wind Farms and Kalshi
Huffman says he would also probe the Administration’s “war on clean energy,” including its terminating offshore wind leases and redirecting money toward fossil-fuel investments. Interior officials have defended the agreements as a way to dispose of projects they regard as unreliable and economically unworkable. Democrats have questioned whether the Administration had the authority to make the deals and whether taxpayer money or federal lease payments were improperly used.
Other investigations would involve government investments, loans and equity stakes in mineral companies. Huffman says he would examine how companies were selected, whether federal safeguards were followed and whether Trump’s family or associates stood to gain financially.
He adds that investigations could not consume the committee’s entire agenda. He plans to pursue legislation on environmental permitting, public lands and energy, as well as tribal water settlements, health care, education and public safety. Citing the committee’s preview over Native American land and communities, he says it may also examine prediction markets such as Kalshi, which tribal leaders contend are encroaching on gaming revenue used to finance government services.
“It's going to be an enormously busy Congress,” Huffman says if Democrats win the House, as most polls suggest. “The whiplash when we go from this to what will be a very fast-moving and unrelenting workload demand—I mean, it's going to be a shock for a lot of members. It's going to challenge me. It's going to challenge all of us.”

Our eloquent hands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
22 minute listen
Signs of the future are marked in our hands, or so any palmist will declare. But do hands also hold signs of the past? Do they have a history? Over decades of research as a historian of medicine and of human bodies, I’d never imagined such a niche question. And then it was sparked in an instant, between one second and the next, in the time it takes to open a manila folder. For another project altogether I was in the UK to research the papers of Charlotte Wolff, a physician trained in Berlin in the 1920s and living in London in the late 1930s, a Jewish refugee. Opening a file labelled ‘Zoo, 1938’, I came across a massive, delicate palm print: it belonged to Mok, a lowland gorilla at London Zoo. Two days after Mok’s death, the keeper had granted Wolff special permission to enter the morgue and collect a pattern that had been too dangerous to acquire in life.
Mok’s palm print was both forceful and touching. Indeed, I was tempted to literally touch, to hold hands across time, across species, and across the worlds of the living and the dead. The emotive power was unmistakeable, yet for all my training as a historian, it was inscrutable to me. I was also puzzled why Wolff, an exceptionally clever physician, seemed to be practising palm-reading, which today is associated with magic and the occult. Could there be such a thing as medical palmistry?
Over time, I learned that the answer is a clear, but unlikely, ‘yes’. Wolff was looking for the so-called ‘simian line’, a particular crease that some humans share with other primate species. Long ago, in embryonic time, the patterns on each of our tiny, clenched palms were formed. For most of us, three main lines were created. For some of us – up to 5 per cent – the so-called head and heart lines fused into a single crease stretching across the palm from one side to the other. Robert De Niro, Hillary Clinton and Benedict Cumberbatch each boast a simian line on their palms. Tony Blair apparently does on both hands, an even rarer distinction. In the 1920s, the London physician Francis Crookshank delighted in announcing that even the Virgin Mary had a simian line, directing people to see for themselves in Renaissance devotional art.
To this day, midwives still quickly check neonatal palms, not because the newborn might be divinely conceived, but because a single crease has a high incidence in those of us with a particular chromosomal anomaly known as trisomy 21. Not everyone with this transverse crease has Down’s syndrome. And not everyone with Down’s syndrome has the so-called (still-called) simian crease. And yet, so strong is the correlation that this sign on the hand was a key element of clinical diagnosis until recently. It is fair, if strange, to say that the history of palmistry is the history of medicine.
As a rule, physicians relish the weird in their own medical history, but I’ve learned that they don’t appreciate this particular claim. Yet, in turning their backs on the medical history of palmistry, they turn their backs on some towering figures.
In the summer of 1663 in Cambridge, young Isaac Newton walked over to the fair on Stourbridge Common and bought himself a new book, Palmistry, the Secrets Thereof Disclosed. It was written by a physician, who instructed that the lines, angles, shapes and hatches on the palm needed to be read strictly and precisely with a measuring compass. Here was a geometry of the hand that needed to be decoded mathematically. No wonder Newton was interested. Yet we also know that Newton attended to ‘occult’ knowledge that purported to be previously unknown or hidden, hence ‘secrets disclosed’. (In fact, physicians still use the word in that plain way: ‘occult pain’, for example, is of unknown or unseen origin.)
Newton was exercised by the learned traditions kept in ancient manuscripts and precious early printed books in Arabic, in Hebrew and in Latin, later circulating in vernaculars across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. He was especially consumed by hermetic natural magic and the mysticism of ancient Jewish Kabbalah that had been Christianised in the Renaissance. This included what was then called ‘chiromancy’, discerning character, health and fortunes from the hand, from the Greek cheir. Medieval and early modern ‘prognostication’ – divining the future – was slowly turning into medical prognostics.
Most early chiromantic texts were written by physicians. From Paracelsus to the Paracelsian physician Robert Fludd, Newton had them all in his library. Sometimes the simian line was clearly illustrated, yet this particular sign had not yet been analysed by the comparative anatomists, the biostatisticians or the primatologists who would later name it.
Both folk palmistry and learned chiromancy were reference points for a modern anatomy of the hand
The hand has a history of natural magic and occult knowledges, but it is also just anatomy, and so it appears in a plainer anatomical canon too. Yet that tradition is enchanted in its own way. One of the 19th century’s most eminent anatomists, Charles Bell, wrote The Hand (1833), a medical text on God’s design. And not long after, humanity’s deep past was being re-told through the human hand. In The Descent of Man (1871), Charles Darwin recounted that, one day, standing upright, the hand of the primate called Homo sapiens was free to grasp and so to evolve differently, uniquely. It is no coincidence that it was in the 1860s that the term ‘haptic’ arose, from the Greek haptikós, not just to touch, but to grasp or perceive. The hand of this new species of primate was set free for matters beyond locomotion, ultimately giving humankind ‘universal dominion’ over all other creatures, as Darwin wrote, quoting Bell. What a revolutionary idea! Friedrich Engels certainly thought so, as he wrangled the human hand into his dialectics of nature, his search for the material drivers of history. Bell’s anatomical textbook had shown the human hand grasping that all-important tool.
Both folk palmistry and learned chiromancy were reference points for a modern anatomy of the hand. In the 1820s, the Czech anatomist Jan Evangelista Purkinje – known for his fingerprint studies – also analysed the crease patterns on human as well as monkey palms, specifying new terms: the lines of opposition, abduction, adduction, extension, and flexion. Yet, in order to clarify, he had to explain these as the life line, the line of Mars, the line of matrimony, the table line, the line of Venus, the line of Rascetta, and the lines of honour and fortune. Traditional palmistry, in other words, was his anatomical reference point. Nearly a century later, when a then-obscure English doctor named Reginald Langdon Down admitted a patient to the family’s private asylum, he recorded ‘Hands, no head line’ in the admission files. Palmists’ terms were his clinical referents too. That was in 1907, just after his own beloved son was born with the syndrome that was yet to be named for his family.
In France, the anatomist Paul Broca had for some time researched palm creases comparatively across humans and other primates, identifying ‘la disposition simienne du pli palmaire’. Over time, le seul pli – the single fold – was the term used in French scholarship, while German anatomists and clinicians referred to vierfingerfurche, the four-finger crease. In English and American studies ‘the simian line’ proved to be an enduring designation. In 1924, an anatomist employed by the London Zoological Society showed clearly that the orangutan had this single transverse line, and sometimes even two in parallel, both running right across the palm.
This was all on Wolff’s mind when she entered the morgue at London Zoo in 1938. Indeed, she had for some time been climbing into the primate cages taking the prints of every live simian she safely could: those of lemurs, spider monkeys, baboons, chimpanzees, orangutans and more. She even took the delicate prints of a hedgehog. Of more stature, perhaps, were the palms of human primates she collected and then interpreted. These were not any old Homo sapiens but very special specimens indeed. As I opened more manila folders in the Wellcome Collection, London, there were the intimate hand-portraits of every interwar cultural luminary imaginable: Aldous Huxley, Virginia Woolf, Vaslav Nijinsky, Maurice Ravel and so many more. Yet the most haunting remained Mok, the dead lowland gorilla.
It’s a delicate history to tell, this comparative anatomy across primate palms that gave rise to the offensive term ‘simian line’. Yet, before we object, sneer, mock, judge or even just enjoy this as the quirky business of early misguided medicine, or worse dismiss it as ‘pseudoscience’, we should note that this is not only an antique history. It tracks right up to our own present, involving some of the most distinguished researchers of the 20th century, Newton’s worthy intellectual descendants.
Around the same time that Wolff was taking Mok’s palm print, in another part of London the medical geneticist Lionel Penrose was beginning a lifetime assessing human palms and finger patterns. He was doing so both geometrically and statistically in a manner more sophisticated than, but not unlike, Francis Galton’s late-19th-century work on fingerprints. It is little known that Galton – often called the ‘father of fingerprinting’– took palm prints too, occasionally wondering if his hypothesis on the individuality of the fingerprint was also discernible in palm lines. This was a tradition of medical and genetic hand-reading that came to be called ‘dermatoglyphics’.
As late as 1990, the simian crease was even sought, detected and analysed prenatally, via ultrasound
In this context, it was the fortune of the so-called simian line to become the perfect exemplar of a classic modern biomedical pair, the visible ‘phenotype’ and its hidden twin, the ‘genotype’. The former is an observable physical trait; the latter is that trait’s unique DNA code or sequence. Sorting out the connection between them was a great driver of mid-20th-century genetics. Over the 1930s and ’40s, before the chromosomal cause of Down’s syndrome was known, clever Penrose could work only with the phenotype – the physical expression – and he was able to statistically correlate the simian line with the syndrome. And then, in the late 1950s, a Paris-based team discovered the genotype that was trisomy 21, the additional chromosome. It was a massive breakthrough, the long-invisible genotype (an extra chromosome) was now visible, a match with its long-visible phenotype (the simian line, le seul pli, vierfingerfurche). We might well say that an occult sign had been revealed.
I expected the medical palmistry – so to say – to then dissipate, to become antiquated, yet to my utter surprise it did not. For decades after the extraordinary chromosomal discovery, these world-leading Paris and London-based geneticists continued to exchange letters with diagrams of hand patterns, still drawing those three – and in some humans, just two – main lines on the palm.
In the 1960s, paediatricians added another palm crease of note, dubbing it the ‘Sydney line’, or sometimes ‘the simian-like line’. As late as 1990, the simian crease was even sought, detected and analysed prenatally, via ultrasound. One study showed that, in seven foetuses with this sign, four had no chromosomal anomaly, and three had trisomy 21. And even today, some of the most prestigious research hospitals in the world explain to parents that their neonatal physician may check the newborn palm, still nominating the ‘simian crease’.
We all know that a straight line can be drawn between any two points. But as a medical historian, can I really draw a line from Newton’s book Palmistry, the Secrets Thereof Disclosed to the prenatal detection of the simian line in the Journal of Ultrasound in Medicine? The first was built from knowledge that is far remote from our own comprehension of the human body. That was a world in which it made every sense that the planet Jupiter and the finger of Jupiter would be connected, a ‘sympathetic’ relation between a celestial macrocosm and a bodily microcosm. Yet I’ve come to appreciate that this apparently magical chiromancy is an archaic version of what modern clinicians do all the time and every day. They read bodily signs.
Medical students are routinely taught the distinction between a symptom felt by the patient, and a sign observed and interpreted by the clinician. This sign (a rash, the colour of nails, a black spot, a pattern in the palm) has that meaning (measles, liver disease, melanoma, Down’s syndrome). And so, all physicians are foundationally schooled in the interpretation of somatic signs. They are medical semioticians, whether or not they would put it that way.
All physicians are medical semioticians, professional and trained readers of bodily signs
The surprising thing is that some physicians put it precisely that way. It was initially strange to me that the London physician who observed the simian line on the Virgin Mary’s palm in the 1920s – Francis Crookshank – was also deeply schooled in the complexities of contemporary linguistics. Pondering the meaning of the simian line that some of his professional colleagues, as well as his patients, displayed, Crookshank began to insist that medicine desperately needed a ‘theory of signs’. One winter’s evening in 1926, he lectured on just that to the Royal College of Physicians and couldn’t understand why his medical brethren first rolled their eyes, and then closed their eyes, falling asleep with boredom. The connection he drew between clinical sign-reading and highly abstract semiotics was just too much. In so many ways, he was speaking a different language, and certainly his essay’s publication in the specialist book The Meaning of Meaning (1923) – to be read mainly by philosophers of language and Oxbridge cultural anthropologists – did nothing to persuade his medical colleagues. It may have been ill-delivered and badly pitched, but the fact is this palm-reading physician was theorising not just the simian line, but everyday clinical business: how signs on the human body are observed, named, and then ascribed meaning. He did so, not only, but not least for the simian line.
All physicians are medical semioticians, professional and trained readers of bodily signs. In his 16th-century treatise on chiromancy, Paracelsus claimed that ‘nothing is so secret in a human being that it does not have an outward sign’. Indeed, a whole language of the hand is discernible within the medical past. It was the 17th-century doctor John Bulwer who set out the origins of sign language in his enchanting book Chirologia, or the Naturall Language of the Hand (1644). He conceptualised the hand as a second mouth, so keen is its capacity to communicate by gesture and by sign. For Bulwer, it was the hand, not the mouth, that could speak a universal language, the ‘chiefest instrument of eloquence’. Two hundred years later, Bell, one of the greatest anatomists of his day, also wrote of the ‘eloquent’ hand. And a century after that, Wolff wrote about the psychoanalytic body that speaks, in A Psychology of Gesture (1945), placing her work on primate hands in just this tradition.
Today, some adventurous and imaginative medical schools take the connection between somatic signs, language and interpretation very seriously indeed, teaching physical examination through the idea of ‘The Body as Text’. ‘Every patient’s body tells a story,’ Stanford’s medical students are instructed. ‘The narrative includes the past and present of a person’s social and medical condition.’ Bulwer, Bell, Crookshank and Wolff would have added ‘and the future’: signs on the hand were not just diagnostic, but prognostic. The Stanford School of Medicine frames the physical examination as an old-school art that needs to be retained, not superseded, by various technologies that ‘see’ inside. This is the art, science and language of decoding the phenotype. It is quite right that Stanford explains this ‘body as text’ method as the interpretation of the phenotype. Yet when their clinicians teach this language of the body, they are perhaps unaware of just how long and distinguished the tradition of decoding somatic signs is.
When dead Mok’s hand first reached out to me – far more than a ghost – I was culturally cornered, stuck thinking that the palm was relevant only to palmistry. Yet of course the hand – including the fingerprints, the palm and its folds, creases and patterns – is plain human anatomy made semiotically and phenotypically meaningful. For centuries, fortune-telling palmists have studied the hand to unlock the future and the past, health and character, but so too have other experts in bodies and minds: physicians, psychologists, psychiatrists, embryologists, anatomists, endocrinologists, primatologists and physical anthropologists.
Having followed a language of the hand both backwards and forwards in time from Mok’s poignant print, it was especially affecting to learn that, as a medical elder in the 1970s, Penrose the curious geneticist was himself pursuing the history of palmistry: one of the final publications of his stellar career was on fingerprints and palmistry, published in The Lancet, no less. For me, Mok’s print became slowly unveiled from its occult state, no longer inscrutable and mysterious, but now known, legible, and clear, a historical secret disclosed.

Ukraine opens first underground kindergarten in Kharkiv Oblast, with 260 children to attend – photos
The first underground kindergarten in Ukraine, Mobil, has opened in the Pisochyn hromada A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories in Kharkiv Oblast.
Source: Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine
Details: The facility can accommodate 260 children and allows them to attend classes in person while staying safe during air-raid warnings.
The underground educational space has eight classrooms. It also has a medical room, canteen, toilets and showers.
The shelter has an autonomous power supply provided by two independent sources of electricity and backup generators. The protective structure is connected to the kindergarten buildings by safe passageways, allowing children and staff to reach the shelter without going outside during an air-raid warning.
Particular attention was paid to accessibility. The kindergarten has lifts and hoists, step-free routes, and facilities for children with disabilities and other people with reduced mobility.
Anastasiia Konovalova, Deputy Minister of Education and Science for Pre-school Education, said, "This year, the state has for the first time allocated separate funding for equipping shelters in pre-school education institutions. Our task is to support hromadas facing the highest security risks and help as many kindergartens as possible resume in-person education."
The underground kindergarten was jointly funded from the state, regional and local budgets. In 2026, the state allocated a separate subsidy for the first time to equip shelters in pre-school education institutions. The total funding for such projects amounts to more than UAH 972 million (US$21.8 million).
Projects of this kind are currently being implemented in nine oblasts: Vinnytsia, Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Sumy, Kharkiv and Kherson.
Background: In 2025, an underground school for 1,000 students was opened in Zaporizhzhia, where kindergarten children will also be able to attend classes.

Gen AI Tools Are Now Being Used to Push ‘Slop Jihad’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Over a decade ago, the Islamic State released a disturbing video that depicted its members lowering men locked in a cage into a swimming pool and drowning them. Today, that video has been reproduced as a SpongeBob SquarePants cartoon depicting fish in orange jumpsuits inside the cage, as SpongeBob lowers the cage into the water while Squidward films the scene.
The video, shared on TikTok, is part of what a new report from the Institute of Strategic Dialogue (ISD) calls “Slop Jihad,” a trend where young supporters of Islamic terror groups like ISIS and al-Qaeda appear to use generative AI tools to create fan edits, cartoons, and memes designed to radicalize a new generation of online backing.
This shift “signals a fundamental transformation in the aesthetics of jihadist propaganda online,” concludes the report, which was shared exclusively with WIRED.
“The principal concern is the growing volume and diversity of material,” says Adam Hadley, executive director of Tech Against Terrorism, a UN-backed counterterrorism organization that has also written a report about the Slop Jihad trend. “Highly stylized AI-generated content can make violent Islamist extremist material more accessible to younger audiences while reducing the visibility of conventional terrorist branding. Users may encounter perpetrator glorification inadvertently through fan edits, cartoons, memes, and other entertainment-oriented formats, after which engagement can drive algorithmic recommendations of related, more overt propaganda.”
Islamic terror groups have long demonstrated their capacity to adapt to new media environments to get their messages to a wide audience online, leveraging new and emerging technologies to aid recruitment and create a decentralized network of propaganda. This was seen in the early 2020s Alt Jihad movement, which sought to co-opt the aesthetics of the alt-right in the Islamic terrorism content.
These groups have also been making use of generative AI technology for a number of years. In 2024, the Islamic State–affiliated news program News Harvest began using AI-generated anchors to help disseminate propaganda videos quickly and cheaply.
But today, the look and feel of the content produced with generative AI is markedly different.
“This is new, and it's still growing; it has not peaked by any means,” says Moustafa Ayad, the research chair in global Islamism and counterterrorism at ISD. “There's always been really shoddy content that's been produced in the support ecosystem, but it wasn't SpongeBob SquarePants as the Islamic State.”
Generative AI tools have also been utilized to quickly and cheaply turn official content from terror groups into animated videos. In one example, one TikTok account was turning the weekly al-Naba newsletter from ISIS into anime.
The Slop Jihad trend has seen some pushback from more traditional supporters who don’t like the new aesthetic. “There seems to be some animosity towards it, because they don't believe the producers of Slop Jihad are true believers,” Ayad says, referring to some reactions to the SpongeBob video. “But again, some accounts that have shared traditional official propaganda are sharing the newer videos. So there seems to be a love-hate relationship with the Slop Jihad content.”
For years now, TikTok has been central to Islamic terror groups' online messaging campaign, taking advantage of the platform’s powerful algorithmic recommendations to spread their message. A report from the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development in 2024 found that TikTok was among the top 10 platforms used to spread terrorist and extremist content.
While Ayad did find a limited number of Slop Jihad videos on other platforms like Instagram and Facebook, the vast majority of the videos were found on TikTok. In total, he found 150 Slop Jihad videos from 71 accounts with more than 5.4 million total views on the platform. Ayad believes the prevalence of this content on TikTok is due to the platform’s For You Page algorithm “that is hyper-targeted to user interests.” He also credits the high level of general AI slop on the platform and “an existing entrenched ecosystem of jihadist support on the platform.”
TikTok contested the findings of the report. “This report's vague methodology reaches poorly evidenced conclusions and doesn't reflect how people use our platform,” a TikTok spokesperson tells WIRED. “We prohibit the presence of violent and hateful organizations, and we use a combination of advanced moderation technology, safety teams, and partnerships to proactively detect and remove violative content, as we keep TikTok a safe space for our community. All the content referenced in this report has been removed from TikTok.”
Dozens of the videos identified by ISD for its report were deleted after WIRED shared them with TikTok.
WIRED shared the ISD report with several outside experts on Islamic terror groups' use of social media to radicalize followers, and all broadly agreed with ISD’s findings. “What is notable here is the ease with which generative AI allows a much broader and more decentralized set of users to remix jihadi figures and imagery and the extent to which that material can circulate across communities whose interest may be driven as much by violence, trolling, or notoriety as by actual commitment to jihadi ideology,” Aaron Zelin, a researcher who specializes in jihadi extremism at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, tells WIRED.
While Ayad admits that some of the wilder Slop Jihad content may be difficult to identify as terror-related, much of it is very clearly supportive of terror groups and ideologies. TikTok has taken down some of the accounts Ayad was monitoring, but many of them have backup accounts in place and have signaled to their followers where they can find them in the case of a takedown.
“Some of the content is surviving for months at a time and continues to evade moderation efforts, whether it's their AI system that's meant to detect terrorist material or not,” Ayad says.

Insta360 X6 Review (2026): A Great 360 and Action Camera Hybrid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Larger sensors provide clearer, sharper video. Low-light performance improvements. 8K/50 fps 360 video. Shoot both 4K linear files and 8K 360 video simultaneously. Smaller body. Built-in storage and microSD card slot.
TIRED
Unresponsive haptic buttons. Mediocre pro recording features.
The combination of good video quality and user-friendly software has kept Insta360 at the forefront of the 360 camera world even as competitors like DJI and GoPro have carved out their own niche. With its latest camera, the Insta360 X6, the company is hoping to leap ahead of the pack again.
The Insta360 X6 brings a slightly larger sensor, faster video frame rates, better low-light performance, and tools to help you spend less time editing and more time filming. While it’s not a huge leap over its predecessor, the X6 is a solid improvement with several new features that might make upgrading worth it for some users.
What’s New
The X6 looks a little bit like if the X5 and the GoPro Max 2 had a baby. It’s shorter, squatter, and a tad bit wider than the X5, but not as small as the Max 2. That might sound like I’m setting it up to say it’s the Goldilocks size, but that’s not really the case. I actually like the individual sizes of the X5 and Max 2 better, the first for its narrower profile and the second for its much smaller overall size.
Along with the smaller size come two other major changes from the X5: the screen is smaller, and the physical buttons at the bottom are gone. Though there is noticeably less coverage, I didn’t find the smaller screen to make much difference. I could still see what I wanted to shoot, but the point of a 360 camera is you don’t need to frame shots. The main thing I use the screen for is making sure that the stitch line isn’t on my main subject.
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
I do miss the X5’s physical buttons on the front, one to record and the other for the menu. There is still a record button, now on the side of the X6, but the onscreen buttons just aren’t as good. They provide haptic feedback (the buttons vibrate when you press them), but they don’t respond 100 percent of the time. I found them noticeably harder to activate compared to the X5’s physical buttons, and I prefer the X5’s front button to start recording.
Another change to the outside is one of the better things about the X6: There are now power contact points on the bottom, which means you can attach a powered selfie stick and charge your camera while you use it. This is a great new feature that I hope other manufacturers copy. And don’t worry, the standard 1/4-inch tripod mount is still there.
Insta360 also says the X6’s new replaceable lens covers are harder than those on previous models. I have never scratched the lenses on my X5, nor did I acquire any scratches during the couple of months I tested the X6. The camera has an IP68 rating, and it’s dustproof and waterproof down to 66 feet.
Speaking of batteries, perhaps my favorite thing about the redesigned X6 is that the battery is now … just a battery. In older X-series cameras, the battery door was part of the battery, which always seemed unnecessary and meant there was no chance of ever using the same battery in another Insta360 camera, like the Ace Pro 2. Now that is potentially possible. If you’re listening, Insta360, give us the same battery for the Ace Pro 3 that’s in the X6. Battery size has also increased from 2,400 mAh to 2,600 mAh compared to the X5.
New Innards
The X6 uses a larger 1/1.1-inch sensor, the same size as the one in the DJI Osmo 360. That’s up from the 1/1.28-inch sensor in the X5 (and note that 360 cameras have two sensors since they have two lenses), and it gives you marginally sharper, clearer video. I did not notice a huge difference when recording in 360 mode. Of the Insta360, GoPro, and DJI cameras I’ve tested, I still find the GoPro Max 2 footage to be the best quality overall, and to GoPro’s point when it launched the Max 2, the X6 only records 7.2K video versus the Max 2’s 8K video.
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
At night, though, the X6 wins. It’s much brighter than the X5 or the GoPro for starters, and while sometimes it does render colors a little wonky, with blues tending toward green and yellows going more orange than they are in real life, it still produces the best 360-degree low-light footage I’ve shot. The Osmo 360 is a close second, but at times I find it has quite a bit of weird blur-like artifacts in low light.
One of the more exciting new features is single-lens mode, which, at least on the spec sheet, goes a long way to making the X6 a viable action camera replacement. I dream of one camera that can do it all, and the X6 is definitely closer than other 360 cameras in fulfilling that wish.
The X6 can now record up to 5K video in single-lens mode (up from 4K in the X5), but even better is the new InstaFrame 2.0 feature, which is Insta360’s name for the ability to record both 360 video and a single-lens shot at the same time. This greatly simplifies editing since you have a flat file to work from, and if you miss the shot in that one, you have the 360 footage to fall back on. This was always a great feature, but in the X5 the non-360 file was capped at 1080p, which made it less than useful. The X6 bumps that footage to 4K for the single-lens recording and up to 8K at 30 frames per second for the 360 footage recorded simultaneously, which makes this very usable and is, in fact, how I shot most of the time.
As I have said many times, no one wants to see raw 360 footage (yeah, yeah, I know VR is going to catch on one day, but I am not holding my breath), and while InstaFrame makes editing it down to a traditional linear video file about as easy as is possible, it is still kind of a pain. Advanced users will also find it annoying that you cannot use Insta360’s I-Log format (video log modes are to video what a RAW file is to still images, and capture a much wider dynamic range) with InstaFrame 2.0, but there are some pretty good preset color modes, and I recommend using them for everyday shots.
With I-Log, the X6 supports 10-bit recording when recording in 360 mode. In single-lens mode, you can only shoot in 8-bit I-Log. The higher the bit rate, the more color information is available (1,024 shades in 10-bit versus 256 in 8-bit). That’s a shame because, at least for my needs, this stops the X6 from replacing an action camera in my kit. Perhaps we’ll get this in the X7. For non-pro users, this is likely a moot point.
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
Other new features in the X6 include 47 GB of internal storage. There’s still a microSD card slot, which is what I used in almost all my testing, but it’s nice to have the internal storage for those times that you forget an SD card, as I do from time to time. Even though I don’t use the internal storage, I love that it’s there as a backup.
The photo tools also got a bump, with 120-megapixel images (up from 72 MP in the X5) and a new AI reframing feature. In this mode, just press the shutter button and the camera will take three photos, one facing you, one facing out at (presumably) your subject, and one of those tiny world images. (I find the first two photo styles useful, but the latter is lame.) You also get the original 360 photo.
To my mind, useful software-driven features, like the triple-photo feature and InstaFrame 2.0, are what have always separated Insta360 from GoPro and DJI. They make it easier to get usable images and video out of the camera.
Finally, I’d like to point out something I haven’t seen mentioned much, but I love how fast the X6 starts up. You press power, and it’s up and running in about 200 milliseconds, which is the fastest start-up time of any action or 360 camera I’ve tested.
360 for Newbies
If you already own the X5, this is very much an incremental update. The new features are nice to have, but the basic video quality is comparable to the X5. If you’ve been thinking of getting a 360 camera but haven’t pulled the trigger yet, the X6 is worth considering. While I prefer the GoPro Max 2 in many shooting scenarios, the X6 wins in low light. I also love the ability to use it as a 5K action camera when you don’t need the 360 footage, as well as the option to shoot 4K and 360 video at the same time, neither of which is possible with the GoPro Max 2. Throw in the very nice editing software Insta360 offers, and you’ve got a great option for 360 camera newcomers.
Scott Gilbertson is Operations Manager for the WIRED Reviews Team. He was previously a writer and editor for WIRED’s Webmonkey.com, covering the independent web and early internet culture. You can reach him at luxagraf.net. ... Read More

How Sudan's civil war is erasing thousands of years of cultural memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

How Sudan’s civil war is erasing thousands of years of cultural memory
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Sudan’s civil war turned its national museum into a battlefield and crime scene, with ancient statues shattered, skeletal remains scorched and vaults of gold looted.
- Archaeological treasures have been sold on the black market to power a war machine that has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced some 14 million people.
- ‘These artifacts and sites, they’re part of us,’ says one museum staffer. ‘Your lose them, you lose your identity.’
KHARTOUM, Sudan — The ancient statues of the deities Heket and Beset, too heavy to move, were used for target practice. The 4,000-year-old skeletal remains from the bio-archaeology lab? Scattered or scorched. The gold vault lays ransacked, the storage rooms firebombed.
-   Share via
Walk through the grounds of the Sudan National Museum and the reminders of the civil war’s devastating impact on this country’s cultural history seem everywhere.
“It was systematic. They entered the depots and stole everything they could,” said Umaima Abdul-Rahman Al-Sanusi, one of the museum’s curators, as her eyes scanned a shattered display case. She was referring to the Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, a paramilitary group that controlled the capital — and the museum with it — from April 2023 until government forces dislodged them in March of last year.
When Al-Sanusi first saw the level of destruction in the museum — where she’s been employed around 15 years — she cried. Even now, more than a year after she and her colleagues returned to the museum, her voice was tight with not-quite-resigned frustration.
“These artifacts and sites, they’re part of us,” she said, her fingers giving a reassuring touch to a statue of the Nubian god Apademak — a lone survivor standing in a courtyard strewn with shattered stone shards and the occasional bullet casing — as she walked past.
“You lose them, you lose your identity.”
Sudan’s civil war, a conflict credibly described as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis, has seen violence matched only by the belligerents’ rapacity in pillaging the country’s riches.
Like gold, oil, gum arabic and other resources, Sudan’s archaeological treasures, a legacy of the successive kingdoms that flourished and died in the Nile Valley over millennia, have been commandeered to power a war machine that has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced some 14 million people.
At least 76 heritage sites and 20 museums have been ransacked by the RSF and run-of-the-mill thieves, officials say, carting off an archaeological haul worth more than $150 million. One museum was turned into a barracks.
The National Museum alone lost almost two-thirds of its inventory, comprising nearly 100,000 artifacts that covered Sudan’s prehistoric age through its Nubian era, the Kingdom of Kush, the Christian era and its Islamic period.
1. Sudanese visitors walk past examples of 10th century Christian art work at the national museum in the capital Khartoum on June 25, 2008. (Khaled Desouki / AFP via Getty Images) 2. Haitem el-Nour, new director of the national corporation of antiquities and museums looks at a collection of antiquities at the Sudan National Museum in the capital Khartoum on August 12, 2020. - (Ashraf Shazly / AFP via Getty Images) 3. Buhen temple in the national museum, Khartoum State, Khartoum, Sudan on January 5, 2019 in Khartoum, Sudan. (Eric Lafforgue/Art in All of Us/Corbis via Getty Images)
Some items were smashed and shattered when the museum’s grounds became a run-and-gun battlefield.
The museum was undergoing renovations before the war, so most of the collections were packed in the main warehouse. The RSF stole the artifacts in the same boxes where they were stored, said Jamal Zaid Al-Abideen, a veteran official at the National Corp. for Antiquities and Museums.
“They didn’t even need to break into the strongroom,” Al-Abideen said bitterly, looking at a heavy metal door secured with multiple bolts. Behind it was the vault that once contained almost 2,000 objects of 24-carat gold, gem-ornamented Nabatean funerary figures and ancient jewelry from the Kingdom of Kush. All gone.
“They had the time to go through the museum director’s desk and find the key. They could loot it all at their leisure.”
Al-Abideen, who was the first civilian to enter the museum after the Sudanese army clawed back Khartoum, walked to a room where staff had gathered all the ordnance found when bomb experts came and sanitized the museum of explosive materials. Lined on the floor was box after box of ballpoint-pen-sized .50-caliber rounds; beside them lay a mound of bullet casings and a half-destroyed drone.
Al-Sanusi joined, and with Al-Abideen continued their macabre tour of the museum’s grounds. They headed to the backyard, where a dozen containers lay in the sun, one for each of the international archaeological missions that had been working in Sudan before the war’s start.
“Everything was packed here for when the research missions were supposed to come back,” Al-Sanusi said, as Al-Abideen heaved a jammed container door open. Inside was a maw of fire-roasted boxes, shards of pottery spilling across the floor, a skull and a scorched femur.
“Now all of it — excavation equipment, notes, samples — it’s all burned. And we don’t even have records for them,” Al-Sanusi said.
“The metal pieces were burned because they thought they could melt them down and find gold in them,” Al-Abideen added.
The ravaging of the museum reflects the destruction seen across Khartoum. The neighborhood where the museum is located — once a well-appointed Nile-side quarter of luxury hotels, architecturally adventurous towers and botanical gardens — became a prime target for the RSF.
The group evolved from the government-supported Janjaweed militias of the 2000s to become the army’s most powerful ally before turning on it in 2023. In Khartoum it went street to street, ransacking what it could, and destroying what it couldn’t. (The RSF denies that its fighters engage in looting.)
Even now, with fighting centered away from Khartoum, the scars persist: Almost no structure, be it the multistory gold souq, the national cinema or the four museums in the capital, stands unscathed. Those buildings not gutted by fire sport a rash of bullet holes or appear gap-toothed where an artillery shell punched through a wall. The mirrored high-rises have no intact windows.
The civil war erupted in April 2023, when the RSF launched attacks across the country aimed at dislodging its rival, the Sudanese military. Before, the two forces had been allies, working together to crush rebellions in Darfur, but also pro-democracy movements that sprung up after the ouster of Sudanese dictator Omar Al-Bashir in 2019.
Since then, the conflict has taken on an ethnic as well as an international dimension, embroiling Sudan’s neighbors but also the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Russia, Ukraine and Iran. The U.S. has sanctioned the RSF for war crimes and genocide; rights groups accuse it of sexual violence, torture and forced disappearances. The Sudanese army too has been accused of war crimes.
The stolen antiquities follow other types of bounty the RSF has ransacked. The pieces are spirited across the border to Egypt, Libya, South Sudan and especially Chad, officials say. But they rarely stop there, said Ahmed Junaid, the Sudan representative for UNESCO, which is supporting national authorities in tracking down lost antiquities.
“We know that some objects went to Europe, Middle East and even Gulf countries,” Junaid said, and from there an unknown number of antiquities entered the regional and international market.
A big challenge for the staff in Khartoum is that there hasn’t been a full accounting of the national museum’s vast holdings from even before the war.
By the museum’s front steps, in the shadow of the main building, Qassem Hassan Nasser leaned in close with a camera and snapped a high-resolution photo of a wooden artifact. Inside, other staff members worked to incorporate paper records into a database. It was all part of a gargantuan effort to stitch together a comprehensive inventory.
There have been some modest successes in tracking down looted antiquities. In January, Sudanese authorities showed off a haul of some 570 items taken from the national museum, including scarab-shaped amulets, along with ancient vases and figurines. They were recovered in Port Sudan, probably before they were to be transported outside the country.
Sudan is hardly the first war-ravaged Middle Eastern nation to have its heritage stolen and sold, said Amr Al-Azm, a Syrian archaeologist and co-director of the Antiquities Trafficking and Heritage Anthropology Research Project.
“In Iraq, Syria, in Lebanon, in Sudan, in Yemen; wherever you have antiquities, it’s a revenue stream,” he said. Much of it can be subsistence looting, with people selling antiquities because their livelihoods have been disrupted by war.
“Then you come to the organized side of things: In all these places, you have a network of criminals and smugglers, and when you get armed, non-state actors, they tap into it. Then they institutionalize the process.”
The money from selling the antiquities is yet another input enriching the RSF’s financial empire, which experts count as one of the world’s largest non-state economies. The funds have enabled it to purchase fighters’ loyalties, as well as advanced materiel, such as drones.
Many looted items appear on Facebook and channels for the encrypted messaging app Telegram, which are based outside the country, Junaid said.
“The scale and the systematic nature of the looting demonstrates this is no longer an isolated or opportunistic case,” he said, “but rather a broader illicit trade taking Sudan’s cultural identity and historical legacy.”
