'Pheromone maxxing': Men avoid showers before dates to boost attraction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:59:40 UTC
18:59:40 KST

'Pheromone maxxing': Men avoid showers before dates to boost attraction
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, September 8: Papers discuss UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Also, could AI change what it means to be human? Finally, "pheromone maxxing" is in; showers are out.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government is set to ban trade with some Israeli settlements in the West Bank, The Times reports. The sanctions come as a response to Israeli plans to construct more than 1,000 settler homes in a key area of the West Bank. Burnham also promised to take a tougher stance in support of Gaza and against the destruction of the two-state solution there.
Fox News reports that Burnham risks clashing with Trump, saying the move could "create an early point of friction" between the two leaders. The Jerusalem Post notes that Israel's Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the expulsion of the British ambassador. Smotrich wrote on X that Israel would not be a "doormat trampled by an antisemitic government" and called the UK a "country conquered by radical Islam" that's trying to save itself by attacking Israel.
Next, The Atlantic writes that "AI is already changing what it means to be human". The author warns that the normalisation of AI bots will come at human expense – the actual dehumanisation of humans. The author argues that this could gradually reshape human moral thinking: humans could move away from love, care and relationships towards cold calculation and robot-like decisions.
Another article in The Washington Post looks into something very human: gut feelings. The author of the piece researches gut feelings and walks us through when to trust them. What we call gut feelings are simply neurochemical signals from the brain that lead to a change in the stomach's electrical rhythms. She says that statistically speaking, gut feelings "aren't necessarily right". They are a bit like the butterflies we feel on a first date – rather inconclusive. She adds that we need to treat gut feelings as stop signs – it doesn't necessarily mean we are doing something wrong; it just means we should slow down and look around before we continue.
Finally, The Indian Express writes about "pheromone maxxing". This latest trend encourages men to embrace their natural body smell and simply skip showering and putting on perfume or deodorant before a date. It stems from the masculinist "looksmaxxing culture" and is built around the idea that stronger and smellier pheromones could attract women more easily. The paper spoke to a psychologist who said that when someone feels insecure, simple and fast hacks like this are used to address deeper issues of "self-esteem, social anxiety or relationship patterns".
You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.

Plane carrying American family of 4 goes missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:58:19 UTC
18:58:19 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
A plane carrying four members of an American family went missing while flying from the Bahamas to Florida, prompting authorities to launch a search.
The five-seat PA-34 Piper departed Great Harbour Cay on Monday for Opa-locka, Florida, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said. Air traffic control later lost contact with the aircraft about 13 miles (21 km) west of Andros Island, the Bahamas’ largest island.
“On the flight this morning was my uncle Mario Lamar, his wife Lili Lamar and two of his grandchildren, Christian Sosa and Sofi Sosa,” Silvi Larrieu, a family member, told CNN.
Police were alerted after receiving a report that “an aircraft may have gone down in the waters off Red Bays,” a settlement on northwestern Andros Island.
Flight-tracking site FlightRadar24 showed the aircraft, tail number N212ML, apparently circling off the Bahamian coast before vanishing from radar. Heavy thunderstorms were reported in the area at the time, although it remains unclear if weather contributed to the incident.
The US Coast Guard said it was helping the Royal Bahamas Defense Force search about 15 miles (24 km) off Andros Island and had deployed an HC-144 Ocean Sentry surveillance aircraft.
An initial search was delayed by bad weather but was expected to resume when conditions improved. 
Police said, “Efforts to locate the aircraft and its occupants remain a priority.”

Gun requirement pulled from Fleet Solid Support contract
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:57:41 BST
18:57:41 KST

The automatic small calibre gun requirement has been removed from the Fleet Solid Support manufacture contract with Navantia UK, at a cost of £1.704 million recorded as a constructive loss, because it no longer matches the Royal Navy’s likely future gun solution, according to a written answer published on Monday.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked about the loss disclosed in the Ministry of Defence annual report and accounts for 2025 to 2026.
Mr Pollard said: “The Fleet Solid Support (FSS) Automatic Small Calibre Gun requirement, which formed part of the manufacture contract with Navantia UK, has been removed from the contract as it is no longer aligned with the Royal Navy’s (RN) most likely future gun solution. The RN gun rationalisation programme, introduced since the FSS manufacture contract was placed, aims to reduce the number of gun variants and bring commonality across the RN’s Fleet, providing longer term value for money.”
Setting out the reasoning behind accepting a loss now, he said: “Although this decision has resulted in some financial loss, changing the requirement now avoids incurring greater losses at a later stage, associated with fitting and then replacing an incompatible system. The FSS ships will now be designed to accept a range of future gun systems that will enhance our warfighting readiness and deterrence.”
The Royal Navy has accumulated a considerable number of small and medium calibre gun types across its fleet over the years, each carrying its own ammunition, spares, training pipeline and maintenance requirement, and the rationalisation programme Mr Pollard describes exists to reduce that spread rather than to change what any individual ship can do.
The saving from commonality is felt in the supply chain rather than on the gun mounting. A fleet operating fewer variants holds fewer distinct ammunition natures, trains fewer specialists and stocks fewer unique components, which is where the longer term value for money he refers to comes from.
The three Fleet Solid Support ships are being built by Navantia UK to carry ammunition, stores and provisions to the carrier strike group and the wider fleet, replacing a capability the Royal Fleet Auxiliary has been without since the Fort-class ships left service.

Germany resorts to legal jugglery to skirt ICJ case over complicity in Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:54:49 UTC
18:54:49 KST

Rather than reckon with its continued diplomatic and military support for Israel during its genocidal war on Gaza, Germany is challenging the legality of a case brought against it at the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
German representatives on Monday challenged ICJ jurisdiction in the case brought by Nicaragua that accuses Berlin of providing political, financial, and military support for the genocide in Gaza.
Hearings in the case are taking place in The Hague.
During the first round of hearings, the German delegation presented its preliminary objections to the court’s judges, arguing that the case cannot proceed because Israel is not a party to the case.
Julia Monar, a legal adviser at the German foreign ministry, said Berlin’s support for Israel did not amount to a violation of international law.
She cited Germany’s financial contributions to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) as evidence of its support for the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination.
Monar also said Germany suspended the approval of export licences for weapons that could be used in Gaza between August 8 and November 23 2025.
She said the processing of arms export licences resumed only towards the end of 2025, arguing that the decision was directly linked to the ceasefire agreement reached in October 2025.
After Germany lifted the export restrictions on November 24 2025, German defence manufacturers were granted licences to supply Israel with military equipment worth $929 million between January and June this year.
According to German magazine Der Spiegel, the information was contained in a written response by the German Economy and Energy Ministry to a parliamentary question submitted by the opposition Left Party, or Die Linke.
Other German representatives said the ICJ must drop the case because there’s no argument between Nicaragua and Germany and the matter falls outside the court’s jurisdiction.
Germany will complete its defence on Wednesday during the second round of hearings, while Nicaragua will present its oral arguments to the court on Tuesday and Thursday.
Nicaragua filed a case against Germany at the ICJ on March 1 2024, accusing Berlin of “facilitating the commission of genocide” by providing Israel with political, financial, and military support.
Nicaragua argued that Germany was Israel’s second-largest arms supplier and could not have been unaware that the munitions were being used in the genocide in Gaza.
It also pointed out that Germany had sent tank shells, drones, and warship ammunition to Israel while cutting aid to Palestinians.

Kenya offers amnesty for migrants after Burundians rush to leave
Government spokesman urges undocumented nationals from other East African countries to formally register at embassies.
Kenya has offered a temporary amnesty to undocumented East African migrants after hundreds of Burundians rushed to their country’s embassy in Nairobi seeking travel documents to return home.
Kenyan President William Ruto’s government last week ordered authorities to close small businesses run by foreigners, starting on Monday.

The order, which Kenya’s Ministry of Trade said applied to foreigners operating without work permits, led to chaos outside Burundi’s embassy on Monday, with some Burundians saying they had been threatened by neighbours since Ruto’s remarks.
Kenya has long drawn migrants from the East African Community, an intergovernmental organisation that allows freedom of movement for citizens of its eight member states, including Burundi.
About 16,000 Burundian migrants and refugees live in the country, according to the United Nations, many of them operating small street businesses.
On Monday, despite no signs of a crackdown, crowds queued outside Burundi’s embassy from the morning to await papers that would allow them to travel home.
Some reported harassment and violence following Ruto’s directive. Jean-Baptiste Ndayizeye, a pastor, told the AFP news agency that his neighbours had been attacked and robbed. “They’ve expelled us like animals,” he said.
Later on Monday, a spokesman for Ruto’s administration urged undocumented nationals from other East African countries, and specifically from Burundi, to formally register at their embassies.
“For the duration of this designated registration period, all individuals undergoing registration will be presumed legally present in the Republic of Kenya,” their statement said.
“This window is designed to bring our brothers and sisters out of the shadows, ensuring they can access health, banking, and legal protections without fear.”
The government also issued a directive to security agencies and local authorities that foreign nationals were not to be “subjected to arbitrary harassment or discrimination”.
“Any elements seeking to exploit recent directives to fuel xenophobic sentiment or mistreat our neighbours will face the full force of the law,” it read.
Following the reports of harassment, Kenya’s junior foreign minister Korir Sing’Oei visited the embassy, apologised to Burundians and assured them police would protect areas where violence had been reported.
“For so many years, you have lived in Kenya together with the Kenyan nationals. You have stayed in peace as neighbours,” he said, promising to help Burundians obtain papers or return home voluntarily.
Critics of President Ruto have accused him of blaming foreigners for Kenya’s economic difficulties before an election next year.

Brazil’s cruise missile testing resumes after years of delay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:52:42 UTC
18:52:42 KST

- Avibras Aeroco and the Brazilian Army successfully test-fired the MTC-300 cruise missile on August 26, resuming certification testing after a roughly four-year pause.
- The missile can strike targets up to 300 kilometers away, and Brazil's army has also revived plans for an upgraded Block II version with improved range and guidance.
Brazil’s Avibras Aeroco and the Brazilian Army completed a successful test launch of the country’s first indigenous cruise missile on August 26, a milestone in a certification process that stalled for roughly four years while the missile’s manufacturer worked through a severe financial crisis.
The test took place at the Army Evaluation Centre’s Marambaia Test Range in Rio de Janeiro, according to a joint statement from Avibras Aeroco and the Brazilian Army. The missile, known as the Tactical Cruise Missile or MTC, is part of the ASTROS artillery system’s family of guided munitions and is designed to strike targets up to 300 kilometers (186 miles) away. The companies said the exercise met all objectives set for this phase of testing.
The MTC-300, also called the AV-MTC 300, has a range of 300 kilometers, a diameter of 450 millimeters and a length of 5.4 meters (17.7 feet). Each ASTROS launch unit currently in Brazilian Army service can carry two of the missiles. The system uses a combination of satellite and inertial navigation to hit within roughly 30 meters of its target, and Brazil has designed two warhead options for it: a high-explosive version and a cluster configuration carrying 66 submunitions. A turbojet engine built by Brazilian company Turbomachine, producing up to 499 kilograms-force (1,100 pounds-force) of thrust, propels the missile to high subsonic speeds of around 1,000 km/h (620 mph) at cruising altitudes between 200 and 800 meters.
Brazil’s army and Avibras began developing the missile in 2012 under the ASTROS Strategic Programme, intending to give the country’s rocket artillery system enough range to strike well beyond its immediate region. Testing stalled in 2022, when Avibras fell into a financial crisis tied to roughly 800 million reais ($133 million) in debt, triggering a prolonged strike involving around 900 employees and effectively freezing the company’s defense programs. The situation began to turn around in May, when Avibras reached an agreement to settle its outstanding labor debts, clearing the way for the company’s restructuring under the new name Avibras Aeroco and the resumption of missile testing.
According to the Brazilian Army, the August test served as part of the missile’s final flight-verification testing, ahead of a last remaining test that will use a live warhead, the final step required before the MTC-300 can be formally validated for service.
Brazil’s army has also revived plans for an upgraded version of the missile, known as MTC Block II, according to guidelines the army published in August for its broader ASTROS-FOGOS Strategic Programme. The Block II upgrade calls for adding an unspecified terminal guidance system, extending the missile’s range and improving its warhead, changes the army has linked to new requirements for coastal defense and for striking moving targets, a description that suggests the upgraded missile could eventually engage ships. The Block II project remains officially listed as “not started.”
Officials attending the August test included Brig. Gen. João Paulo Zago, head of the Army Evaluation Centre; Brig. Gen. Marcelo Gurgel do Amaral Silva, manager of the army’s FOGOS Strategic Programme; and Brig. Gen. Moisés da Paixão Junior, manager of the Field Artillery Sub-programme, alongside representatives from the Army Projects Office, the Manufacturing Directorate, the Military Institute of Engineering and the Army Technology Centre.
Avibras’s pause since 2022 gave rise to competition it did not previously face in Brazil’s missile industry. Other Brazilian firms have since disclosed their own cruise missile programs, including the AATD, reported to have a range of up to 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles) using the same turbojet engine as the MTC-300, and the MCX, described as an export-friendly medium-range cruise missile with a satellite datalink. Separately, Brazilian company SIATT integrated Brazil’s MANSUP anti-ship missile onto Marine Corps ASTROS launchers in 2025, despite legal action from Avibras at the time, and is developing its own coastal defense missile system.

Spain seizes more than 1.2 tons of cocaine hidden in coconut shipment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:52:35 UTC
18:52:35 KST

Alyssa Mcmurtry
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Spanish authorities have seized more than 1.2 tons of cocaine hidden in a shipment of coconuts in the southern province of Seville, Spanish police said Tuesday.
Authorities intercepted 1,238 kilograms (2,729 pounds) of cocaine concealed at the back of a truck trailer and beneath pallets carrying coconuts, according to a statement.
Two people were arrested on suspicion of drug trafficking.
The operation began in December after investigators identified a company in Dos Hermanas, Seville, that they suspected was being used to bring drugs into Spain.
Investigators later identified a suspicious shipping container and placed it under close surveillance.
Authorities moved to intercept the shipment just as the driver was preparing to deliver it to a warehouse. The shipment was intercepted as it was being received, while searches of two properties in Seville province led to the seizure of cash and electronic devices deemed to have significant evidentiary value.
The investigation remains open, and authorities said further arrests are possible.
Spain is a major entry point for cocaine into the EU, particularly for shipments arriving from Latin America.
Spanish authorities seized 124 tons of cocaine in 2024, accounting for 37% of all cocaine seized across the EU that year, according to the European Union Drugs Agency's latest European Drug Report.
Spain, France and Belgium together accounted for 67% of the 330 tons seized across the bloc in 2024.
While the overall quantity of cocaine seized declined from the previous year, the number of seizures increased, with the EU agency pointing to criminal groups' growing use of smaller, fragmented shipments to make detection more difficult.

Russian strikes killed two people in Kyiv overnight, while a Moscow-backed official said a Ukrainian attack also killed two people in Crimea, ending a three-day halt in attacks Tuesday.
The warring countries had paused attacks on each other's capitals over the weekend as U.S. envoys made a renewed push to narrow the differences between Moscow and Kyiv and steer them toward a peace settlement.
With neither side able to deliver a knockout blow in the war that started after Moscow’s February 2022 invasion and with armies on the front line largely stuck, Russia and Ukraine have in recent months intensified their air war in an effort to grind each other down.
The visit to Moscow and Kyiv by Washington envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff produced no significant breakthrough that might stop the fighting.
The main targets of Russia's overnight attack were Kyiv and the southern Odesa region. At least 16 people were wounded in Kyiv, Ukraine’s Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said. There was no immediate tally of casualties in Odesa.
Explosions were heard in Kyiv for nearly five hours, according to Vyhivskyi. More than 50 sites were damaged in Kyiv during the Russian overnight attack Tuesday, including residential buildings, dormitories, schools, shops, gas stations and a flour production plant, he said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called it "a horrific attack" and accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of undermining U.S. peace efforts.
"His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy," Sybiha said on X, referring to Putin. "Strike after strike on residential buildings brings him no closer to winning this war – it is nothing but senseless terror."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram that the attack was complex and appeared deliberately designed to cause maximum damage, involving ballistic and cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles and Shahed drones.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces overnight launched a massive strike with "land-, air-, and sea-based precision weapons, as well as long-range unmanned aerial vehicles" on Ukrainian military industry facilities. It provided a detailed list of its targets.
The targets included places storing Ukrainian drones and cruise missiles, as well transport, logistics and distribution centers for military cargo in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, the ministry added.
Infrastructure in the port of Chornomorsk in the Odesa region used for "unloading military cargo" also was struck. Additionally, the Russian forces hit a tanker carrying fuel and lubricants for the Ukrainian armed forces, the ministry said.
In the meantime, a Ukrainian attack on Crimea killed two people and wounded one, the peninsula’s Russian-installed Gov. Sergei Aksyonov said.
The Russian attack caused damage and fires in at least five districts of the capital, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. The Kyiv City Military Administration said civilian infrastructure was damaged in at least 16 locations.
A 26-story non-residential building was hit in the Holosiivskyi district. Rescuers saved one person during a search and two people were evacuated from an apartment in a 16-story residential building, officials said.
People also were trapped in a five-story, residential building in Solomianskyi district, according to authorities.
Kyiv resident Iryna Barisenkova, 61, said she heard explosions while traveling on public transport and was told there was a large fire near the Darnytskyi Vehicle Repair Plant on the capital’s left bank.
"Everything was thundering on the left bank," Barisenkova said. "It was just brutal."
Barisenkova said she had slept well during the previous two nights while Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Kyiv and then stayed in the city.
"We got some rest, thanks to them," she said. "Let them come more often so they don’t shell us."

Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has taken the unprecedented decision to expel 10 members of staff of the Russian Embassy.
Source: Orbán on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Orbán said that 10 members of the Russian diplomatic mission "had engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention".
A representative of the Hungarian Foreign Ministry has informed the Russian ambassador in Budapest that the individuals must leave the country.
However, Orbán stressed that the decision does not imply any break in diplomatic relations with Russia.
Quote: "This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty. It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules."
Details: The decision is unprecedented in terms of the number of diplomats Hungary is expelling. Viktor Orbán's previous government took a similar step in 2018, when Hungary expelled just one member of the Russian diplomatic mission in solidarity with the UK following the poisoning of former Russian spy Sergei Skripal on British soil.
Background:
- In 2022, an investigation by Hungarian outlet Direkt36 and the RTL channel found that while most EU countries expelled Russian diplomats following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in Hungary their number increased by almost a third.
- Earlier, journalists working with European security services established that Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin had tasked a group of political strategists and Russian military intelligence with interfering in Hungary's parliamentary elections in April to ensure Viktor Orbán's victory. The plan involved stationing experts in social media manipulation at the Russian Embassy in Budapest.
- In May, Hungary quietly expelled a Russian intelligence officer who, operating under diplomatic cover, had infiltrated right-wing and foreign policy think tanks close to Viktor Orbán's government.

Presidential commissioner: Russia again using American processors in Kinzhals, Russian equivalents failed
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:50:26 EEST
18:50:26 KST

Russia continues to use foreign electronic components in complex weapons systems, including American processors in Kinzhal missiles, stated Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk in a comment to the Interfax-Ukraine agency.
"In 2023, Russia replaced American Texas Instruments processors with its own microcircuits. However, in a newer 'Zarya-61' sample found in a missile shot down in May this year, this replacement is no longer present. American processors are being used again," he said.
According to him, the research results directly indicate that Russian equivalents failed to yield the required result. At the same time, Russia continues to receive foreign electronics for missile and drone production through various supply chains.
In particular, 96 foreign components were identified in a Geran-4 drone shot down on August 12 in Kyiv region. Among the manufacturers are Texas Instruments, Amphenol, Diodes Incorporated, Kyocera AVX, Kemet, ON Semiconductor, and Vishay Intertechnology. Seven components were produced in 2026, and three more in 2025.
In an Iskander-M missile found at a strike site in Kyiv region in early July, 147 foreign-made components were discovered, including those produced in the U.S., Belarus, Switzerland, Germany, China, and Japan. At least 21 components were produced in 2025, with 2026-manufactured components also present.
Vlasiuk noted that Russia uses electronics of varying ages. Specifically, a "Zarya-61" board assembled in May 2025 contained components manufactured in 2021–2024, while another board contained a Texas Instruments processor marked 1986 and AMD microcircuits from 1996.
"Meaning Russia can use foreign electronics that are not the most modern if they remain suitable for a specific system, while parallelly incorporating newer components," he said.
According to Vlasiuk, the Iskander-M also contains 36 Russian-made components and 11 Belarusian ones, though this is insufficient for complex systems.
"They have to combine their own component base with foreign ones, while sourcing them across different markets and through various supply chains," he noted.
"Every manufacturer, every law enforcement agency, or export control body has all the information sufficient to stop such deliveries to Russia," Vlasiuk emphasized.

Expert insights: Who notices the (Danish) elephant in the room?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:50:00 UTC
18:50:00 KST

The author: Signe Biering Röpke is an executive coach, trained in psychology, with a background in diplomacy. She is also a career columnist for The Copenhagen Post.
When I began working as a Danish diplomat nearly 30 years ago, we received no cultural training. We were trained in foreign policy, strategy, administration and financial management. Culture was something the ‘other’ had. Something to notice when posted abroad, not something we ourselves brought into the picture.
And I did notice and learn – sometimes successfully, sometimes through fairly painful mistakes.
Today, the Foreign Service prepares diplomats to understand not only other cultures but also Danish culture. That second part is crucial. Learning about another culture from the outside is one thing. Seeing your own culture from the outside is quite different.
And culture is still challenging for Danes to ‘see’. Danish culture is remarkably good at not being seen by Danes.
Many Danes experience Danish culture as the practical and sensible way. Flat hierarchies make sense. Informality makes sense. Trust seems natural. Speaking Danish when most people in the room are Danish is practical. If internationals remain here long enough, we assume, they will eventually understand why our way works rather well.
In the Danish cultural imagination, our culture is not one possible way of organising society and working life, weighed against many others and found preferable to us. It is simply the way things are done. This is a mental habit most of us are not aware we have. It rarely occurs to us that a colleague might see something quite different, because it rarely occurs to us that there is something else to see.
This is where things get complicated for internationals trying to raise cultural questions at work.
If you point out that colleagues repeatedly switch to Danish, you may be told that it mostly happens when no international is in the room – which obviously does not solve the issue for you. If you ask about hierarchy, you may be talked through the organigram, without mentioning informal networks. If you ask how opportunities arise, you may be shown the procedure for career progression, without clarifying you who usually gets promoted.
Danish work culture prides itself on being direct, transparent and flat-ish, and much of the time this is true. But a great deal of what happens – who meets over coffee, who is taken seriously in a meeting, what “flat” means in practice – is implicit, part of the tacit knowledge. We don’t know that we know how to navigate our own culture.
This is why an international’s observations and questions often create social awkwardness rather than being received as helpful.
Culture is rarely the only explanation for what happens. Personality, professional background, organisational habits, power and economics all matter too. But culture may still be one part of the explanation.
The issue cannot change if nobody speaks about it. But it is difficult to raise it in a way Danish colleagues can hear.
And that tells us something about who holds the cultural power.
Still, we need to talk about it, even if doing so is an act of psychological courage: staying with an uncomfortable observation and continuing to name something others don’t name, without having to be the one to ‘fix it’ just because you name it.
How can you talk about culture while consuming as little of your own energy as possible?
It is worth adding that – for the Dane – hearing the observation without becoming defensive takes courage as well. A ‘brave’ response would be to wonder why they themselves didn’t see the elephant – and ask what it looks like from where the international is standing.

Swiss simulate landslides using 3D model of Blatten
Researchers at the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research (SLF) have created a detailed 3D model of the Blatten region in southwestern Switzerland to study mass movements. The experiments are intended to help assess natural hazards more reliably.
The experiments are intended to improve the reliability of computer models which cantonal and municipal authorities will use in future to assess risks to settlements and infrastructure, the SLF announced on Tuesday. For the experiments, the landscape around Blatten was recreated on a scale of 1:577.
The model is housed in a former military bunker near Davos. It measures 5.4 metres by 4.5 metres and consists of 56 individual parts, which took around 100 days to print. According to the researchers, this represents a long-term investment in research.
More
                
        Climate solutions

In the experiments, a mixture of water, sand and clay is channelled over the model. Cameras, lasers and sensors measure, among other things, the speed, the discharge level and the deposits resulting from the artificially generated mass movement.
“We are currently particularly interested in the influence of terrain curvature on flow dynamics,” said Johan Gaume, head of the Alpine Landslides research group at the SLF.

Rutte: coronavirus curfew and school closures were “unavoidable”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Rutte: coronavirus curfew and school closures were “unavoidable”
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Former prime minister Mark Rutte has defended the nationwide curfew imposed during the coronavirus lockdown, insisting it was “unavoidable”.
Giving evidence to the parliamentary inquiry into the government’s pandemic response, Rutte said there was “no alternative” to the drastic measure, which was in force for three months until the end of 2021.
Earlier witnesses including Hubert Bruls, the chair of the group of regional safety boards that were responsible for enforcing the lockdown rules, questioned whether the curfew was effective and said the government had failed to explain why it was necessary.
Riots broke out in several towns and cities during protests against the curfew, while in a poll by RTL this year 35% of people named it as the “most severe” of all the pandemic restrictions.
But Rutte said the curfew and other unpopular measures, such as shutting the schools, were essential to keep infections down and stop the health service reaching the “code black” crisis point.
He also defended the decision to close schools for a third time in December 2021 as the delta variant spread from the UK, after the education minister in his cabinet, Arie Slob, earlier said he was against the shutdown.
Delta variant
“The Delta variant meant that we had to take lockdown measures from October and November,” Rutte said.
“Then the Omicron variant appeared and all we knew was that it was highly infections. If it had been as debilitating as the Delta variant, code black would have been inevitable.”
Rutte also said he clashed with health minister Hugo de Jonge over vaccination policy. He was willing to set an example as prime minister by taking the jab, but it should be a matter of individual choice, while De Jonge believed the government should press people to take responsibility.
Rutte added that strict rules such as curfews would not have been needed if everyone had stuck to the basic rules announced at the start of the pandemic in March 2020.
“If everyone had said: I’ll keep to the one and a half metre rule, sneeze into my elbow, not shake hands and ventilate enough, then in theory we wouldn’t have had to take those measures,” he said.

Second-hand smoke causes 1.7 mln deaths globally: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:45:57 UTC
18:45:57 KST

Notices warning against littering, smoking, and unauthorized entry ,written in multiple languages, are seen outside an apartment building near Shinjuku Station in Tokyo on September 7, 2026. (AFP Photo)
More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published on Sept. 8 in The Lancet.
Tobacco remains a leading cause of disease globally, the study said, noting many “non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke” were among the estimate total of 8 million people who died in 2023 of smoking-related illnesses.
“Exposure to second-hand smoke is a globally recognized health risk, with no safe level of inhalation,” it said.
By reviewing studies published in the U.S. National Institutes of Health database PubMed along with population surveys, Sept. 8's study sought to estimate the prevalence of exposure to second-hand smoke and quantify the burden of disease in 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Among the approximately 2.7 billion people exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023 were 767 million children aged 0 to 14, the study found.
This exposure is estimated to have resulted in 1.66 million premature deaths and causing premature disability and illness, leading with ischemic heart disease, a heart condition caused by insufficient oxygen supply to the heart muscle.
In children, exposure to second-hand smoke is estimated to have caused 5.2 million respiratory tract infections in 2023, it said.
People in proximity to someone lighting up are exposed to both the “sidestream smoke” from the burning tobacco product and smoke exhaled by the active smoker, the study explained.
“The sidestream component, which dominates the air non-smokers breathe, is unfiltered, carrying higher per-unit concentrations of the toxic and carcinogenic compounds” than that being inhaled by the active smoker, it said.

Tehran metro takes on a new role in urban tourism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

Tehran metro takes on a new role in urban tourism
TEHRAN - Tourism maps have been installed at 24 metro stations in Tehran to help passengers discover historical, cultural and tourism attractions located around the stations, the Tehran Municipality Tourism Headquarters said.
“Tehran, with more than 10 million people and an extensive public transportation network, has considerable potential for using the metro for tourism,” Amir Ghasemi, head of the headquarters, said at a ceremony unveiling the maps on Tuesday.
“The initiative was designed to make greater use of Tehran’s extensive metro network as a tool for urban tourism, in addition to its conventional role as a public transport system.”
He added that the idea of using the metro network to promote tourism was first raised about two years ago and was subsequently developed by the municipal tourism headquarters with the participation of people who had conducted field research on Tehran’s history and attractions.
Ghasemi cited Tokyo, Paris, London and Barcelona as examples of cities where metro systems have been used from a tourism perspective, saying Tehran was also moving in that direction.
He said the maps were developed as tourism infrastructure rather than as a conventional contracted project, with field researchers documenting attractions and features across the city.
A team based at Tehran’s Aslani Historical and Cultural House mapped metro routes according to nearby tourism attractions and prepared the maps unveiled under the initiative, he said.
According to Ghasemi, an initial assessment identified 40 metro stations with significant tourism potential. Maps have so far been installed at 24 stations, including at entrances, exits and on platform areas.
The assessment covered historical sites, museums, shopping and entertainment facilities, green tourism attractions, religious sites and essential public services. It also considered connections with other forms of public transportation, including Tehran’s bus rapid transit network.
Ghasemi said most information about commercial, medical, architectural and environmental sites had been collected through fieldwork over the past two years. As a result, facilities established during the past four or five months may not yet appear on the maps and will be added in future revisions, he said.
The maps generally cover attractions within a 500-metre radius of each station. The radius for Tajrish station was expanded because the Simin and Jalal House and Nima House are located about 700 meters away.
Ghasemi said the selection of stations was based primarily on Tehran’s historical fabric and tourism potential, with an effort to include less-known areas.
More than 1,020 symbols and graphic categories have been used in the maps. Their color schemes correspond to the colors assigned to Tehran’s metro lines to make them easier to read.
The stations covered by the project include Tajrish, Haqqani, Taleghani, Saadi, Imam Khomeini, 15 Khordad, Khayyam and Mohammadiyeh on Line 1; Baharestan, Mellat and Hasanabad on Line 2; Moniriyeh on Line 3; and Darvazeh Dowlat, Darvazeh Shemiran, Theater-e Shahr, Shohada Square and Ferdowsi on Line 4.
On Line 6, the selected stations are Maryam-e Moqaddas (Holy Mary), Laleh Park and Kargar, while Qiyam, Molavi, Helal Ahmar and Milad Tower are included on Line 7.
The maps for Milad Tower and Haqqani stations have not yet been installed because they require further updating and completion, Ghasemi said.
Ghasemi also called for greater use of the metro in organized tourism tours, saying municipal districts had been informed about the initiative.

Germans in Finland express concern following far-right AfD's state election win

The far-right Alternative for Germany's (AfD's) election win in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt has not come as a surprise to Germans living in Finland.
The AfD garnered 43.8 percent of the vote, well ahead of its nearest rival, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which came in distant second on 17.2 percent.
Robert Stark, who holds dual Finnish-German citizenship but has lived in the Helsinki region for nine years, told Yle that the AfD's rise in popularity has been evident for a decade.
"For the past 10 years, the AfD has been the only party that has been setting up bouncy castles at family celebrations. It has been the only party that has been present and talked with people," Stark said.
He added that there should be more awareness in Finland about the fact that AfD is a pro-Russian party that opposes the EU placing sanctions on Russia.
"They don't even talk about war, but about a special military operation."
In his view, many Germans want to see the return of more traditional values in the country, to a time before so-called woke culture. Russian President Vladimir Putin's rhetoric about the ills of Western society therefore appeals to them, he noted.
"This is a bit like the 1920s and 30s, but even more extreme, when the world's richest person supports Germany's far-right party," Stark said, referring to the period when Germany transitioned from a fragile democracy into a totalitarian Nazi dictatorship.
AfD appeal to people's dissatisfaction
Pastor Hans-Christian Daniel, a resident of Espoo, moved to Finland over 50 years ago but told Yle that he still follows his native country's politics closely.
He believes the AfD's success is down to the fact that the party knows how to appeal to people's dissatisfaction with emotions instead of facts — whether the topic is the price of gasoline or unemployment figures.
"The success in the elections was due to AfD saying it is an alternative for Germany, but they don't show what that alternative actually would be," he said.
Daniel is especially concerned about the AfD's immigration policies and rhetoric, which he believes are reminiscent of the views espoused by Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party about Jewish people during the 1920s and 1930s.
"Back then they said "Kauft nicht bei Juden," meaning don't buy from Jews. AfD's message about immigrants is very similar," Daniel said.
AfD's victory is very significant, as a far-right party has not governed a German state since the end of World War II. The party however fell short of an outright majority, meaning it will need to form alliances with other parties or individuals in order to take power in the eastern state.

The unending Iran war and Israel’s new low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:43:11 UTC
18:43:11 KST

Somewhere in America this week, a young woman is calculating whether she can make her student loan payment, her car payment, and her credit card minimum before the month ends.
A strategist is calculating whether her debt is the right price for her body in a ground war against Iran.
The average American carries $63,500 in total debt as of 2026, a burden concentrated most heavily among the 25-to-44 age cohort the Pentagon needs most, accumulated not through recklessness but through the ordinary arithmetic of surviving in a political economy that privatised education, defunded public institutions, and handed the next generation the bill.
That bill is now being proposed back to her as an exchange: twenty-four or thirty-six months in uniform on Iranian soil, and her debt would be discharged.
Jaff calls this voluntary enlistment. His proposal describes a state that created the conditions of economic coercion and would now harvest that coercion as military labour, with no fingerprints on the compulsion because the mechanism is financial rather than legal.
Voluntary only in the sense that a person drowning is free to choose which hand pulls them out.
The strategist who devised the diabolical plan is purportedly a retired Canadian Armed Forces officer who also claims to be “an expert in international security, crisis management, and geopolitical risk”.
The fact that an Israeli news portal published the so-called ‘opinion’ is itself a reflection on Israeli society and its intelligentsia, and the moral depths to which they have fallen over the years, waging unnecessary wars across multiple fronts and constantly keeping the region on the boil.
Sovereign debt as imperial labour
Every American war has found the economic mechanism that converts the most financially exposed generation into military labour.
The GI Bill for the Depression-era poor. College deferments that sent working-class Americans to Vietnam while the affluent studied. Citizenship pathways that enlisted non-citizen recruits after 9/11.
The Iran war has found its proposed mechanism in the $1.86 trillion student debt burden, which Jaff proposes selectively discharging in exchange for military service.
What distinguishes this proposal from its predecessors is not the desperation it reflects but the candour.
Previous mechanisms concealed the coercive logic inside the language of patriotism, opportunity, and civic duty.
Jaff's proposal openly calls for the state to discharge the debt it permitted to accumulate, through the institutions it defunded, against the generation it failed, in exchange for bodies it needs for a war it cannot staff through any other means.
The legal question of whether this constitutes compelled service is less important than the political one.
Consent obtained against conditions of severe economic dependency, where the alternative to enlistment is decades of debt servitude in a labour market that cannot absorb the generation it produced, is not consent in any sense that the word has historically carried moral weight.
What Jaff's proposal presents as voluntary enlistment is more precisely a population whose options have been so systematically narrowed that the state's offer of relief functions as compulsion without requiring compulsion's legal form.
Under Jaff's proposal, the Pentagon would not need a draft when economic conditions could make enlistment the rational choice for millions of people who had no hand in engineering those conditions.
The debt proposal is not the only instrument this strategic vision has produced.
Self-determination as imperial weapon
The ICJ affirmed in its 2004 Advisory Opinion that the right of peoples to self-determination has an erga omnes character. In its 2024 Advisory Opinion on Israel's policies and practices in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, the Court further held that, in cases of foreign occupation, the right to self-determination constitutes a peremptory norm of international law, or jus cogens.
Yet the architects of this proposal have spent seven decades watching Security Council resolutions on Palestine and Kashmir gather dust, dismissing liberation struggles as terrorism when their success threatened strategic interests, and treating the principle as a procedural inconvenience rather than a binding obligation.
Now they propose to deploy that same principle as an instrument of partition against a sovereign state they need to dismember.
The record is specific and verifiable. Fourteen Security Council resolutions on Kashmir remain unimplemented since 1948.
The US has used its Security Council position to obstruct resolutions on Palestinian statehood and ceasefire with a consistency that spans administrations, parties, and decades.
The US designated the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine a terrorist organisation in 1997. Jaff now proposes that Congress recognise the independence of minorities within Iranian territory as a coercive instrument of partition, not because Washington's position on liberation movements has changed, but because the geography has.
Jaff's proposal deploys the language of minority recognition and liberation as an instrument of imperial partition when it serves the dismemberment of a resistant state, while contrasting with the denial of the same language to Palestinians and Kashmiris whose liberation threatens the territorial integrity of allied states.
It is the international order functioning as designed.
That a proposal invoking the language of minority liberation to serve the logic of imperial partition appears without caveat or editorial distance in an establishment publication of a state whose founding required the displacement of another people's self-determination, and whose government has spent the last three years arguing before international courts that Palestinian statehood cannot be recognised while simultaneously prosecuting a war that has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, is not a new low in strategic thinking.
It is strategic thinking finally dispensing with the pretence that the principle was ever meant to apply universally.
Taken together, Jaff's two proposals answer a question that strategic discourse has never stated so plainly: that the bodies of economically precarious young Americans and the identities of minority peoples in resistant states are resources to be allocated, discharged, or recognised according to the needs of imperial power.
What has changed is not the logic but the candour, a candour that signals the project no longer requires the consent, the silence, or even the ignorance of the people it is built upon.
That it required a state whose accumulated conduct across Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, and now Iran has progressively dismantled every threshold of restraint for strategic discourse to reach this level of candour about who counts as raw material and who counts as sovereign is itself the measure of how far that threshold has moved.
The question is not whether the proposal is morally wrong. That was settled before it was published.
The real question is whether the international institutions, the allied governments, and the publics whose taxes fund these wars will continue to extend to this project the diplomatic cover, the legal abstention, and the studied silence that have made each successive escalation possible, or whether the candour that produced this proposal will finally produce the reckoning it has made unavoidable.

Ministry hopes to choose location for Estonia's nuclear power plant by spring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:43:00 UTC
18:43:00 KST

Ministry hopes to choose location for Estonia's nuclear power plant by spring
In Estonia, a nuclear power plant can only be built on the coast to ensure sufficient cooling water, but dozens of other requirements must also be met.
The International Atomic Energy Agency's guidelines set out numerous conditions that must be considered when selecting a site for a nuclear power plant. A Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications table lists 40 criteria, Agnes Lihtsa, an adviser on national spatial plans in the ministry's land and spatial policy department, said.
"These are not only nuclear safety requirements, but also geological criteria, hydrological criteria such as the availability of cooling water, as well as what natural or environmental assets would be affected by the project, and socioeconomic criteria," Lihtsa said.
She gave examples of the factors that need to be considered when selecting a site. According to Lihtsa, six potential sites are under consideration, located in the Kunda and Lüganuse areas.
"The most important factor is the availability of cooling water and in Estonia the only place we can get it is from the sea. We don't have a single river with sufficient flow to provide the necessary cooling water, so it has to come from the sea," Lihtsa said.
Even along the coast, there are not many suitable locations, Lihtsa said, as a nationwide spatial analysis conducted in 2023 found.
"Based on the various criteria, the Kunda area and the Lüganuse-Toila area emerged as possibilities. Both are on the coast and each has three potential sites."
Geological conditions are also important, Lihtsa said. "The bedrock on which the plant is built has to be very stable," she said.
Proximity to transmission lines is important so the plant can be connected to substations. There are currently two potential connection points: one substation near the city of Rakvere and another in Püssi. Proximity to ports must also be considered to allow for the delivery of nuclear fuel, for example, or components needed to build the plant.
People generally do not want a nuclear power plant in their backyard, so officials are trying to find a site with as few nearby residents as possible. In August, the ministry also held public information meetings in the municipalities covered by the planning area to gather broad feedback and it received plenty, Lihtsa said.
"Local residents were mainly concerned about how the location of a nuclear power plant would affect property values, groundwater or the natural environment they are accustomed to," Lihtsa said. According to her, the feedback covered the full spectrum, "from simply saying they don't want it to detailed letters dozens of pages long."
The proposals are still being analyzed, but it is already apparent that the process for assessing the potential sites and making a selection will need to be explained in greater detail.
"We will probably need to spell out our methodology even more clearly so that everyone has the same understanding of how the comparison works, how the different sites are assessed and how the preferred site is identified."
The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications hopes to have progressed far enough with its analyses by spring to identify a preliminary site.

Korea’s Hanwha brings lasers and drones to Poland’s biggest defense show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:42:52 UTC
18:42:52 KST

- Hanwha Aerospace and Hanwha Systems are showcasing air defense, laser weapons, unmanned systems and artillery at MSPO 2026 in Poland, building on a partnership dating to 2014.
- Hanwha is pursuing a third K9 howitzer contract with Poland while already building Chunmoo missiles at a new Polish facility under a roughly $4 billion deal signed in December.
South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace and Hanwha Systems opened a joint exhibit at MSPO 2026 in Kielce, Poland, on September 8, presenting an expanded lineup of air defense, unmanned and artillery systems built around the company’s decade-long defense partnership with Warsaw.
The two companies are sharing a stand at the exhibition, which runs through September 11, under the slogan “Proven Partnership. Strategic Capabilities. Sovereign Defence.” Hanwha’s relationship with Poland dates back to 2014, when its K9 chassis was selected for the Polish Krab self-propelled howitzer, and has since expanded through the K9 howitzer program and the Chunmoo rocket launcher system, known in Poland as Homar-K.
The company’s newest offerings center on layered air defense. Hanwha is showing its L-SAM long-range surface-to-air missile launcher, the H-SHORAD short-range air defense system, the H-Shield counter-drone system, and a 40mm wheeled counter-UAS vehicle, all designed to link into Hanwha Systems’ command-and-control network alongside interceptor drones. Hanwha Systems is also displaying Cheon gwang, South Korea’s first operational laser weapon system, along with a 50-kilowatt laser mounted on an armored vehicle and a smaller 20-kilowatt tactical laser vehicle. The company says each laser shot costs roughly 2,000 South Korean won, or about $1.50, and can down a small drone within seconds.
On the ground, Hanwha is presenting its manned-unmanned teaming concept through a display combining the K9A1 howitzer with an unmanned rocket launcher and its H-UGV ground vehicle, an arrangement where the crewed howitzer provides firepower while unmanned systems handle reconnaissance and maneuver, keeping soldiers farther from direct fire. The stand also includes the export version of the K-NIFV infantry fighting vehicle and an active protection system meant to improve vehicle survivability. In the naval domain, Hanwha is showing unmanned surface vessels built for Baltic Sea operations, including the Striker-S, which pairs an unmanned boat with a Chunmoo rocket launcher.
Hanwha is also exhibiting the upgraded K9A2 howitzer alongside a new 155mm ammunition package that includes a trajectory-correcting fuze and a modular propellant charge system intended to improve accuracy. The company is pursuing a third execution contract with Poland for K9 howitzers, a follow-on to earlier deals that have made Poland one of the largest operators of the K9 family. Hanwha’s existing Homar-K contracts with Poland include a roughly $4 billion deal signed in December, covering Chunmoo CGR-080 guided missiles to be built at a dedicated production facility inside Poland, with deliveries beginning in 2030, part of a broader push to localize Korean weapons manufacturing on Polish soil. Hanwha is displaying four Chunmoo guided rocket variants at MSPO alongside maintenance tools including a predictive health-monitoring system and a K9 turret simulator.
On September 9, Hanwha Systems plans to publicly demonstrate a satellite-imagery analysis system for the first time, using artificial intelligence to process electro-optical, infrared and synthetic aperture radar imagery from satellites currently in operation, aiming to automate object detection and flag unusual activity for military analysts.
“Hanwha is proud to be a trusted defense and industrial partner in Poland,” said Jacek Cyrek, CEO of Hanwha Aerospace Europe. “At MSPO 2026, we are expanding our local footprint into air defense, MUM-T, and space AI, building true defense sovereignty and industrial capability together on Polish soil.”

What would Germany's AfD do in first 100 days if it takes power in Saxony-Anhalt?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:42:09 UTC
18:42:09 KST

What would Germany's AfD do in first 100 days if it takes power in Saxony-Anhalt?
BERLIN, Sept 8 - The far-right Alternative for Germany's (AfD) Ulrich Siegmundis the most likely next leader of the eastern state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt after a historic election win.
The 35-year-old former fragrance salesman has laid out 10 points that he would like to achieve in the first 100 days of office as part of his "Vision 2026" election manifesto.
The AfD won nearly 44% of the vote on Sunday, but fell short of an absolute majority in the state legislature. It hopes to poach individual conservative lawmakers to be able to govern.
MEDIA AND CULTURE
Public broadcasters have been one of Siegmund's primary campaign targets, which he says are biased and bloated.
His first point of action would be to withdraw from an agreement between Germany's federal states that regulates media practices.
He said this would be a first step towards abolishing a public broadcasting licence fee of €18.36 ($21.33) a month that households are required to pay to support channels such as ARD and ZDF, regardless of whether they own a television or radio.
In its place, the party would institute a tax-funded model.
Other points include flying Germany's flag at public buildings and starting a "think German" campaign aimed at rekindling national pride.
The proposal would challenge Germany's postwar political culture, which places strong emphasis on remembrance of Nazi crimes and often treats overt displays of nationalism with caution.
An AfD-led government would also offer a 50% subsidy for people who volunteer to help with disaster relief and emergency medical services to get their driver's licences. A licence can cost up to €4,000.
MIGRATION
The AfD candidate also promises "deportations from the first minute," in an echo of U.S. President Donald Trump's election campaign. Siegmund said he would achieve this by significantly increasing the number of spaces to hold people awaiting deportation.
When challenged on the campaign trail, he denied that the deportation would apply to gainfully employed foreigners settled in the state with a legal right to reside and said it would apply only to those with no right to stay.
In schools, he would create separate classrooms for refugee children who have no prospect of remaining in Germany, and his interior ministry would also compel all municipalities to create obligatory work programs for asylum seekers.
GOVERNMENT AND POLITICS
Siegmund promises to cut off taxpayer funds that go towards political foundations, saying he does not want to contribute any more money "for the cronyism of the established parties."
He also wants to reduce the number of ministries through merging functions and avoiding redundancies, and eliminate one ministry entirely - without naming which one.
Siegmund also wants to initiate a review of how the state government responded to the COVID-19 pandemic, alleging that there are numbers, dates and facts that the public should be made aware of and that require the previous government to take responsibility for to avoid a similar situation in future. Israeli firm unveils satellite that spots 25-centimeter details
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:39:22 UTC
18:39:22 KST

- ImageSat International unveiled EROS NOVA, a new satellite capturing imagery at 25-centimeter resolution with onboard AI processing, on September 8.
- The satellite combines high-resolution optical imaging, infrared sensing and video collection, joining ISI's existing RUNNER and KNIGHT satellite platforms.
Israeli satellite company ImageSat International unveiled a new Earth observation satellite on September 8 designed to capture imagery sharp enough to identify small objects on the ground from orbit, while processing some of that data in space before it ever reaches an analyst.
The satellite, called EROS NOVA, will capture imagery at a native resolution of 25 centimeters, according to ISI, meaning objects roughly that size become distinguishable in the images it produces. The company describes the resolution tier as Very-Very-High-Resolution, sitting above the high-resolution imagery typical of most commercial Earth observation satellites.
EROS NOVA combines that high-resolution optical imaging with short-wave infrared sensing and video collection on a single satellite, letting customers pull different types of information from one platform rather than tasking separate spacecraft for each capability. Short-wave infrared imaging can help distinguish materials or detect activity that isn’t visible in ordinary daylight imagery, such as certain camouflage or recent ground disturbance.
The satellite will also carry onboard artificial intelligence and processing hardware that ISI says can analyze selected data while the satellite is still in orbit, rather than waiting for all of it to be downlinked to ground stations first. ISI says that approach is intended to prioritize the most operationally relevant imagery and shorten the time between when the satellite captures something and when an analyst or military user can act on it.
“EROS NOVA represents the next generation of space-based intelligence, bringing together advanced imaging, multiple sensing capabilities and onboard intelligence in a single satellite platform,” said Noam Segal, CEO of ISI. “It is designed to help intelligence organizations extract greater value from every collection and respond more rapidly to evolving operational needs, providing greater flexibility and a faster path from satellite collection to operational insight.”
EROS NOVA is the latest addition to a satellite lineage ISI has operated since 2000, when it launched EROS A, the first in a series of Israeli-built commercial reconnaissance satellites developed with Israel Aerospace Industries. That original satellite captured imagery at a resolution of 1.8 meters; ISI’s EROS C series, whose most recent satellite launched in December 2022, brought that down to well under a meter. ISI has since built out a wider satellite family beyond the EROS line, including the RUNNER microsatellite, developed with Terran Orbital and capable of sub-meter, wide-swath multispectral video, along with the KNIGHT platform, which EROS NOVA is now set to complement rather than replace.
ISI has operated as a joint venture since 1997 and has been controlled by Israeli private equity fund FIMI since 2017. The company markets itself around what it calls “sovereign” intelligence capabilities, meaning it builds and sells complete satellite systems, ground infrastructure and analytics software that let a customer country operate its own independent space-based intelligence capability rather than relying on imagery purchased from an outside provider.

Ukrainian company unveils RAM-2X strike drone for first time, used to hit over 450 targets – photo, video
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:38:00 EEST
18:38:00 KST

Ukrainian company unveils RAM-2X strike drone for first time, used to hit over 450 targets – photo, video
Ukrainian company Ukrspecsystems, which develops reconnaissance and strike drones, has publicly unveiled its RAM-2X strike UAV with an X-shaped wing for the first time. The drone was presented at the MSPO defence exhibition in Poland.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda
Details: The RAM-2X was designed to strike high-value targets at ranges of up to 180 km. The drone can remain airborne for more than two hours and has a high degree of automation. It can carry a 2.7 kg or 3.5 kg explosively formed penetrator warhead.
"Each type of equipment performs its own task, and every target requires an appropriate means of engagement. Following a comprehensive approach, we are developing strike systems in several subclasses at once, built around standardised components, a common ground station and unified software," Ukrspecsystems representatives said.
The RAM-2X can also use various AI assistant models to improve its effectiveness and operate with different communications systems. The drone can use several radio-frequency bands or Starlink.
In addition, the RAM-2X can operate together with a SHARK-M reconnaissance UAV acting as a communications relay. In this configuration, the reconnaissance drone provides targeting data and helps overcome enemy electronic warfare systems.
Ukrspecsystems says RAM loitering munitions have struck more than 450 targets. Although footage of these drones being used in combat has regularly appeared in the public domain, the company was unable for a long time to publicly confirm its connection to RAM due to security restrictions.
Ukrspecsystems has now decided to open its own "X-Files", a series of publications featuring footage of the drones being used in combat. The first compilation focuses on strikes against Russian air defence systems. Its publication was approved by the military.
RAM-2X drone strikes on targets. Video: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
"These are targets that are themselves designed to hunt drones. There are simply no more difficult targets for a strike drone. Secondly, because of their value, they are better camouflaged and positioned further from the front line. That is why striking an air defence system or radar demonstrates the key capabilities: the system's ability to overcome electronic warfare and enemy defences and operate far beyond the line of contact," Ukrspecsystems representatives explained, describing why they chose to publish footage of strikes on air defence systems first.
Background: Ukrspecsystems previously announced that it had developed a ready-to-use medium-range strike drone similar to the US Hornet.

INTERVIEW – ‘Tens of thousands of widows’ bear growing burden of holding Gaza families together: UN official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:35:00 UTC
18:35:00 KST

INTERVIEW – ‘Tens of thousands of widows’ bear growing burden of holding Gaza families together: UN official
UN Women says nearly 1 in 4 Gaza households now headed by women, roughly double than before Israel launched its war on the besieged Palestinian territory
Beyza Binnur Donmez
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
GENEVA
Women-headed households face greater barriers to aid, protection risks, and psychological trauma
68% of women-headed households reported unmet shelter needs, compared with 55% of male-headed households, says UN agency
Women now head nearly one in four households in Gaza, roughly double the pre-war rate, and the proportion is expected to have "risen further" in 2026 as deaths, disappearances, injuries, and displacement continue to reshape Palestinian families, according to UN Women.
The agency's latest Gender Alert estimates that women head around 86,290 households in Gaza, compared with around one in nine before October 2023. The estimate is based on data collected at the end of 2025.
Sofia Calltorp, director of UN Women’s Geneva Office and chief of humanitarian action, told Anadolu that developments since the data was collected mean the actual proportion is likely to be higher today.
"Definitely, we can expect that the actual proportion of women-headed households has risen further in 2026," Calltorp said.
She noted that despite the October 2025 ceasefire, more than 1,330 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 11 months, while thousands remain missing and many have sustained lifelong disabilities from injuries caused by bombardment.
The report also cautions that its estimate does not capture the full scale of women assuming responsibility for their families. Some households remain formally classified as male-headed even when women have effectively taken over because husbands are missing, detained, separated, severely injured, disabled, or otherwise unable to fulfill their previous roles.
Calltorp said there is no single factor driving the increase, pointing to deaths from Israeli bombardment and military ground operations, forced displacement, missing people, and injuries resulting in lifelong disabilities.
"This has left behind tens of thousands of widows who are now heading households," she said.
Greater needs, less access to aid
Women assuming responsibility for their families are doing so amid severe economic and humanitarian pressures.
According to the report, 68% of women-headed households reported unmet shelter needs, compared with 55% of male-headed households.
Women-headed households were also more likely to have had their homes damaged or destroyed, at 74% compared with 67% of male-headed households.
Economic insecurity was also more severe, with 67% reporting unmet cash needs, compared with 55% of male-headed households.
They were also displaced an average of eight times since October 2023, compared with seven times among male-headed households.
Despite their greater needs, 18.3% of women-headed households reported receiving no assistance, more than twice the 8.7% of male-headed households.
Calltorp said repeated displacement makes it harder to maintain stable shelter and consistently access assistance systems, while limited resources can restrict women's ability to travel and meet eligibility requirements.
"This creates a bit of a vicious circle where women that also have greater cash needs have more difficulties in accessing support," she said.
Protection risks, psychological toll
Women heading households also face heightened protection concerns. The report found that 19% reported gender-related protection concerns, compared with 8% of women living in male-headed households.
Calltorp said women and girls are forced to limit their food and water intake while prioritizing their families, and many live in shelters that do not provide adequate privacy. She recalled that hundreds of thousands of women and girls are already experiencing crisis-level food insecurity.
They can also face protection risks and harassment while going out to collect aid, food, and other essential items for their families, she said.
"The security environment has totally collapsed, leaving those women and girls without much protection at all," Calltorp said.
The burden of becoming responsible for a household while simultaneously coping with loss is also taking a heavy psychological toll.
The report found that women heading households reported their children's health needs at more than three and a half times their own, suggesting that their own health and psychosocial burdens may be underreported as they prioritize other family members.
Calltorp said women caring for their families alone while facing such risks are experiencing "extreme psychological and emotional trauma."
Many, she said, have lost their husbands and the fathers of their children and must manage their new responsibilities while also grieving.
Legal and documentation barriers can further complicate their lives.
The report calls for assistance with civil documentation, death registration, widowhood, custody, guardianship, and inheritance, including for women whose husbands are missing or detained and who may not fall into formal widowhood categories.
Calltorp said legal assistance is "really critical" to ensure women can secure necessary documentation, access humanitarian support, and care for their families.
'Assistance must be brought closer to women'
Calltorp called for changes to how humanitarian aid is delivered, including mobile registration, accessible distribution points, and alternatives for women unable to travel because of childcare, disability, or caregiving responsibilities.
"First of all, assistance must be brought closer to women," she underscored.
She said protection against gender-based violence should also be built into aid delivery so women can collect assistance safely, while cash, shelter, and livelihood support should be integrated to prevent women solely responsible for households from having to navigate multiple systems.
Legal assistance should also be expanded, she added, particularly to help women obtain civil documentation and address issues related to death registration, widowhood, and guardianship.
But Calltorp said implementing these measures depends fundamentally on humanitarian access.
"We need to make sure that humanitarian access is fully granted, so that we can come in and support the women and girls in Gaza," she said.

Latvian ports are not refusing to accept domestic grain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:34:57 UTC
18:34:57 KST

The Ministry of Transport has no information about Latvian ports refusing to accept domestic grain, the ministry told BNN.
Companies providing transportation services strictly comply with all applicable sanctions, while the competent authorities carry out rigorous controls and supervision throughout the logistics chain. At the same time, handling and storage capacity is sufficient to accommodate all declared domestic grain shipments, according to the information report On Solutions in the Area of Grain Transit, which was reviewed at an extraordinary government meeting on Friday, the 4th of September.
The government also decided that ports and state-owned Latvijas dzelzceļš must ensure priority access for the transportation of products from Latvian farmers.
Asked how soon laboratory testing to determine the origin of grain would begin, the Ministry of Transport said the government had decided at the meeting to grant the Food and Veterinary Service (PVD) the right to inspect grain cargo in transit at Latvian ports, including verifying its origin. At the same time,
the ministry noted that this issue does not fall within its area of responsibility.
In an interview with Latvijas Radio, PVD Director General Māris Balodis said the service currently does not inspect transit cargo. However, if the government amends the Cabinet regulations governing border controls, the PVD will be authorised to inspect the documentation accompanying such cargo and take grain samples to analyse their possible geographical origin.
Balodis also said that several foreign laboratories would have to be involved in determining the geographical origin of grain transported in transit, stressing that the procedure is not inexpensive. The PVD Director General added that it would be a paid service, with the cost covered by the cargo sender.
The analyses would take approximately one month, while testing a single shipment could cost an estimated 900,000 euros. Balodis explained that the PVD would take a grain sample after receiving advance payment. If the cargo sender refuses to pay, the shipment would not be allowed to cross Latvia’s border.
The government is expected to take a specific decision on granting these powers in mid-September.
