UN Security Council to decide future of Lebanon peacekeeping mission as UNIFIL exit looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:34:43 UTC
18:34:43 KST

The UN Security Council will decide the future of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) after the end of the peacekeeping mission’s mandate, the force’s spokesperson has said.
In an interview with Anadolu, Dany Ghafri said the council has several options regarding how to continue implementing Resolution 1701, including monitoring, observation and assistance to the Lebanese army.
UNIFIL’s mandate expires at the end of 2026 amid international discussions over its future, while Lebanon insists on maintaining the mission’s presence as a key element of stability in the south.
UNIFIL has been deployed since 1978 under Security Council resolutions to monitor the cessation of hostilities between Lebanon and Israel and help maintain security and stability in the area.
Israel occupies areas in southern Lebanon, some for decades and others since the previous war between 2023 and 2024, while it advanced more than 10 kilometres into Lebanese territory during its current assault.
Mission operations
Ghafri said Security Council Resolution 2790, issued in August 2025, extended UNIFIL’s mandate for a final time until December 31 2026.
UNIFIL continues, under current circumstances and capabilities, to carry out all tasks required of it under Resolution 1701, he said.
“But by the end of December 31 2026, the mission’s operations will stop, and UNIFIL will begin a gradual and safe withdrawal during 2027,” he added.
“UNIFIL is preparing plans for the withdrawal in coordination with troop-contributing countries and with the Lebanese government and army,” Ghafri said.
“The mission is expected to hand over its tasks to Lebanese authorities,” he added.
Since March 2, Israel has been carrying out an assault on Lebanon that has killed at least 4,362 people, injured 12,378 others and displaced more than 1 million, according to Lebanese authorities.
Lebanon’s government and lawmakers have called for reconsidering Resolution 2790, warning of a vacuum in southern Lebanon after UNIFIL’s withdrawal.
On Thursday, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun stressed Lebanon’s commitment to UNIFIL remaining in the country given the “important role” it plays.
If an extension of UNIFIL’s mandate is not possible, Lebanon would welcome any “brotherly or friendly” country willing to continue aspects of the mission’s work, Aoun said.
The president added that contacts are under way “to find the legal formula for such an international presence” to support the Lebanese army and residents of the south in humanitarian, social, health and educational fields.
Major challenges
Ghafri said UNIFIL currently consists of around 7,500 peacekeepers from nearly 50 countries.
Asked about the Lebanese army’s ability to assume the security tasks carried out by UNIFIL, he said the situation in the mission’s area of operations has “changed radically” since Resolution 2790 was issued.
“The Israeli army is present in a large part of UNIFIL’s area of operations,” he added.
Ghafri noted that Israeli airstrikes and shelling continue, although at a lower pace than what southern Lebanon witnessed in March and April.
“We are still living in an area facing major security challenges,” he said.
He added that since the cessation of hostilities understanding in November 2024, the Lebanese army has carried out a major redeployment in UNIFIL’s area of operations, with the mission helping facilitate the deployment.
Resolution 1701
On the future of implementing Resolution 1701 after UNIFIL’s mandate ends, Ghafri said: “Resolution 1701 remains valid, and its principles remain in place.”
“The resolution addresses the extension of state authority, strengthening the capabilities of the Lebanese army, the withdrawal of the Israeli army, the return of residents to their areas, and the exclusivity of arms or disarmament of armed groups,” he continued.
The Lebanese government is implementing a plan to place all weapons, including Hezbollah’s arms, under state authority, while Hezbollah insists on keeping its weapons and says it is a resistance movement against Israeli occupation.
“Any sustainable agreements or solutions reached in the area would be based on the principles of Resolution 1701,” Ghafri said.
He called on all parties to commit to implementing the resolution and to stop violence and hostilities in southern Lebanon to provide a safe life for residents on both sides of the Blue Line.
Asked about UNIFIL’s role in implementing a US-mediated framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel, Ghafri said the agreement “does not include a role for UNIFIL and does not mention Resolution 1701.”
“But the principles of Resolution 1701 remain in place, and the framework agreement and the cessation of hostilities understanding can be included within those principles,” he said.
UNIFIL, Ghafri added, is “ready to assist if asked to do so.”
Under US sponsorship, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed the framework agreement on June 26. It provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from all occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the Lebanese army’s deployment there and the disarmament of armed groups.
UN options
On the future of the UN presence in southern Lebanon after UNIFIL’s withdrawal, Ghafri said the Security Council asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to present options by June on how to continue implementing Resolution 1701 after the mission leaves.
“Guterres sent a letter to the council on June 1 outlining options for how the UN presence in southern Lebanon could continue for the purpose of monitoring, observation and assisting the Lebanese army,” he said.
The letter is now with the council, which can meet to discuss the options, adopt one of them, amend them, or take no decision, he continued.
“If the council does not take any decision by the end of 2026, UNIFIL will continue implementing Resolution 2790,” which provides for ending its operations by the end of this year and beginning withdrawal in 2027, he said.
Israeli assault
On security developments in southern Lebanon, Ghafri said the first days of the ceasefire saw a decrease in the intensity of airstrikes inside UNIFIL’s area of operations.
“Unfortunately, this trend has risen again, and we began seeing large numbers of projectiles from the Israeli side, while we have not monitored projectiles from the Lebanese side since June,” he said.
“The UNIFIL monitors the presence of the Israeli army inside Lebanese territory north of the Blue Line, which constitutes a violation of Resolution 1701,” he added.
Ghafri said the mission has repeatedly asked the Israeli army to withdraw from areas it occupies in southern Lebanon.
“UNIFIL has monitored demolitions and explosions in those areas, as well as major damage to civilian infrastructure,” he continued.
He warned that this is “very dangerous,” not only because of the physical impact of explosions and bulldozing, but also because of its psychological impact on the return of residents to UNIFIL’s area of operations in the coming period.
“The mission’s goal is to restore stability to its area of operations before the end of its mandate, and this must be accompanied by the safe return of residents to their villages,” he stressed.
Pilot zones
Regarding the “pilot zones” included in the framework agreement, Ghafri said two out of three are located within UNIFIL’s area of operations.
“The mission cooperates with the Lebanese army within its area of operations, and UNIFIL can respond to any request submitted by the Lebanese army,” he said.
“UNIFIL, within its capabilities, also assists residents who have returned to their areas as well as displaced people in other areas, including Sidon and the capital Beirut,” he added. “The assistance includes food, clothes and medical aid.”
In addition to occupying Lebanese territory, Israel occupies Palestine and territories in Syria and refuses to withdraw or allow the establishment of an independent Palestinian state as stipulated in UN resolutions.

Poland unveils new precision strike drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:34:39 UTC
18:34:39 KST

- FlyFocus unveiled TASACK, a 15-kilogram precision loitering munition with a 110-kilometer range and a point-and-click targeting interface, at MSPO 2026 in Poland.
- The system uses mostly Polish-made components and is expected to reach production readiness in the first quarter of 2027.
Polish defense technology company FlyFocus unveiled a new precision loitering munition called TASACK on September 8 at MSPO 2026, the international defense industry exhibition in Kielce, Poland, positioning the system as a lower-cost, easier-to-operate alternative to conventional first-person-view attack drones.
The 15-kilogram (33-pound) aircraft can fly up to 110 kilometers (68 miles), carries a 5-kilogram (11-pound) payload, and reaches speeds of up to 300 km/h (186 mph), according to FlyFocus. Unlike typical FPV drones, which require operators to manually fly the aircraft using first-person video and extensive training, TASACK uses what the company calls a point-and-click interface, letting an operator select a target on screen rather than pilot the drone by hand into it.
A stabilized electro-optical and infrared gimbal handles target identification and tracking, and lets the drone approach a target from different angles, from a flat, direct trajectory to a near-vertical dive, depending on what the mission calls for. FlyFocus says the system achieves a targeting accuracy of 1 meter CEP50, a measure of how tightly half of a weapon’s strikes cluster around the intended aim point. The drone runs on electric power, can stay airborne for up to 1.5 hours, and maintains a datalink out to 80 kilometers (50 miles). Navigation combines GPS with inertial guidance as a backup, with radio-based navigation available as an option, and the modular airframe can be fitted with different warheads depending on the mission. FlyFocus says the system can be readied for launch in five to seven minutes.
“TASACK has been designed around what we believe matters most for this class of system: precision, simplicity and the ability to manufacture at meaningful scale,” said Igor Skawiński, CEO and co-founder of FlyFocus. “Modern militaries need sophisticated capabilities, but they also need systems that can be produced affordably, deployed quickly and adapted as battlefield conditions change. Our objective with TASACK is to bring those requirements together in one platform.”
Most of TASACK’s components, including its gimbal, are built in Poland, continuing a supply chain approach FlyFocus has followed since its founding. The company, established in 2017 by Skawiński and Albert Świerczyński, has built its product line around NATO-aligned components rather than the Chinese-made parts, such as batteries and flight controllers, that dominate much of the broader European drone industry. FlyFocus raised its first institutional funding round in February, a €4.5 million ($5.3 million) round led by ffVC with participation from the NCBR Investment Fund, Poland’s state-run research and development investment arm, which the company is using in part to build a new manufacturing facility in Poland.
TASACK joins a portfolio that already includes the Polaris ISR drone, the tethered CableGuard surveillance system, and the Striker deep-strike loitering munition, a much larger system with a stated range exceeding 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) and a payload of up to 40 kilograms (88 pounds) that FlyFocus tested near Kyiv in June, with what the company described as positive feedback from Ukrainian operators. TASACK shares a common ground control interface with those existing platforms, which FlyFocus says reduces the retraining needed when operators switch between systems. Both the Polish and Ukrainian defense ministries are current FlyFocus customers, and the company has said its systems have seen use in Ukraine under combat conditions.
FlyFocus said TASACK is expected to reach production readiness in the first quarter of 2027.

No decision yet on drone defences for Army’s new vehicles
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:33:23 BST
18:33:23 KST

The Ministry of Defence has taken no decision on including a hard-kill counter-drone active protection system within the Mechanised Infantry Programme, though such opportunities are being explored, according to a written answer published on Monday.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked what assessment had been made of the potential benefits of including such a system in the programme.
Pollard said: “Hard-Kill Counter-UAS opportunities are being explored, but no decision has been taken to include a hard-kill Counter-UAS active protection system within the current scope of the Mechanised Infantry Programme. However, the Department continues to evaluate emerging technologies and capability options to ensure Army platforms remain effective against current and future threats.”
Soft-kill systems work by interfering with the threat, jamming its guidance, decoying its seeker or obscuring the target behind smoke, and they consume nothing physical when they operate. Hard-kill systems physically destroy the incoming round, typically by firing an interceptor or a projectile pattern into its path.
The Mechanised Infantry Programme
The programme is delivering the Boxer to the British Army, a wheeled armoured vehicle built around a drive module and interchangeable mission modules, produced in Britain by WFEL at Stockport and Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land at Telford under a contract for more than 600 vehicles.
The Boxer is intended to carry the Army’s mechanised infantry battalions, and the vehicles began arriving with units over the past two years. The question of what protective equipment they carry has been raised repeatedly since the invasion of Ukraine, where losses among armoured vehicles to small drones have run at a rate nobody planning armoured forces in the 2010s anticipated.
The department’s broader general position on counter-drone work has been set out through a series of related efforts, including the Request for Information issued in July for electronic warfare systems for the Armed Forces of Ukraine, which sought equipment able to disrupt drone control links from soldier-portable, vehicle-mounted, uncrewed and emplaced configurations, and which the department noted was the only category where a combat-proven answer to fibre-optic drones was being sought.

China’s maritime strategy: From chokepoint vulnerability to a new geography of power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:33:21 UTC
18:33:21 KST

Vusal Guliyev is an Indo-Pacific and Eurasian affairs analyst at the Center for Analysis of International Relations and Multiculturalism (AIR Center) based in Baku, Azerbaijan.
The geopolitics of the 21st century are increasingly shaped not only by who controls territory, but also by who can secure, regulate, or disrupt the movement of goods across seas, straits, and strategic corridors. This transformation is particularly significant for China. As the world’s largest trading nation and one of the world’s largest energy importers, it remains heavily dependent on maritime routes that pass through strategically exposed chokepoints.
This dependence has long shaped Beijing's efforts to diversify its connectivity and reduce its exposure to maritime chokepoints. Yet China's evolving maritime strategy suggests that bypassing one chokepoint does not necessarily eliminate vulnerability. Instead, it may simply shift that vulnerability to another geographical, political, or infrastructural node. As Beijing expands its presence across the Arctic, Indian Ocean, and Eurasian land corridors, it is not escaping the geopolitics of chokepoints so much as navigating an increasingly complex network of them.
The traditional “Malacca dilemma” captures China’s exposure to a narrow maritime passage through which substantial volumes of its energy supplies and commercial traffic transit. In the event of a major geopolitical crisis, disruption in Southeast Asia’s Strait of Malacca, the Strait of Hormuz, or Bab el-Mandeb could impose high economic costs on Beijing and expose the vulnerabilities of China’s maritime-dependent economy.
China has therefore pursued a broad diversification strategy to reduce its reliance on vulnerable maritime routes. Pipelines from continental Eurasia, investments in ports, railways, and logistics infrastructure, and the development of overland corridors have all expanded Beijing’s strategic options. The Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in this context represents more than an infrastructure and connectivity program. It also serves as a mechanism to reduce exposure to individual maritime chokepoints and enhance the resilience of China’s trade and energy networks.
The Arctic has emerged as an increasingly important component of this strategy. China’s 2018 Arctic Policy formally introduced the concept of the “Polar Silk Road” and identified Arctic shipping routes as potential international trade routes. Beijing has subsequently sought a greater role in Arctic infrastructure, navigation, resource development, and scientific cooperation.
The Northern Sea Route (NSR), in particular, offers the potential to shorten some Asia–Europe maritime journeys and reduce reliance on the Suez Canal and, indirectly, the maritime routes connecting East Asia with the Indian Ocean. Yet the Arctic is far from being a frictionless alternative. Navigation remains constrained by seasonal conditions, specialized infrastructure, limited port capacity, and dependence on icebreaking capabilities. Moreover, China’s growing involvement in the Arctic is increasingly intertwined with its relationship with Russia, creating a different form of strategic dependence.
China’s geographical diversification, therefore, does not eliminate the chokepoint problems. By developing alternative routes, Beijing can reduce its exposure to any single maritime passage, but each alternative introduces its own political, geographical, infrastructural, and strategic vulnerabilities. This broader pattern highlights a fundamental shift in maritime power. The strategic importance of a route increasingly depends not only on who controls the territory surrounding it, but also on who can influence access to it.
The significance of contemporary maritime competition lies precisely in this transformation. A state does not necessarily need to occupy territory to exercise strategic influence over it. The ability to make a maritime route secure, vulnerable, costly, or politically uncertain can generate significant geopolitical leverage.
The Red Sea demonstrates this dynamic clearly. Attacks on commercial vessels since late 2023 have forced shipping companies to reassess the security and economic viability of one of the world’s principal maritime corridors. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has recorded dozens of attacks on international shipping linked to wider Mideast conflicts, while renewed attacks in July 2026 once again raised concerns about the implications for global supply chains and freedom of navigation.
The Strait of Hormuz presents an even more consequential example because of its central role in global energy markets. According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), approximately 14.6 million barrels of oil and petroleum liquids per day passed through the strait in the first quarter of 2026 despite disruptions during the period.
These developments demonstrate that maritime power increasingly rests on the ability to control or threaten access. Even relatively small actors can impose high costs on major trading economies without possessing conventional blue water navies. At the same time, major powers are being compelled to devote greater resources to protecting commercial shipping, securing alternative routes, and maintaining freedom of navigation.
The emergence of so-called shadow or dark fleets adds another dimension to this changing maritime order. The term generally refers to vessels operating through opaque ownership structures and often relying on complex registration, insurance, and ship-to-ship transfer arrangements to transport sanctioned or politically sensitive commodities.
This phenomenon illustrates how maritime competition is extending beyond conventional naval confrontation. Shadow fleets can complicate sanctions enforcement, obscure the origins and destinations of cargoes, and create additional safety and environmental risks. The IMO has identified substandard and dark-fleet shipping as a growing maritime concern, particularly because some vessels may operate without adequate insurance or in violation of established safety standards.
China’s alleged reliance on or involvement in trade involving shadow fleet vessels should therefore be understood within the broader transformation of maritime governance. The issue is not simply whether Beijing uses particular vessels to circumvent restrictions, but whether the growing opacity of maritime transportation is weakening the ability of states and international institutions to monitor and regulate strategic flows.
The simultaneous contestation of multiple chokepoints presents China with a complex strategic challenge. The Indo-Pacific, Middle East, Arctic, and Eurasian land corridors are increasingly interconnected, meaning that instability in one region can alter the strategic and economic value of routes elsewhere. This dynamic is reshaping the maritime policies of not only China and the US but also India, Japan, Europe, and other regional powers. Naval deployments, port-access agreements, maritime partnerships, coastal infrastructure, and logistics hubs increasingly serve both economic and strategic purposes. As a result, the distinction between commercial connectivity and military security is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain.
China is responding by strengthening its maritime capabilities while simultaneously developing alternatives to maritime dependence. The result is a strategy built around redundancy, involving the expansion of ports, pipelines, rail connections, naval capabilities, and alternative geographic routes. Yet redundancy has clear limits. Every alternative corridor carries its own political and strategic vulnerabilities. Arctic routes depend on a contested northern environment, land corridors depend on the stability and sovereignty of transit states, and maritime routes remain exposed to naval competition and conflict. China’s expanding connectivity network therefore provides greater strategic flexibility without eliminating strategic exposure.
The emerging maritime order is consequently not one in which China is simply becoming more powerful or more vulnerable. Rather, it is one in which power and vulnerability are increasingly produced by the same networks. China’s efforts to overcome the Malacca dilemma are creating a broader geography of strategic connectivity in which the central question is no longer simply who controls territory, but who can keep the world’s critical passages open. The challenge is therefore not simply to build a stronger navy or find an alternative to every chokepoint. It is to ensure that no single disruption, whether military, political, economic, or infrastructural, can simultaneously threaten the networks on which China’s global power depends.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

Israeli forces impose siege on Anata, Shuafat in occupied East Jerusalem

Israeli forces have imposed a tight siege on the town of Anata and the Shuafat refugee camp in occupied East Jerusalem since early Tuesday, carrying out raids, arrests and searches of homes, shops and other facilities, according to Palestinian authorities.
The Jerusalem Governorate said in a statement that Israeli forces had closed roads leading to Anata and the Shuafat camp since dawn, preventing Palestinians from moving in and out of the areas.
The siege and curfew forced schools and kindergartens in the town and camp to suspend classes, while Israeli forces prevented shop owners from opening their businesses, it added.
The restrictions have largely paralyzed commercial activity and daily life for around 80,000 Palestinians.
The governorate said Israeli forces were carrying out a large-scale arrest campaign, estimating that around 100 Palestinians had been detained, including a woman, while raids and field interrogations continued.
Israeli forces also raided dozens of homes in Anata and Shuafat, searching and questioning residents, and stormed several shops and private facilities, breaking down doors at some premises and damaging their contents, it added.
Israeli forces remained deployed in neighborhoods and main streets, while tight military restrictions continued at the Shuafat checkpoint, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
Local sources told Anadolu that Israeli forces were allowing people to enter the area in some cases while preventing them from leaving.
Dozens of Palestinians were forced to spend hours overnight in their vehicles after the siege prevented them from reaching their homes, while people from outside Anata and Shuafat were stranded when roads were closed.
The Jerusalem Governorate also said Israeli forces were preventing ambulance crews from reaching patients and emergency cases, warning of the potential consequences for residents.
It condemned the continued siege and restrictions, calling the measures a “dangerous escalation” and “collective punishment” affecting the lives and basic rights of tens of thousands of Palestinians.
The Israeli army announced Monday that it had launched what it called a “focused” operation in Anata and Shuafat, without specifying how long it would last.
The Jerusalem Governorate said the raids resembled an Israeli military operation carried out in the Qalandia refugee camp in early August and accused Israel of pursuing a policy of collective punishment against Palestinian communities surrounding Jerusalem.
The latest raids come amid a sharp rise in violence across the occupied Palestinian territories. UN data indicate that attacks by Israeli occupiers have reached “unprecedented levels,” with more than 1,400 attacks resulting in casualties or property damage documented in 2026.
Around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 516 illegal settlements and outposts across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem.

We need missiles, you know. What is Freyja

Cabinet considers visa blocks for Russian athletes
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch cabinet will do everything it can to prevent athletes from competing under the Russian flag at international sporting events, including the upcoming 2030 winter games in Heerenveen, sports minister Mirjam Sterk has said.
She told De Telegraaf that the government is actively lobbying the International Olympic Committee to reverse its decision to readmit Russian athletes, which it made this summer, clearing the way for the 2028 summer games in Los Angeles.
Russians were suspended in 2023 after the Putin regime began using sports bodies from occupied Ukrainian territories.
The cabinet’s stance would have consequences for the 2030 winter games at Thialf in Heerenveen, which will be the first Olympic competition on Dutch soil since 1928.
Asked what would happen if Russian skaters qualified to race there, Sterk told the paper: “You would have to look at what that means for the visas.”
“The cabinet considers the participation of Russian and Belarusian athletes and teams under their own flag and national symbols at sporting events in the Netherlands undesirable and will do everything within its power to prevent it,” she said. “That applies to individual athletes, national teams and club teams from both countries.”
Pressure on IOC funding
 The Netherlands is one of nine EU countries, led by Estonia, that asked the European Commission in July to cut the IOC and other federations that readmit Russia out of Erasmus+ and other EU funding programmes.
Sterk said the primary responsibility lies with the sports federations, but that the Netherlands is raising the issue with them directly. “Russia also uses this to make political statements,” she said.
D66 MP Hanneke van der Werf backed the minister but said the message should have been made “much more emphatically and more widely” at the time. “Sport is not separate from reality when a regime deliberately uses it for political ends,” she told the Telegraaf.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect as US trade talks stall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:29:58 UTC
18:29:58 KST

Breadcrumb
Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect as US trade talks stall
Canada's retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect just after midnight on Tuesday as Prime Minister Mark Carney increased economic pressure on his country's biggest trading partner after negotiations collapsed last month, intensifying an 18-month-old trade war.
The counter-tariffs cover $20 billion of US goods, with duties ranging from 15% to 50% across products from steel and furniture to clothing and electronics.
The dollar-for-dollar retaliation marks an escalation in the dispute between the neighboring countries, and US and Canadian officials have traded blame for scuttling a deal that seemed close to fruition two weeks ago. The rising tensions create uncertainty about the broader US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement, which is up for annual reviews after US President Donald Trump declined to extend it for another decade.
"What we are worried about is an escalatory spiral," said Michael Harvey, executive director of the Canadian Agri-Food Trade Alliance and a member of Carney's advisory committee on bilateral US economic relations.
"But at the same time, we totally understand that the prime minister needs to find areas of leverage," Harvey said.
Trump's tariffs implemented last month hit sectors including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment, covering $20 billion, or 5%, of Canadian exports to the US
According to Canadian and US government data, Canada has shipped almost 68% of total exports to the US this year, out of which roughly 80% moved duty-free due to exemptions under the USMCA pact. Protections under the agreement have provided the domestic economy some resilience.
The new tariffs, imposed under a Depression-era US law, do not allow Ottawa to exercise USMCA exemptions.
Concerns about the USMCA's future have fuelled uncertainty about investment and growth, as Canada wages a trade war against an economy 13 times its size.
Polls show Carney has broad support from Canadians, but it could disappear within months as the consequences of the trade war sink in, according to political analysts.
Just 20% of Americans approved of Trump's tariffs on Canadian goods, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
Carney said last week his government was ready to sign a trade deal that benefits both countries.
Trump threatened last month to raise US tariffs on all cars, trucks and automotive parts from Canada to 50% starting 1 January, and signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America".
A government source said there are currently no talks between the two sides among ministers or government officials.
"The Canadian government needs to keep channels open to the United States and not go overboard in terms of rhetoric and reacting to the rhetoric from the American side, while waiting for the American decision-making process to come back to economics," Harvey said.

Herzog rejects UK settlement trade ban, warns it would be ‘gross interference’ in Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:29:55 UTC
18:29:55 KST

President Isaac Herzog on Tuesday urged Britain and other governments to halt plans for sanctions against Israel over its policies in the West Bank, calling the expected measures a “grave miscalculation” and “gross interference” in Israel’s democratic election.
“Later today, we expect to see headlines announcing certain British trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in Judea and Samaria, and other nations may join,” Herzog said at an event marking 30 years of Israeli participation in the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation program. “If this happens, I believe it will prove to be a grave miscalculation, a decision that will fall on the wrong side of history.”
According to information received by senior Israeli officials, Britain is seeking to persuade other countries to join the measures, with France considered among the governments that could follow London’s lead.
Herzog argued that imposing sanctions in the run-up to Israel’s election would amount to direct foreign interference. “In the current context, it would be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation. And it will serve no one,” he said.
He also warned that restrictions targeting settlements could hurt Palestinians employed by Israeli businesses. “It will directly harm, unfortunately, Palestinians, robbing them of business and employment,” Herzog said. “And, ultimately, it will undermine the interests and national security of freedom-loving nations.”
“Sanctions are not a solution. Dialogue is,” he added. “I say to all foreign governments: Stop! Step away from the dead-end of sanctions and boycotts. And turn toward constructive dialogue and toward cooperation.”
Britain is expected to announce measures later Tuesday targeting trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Bloomberg reported that British diplomats have told their American counterparts that the measures being prepared at this stage are largely symbolic and are not expected to have a significant impact on Britain’s broader trade or security relationship with Israel. According to the report, London has also been working diplomatically to limit potential friction with the Trump administration over the move.
The New York Times reported Monday that Britain was preparing what officials described as broad economic restrictions targeting Israeli settlements, including a ban on goods produced there and possible sanctions against companies involved in settlement construction.
British officials have also considered personal sanctions against individual Israelis and restrictions involving goods originating in east Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, although it remains unclear which measures will be included in the final package. Israel does not currently expect a major expansion of Britain’s restrictions on arms sales.
London has described the emerging policy as part of a broader “reset” toward Israeli settlements. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said his government is examining measures aimed at preventing trade with settlements.
Israeli officials are waiting to see whether Britain confines the measures to economic activity connected to settlements or also imposes sanctions on specific individuals. Officials assess that the European Union is less enthusiastic about taking such steps immediately before Israel’s election, partly out of concern that they could strengthen Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu politically.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar warned last week that Israel would retaliate if London moved ahead.
“If Britain acts against the State of Israel, the State of Israel will act against Britain,” Sa’ar told ynet last week, referring to possible British measures linked to Israel’s advancement of construction plans in the E1 area.
Herzog, however, framed his appeal more broadly, urging foreign governments to abandon sanctions and boycotts altogether in favor of engagement.
“Stop,” he said. “Step away from the dead-end of sanctions and boycotts.”

U.S. and Indonesia test rocket systems in joint drill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:29:05 UTC
18:29:05 KST

- U.S. and Indonesian forces combined HIMARS, ASTROS II and Vampire rocket launchers with F-16s and Apache helicopters in a live-fire exercise September 4 and 7 in Baturaja.
- The drill is part of Super Garuda Shield 2026, a 21-nation exercise running through September 11 involving roughly 4,700 personnel across Indonesia.
U.S. and Indonesian forces fired rocket artillery and flew combat aircraft together during a live-fire exercise at Baturaja Combat Training Center on September 4 and 7, part of the ongoing Super Garuda Shield exercise in Indonesia.
The ground-fire portion combined U.S. Army M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems with Indonesian Army ASTROS II Mk6 launchers and Indonesian Marine Corps RM-70 Vampire launchers. In the air, Indonesian F-16 fighters flew alongside U.S. Army and Indonesian AH-64 Apache attack helicopters.
“Today was a great example of working together to conduct safe and responsible training,” said U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Ed Matthaidess, Army Forces commander for Super Garuda Shield, after the September 4 event. “It’s a huge coalition effort, a lot of synchronization goes into that.”
“The combined joint land strike demonstrated what the United States and Indonesia can achieve when we train together,” said U.S. Marine Corps Maj. Jonathan Bowman, fires and effects coordinator for Marine Rotational Force-Darwin. “We are grateful to our Indonesian counterparts and hosts for their support and for the opportunity to learn from one another. Exercises like Super Garuda Shield strengthen the cooperation we need to operate together effectively.”
Getting different rocket systems and aircraft from two militaries firing on the same range required participants to reconcile differences in equipment and procedure well before anyone pulled a trigger.
“Executing joint and multinational fires coordination is among the most demanding tasks in modern combined arms warfare,” said U.S. Army Capt. Eric Brown, a fires planner with the 4th Infantry Division.
Brown said aligning Army, Marine Corps and Indonesian capabilities meant working through differing technical requirements and doctrine, and credited the Army’s Next Generation Command and Control technology with helping units share targeting data and synchronize fires in real time.
For the crews on the ground, that coordination came down to repetition.
“Lots of practicing, lots of run-throughs,” said U.S. Army Sgt. Madeleine Rocha, a HIMARS crew member with the Iowa Army National Guard. “We made sure that everything runs seamlessly.”
Rocha said training alongside Indonesian and other partner forces gave crews a chance to see how other militaries approach the same problems and adjust their own procedures as the exercise progressed.
The live-fire event is one piece of a much larger exercise. Super Garuda Shield 2026, running from August 31 to September 11 across sites including Bandung, Jakarta, Lampung, Baturaja and North Kalimantan, involves roughly 4,700 personnel from 21 countries this year, according to Indonesia’s military. Originally a bilateral drill between the U.S. and Indonesia dating back to 2007, the exercise expanded into its current multinational format in 2022 as regional security concerns in the Indo-Pacific grew, and this year’s iteration also included a coordinated multinational parachute jump into Baturaja involving Indonesian, American, Indian, Japanese and French troops.
Indonesia has continued to describe its participation as consistent with a foreign policy of strategic non-alignment, having also conducted separate military exercises with China this year, even as it deepens training ties with the United States and other Western partners.

Wildfires continued to burn in Türkiye’s southern provinces of Antalya and Adana on Sept. 8, prompting evacuations and mobilizing more than 1,000 personnel as strong winds hampered firefighting efforts.
In Antalya’s Aksu district, a fire that broke out in the Karaöz area spread rapidly under winds reaching 30 kilometers per hour, advancing toward residential areas and eventually reaching the Döşemealtı district. Authorities evacuated 254 homes and 720 people in Aksu and neighboring Kepez, while further evacuations were underway in Yeşilkaraman.
Officials also evacuated animals, including those from a municipal shelter, as emergency teams established a mobile coordination center, temporary communications infrastructure and aid stations. Power outages affected almost 3,000 subscribers in the area.
Firefighters tackled the blaze from the air and ground using aircraft, helicopters, water tankers, heavy machinery and security vehicles. Authorities said the fire’s intensity had decreased and expressed hope it could be brought under control. Smoke and ash from the blaze reached Antalya city center.
Meanwhile, a separate wildfire in Adana’s Kozan district spread across the Doğanalanı and Düzağaç areas, forcing the precautionary evacuation of nearby settlements. Seven homes were destroyed, according to local reports.
The General Directorate of Forestry said fires in Antalya’s Serik, Kayseri’s Yahyalı, and Adana’s Karaisalı and Feke districts had been brought under control, with cooling operations continuing.

TBILISI, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- A groundbreaking ceremony for the Imereti wind power plant project, an investment by Sichuan Energy International Investment Co., Ltd., was held Monday in Tbilisi, marking the official start of construction of the first Chinese-invested new energy project in Georgia.
Margalita Arabidze, head of the Department of Energy Policy and Investment Projects of the Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development of Georgia, said in her remarks that electricity consumption in Georgia has grown steadily in recent years and that developing domestic energy resources is a top priority for the country's energy sector.
She said Chinese companies would play an important role in developing wind power in Georgia, noting that projects such as the Imereti wind power project would increase the share of green energy in the country's energy mix and contribute to its energy independence.
Davit Narmania, chairman of the Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission, said the project would help strengthen Georgia's energy system, while contributing to the country's socioeconomic development and creating additional opportunities for further economic growth.
Chinese technologies and equipment have already been widely used in Georgia's energy sector, he said, adding that the project would serve as an example of effective technological cooperation between Georgia and China.
Dai Chunyong, charge d'affaires ad interim of the Chinese Embassy in Georgia, said the Imereti wind power project reflects Chinese companies' confidence in Georgia's energy sector, noting that China stands ready to work with Georgia to share development opportunities and improve the well-being of both peoples.
He said new energy and other projects invested in or undertaken by Chinese companies would help reduce carbon emissions and promote Georgia's economic development.
The Imereti wind power project is located in Sachkhere Municipality in Georgia's Imereti region. The first phase is planned to have an installed capacity of 104 megawatts. Once operational, it is expected to generate about 340 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, enough to meet the electricity needs of more than 90,000 local households. ■

China's Tianyu Telescope to be commissioned for scientific observations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
17:27:59 CST
18:27:59 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- The Tianyu Telescope, located in Lenghu, northwest China's Qinghai Province, has successfully captured an image of the North America Nebula and the Pelican Nebula in the constellation Cygnus, along with more than one million surrounding stars in the Milky Way in a single exposure.
This feat signals the telescope's transition to the scientific observation stage, according to People's Daily on Tuesday.
Initiated in 2022 and led by the Tsung-Dao Lee Institute (TDLI) of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, with the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences responsible for its development, the telescope is expected to begin formal scientific survey operations in October 2026.
The Tianyu Telescope covers a sky area of nearly nine square degrees in a single exposure, equivalent to more than 40 full moons.
Many violent events in the universe, such as stellar explosions and gravitational-wave flashes from neutron star mergers, often fade away within seconds to minutes. When space telescopes or gravitational-wave detectors send out alerts, the Tianyu Telescope can rapidly slew toward the target and "rewind" the sky area under its real-time monitoring, restoring the celestial view from seconds before the burst, said the report.
The Tianyu Telescope will carry out sustained photometric monitoring of hundreds of millions of celestial objects, capturing subtle variations in their brightness to discover exoplanets, various types of variable stars, supernovae and small bodies within the solar system, Feng Fabo, an associate professor at the TDLI and project director of the Tianyu Telescope, was quoted as saying by the newspaper.
The Tianyu project has already attracted research teams from Britain, Belgium and Chile, and its data will be coordinated with multiple survey projects both at home and abroad.
Moving forward, the Tianyu Telescope will undergo a phased transition from commissioning observations to stable operations, and from remote-controlled to fully-automated observing modes. ■

Zelensky gives cautious backing to Trump envoys' 'good' ideas to end Russia's war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:27:44 UTC
18:27:44 KST

Zelensky gives cautious backing to Trump envoys' 'good' ideas to end Russia's war
U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, brought Kyiv some "pretty good, decent" ideas on how to end Russia's war against Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters on Sept. 8.
Zelensky said it remains unclear whether the proposals can actually work.
"We need to understand whether we can implement them and make them effective," the Ukrainian president said. "I don't know yet if it will work out."
His comments came days after Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Moscow and Kyiv with revised peace proposals in an apparent attempt to restart negotiations that have been deadlocked for months.
Zelensky stopped short of disclosing the details of the U.S. proposals but pointed to two issues that could play an important role in any potential agreement: grain and energy.
"Grain and energy are sensitive issues for Ukraine and Russia," he said.
Grain, energy
One new proposal discussed during the talks involved a potential truce in the air, either focused on energy infrastructure or halting aerial strikes altogether, one person familiar with the negotiations previously told the Kyiv Independent.
Russia has not agreed to the proposal so far.
Both Ukraine and Russia have repeatedly targeted each other's energy infrastructure throughout the war. While Ukraine has targeted Russia's energy exports to cut off a key source of funding for the war, Moscow has focused on destroying Ukrainian power plants and substations in an effort to trigger blackouts across the country.
The issue has become particularly urgent for Kyiv ahead of another winter, when Ukrainian officials expect Russia to intensify attacks on the country's energy grid.
Last winter, Kyiv faced a major Russian campaign against its energy infrastructure, causing mass blackouts amid freezing temperatures.
Grain has also emerged as another sensitive issue.
Russia has intensified attacks on shipping corridors in the Black Sea, including deadly strikes on civilian grain ships. The campaign has contributed to declining exports, rising costs, and a shrinking number of vessels willing to dock at Ukrainian ports.
Zelensky said the consequences extend far beyond Ukraine and Russia.
"These are pressing issues for the entire world," he said. "And these are pressing issues for India today, for the Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Asia, and many other countries. We are ready to find a compromise here."
read also
Meeting with Trump
Zelensky said he hopes to meet Trump around Sept. 20 and plans to raise Ukraine's need for additional anti-ballistic missiles.
"We need a package of anti-ballistic missiles from the U.S. They heard in detail what we need," Zelensky said. "I count on meeting with President Trump to raise this topic."
Ukraine faces a shortage of missiles capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles, which Moscow has increasingly used against Ukrainian cities.
Zelensky did not disclose the details of the proposed support package.
"I cannot disclose all the details here," he said. "We have agreed with the American side that we will prepare everything and then communicate with the Europeans."
Moscow's demands remain
Despite the renewed U.S. push, the central obstacles to a peace deal remain unchanged.
The negotiations have been effectively deadlocked since earlier this year as Moscow continues to reject a ceasefire along the current front lines and demands that Ukraine cede Donbas — the strategically important, partially occupied region in eastern Ukraine — and abandon its NATO membership aspirations.
The Kremlin has not signaled that it is prepared to compromise on its territorial demands.
At the same time, Ukrainian officials warn that Russia is preparing to escalate attacks on Ukrainian cities and the country's energy infrastructure over the winter.
"Putin still hopes to break us this winter and isn't willing to agree to anything," one Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent.

Singapore sees record-low major injury rate in H1
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
17:27:35 CST
18:27:35 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's workplace safety and health performance remained broadly stable in the first half of 2026, with the annualized major injury rate falling to an all-time low, although the fatal injury rate rose, the Ministry of Manpower said on Tuesday.
The annualized major injury rate, excluding platform workers, improved to 14.6 per 100,000 workers in the first half from 15.8 a year earlier, the ministry said in a statement.
However, the overall fatal injury rate increased to 1.1 per 100,000 workers from 0.97 in the first half of 2025 and 0.96 in the second half of 2025, with 21 workplace fatalities recorded. Vehicular incidents were the leading cause, accounting for nine deaths.
The increase prompted the ministry and the Multi-Agency Workplace Safety and Health Taskforce to step up safety measures after seven workers died over four weeks in late May and June. These included tougher penalties and a two-week nationwide voluntary Safety Time-Out.
The ministry is also reviewing further measures to strengthen workplace safety ownership and accountability, including tougher enforcement, it said.
Minister of State for Manpower Dinesh Vasu Dash said the rise in fatal injuries, particularly those involving vehicles, remained a serious concern and urged employers and workers to stay vigilant. ■

3 artworks stolen from France's Renoir Museum
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
17:27:29 CST
18:27:29 KST

PARIS, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Three works of art were stolen early Tuesday from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer in southeastern France's Alpes-Maritimes department, the French daily Le Monde reported.
Two thieves were spotted by the town's video surveillance cameras and fled, Cagnes-sur-Mer Mayor Bryan Masson was quoted as saying. The thieves took four works of art from the museum but dropped one as they fled, the mayor said.
Masson said his office estimated the value of the stolen artworks at 9 million euros (10.45 million U.S. dollars), adding that the perpetrators were "currently being actively sought."
The French judicial police have taken over the investigation.
Created in 1960, the museum is housed in the final home and estate of the famous French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir.
The museum holds a collection including about a dozen original paintings by Renoir, as well as his furniture, personal belongings, photographs and archives. ■

Study shows New Zealand student performance stabilizes after years of decline
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
17:27:29 CST
18:27:29 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's student performance in science and mathematics has improved or stabilized after more than 20 years of decline, while reading fell to a new low, according to the 2025 Program for International Student Assessment (PISA).
New Zealand students remained above the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) average in all three subjects, ranking ninth in reading, 10th in science and 16th in mathematics, broadly similar to 2022 results, a government statement said on Tuesday.
New Zealand's average science score rose from 504 to 509 points, while mathematics increased by one point to 480. Reading fell four points to 497, driven by a decline in boys' scores. The changes were statistically insignificant, Radio New Zealand reported.
Positively, New Zealand students were amongst the highest performers in computational problem-solving, the statement said.
Education Minister Erica Stanford said in the statement that the results indicated achievement was stabilizing after years of decline, but more needed to be done to raise performance.
However, New Zealand did not meet the OECD participation requirements for PISA 2025, with only 52 percent of selected schools and 76 percent of students participating. The results may therefore be more positive than those from a fully representative sample and should be treated with caution, the statement said.
Nearly a quarter of New Zealand students were low performers in reading, while 29 percent were low performers in mathematics, according to the PISA 2025 results. ■

Taiwan flu epidemic begins as severe cases, deaths climb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:26:48 UTC
18:26:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Centers for Disease Control said Tuesday that the country has entered a flu epidemic period, with 105 severe cases and 19 deaths reported in one week.
CNA reported that health authorities recorded 115,136 flu-related outpatient and emergency visits from Aug. 30 to Sept. 5, up 11% from the previous week. Flu-related visits accounted for 11.2% of all outpatient and emergency visits, exceeding the 11% epidemic threshold.
Taiwan reported 105 new severe flu cases from Sept. 1-7, including 97 linked to H1N1, four to H3N2, and four to untyped influenza A. Authorities also reported 19 deaths, including 18 linked to H1N1 and one to untyped influenza A.
Laboratory monitoring shows influenza A remains the main type circulating in Taiwan. H1N1 accounted for 79.4% of detected flu viruses.
Taiwan has recorded 1,329 severe flu cases and 253 deaths so far this flu season. Most severe cases involved people aged 65 or older and those with chronic health conditions, while 68.6% of severe patients had not received this season’s flu vaccine.
COVID-19 infections continued to decline but remained at epidemic levels, health authorities said. Taiwan recorded 20,199 COVID-19-related outpatient and emergency visits from Aug. 30 to Sept. 5, down 9.7% from the previous week.
Authorities also reported 73 new severe local COVID-19 cases and 15 deaths from Sept. 1-7. Since October last year, Taiwan has recorded 622 severe local cases and 106 deaths.
Most severe COVID-19 cases involved people aged 65 or older and those with chronic health conditions. Among severe patients, 84.9% had not received this season’s COVID-19 vaccine.
Health authorities advised people with symptoms including a sore throat, cough, stuffy or runny nose, fever, fatigue, headache, or muscle pain to seek medical care. They said anyone experiencing difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, low blood pressure, or a high fever lasting more than 72 hours should seek treatment immediately.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Breeze Development Co. plans a major overhaul in Taipei’s Xinyi District following the loss of the Taipei Main Station mall, the company said at its 25th anniversary celebrations Tuesday.
Shin Kong Mitsukoshi Department Store Co. started managing the station mall on July 25 after defeating Breeze in the bidding process. Breeze had been in charge of the complex for almost 20 years.
The change is expected to reduce revenue during the anniversary sales period to NT$5.7 billion (US$180.78 million) from NT$6 billion last year, the company said. Its overall revenue target for 2026 is NT$35.5 billion, similar to last year, per UDN. Sales for the first eight months of 2026 rose between 7% and 10%.
Breeze Chief Strategy Officer Michelle Liao (廖曉喬) said the company was stepping into its next 25 years by preparing a major renovation project in Xinyi District. The project is scheduled for 2029-2030, but details are not yet ready to be announced, she said.
The group’s top malls are the original Breeze Center on Fuxing South Road and two malls in Xinyi District.
Liao also mentioned plans to strengthen ties with South Korean brands and sell more of their products. Cooperation would take several forms, including limited-time offers, while food and technology would join fashion in the available product range, UDN reported.

Taiwan's Ability posts 10-year monthly revenue high in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:26:26 UTC
18:26:26 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Ability Enterprise Co. posted its highest monthly revenue in a decade in August as it shifts from traditional camera manufacturing toward AI and smart imaging products.
The company reported August revenue of NT$1.3 billion (US$41 million), up 34.7% year-on-year. Consolidated revenue for the first eight months of the year totaled NT$8.3 billion, an increase of 50.06% from the same period last year, according to CTEE.
Ability is expanding beyond conventional camera products into areas such as edge AI, machine vision, and smart sensing, building on its experience in optics and imaging. The shift comes as AI applications expand from cloud-based systems to physical devices and machines.
Ability said 2026 marks an important stage in its transformation, with three new product lines — robot vision, drones, and AI smart lenses — moving from development and certification into mass production and shipments. With existing projects expanding and new customers and models being added, the company remains positive about its future operations.
Ability expects robot vision to become a major growth driver. The company has developed next-generation sensing and vision modules with Japanese and US customers for use in humanoid robots, service robots, and automated guided vehicles.
As AI-powered robots move from the concept stage toward commercialization, machine vision is becoming an important technology for helping them perceive their surroundings and identify objects.
For drones, Ability has developed high-end camera lenses and optical modules for environmental monitoring, infrastructure inspections, and public safety. The products have completed customer certification and are now entering delivery.
For the European market, Ability's AI smart lenses combine AI processing and image sensing for smart cities and traffic management. Ability expects orders to increase in the second half of the year.

Taiwan’s Wistron raises NT$46.4 billion in global share sale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:26:05 UTC
18:26:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Wistron Corp. is raising about NT$46.4 billion (US$1.47 billion) through a global share sale to fund purchases of raw materials in foreign currencies, Reuters reported Monday.
Wistron priced the offering at about NT$1,858.60 per global depositary receipt (GDR), near the bottom of its marketed range of about NT$1,852 to NT$1,887. The company will issue 25 million GDRs representing 250 million common shares, with each GDR equivalent to 10 Wistron shares, per CNBC.
The offering price is equivalent to about NT$185.86 per share, a 5.5% discount to Wistron’s Monday closing price of NT$197. The new shares will dilute existing shareholders by about 7.29%, although Wistron said it does not expect the dilution to materially affect shareholder interests.
The fundraising comes as Wistron expands production to meet strong demand for AI servers. The company has approved additional spending to expand capacity in Taiwan and opened a roughly NT$22.1 billion plant in Texas in July to manufacture Nvidia’s latest AI systems.
Wistron said in August that demand for AI servers from cloud computing firms and business customers continued to exceed supply. Its Q2 net profit rose 128% year-on-year, while revenue climbed 64%, and its shares have gained about 30% this year despite closing 0.5% lower Monday.

U.S. and Russian warplanes to appear together at Egypt’s airshow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:24:47 UTC
18:24:47 KST

- The U.S. Air Force is sending F-16s, F-15Es, A-10s and C-130s to Egypt's El Alamein International Airshow, opening September 8 alongside more than 80 countries.
- Russia is separately showcasing its Su-57E stealth fighter at the same airshow, putting American and Russian military aircraft on display together.
American and Russian military aircraft will appear at the same airshow this week, as the U.S. Air Force sends fighters and cargo planes to Egypt’s El Alamein International Airshow alongside a Russian delegation set to showcase its Su-57E stealth fighter.
The 2026 Egypt International Airshow officially opens September 8 at El Alamein International Airport, drawing participants from more than 80 countries and more than 50 aircraft on display, according to a statement from U.S. Central Command. The event marks its second iteration and is intended to highlight Egypt’s aerospace capabilities while reinforcing the decades-long U.S.-Egypt defense relationship.
The U.S. Air Force and the Texas Air National Guard are sending personnel and aircraft to the show, including C-130J Super Hercules and C-130H Hercules cargo planes, A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft, F-16 Fighting Falcon fighters, and F-15E Strike Eagle strike fighters. The U.S. delegation is also opening a pavilion featuring more than 25 American aerospace and defense companies.
“The United States is proud to participate in the El Alamein International Air Show 2026 and to open the U.S. Pavilion, featuring more than 25 American companies from among the world’s leading aerospace and defense innovators,” said Eric Gaudiosi, Charge d’Affaires ad interim at the U.S. Embassy in Cairo. “Our strong presence reflects the depth of the U.S.-Egypt partnership and our longstanding cooperation across the aviation, aerospace, defense, space, and commercial sectors. We look forward to building new partnerships and expanding opportunities that benefit both our countries.”
Russia is also attending the show with its own aircraft. Russia’s state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, has said it will fly its Su-57E stealth fighter in a demonstration and display it on the ground, alongside the public debut of two new weapons built for the jet, according to Russian state media reports covered separately by The Defence Blog. Rosoboronexport CEO Alexander Mikheev has said the company has signed new Su-57E export contracts ahead of the show, though he has not named the buying countries or disclosed contract values, and Russia’s claims about the jet’s proven combat record have not matched independently documented losses of the aircraft during its war in Ukraine.
Egypt has maintained defense ties with both Washington and Moscow for decades, operating American-made F-16s alongside Russian-made air defense systems and other Soviet-legacy equipment, a balancing act reflected in this week’s airshow drawing military hardware from both countries onto the same tarmac. The U.S.-Egypt defense relationship dates back to the 1978 Camp David Accords, and Egypt remains one of the largest recipients of U.S. military aid in the world.

How the US war is driving up the cost of survival in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:22:20 UTC
18:22:20 KST

Breadcrumb
The things Iranians can no longer afford: Surviving the US war, sanctions and soaring inflation
"If you sit in my car right now, you would think it sounds like an old tractor," says Mohsen, a 40-year-old father of a three-year-old girl in Tehran. He knows his car is breaking down, but taking it to a mechanic is a luxury he can no longer afford.
"When I prioritise my family's expenses, repair costs never make the cut."
Mohsen earns a fixed monthly salary of 50 million tomans as an office employee. At the start of the Iranian calendar year, that amount was worth roughly $300.
Today, as Iran's currency continues its freefall amid tightening US sanctions and regional geopolitical turmoil, his wages translate to less than $200.
His predicament has become the new normal for Iran's middle and working classes.
While sanctions, and US sanctions in particular, are said to target the government, the reality on the ground tells a different story.
The intersection of international isolation, recent escalations, and domestic economic vulnerability has placed an unprecedented squeeze on ordinary citizens, reshaping their dietary habits, access to healthcare, and basic social lives.
According to the Statistical Centre of Iran, annual inflation reached 69 percent in August. The macroeconomic horizon offers little optimism: the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects a stark reality for 2026, forecasting a 5.4 percent contraction in real GDP alongside consumer price inflation hovering at 68.9 percent.
For salaried employees like Mohsen, the gap between a fixed income and skyrocketing prices means constantly recalibrating how to survive.
"Being an employee in Iran means you agree on a fixed salary at the start of the year, and no matter what happens in the country, whether there is a war, intensified sanctions, or a blockade, your income stays the same," he explains.
He used to buy meat for his family every week; now it's a once-a-month purchase. Fresh fruit has seen a similar reduction.
Hoping to supplement his income, Mohsen recently registered with a ride-hailing app to work evening shifts, but the embarrassing mechanical noises of his deteriorating car forced him to stop.
Still, he considers himself one of the lucky ones. Because of an inherited property, he doesn't pay rent. "Looking at the terrifying housing market right now, almost all my colleagues are tenants who give up a massive chunk of their salaries just to keep a roof over their heads."
His primary anxiety is no longer his own comfort, but whether he can secure a baseline of welfare for his young daughter.
The rising cost of survival
The Iranian government is acutely aware of this mounting pressure. Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh recently acknowledged the severe impact of inflation on daily life during a televised interview, announcing plans to increase the value of electronic coupons (Kala-barg) for lower-income brackets.
Currently, the state allocates a one-million-toman monthly credit to each citizen, restricted to basic goods such as meat, chicken, and milk. But the sheer speed of price hikes is rapidly eroding the effectiveness of this safety net.
The crisis extends far beyond the dinner table, altering family dynamics and fraying the social fabric.
Nasrin, a 39-year-old single mother and teacher in southern Tehran, can no longer afford private kindergarten for her five-year-old daughter, and public options in her area are virtually nonexistent.
When schools reopen for in-person classes this autumn, she will have no choice but to bring her child to the girls' elementary school where she works.
"Instead of playing with kids her age, she will have to sit in my classroom or the school office from early morning until noon," Nasrin says.
She admits that without her own parents' help providing basic groceries, surviving on a teacher's salary would be nearly impossible.
Beyond food and childcare, the cost of basic healthcare has surged, turning routine illnesses into financial emergencies.
Despite theoretical humanitarian exemptions in US sanctions, the medical supply chain has been choked by a combination of factors: pervasive "de-risking" and over-compliance by international banks, the Iranian government's severe shortage of foreign currency, and an ongoing maritime blockade.
A recent market analysis by Ham-Mihan highlighted staggering year-on-year price hikes for domestically produced and imported essential medications between September 2025 and September 2026.
The price of a standard package of Amoxicillin jumped from 320,000 to 1.23 million tomans. Acetaminophen with codeine surged from 137,000 to 650,000 tomans, and Clarithromycin more than tripled to 1.58 million tomans. Gabapentin, used for nerve pain, rose from 300,000 to 960,000 tomans.
These figures represent just a fraction of a broader, systemic pharmaceutical crisis that leaves patients with chronic or rare conditions highly vulnerable.
Feeling the squeeze
The physical and technological infrastructure ordinary Iranians rely on is also buckling under the weight of the geopolitical standoff.
Recent US strikes targeting Iran's petrochemical facilities have disrupted gasoline supplies, sparking widespread anxiety over potential fuel price hikes.
The economic daily Donya-e-Eqtesad recently warned that given Iran's structural dependence on energy subsidies, any sharp increase in petrol prices could trigger catastrophic disruptions across production chains and urban life.
At the same time, digital connectivity, a lifeline for education, business, and youth culture, is becoming prohibitively expensive.
Following the recent 40-day war, basic technological goods have seen massive markups. The Samsung Galaxy A07, considered an entry-level economy smartphone, now costs at least 50 million tomans on the local market, more than double a standard worker's monthly wage, up from under 20 million tomans just weeks earlier.
For the younger generation, this economic siege means the systematic stripping away of small, daily joys and personal milestones.
Fatima, a 27-year-old social media expert in the private sector, recently had to take out a new bank loan just to pay off the overdue instalments on previous debts.
"Every day, it gets harder to make my money last until the end of the month," she says. Her daily cafe routine was replaced by home-brewed coffee, which has now disappeared entirely, too. She's downgraded to the cheapest available brand of cigarettes. Cosmetics, like sunscreen, are being phased out of her budget, and dining out with friends is a relic of the past.
Yet Fatima's frustration is directed as much at the international actors shaping her reality as at the domestic situation.
Walking through Tehran in a short-sleeved T-shirt and jeans, without a headscarf, a direct defiance of the country's mandatory hijab laws that carries heavy risks of arrest, the severing of mobile networks, and loss of basic state services, she reflects on the geopolitical messaging directed at Iranians.
"The US President tweets asking why the Iranian people don't pour into the streets," Fatima says. "It's ridiculous. They torture us, so we protest? We are in a daily struggle. Just the way we look when we step outside is a struggle in itself."
Ariya Farahmand is an Iranian journalist

Swiftsure is the demonstrator for a programme that has to deal with a substantial number of boats. Decommissioned submarines are held afloat at Devonport and at Rosyth, where seven laid-up vessels are stored and where work under the Submarine Dismantling Project began in 2016.
Defuelling of decommissioned submarines at Devonport stopped in 2004, and the recommissioning of 14 Dock there is intended to allow legacy defuelling operations to resume, work Mr Pollard confirmed last week forms part of the £7.1 billion being invested in the naval base and dockyard over the next decade under Project Royal Oak. He said the department is exploring opportunities to accelerate work on 10 and 14 Dock following the nuclear regulatory review.
Graeme Downie, the Member of Parliament whose constituency covers Rosyth, has been pressing the department for news on submarine recycling at the yard alongside other work, saying last month that he hoped to hear good news soon.

As sanctions, isolation and strained alliances mount, who will be Israel’s next foreign minister?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:19:36 UTC
18:19:36 KST

Sanctions pressure is growing, relations with key Western governments are deteriorating and Israel’s international standing is emerging as one of the biggest challenges awaiting the next government. 
After years of war, repeated confrontations with European governments and mounting criticism of Israeli policy in the West Bank, ties with several countries have fallen to some of their lowest points in decades. In a growing number of capitals, officials are no longer limiting themselves to condemnations and are considering concrete measures against Israel.
European governments have in recent months discussed a range of possible steps, including in response to plans to advance construction in the E1 area. Diplomatic officials say one of the main questions is timing: some European capitals fear sanctions imposed shortly before Israel’s election could strengthen Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and right-wing parties by allowing them to portray the measures as foreign interference. Britain, however, is moving toward restrictions on trade in goods, and in some cases services, originating in Israeli settlements, while considering additional measures as part of a broader shift in policy toward Israel.
The deterioration is increasingly visible beyond official diplomacy as well. Israelis have reported cases across Europe in which they were refused accommodation or services because of their nationality or origin. In Germany, authorities opened an investigation after an Israeli family seeking to book a room at a Bavarian hotel received a message saying Jews were not welcome.
Against that backdrop, the identity of Israel’s next foreign minister could become far more consequential than an ordinary coalition bargaining question. Whoever takes the job will have to manage relations with Washington and Israel’s regional partners while trying to prevent further sanctions, repair strained alliances and reverse a broader trend of diplomatic isolation.
Right-wing government: Sa’ar wants to stay, Katz could return
If Netanyahu forms another government, the natural candidate to remain foreign minister is Gideon Sa’ar. He wants to stay in the post and continue a strategy centered on expanding Israel’s circle of friendly governments, with particular emphasis on Latin America. Sa’ar designated 2026 the Foreign Ministry’s “Year of Latin America,” seeking to capitalize on political shifts across the region.
During his tenure, Israel restored diplomatic relations with Bolivia after years of rupture, while a change of government in Colombia led to the full restoration of ties and a decision to move its embassy to Jerusalem. Israel and the United States also established a joint strategic dialogue focused on Latin America. Jerusalem has meanwhile begun a cautious rapprochement with Venezuela, where consular services were restored in August, 17 years after relations were severed. The next major target is Brazil, where Israeli officials hope future political change could create an opening to repair badly strained relations.
Even if Sa’ar wants to stay, however, the Foreign Ministry could become a focus of internal coalition bargaining. Defense Minister Israel Katz has already served twice as foreign minister. His preference would likely be to remain at the Defense Ministry, but if that portfolio goes elsewhere during coalition negotiations, Katz could seek a return to the Foreign Ministry, forcing Netanyahu to choose between Sa’ar and one of Likud’s most senior figures.
Centrist government: Lapid leads, Bennett and Lieberman in the picture
If parties opposed to Netanyahu form the next government, Yair Lapid would begin as the leading candidate for foreign minister. Lapid held the post from 2021 to 2022 and built direct relationships with governments in Europe and the United States. Within B’Yachad, he would also be a natural candidate for a senior portfolio if Naftali Bennett becomes prime minister.
A Lapid-led Foreign Ministry would likely put repairing relations with Europe near the top of its agenda. While the current government has relied partly on friendly states to block measures against Israel inside European institutions, a centrist government could try to rebuild direct dialogue with Brussels, Paris, Berlin and London and prevent punitive measures from gaining momentum in the first place.
Lapid would not necessarily be the only option. Bennett himself could seek the Foreign Ministry if he does not receive the defense portfolio, or if a rotation agreement leaves him outside the Prime Minister’s Office for part of the government’s term. Avigdor Lieberman could also enter the picture. The Yisrael Beytenu leader served twice as foreign minister, from 2009 to 2012 and again from 2013 to 2015, and his candidacy would depend largely on which portfolio he prioritizes in coalition negotiations.
The first mission: stop the snowball
Whoever gets the job will inherit a diplomatic crisis that is already moving. The European Union has imposed additional sanctions this year on settlers and Israeli organizations while continuing to debate broader measures, including restrictions involving trade with settlements. More sweeping steps have so far encountered opposition from individual EU governments, including Czechia and Slovenia, preventing the formation of the majority required for some measures.
The challenge for the next foreign minister will therefore be twofold: preserve the governments still willing to help Israel block punitive action, while expanding that group before it shrinks further. As criticism of Israel spreads, relying on a small number of friendly capitals becomes increasingly precarious.
Whether the job goes to Sa’ar, Katz, Lapid, Bennett, Lieberman or another candidate, the task will be the same: stop the diplomatic snowball before sanctions, isolation and strained alliances become much harder to reverse.
