The law on mandatory shelters has entered into force in Ukraine — what has changed
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:00:50 EEST
18:00:50 KST

The law on mandatory shelters has entered into force in Ukraine — what has changed
Kyiv • UNN
Law No. 4778-IX strengthens civil protection and requires shelters to be planned for new facilities. Centers and classes for safety are also being established.
On Tuesday, September 8, a Law entered into force in Ukraine that strengthens civil protection requirements and provides for the mandatory construction of shelters in new residential, public, and infrastructure facilities. This was reported by UNN.
Details
Law No. 4778-IX was adopted back on February 10 of this year. It concerns amendments to certain legislative acts of Ukraine on preventing emergencies and eliminating their consequences, establishing a fund of civil protection protective structures, and creating safety classes and centers.
This regulatory legal act enshrines in law the concepts of "safety center," "safety class," and "protected space."
From now on, local self-government bodies will be able to establish safety centers for a comprehensive response to hazardous events. One such facility may simultaneously house a fire and rescue unit, an emergency medical care base, and a police station.
Special safety classes may also be established in educational institutions, where children will be taught fire safety and civil protection rules, as well as how to behave during emergencies, including those involving explosive objects.
In addition, the planning of civil protection protective structures and dual-purpose structures is now mandatory in urban planning documentation.
The law separately addresses the certification of emergency and rescue services, rescuers, and Ukrainian citizens being hired by emergency and rescue services. It is conducted to verify their readiness to carry out emergency rescue and other urgent operations, extinguish fires, and obtain authorization to perform such work.
A specific feature of the certification of emergency and rescue services staffed with divers equipped with special gear for underwater operations is the preliminary certification of the diving units of those services to determine the list of underwater operations they are capable of performing. Emergency and rescue services, rescuers, and Ukrainian citizens being hired by emergency and rescue services are subject to certification. Periodic certification of emergency and rescue services and rescuers is conducted at least once every five years. The certification of emergency and rescue services, rescuers, and Ukrainian citizens being hired by emergency and rescue services is conducted by an interagency certification commission established by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine. The regulations governing the interagency certification commission are approved by the central executive body responsible for formulating state policy in the field of civil protection

'Tirana teeth': Albania hopes to be the new Turkey for dental work
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:28 BST
18:00:28 KST

'Tirana teeth': Albania hopes to be the new Turkey for dental work
- Published
Anthony Hook is sitting in a dentist's chair, grinning toothily into a handheld mirror. He has been asked to pose for photos showing off his new smile – and he is only too happy to oblige.
The 58-year-old window cleaner from Bolton, in Greater Manchester, is the proud owner of a sparkling new set of "Tirana teeth".
That is not a brand name – at least, not yet. But it would be a fitting slogan as Albania moves decisively into the medical tourism business.
Tirana, its capital city, is the focus of operations. And once you spot the first tooth, you start seeing them everywhere. They seem to be all over the city centre.
Rest assured, these are not the physical remains from a night out that ended in a punch up. Rather, they are the kind of larger than life-size illuminated molar that – in these parts at least – advertise that a dental clinic is not too far away.
In Tirana's metropolitan area alone, there are almost four hundred dental clinics – and most of them are in the city centre. That's more than enough for a population of around 600,000 people.
So, it is not surprising that dozens of dentists are now targeting customers from further afield. They have set up websites and signage in English and Italian, as well as Albanian.
Dental implants in Albania are typically around €600 ($700; £516) per tooth, similar in price to what is charged in Turkey, which has long been the main overseas destination for people in western Europe who are seeking much cheaper dental work than they can get at home.
The same treatment in the UK, France or German can easily cost four times as much.
For Hook the appeal was irresistible. He made his first visit to Tirana to watch England's footballers play Albania last year – but then found himself intrigued by all the signs for dentists. That nudged him into doing something about his missing teeth.
He thought he's give Albania rather than Turkey, because he was concerned by media coverage of dental or hair transplant work in Turkey that had gone wrong.
In fact, even the UK Foreign Office warns that it is "aware of seven British nationals having died in Turkey in 2025 following medical procedures"., external It adds that "some British nationals have also experienced complications [after surgery in Turkey], and needed further treatment or surgery following their procedure."
Hook says he wouldn't go to Turkey "because I have heard so many bad things", adding that he investigated thoroughly before taking the plunge in Tirana.
"I went onto the internet and looked into it properly. It took me two days to research it because I'm not one for jumping into anything."
Several return trips later, Anthony now has a mouthful of impressive implants – and, unsurprisingly, he is all smiles. "I'd come here once a month for a holiday if I could," he chuckles.
Elite Dental is one of the biggest clinics in Tirana. It is fully licensed by the Albanian health authorities – and so are all of its 15 resident dentists.
The man who runs the place, Ardtur Dema, says he is "not in favour of damaging proper teeth for aesthetics". Instead he says the priority is "changing people's lives" through restoring their ability to chew, and indeed – to smile.
Dema believes that as long as Albania remains outside the EU, prices for treatment are likely to remain low. At the same time, low-cost airlines have greatly expanded their flight network to and from Tirana, meaning that he is as likely to see a patient from Turin as he is from Tirana.
But Dema is concerned that the explosion of tourism could lead to less scrupulous operators ruining the business for everyone. He is a member of the newly-established Albanian Medical Tourism Association – but many others are not, at least not yet.
Albania's Prime Minister, Edi Rama, tells the BBC that the government is playing catch-up after five years that have seen overall international arrivals to Albania more than double. Some sort of official seal of approval for medical tourism facilities is a possibility – but the government has yet to sort out the details.
"It's a new industry that is within the tourism industry umbrella that is showing a big potential and where there are very good people," says Rama.
He adds that the government wants to help all the reputable providers "survive", and to guard against any informal "bad competition".
Along with dental treatments, some visitors to Albania are starting to think "hairline" as well as "coastline".
Some transplant clinics are employing Turkish specialists – others are actually branches of businesses based in Turkey.
Vatanmed, in Tirana, is one of the latter. Sales specialist and health consultant Ayşe Mina Kasemi describes the business as a "global brand", with 15 clinics across a number of countries. That scale, she suggests, makes it "a safe place to trust" for the international patients arriving for treatment.
Besides that, Ayşe notes, Albania has its own appeal.
"When people decide to have a hair transplant operation here in Albania, they also want to have a holiday here, because Albania is a very beautiful place," she says, while adding a note of caution for hair transplant patients. "For the first two or three days, they have to be careful – they are not allowed to be exposed to the sun."
That is not a factor that concerns Anthony Hook. He happily sports a shaven head – and has no intention of following his dental treatment with a radical rug rethink. So enjoying Albania's beaches and scenery was very much part of the attraction of getting his teeth fixed here.
"There's a lot to do in Tirana… there's a lot to do along the coast there, it's absolutely stunning," he says. "I want to do it now before it gets too popular and it's ruined like everywhere else."
With his new teeth, enjoying Albania's cuisine will doubtless also be part of Anthony's programme. Apart from anything else, that smile is going to dazzle in the holiday snaps.

Ukraine’s first underground kindergarten opens in Kharkiv region
Ukrinform reports this, citing the Ministry of Education and Science .
1 / 10
“The new educational space is designed for 260 children and makes it possible to organize a full-fledged in-person educational process even during air raid alerts. The underground facility is equipped with eight classrooms, a medical room, a dining room, restrooms, and showers. The shelter is autonomous thanks to two independent power sources and backup generators,” the statement says.
The shelter is connected to the kindergarten buildings by safe passageways, allowing children and staff to reach it without going outside.
Particular attention was paid to creating a barrier-free environment. The facility has elevators, lifts, and step-free routes, as well as all the necessary conditions for children with disabilities and other people with reduced mobility.
The Ministry of Education and Science recalled that in 2026, the government allocated separate funding for the first time to equip shelters in preschool education institutions. This includes support for communities facing the highest security risks.
The underground kindergarten was built through co-financing from the central government, regional, and local budgets. In 2026, a government subsidy for equipping shelters in preschool education institutions was provided for the first time. The total amount of funding exceeds UAH 972 million.
Projects are currently being implemented in nine regions of Ukraine: Vinnytsia, Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Sumy, Kharkiv, and Kherson regions. During the project selection process, priority was given to communities facing the highest security risks, particularly in frontline regions, as well as facilities where construction work had already begun.

The construction and reconstruction of shelters in preschool education institutions are being carried out by territorial communities with financial support from the European Union under the Ukraine Facility.

Firmly attached to a specific desire, my ability to see reality is occluded. My attention cannot…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:58:01 UTC
17:58:01 KST

Firmly attached to a specific desire, my ability to see reality is occluded. My attention cannot reach what is happening in and around me, because I’m seeing everything through the lens of my desire and its possible satisfaction. I’m ignoring important information and putting too much emphasis on the evidence that supports my desire.
With my attention so heavily restricted, I can’t get an accurate picture of things, which means it’s easy for me to fall into delusion. This is especially true when the desire is intense and its object is present, which is often what happens when it involves another person. Sometimes these delusions are glaringly obvious, but often they are more subtle.
The most common subtle delusion in a relationship is to believe that an agreement has been reached when no such agreement actually exists. I believe that we have agreed that our relationship will go in a certain way, but we have not. It is my own attachment to a particular ideal of the relationship that has deluded me into thinking I’m living in this imaginary world when I’m actually living in another.

Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.

Lorenzo Tondo
in Palermo
According to the National Research Council (CNR), the summer of 2026 was the hottest recorded in the Italy since 1950, as the country battled a wave of wildfires and the largest glacier in the Dolomites suffered a record loss of mass.
The CNR said on Monday that temperatures during the summer months even surpassed the previous record set in 2003, an exceptionally hot summer that had long been seen as difficult to repeat.
The average temperature across Italy this summer was 24.3C, measured 2 metres above the ground, compared with 23.6C in 2003, said Lorenzo Arcidiaco of the CNR.
The average temperature in August was 25.6C, beating the previous records of 24.6C in 2024 and 24C in August 2017, Arcidiaco said.
“The data suggest that 2026 will end as the hottest year since 1950.”
Meanwhile, wildfires that have hit Sicily in recent days continued to burn on Monday, forcing thousands of residents and tourists to leave their homes and holiday accommodation.
Firefighters were battling blazes in several parts of the island, days after the death of Salvatore Giglia, 26, who suffered severe burns while trying to fight a fire near his home and land in Ciminna, near Palermo.
In Palermo province, fires broke out in Castronovo di Sicilia and Bolognetta, while in Trapani province flames burned woodland near the Zaffarana dam.
The extreme temperatures have also taken a heavy toll on the Marmolada glacier, the largest in the Dolomites.
The glacier suffered a record loss of mass this summer, according to data presented on Monday by the University of Padua, the Veneto environmental protection agency and the Italian Glaciological Foundation.
The Marmolada retreated by an average of about 23 metres over the summer and its surface area fell from 92 hectares to 83 hectares.
Experts said the only comparable loss was recorded in 2022, when part of the glacier collapsed after a heatwave brought unusually high temperatures, killing 11 people.

Ushakov said Putin gave Trump an “objective and detailed assessment” of developments on the battlefield. Putin has repeatedly sought to portray Russian forces as making gains at the front, while at times claiming the capture of Ukrainian territory that remains outside Russian control.
According to Ushakov, Trump argued during the call that ending the war in Ukraine could pave the way for a broader restoration of US-Russia relations.
Ushakov also said Putin stressed to Trump that Russia had “no hostile plans whatsoever” towards Europe.
Trump has in recent days insisted that Putin would not attack Nato territory, playing down concerns in European capitals that Russia could eventually test the alliance with some form of military incursion.
Putin, Trump discusses weekend envoy talks on Ukraine, Kremlin says
Meanwhile, we have just heard from the Kremlin on a phone call between US president Donald Trump and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
The pair talked about the visit of US peace envoys to Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend, and prospects for their bilateral relations.
Kremlin claims that Trump would like to see US-Russia ties restored during his presidency, while Putin assured him that he had no hostile plans towards Europe.

That is why today we summoned the Serbian Chargé d’Affaires. Glorification of a convicted war criminal directly undermines trust, fuels division and is incompatible with the process of reconciliation within Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region.

First Lady: barrier-free approach works only when everyone is responsible for it simultaneously
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:57:02 EEST
17:57:02 KST

First Lady of Ukraine Olena Zelenska believes that the barrier-free policy works only when everyone is responsible for it simultaneously: the state, the public, and business.
"A barrier-free approach works only when everyone is responsible for it simultaneously. The state lays down standards and strategy. Public organizations keep in touch with the real needs of people—without this, no standard will work. And business transforms all of this into specific services, products, and internal corporate culture," Zelenska said in a video address to the III Annual Forum "My Barrier-Free Space. Lessons Learned" on Tuesday in Kyiv.
She recalled that the National Strategy for Creating a Barrier-Free Space is being implemented in the country.
According to her, the state, together with business, is building an entire barrier-free infrastructure: barrier-free driving schools, "Superheroes' Schools," barrier-free routes, barrier-free Administrative Services Centers (CNAPs), and adaptive sports.
"This year, this joint effort is reaching a new level. As part of the Barrier-Free Strategy, we declared the year of education and enlightenment. This is already tangible. Nearly 30 projects are currently being led by various ministries. Barrier-free commissioners are appearing in communities, and the network of advocacy ambassadors is expanding," Zelenska added.
At the same time, the First Lady emphasized that institutional mechanisms and services are not everything, as respectful treatment and communication are equally important.
"And each of you can become part of this process, implementing it at your own level. Moreover, it is worth starting from childhood. Therefore, this school year did not accidentally begin with the lesson 'Language of Dignity'," Zelenska said.
She expressed hope that this year barrier-free language would become a general rule.
"Someone will ask: what will change if we say 'invalid' [disabled person] or 'person with a disability'? I will say this: something important will definitely change—this person will finally take first place. Both in our speech and in our actions. And this applies not only to children at school, but at any level—in the state, in the community, in a company. Language itself shows whom we put first. Therefore, dignity is not about loud statements, but about daily phrasings—how we recall each other, how we write, how we speak," the First Lady stressed.
The Interfax-Ukraine news agency is an information partner of the event.
The III Annual Forum "My Barrier-Free Space. Lessons Learned" was initiated and organized by Oschadbank with support from Visa and the European Business Association within the framework of First Lady Olena Zelenska's "Barrier-Free" initiative. Oschad, along with its partners, works to ensure that accessibility and inclusion become an established societal norm.
As reported, in December 2022, First Lady Olena Zelenska presented a section on the Diia portal—"Diia. Barrier-Free," which encompasses articles useful for Ukrainians during various life periods. The portal features extensive information for internally displaced persons, people with disabilities, parents, elderly individuals, and job seekers.

Netanyahu rejected Shin Bet recommendation to assassinate Sinwar before Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:56:27 UTC
17:56:27 KST

Less than a week before the October 7 attack, then Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on October 1, 2023, and recommended carrying out a targeted assassination of Hamas leader in Gaza Yahya Sinwar, along with a series of additional assassinations targeting senior figures in the organization.
Notably, the report comes after N12 News reported in January that Netanyahu had turned down the chance to kill Sinwar 11 times before October 7.
Israeli media also previously reported in 2025 that Bar asked Netanyahu to approve Sinwar's assasination days before the massacre.
According to a security source, Bar told Netanyahu that the Shin Bet had identified that Hamas was "preparing something extreme," and also used the term "earthquake" during the conversation.
The source confirmed that the information was presented to the prime minister and that the recommendation to act against Sinwar and other senior Hamas officials was put before him, but Netanyahu did not accept it. "The reports that have emerged recently on this matter are accurate," the security source said.
The account takes on additional significance in light of Haaretz's recent report alleging that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed also warned Netanyahu, about a week and a half before the attack, that Sinwar was planning a significant move against Israel.
According to the investigation, MBZ called Netanyahu from the presidential palace in Abu Dhabi, and the two spoke for about 45 minutes. During the conversation, the UAE president warned that Sinwar was preparing for a major move that could lead to bloodshed, destabilize the region, and even harm the Abraham Accords.
President Isaac Herzog, who maintains close relations with MBZ, told Haaretz that the UAE president had already been concerned about the situation before the war. "He spoke to me about it a lot in the months before the war," he said.
'Something is about to explode,' said MBZ
According to the investigation, MBZ's source was a close adviser, a Palestinian who had emigrated from Gaza to Abu Dhabi years earlier and maintained contacts in the Strip. The adviser said that bin Zayed warned Netanyahu that Israel needed to prepare. "The emir explained that, in his assessment, Sinwar was preparing for a significant event. He told Netanyahu that Israel would be better off being prepared."
At the same time, MBZ recommended pursuing an economic solution in Gaza and reducing tensions in the West Bank in an effort to prevent further deterioration. According to the report, Netanyahu received the warning relatively calmly and said that, in his assessment, Hamas intended to act specifically in the West Bank. He also reassured MBZ that Israel was prepared for any scenario.
MBZ later shared his concern that "something is about to explode" with then CIA director William Burns. However, according to the same report, the warning delivered by the UAE president to Netanyahu was not brought to the attention of the heads of Israel's security establishment. The heads of the Shin Bet and Mossad, as well as the IDF chief of staff, were unaware of the warning the prime minister had received.
A different outcome?
Meanwhile, the security establishment rejects the claim that the outcome could necessarily have been changed if the prime minister or defense minister had received an update during the night between October 6 and 7.
According to security officials, the intelligence picture available to the Shin Bet and Military Intelligence that night was partial and did not provide sufficient clarity about Hamas's offensive intentions. Some of the information, they said, was even consistent with signs of continued routine inside Gaza and did not clearly indicate that a large-scale attack was about to be launched within hours.
The security establishment maintains that even if Netanyahu or the defense minister had become involved at that stage, convening an assessment at the political level, building an intelligence picture and making decisions would have taken enough time that the discussion itself would have come close to the time the attack began.
A security source familiar with the events of that night rejected Netanyahu's version, according to which he would have acted in a way that changed the situation on the ground had he received an update during the night.
According to the officials, the intelligence available at the time did not provide a clear picture that Hamas intended to launch a comprehensive attack. They also said the remaining timeframe was too short for the IDF to move significant forces into position or launch a disruption operation that could have prevented the attack.

Türkiye’s civil aviation fleet reaches 846 aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:55:12 UTC
17:55:12 KST

Türkiye’s civil aviation sector continued its growth momentum in the first half of the year, with the fleet of airline operators expanding to 846 aircraft and total seat capacity exceeding 166,000.
According to data from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (SHGM), a total of 111 million passengers traveled by air during the January-June period, including 50 million on domestic routes and 61 million on international routes.
Cargo traffic also increased during the period. Domestic flights carried 441,000 tons of freight, while international services transported 2.06 million tons, bringing total cargo volume to 2.5 million tons.
As of the end of the first half, Türkiye had 14 airline operators, 49 air taxi operators, 101 general aviation operators, 72 balloon operators, 13 ultralight aircraft operators, 165 maintenance organizations, 48 ground handling companies and 15 landing strips.
Air taxi operators had a total of 259 aircraft, while general aviation operators operated 632 aircraft. Balloon operators had 528 aircraft and ultralight aviation operators had 35 aircraft.
Türkiye’s aviation growth was not limited to passenger and cargo traffic. Over the past 23 years, the sector’s turnover increased 805-fold, surpassing 2.46 trillion Turkish Liras.

Finland Builds 200 km Fence Along Its Border With Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:54:25 UTC
17:54:25 KST

Finland has completed a 200-kilometer fence along its eastern border with Russia after more than three years of construction.
The Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported the completion.
The construction work lasted over three years.
Finland’s Interior Minister Mari Rantanen announced the completion of the fence on September 7 during a press conference near the Nuijamaa border crossing in southeastern Finland.
The largest section of the fence, about 140 km, runs through southeastern Finland. Another 35 km is located in the North Karelia region, while around 25 km runs through Kainuu and Finnish Lapland.
The project is estimated to have cost around €380 million. Construction began with a pilot section near Imatra in April 2023. During the project, Finland stayed ahead of its planned construction schedule.
Finland’s border with Russia is approximately 1,340 kilometers long. It is the longest land border with Russia among EU and NATO countries.
In 2023, Finland closed its border with Russia amid accusations that Moscow was using so-called “instrumentalized migration.”
Meanwhile, the Finnish government proposed extending the border security law for another two years. The law is intended to strengthen the government’s ability to respond to similar hybrid operations.
In addition to the border fence, the Finnish government is considering restoring drained wetlands to create a natural barrier against a potential Russian ground invasion.
Finland’s Defense and Environment ministries are expected to begin talks this autumn on launching a pilot project to restore peatlands.
The Finnish Defense Forces are also calling on reservists who have previously volunteered for such duties to help strengthen security in border areas. They will assist with protecting the border and airspace in different parts of the country.

Culture minister to decide on future of far-right broadcaster ON
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Culture minister Rianne Letschert is under pressure to pull the plug on far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON) when she meets director-general Peter Vlemmix later on Tuesday.
The channel has been repeatedly criticised for breaching journalistic and ethical standards, most recently in an item that used footage of a speech by Adolf Hitler to introduce a discussion about the “cosmopolitan elite”.
Letschert initially said she was unable to intervene because the public broadcasting service NPO had not asked her to withdraw ON’s licence.
But last week the media regulator CvdM said in a letter to the minister that the broadcaster had failed to comply with its legal obligations, clearing the way for Letschert to take ON off the air.
More than two-thirds of MPs want the publicly funded channel to be removed in the wake of the latest controversy, including all three coalition parties D66, CDA and VVD, RTL Nieuws reported. Parliament is due to debate its future later this month.
ON’s editor-in-chief Joost Niemöller stepped down a week ago because of a ”difference of view about the editorial direction and recent programming”, according to a statement by Vlemmix.
Niemöller was one of the panellists on the show that sparked the row, after he said he agreed with “certain things of Hitler’s” but condemned the Nazi leader’s anti-Semitism.
Vlemmix has said the broadcaster will continue its “fight for survival” and accused the media regulator of overlooking improvements made over the past year.

Macron urges EU ban on social media for under-15s in letter to Von der Leyen
Unknown

Macron urges EU ban on social media for under-15s in letter to Von der Leyen
- French President Emmanuel Macron urges an EU-wide ban on social media for children under 15 after France’s national bill was rejected.
- Macron wants a strict ban to protect children’s mental health, pushing ahead of the 2027 French presidential election and lobbying other EU countries.
- European Commission plans a tiered access system for under-13s, but Macron seeks a tougher approach with a full ban until age 15.
AI generated
PARIS – French President Emmanuel Macron has urged the European Commission to back a European Union-wide ban on social media for children under 15 after France failed to enact its own legislation, his office said on Sept 8.
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen dated Aug 29 and seen by Reuters and other media, Macron said it had become urgent to introduce a bloc-wide ban through new EU legislation after France’s Constitutional Council struck down a national bill this summer before it was due to take effect in September.
“I believe it has now become essential to go further and, through a new European legislative text, harmonise a ban on access to social media platforms for children under the age of 15, in order to protect all children across the union,” Macron wrote.
Following Australia’s landmark social media ban for children adopted in 2025, several European countries are considering their own curbs amid growing concern over the impact of social media on young people’s mental health and safety. But some countries, especially in Scandinavia, believe it is best left for parents to decide.
Macron, now in his final year as French President, has taken up the cause as a priority before the next French presidential election in 2027, and has been lobbying other EU governments to back restrictions.
He said France would separately rework the legislation struck down by the constitutional council, though political fragmentation in parliament and difficult budget negotiations could complicate efforts to pass a new law.
Von der Leyen said in July that the European Union would move to limit young children’s access to social media across the 27-member bloc, citing proposals from two experts recommending a tiered system.
Under that approach, children under 13 would be allowed only limited, supervised access, with restrictions eased gradually as they get older.
Macron is seeking a tougher approach, pushing for a blanket ban on social media access until the age of 15, ahead of von der Leyen’s flagship State of the Union speech to the EU parliament later in September. REUTERS

Warm temperatures of up to +32° and no rain: what the weather will be like in Ukraine on September 9–10
Kyiv • UNN
On September 9–10, it will be dry, sunny, and warm in Ukraine, with temperatures reaching up to +32°. On September 10, the wind will strengthen, helping to disperse the smoke in Kyiv.
On Wednesday, September 9, sunny weather without precipitation is expected in Ukraine. The air temperature will rise to +32°, while Kyiv will see up to +27°. Meanwhile, on September 10, summer weather will also prevail in Ukraine. This was reported by weather forecaster Natalka Didenko, according to UNN.
Details
According to Natalka Didenko, an anticyclone—an area of high atmospheric pressure—will continue to determine the weather over Ukraine. As a result, no rain is forecast in any region of the country.

More than 20 countries have invested billions of dollars in the programme which aims to ensure a predictable flow of lethal and non-lethal support for Ukraine, with military hardware purchased mainly from the US.
The equipment "will be delivered before the winter, helping Ukraine defend its critical national infrastructure, innocent civilians and armed forces from Russian attacks," the ministry added.
Ukraine relies on advanced air defence systems, chiefly US Patriot interceptors, to protect its skies from Russian ballistic missile strikes.

The broken illusion: US fails to subdue Iran in war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:47:05 UTC
17:47:05 KST

A war becomes a victory for a great power when it can achieve the objectives it set for starting it; inflicting damage or carrying out extensive attacks alone is not a sign of victory. Now, the more time passes since the start of America's war against Iran, the more the gap between the victory narrative in Washington and the reality on the ground becomes apparent.
America's failed war against Iran has gradually turned into a domestic issue in the United States. What was initially supposed to be a display of Washington's power and proof of its ability to impose its will on Tehran is now facing serious questions about the human, military, and economic costs of the war. Under such circumstances, opposition to the Trump administration's policies is no longer raised only by foreign critics, but a number of American politicians are also warning about the results of this war.
Chris Murphy, the Democratic senator from Connecticut, pointing to the consequences of the war against Iran, has presented a picture of the costs that, according to him, the United States has incurred as a result of this conflict. Murphy announced that 18 Americans have been killed, billions of dollars in damage have been inflicted on US bases, and the country's missile stockpiles have been severely depleted. He also pointed to the economic pressures on American farmers and the rise in gasoline prices to around five dollars; an issue that shows the consequences of the war no longer remain confined to military bases and the battlefield, but have spread into the daily lives of American society.
But the most important part of Murphy's remarks is not his reference to casualties and damages, but his assessment of Iran's situation. The American senator has stressed that Iran is "stronger than ever" and that Trump, in contrast, has become dangerously delusional. These words in effect constitute a direct blow to the US government's narrative about the outcome of the war; a narrative that tries to present extensive military strikes as equivalent to victory.
The main problem with this narrative is that victory in war cannot be measured solely by the number of attacks, the amount of bombs used, or the damage inflicted on the opposing side's infrastructure. The real criterion is the achievement of political and military objectives. If the goal of the war was to weaken Iran, destroy its capacity for resistance, and force Tehran to accept Washington's demands, then Iran's continued ability to confront, respond, and rebuild its capacities shows that these objectives have not been achieved.
On the other hand, the United States has paid considerable costs to continue this war. The depletion of missile stockpiles, increased pressure on military bases, American casualties, and the economic effects of the war are all part of the cost Washington must pay to continue the conflict. These costs become even more significant when the opposing side still retains the ability to continue the war. In a war of attrition, the issue is not only who has inflicted more damage; the decisive question is who has greater capacity to absorb the blows and keep going.
This is where Trump's claim of victory faces a serious challenge. The US government can speak of the success of military operations and the damage inflicted on Iran, but if these operations have not been able to deter Tehran from continuing its resistance, the final result will fall far short of the classic definition of victory. Military victory must ultimately lead to a lasting political achievement; otherwise, large-scale attacks may simply turn into a cycle of attrition that imposes costs on both sides.
From this very perspective, Murphy's remarks gain greater significance. He is effectively drawing the attention of American public opinion away from images of attacks and displays of military power toward the bill for the war. A bill that includes human casualties, the consumption of weapons stockpiles, damage to bases, economic pressure, and the rising cost of living for the American people. When such costs are set alongside the failure to achieve the war's primary objectives, the question about the real success of these operations becomes unavoidable.
In this context, the claim that "Iran has become stronger" should also be examined within the same framework. Power does not mean merely an increase in the number of military equipment. The ability to maintain political cohesion, continue economic activity, rebuild defensive capacities, preserve the ability to respond, and most importantly, prevent the enemy from imposing its political will are all part of a country's power in wartime. If Iran, after enduring heavy attacks, still retains the ability to continue the confrontation, this in itself shows that the American strategy has not been able to achieve the result for which it was designed.
In contrast, the United States also faces an important issue: prolonged wars carry costs for Washington far beyond military operations. They consume weapons stockpiles, put forces and equipment at risk, create economic pressure, and can ultimately deepen the political divide within the United States. The longer the war drags on, the more serious this question becomes: whether its achievements have been worth such a cost.
For this reason, the war against Iran cannot be assessed solely through images of attacks and official American statements. The reality on the ground becomes clear when the stated objectives are compared with the actual results. If the United States, despite using its enormous military capacity, has not been able to force Iran to surrender, has not been able to eliminate its capacity for resistance, and has simultaneously faced casualties, depleted weapons stockpiles, and economic pressure, then speaking of victory will be difficult.
America has lost this war; not only because of the heavy costs, but because it has not been able to achieve its primary objectives. The more important issue is that this failure is no longer raised only in the analyses of Washington's opponents. Now the voice of criticism is also being heard from within the American political structure, and politicians like Chris Murphy are warning about the gap between the war's costs and its achievements.
Ultimately, what is collapsing today more than anything else is not just a military strategy, but the illusion of an easy American victory against Iran; an illusion that imagined a country could be forced to surrender through firepower. The reality of the war, however, has shown that real power is not limited to the ability to attack; sometimes more important than that is the ability to stand, to respond, and to keep going. And Iran, at least according to the existing realities, is still standing.
MNA

Sweden to Buy U.S. HIMARS, Plans to Produce PrSM Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:46:15 UTC
17:46:15 KST

Sweden will purchase U.S.-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket systems for approximately SEK 7 billion ($729 million) and will cooperate with Finland on their operation.
The Swedish government announced the deal on its official website.
The first HIMARS rocket systems, manufactured by Lockheed Martin, are expected to be delivered in 2027.
The Swedish Armed Forces will fund the purchase through its investment plan and the country’s 2025–2030 defense program.
The HIMARS rocket systems will expand the Swedish Army’s long-range strike capabilities and strengthen NATO’s defensive posture in Northern Europe.
They will complement existing Archer artillery systems and mortars while ensuring interoperability with weapons systems operated by other NATO countries.
According to Swedish broadcaster SVT, the deal involves more than ten HIMARS launchers and a large quantity of GMLRS guided rockets. The Swedish government’s official announcement did not specify the exact number of systems.
Meanwhile, Saab and Lockheed Martin have signed a letter of intent to potentially integrate GLSDB munitions into the new systems.
The companies are also considering producing PrSM precision-guided ballistic missiles in Sweden. HIMARS and other systems, including the Patriot air defense system, use the missiles.
However, the Swedish government’s official announcement does not yet specify which type of missile it plans to manufacture in Sweden.
HIMARS is a U.S.-made highly mobile wheeled multiple launch rocket system designed to conduct precision strikes and rapidly relocate to new firing positions. It can carry six GMLRS rockets, two PrSM missiles, or one ATACMS missile.
PrSM is a surface-to-surface ballistic missile with a range of 60 km to more than 500 km, developed to replace ATACMS. A single HIMARS launcher can carry two PrSM missiles instead of one ATACMS, or a pod containing six GMLRS rockets. The missile is also compatible with the tracked M270 launchers.

From the airport to a new life: ynet Global Aliyah Summit answers biggest questions facing new olim | Live

The decision to make aliyah can take years. But once the ticket is booked and the suitcases are packed, questions about identity and belonging quickly give way to much more practical ones.
What do you do when you land? Which documents do you need? How do you choose a health fund, open a bank account, transfer money, find work or rent a home? And if something happens in the middle of the night, who do you call?
Today, September 8, ynet Global is holding its Global Aliyah Live Summit, a day of broadcasts devoted to answering those questions and helping prospective and newly arrived immigrants understand what life in Israel actually looks like after the plane lands.
Follow the live broadcasts and continuing coverage on this page throughout the day.
The summit brings together senior public officials, Aliyah and absorption organizations, specialists in healthcare, banking, employment and housing, and new immigrants who are experiencing the process firsthand.
Broadcasts will be held in Russian, English and French, with coverage also appearing across ynet and ynet Global.
Today’s broadcast schedule, Israel time
13:00-14:00 — Live broadcast in Russian, in cooperation with Vesti
14:00-17:00 — Live broadcast in English on ynet Global and ynet
17:00-18:00 — Live broadcast in French on ynet Global
You landed in Israel. What happens next?
One of the summit’s central discussions focuses on the first 24 hours after aliyah, when months or years of planning suddenly become reality.
After the flight, the welcome and the first photo in Israel comes a new challenge: navigating a bureaucracy and public-service system that can be unfamiliar even to people who prepared extensively before arriving.
Which documents do new immigrants receive? What must be done immediately and what can wait? When should they register with a health fund, open a bank account or begin dealing with government offices? What benefits are available and how are they accessed?
Today’s summit brings those steps together, giving new immigrants a practical guide to the first days of building a life in Israel.
What should be done before the flight?
Some of the most important preparations begin before an oleh ever reaches Ben Gurion Airport.
The summit will address which documents should be brought to Israel, what arrangements should be made with banks overseas, what to do with savings and other assets abroad and when to begin looking for work.
New immigrants will also discuss the less technical side of leaving: saying goodbye to family and friends, leaving a job, packing a home and confronting the uncertainty of having to build a new routine in another country.
Money, banking and buying a home
Opening an Israeli bank account can raise questions that go far beyond simply choosing a branch.
A financial panel featuring experts and representatives including Bank Leumi and mortgage advisers will examine how newcomers should navigate the Israeli financial system.
Among the issues: transferring money from abroad, handling overseas income and assets, understanding Israel’s credit system, foreign currency and international transfer fees.
The summit will also look ahead to one of the largest financial decisions many olim eventually face: buying a home in Israel.
Mortgage advisers will discuss what new immigrants should know before entering the Israeli property market and what needs to be checked before taking out a mortgage.
Bringing your career to Israel
For many new immigrants, moving countries also means confronting the possibility of starting again professionally.
A doctor, engineer, teacher, executive, entrepreneur or tech professional may arrive with a decade or more of experience only to discover that the Israeli job market does not automatically recognize the career they built overseas.
Employment specialists taking part in the summit will discuss when to start searching for work, how to adapt a résumé for Israel, how to build a local professional network and which professions require Israeli licensing.
The sessions will also address entrepreneurship, retraining and starting a business.
The goal is not simply to help olim find their first Israeli job, but to help them preserve and use the skills and experience they already have.
Healthcare and the number every newcomer should know
Israel’s healthcare system can also require an adjustment for immigrants arriving from countries with very different models of medical care.
Representatives from Clalit Health Services will explain how to join a health fund, choose a doctor, make appointments and begin using the services available to new immigrants.
The summit will also cover medical emergencies.
A dedicated segment will explain what happens when someone calls Magen David Adom at **101**, what information dispatchers need and what newcomers should expect from Israel’s emergency medical system.
Among the many new numbers an oleh needs to learn, 101 is one worth knowing from the first day.
Hearing from olim themselves
The summit is not only about officials and experts.
New immigrants at different stages of the aliyah process will discuss what surprised them after arriving, what proved more difficult than expected, where bureaucracy caused problems and what they wish they had known before boarding the plane.
They will also talk about finding jobs and apartments, building communities and adjusting to everyday Israeli life.
That firsthand perspective is central to today’s event. Sometimes the most useful advice for someone preparing to make aliyah comes from someone who made the same move only weeks or months earlier.
The organizations behind aliyah
The Global Aliyah Live Summit features representatives from many of the major organizations involved in bringing immigrants to Israel and helping them integrate, including the Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, the Jewish Agency for Israel, the World Zionist Organization, Keren Hayesod, Ofek Israeli, Nefesh B’Nefesh, Clalit Health Services, Bank Leumi, the Jerusalem Municipality, Masa Israel Journey and Magen David Adom.
Participants also include the minister of Aliyah and Integration and the chairman of the Jewish Agency, who will address the broader questions surrounding immigration to Israel: Who is making Aliyah today? What has changed in recent waves? What barriers remain? And what does Israel need to do not only to bring new immigrants to the country, but to help them build successful lives once they arrive?
Aliyah does not end at the airport
ynet Global’s Global Aliyah project has followed prospective and new immigrants throughout the year with guides, personal stories and practical information about life in Israel.
Today, that conversation goes live.
The summit is designed for those who have already booked their flights, those planning Aliyah in the coming months and those still sitting in Paris, London, New York, Toronto, Moscow or elsewhere wondering whether the time has come.
Throughout the day, the broadcasts will address the large and small questions behind starting a new life: work, money, healthcare, housing, bureaucracy, community and belonging.
Watch the Global Aliyah Live Summit and follow continuing coverage on this page throughout the day.
Because aliyah does not end when you land at Ben Gurion Airport.
That is where it really begins.

Russia opened an ancient tomb – and found a message for today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:45:26 UTC
17:45:26 KST

Russia opened an ancient tomb – and found a message for today
In the dim interior of Moscow’s Cathedral of the Archangel, a candle softly flickered. Russian President Vladimir Putin stood by an open white stone sarcophagus, made the Sign of the Cross, and bowed his head. Only a few inches remained between the Kremlin of the 21st century and an ancient Russian ruler who died more than 600 years ago. The Russian president called the uncovering of the relics a “miraculous discovery.”
Several weeks earlier, restorers had removed the sagging floor near the cathedral’s southern wall. The old stone lid, which was in danger of collapsing inward, was carefully lifted. Beneath the burial cloth lay the remains of Prince Dmitry Donskoy, a warrior prince canonized by the Orthodox Church and venerated in Russia as the holy savior of Rus’.
On August 18, Patriarch of Moscow and All Rus’ Kirill held a prayer service at the sarcophagus. Particles of the relics were placed in reliquaries for veneration by the faithful; one of them may be delivered to Russian troops at the front. Thus, the warrior prince who once led a united Russian army against the nation’s fiercest enemy will once again stand alongside the nation’s army, in a completely different era and war.
On September 6, one of those reliquaries was carried at the head of a major religious procession through Moscow. Led by Patriarch Kirill, the procession drew around 100,000 people and followed a 6.5-kilometer route from the Cathedral of Christ the Savior to Novodevichy Convent. More than six centuries after his death, Dmitry Donskoy once again led a procession through the Russian capital.
Grand Prince Dmitry Ivanovich of Moscow, better known as Dmitry Donskoy, is a fairly common example of a historical figure remembered by virtually all his compatriots, but known only to specialists outside his country. This 14th-century prince played a huge role in the history of Russia, which was then still known as Rus’. His contributions to the fate of Russia as a warrior and statesman were recognized during his lifetime, but after his death, Dmitry gradually became a symbolic figure of the struggle for independence.
The uncovering of his relics could hardly have remained only an ecclesiastical or archaeological event. Modern Russia once again speaks the language of sovereignty, unity, and resistance to an external adversary – the same concepts which national memory associates Dmitry Donskoy.
To understand why Dmitry Donskoy is venerated by Russians centuries later, we must return to where his name became history – the field between the Don and Nepryadva rivers on the morning of September 8, 1380.
An existential enemy
Despite Russia’s long and dramatic military history, it didn’t have many long-standing adversaries with whom it was forced to fight again and again. The list of Russia’s historical adversaries isn’t topped by Poland, Germany, or Türkiye, as one might expect from a brief look at Russian history. The most formidable enemy, one that called into question the very existence of the Russian people, was a state that no longer exists on the world map – the Golden Horde, one of the major powers into which Genghis Khan’s empire was divided after his death.
In 1237, the still formally united Mongol state began its great march westward. Rus’ was one of the countries that fell prey to the Mongols. From this moment on, an epic struggle began, encompassing several dozen wars, not to mention isolated raids and minor border conflicts. Until the second half of the 15th century, Rus’ remained a vassal state to the steppe kingdom.
Regular and heavy tribute payments served as the basis of this dependence. If the people of Rus’ attempted to avoid them, a punitive expedition would arrive, destroying everything in its path, after which the survivors would go back to paying tribute. Horde officials known as the ‘baskaks’ were responsible for its collection. As is usually the case, the baskaks abused their power and engaged in extortion. Whenever they overstepped the boundaries, another rebellion would break out, followed by a new punitive campaign.
The Mongols also skillfully manipulated the Russian princes. There was no single leader in Rus’ at the time, so the princes traveled to the khan’s headquarters to intrigue against each other, turning to the Mongols as arbiters. The winners of this vile contest received a ‘yarlyk’ or charter to rule, along with the obligation to pay tribute and support the Mongols against those attempting to shake off their rule. This period in Russia is still called “the yoke,” calling to mind the yoke meant for draft animals. It aptly describes the severity and humiliation of the situation in which Rus’ found itself for many years.
Everything comes to an end, however; and by the 14th century, the Golden Horde had plunged into a protracted crisis. The khans were more likely to slaughter one another due to intrigues than to wage war on their neighbors. The nomadic empire was weakening.
The rise of Moscow
Some Russian principalities freed themselves from the yoke, falling under the control of other states, primarily the young and dynamic Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Lithuania’s time as a great Eastern European power was short but brilliant. The western principalities of Rus’ gravitated toward the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; this is how the future country of Belarus began to take shape. In the eastern part of Rus’, however, the control of the Horde was more strict, and events took a different course.
In 1325, Ivan Kalita became Prince of Moscow. ‘Kalita’ is a nickname meaning ‘money bag’ as he was indeed a sort of bagman, an unscrupulous schemer who based his power on the flow of money. He managed to ‘sell’ himself to the Horde as the most loyal of the princes and, most importantly, persuaded the khans to entrust him with collecting tribute from all of Rus’.
Baskaks and other options involving Horde officials were not very convenient for the khan: firstly, baskaks sought to pocket the money for themselves; secondly, dealing with one prince was easier: tribute collection proceeded more smoothly, a specific person could be held accountable, and naturally, the Russian prince had a better understanding of the country’s inner workings than the Mongols.
In this case, ‘Mongols’ is a very loose term. The rulers of the Golden Horde were the Chinggisids, descendants of Genghis Khan, and indeed Mongol by origin. However, the Horde’s majority at the time were descendants of numerous nomadic peoples who inhabited the steppe belt stretching from present-day Ukraine to present-day Kazakhstan. In Russian tradition, they were collectively called Tatars. Modern Tatars living in the Russian Republic of Tatarstan and the Crimean Tatars are descendants of some branches of the former Horde, but the historical meaning of this word is much broader, and at various stages included all Muslim peoples south and east of Russia, right up to the peoples of the Caucasus Mountains. In Russian, the name Tatar-Mongols is often used to refer to the entire group of peoples of the Golden Horde.
Ivan Kalita’s position as a go-between was disreputable but highly lucrative. He profited from the cash flow but managed to strike a fine balance, avoiding further rebellions within Rus’ while satisfying the khan’s demands. His accounting tricks still allowed him to keep some of the money for himself. He also used his position to quietly undermine his rivals, particularly the powerful prince of Tver. Now a smaller city northwest of the modern capital, at the time Tver was a serious rival of Moscow.
By 1340, when Ivan Kalita died, Moscow had become the richest and most powerful principality in Rus’.
Kalita’s successors – his elder son Simeon and later his younger son Ivan – were not as cunning as he, but managed to preserve their father’s gains. The principality was supposed to be headed by Simeon’s heirs, but both Simeon and his sons fell victim to the plague. The cause of death of his younger son Ivan is unknown, but he was 33 years old at the time and may have fallen victim to the same disease. Be that as it may, in 1359 rule over the principality was formally passed on to a nine-year-old boy named Dmitry Ivanovich.
The birth of a legend
Dmitry Donskoy’s personality is almost buried beneath the legend surrounding him. Generations of chroniclers and writers have described the prince as a chivalrous man and a patriot with deep convictions. Such a person was of course supposed to be ideal, and Dmitry was characterized as exceptionally virtuous and wise beyond his years.
More specifically, we may add the following about his character: Dmitry was certainly a religious man, and his faith was sincere. His guardian was Metropolitan Alexei, an authoritative figure and a shrewd politician who played a huge role in Dmitry’s development and the preservation of the principality. Dmitry always had a warm relationship with the Orthodox Church, not least because of the positive influence of Metropolitan Alexei, the most important Orthodox hierarch of his time.
The second important factor was that, after his father’s death, Dmitry was thrown headlong into the brutal maelstrom of politics. He had to learn self-control and military skills literally from childhood. Lithuania pressed in from the west, vying with Moscow as a rallying point for the Russian principalities; the Horde pressed from the south; and the independent principalities were in a state of constant feudal competition. In short, it was the ‘normal’ reality of medieval life. Thus, from childhood, Dmitry was exposed to the harsh school of politics, intrigue, and war. Young Dmitry had to endure short but intense wars with Lithuania. Moreover, Regent Alexei could not protect Dmitry forever, and the latter was forced to negotiate with the Horde and participate in campaigns against other princes. Dmitry besieged Tver, which had long been a thorn in Moscow’s side, and forced Prince Mikhail of Tver to pledge his loyalty to him.
In 1375, Prince Dmitry, who was then 25 years of age, concluded a treaty with Tver. Prince Mikhail of Tver called himself Dmitry’s “younger brother” (behind this elegant formula was actually a vassal treaty) but from a historical perspective, the key to the treaty was the phrase “If God changes the Horde”: if Moscow fought the Horde, Tver was obliged to join the fight. Apparently, Dmitry earnestly hated the Horde and wanted to fight it. Such an opportunity soon presented itself.
The rebellious prince
The Horde was rocked by coups. Its de facto ruler was the military commander Mamai. In Russian tradition, Mamai is often referred to as a khan, but this is incorrect. He was a ‘beklarbek’, i.e., one of the top-ranking officials. However, this position afforded him powers almost equal to those of a khan. Mamai ruled the Horde like an ‘eminence grise’, outliving a dozen khans while hiding behind the back of the nominal ruler Muhammad Bulak. Mamai maintained his rule by means of poison, dagger, and intrigue. In 1363, it was Mamai who granted the charter to young Dmitry. However, in the 1370s, Dmitry, feeling powerful enough, refused to pay tribute to the Horde.
This was a bold challenge. At that time, the Horde seemed almost invincible to the Russians. Psychologically, someone had to finally stand up and say “No”, and the most powerful prince of eastern Rus’ did so. Dmitry convened a congress of princes who expressed their support for him.
This certainly meant war, but this was no longer a rebellion of isolated outcasts. Dmitry spoke on behalf of all Rus’. Not everyone was ready to support him, but Moscow was not alone; it could count on the support of different corners of a country which, though humiliated, was still alive.
The war began dismally: a Horde detachment managed to surprise and defeat a small Russian force on the Pyana River. The river’s name in Russian sounds similar to the word ‘drunk’ [pianaya] and alas, in this case, “nomen est omen”: the Mongols took the Russians by surprise when they were relaxing in their camp. After the defeat in the field battle, Nizhny Novgorod, a large city approximately 400 km east of Moscow was devastated. However, during the very next skirmish, on the Vozha River, things took a different turn. This time, Dmitry, who personally led the army, surprised the Mongols at the crossing and pushed their detachment into the water.
Mamai faced a serious problem. Rus’, which was seemingly subjugated long ago, now rebelled. Moreover, Mamai was in serious trouble: Khan Tokhtamysh, a protégé of the mighty Tamerlane, rose up against him. Mamai needed to act quickly and brutally.
Another punitive expedition was organized against Rus’. This time, Mamai, a contender for power in the Horde, led it himself. It was late summer 1380.
Preparing for battle
Mamai saw that this time, he would meet with significant resistance and focused on the political preparations for the campaign. He negotiated with the Grand Duke of Lithuania Jagiello. As a rival of Moscow, Jagiello saw advantage in weakening Dmitry. Prince Oleg, the leader of Ryazan, which bordered the Horde, took an ambiguous stance. A century and a half earlier, in 1237, Ryazan had fiercely resisted the invasion, but the city had been completely devastated, and its inhabitants had almost entirely perished. Now, the descendants of the few survivors did not want to get involved.
Prince Oleg demonstrated exceptional political flexibility, expressing loyalty to both sides but refusing to lend troops to either. Meanwhile, Dmitry was gathering troops – his own and those of his allies – in Kolomna, a city southeast of Moscow. He did not have the full might of Rus’ at his disposal, but commanded a considerably large force assembled from various principalities: his own domain, which included the cities of Moscow and Vladimir; detachments from Novgorod and Pskov; and his cousin’s forces from Serpukhov. Moreover, individual detachments arrived from Ryazan, despite Prince Oleg’s ambiguous stance, and there were also troops from the Rostov Principality, Nizhny Novgorod, Yaroslavl, Bryansk, and Starodub. Small groups even came from the Lithuanian Principality – these were the detachments of the exiled princes, Jagiello’s half-brothers.
Admittedly, these troops likely numbered about 10,000 men – which is not a staggering number. However, we should remember that we’re talking about the 14th century, and at the time, Rus’, though large, was a sparsely populated country and could not assemble huge armies.
To dispel the fog of war, watchmen – i.e., reconnaissance detachments – were sent ahead to the steppe border. The first detachment went into the steppe and disappeared; a second detachment had already been dispatched from Moscow to search for it when a scout from the first group emerged from the steppe. This was Vasily Tupik, whose group managed to kidnap Mamai’s confidant. The scouts forced him to provide information about the enemy’s whereabouts and plans. This information was so vital that the name of the soldier who obtained it was written down in the chronicles, and thus remained in history.
Dmitry did not march directly towards Mamai. Instead, he first made a surprise dash west. This was done to accomplish two goals. Firstly, along the way, he ‘picked up’ several units that hadn’t made it to the general assembly. Secondly, he created a convincing illusion that he was busy attacking Jagiello’s Lithuanian army. Jagiello, unwilling to engage in a pitched battle with the strong Russian army, slowed his march. So, by the time Dmitry turned back and embarked on the campaign against Mamai, it was hard for the Lithuanian prince to catch up. By the morning of September 8, Dmitry had crossed the Don River which separated him from the army of the Horde.
This was a very risky maneuver. The Don is a large river. In case of defeat, the Russian army would have been pushed towards the river and easily annihilated. However, Dmitry wanted to avoid lengthy maneuvers. Time wasn’t on his side: the threat of Jagiello’s Lithuanians in the rear was still present, and no one knew what Oleg of Ryazan was up to. Therefore, he had to defeat Mamai in open battle, and do it quickly.
Dmitry employed a good deal of imagination in planning the battle. Historically, the Mongols possessed highly maneuverable cavalry. Dmitry occupied a battlefield bordered by forests, rivers, and ravines on the flanks; this protected his army from encirclement. But the Horde didn’t yet know the biggest surprise. The weakest link in the Russian position was the left flank, positioned next to a large oak forest. But it was precisely here that Dmitry had an ace up his sleeve – a powerful detachment of heavy cavalry led by the experienced commander Bobrok. Bobrok was an old, experienced warrior with strong nerves, and his task was to carry out a surprise attack when the situation became critical.
Before the battle began, Dmitry exchanged armor with boyar Mikhail Brenk. It was a cruel decision: both Dmitry and Mikhail Brenk knew that the enemy would try to kill the man wearing the prince’s armor. But Dmitry needed freedom to move around the battlefield and issue commands. However, he also took care to issue detailed instructions to the commanders.
The battle began on the morning of September 8.
Kulikovo Field
The chronicle states that the battle began with a duel between two fighters. A warrior monk, Alexander Peresvet, rode out from the Russian side. A former warrior from Bryansk, he had retired to a monastery some time earlier, but left for the campaign against Mamai, with the full understanding and approval of the abbot. Peresvet encountered a steppe warrior, known as Chelubey in the chronicles. The name sounds Turkic, which is logical: Mamai’s main forces were composed of various Turkic peoples. According to the chronicle, both warriors struck each other with spears and died. Apparently, they engaged in a head-on clash, and neither turned away.
Mamai seized the initiative in the battle. Apparently, the steppe army had a numerical advantage, as the Russians spent almost the entire battle on the defensive.
The size of the armies that fought at Kulikovo Field is a matter of debate. The biggest estimates place the number of participants at 100,000-150,000 men on each side. This is highly questionable. Firstly, such a number of men is dramatically at odds with the logistical capabilities of the time. Considering that both armies consisted almost entirely of cavalry, 150,000 warriors would have required forage for at least 300,000 horses (main + spare horse for each warrior), which is absurd. Not to mention that such numbers of men would require supply by rail. Later, when Russian military bureaucracy allowed for more precise troop estimates, 100,000-man armies ‘disappeared’ from the accounts and were replaced by armies of standard European size, i.e., 10,000-20,000 fighters. Considering that not all principalities of Rus’ took part in the battle of Kulikovo, one must agree with those researchers who limit the number of participants to 10,000-15,000 warriors on each side.
The Horde launched a series of attacks in various areas. They persistently sought out weak points and fought in waves for several hours. Of course, we’re not talking about hours of nonstop fighting. Cavalry armies fought on both sides and the battle resembled a series of skirmishes. The detachments charged at each other, fought for several minutes, then dispersed, making way for fresh reserves.
The Advance Regiment was positioned ahead of the main body of the Russian army. Under the Horde’s attacks, it retreated toward the Grand Regiment, the main line of the Russian army. The right flank repelled all attacks and was in least danger. The center fought very hard, but stood firm and did not crumble. The battle raged past midday. Mikhail Brenk, who had exchanged armor with Dmitry, was killed in battle. The prince himself not only commanded the battle, but actively participated in it and was wounded. This had no effect on morale; everyone knew Prince Dmitry was somewhere among the fighting ranks, but his simple, unadorned armor made it difficult to know his exact whereabouts.
The left flank of the Russian army was in danger, however. This regiment was retreating and the princes that commanded it had perished in battle. A small reserve detachment came to its aid, but stabilized the situation only briefly. The Horde forded the narrow Smolka River and pushed the Russians further and further back. The battle had reached its climax; both armies suffered heavy losses and were terribly tired. However, the Horde army had inflicted serious damage on the Russians’ left flank and was about to move into the rear of their center.
That’s when Bobrok’s Ambush Regiment struck the Horde army.
The old commander had calculated the moment with perfect precision. He arrived when the enemy was already exhausted by the long, hard battle, but the Russian line of defense had not yet crumbled.
Fresh cavalry reserves are a terrifying force at the end of a major battle. After several hours of heavy fighting, the Horde army was hit from the flank as if struck by a train. The balance of power didn’t just shift: the Horde panicked. Now, instead of the Russian left flank, the Horde’s right flank began to crumble. Mamai had no reinforcements left, as he had thrown all his forces into battle.
Some time after the attack by the Ambush Regiment, the enemy wavered and began to scatter.
The pursuit of the Horde was led by Dmitry’s cousin, Prince Vladimir of Serpukhov. Mamai fled, and most of his army followed on exhausted horses. The Russians relentlessly pursued the enemy for about 30 kilometers.
The Russians suffered heavy losses. For several more days, the army stood “on the bones,” picking up the dead, nursing the wounded, and gathering all the weapons and equipment they could find.
Prince Dmitry was found among a pile of corpses. He was alive, but gravely wounded; his armor was mangled, and he was unconscious. He fought the most important battle of his life at the forefront of his warriors, with a war club in hand, and nearly paid for the victory with his life. Unfortunately, the chroniclers did not specify in what circumstances he was wounded, but the location where he was found speaks for itself: it was, of course, the left flank.
From that moment on, Prince Dmitry of Moscow would be known by the name that would become part of history: Dmitry Donskoy, i.e., Dmitry of the Don.
On September 14, the army turned back.
Afterword
The Battle of Kulikovo had a huge psychological impact. The Russian army routed the Horde in a proper pitched battle – it didn’t hide behind fortified walls, and didn’t just defeat a single detachment; it utterly destroyed the enemy’s main field army. This was not accomplished by any single principality but by a broad alliance. Men who had seen the backs of the fleeing Horde army with their own eyes returned to Nizhny Novgorod, Pskov, Novgorod, and Yaroslavl.
After the battle, the Lithuanian army quietly retreated home.
The struggle for independence did not end there, of course. After this defeat, Mamai lost the internal struggle in the Golden Horde to Khan Tokhtamysh, fled to Crimea, and was killed there. Tokhtamysh set about restoring the Horde’s former glory. In 1382, he launched a new campaign against Rus’, and this time succeeded in taking Moscow while Dmitry was gathering a field army. Dmitry, through gritted teeth, paid tribute for the previous two years (but not for the earlier years). However, the Battle of Kulikovo marked a new style of relations between Rus’ and the Horde. Tokhtamysh made no attempt to install anyone else as ruler of Moscow. The idea of independence and political unity took hold in Rus’, and Moscow clearly headed this process. The Russians were still paying tribute, but they already saw that they could seize the opportunity to avoid it. The gaps between payments grew wider and successful battles with the Horde became more frequent.
In 1395, Khan Tokhtamysh suffered a terrible defeat at the hands of Tamerlane, with whom he had fallen out. The Horde was falling apart and the Russians accelerated this process as best they could.
In 1389, Dmitry Donskoy died before reaching the age of 40. The cause of his early death is unknown. However, he left behind a powerful legacy: a large principality that became the leader in the unification of Rus’; a son who continued his policies; and, finally, the idea of a unified state that would never again lose its independence.
At the end of the 14th century, ‘Zadonshchina’ – a literary monument about the Battle of Kulikovo – was published.
In 1480, Ivan III formalized the complete political independence of Rus’; By this point, its dependence was more of a formality and Ivan III sealed the recognition of the new reality.
In 1783, Empress Catherine II annexed Crimea – the last fragment of the Golden Horde to be incorporated into Russia. The great conflict thus ended, and all debts were settled.

Indonesia on Tuesday said that all airports affected by volcanic ash from Mount Anak Krakatau had resumed operations following safety assessments, as conditions improved after days of aviation disruption.
Berton Panjaitan, a spokesperson for Indonesia’s National Disaster Mitigation Agency, told Anadolu that restrictions had been lifted at all seven airports closed to air traffic on Sunday and Monday.
“The situation has significantly improved. As of today, there are no airports that remain closed due to the impact of volcanic ash from Mount Anak Krakatau,” Panjaitan said in a statement.
“All previously affected airports have resumed operations following safety assessments and inspections,” he added.
Volcanic ash from Anak Krakatau began affecting Indonesian airspace on Saturday, initially forcing eight airports to suspend operations.
Panjaitan, however, cautioned that the volcano remained active and conditions could change quickly.
“We remain vigilant because Mount Anak Krakatau is still active and volcanic ash dispersion can change rapidly,” he said.
Aviation authorities continued to monitor ash conditions and would adjust flight operations if necessary, he added.

The European commute: Which EU country spends the most time getting to work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:44:56 UTC
17:44:56 KST

Just how long do Europeans spend getting to work? Across the continent, the daily average commute sits at 48 minutes, but that hides a massive divide.
For millions of workers across the continent, the daily journey to the office is an unavoidable ritual. But just how long do Europeans actually spend getting to work?
According to new research from talent management company SD Worx, the daily average commute across Europe sits at 48 minutes. However, that continental average masks how differently nations experience geography, traffic, and worker mindsets.
While the European average hovers around three-quarters of an hour, individual countries experience vastly different realities on their roads and rail lines.
Countries such as Italy and Slovenia manage to keep daily travel times relatively brief, hovering around 35 minutes.
At the opposite end, countries push much closer to the hour mark. Sweden and Ireland report hefty averages of 57 and 56 minutes, respectively.
Taking the top spot overall, Belgium officially crosses the one-hour mark at 61 minutes a day. This is driven by the fact that 13% of its workforce are "super-commuters", according to SD Worx, spending two hours or more on the road—the highest rate in Europe—with 14% travelling over 120 kilometres daily.
Distance vs. congestion: The Netherlands and Romania
The data also reveals fascinating differences in why commutes take as long as they do. For instance, the Netherlands and Romania both average 53 minutes for a daily commute, but the underlying dynamics are entirely polar opposite:
Workers in the Netherlands cover 63 kilometres on average, leaning on efficient infrastructure to handle long-distance travel.
In Romania, workers spend that same 53-minute window covering much shorter geographic distances, where heavy traffic and urban congestion eat away at the clock.
The commuting paradox
Perhaps the most intriguing takeaway from the research is how workers psychologically handle their travel times.
Even in Belgium—where the average commute surpasses the 57-minute limit that people generally consider "acceptable"—only 34% of workers view that time as wasted.
Despite enduring some of the longest transit times on the continent, demand for more remote work among Belgian employees sits at just 32%, staying right below the international average.
Across Europe, the daily commute remains a patchwork of infrastructure challenges and personal routines, proving that the time we spend getting to work is about much more than just kilometres on a map.
