US officials discuss smaller Mideast footprint after Iran conflict: CNN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:15:01 UTC
16:15:01 KST

Busra Nur Cakmak
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
US military and intelligence officials have begun discussing a potential reduction in personnel and facilities permanently stationed in the Middle East if the Trump administration succeeds in ending the conflict with Iran, CNN reported, citing six sources.
The informal discussions could lead to another shift in Washington's military and intelligence posture in a region where the US dramatically expanded its presence following the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, according to the report.
Officials are considering possible cuts even as about 50,000 US troops remain deployed across the Middle East alongside significant military assets, including two aircraft carriers and more than a dozen guided-missile destroyers.
The US military has developed several possible options for changing its force structure in the region as early as next year, two sources told CNN. No formal force posture review has been ordered, however.
Shifting defense burden to regional partners
Senior Pentagon officials have also privately indicated that they want to reduce troop levels in several Gulf countries while shifting more of the defense burden to regional partners, the report said.
At the same time, the Pentagon is examining ways to strengthen defenses for forces expected to remain in the region, including potentially moving some installations underground to protect them from Iranian missile and drone attacks.
The idea gained urgency after Iranian strikes during the conflict exposed vulnerabilities at US facilities, according to CNN.
"The vulnerabilities were always known, but the US never acted on it with urgency," a US official told the network.
Iranian attacks have caused significant damage to American facilities across the region, the report said. A CIA outpost in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was effectively destroyed, while US military installations in Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait were also struck, according to CNN.
Officials are considering whether some intelligence and special operations missions could be conducted without permanent regional bases, with personnel and equipment instead deployed from the US for specific missions before returning home.
May choose not to rebuild damaged facilities
Washington may also choose not to rebuild some facilities severely damaged or destroyed in Iranian attacks because of the costs involved.
Pentagon comptroller Jules "Jay" Hurst III said in April that decisions on repairing damaged facilities would depend partly on Washington's future regional posture.
Despite discussions about a smaller footprint, the US and Iran remain far from a settlement. Tehran continues to target US forces and bases, including attacks on American installations in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates last week.
Pentagon officials broadly expect the US to retain some large permanent bases in the Middle East, though reconstruction could depend on host countries contributing to costs that could reach billions of dollars.
US forces are also expected to remain vulnerable to Iranian attacks in the near term.
Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said last week that US Navy personnel would not return soon to Bahrain, the traditional home of the 5th Fleet.
"We're not getting back in there anytime soon," Caudle said.

Thieves steal works worth $13 million from France’s Renoir museum: Mayor

- The museum, located in Renoir's last home, houses his personal items and paintings, and police responded within five minutes.
- This theft follows a major Louvre robbery last year, where stolen items worth US$100 million remain missing despite arrests and investigations.
AI generated
Marseille – Two thieves broke into a museum dedicated to French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir in southern France on Sept 8, stealing “four works of art”, two of which they dropped as they fled, a mayor said.
“The museum and police sirens forced the burglars to hurry, stealing only four works from the Renoir Museum out of the 12 the museum holds,” said Bryan Masson, the mayor of the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer.
Of those four, two were “left behind in the gardens of the Renoir museum”, added the far-right official, whose office earlier estimated the value of the stolen works at €9 million (S$13 million).
The Renoir Museum was opened in 1960 in the painter’s last home before he died at age 78 in 1919.
Its collection includes objects and furniture that belonged to Renoir, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as portraits, landscapes and nudes painted by the artist.
Some of his more famous works are on display at the Musee d’Orsay in Paris, as well as in London and New York.
‘Just five minutes’
The mayor said it took just five minutes for the authorities to respond.
“The museum alarm went off at 5.48am. At 5.53am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene,” he said.
A spate of heists at French museums, including at the Louvre in Paris, has highlighted inadequate security in some cases and led to questions about whether criminal gangs see them as soft targets.
The theft comes less than a year after eight items valued at around US$100 million (S$126 million) were stolen during a daylight robbery from the Louvre.
The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the stolen items have still not been found despite extensive searches by French investigators in the Paris region and exchanges with police in Belgium, Italy and beyond. AFP

Zaporizhzhia and the Dnipro region were also attacked
What is Freyja
Freyja is a Ukraine-initiated project for a joint European antiballistic system, the first track of the Antiballistic Coalition, which includes 10 states and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
The project is built around the Ukrainian FP-7.x interceptor missile developed by Fire Point, while other components are supplied by European manufacturers. As UNN reported, Fire Point’s General and Technical Director Iryna Terekh said that development had reached the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem—radars, a launcher, a data transmission channel, and a command center—and that tests are being conducted up to twice a week. The system’s first interception of a ballistic target is scheduled for 2027.

The central bank has raised its 2026 economic growth forecast to 3.3%, citing strong exports amid the continuing semiconductor supercycle.

Russia Pounds Kyiv Hours After US Envoys Depart Ukrainian Capital
Unknown

2026-09-08
07:06:12 UTC
16:06:12 KST

KYIV -- Russia hammered the Ukrainian capital with drones and ballistic missiles, killing at least five people in a major attack hours after White House envoys left Kyiv amid a renewed push for peace negotiations.
The September 8 bombardment followed a lull in near daily attacks, underscoring Moscow's intent to press forward in its nearly 4 1/2-year full-scale war on Ukraine despite astronomical casualties.
Emergency workers pulled bodies from the rubble in one district of Kyiv while firefighters battled to put out fires from the attack, which also included jet-powered drones -- a relatively new weapon that Ukraine has struggled to defend against.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitshcko said five people were confirmed dead, and emergency officials reported at least 16 people were wounded.
The Russian attack included dozens of ballistic and cruise missiles along with more than 160 drones, Ukraine's military said.
The onslaught came after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner departed Kyiv following meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other officials.
Prior to Kyiv, the pair visited Moscow for talks with President Vladimir Putin.
It was the first time the White House officials had traveled to Kyiv; by contrast, Witkoff has met with Putin eight times since the beginning of 2025.
US efforts to push peace negotiations have been dormant in recent months as President Donald Trump's administration has prioritized the war with Iran, now in its sixth month.
That conflict has severely depleted stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles, which are the only weapon effective against Russian ballistic and hypersonic missiles. European countries that operate Patriot systems have been working to help make up the shortfall and maintain supplies to Ukraine.
In recent months, Ukraine’s ability to defend against the nearly daily Russian assaults has been severely constrained by a lack of missile interceptors, above all US-built Patriots.
The European Union will provide Ukraine $3.7 billion "to purchase crucial products for Patriot air defense systems," EU chief Ursula von der Leyen announced hours after the attack. Britain also announced $135 million to help Ukraine boost air defenses including Patriot missiles.
Trump and Putin spoke by telephone on September 8, and Putin gave his assessment of the battlefield, Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov said. He also said Putin stated that Russia had no hostile plans toward Europe, something a growing number of European nations have voiced concern about.
Trump, Ushakov said, told Putin that he wanted a swift end to the war, which he said would allow Russian-US ties to be fully restored.
The White House had no immediate comment on the phone call.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha called on Kyiv's allies to "to act and increase pressure on the aggressor."
Russia's Defense Ministry said the attack on September 8 targeted Ukrainian defense and military logistics facilities.
EU Ambassador Katarina Mathernova said she spent the night in a shelter as "Kyiv was exploding and burning."
"What happened in Kyiv last night was hell," she wrote on X. "I would not wish it on anyone who lives in peace and falls asleep safely in their own bed."
After meeting Zelenskyy, Witkoff described discussions as constructive and said Washington had heard "new ideas" from Moscow. Kushner said the United States was working on a broader "peace package."
Zelenskyy, for his part, called his discussions with the Americans "very substantial" and said Ukraine was prepared to move toward trilateral talks involving Kyiv, Washington, and Moscow.
National-security advisers from Britain, France, and Germany also joined part of the Kyiv discussions.
The Kremlin has shown no indication it has softened its hard-line position on its war aims. In comments to reporters after the September 5 meetings with Putin, Ushakov said Russia would press forward to "eliminate" the "root causes" of the conflict.
"Root causes" is a phrase representing a grab bag of Russian grievances dating back to before the 2022 invasion, including the assertion that Zelenskyy is not a legitimate president and the Ukrainian government was oppressing native Russian speakers in Ukraine.

Trial into deadliest migrant Channel crossing begins in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:05:54 UTC
16:05:54 KST

As the defendants face trial, survivors' testimony and a parallel probe into French naval response raise urgent questions about how the waters are policed.
Fourteen defendants go on trial in France on Tuesday over a 2021 Channel crossing that killed 31 people, including a seven-year-old, in the worst small-boat disaster involving migrants in those waters.
Prosecutors allege the accused, said to have ties to smuggling operations, bear responsibility for the sinking that claimed 27 confirmed lives — most of them Iraqi Kurds — when an overloaded dinghy went down in the early hours of 24 November, 2021.
Four victims have never been found, and just two men made it out alive.
That morning, a French fishing boat spotted bodies drifting in the Channel near Calais, not far from British territorial waters. The two survivors later described how the flimsy vessel started losing air and taking on water after hours at sea, with passengers being swept overboard and drowning one by one — this despite roughly a dozen frantic calls placed to both French and British rescue authorities.
Those who died ranged in age from seven to 46 and came mainly from Iraqi Kurdistan, and included Afghan, Ethiopian and Egyptian nationals among the dead.
Distress calls ignored by authorities
Given the scale of the loss of life and the involvement of 114 civil parties — among them bereaved families and roughly a dozen relatives who made the trip from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan — the trial has drawn considerable attention.
Most of the 14 defendants, the majority Afghan nationals, face charges of manslaughter and organised facilitation of illegal immigration. Two, including one Afghan national, will be tried in absentia under active arrest warrants.
Adding to the case's profile is a separate, still-unresolved inquiry. Since 2023, seven members of the French military — five staff at a maritime rescue coordination centre and two crew members of a patrol boat — have been investigated for failing to render assistance to someone in peril.
A UK government inquiry published in February concluded that faster action by French and British authorities could have prevented some of the deaths.
Nearly 12 hours passed between the initial distress calls and the moment a French fishing vessel finally located the boat — by then, most aboard had already drowned.
Matthieu Chirez, an attorney representing 113 of the civil parties, said accountability must extend to everyone who played a role in the tragedy.
Fellow lawyer Emmanuel Daoud voiced hope that the three-week proceedings would encourage the public to see migrants not as "statistics or commodities, but human beings in search of a better life".
Defendants claim they are also migrants
According to prosecutors, those on trial helped launch a vessel that was uncertified, poorly built, overcrowded, and lacking sufficient life jackets — unfit for any open-water voyage.
Investigators argue that responsibility also falls on those who transported, sheltered, or escorted the victims beforehand, framing these actions as links in a "chain of successive events" culminating in the disaster.
The defendants have pushed back, denying involvement in smuggling. Some claim they themselves were simply migrants attempting the crossing.
Prosecutors have been handed phone data and location records that investigators claim tie several of the defendants to the departure point and to coordinating Channel crossings — evidence that helped uncover two separate smuggling networks run by Afghans and Iraqis.

====================================================================================================

High-end boom masks Swiss watch industry polarisation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:05:00 UTC
16:05:00 KST

High-end boom masks Swiss watch industry polarisation
After three years of turbulence, Swiss watchmakers are searching for signs that the worst is over. Wars, tariffs, a soaring gold price, the strong Swiss franc and weaker luxury demand have all taken their toll. Now, export values have stabilised and volumes are rising again.
But recovery is an increasingly difficult concept to apply to the Swiss watch industry as a whole. While some manufacturers are cutting production and relying on state support to protect jobs, makers at the very top of the market are struggling to keep up with demand. A tiny fraction of watches now accounts for most of the industry’s growth.
“This year has presented a lot of challenges and there is a lot of uncertainty in the industry,” says Yves Bugmann, president of the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry (FH). “I hope that the situation will improve over the next few months.”
    
        External Content    
    
        
    
In the first half of the year, Swiss watch exports were worth CHF12.2bn ($15.1bn), down 0.6 per cent year-on-year. But the headline figure disguises growing polarisation.
Last month, Swiss watch industry consultancy LuxeConsult published a report based on FH data showing that 75 per cent of the market’s value growth had been added by watches accounting for only 1.3 per cent of volumes. “Growth of ultra-luxury was spectacular,” says Oliver Müller, LuxeConsult’s founder and author of the report. “And it shows where the whole market is going.”
The picture was less comfortable lower down the market. Watches priced between CHF25,000 and CHF50,000 were the hardest hit, falling 8.3 per cent, while “accessible luxury” watches priced between CHF7,500 and CHF12,500 rose just 0.5 per cent, helped by steel models from Rolex, Omega and Cartier. “The brands have to adapt to a new situation in which it became very complicated for retailers to continue to replenish their stocks,” says Müller.
‘Fatigue with existing brands’
At the same time, first-half export volumes rose 2.3 per cent, driven largely, according to Müller, by Swatch Group brands Longines, Tissot, Hamilton and Swatch.
More
Time’s up for Swatch?
The uptick was unexpected. Annual Swiss watch exports fell from 17 million units in 2023 to 14.6 million in 2025, according to FH data. Many brands and suppliers have sought to protect jobs and skills through RHT, Switzerland’s state-backed short working hours scheme.
The industry’s problems haven’t curtailed the rush of new watch brands. This week, House of Brands has revived Gallet after a hiatus stretching back to the 1980s, following its reintroduction of Universal Genève in the spring. In July, former Audemars Piguet chief executive François-Henri Bennahmias announced N3W5, which is due to launch its first watches next autumn. And earlier this year, Niton, another defunct dial name, was resurrected by former Girard-Perregaux executive Leopoldo Celi.
Bennahmias, whose watch company will sit under the umbrella of his The Honourable Merchants Group, believes the market is ripe for disruption. “Four years ago, the watch industry was on fire and even the lousiest brands were selling,” he says. “Now, the market is down, but is this a sign people don’t have money? No. They’re tired of the same things. To get on people’s radar, you have to do something out of the ordinary.”
Georges Kern, chief executive of House of Brands, agrees. “There’s fatigue with the existing brands,” he says. Gallet, also a sister brand to Breitling, will sell watches priced between £2,220 and £5,300, considered the gateway to luxury watches. “Saying there’s no business at this price point is nonsense,” Kern continues. “We’re not surfing on a wave any more, so you have to take market share from others, which means you need to be better than them. The retailers are happy to have something new. They don’t want the 20th version of something they already have.”
While establishment watchmakers are battling to protect volumes, many of the younger independents making short-run pieces are struggling to keep up with demand. Three years ago, industry veteran and former Hublot supremo Jean-Claude Biver created a company in his own name with his son Pierre. With a focus on high-end horology and hand-finishing, Biver watches can carry price tags up to CHF500,000.
“We arrived at the right moment,” says Pierre, now Biver’s chief executive. “The market came down after Covid, but it wasn’t a bubble bursting. There was a plateau and results are back up again now. That’s brought collectors confidence, but for independents launching now, they are faced with a bigger challenge because the market is looking for brands that feel safe.”
+ Swiss watchmakers feel pinch amid luxury slump
That, says Biver, is fuelling demand for watches made by independent sector totems such as FP Journe, Kari Voutilainen and Rexhep Rexhepi, a view borne out by recent auction results. In June, Phillips sold an FP Journe Chronomètre à Résonance for $13.9 million, making it the fifth most expensive watch ever sold. Biver will make around 100 watches this year. “We are limited not by desire but by our capacity,” says Pierre.
Niton’s owner Celi, whose watches start at CHF44,750, expects annual production never to exceed 500 pieces. “Small specialist brands are where the volumes will be diluted,” he says. “Big brands doing most of the volumes, that’s not the future.”
More
Rising June Swiss watch sales bucks 2026 trend
China down, US up
The market is also being reshaped geographically. Before the pandemic, China and Hong Kong were key markets for the Swiss watch industry, but both have since shrunk. Exports to China are down 7.1 per cent this year.
This autumn, Switzerland is due to sign a trade agreement with China that will reduce almost all export tariffs to zero. “It could give us a boost,” says Bugmann. “We paid CHF100 million a year in customs duties [to China] that will be eliminated over the next few years.”
Kern is less convinced it will change demand. “It’s only 3.5 per cent,” he says of Chinese tariffs, noting that brands with global distribution constantly balance pricing to accommodate regional currency and tariff fluctuations. “Nobody will decrease prices in China. Brands will enjoy a higher margin there.”
Meanwhile, the US has become the industry’s largest market. Exports for the seven months to July are approaching SFr3bn, close to 20 per cent of the total and almost as much as the next three largest markets combined. “I expect the US to show good performance for the next few months,” says Bugmann.
Many brands are now spinning the globe for signs of life. South Korea and Mexico are growing strongly, but it is India that is outperforming the market, albeit from a low base. Exports are up 30 per cent this year. Another Swiss trade deal means tariffs on most goods exported to India will drop to zero by 2031. “India today is as significant as any major European market,” says Kern.
Increasingly selective customers
But the industry’s longer-term challenge may have less to do with geography than value. Prices have risen sharply since the pandemic even as volumes have fallen, leaving consumers increasingly selective about what they are prepared to buy.
+ Six things you should know about the watchmaking industry
“Consumers are more and more aware of the comparison between quality and price,” says Pierre Biver. “Rolex and Cartier are able to produce some of the best quality at their price point. Someone buying at over one hundred thousand, they still want quality for what they’re paying. The challenge is how do you put enough value in the products?”
The pressure is particularly acute among suppliers and manufacturers still dependent on RHT. Bennahmias argues the scheme can preserve jobs in the short term but cannot resolve overcapacity. “It’s putting a band-aid on something that’s more important than a cut, but without it people won’t have jobs,” he says. “With this erosion of the supplier network, we’re putting the entire industry at risk.”
Kern says he stopped using RHT before the summer. “I think we’ve reached the bottom,” he says. “Companies have to adjust capacities and then take market share.”
There are other signs that consumers have not lost their appetite for watches altogether. Prices on the secondary market are rising: online marketplace Chrono24 said its price index increased 5.5 per cent in the first half of 2026, led by Cartier, Tag Heuer and Tudor.
Manufacturers are also taking a greater interest in the used market. Rolex’s certified pre-owned business, launched in late 2022, is growing, while Audemars Piguet is expected to introduce a programme of its own this autumn. “It will be another boost to the secondary market,” says LuxeConsult’s Müller. “It brings trust, and trust brings more transactions.”
Yet with prices still climbing — Rolex has raised them twice this year — and volumes uncertain, the shape of any recovery remains difficult to predict.
“With the exceptions of Rolex and Cartier, brands are squeezed, which is why they are moving upmarket,” says Luca Solca, head of luxury goods research at Bernstein.
“For new brands to succeed, they will need to have something unique to say with a focus at the high end. But the market is crowded and not growing very much, so I don’t see how new entrants could survive. It would be a rare exception that does,” he adds.
Bennahmias is more confident. “There is no bad or good time to launch,” he says. “There is always room to launch new things.”
“Watches are an eternal symbol of wealth and power,” says Pierre Biver.

Report: Iran’s offshore oil stockpile could run out by October as US blockade dries up revenues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:03:58 UTC
16:03:58 KST

Iran’s oil revenues are rapidly drying up as a U.S. naval blockade prevents new crude shipments from leaving the Persian Gulf and the stockpile already positioned outside the blockade dwindles toward exhaustion, The Wall Street Journal reported.
No Iranian crude has crossed the blockade since the U.S. Navy reinstated it in mid-July, according to shipping-data firm Kpler. Iran is still loading limited amounts of oil onto tankers inside the Gulf, but those barrels remain trapped there.
Meanwhile, Iranian crude already aboard vessels beyond the blockade, which Tehran can still deliver and sell, has fallen from roughly 90 million barrels in mid-July to about 29 million. Kpler estimates that if deliveries continue at their current pace, mostly to China, that floating stockpile could be exhausted by mid-October. Payments for cargoes already delivered could largely dry up by mid-December.
The squeeze is hitting Iran six months into the war, as the rial weakens, inflation surges and the economy contracts. Oil typically finances about one-third of the state budget and also helps fund the military, including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Iran loaded about 255,000 barrels a day onto vessels inside the Gulf in August, according to Kpler, roughly 85% below the average recorded between February and April. Those newly loaded barrels have not made their way toward overseas buyers.
Tehran is still benefiting from crude moved abroad during a temporary easing of the blockade after U.S.-Iran diplomatic contacts in June. That window allowed Iran to transfer large quantities beyond the Gulf for later delivery, but those reserves are now shrinking quickly.
Chinese refiners have increasingly turned to Saudi, Iraqi and Emirati crude, Gulf energy officials told the Journal. Iranian oil has become scarce enough that in some cases it costs refiners more than competing supplies. Iraq has offered discounts approaching $30 a barrel on some grades.
The blockade also appears to be forcing Iran to reduce production. Domestic inventories have not risen significantly despite the collapse in exports, suggesting Tehran has cut output closer to what it needs for domestic consumption, according to Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler’s head of crude-oil analysis.
Alternative routes offer little relief. Iran can move only limited volumes by truck or rail, with Falakshahi estimating that trucks could carry no more than about 40,000 barrels a day, compared with prewar exports of nearly 2 million barrels daily.
The pressure is also spreading to petrochemicals, Iran’s second-largest source of foreign-currency earnings after oil. Kpler estimates that loadings in August were about two-thirds lower than at the beginning of 2026.
For Tehran, the lost revenue is compounding an already severe economic crisis. Official inflation is running above 80% year over year, while the International Monetary Fund forecasts a 5.4% contraction this year. The rial has also lost almost 15% of its value against the dollar since President Donald Trump announced his latest economic pressure campaign in August.
Washington is betting that the mounting economic pain will force Tehran to make concessions, but Gulf officials and analysts cited by the Journal remain skeptical. Some warn that instead of backing down, Iran may choose further military escalation as the economic pressure intensifies.

Mistral announced Tuesday that it had raised three billion euros ($3.5 billion) in what it described as the largest-ever European tech fundraising, valuing the French AI firm at over 21 billion euros.
The startup, which is considered Europe's leading AI model developer, said the funding round led by chip giant Samsung would accelerate its research and help it to expand internationally.

While still an upstart compared to the AI giants OpenAI or Anthropic, Mistral says it is carving a niche by offering models that companies can run themselves with their own data.

Nijmegen streets sealed off over gunfire report after Overasselt
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Armed police sealed off several streets in eastern Nijmegen on Monday evening after residents reported hearing what sounded like automatic gunfire. It turned out to be a false alarm, a week after the deadly attack in nearby Overasselt.
Officers ordered people around the Hengstdalseweg to stay indoors and out of sight, a police helicopter came in and the DSI special intervention unit of heavily armed police was called in. Police later said they had found no evidence that any shots had actually been fired.
“We are extra alert to reports like this at the moment,” a spokesperson told regional broadcaster Omroep Gelderland. A spokesperson told news agency ANP that the scale of the response was linked to the attack in Overasselt, roughly 10 kilometres to the south, in which two police officers were hit.
Belgian arrest
 Police said on Sunday that a 26-year-old Belgian national had been arrested in Amsterdam on Friday in connection with the attack, bringing the total number of arrests to 35. Two people released earlier remain suspects.
Specialist teams backed by riot police are continuing to search Overasselt and the surrounding area for evidence.
Previous convictions
 Several of the men being held have previous convictions for firearms offences, kidnapping and fraud, the AD reported on Monday, citing the list of suspects brought before an examining magistrate on Friday. Police declined to comment on the report to broadcaster NOS.
One 23-year-old from Amsterdam was jailed for four years after firing on a house in Antwerp in 2022, the AD said. The intended target was a relative of kickboxer Jamal Ben Saddik, but the gunmen hit the wrong address.
A second Amsterdam man was given 15 months, six of them suspended, for kidnapping and robbing an elderly man at gunpoint in 2024. A third, aged 20, appeared in court over a shooting late that year and is suspected of firing the fatal shots in Overasselt, according to the paper. Prosecutors have not said who they believe pulled the trigger.

Volkswagen Plant to Be Converted for Air Defense System Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:02:47 UTC
16:02:47 KST

Volkswagen has agreed to a potential sale of its Osnabrück plant, which is planned to be converted into a production center for air defense systems in cooperation with Israeli company Rafael.
According to Volkswagen Group, it has agreed on the key deal terms with the state of Lower Saxony and Israeli investment company Aurelius Capital.
Under the preliminary plan, Aurelius will become the majority owner of Volkswagen Osnabrück GmbH, while Lower Saxony will also acquire a stake in the company.
The new owners intend to gradually transform the automotive plant into a center of expertise in security and defense. The first major project will be a partnership with Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.
The facility could produce air defense systems and components for Germany and other European countries. Rafael would provide its technology and expertise, while the plant’s workforce would establish production processes and manufacture the systems at scale.
Volkswagen has not officially specified which systems it plans to produce. At the same time, the Financial Times reports that the project involves components for Israel’s Iron Dome defense system.
The agreement came just days after Volkswagen announced a major restructuring. Amid weak demand, high costs, and competition from China, the automaker is considering closing or repurposing up to four plants in Germany.
In March 2026, it was reported that Volkswagen and Rafael were in talks about potentially producing transport platforms, launchers, and generators for Iron Dome in Osnabrück. The plant was not expected to produce missiles.
The facility has the infrastructure, skilled workforce, and experience needed for small-batch production of complex equipment. In the future, it is also expected to serve as a base for bringing in other defense companies and launching new projects.
Volkswagen plans to stop producing vehicles in Osnabrück in summer 2027 as part of its cost-cutting measures. The automaker has pledged to transfer its production infrastructure and expertise in product development and industrialization to the new entity.
According to Daniela Cavallo, chairwoman of the General and Group Works Councils of Volkswagen AG, the agreement creates the prospect of preserving jobs for more than 1,200 employees. The transition to defense production at the facility is currently planned to take place in stages.
The deal has not yet been finalized: the parties still need to determine the ownership structure, allocate responsibilities, and obtain corporate and regulatory approvals. The parties have not disclosed the financial terms of the potential sale.

Trump’s Ukraine plans ‘scared Europeans to death’ – Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

Trump’s Ukraine plans ‘scared Europeans to death’ – Lavrov
European leaders were “scared to death” by US President Donald Trump’s proposals for resolving the Ukraine conflict and worked relentlessly to sabotage Washington’s compromise efforts, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
In an interview published on Tuesday, Lavrov accused European NATO members of seeking to prevent Trump from returning to the ideas he had discussed with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Alaska last year. He also pointed to a phone call between the two leaders on July 4 this year.
“Europe understands that if the Americans suddenly return to their original proposals... as was the case in Anchorage, Europe was simply scared to death,” Lavrov said. According to him, European leaders “immediately rushed” to coax Trump into abandoning his own initiatives.
Lavrov recalled French President Emmanuel Macron’s remarks at a NATO summit in June, at which the French leader had effectively boasted that the Anchorage initiative had been “buried” and that Washington was once again aligned with Europe in a united front against Russia.
“If Western diplomacy comes down to restraining countries that put forward reasonable, balanced, compromise initiatives, then so be it,” Lavrov said. Moscow would then pursue its objectives “not at the negotiating table,” which he said Russia would prefer, “but on the battlefield.”
Lavrov’s remarks come as the Trump administration makes a renewed push to revive stalled diplomacy. US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Saturday for more than three hours before traveling on to Kiev the following day.
The White House said the sides discussed “substantive plans for next steps” toward ending the conflict, while Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov described the meeting as “extremely frank” and said the American envoys had presented a number of ideas on possible avenues toward a settlement.
Lavrov, however, argued that most of the public talk about diplomacy coming from Kiev and its Western sponsors is intended to secure another pause in the fighting and give their Ukrainian proxies time to rearm and regroup. Despite the renewed US effort, Lavrov insisted that no constructive peace negotiations are currently under way.
“Nothing is happening on the diplomatic front,” he said, adding that developments are instead unfolding “on the real front,” where Russian forces are advancing.
The foreign minister also warned that Moscow intends to follow through on threats of retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure. Russia had warned that such strikes would trigger a response “much heavier for Ukraine,” he said, adding: “This is happening now.”
The top Russian diplomat also took aim at London, which has vowed to remain with Kiev to the end. “I feel sorry for Britain,” he said, since that end “will not be a happy one.”
Addressing European preparations for a possible future conflict with Moscow, Lavrov reiterated Putin’s position that Russia has no intention of attacking Europe. If European countries were to attack Russia, however, he warned that it would be “a fundamentally different war” and “very short.”

Estonian MP: US administration has no idea how deep the roots of the Ukraine war go
Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Marko Mihkelson said Moscow sees no need for a breakthrough in peace efforts and believes it can intensify attacks on Ukraine's infrastructure as winter approaches.
The latest meeting between Vladimir Putin and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also failed to deliver any breakthrough because Putin has no need for one.
"Russia senses that as winter approaches, it has an opportunity to destroy Ukraine's economic infrastructure to the greatest possible extent. Ukraine's air defense problem is growing and serious," said Marko Mihkelson, chair of the Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee.
"Dear colleagues, I warmly welcome you to Moscow. The situation we have to deal with today is, of course, complicated," Putin said.
"The Russian side gave a clear and comprehensive assessment of the situation that has developed in the course of the special operation. In particular, the tangible successes of the Russian army in the combat zone were noted, confidence was expressed that the objectives that had been set would be achieved and, naturally, the need to address the root causes of the conflict was emphasized," Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said.
"The Trump administration certainly does not have a good understanding of just how deep the roots of this war really go. In Moscow, Putin once again reminded Witkoff and Kushner that this war cannot be ended until the root causes are addressed. We know that the root cause has not been some desire by NATO to expand, but rather the desire to restore the Russian Empire and shift borders through force and violence, as Russia does every day against Ukraine," Mihkelson said.
The meeting in Moscow also explored opportunities for doing business with Russia.
"Economic issues were also discussed in considerable detail, as were potential major Russian-American projects that would benefit both sides," Ushakov said.
"Kushner and Witkoff are not ordinary diplomats. Above all, they also represent interests that extend beyond conventional diplomacy and by that I mean economic interests in particular. The desire to restore some kind of normal interaction between the United States and Russia unfortunately gives Putin confidence that he can manipulate anyone who comes to talk to him," Mihkelson said.
One tangible benefit, however, may be that Kyiv was not bombed while the U.S. envoys were in Ukraine.
"When I arrived at Kyiv's train station in the morning, a good colleague from the Verkhovna Rada was there to greet me cheerfully and said, 'You know how wonderful it is? We got to sleep last night.' For the past 10 days or so, Russian airstrikes have been taking place here without interruption," Mihkelson said. (Air strikes on Kyiv resumed in the early hours of Tuesday — ed.).
What was actually discussed in Moscow and what was agreed upon, however, is something we will probably only find out later, when the memoirs are written.
"We were just sitting on the terrace — me, Jared and Kirill — and then Yuri joined us, and we talked about how, when we eventually retire, we'll have all these incredible stories and memories to tell, and these are the most extraordinary ones of all," Witkoff said.

====================================================================================================

Youth clubs, trade unions, pubs: here's how Burnham can fix Britain's social recession | Gordon Brown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:00:30 UTC
16:00:30 KST

Prime minister Andy Burnham has hit the ground running, tackling head-on three of the public’s burning concerns: falling standards of living, failing public services and a remote, out-of-touch, over-centralised Whitehall. Now, this autumn, a fourth challenge, reversing the decades-long decline of civic engagement, is about to move centre stage to achieve his ambition to put citizens back in control of their communities.
For while there are tens of thousands of local champions bringing towns, cities and villages together, Britain is suffering a civic recession, a hollowing out of the associations, clubs and organisations that once were the beating hearts of our communities.
It is a sobering fact that almost 50% of British adults are not members of any community organisation of any kind, neither a civic association nor church nor faith group, nor even a sports club.
Trade union membership has halved from more than 13 million in 1979 to less than 7 million in 2025. Then there is the widespread collapse in religious adherence – the fall in Church of Scotland membership from 1.3 million in the 1950s to less than 300,000 today being one of the most dramatic indicators. The long-established Women’s Institute has seen its UK membership fall from a peak of 470,000 in the 1950s to about 170,000 today. Since 2000, the UK has lost about 1,200 youth centres. Working men’s clubs – which were once at the centre of industrial communities – have fallen from a peak of 4,000 in the 1970s to about 1,800 now, their membership dwindling from 4 million to under 1 million. And the number of pubs in the UK, the heart of many communities, has dropped from 75,000 in the 1960s to about 45,000 today. For a fleeting moment, the boost in volunteering during the pandemic obscured a drop from 27% of all adults a decade ago to just 17% now.
But the breakdown is not just in formal memberships, but in informal, everyday relationships too: young people in particular are vulnerable, with soaring numbers in England reporting having no close friends at all.
If our physical infrastructure – our roads, railways and airports – broke down, there would be a public outcry and a demand for their immediate repair. If our financial infrastructure collapsed – if cash machines shut down and bank transfers failed – there would be panic. But the breakdown of our civic infrastructure is happening in plain sight and it needs urgent remedy.
This change is not unique to Britain. A survey of more than 30,000 people in 20 countries provides compelling evidence that, in tandem with economic decline, civic decline helps explain the widespread loss of trust, nostalgia for the past and lower levels of tolerance that are the surface manifestations of what is a deep and widespread dissatisfaction with the status quo. It should not be a surprise that many now talk despairingly of a broken society as well as a broken economy.
This sense of decline, combined with social isolation and a feeling that “traditional values” have been lost, encourages a zero-sum view of the world: the belief that life is an endless struggle between “us” and “them” – whether “them” is defined as immigrants, foreigners or simply “others”. In this view, our very commitment to democracy and a rules-based international order becomes tenuous: widespread dissatisfaction means that people agitate for their government to exclusively pursue the interests of a narrowly defined population. The fact is that someone who is not involved in their local community and has little contact with people of different ethnicities or religious views is much more likely to support rightwing populist nationalist parties and to oppose cooperation between countries.
So No 10’s plans to transfer power from the centre to regions are best seen as what is called a “double devolution”; extending spending and decision-making power beyond local authorities downwards to local communities to empower a new generation of active citizens. But this must be complemented by a boom in civic participation. An opt-out national community service for young people, a remodelled Pride in Place programme to put local people and not politicians in control, legislating participatory budgeting to allocate funding for local services, and designing services to be much more accessible to people should all now be under consideration as part of a nationwide consultation on rebuilding community life.
Learning from a Danish law that requires municipalities to fund voluntary associations and provide venues for their activities, a UK civic capital fund could go further and guarantee support to all those who want to form or join clubs in their neighbourhoods, with only one stipulation: they are open to all and contribute to the common good. Such a fund could assist with travel, venue hire, membership fees and anything that constitutes a “participation tax”.
Promoting civic education and introducing volunteering hours to the school curriculum have proved to be effective, from Ontario, where pupil volunteering is mandatory, to Sweden, where school councils are given real decision-making powers. An Erasmus-style exchange – this time between the nations and regions of the UK – could help young people connect across religious, ethnic and ideological divides.
Recent evidence shows areas without quality local news see the least civic activity and are more prone to online misinformation. So support should be given to local newspapers and websites, including through an expansion of the BBC local democracy reporting service. Online community groups also have a role to play: in my own home town, the Facebook page Love Kirkcaldy has nearly 60,000 members – roughly as many as the population of the wider town itself. The page acts as a community noticeboard but also now brings people together face to face in clubs. Such forums help us to better get to know our neighbours, and restore faith and trust in democracy.
Between them, measures like these can rebuild an ethic of mutuality and civic obligation. The distinctive feature of a successful community organisation is not just that we belong to it but that it belongs to us. And while governments, local and national, can create the conditions for a stronger civic society, the most effective way to build one is the simple act of one person inviting another person to join in.
It is when neighbours no longer talk of “the school”, “the hospital”, “the library” and “the community centre”, or even “my school”, “my hospital”, “my library” and “my community centre”, but instead speak of “our school”, “our hospital”, “our library” and “our community centre”, that we will know a community has been reborn and there is a renewed sense that we are all part of a shared future.
- 
  Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010
- 
  The future starts with us: Gordon Brown in conversation 
On Thursday 10 September, join Hugh Muir and Gordon Brown to discuss the intricate connections between global instability and civic decline, as explored in Brown’s new book, The Future Starts With Us. Book tickets here

What role for science in Swiss democracy and worldwide?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

What role for science in Swiss democracy and worldwide?
In Switzerland, science enjoys greater public trust than the police, government or parliament. But what exactly is the role of science in a democracy, and how does it differ in dictatorships?
For many years, the police were the institution that the Swiss population trusted most. This emerges from the yearly Security Study by the federal technology institute ETH ZurichExternal link. Today, however, another body comes out on top: science.
For Naomi Oreskes, a science historian at Harvard University, this is good news. It shows that the Swiss public values “high-quality information” more than its counterpart in the United States.
The Security Study has been examining levels of trust in science since 2018External link. At the time, it justified the introduction of the category based on trends seen “particularly in the United States”.
    
        External Content    
    
            
‘Follow the Science’
In countries such as Switzerland, the Covid-19 pandemic propelled debate about the role of science in society into the political limelight.
According to political scientist Eri Bertsou, the rhetoric at the start of the pandemic set off her “personal alarm bells”. Her research at the University of St Gallen focuses, among things, on technocracy – that is, the idea that political decisions should be based more heavily on expert knowledge.
In spring 2020, then-British Prime Minister Boris Johnson justified government decisions with the slogan “Follow the Science”. “I remember thinking: gosh, this isn’t good,” says Bertsou. It was the use of the definite article, “the”, rather than the actual policy choice that she was reacting to. “The science, as if there were one settled answer to follow. There wasn’t one at the time.” Data was constantly coming in, and assumptions were being rethought.
“Scientific assessments and models changed accordingly over the course of the pandemic.” says Bertsou. When governments then modified their pandemic policies, science was blamed. “Precisely because governments had claimed to be following it.”
The idea that science can provide clear-cut answers to politically complex questions sounds tempting. But the role of science, Bertsou says, is to contribute its findings as a basis for democratic debate: “The decision must lie with those who have to live with the outcomes.”
However, the “Follow the Science” slogan conveyed the message that political decisions could derive directly from scientific findings. “In so doing, the boundary between scientific advice and political responsibility blurred,” Bertsou explains.
She has noted a strong polarisation of public attitudes towards science in many places. These attitudes are “context-specific”. Thus, in Eastern Europe after the end of the Cold War, it was mainly people on the political left who were sceptical of science. Today, attitudes there have aligned more closely with Western Europe where, as in the United States, right-wingers tend to be more sceptical. The same holds true for Switzerland, where the Security Study shows that trust decreases “the further to the right one moves on the political spectrum”.
Bertsou is not surprised to see such high trust in science among the Swiss population as a whole. “My guess is that in a world full of uncertainties, there is an additional need to have something to guide one.” Data from a study across 68 countriesExternal link, in which Bertsou was involved, show that many people want scientists to be more active in politics.
Trust is often regarded as a vanishing commodity. In recent years, dwindling public confidence in institutions in many countries has given rise to growing concern.
>>Trust in politics and the authorities is also comparatively high in Switzerland. Read our latest article on the subject here:
More
High Swiss trust in government sparks little interest abroad
Yet Bertsou says that trust does not disappear – it merely shifts, just like in the law of conservation of energy: “Trust is relative; you have to direct it somewhere.” Those who lose trust in politics may place it in a populist figure – or in science. If politics is perceived as corrupt, some people pin their hopes on experts whom they see as being outside the system.
Technocracy – or the call to “follow the science” – can capitalise on the promise that there is an objectively correct, scientifically justifiable policy.
When science serves the authoritarian state
In dictatorships, there is no critical tension between science and government, says political scientist Ralph Weber, who conducts research on China at the University of Basel. “On the contrary. In China, science is supposed to help the Party exercise its rule.” It is no coincidence, he adds, that authoritarian governments often have a technocratic understanding of science: the notion of a “best solution” is closely linked to autocratic rule.
This may sometimes be efficient. However, open discussion is precisely one of the strengths of science in democracies. “We can debate what the problem actually is. Authoritarian states bypass this. The regimes decide and the problem is laid down from above,” says Weber.
During his research and advisory work with a “wide variety of members of the scientific community”, Weber is often confronted with the question of who scientists should cooperate with and how. Modern science operates as an interconnected global network, but science has a different function and self-image in authoritarian states – and this poses challenges for democratic countries such as Switzerland.
More
Our democracy newsletter
On the one hand, it’s all about “keeping ahead in the global competition for knowledge and innovation”, says Weber. At the same time, though, it is vital to avoid inadvertently contributing to a further weakening democracy in the long term.
For Weber, this means staying open without being naïve. What is needed is investment in “fully informed scientific cooperation”. Exchange, research and cooperation should be facilitated. But “if someone is conducting research into hydraulics with China, they should be able to gauge what the lack of distinction between civilian and military research means for the project.” No one should be completely taken aback afterwards to discover that their findings have contributed to the construction of long-range missiles.
When Weber talks about challenges in cooperation, he is no longer thinking solely of authoritarian states such as China – but rather, globally, of democracies that “face many internal authoritarian challenges”, such as India and the United States. The proportion of democracies worldwide has decreased in recent decades.
Like many others, Weber is currently concerned about the situation in the United States. “We are witnessing first-hand how a traditionally strong scientific partner is changing.”
>>When is a democracy no longer a democracy? Read our article on this issue:
More
When is a democracy no longer a democracy?
Challenges for universities: from YouTube to Trump
Weber is surprised at the high level of trust that the Swiss place in science.
He has rather observed that, “not least as a result of digitalisation”, scepticism towards science is on the rise. In his student days, he would have thought long and hard before daring to contradict his professor, but today, thanks to digital channels, people are readier to question societal authorities. “This goes hand in hand, however, with a blurring of the line between opinion and knowledge. In the worst-case scenario, I look for something on YouTube that reinforces my opinion and then declare that to be knowledge.”
This puts universities on the spot. “They need to demonstrate their value to society and find the right language to convey how scientific knowledge is generated,” says Weber; for example, to explain that the humanities and social sciences often produce a different kind of knowledge than laboratory evidence, or what the difference is between objective knowledge and well-founded interpretation.
Harvard historian Oreskes is also calling for better communication on the different ways that science contributes to the public good. Many scientists, she notes, are struggling to deal with the growing polarisation and loss of trust in science among sections of the United States population.
The “leaders of the scientific communities” should consider, in dialogue with disciplines such as sociology and political science, how science can better “address human needs” and demonstrate “how our work does help the societies we live in”.
She sees science as a force against authoritarianism. “Science, as an enterprise, threatens authoritarian governments, because science is a source of independent thinking and with that, potentially a source of an independent voice.” Even though, of course, not all scientists have championed democratic principles at all times.
Science as a whole is a value-driven endeavour, Oreskes argues. The search for truth remains paramount.
A high level of trust in science is justified because it has “a strategy for identifying and correcting error”. It is also necessary “because science involves complex questions that none of us can answer on our own”.
In the Security Study, trust ratings for science were consistently higher than for the Swiss government.

The fight against transnational fraud rings has become a regional priority, Hsiao said. He cautioned Taiwanese against being lured into fraud operations by promises of high salaries, free air travel, and accommodation in Southeast Asia.

Taisun seeks NT$1 billion over Taiwan cooking oil scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:56:02 UTC
15:56:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taisun Enterprise filed a civil lawsuit in Taipei District Court on Tuesday against four companies, seeking NT$1 billion (US$31.7 million) in damages over losses associated with contaminated cooking oil.
The defendants are Central Union Oil, Fwusow Industry, Formosa Oilseed, and Namchow Holdings. Taisun Marketing Vice President Niu An-ze (鈕安澤) said the company is seeking damages partly because abnormalities in oil were discovered three times beginning May 13 but were not reported to the relevant authorities as required, per CNA.
Niu said multiple abnormal signals appeared in the oil supply chain and the responsibilities of each company in handling the information should be clearly defined. If the information had been disclosed promptly, risk controls could have been initiated earlier, he said.
Taisun lawyer Chen Cheng-hsi (陳政熙) said a comparison of the prosecutors' indictment, Namchow's public statement, and other evidence revealed significant discrepancies in when the companies obtained information about the abnormalities, the extent of their knowledge, and their subsequent handling of it. Chen said the first key issue was whether the information was communicated promptly.
Namchow's public statement indicated that on May 13, an oil sample from a Fwusow Industry tanker tested positive for benzo(a)pyrene at 4.6 micrograms per kilogram, exceeding the legal standard. A May 22 retest also exceeded the standard, while SGS testing produced a result of 8.0 micrograms per kilogram on June 4, per UDN.
Chen said Taisun and Namchow simultaneously received soybean cooking oil from Central Union. Taisun submitted its finished product to SGS for testing on April 10 and received a passing report on April 21, leading the company to conclude that its product met safety standards.
If information about the first abnormal test results in May had been promptly disclosed and reported, Central Union and its shareholder companies could have begun source tracing, cross-testing, and risk controls earlier, Chen said.
Niu said Taisun would also have had an opportunity to re-examine its products and raw material sources. He added that Taisun had hoped the three major shareholders would jointly reform Central Union and rebuild its food safety and corporate governance systems, per CNA.
Taisun said that as additional evidence emerged, it would no longer remain silent about responsibilities it believes should be pursued.
The lawsuit comes after Taichung prosecutors indicted Central Union, Fwusow, Formosa Oilseed, and Taisun, along with 15 individuals, in August over oil containing excessive levels of benzo(a)pyrene. Prosecutors said the oil had been supplied to downstream food businesses and alleged that reporting of the problem was delayed.

Prompting makes perfect: Award-winning AI artist Nóra Bereczki on new frontiers for photography
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:55:21 UTC
15:55:21 KST

Is an AI-generated image really art? What role will AI play in schools and will machines take our jobs? Award-winning Digital Umami creator Nóra Bereczki gives her artistic impression on the creative processes, photography and education.
Artificial intelligence is transforming our entire world, from street billboards to brain surgery. Art is no exception. An ever-growing number of creators use AI models, while a lively debate is under way over whether works created in this way can even be regarded as artistic creations.
Enter Nóra Bereczki, an AI artist working under the alias Digital Umami who's attracting increasing attention. Her video series that bring Hungarian poets and writers to life has appeared widely on social media, and this summer she won an image-generation software contest from among 52,000 entrants, taking home the $100,000 grand prize.
Her winning series is titled Dolce Impossible, inspired by the Mediterranean summer. It consists of ten images that depict typical holiday scenes, which many people can relate to, but each of them contains a surreal element. For example:
What is the difference between an average AI-generated image and art? Why is it dangerous to see artificial intelligence not as a tool but as a partner? What role can AI play in education? How should we prepare our children for the new world shaped by artificial intelligence? And will machines really take our jobs? These are just some of questions we discussed with Nóra Bereczki.
First of all, how did you first come into contact with artificial intelligence?
Professionally, I work as a marketing consultant, and I am very interested in technology. My last workplace before I went on maternity leave was a robotics and industrial automation company. My husband also works in AI, and we talk a lot about the topic, follow what is happening and how the technology is developing.
AI tools broke into the wider public consciousness in 2022, and that was when I began to think about how they could be effectively built into a company's marketing strategy. Alongside marketing, I have been involved in analogue and digital photography for more than 20 years, and image-making is my passion, so I started testing these AI tools separately as well. Hobby projects followed, I kept a close eye on how the technology was evolving, and the hobby gradually grew into something bigger.
If I understand correctly, you use AI to realise your own ideas for images. Have you finally found a tool that lets you do anything you can imagine?
You're on the right track. When I walk down the street, I constantly see frames and think in terms of compositions. There are a huge number of such ideas in my head, and many of them I cannot realise through classical photography. AI, however, is perfect for expressing these ideas visually.
A good example is one of the images in my award-winning series. On a beach, a huge, human-sized lobster stands facing a three-year-old girl. The scene itself had already existed in my mind. Of course, it would be possible to try to create it as a traditional photo production, but it would require substantial organisation, post-production and budget. With the help of AI I was able to realise the visual idea I had imagined.
Perhaps this is also why I don't see AI as something that replaces photography for me. It has become another tool on the palette. I like mixing different technologies and genres; for example, I often combine my own analogue photographs with AI. I always try to decide which tool suits a particular idea best. Sometimes that tool is AI, and sometimes it is not needed at all.
Has it ever happened that you had an idea, but AI overrode it and you liked the new version so much that you decided to go with that instead?
It's one thing when someone is just experimenting with image-generating tools, types in something like "blue dog", the model produces something artistic, and the user likes the result and feels a sense of achievement. And it's another thing when someone sits down in front of AI with a specific vision, and the question is whether they can carry that vision through.
In my view, an AI-generated image becomes a human creation when the artist is able to carry through the vision they imagined. When they do not leave the outcome to the random results produced by the model, but really get what they originally wanted.
I also have an AI image on my bookshelf, and it really was created in the rather random way you described. In your case, I imagine producing such an image is quite a long process.
If someone makes an AI-generated, random image that brings them joy, that's great. But I generally approach things with a fairly clear picture in my mind of what I want to see. I know what elements I want the image to be built from, what the composition, lighting, texture, aspect ratio or even the camera angle should be, and I try to pass all this on to the model as precisely as possible.
From there, it becomes an iterative process: I look at what it understood from what I imagined, and if something isn't right, I refine it. Sometimes the desired result appears very quickly, other times it takes many rounds. For me the crucial thing is not to let the first interesting generated image determine the direction I go in, but to have a vision and consciously steer the outcome towards it.
Does that require very long instructions?
Not necessarily. A prompt doesn't become good simply by being long. It matters more that it is well thought-through and clear. But to really get back what I imagined, you have to decide on a lot of small details.
For example, it can happen that I specify almost everything except that the scene should take place in daylight, and the model generates a night-time image. In that case, you need to fine-tune the instructions and generate again. At the same time, you have to make sure not to overload the prompt, because beyond a certain point too many instructions can actually worsen the result. And of course different models vary greatly in how precisely they interpret textual instructions.
When social media became widespread, the mantra was that everyone could now be a content creator. Thanks to AI this is now exponentially more true. But is there a threshold someone has to cross in order to create works of art with artificial intelligence? For instance your background in photography?
In technical terms, I think the entry threshold is now very low. AI provides a sense of success incredibly quickly: you type in a few sentences and within seconds you get a striking image. As a result, vast amounts of content are being produced, and it's no coincidence that the term "AI slop" has appeared to describe low-quality content generated at scale.
The artistic threshold is, in my view, a completely different question. What I see is that behind the works that really manage to stand out from this noise, there is very often some kind of relevant background knowledge. It might be photography, film, graphic design, painting or another visual field. The knowledge, experience and visual sensitivity someone has built up over the years matter a great deal: how composition, light, colour and rhythm work, or how to tell a story visually. For me, my photographic background is clearly a huge asset.
At the same time, one of the most exciting things about AI is precisely that it can put tools into the hands of people who have always had a creative mindset or sensitivity but never found the right medium for it. I know someone who used to work in a completely different field, yet always felt a strong need for self-expression. In AI they found the tool that finally lets them visualise their ideas, and they are producing fantastic work.
Hungarian creators, incidentally, are very strong in this field internationally as well. Dávid Szauder, for example, attracts significant international attention, and then there is Laci Gaál, who lives and works in Vietnam and is also internationally recognised. It is telling that they too have a prior visual background: Dávid Szauder comes from fine art, while Laci Gaál comes from film.
One of your projects, the AI videos presenting Hungarian poets and writers, has already been used by several teachers in literature classes. The obvious question is: in your view, how can artificial intelligence be used in education?
I would divide this into two parts. One is when the teacher uses AI. I have spoken to several teachers who are specifically interested in the technology and are creating very exciting things with it: quiz apps, interactive teaching materials, or tools that help visualise scientific phenomena that are hard to imagine. To do this, however, the teacher has to understand the tools and their limitations.
If we want to embed the use of AI in education at system level, I think we first need to prepare teachers. Not only in how to use a model, but also in when it is appropriate to rely on it, how to check what it says, and what data protection, copyright and ethical issues arise. This is a particularly difficult task with a technology that develops faster than we can adapt to it. At the same time, it is necessary to prepare education systems for AI's presence, because pupils will encounter it in their everyday lives and later in the labour market. Across the world, in several countries and education systems, initiatives have already been launched on how to incorporate AI and AI literacy into education.
And what is the other case?
The other is when the child themselves uses AI for learning at home, and here parents have a crucial role. As a parent, this concerns me a great deal: at what point would I first put such a tool into my own children's hands? In part this is a question of age, but it also depends on what skills need to be in place beforehand.
I think a child first has to learn to study without AI. They need to experience what it is like to delve into something, think through a problem independently, search for information, make mistakes, try again and think critically. And of course they also need to learn what AI is, how it works, in what ways it can be useful, and what its limits and risks are. That is why, for example, in the early years of primary school I don't yet see a place for simply sitting children down in front of ChatGPT or other generative AI tools.
Once those basic competences are in place, I think AI can offer huge opportunities, especially in personalised learning. It can explain the same material in different ways, adapt to the child's pace, offer different examples to those who didn't understand something the first time, or suggest alternative learning approaches to pupils for whom traditional methods are less effective. For a child with ADHD, for example, it can help break the material down into shorter units, make it more interactive or link it to their interests.
So in my view the question is not whether we should use AI in education, but when and for what purposes, and on what foundations.
Let me quote you from an earlier interview: "The question is not whether the tool is artificial, but whether the thought behind it is human." Are you saying that anything that is not born of a human thought but of artificial intelligence cannot be an artistic work? That it cannot be art if I tell AI to create a beautiful work that expresses the pain of passing time?
It's hard to say, because what you described could easily slip into the category of experimental art. Many works of art have been based on a random situation like that. But even in such cases there is, once again, a human thought: the artist's aim was to have the artwork emerge with the help of chance.
In my own creative process, the starting point is usually some inner tension, a feeling, thought or question that I want to release in some way. Then comes the vision of how I want to show it, and I choose the tool to do so, which may well be AI.
So the idea comes from the human, and AI is the tool for realisation. It's like using a robotic arm to lift something heavy. Many people, however, don't treat artificial intelligence as a tool but as a companion.
Yes, and for me this is where one of the truly problematic aspects of the technology begins. I have done interviews where people referred to AI as a creative partner, and I have to admit that gives me chills. I very consciously see it as a tool. Creative intent, decision-making, control and ultimately responsibility must remain with the human.
We can already see people giving names to the models they use, talking about them as personalities, or feeling emotionally shaken when an update changes or removes the version they were used to. In other words, a real emotional bond can form with something that is, in fact, a technological system. I consider this dangerous because AI can imitate human communication in a highly convincing way without there being a person on the other side who feels, understands or cares about us. The better it becomes at this, the more important it will be for us not to lose sight of that distinction.
There is, for example, a deeply disturbing video in which a grandmother receives a ChatGPT subscription, and by the time her grandchild explains that she isn't talking to a real person, she already wants to invite them round because they've become such good friends. These are things I find very worrying.
And we can't really blame the grandmother for believing she was talking to a human being.
The technology is developing much faster than we are learning to live with it as a society. We're long past the point where you can spot an AI-generated image because a person has six fingers. It is becoming ever harder to decide, on the basis of our senses alone, whether something is real.
It is hugely important that we prepare our children for this new world. I already talk to my kids about the fact that just because they see something in a picture or a video doesn't mean it really happened. In their world, the basic assumption won't be "I'll believe it when I see it".
Perhaps the most common anxiety around artificial intelligence is that it will take away our jobs. How real do you think that threat is?
I think it's an absolutely valid concern. We are facing very serious changes in the labour market; it's just that no one yet knows exactly how extensive they will be.
Stanford University recently published a study showing that in the United States, job prospects for young people in professions most exposed to AI have already clearly worsened. The researchers looked at what percentage of 22 to 25-year-olds qualified for a given profession are employed, and found that in the summer of 2025 there was a 15 percent gap compared with professions less affected by AI, and by the summer of 2026 that disadvantage had already grown to 19 percent. At the same time, of course, new positions that did not previously exist are also emerging; I see more and more job ads specifically related to AI.
And how should we respond to that challenge? What should we do, if for instance as journalists we are worried about whether we will have jobs in the long term?
What I think we absolutely must not do in this situation is stick our heads in the sand and tell ourselves things will somehow work out. It is worth regularly thinking through how our own profession might change, what new knowledge we will need, whether we should retrain or even look for a new professional direction in the longer term. And I think we should get to know these technologies even if we disagree with them or are unhappy about their spread. They will affect our work and our environment regardless.
As parents, we also have to keep in mind how we prepare our children for a world and a labour market that will probably be very different from the one we grew up in. We need to keep an eye on the trends. No one knows exactly what will happen, but it is already clear that we are headed for a great many changes.

'To stop love jihad': Maharashtra minister Nitesh Rane backs VHP's call to bar Muslims from Navratri events

Maharashtra inister Nitesh Rane (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Maharashtra minister Nitesh Rane expressed support for the Vishva Hindu Parishad's (VHP) call to bar Muslims from the Navratri events in the state, alleging that otherwise this would lead to an increase in "love jihad" cases.Attendees at such festivities should undergo identity checks and recite the Hanuman Chalisa before entry, the BJP leader told PTI Videos on Monday.
"Love jihad" is a term used by right-wing activists to allege a ploy by Muslim men to lure women (mostly from the Hindu community) into relationships for religious conversion."Those who do not follow idol worship should not participate in Hindu religious events. Those coming for garba should show their identity and chant the Hanuman Chalisa before being allowed entry," Rane said, extending support to the VHP's demand.
The VHP last week announced that Muslims "would not be allowed" entry to garba and dandiya venues across the state during the upcoming Navratri festival, and issued "guidelines" for organisers to verify participants' identities by checking their Aadhaar cards and applying tilak on their foreheads.
