’I’m in survival mode’: Farmers turn to new crops for earnings in the face of repeated droughts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:52:48 UTC
15:52:48 KST

A grain being developed in the US could offer farmers a way to improve soil health while making crops more resilient to drought and heavy rainfall.
Bryce Black kneels in a wheat field battered by intense drought. He holds two strands, remarking on how small the seed head is compared with what's normal.
After a late October rain last year, the fourth-generation farmer was optimistic about his 1,800 acres (728 hectares) of winter wheat. But a dry winter and spring brought extreme drought when the wheat needed moisture to establish itself. He ended up harvesting about 1,500 acres (607 hectares), but the yield was the lowest he's had since taking over his family's farm in 2017.
“It was just a grit your teeth and get through it type of deal,” says Black, who also grows corn, soybeans and milo on his family’s 4,500-acre (1,821 hectare) farm. “It is disheartening, you know? And it’s kind of hard to know what to do.”
When these weather events occur, farmers often look for new ways to protect their crops and their bottom line.
What is a perennial grain?
Some farmers are putting perennial grains in rotation to build resilience against extreme weather like drought and intense rainfall. Researchers are working to develop perennial versions of common annual grains like wheat, sorghum and rice, but the work is slow. And widespread adoption by farmers is challenging because perennial crops don’t yield as much, harvesting can be difficult and the market is still developing.
Despite the challenges, Black is intrigued. “I’m in survival mode,” he says. “If you can plant something and then you don’t have to go back for four or five years … that would save so much money, so much labour, everything. That’s what makes it enticing.”
Five years ago, David Mueller planted a 12-acre (5 hectare) field of Kernza, a perennial grain similar to native grasses found in parts of Europe and western Asia.
Perennial grains don’t require yearly planting, harvesting and replanting. Instead, they are planted once every few years.
Researchers say their root systems, which can reach several feet down, can access water deeper in the ground. That helps them better withstand short-term drought. And when heavy rain hits, the larger root structures can absorb excess water that would otherwise run off and erode the soil. Those deeper roots also sequester more carbon, reducing pollution in the atmosphere.
Inside the institute developing perennial crops
Kernza is one of several perennial grains under development at The Land Institute in Salina, Kansas, about an hour’s drive north of Mueller’s farm. The institute, which formally began domesticating Kernza in 2001, works with researchers and farmers around the world to develop perennial versions of wheat, rice, sorghum and other grain and oil seeds.
Some farmers in Southeast Asia and parts of Africa have started planting and harvesting perennial rice in their fields. Kernza, though, is furthest along and was first harvested on a farm in 2010.
In the US last year, Kernza was cultivated on 3,511 acres (1,421 hectares), compared with 37.2 million acres (15.1 million hectares) of winter, spring and Durum wheat harvested or planted in 2025-26.
Mueller's Kernza field is one of almost 100 acres (40 hectares) he has planted since 2018. He's used the crop to rebuild soil with drainage issues or to reestablish organic matter on his family's farm in Halstead, Kansas, where they also farm about 600 acres (243 hectares) each of corn and soybeans.
He also said Kernza uses about a third of the fertiliser that wheat needs, and because it's planted once every few years, he doesn't have to run gas-burning farm equipment as often.
“Not only are we able to utilise those acres profitably, but then we also build up that soil and work on some benefits to make it hopefully profitable to raise other crops on those fields in the future,” Mueller said.
Soil degradation is a serious threat
A 2024 United Nations report suggests that by 2050, soil degradation could cause more than $20 trillion in losses to the global economy. Farming perennials is less disruptive to that carbon-capturing soil.
Soil serves as a reservoir, capturing planet-warming carbon dioxide from the atmosphere that plays a role in climate change, experts say. Annual cultivation - the plow, plant, harvest and repeat cycle - strains soil formation, which takes thousands of years and rapidly degrades the farmland. Perennial roots can also bring that carbon deeper into soils, where it is less likely to be disturbed, says Laura van der Pol, The Land Institute's lead soil ecologist.
And soil that has more carbon in it tends to be better for plants.
“Incorporating perennials into our agriculture seems like really the only option to have soil for generations if we want to continue to grow food,” van der Pol said. “It’s hard to imagine getting to a place where we could have soil and abundant food without a perennial option.”
Lower yields and harvesting can be challenging
Pilot programs involving perennial grains are in the works around the world, testing how to grow them in different regions, climates and soils, but the research is early and slow-moving.
Chief among the challenges is the crops' grain yield, says Lee DeHaan, who leads the Institute’s Kernza domestication program. Kernza farmers are getting yields of about 20 to 40 per cent of what they might get from a wheat crop in the area. That's because a perennial crop has to use energy not only to grow seeds for grain, but also to grow roots to penetrate the soil so it can survive for more than a year. That contrasts with annual crops, which are engineered to put as much energy as possible into making as much seed as they can in one growing season.
Researchers at Cornell University also have found that establishing a Kernza field can be difficult as it contends with weeds in its first year. Finding the right seeding rate to maximise yield is also still being studied, says Matthew Ryan, a sustainable cropping professor at Cornell University.
Mueller says new varieties of Kernza are yielding more than previous ones, but the yield can decline as the crop ages. Yields on perennial rice are similar to annual ones, officials at The Land Institute say.
Harvesting Kernza specifically can be challenging. The grain is smaller than wheat, for example, and farmers and researchers are still finding the best ways to adapt farm equipment so the kernel isn't damaged during harvest.
Still, Ryan says farmers who experience crop loss due to drought or major flooding may be prompted to think about ways to build more resilience into their operations.
“I think farmers, more than other people, realise that the climate is changing,” he says. “They prompt people to think, and I feel like they are driving farmers to practice this.”

SIX launches new service for European stock market data
The Swiss stock exchange operator SIX is launching a new service for real-time stock market data. The platform gives professional market participants and retail investors access to price data from stock exchanges in Switzerland, the UK and 16 EU markets.
According to a statement issued on Tuesday, at the heart of the service, known as “SIX Market Signal”, is a real-time data feed called 1BBO. This displays the best available bid and ask prices for each share. The data is sourced from, among others, the SIX Swiss Exchange, the Spanish stock exchange BME and the trading platform Aquis Exchange.
For institutional clients, this is intended to make stock market data more easily accessible even outside the actual trading departments. SIX cites asset management, comparative analysis and compliance as possible areas of application. Retail investors, meanwhile, can access real-time stock market data directly.

Second phase of RAF air command system cancelled
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:50:51 BST
15:50:51 KST

The Ministry of Defence has cancelled the second phase of Project Guardian, a Royal Air Force command and control system developed to protect British and NATO airspace, writing off £9.476 million in a constructive loss recorded in its annual report and accounts, according to a written answer.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked for further information on the loss disclosed in the Ministry of Defence annual report and accounts for 2025 to 2026.
Mr Pollard said: “Project GUARDIAN is a Royal Air Force advanced Command and Control system developed to protect UK and NATO airspace. A strategic decision was taken to cancel the second phase of this system, UKV2.”
Setting out the reasoning, he said: “A number of factors led to the cancellation, including evolving capability requirements, the increased technical complexity in delivering a compliant solution and a wider reprioritisation of capabilities across the portfolio.”
He said: “The constructive loss reflects historical project costs for activities that had been undertaken during the Demonstration and Manufacture phase of the programme.”
A constructive loss
Constructive loss is the term used in government accounting for money spent on something that has produced no usable output, as distinct from a cash loss where funds have gone missing or a fruitless payment where a service was paid for and not received. Departments are required to disclose them in their annual accounts, which is where this figure came to light and why the question was asked.
Guardian
Guardian is the computer system behind the Recognised Air Picture, the real-time depiction of every aircraft in the airspace Britain controls or patrols, with each contact identified as friendly or hostile. It links the radars and radios of the United Kingdom and NATO, allows communication between the ground and aircraft, and enables the Royal Air Force to despatch fighters to identify, intercept and escort aircraft flown aggressively or suspected of being a threat.
The programme replaced the previous UKASACS Command and Control System, with IBM awarded a £60 million contract in April 2018 to develop and install it, carrying a further £20 million of costed options which would have taken the total to £80 million. Announcing it at the time, then Defence Secretary Gavin Williamson said the system would give the Royal Air Force the upper hand in the face of rapidly changing and intensifying global threats.
Initial operating capability was declared at the Control and Reporting Centre at RAF Boulmer in Northumberland, with the system also installed at 78 Squadron at Swanwick in Hampshire. Defence Equipment and Support has said the two centres operate around the clock, with 50 dual workstations at Boulmer and 29 at Swanwick, which when fully manned could be staffed by more than 100 battlespace management personnel.
The original 2018 announcement also covered the replacement of systems at Royal Air Force bases in the Falkland Islands, where 1435 Flight holds quick reaction alert over the islands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

After Sunday's talks in Kyiv, Witkoff and Kushner said they had held "meaningful discussions" and were encouraged. The visit was part of a trip that began in Moscow in the latest push to end Russia's full-scale invasion more than 4-1/2 years since it began.

====================================================================================================

How Material Intelligence Solves What BIM Can’t
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

The original promise of BIM (Building Information Modeling) went far beyond the three-dimensional representation of a building. Its ambition was to turn the model into a coordinated information structure, in which geometry, components, systems, and data remained connected as the project evolved. Changes to one element could be reflected across corresponding plans, sections, elevations, and quantities; clashes between different disciplines could be identified before construction; and information associated with building components could follow the project through different stages of its life cycle.
In the early 2000s, Dave Lemont, now Executive Chairman of Acelab, was among a small group involved in shaping this vision during the period following Autodesk's acquisition of Revit Technology Corporation, when the strategy and terminology around BIM were still being discussed. Two decades later, this approach has moved well beyond pioneering practices and become part of the everyday workflow of much of the construction industry and its scope has also expanded into areas such as scheduling, cost, and management.
Yet, according to Lemont himself, models never fully delivered on that promise. One of the most persistent gaps appears in the transition between the modeled element and the product that will ultimately be specified. A model may define the geometry, composition, and performance requirements of a wall, roof, or facade, but decisions about which product to use, from which manufacturer, with which certifications, environmental data, specification section, keynote, and technical documentation are still commonly distributed across platforms, spreadsheets, PDFs, and databases. Also, product information changes continuously: lines are discontinued, formulations change, and new certifications are introduced. Even a well-organized internal library therefore requires constant maintenance if the information it contains is to remain reliable.
The issue is not necessarily BIM's ability to store this information, but rather how well it can keep it structured and synchronized throughout the process. When a product selection changes without specifications, schedules, drawings, and other documents being updated at the same time, discrepancies can emerge between what was selected, specified, and documented. And the later these inconsistencies are identified, the more costly they tend to become.
The idea behind material intelligence is to bring product information into the project's working data, so it remains connected across selections, specifications, and documentation. Performance, certifications, environmental impact, cost, and technical information can then be linked to material selections and updated as those selections evolve. It is less about adding more data to the model than about keeping the information behind material decisions current and consistent throughout the project.
Acelab's Material Hub is one example of how this approach can be applied in practice. Built around this gap, it organizes product and material information as structured data and keeps it connected to the documentation that depends on it as the project develops. In this sense, it extends BIM's coordination logic to specification decisions. The platform brings together data related to aesthetics, performance, certifications, embodied carbon, and cost, linking it to specifications, schedules, and drawings developed in Autodesk Revit. This information is organized into three layers:
- Database: brings together more than 200,000 products, sorted according to performance information, certifications, and sustainability metrics, treating them as structured data rather than simply catalog content.
- Library: maintains each firm's history of products and material decisions, preserving knowledge accumulated across projects, including previous experience with use, installation, and sourcing.
- Collaborative workflow: allows architects, specifiers, manufacturers, contractors, and owners to work from a shared source of material information, reducing the need to reconcile different versions scattered across emails, PDFs, and other documents.
This becomes even more relevant in interiors and FF&E (Furniture, Fixtures, and Equipment), where not every selection necessarily corresponds to an object in the model. A paint color, wallcovering, or fabric, for example, may exist in schedules and specifications without ever becoming a Revit family or modeled object. In these cases, coordination has to happen through the information and documentation itself rather than through geometry alone.
Part of the project documentation can then be generated directly from specification decisions. Through what Acelab calls Smart Docs, information associated with selected products feeds specifications, schedules, keynotes, and sustainability reports, reducing the need to update each document separately when a selection changes. According to data provided by Acelab, firms using this workflow report reductions of up to 50% in the time spent on material documentation.
What Changes for the Project Team
The main shift is that material decisions can enter the project earlier. Things like performance data, certifications, environmental impact, and cost can be considered while solutions are still being developed, rather than being addressed primarily during documentation. Because those decisions remain connected to specifications, schedules, and drawings, they can also be easier to track as the project moves from design to construction.
BIM established a framework for coordinating a building's geometry and components across disciplines. Product and material information, however, has often remained less integrated into that process. The next step for BIM is to bring these decisions into the same coordinated information environment, helping reduce inconsistencies, rework, cost overruns, and material waste.

====================================================================================================

Rethinking drone warfare: Germany's military needs more than new technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:44:43 UTC
15:44:43 KST

Ukraine is relying on hundreds of thousands of drones in the war and constantly upgrading its systems. The Bundeswehr is also rearming, but still has ground to make up in procurement, training and adaptation.
Ukraine is now said to be producing around 500,000 drones a month to defend itself against Russia's full-scale invasion. That's according to Ukrainian media, which also report that this output has almost doubled in the space of a year. But the sheer number of drones is not decisive for the Ukrainian army: the unmanned systems are being upgraded and adapted almost every week.
One of the companies driving this ongoing drone revolution and evolution is the Ukrainian firm Buntar Aerospace, which has added a new feature to its Buntar Copilot software, allowing reconnaissance drones to be controlled entirely remotely. It means only a small team remains at the launch site, while missions can be run from hundreds or even thousands of kilometres away.
"The main goal is to ensure the safety of experienced crews. Once the drone is airborne, the pilot can carry out the mission from a safe location while the launch team quickly leaves the area," Bohdan Sas, one of Buntar's founders, told Euronews.
Unlike other firms, Buntar does not rely on external remote-desktop software but has built it directly into its own mission-planning platform. The reason, Sas said, is simple: "Warfare has changed, and remote control has now become an indispensable standard."
How quickly innovation can advance in war
Not only do soldiers have to adapt to the realities of war; systems do too, as the example of Kaban shows. The Ukrainian company Kaban Robotics converts existing vehicles such as the US HMMWV (High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle, better known as the Humvee) so that they can be operated remotely from a safe distance.
The advantage is that rather than designing an entirely new unmanned vehicle, existing hardware can be adapted relatively quickly for new tasks. The pace of further development is even more striking. According to the system's lead developer, new functions are introduced directly in response to feedback from Ukrainian soldiers.
In one case, soldiers suggested as a vehicle was being handed over that the exterior lights should switch off automatically if communication was lost. The modification was implemented in around 15 minutes.
The cameras too were adapted straight from frontline experience: because oncoming headlights could dazzle the main camera at night, a function was added enabling the driver to switch to the thermal-imaging camera at the push of a button.
As Kaban told Euronews: "Sometimes the time between a suggestion from military personnel and the implementation of a new feature is not measured in months or weeks, but literally in minutes."
Is the Bundeswehr adapting to modern warfare?
Drones also play a major role in the German armed forces. Germany is now trying to ramp up industrial production. A few months ago, the Bundestag's budget committee approved, with conditions, the delivery of thousands of so-called "kamikaze" drones for the Bundeswehr. These are relatively inexpensive systems designed to engage individual enemy targets precisely over long distances.
Germany may not yet be producing as many drones as Ukraine, but output has been ramped up sharply. Bavaria in particular has become a hub for numerous drone manufacturers, including Quantum Systems, Helsing, ARX and Airlogix, which have reportedly begun mass production of more than 5,000 long-range combat drones for Ukraine. And Bavaria is not set to be the only site: according to a report in the newspaper Welt, another production facility is already planned in eastern Germany.
In last year's report by the parliamentary commissioner for the armed forces, Henning Otte, he wrote that "the armed forces are, however, lagging far too far behind in the acquisition of modern unmanned systems."
During a troop visit, criticism was voiced that the KZO and LUNA drones were already outdated when they were introduced. The priority now, he argued, is to get new systems "into series production quickly" and deliver them to the troops in large numbers.
The problem, however, is not just production. Otte also criticises the Bundeswehr's procurement processes as overly bureaucratic. In his view, more money on its own is not enough. He writes that the "blanket invocation of underfunding of the Bundeswehr" is no longer an excuse. Instead, procurement needs to be accelerated and the forces relieved of "non-military bureaucracy."
When it comes to drones, security expert Dr Frank Sauer therefore sees technology as the lesser problem. "Catching up and closing the gap is quite possible here and in fact already under way, albeit at much higher prices per drone, which is why German products are not particularly popular in Ukraine," he told Euronews.
"The real issue is how we handle these new systems, internalise the changed geometry of the battlefield, and develop new tactics and procedures along with the organisational 'muscles' that go with them. I fear we are still too wedded to the old ways and not learning fast enough."
Freuding: 'Everyone must learn it, everyone must be able to do it'
Lieutenant General Dr Christian Freuding told the RND news platform in an interview that basic training already includes an introductory course in operating drones.
"Everyone must learn it, everyone must be able to do it," said Freuding, emphasising that every soldier has to be a drone reconnaissance operator or a counter-drone specialist.
For the German armed forces, the challenge therefore lies not only in procurement but also in their ability to adapt and learn from current conflicts. How far the Bundeswehr is adjusting to the new form of warfare could be seen at this year's "Freedom Shield I" exercise in Lithuania: soldiers had to fly drones themselves and protect against them using improvised drone cages of their own design.
Kevin, a tank commander from Augustdorf-based Tank Battalion 203, told Euronews after the exercise that it was the first time he had flown a drone. Learning how it worked took three minutes, he said.

SHENZHEN, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Inside a flagship store of Chinese drone maker DJI in the city of Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, British visitor Annabel Grainger was busy taking photos of products to share with her friends back home.
"My friends wouldn't have seen anything like that before," she said.
A thriving tech hub, Shenzhen has emerged as a magnet for global tech aficionados. The city's wide range of high-tech products, including artificial intelligence (AI) glasses, AI 3D printers, AI robots, drones, and handheld gimbal cameras, have generated considerable buzz on international social media platforms such as Instagram and TikTok.
An average of nearly 8,000 foreign buyers visit Huaqiangbei, Shenzhen's mega electronics marketplace, each day this year. From January through July, sales of AI products surged more than 55 percent from a year earlier in this area. Industry insiders noted that a complete industrial chain and high-density industrial clusters have taken shape in Huaqiangbei's AI sector, covering the full spectrum from AI chip solutions and agent development to on-device model deployment and scenario testing.
These advantages, they said, have facilitated the deep integration of AI technologies into hardware products, while boosting production efficiency and significantly lowering costs.
"It takes several weeks to make a prototype in Europe, but it can be done in half a day in Shenzhen," Dutch engineer Henk Werner said.
"In Shenzhen, if you need to upgrade a product, you can pull together all your suppliers within a day and have a cooperation agreement inked by the evening," said Leng Xiaokun, founder of Leju Robotics, highlighting the city's core advantage in having a complete industrial chain.

In a bid to incentivize enterprises to double down on fundamental core technologies over the long haul, Nanshan District in the city, home to a vibrant tech ecosystem, has set up a seed fund and an angel fund totaling 500 million yuan (approximately 73.7 million U.S. dollars), aimed at offering lead investment support to early-stage ventures.
"Though the research and development of the fundamental components and algorithms of humanoid robots often yields no direct returns for several years, Shenzhen's patient capital provides a guarantee for technological breakthroughs," Leng noted.
Leveraging an international cooperation center based in the city's Longhua District, a host of advanced technology firms have successfully introduced their AI-powered intelligent computing terminals and other smart products and solutions to markets across North America and Southeast Asia.
Shenzhen has also jointly built cooperation platforms with ASEAN member states. The Shenzhen-Singapore cross-border data verification platform, now in trial operation, is designed to address challenges related to secure data flows in AI and other industries.
Adjacent to Hong Kong, Shenzhen was one of China's first special economic zones and has since evolved, over four decades, into a global hub for innovation and advanced manufacturing.
The number of AI enterprises in China had surpassed 6,000 last year, while the output value of the core AI industry was projected to exceed 1.2 trillion yuan during the same period, representing a year-on-year increase of almost 30 percent.
Moreover, China was home to more than 140 humanoid robot developers in 2025, with shipments reaching 14,400 units -- accounting for 84.7 percent of the global market, an industry research report said. ■

China to bolster IP protection in emerging fields including AI

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:44:20 CST
15:44:20 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- China will refine intellectual property (IP) rules for artificial intelligence (AI), algorithms and other emerging technologies, as part of a broader push to modernize its copyright regime for the digital economy.
This move forms part of the country's recently released 15th five-year plan for intellectual property protection and utilization, which maps out IP development priorities from 2026 to 2030.
According to the plan, China will refine IP protection rules for emerging fields and specific sectors, including algorithms, AI-generated content and platform-economy-related IP issues.
To support the development of new quality productive forces, China will strengthen copyright services and safeguards for new technologies and industries such as blockchain, big data, cloud computing and artificial intelligence, the plan said.
In recent years, Chinese films, TV series, web novels and video games have gained growing popularity overseas. Revenue from Chinese self-developed games in overseas markets surpassed 20 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, while the country's online literature has reached hundreds of millions of readers in more than 200 countries and regions.
The global expansion of these digital cultural products has heightened the need for stronger copyright safeguards. In the next five years, China will enhance copyright protection and transaction rules in fields like online publishing, online audiovisual services, and online literature and arts, the plan noted.
It will also improve its international IP protection system to achieve better dispute resolution and risk control, and create a case database of cross-border IP disputes, the plan said.
The country will step up IP cooperation through the World Intellectual Property Organization and other multilateral mechanisms, strengthen IP consultations with major trading partners, and help shape international IP rules and standards in emerging fields, the plan added.
The plan set the goal of making decisive progress in building China into an IP powerhouse by 2030, with its IP competitiveness ranking among the world's best by 2035. Another target is to raise the share of copyright industries' value added in GDP to 7.53 percent by 2030.
To this end, the plan urged high-quality development of copyright industries, better transformation and commercialization of copyrighted works, and stronger international promotion to bring more Chinese works to global audiences.
Via these measures, China aims to foster a more robust IP ecosystem that supports innovation and cultural creation, laying a solid foundation for high-quality development in the digital era. ■

"As business priorities evolve and operating conditions remain uncertain, hiring decisions are becoming more targeted, selective and closely aligned to areas that deliver the greatest value," Teo added. ■

Study finds strong genetic link between gut health, depression
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:44:14 CST
15:44:14 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have identified a strong genetic link between gut-related health conditions and depression, offering new insights into why physical illnesses often accompany the mental health condition.
Physical illnesses can contribute substantially to poor health outcomes in people with depression, who die up to 12 years earlier than those without the condition, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute.
The study, published in Nature Genetics, examined the genetic relationship between major depressive disorder and four groups of physical diseases: cardiovascular, metabolic, gastrointestinal and immune disorders.
While all four groups were genetically linked to depression, gastrointestinal diseases including irritable bowel syndrome, gastroesophageal reflux disease, gallstone disease and peptic ulcer disease showed the strongest association, the statement said.
Researchers found that genetic risk factors linked to these physical illnesses overlapped with almost half of those involved in depression.
Lead author and QIMR Berghofer PhD Student Damian Woodward, said the findings highlighted the importance of looking beyond the brain when treating depression.
"We found gastrointestinal diseases had the strongest shared genetic relationship with depression, confirming that the gut-brain axis plays a key role in why depression commonly occurs alongside physical illness," Woodward said.
"The gut is often referred to as the second brain, sharing many of the same signaling chemicals and containing a high number of nerve cells," Woodward said, adding that the study identified genetic factors affecting communication between the gut and brain that may contribute to depression, gut dysfunction and immune-related conditions.
Researchers hope the findings will help identify new treatment opportunities, including repurposing existing medications, and reduce the health burden associated with depression. ■

The move aims to improve ecosystems in the region, sustainably manage watersheds and mitigate climate change. It will also greatly assist local people in their agricultural activities and bring other benefits, the report said.
The designation will also help conserve forests and wildlife species, improve ecosystems, support the socio-economic development of local people, improve the climate, further develop agriculture and horticulture, and enhance the sustainability of village water sources, it added. ■

Netanyahu accused of ‘Criminal negligence,’ following bombshell report that the prime minister was warned about Oct. 7 attack plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:42:30 UTC
15:42:30 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- Lawmakers react to new bombshell report that Netanyahu was warned about Oct. 7 attack plans
Lawmakers react to new bombshell report that Netanyahu was warned about Oct. 7 attack plans
An extensive investigation reveals that UAE leaders warned Netanyahu that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major operation, yet the prime minister did not brief Israel's security chiefs
An investigation conducted for the new book "Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment," researched by Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval, reveals that UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on a secure line about ten days before October 7, 2023, and warned him for 45 minutes that Sinwar was planning a major operation against Israel. According to the report, bin Zayed feared the event would destabilize the region and threaten the Abraham Accords.
Netanyahu reportedly responded calmly, telling bin Zayed he believed Hamas intended to operate in the West Bank and that Israel was prepared for any scenario. None of Israel's security chiefs, including the heads of the Shin Bet and Mossad and the IDF chief of staff, were briefed on the warning, the investigation found.
The report traces the warning back to a secret Israel-Hamas channel, approved by Netanyahu, that had been negotiating a temporary truce and prisoner arrangement since early 2023. In September 2023, Sinwar abruptly cut off contact with the channel and told a Fatah intermediary, referred to as "Coal Eyes," to warn Israel he was preparing "the mother of all surprises," using the word "zilzal," or earthquake.
The warning was relayed to bin Zayed's adviser and eventually to Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar, who briefed Netanyahu by phone on September 15. A security meeting held two days later ended without a decision.
According to the investigation, Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel separately warned Netanyahu around the same time of "something unusual, a terrifying operation," while Netanyahu told him Israel's focus and forces were on the West Bank, not Gaza.
The investigation states that on October 1, Bar again recommended targeting senior Hamas officials including Sinwar, and Netanyahu replied, "Prepare plans for me and I will consider them," a response a senior defense official described as his standard way of postponing decisions. Throughout this period, the report says, Netanyahu never disclosed bin Zayed's warning to his security chiefs. A senior Shin Bet official told the authors that had the warning been shared, "it could have changed our entire assessment picture."
In response to the investigation, the prime minister's office said "Prime Minister Netanyahu didn't speak to the president of the UAE during the period in question and received no warning from him," calling the report "an absolute lie." Former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar and former IDF Chief of Staff Herzl Halevi said they were never informed of the warning attributed to bin Zayed.
The book's researchers reached out to bin Zayed for comment but did not receive one.

UK to announce a trade ban on Israeli West Bank goods

UK to sanction Israeli West Bank settlements in support for two-state solution
- The UK will ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank to support the two-state solution, despite Israeli and US criticism.
- The sanctions target mainly agricultural products and aim to oppose settlement expansions like the E1 project near Jerusalem.
- The move strains UK-Israel relations further, with concerns over enforcement difficulties and potential impacts on UK-US trade ties.
AI generated
LONDON/TEL AVIV – Britain will announce a trade ban on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank later on Sept 8, a senior minister said, the latest in a series of sanctions against Israel as it faces growing diplomatic isolation.
The US, through its ambassador to Israel, has already criticised the move, which London has framed as a sign of fresh support for the two-state solution, which Israel opposes.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog accused Britain of interfering in Israel’s upcoming elections, due in late October, while Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the British ambassador in Tel Aviv to be expelled.
Ed Miliband, who became Britain’s foreign minister in July, had flagged that he wanted to reset policy on Israel and will announce the trade sanctions later on Sept 8.
The impact on the £6 billion (S$10.28 billion) of annual bilateral trade is likely to be minimal, with details unclear of how the UK will differentiate between goods originating in West Bank settlements and products made in Israel.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, in office since July, discussed the Middle East in a call with US President Donald Trump on Sept 7, when he stressed “the importance of the two-state solution”, according to his office.
Opposition to E1 settlement plans
UN bodies and most governments, including Britain, consider Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal and regard the West Bank as territory under military occupation.
Israel says the territory is disputed rather than occupied, and asserts that Jews have a historical claim to the land.
The focus of recent concerns is Israel’s E1 settlement project in the West Bank not far from Jerusalem, which would cut across land the Palestinians seek for a future independent state.
Britain and other European nations criticised the E1 settlement plans in August, and UK work and pensions minister Pat McFadden said on Sept 8 the rate of settlement activity made the need for sanctions urgent.
By moving ahead with sanctions, Burnham’s government is sticking with the policy direction of his Labour Party predecessor, Keir Starmer.
Under Starmer, Britain in 2025 joined other countries to recognise a Palestinian state as a means to promote a two-state solution, and in June it sanctioned Israeli networks involved in financing, enabling and carrying out violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
While several Labour lawmakers welcomed Miliband’s move, one described the ban as not going far enough for some and going too far for others, especially those with large numbers of Jewish voters in their constituencies.
Souring relations
Israel-UK relations have become increasingly strained in recent years with London criticising Israel’s conduct in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank and rising settler attacks on Palestinians.
President Herzog, whose role is largely ceremonial, said the sanctions would be a “grave miscalculation” that would fall on the “wrong side of history”.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee told the BBC that the sanctions amounted to “discrimination against the Jewish people”.
He warned they could potentially limit the UK’s ability to do business in some US states that prohibit companies that boycott Israel from being eligible for state government contracts, procurement or public investment.
McFadden said Israel would remain an important trading partner for the UK.
Goods originating from settlements are mainly agricultural, including fresh produce and wine, and make up only a tiny fraction of Israel’s total trade flows.
The Israeli prime minister’s office and foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Foreign diplomats say an import ban could be difficult to enforce as some goods from Israel may use products from settlements without identifying their origin.
Spain, Ireland and the Netherlands have each moved to ban imports of goods originating in Israeli settlements in the West Bank, though not all the bans have come into effect.
Other countries including France, Canada and Norway also issued sanctions in 2026 targeting settlements. Finance Minister Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir have been sanctioned by some countries, including the UK. REUTERS

Rail giant and subsidiaries of Malaysian engineering firm Gamuda Berhad win bid as joint venture, in deal reportedly worth A$880 million
The company said on Tuesday that it and its two partners – both subsidiaries of Malaysian engineering firm and developer Gamuda Berhad – won the bid as the joint-venture Riverside Link Consortium, with Australian media reporting the deal to be worth about A$880 million (US$635 million).
The deal is a major part of the Sydney Metro West project in New South Wales.
It will be key to the growth and development of Parramatta, a commercial and financial centre located 24km (15 miles) west of Sydney and regarded as the city’s second central business district.
“The project provides an opportunity for the MTR Corp to apply our experience in integrating transport infrastructure with residential, commercial and community development opportunities to create well-connected, vibrant and people-focused urban precincts,” David Tang Chi-fai, the rail giant’s managing director for property and international business, said.
The joint venture will be responsible for designing and building the Parramatta metro station by 2032. The facility is expected to cut train travel times from Parramatta to Sydney’s city centre to about 20 minutes.
The development also covers offices, retail and residential properties at and around the new station, which will be completed in stages following the opening of the railway.

eBay to investigate how banned gender-test kits were sold in India — report
US e-commerce platform eBay is conducting an internal review of its platform's safeguards after news agency Reuters found that several gender-prediction kits were listed for delivery to India. New Delhi has banned the use of such kits under a law aimed at preventing sex-selective abortion.
Reuters identified nine listings, including kits from brands SneakPeek and Peekaboo, which were being offered by third-party sellers with shipping to India. The platform removed the listings after being notified last week.
"These listings violated local regulations and eBay's policies, and we are reviewing these controls, including the relevant shipping and checkout experience, to determine whether further enhancements are appropriate," eBay told Reuters in a statement.
"eBay has controls in place intended to prevent certain gender-prediction products from being visible in India," it added.
While eBay does not have a dedicated Indian shopping site, the company does ship to India, functioning purely as a marketplace for third-party sellers.
India has a strict prenatal gender determination law dating back to 1994, which followed a steep decline in the ratio of girls born after ultrasound technology spread. With patrilineal inheritance being the norm, people misused the technology to abort female fetuses.
Under the law, violations carry prison terms of up to three years, with repeat offenses being hit with harsher penalties.
Separately, India's Health Ministry has pressed Google to remove search results linking to Peekaboo's website, according to notices reviewed by the news agency.
 
Manipur singer killed after confronting group drinking outside Delhi home
A group of men has been apprehended for beating Manipuri musician Chongtham Vikram Singh to death outside his apartment in Southeast Delhi, local media reported.
The 54-year-old lived in Kilokari village, where he was allegedly assaulted by a group of delivery workers and local eatery staff after he confronted them for drinking and creating a nuisance outside his residence, police said.
Seven people have been arrested, and a juvenile has been detained in relation to the assault.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi slammed local authorities and Home Minister Amit Shah, raising concerns over the safety of people from the northeastern states of India in Delhi.
"A father, killed outside his own home, in his own country's capital. After many such incidents, every Northeast family in Delhi is asking the same question today - are we safe here?" he wrote on X.
Chief Minister of Manipur, N Biren Singh, also offered condolences to his family, urging Delhi Police to take swift action on the matter. He also shared CCTV footage that claimed to show the accused heading downstairs after assaulting Singh.
The incident has raised concerns among New Delhi's Northeast community. The area that comes under the Sunlight Colony police station is known to have a sizeable population from the region, the Telegraph newspaper reported. In 2023, a group of men assaulted a Manipuri family in the area.
Iran hails 'civilizational' relationship with India ahead of BRICS summit
Iran highlighted its "long-standing, historic and civilizational relationship" with India ahead of President Masoud Pezeshkian's visit to New Delhi for the upcoming BRICS summit.
Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei emphasized the importance Tehran places on its ties with New Delhi during a press conference.
He highlighted President Pezeshkian's bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, to reaffirm Iran's plans to engage diplomatically with India to deepen economic collaboration.

The 18th BRICS summit will be held from September 12 to 13 at the Bharat Mandapam convention center in the Indian capital.
BAPS apologizes over Eiffel Tower row, denies preventing access
A Hindu religious group has apologized after the Eiffel Tower in Paris, France, was closed on Monday after staff went on strike to protest the exclusion of female workers during a visit by the organization.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), however, reiterated that their tour was pre-coordinated with the tower's team, adding that no person was denied access. BAPS also offered apologies to anyone hurt or inconvenienced.
"We understand the concerns raised and take them very seriously. Given the size of our delegation, the visit was organised in coordination with the Eiffel Tower team at the beginning of normal opening hours to minimise any inconvenience to other visitors," BAPS said in a statement on social media.
"To our knowledge, at no point was anyone denied access to the Eiffel Tower. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise to anyone who may have been hurt or inconvenienced by this situation," the statement added.
Around 100 men from BAPS were visiting the landmark. The company that operates the Tower, SETE, said that the group had requested a visit as part of which the "interactions with women" would be limited.
SETE accepted that the decision was a mistake: "These conditions should not have been accepted."
On Sunday, BAPS conducted the consecration ceremony of France’s first traditional Hindu temple in Bussy-Saint-Georges, near Paris.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi virtually addressed the inauguration gathering, adding that "India and France’s relations have reached new heights."

ynet has learned that Gvili is expected to be placed at No. 9 and Medan at No. 11.

Europe must take responsibility for protecting its southern border, Prime Minister Bart De Wever (Flemish nationalist N-VA) insisted, following a meeting with his Italian counterpart, Giorgia Meloni, in Rome. He thanked Meloni in Italian for the warm welcome.
PM De Wever calls for ‘credible migrant return policy’, has a go in Italian (VIDEO)
At the European level, De Wever and Meloni often champion the same position together – for example, on tackling economic problems and migration. The war in Ukraine was also discussed during their talks in the eternal city.
“I fully understand that we must strengthen Europe’s southern border. We talk a lot about the eastern border and the threats there, but we must not forget that we have a southern border, a border on the Mediterranean. Europe must take responsibility for securing that border,” said De Wever.
European Migration Pact
De Wever met Meloni following a summer in which, unexpectedly, tens of thousands of people from Morocco stormed the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in the continent of Africa. Italy promptly introduced border controls for travellers from Spain, a measure that was extended again last week for a further 15 days.
Meloni also made a case for better protection of the external borders. “I remain firmly convinced that the Schengen area can only be maintained if the Union’s external borders are protected and if everyone plays their part in the fight against people smugglers,” she said.
De Wever also called for the full roll-out of the new European migration pact, including a stronger return policy. “Only with a credible return policy can we make European migration policy a success,” argued the Belgian leader.
Geopolitical instability
De Wever’s Flemish nationalist N-VA and Meloni’s Fratelli d’Italia party form part of the same political group (ECR) in the European Parliament, and the two politicians are also “comrades-in-arms” in the European Council, according to De Wever. The Prime Minister praised Meloni’s “leadership” and the “excellent” bilateral relations with Italy. The fact that he did so in Italian earned him a round of applause from his hostess.
Belgium and Italy are on the same wavelength not only on the issue of migration. According to De Wever, both countries are also fighting the same battle to strengthen European competitiveness and combat high energy prices that are hampering European industry. The Prime Minister also expressed his appreciation for the cooperation in the fight against organised crime.
On the geopolitical front, according to De Wever, both countries hope for a swift end to the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. “We believe we must make greater diplomatic efforts to bring an end to the conflict on our own continent,” said the Prime Minister.
Geopolitical instability has led to rising defence budgets and rearmament programmes across Europe. Belgium and Italy also wish to join forces in this area. “Greater cooperation is on the agenda, and we are very keen to do more with Italian industry,” the Prime Minister added.

Bridge between Russia and North Korea opens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:35:43 UTC
15:35:43 KST

The first bridge connecting Russia and North Korea has opened across the Tumen River, allowing for easier movement of goods and passengers between the two countries, but Ukraine has warned that it is being built as a corridor for military purposes, writes the BBC.
North Korean state media has announced that the bridge will be used for personnel exchanges, tourism and trade. Meanwhile, the Ukrainian human rights group Truth Hounds has indicated that the bridge is intended primarily for the creation of a secret military logistics corridor.
Relations between Russia and North Korea have become closer since the start of a full-scale war in Ukraine, and Russian dictator Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un have previously spoken of their determination to help each other if either country is attacked by military aggression.
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin described the bridge as a new symbol of friendship, while North Korean Prime Minister Pak Thae Song said the opening of the bridge was a historic event. Russian state media
TASS reported that up to 300 vehicles and 2,323 people can cross the bridge each day.
The BBC reported in May that satellite images showed the kilometre-long bridge with several new access roads, a border checkpoint, surrounding infrastructure and parking lots.
There are air links between Russia and North Korea, as well as a railway, but the only land route until now has been planks placed on the railway tracks, allowing cars to cross. Reuters reported that the Russian government had planned to use the bridge for freight transport only for now, with passenger traffic to be opened later.
Mishustin said the bridge would allow for further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation. The most immediate impact is likely to be increased arms exports from North Korea to Russia. Researchers at South Korea’s spy agency estimate that North Korea has already shipped 7 billion to 14 billion dollars worth of missiles and artillery shells to Russia by sea. It is believed that around 11,000 North Koreans are currently actively fighting in Ukraine.
Truth Hounds recently reported that, under a cooperation agreement signed in 2024,
the bridge could be used to transport North Korean soldiers, construction workers and high-ranking military personnel
to Russia, while Russia would be able to more quickly transport technology and resources to North Korea.
Construction of the bridge began in 2025 and took 495 days to complete.
Since it was authorized in 2024, Russian tourists have been flocking to North Korea. They are welcomed in the capital Pyongyang and the beach resorts of Wonsan-Kalma, while tourists from other countries are not allowed to visit the communist country.
The bridge will allow for the expansion of the flow of North Korean workers into Russia. South Korea estimates that around 10,000 North Koreans work on Russian construction sites and in logging. Although the UN prohibits countries from using North Korean labor, many North Koreans come to Russia on student visas.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday she hoped US negotiators who visited Kyiv over the weekend had seen for themselves that Russia is not genuinely interested in ending its war against Ukraine.
“I’m happy to see that for the first time the special envoys have also visited Kyiv,” Kallas told reporters in Vilnius. “What it meant for the Ukrainians was three days without bombing of civilians. I think that’s the positive side of this visit.”
“I hope that they also heard what the situation on the ground is and Ukrainians also showed them that Russia is not really interested in peace – the opposite,” she said.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over the weekend in a renewed effort to end the fighting.
Moscow and Kyiv agreed to suspend strikes while the negotiations were taking place.
Witkoff on Monday praised the weekend discussions in Moscow and Kyiv and suggested they could lead to a schedule for new three-way peace talks. The Kremlin also said Monday that it had not ruled out three-way negotiations involving the United States and Ukraine.
The talks remain complicated by disagreements over Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, parts of which Russia does not control but which Moscow has demanded as part of a potential peace settlement.
Kallas said Europe cannot serve as a neutral mediator between Russia and Ukraine because it is directly affected by the conflict.
“In the end, when there is going to be a peace agreement, there are also a lot of asks for Europe to be very clear that these are not some things that we are giving without getting anything in return,” she said.
Kallas warns of growing Russian threat
During her visit to Vilnius, Kallas also warned that political parties in Europe that downplay the threat posed by Russia are gaining support.
Her comments followed an election victory by Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, in a state election Sunday.
Following a meeting with Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, Kallas said sabotage and other security threats were moving closer to Europe.
“At the same time, the parties that are sort of blind to this threat and say that we should not do anything with this because it’s not our concern, are gaining ground,” she said.
“I’m just afraid that we might wake up in a situation where we haven’t done enough to be able to deter the threats and defend ourselves,” Kallas added. “But of course it’s up to the German people, as a democratic country, to make their choices.”
Sinkevičius said victories by far-right parties should serve as a warning to mainstream political forces that they are failing to meet voters’ expectations adequately.
“I would hope that such cases do not recur and that this does not become a new trend across European countries,” he said.
But he said the AfD’s victory in one German state would not affect relations between Germany and Lithuania.
“Germany has remained and will remain Lithuania’s most important strategic partner,” Sinkevičius said.

One campaign, two realities: Adidas features former Israeli soldier as Gaza amputees struggle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:31:54 UTC
15:31:54 KST

For Palestinian amputees in Gaza, an Adidas campaign featuring a former Israeli soldier who lost a leg has come to embody two starkly different realities.
Former Israeli soldier Shalev Biton appeared in a local campaign promoting Adidas’ “Single Shoe” service, designed for amputees and others who need only one shoe.
In Gaza, meanwhile, thousands of Palestinians who lost limbs in brutal Israeli attacks continue to struggle to obtain basic prosthetics, replacement parts and rehabilitation.
The contrast has angered amputees in the enclave, who question why a former Israeli soldier was chosen for such a campaign while their own needs remain largely unmet due to the Israeli blockade despite a ceasefire deal.
‘How can Adidas do this?
Omar Haliwa, 14, lost his leg in an Israeli strike while on his way to collect water. Several relatives who were with him were also killed.
“How can Adidas bring an Israeli soldier and put him in an advertisement while we, the wounded of the war in Gaza, are suffering so much?” Haliwa says.
He said losing his leg changed his life completely, while attempts to obtain a suitable prosthetic repeatedly ran into shortages of raw materials at Gaza’s prosthetics centres.
For Haliwa, seeing a former Israeli soldier receive services tailored to amputees while Palestinians struggle to obtain basic prosthetic limbs was painful.
He urged Adidas to pay attention to Palestinian children and young people who have lost limbs in Israeli attacks.
‘We have nothing’
Kifah al Fakhouri, who lost her leg in an Israeli strike on a seaside cafe in Gaza City, said she was shocked by the campaign.
“I would have liked Adidas to pay attention to the needs of the people of Gaza and Palestine, because we have thousands of amputees,” she says.
“This soldier lost his leg in 2021 and now has a prosthetic limb and resources. We in Gaza have nothing — no treatment, no equipment, no supplies.”
Fakhouri said prosthetic limbs available in Gaza often fail to meet patients’ needs, with some too heavy or unsuitable for everyday use.
Amputees need modern joints, replacement parts and better prosthetics to regain mobility, she said, adding that losing her leg affected her work, movement and virtually every aspect of daily life.
Ahmed Jawadi al Balawi, another Palestinian who lost a leg during the war, said his prosthetic had already worn out and needed maintenance and replacement parts.
“Look at us with mercy,” he said.
“They do not need help the way we do. They have resources. We have nothing. We make something out of nothing.”
Balawi said many amputees in Gaza are forced to use old or poorly fitting prosthetics and struggle to find shoes and accessories compatible with them.
Nabil Abdullah Mahmoud Ibrahim lost his leg when an Israeli drone struck him while he was playing football with other children at a school sheltering displaced Palestinians in northern Gaza.
“Shouldn’t Adidas support Gaza, when so many people here have lost limbs?” he asked.
He said Palestinians with amputations should receive the same support and opportunities available to others living with similar injuries.
More than 8,000 amputees in Gaza
Munir al Barsh, director-general of the health ministry in Gaza, said estimates indicate that more than 8,000 Palestinians have lost limbs during Israel’s genocide in Gaza, including more than 3,000 children.
He said Gaza has trained specialists capable of producing and fitting prosthetic limbs, but restrictions on the entry of raw materials and medical supplies have prevented many patients from receiving suitable prosthetics.
“The priority should be the Palestinian child who has lost a leg or an arm and needs rehabilitation,” Barsh said.
He urged international organisations and global companies to support Palestinian amputees and help provide prosthetics and rehabilitation equipment.
Boycott calls
The controversy intensified after images from the campaign spread widely online, with pro-Palestinian users contrasting Biton’s access to prosthetics and specialised services with the conditions facing thousands of amputees in Gaza.
Israel’s Channel 15 said posts about the campaign drew millions of views, while calls to boycott Adidas spread across social media.
Amid the backlash, Adidas Arabia, the sportswear company’s regional Middle East social media account, issued an apology over the campaign, saying an image used in a recent local activation had raised “concerns and strong reactions.”
“It was never our intent to cause offence, and we apologise for anyone affected,” the statement said, stressing that the promotion was a local initiative rather than part of a global campaign.
Adidas Arabia also said the company would continue to “listen, learn and work” to ensure its actions reflected its stated inclusive values.
For Gaza’s amputees, however, the controversy exposed a gulf that went far beyond a single advertisement.
One campaign had put an amputee in the spotlight. Thousands of others in Gaza were still waiting for the chance to walk again.
Israeli occupation forces have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and wounded over 174,000 in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza that has destroyed or damaged much of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure since October 2023.

Germany news: Gas reserves historically low ahead of winter
