====================================================================================================

‘So big and so close’: going on a bear hunt in northern Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:00:28 UTC
15:00:28 KST

Once upon a time, in the woods outside Pola de Somiedo, lived a family of Cantabrian brown bears. The villagers reported sightings of a mother bear who had lost a leg to a hunter’s trap, her two cubs and two adult males, either of which might have been the father. In those days, at the end of the 1980s, they seemed to be the last of their kind in this part of Asturias. Meanwhile, the wider population dropped to about 60 bears across the surrounding Cantabrian mountain range that gave the species its name.
They have since clawed their way back from the edge of extinction here in northern Spain, and nature guide Luis Frechilla believes their numbers may now be upwards of 500 again. “They’re still classed as endangered,” he tells me, until the official count hits 1,000. But relative abundance makes them much easier to see today in Somiedo natural park – one of Spain’s first such protected areas, established in 1988.
Setting his scope on a tripod in a steep-angled pasture, Frechilla spots a bear almost as soon as we start looking. A juvenile, apparently, which means the animal is old enough to be foraging alone, but it’s still too small, and too far away, for him to tell if it’s a male or female. Another bear-spotter standing near us seems more willing to take a guess.
“Ooh, look at his little ears,” she says delightedly, beaming behind binoculars. No expert myself, I watch that distant fuzzy shape move across the viewfinder and along the sharp ridges opposite, blinking in and out of sight like a cursor on the trend line of a graph. I’m not sure that we are close enough to call this an encounter, but it is an experience.
The sun drops behind the peaks; the birds sing a dusk chorus in the birches and oaks; cowbells ring through the valley from the dairy herds that help this region of so-called “Green Spain” look and sound like the Swiss Alps. It gets cold at night up here, and it’s been known to snow in summer, though my own visit in late spring sees the mountaintops looking whiter than anyone around here can remember so deep into May.
That weather, and the sheer calorific spend of living and working at a median altitude of 1,300 metres, has made the traditional cuisine much sturdier here than elsewhere in Spain.
Down at the village inn, Casa Miño, we share a bottle of regional cider and a cachopo (beef fillet topped with serrano ham, peppers and goat cheese, and pounded into a single solid unit the size of a solar panel). I want fabada, too, the famous Asturian stew of white beans, pork belly and blood sausage. Frechilla says it’s a winter dish, customarily eaten for lunch – too heavy for the body to process later in the day. But I would order fabada at midnight in a heatwave, and keep eating it even while they loaded me into the ambulance.
The bears, meanwhile, don’t have much to feed on at the moment. They only woke from hibernation a few weeks ago, explains Alicia Madrid the next day, on a forest trail above the century-old hydroelectric power station at La Malva. A biologist with the conservation group Fundación Oso Pardo, Madrid tells me that Cantabrian bears don’t hibernate as long or deeply as other brown bears and are generally smaller and lighter than American grizzlies.
“They’re adapted to this terrain, and they can’t be too heavy because they have to climb a lot,” she says. Their paw prints in the mud look big enough to me, and the bite marks where they chewed clumps of long grasses, and the hairs shed where they scratched their backs against trees. Madrid shows us, too, the hefty rocks they overturned looking for insects. Further into the summer, there’ll be plenty of berries, acorns, chestnuts and maybe some meaty carrion to fatten them up.
The foundation has played a major role in the regrowth of bear populations, building bio-corridors with strategic placements of trees and bushes full of all the things they like to eat. Another key factor is the hunting ban, introduced in 1973. The trick now, says Madrid, is coaxing isolated cohorts to breed with other groups and boost genetic diversity.
Also: managing the tourists who come to see them, and balancing ecological imperatives against financial incentives. Later, after a long hike through the Valley of the Lake to reach the aptly named Lake of the Valley, I overhear Frechilla fielding the related concerns of two local women. Against a backdrop of blue sky, bright wildflowers and silver waters, the women seem to argue that conservation efforts amount to commercial exploitation. Frechilla gently insists that Somiedo natural park is a model of good practice in Spain. Much of the bears’ territory is closed to the public, and spotting expeditions are only permitted in the company of licensed guides. Nature tourism, he says, keeps villagers in jobs where farming culture cannot, and is proving vastly more sustainable than hunting bears for sport. As for protecting humans, there has been only one bear attack in recent memory, on an elderly lady whose evening stroll led her between a mother and cubs. She survived.
For now, at least, most residents seem willing to share the bears with outsiders. That evening, a small crowd gather by the side of a winding back road near Saliencia, some sitting comfortably on camping chairs with spotting scopes in their hands. Everyone is watching a large male bear – so big and so close that they don’t need the viewing equipment – as he lopes across a meadow to take a quick splash in the river. Another male is spotted in the treeline above, and the two circle each other at a distance for a while. There is some speculation that they might fight for this turf, and a man with two leashed greyhounds seems ready to take bets on it. Frechilla shakes his head.
“Maybe later in the season, when they’ve gained enough weight.”
These bears are doing better now, but it’s still a tough life. The reality of their ongoing baby boom is that only 30% of juveniles will survive on their own, after a year of maternal supervision. This is surely why I find it so moving when we follow reports of another sighting in the twilight: a mother and her two young cubs have been seen climbing a slope called El Diente, or “The Tooth”.
It’s getting dark and cold, but we can see them through the scopes, about a mile away from us across the high mountain pass at La Peral. I watch the mother bear waiting and cajoling as needed while the siblings struggle up the vertical planes of rock like toddlers trying to climb a baby gate. On the ridgeline, they turn to silhouettes, play-fighting against a white sky.
They disappear over the far side, but then a little one comes back, seeming to wave goodbye with both front paws in the air. I remember a story I read to my daughter once, which put a poignant time limit on the usual fairytale ending: “And they all lived happily together, for as long as they could.”
The trip was provided by the Spanish Tourist Office, Turismo Asturias and Casa Miño in Pola de Somiedo. Bear-spotting tours with nature guide Luis Frechilla can be organised through Wild Spain Travel. For more information on the Cantabrian brown bear and related conservation efforts, visit Fundación Oso Pardo

China targets fourfold boost in AI computing capacity by 2030 in major tech push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:00:20 UTC
15:00:20 KST

China targets fourfold boost in AI computing capacity by 2030 in major tech push
The nation’s intelligent computing capacity hit 2,185 eflops at the end of June, up 177 per cent from a year earlier, according to MIIT
China plans to deploy artificial intelligence computing clusters containing 100,000 accelerator cards and sharply expand the country’s intelligent computing capacity over the next five years, as Beijing steps up investment in the infrastructure underpinning its AI ambitions.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), in a five-year industry plan released on Monday, set a target of 9,800 eflops of intelligent computing capacity by 2030, and called for 3.8 trillion yuan (US$532 billion) in cumulative information infrastructure investment over the 2026-2030 period.
The plan calls for the “orderly deployment” of intelligent computing clusters with 10,000 graphics processing cards or those using 100,000 or more cards, alongside inference computing facilities tailored to different applications. It also calls for greater efforts to adapt infrastructure to home-grown computing chips.
The targets extend a rapid expansion already under way. China’s intelligent computing capacity had reached 2,185 eflops – short for exa floating-point operations per second – by the end of June, up 177 per cent from a year earlier, and the country had built 52 intelligent computing facilities each equipped with more than 10,000 accelerator cards, according to MIIT.
That means China would need to more than quadruple the June level to reach the 2030 target. By the end of July, capacity had already risen to about 2,450 eflops, according to the National Data Administration, an agency overseen by the National Development and Reform Commission.
The expansion builds on the “East Data, West Computing” project launched in 2022, which seeks to shift power-intensive computing workloads from densely populated eastern regions towards western areas with cheaper land and abundant energy. China has since formed a network centred on eight national computing hubs, 10 data-centre clusters and three regions focused on coordinating computing facilities with power supplies.

Australia proposes hefty fines for big tech over duty to protect young users
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:57:10 UTC
14:57:10 KST

Social media giants face US$78 million fines if they fail to protect young users from harmful content, Australia's prime minister said on Tuesday as he unveiled draft laws reining in big tech.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese released draft laws that would place a "duty of care" on the firms behind popular platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and Instagram.
Social media companies would be held responsible for protecting under-18s from pornography, online bullying, content that glorified crime, and content that encouraged eating disorders.
"We took action because the community said 'enough is enough'," Albanese told reporters.
"We would no longer let Australian kids be treated as commodities instead of children."
Social media firms face mounting scrutiny over their use of allegedly addictive algorithms and stand accused of directing users to extreme content to keep them scrolling.
The draft laws build on Australia's world-first social media ban for under-16s, which came into effect late last year.
Companies found to be flouting their "duty of care" could be fined up to Aus$109 million ($78 million), Albanese said.
The legislation includes a requirement that platforms allow users to "opt out" of powerful algorithms that determine what comes up on social media feeds.
"This will give Australians greater choice over their platforms and what they see," Albanese said.
It would require firms like Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said big tech was facing a "reckoning".
"Their platforms and tools have infiltrated our daily lives in ways that we could never have imagined," she told reporters on Tuesday.
"Some good, but some with terrible consequences."
Data last month found that under-16s in Australia were increasing their use of social media apps such as Instagram and TikTok despite the ban.
The draft laws would be introduced to parliament later this year after consultation with social media companies, industry bodies and civil society groups.

The monastery was built during the Middle Ages. (AA Photo)
The rock-cut Çukurayva Monastery in the eastern province of Kars’ Kağızman district bridges the Middle Ages and the modern era through its remarkably preserved architecture.
Located near Çukurayva village, about 1.5 kilometers west of the village, the monastery draws attention with its main church, chapels and living spaces carved directly into the rock.
The monastery, dated to the 10th century based on its plan, architectural features and decoration, centers on a cross-shaped church.
The main church and two chapels accessible from its northern section are covered by domes supported by squinches. The structure also stands out for its cross motifs painted with red ochre.
Kafkas University academic Associate Professor Muhammet Arslan told state-run Anadolu Agency that the monastery was built during the Middle Ages.
Arslan said the exact construction date of the monastery is unknown, adding that it is dated to the 10th century based on its plan, architectural features and decoration.
Pointing to motifs made with ochre inside the monastery, Arslan said: ”The main structure of the monastery is a church, and we should emphasize that it is a rock-cut church. It was built in a cross-shaped plan and covered with a dome supported by squinches. One of the elements that makes this place special is the cross motif painted with red ochre at the center of the dome.”
”There are also two chapels accessed from the northern arm of the cross-shaped plan. The chapels were built on a square plan and are each covered with a dome supported by squinches.
As in the dome of the main church, we can also see similar cross motifs painted with ochre at the center of the chapels’ domes,” he added.
Call for archaeological work around monastery
Harun Ağdaş, head of the Kağızman Mountaineering and Outdoor Sports Club, said the monastery is highly important for the region and that they occasionally organize hikes to the site.
Ağdaş called for archaeological work to be carried out around the monastery.
Visitor Sergül Keskin also highlighted the monastery’s importance for regional tourism. ”It is a cave worth seeing. We invite all nature lovers and visitors interested in history to come here,” she said.

Türkiye’s museums, heritage sites draw nearly 66 million visitors in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:54:01 UTC
14:54:01 KST

Türkiye’s museums and archaeological sites attracted nearly 66 million visitors in 2025, according to the latest cultural heritage statistics released by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK).
The number of museum and archaeological site visits rose 6.8 percent year-on-year to 65.86 million. More than half of all visitors, 52.9 percent, visited museums and sites operated by the Culture and Tourism Ministry, while private museums accounted for 21.9 million visits, up 10.8 percent from the previous year.
The country had 664 museums in 2025. Of these, 220 were operated by the ministry, 426 were private museums and 18 were managed by the Presidency of National Palaces. Türkiye also had 148 archaeological and historical sites open to visitors.
Among provinces, Istanbul remained by far the country’s leading museum destination, recording 18.3 million visits. İzmir followed with 4.65 million and Ankara with 4.64 million.
The figures underline the continued popularity of some of Türkiye’s best-known cultural attractions. Istanbul’s Topkapı Palace, Hagia Sophia, Galata Tower and Dolmabahçe Palace, as well as major archaeological destinations such as Ephesus in İzmir and Hierapolis-Pamukkale in Denizli, have consistently ranked among the country’s most visited heritage attractions in recent years.
The country’s museums housed more than 4 million artifacts in 2025, with coins making up the largest category.
Interest in museums was also reflected in the sale of 6.8 million Museum Cards, which provide access to participating museums and archaeological sites.
Beyond museums, Türkiye recorded 130,632 registered immovable cultural heritage assets. Istanbul had the highest number, with 34,558 registered assets, followed by İzmir and Muğla.
The statistics also point to the scale of Türkiye’s protected natural heritage. The number of national parks increased to 50, covering nearly 942,300 hectares, while the number of nature parks reached 274. The country also had 32 nature conservation areas and 111 natural monuments.

The Finnish Border Guard marked the completion of the barrier at the Nuijamaa border crossing in southeastern Finland on Monday, capping a project conceived after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine reshaped the Nordic country’s security policy.

“The state’s most important duty is to see to the safety of its nationals,” Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said at the event.
“The eastern border fence is a necessary part of an effective border surveillance system in these unpredictable times,” she added.
The fence covers selected sections of Finland’s 1,340-kilometer frontier with Russia – the longest border Russia shares with any EU or NATO member.
Rantanen said Finland could eventually extend the barrier and called for additional EU funding to help eastern member states strengthen their borders.
The 200-kilometer barrier consists of dozens of separate sections concentrated in areas deemed most vulnerable.
The system includes a 4.5-meter-high fence, technical surveillance equipment, patrol roads and a 25-meter-wide cleared strip along the frontier. The project cost €356 million.
What to Make of Witkoff and Kushner’s Return to Russia-Ukraine Peace Talks
                                                                                                                                                                         
From non-alignment to NATO
Finnish political parties agreed in October 2022 on the need to build a partial fence along the Russian frontier, months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Pilot sections were built in 2023, with large-scale construction beginning in 2024.
The decision came amid a historic shift in Finland’s security policy. The country joined NATO in April 2023, ending decades of military non-alignment in response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The fence took on added importance after Helsinki accused Russia of facilitating the movement of migrants toward its border in late 2023 as a form of hybrid pressure.
Around 1,000 asylum seekers from third countries arrived at the frontier from Russia that autumn, prompting Helsinki to progressively shut its eastern border crossings before closing them all in December.
Russia denied orchestrating the influx.
Border crossings to remain shut
Rantanen said on Monday the crossings would remain closed, citing the continuing war in Ukraine and concerns over Moscow’s hybrid operations.
“The border crossings with Russia will not be opened because the security situation related to the military attack on Ukraine and hybrid operations has not changed,” she said.
The fence is part of a broader push by Finland to bolster its preparedness amid heightened security concerns over Russia.
Last week, more than 2,000 people took part in a two-day drill in the central city of Kuopio, billed as Europe’s largest civil defense exercise since the end of World War II.
The drill tested how authorities and civilians would respond to cyberattacks, disruptions to electricity and water supplies, and the threat of missile strikes from Russia.

Turning crisis into an opportunity to work better
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:52:29 UTC
14:52:29 KST

By Signe Bāliņa, President of the Latvian Information and Communications Technology Association (LIKTA).
We have become accustomed to using the e-services provided by the state and municipalities in our everyday lives. They are practical and convenient, which is why we become frustrated when one of them is temporarily unavailable or when a long-promised digital service takes too long to implement. The governance crisis that has emerged in Latvia’s public information and communication technology (ICT) sector provides a timely opportunity to improve cooperation between the public and private sectors on ICT projects that matter to society, modernise governance in the sector, and strengthen project management.
There is no doubt that Latvia’s ICT sector is a source of national pride. Its annual turnover amounts to €5.8 billion, and it is the country’s fourth-largest taxpayer. Public-sector procurement accounts for only 5% of the industry’s total turnover, yet the consequences of shortcomings in public ICT projects are felt across society. In the view of the Latvian Information and Communications Technology Association (LIKTA), efforts should currently focus on three areas: strengthening the competence of contracting authorities, reinforcing a unified national digital architecture, and modernising the public procurement system and its requirements.
When working on public-sector projects, LIKTA members regularly encounter weak ICT project management on the contracting authority’s side. This means that organisational leaders often struggle to maintain control over projects and remove obstacles that arise during implementation. ICT projects are also frequently implemented in isolation from other organisational processes and from the broader needs of Latvia’s e-government ecosystem.
In our view, Latvia should adopt best practices from other EU Member States and organise public-sector ICT projects in the same way as the private sector does. An ICT project should address the needs of the organisation as a whole, including change management. The objectives of the ICT system should be defined in advance, together with its total cost of ownership (TCO) and the expected efficiency gains. Each project should have a clearly designated business owner with the authority to make decisions, remove obstacles and take responsibility for measurable results. Finally, before launching a procurement procedure, a feasibility assessment should be carried out. This should include dialogue between the contracting authority and the industry, examining comparable examples, assessing similar systems already available on the market, and evaluating whether developing a new system is justified.
Second, all stakeholders should focus on developing public e-services as part of a unified digital platform. This is not currently the case: approximately 1,000 different state information systems are used across Latvia’s public sector. Those responsible for individual systems often do not see how their system fits into the country’s broader ICT architecture.
LIKTA therefore proposes considering the establishment of an empowered and competent national ICT council capable of prioritising projects and assessing their compliance with the overall national ICT architecture. This would help ensure interoperability between systems and prevent inefficient use of resources. At the same time, knowledge and expertise should be concentrated in competence centres to ensure professional project management and consistency of ICT architecture across the public sector.
An excellent example of such knowledge consolidation is the ICT Governance Leaders’ Forum organised by the Ministry of Smart Administration and Regional Development (VARAM). Good examples from other sectors include the services provided by State Real Estate (VAS “Valsts nekustamie īpašumi”) in organising construction procurement and managing projects, as well as the technical specification standards for road construction and maintenance maintained by Latvian State Roads (VAS “Latvijas Valsts ceļi”).
Together, these measures would move us closer to a situation in which every solution forms part of a centrally managed ICT portfolio, with clear accountability, measurable KPIs and regular reporting throughout its entire lifecycle.
Third, Latvia should significantly modernise its approach to public-sector procurement. LIKTA has prepared a range of proposals covering various aspects of procurement, including the assessment of bidders’ qualifications. Most importantly, high-quality tender evaluation criteria should ensure that contracts are awarded to bidders capable of providing higher-quality services and delivering the outcomes intended by the contracting authority.
For example, the State Revenue Service already includes a practical assignment in its procurement documentation, where the level of detail demonstrated in completing the task and the assessment of the required workload form part of the evaluation of the most economically advantageous tender. LIKTA proposes making such assignments a binding reference standard throughout the entire duration of the contract.
In LIKTA’s view, procurement requirements should also include bidders’ financial indicators, such as liquidity ratios, turnover generated from relevant development projects, and mandatory state social insurance contributions. This would provide greater confidence that a company will be able to maintain the necessary team of specialists throughout the contract period and that it does not face significant insolvency risks. In other words, the risk of awarding contracts to bidders with insufficient in-house capacity that rely on a difficult-to-manage network of subcontractors should be reduced.
For smaller ICT system development and maintenance contracts, LIKTA believes that competition could be strengthened by transforming the existing Electronic Procurement System (EIS) e-catalogues into dynamic purchasing systems. Here too, regularly updated information about team capacity and available work assignments would be important. This would promote stronger competition than procurement based on narrowly specified lists of projects.
High-quality procurement of ICT services requires appropriate quality assessment, a proportionate allocation of risks between the contracting authority and the supplier, and clear, objectively verifiable acceptance criteria. Nobody remembers the e-service procurements that worked well, but everyone feels the consequences when information systems fail or provide an inadequate user experience.

EU condemns glorification at Mladic funeral in Serbia

Serbian national military servicemen fire a three-volley salute during the funeral of war criminal Ratko Mladic, who died last week while serving a life sentence for genocide and other atrocities during the war in Bosnia, at the Topcider Cemetery, in Belgrade, Serbia, Sept. 7, 2026. (AP Photo)
The European Union has condemned the public glorification of Ratko Mladic after thousands attended the convicted war criminal’s funeral in Belgrade, which featured military honors and was joined by several Serbian government ministers.
The EU’s diplomatic service said Mladic’s crimes were among “the most heinous crimes known to humankind.”
“Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values,” it said, adding that such acts had no place in the bloc or its candidate countries.
Serbia has been an EU candidate since 2012.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos earlier canceled a planned visit to the country over what she described as the glorification surrounding Mladic’s death.
The former Bosnian Serb military commander died on Aug. 27 at the age of 84 in a U.N. detention facility in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence.
Mourners began gathering early on Sept. 7 at Belgrade’s Serbian Orthodox Church of St. Luke, where Mladic’s coffin was placed on public display.
His military cap and saber rested on the coffin as uniformed soldiers and war veterans stood nearby.
Serbian Orthodox Patriarch Porfirije led the service, while large screens were installed outside the church for crowds unable to enter.
Although the ceremony was not formally designated a state funeral, the Serbian government had sent an aircraft to return Mladic’s body from the Netherlands, and soldiers carried his flag-draped coffin.
Defense Minister Bratislav Gasic and Justice Minister Nenad Vujic attended the funeral. President Aleksandar Vucic was absent, but his son Danilo was among the mourners.
Following the service, the coffin, draped in the flags of Serbia and Bosnia’s Serb entity Republika Srpska, was taken in procession to Topcider Cemetery.
Some supporters carried banners describing Mladic as a hero and chanted his name.
He was buried with military honors, including a three-volley rifle salute, beside his daughter Ana, who died in 1994.
The U.N. International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia convicted Mladic in 2017 of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. His life sentence was upheld on appeal in 2021.
The convictions included his role in the 1995 Srebrenica genocide, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed, and the siege of Sarajevo.

NEW YORK, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- The Iran war has cost U.S. consumers an estimated additional 100 billion U.S. dollars in energy costs, a figure that is rising by roughly 1 million every two minutes, according to a real-time estimate from Brown University as of Monday.
The Iran War Energy Cost Tracker from Brown's Watson School says higher gasoline and diesel prices have cost the average U.S. household more than 760 dollars since the war began on Feb. 28.
The U.S. national average price for diesel rose to a record 5.90 dollars per gallon on Monday, surpassing the record 5.85 dollars set on Friday, according to the American Automobile Association.
Texas has borne the biggest share of the cost increase, with consumers paying around 11 billion dollars in extra gas and diesel costs since the war began. It is followed by California and Florida, at about 8 billion dollars and 5 billion dollars, respectively.
U.S. consumers are expecting a longer period of higher fuel prices than they anticipated when the war began, the tracker shows. The rising costs have translated into higher transportation expenses for many everyday goods. Some businesses have already passed those costs on to consumers in the form of additional fees. ■

Feature: Chinese stories find new ways to reach global audiences through immersive technology
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:51:09 CST
14:51:09 KST

VENICE, Italy, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- At a screening venue on a small island near Venice's Lido in Italy, a foreign visitor put on a virtual reality headset and stepped into a Chinese story.
Outside the screening room, more viewers waited in line for their turn to experience The Pigeon Ring, a Chinese immersive work that explores family, memory and the bonds between generations.
The scene at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival is a vivid example of how immersive storytelling is opening up new possibilities for Chinese creators to reach audiences around the world.
Established in 2016, the Venice Immersive section is an official section of the festival and has grown into one of the world's largest events dedicated to immersive arts and media. It showcases creative extended reality (XR) works ranging from immersive videos and virtual and mixed reality experiences to virtual worlds and immersive installations.
The Pigeon Ring, directed by Zhang Yuqi and Tao Shixin, has been selected for the Venice Immersive competition this year. It tells a story of a granddaughter who accompanies her grandfather back to their old family home in search of a lost pigeon ring. What begins as a seemingly ordinary family journey gradually unfolds into a story of memory, companionship and affection.
"Most of the audiences who have come to see the work over the past few days have been from overseas," Zhang and Tao told Xinhua. "Many foreign viewers shed tears after watching it. Perhaps the work has touched something that people can emotionally relate to."
That emotional connection across cultural boundaries has also left a deep impression on Michel Reilhac, co-curator of Venice Immersive.
He described the work as "very moving," noting that without featuring broad narratives and spectacular visual scenes, The Pigeon Ring focuses on a much smaller story -- an ordinary family story -- yet manages to generate a powerful emotional impact.
"It's not relying on special effects, but on the heart of the story itself," Reilhac told Xinhua, adding that this makes Chinese works accessible to and appreciated by international audiences.
Behind these stories and emotional experiences lies another important force: rapidly evolving technology.
Liz Rosenthal, co-curator of Venice Immersive, highlighted the use of Gaussian splatting, an advanced 3D rendering technique, in The Pigeon Ring, describing it as a particularly innovative approach.
"It really takes you into the story in a way that we haven't seen before," she said. "It's almost like stepping into a film."
"China has made incredible progress in artificial intelligence, robotics and all kinds of digital technologies," said Reilhac, adding that the country's technological development is moving in a highly forward-looking direction and is helping creators produce increasingly sophisticated immersive works.
The co-curator also commended the development of talent training at Chinese universities. Recalling a recent visit to Shanghai Theatre Academy, Reilhac said he was impressed by the openness of young Chinese creators and artists toward international collaboration.
He noted that, alongside The Pigeon Ring, a number of works by young Chinese artists are being presented at the festival's immersive section, with some creators still studying at university.
"It's very important for us that we represent new voices, new artists alongside the more established ones," he said. ■

UK prepares settlement trade restrictions

London has argued that illegal settlement expansion threatens the prospects for a two-state solution and has pledged further action in response to Israel’s settlement policies.

Minister: Ukraine was discussed at Tallinn dinner with Donald Trump Jr.
Ukraine was high on the agenda in a meeting between Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) and Donald Trump Jr., the minister said.
Trump Jr. was in Tallinn recently, departing Monday morning according to Delfi.He was in town discuss security and economic policy at the same time high-level U.S. negotiators were in Ukraine, while he also attended functions organized by the casino industry.
While US peace negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were in Moscow and in Kyiv, Donald Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr., was in Tallinn. Please, tell us what was he doing here?
He had some meeting of his own, but I also got the opportunity to attend a dinner, at the invitation of the U.S. side. Frankly, it was very interesting to meet someone who is not an active politician but who is nevertheless a very influential individual, to get a view of his attitude towards us, plus there was also an opportunity to talk about our own views on both security and economic policy. Perhaps contacts like these, with unconventional people close to the U.S. presidential administration, may prove handy one day.
Delfi has written about this expensive invite party held by casino company Studioworks at the Euroopa Liidu Maja in quite colorful terms, pointing out that it brought together a rather motley crew. Are you sure that conducting business in this kind of company is now the direction of our foreign policy?
It is not my place to comment on what Delfi writes, but those are two different events: One was a dinner with 13 people and the other was some other event. I had the opportunity to speak with Donald Trump Jr. at considerable length, and about important issues.
Did you also ask for any kind of support for Ukraine, and did you get any positive response?
Ukraine was discussed quite actively at the table.
And how was it discussed at the table?
I'll leave the details to one side.
Then you should also know what took place in Moscow, as you happened to have an excellent contact at hand to ask about it.
Speaking seriously, I had a call with the Ukrainian foreign minister today, and he gave me an overview of what was talked about. In his assessment, there was no major breakthrough between Ukraine and Russia or on the peace process as a whole. But I will get an opportunity this week to find out more precisely through direct discussions.
However, I am still interested in this: When you did speak with Donald Trump Jr. about Ukraine, what was his attitude? How could it be that we have a freedom of the media in which Estonia ranks second and America is quite some way far behind – I understand all that – but how can it be that the son of such an influential president comes here yet we do not know what he was doing here?
We do know what he was doing, but those questions need to be put to those people who organized his visit here. The issues I discussed were related to security and economic policy.
Come on, you posed for a photo with an American rapper. I don't know whether that was related to security or economic policy, but what was that rapper's name? I've already forgotten.
I genuinely don't know the rapper's name. There were a lot of people there.
The one you posed for a photo with and who wrote in his social media post that he had taken a photo with the 'prime minister'?
You'll have to ask him about what he writes on his social media.
Among the people you were there with were also – at least according to Delfi – was a New York mafia boss, I don't know whether former or current, some casino people and some beauty queens. The whole thing had a bit of a 1990s vibe to it, I have to say.
You are now conflating two different events.
Then explain exactly what went on. Am I right in understanding that Donald Trump Jr. was here conducting casino business?
You will have to ask him and the people who organized his visit here. I attended a dinner where neither the casino business nor any business activities were discussed.
You didn't ask why he was here either? Do you know why he came here?
My understanding was that he had business meetings here, so that is for him or his team to comment on.
When I think about it, it still could have been on casino business, as it was a casino company's party that you were invited to. Were you there primarily as foreign minister, or were you carrying out Eesti 200 politics?
I was there at the invitation of the U.S. side, we held talks, and I think it would be pointless not to make use of a contact like that when a person like that comes to Estonia and is willing to discuss issues that are of interest to us, and that is what actually happened. There was no party at the dinner table where the 13 of us were seated.
So what did go on there?
There was a discussion on various topics, as I already said.
Who else from the government was invited?
No one else from the government was invited. It was a personal invitation for me.
All right, let's change track. In the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, the far right achieved a historic election result, winning nearly 44 percent of the vote. Can you imagine that one day you could be Estonia's foreign minister at a time when the far right is in power in Germany?
Anything can happen. We saw the elections in that state and unfortunately the rise of extremist forces is indeed a reality not only in Germany but across Europe more broadly. I had thought that Germany's extraordinary step of publicly attributing the Leipzig terror attack to Russia may also be an attempt to make its people understand that Russia genuinely poses a direct threat to them. Russia really is carrying out attacks against Germany and the German people.
But it seems to be having the opposite effect. When we watched Epp Ehand's report from Germany, a great many people there seemed to feel that Russia is a much more normal country than Ukraine. It seems to be some kind of trend. What is the point of us making all this effort to help Ukraine if Germany itself starts leaning towards Russia?
We have to make the effort. It is in our own security interests, it is in Europe's interests, and we should not draw definitive conclusions from the election result in a single state.
But as Epp Ehand said, that is actually the trend.
All of that is there, and I talk to Germans quite a lot and they are highly concerned. Voter turnout was also very high. The question is whether the majority of Germany can somehow consolidate itself, also looking at the results of this particular state election. Will there be a debate about what is genuinely in the security interests of Germany and Europe, or will we indeed at some point see a Germany whose government says that relations with Russia are normal and that we want the good old days back? That would certainly not be in Estonia's interests.
What will happen to the EU if the far right comes to power in Germany?
We saw what happened in Hungary, under Viktor Orbán. I would not get ahead of events, though the issue is actually very serious, because the current model, in which 27 member states try to reach a consensus on security and foreign policy, would turn into something entirely different. I would also remind you that France has elections coming up next year and the far‑right presidential candidate there is also getting increasingly popular. Europe is facing some very serious and important questions.
One of the things we are also facing up to is climate change. Of course, you are the foreign minister, not the climate minister, although perhaps you could still become one. Do you also think about the possibility that climate change around the world could at some point put Estonia in a completely different foreign‑policy position from the one it is in today?
Foreign‑policy problems arising from climate change already exist in Europe, for example when we talk about migratory pressure from Africa. That is a reality. I remember that when I was social security minister in 2015, it directly affected Estonia's domestic politics too, even though climate refugees did not actually want to come here. EKRE also emerged around that time, and one of its platforms was immigration, which may now also be helping AfD come to power in Germany, for instance.
Those direct links stemming from climate change, such as migration pressure or changes in the economic situation, will certainly be reflected in the domestic politics of democratic countries. Domestic politics, in turn, shapes foreign policy to a very large extent, so we certainly think about it. But if you ask whether we are prepared for it, or whether Europe, for example, has some well‑thought‑out strategy, I can say that in reality it does not, and the problems are dealt with one by one. The root causes of these problems are very often not purely scientific; they are also a matter of belief, and we see conflicts and divisions in different societies, not only in Europe.
Finally, I would ask this: When I usually interview a foreign minister, there is at least some hope that I will meet them again the following year. What do you think will have become of you six months from now? Will you still be in politics, or will you have left?
It is very hard to say. According to my original plans, I took the job of foreign minister for about a year, yet I am now already in my fourth year. I think the elections are in March, then forming a new government usually takes a couple of weeks or a month, and ultimately the voters will decide. Whether I am still in politics then or not, the good thing about foreign and security policy, at least, is that fortunately it is not a matter of day‑to‑day politics. We have agreed on certain fundamental principles, and in that sense I am not worried in terms of the elections, as Estonia's foreign and security policy will certainly continue on the same trajectory.

An election poster of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party reading "Migration needs borders" is fixed in front of the headquarters of Germany's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party in Berlin on Sept. 7, 2026. (AFP)
Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has set its sights on federal power after its record state election victory, a result that has deepened unease among the country’s immigrant communities, including its large Turkish population.
At a press conference in Berlin on Sept. 7, AfD co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla appeared alongside lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund and presented the result as a springboard for the 2029 federal election.
“We will be the strongest force across Germany at the next federal election,” Weidel said.
She said an AfD-led federal government would seek to stop irregular migration and deport people convicted of crimes and rejected asylum seekers.
According to provisional official results, the AfD won 43.8 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6, more than doubling its 20.8 percent share in 2021.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) fell to 17.2 percent from 37.1 percent.
The AfD secured 39 of the 83 seats in the state parliament, three short of an outright majority.
The result has left the state facing difficult coalition arithmetic.
Germany’s mainstream parties have long ruled out cooperation with the AfD under the political “firewall” intended to keep the far right out of government.
Forming a majority without the AfD would require all five other parties represented in parliament to work together.
Siegmund said the AfD would speak with every parliamentary group and individual lawmaker but would seek a stable majority rather than lead a minority administration.
The party’s state branch has been classified as a proven right-wing extremist group by local domestic intelligence.
Its campaign included stricter deportation policies and a proposed task force to remove migrants who do not work or integrate.
Siegmund sought to allay concerns after the vote, saying no one should be afraid and that an AfD-led government would operate under the rule of law.
The result has nevertheless intensified concern among Germany’s Turkish community.
International relations expert Canan Tercan told daily Hürriyet that the outcome could push other parties toward tougher positions on migration and security.
“For Turks, the AfD’s policies should not be assessed only through the question of ‘who will be deported,’ but also through the future legal and social position of migrants in Germany,” she said.
Tercan noted that the party’s official documents did not call for German citizens to be deported solely because of their immigrant roots.
However, she said tougher positions on immigration, naturalization and dual citizenship, along with policies affecting Muslims, could have broader consequences for the Turkish community.
Cihan Günyel, a Turkish political scientist and foreign policy expert, said the AfD’s attempts to attract Turkish and other immigrant-origin voters reflected electoral pragmatism.
“When we look at its ideological structure, it is not inclusive and is anti-immigration,” he said.
Merz, meanwhile, ruled out resigning after acknowledging that the CDU had suffered its worst defeat in the state in decades.
“Giving up is not an option for me,” he said.
State elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sept. 20 will provide the next test of whether the AfD can extend its gains.

"Everyone knows that Canada doesn't let our Great Dairy Farmers sell into the Canadian Market, and that the only reason Canada makes Autos is because of previous disastrous Trade Agreements while other Presidents were in Office," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

After trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, the US moved to impose 50% tariffs on key Canadian goods.

UAE gave explicit warning to Netanyahu of Hamas plans days before October 7, new book says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:41:44 UTC
14:41:44 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu received an explicit warning about a major operation being planned by Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar shortly before the October 7 attack, according to a new book by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval. The account also alleges that Netanyahu received a separate warning from Egypt in the days before the massacre and later declined to authorize a renewed proposal to target senior Hamas leaders, including Sinwar.
The book, Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment, says Sinwar warned that he was preparing a “big surprise” for Israel and twice used the Arabic word zilzal, meaning “earthquake.” The investigation follows an earlier report by Yedioth Ahronoth journalist Smadar Perry, published during the first days of the war, that Egypt had warned Netanyahu of “something unusual, a terrible operation” being prepared by Hamas.
“The story starts earlier,” Eldar said Tuesday, discussing the investigation published by Haaretz. He said the episode began during indirect talks involving Israel, Hamas and Fatah over the return of the bodies of Israeli soldiers Hadar Goldin and Oron Shaul and the release of Hisham al-Sayed and Avera Mengistu, then held in Gaza. When the talks stalled in early September 2023, Eldar said, Sinwar disappeared completely and dropped off the Shin Bet’s radar.
According to Eldar, Sinwar then contacted a Fatah figure and told him: “Pass on to the Israelis that I’m planning a big surprise for them if they don’t make progress.” Sinwar used the word “earthquake,” Eldar said. The Fatah figure, alarmed by the conversation, passed the message to an associate who now serves as an adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. Sinwar later repeated the message: “Pass it on to the Israelis, I’m planning an ‘earthquake’ for them.”
The call on a special app
Eldar said then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar received the information on September 15 and passed it to Netanyahu. About a week and a half later, according to the investigation, bin Zayed sought to make sure Netanyahu had received the warning and called him through a special communications system developed by the UAE.
“They have conversations through a unique system. A representative from the embassy arrives with the application, with a phone, and they hold a conversation that lasts 45 minutes,” Eldar said.
During that conversation, the investigation claims, Netanyahu sought to reassure the UAE president, telling him: “We are prepared in Gaza.” Netanyahu reportedly assessed that if trouble erupted, it was more likely to occur in the West Bank. The book says Netanyahu did not subsequently brief then-IDF chief Herzi Halevi, Bar or then-Mossad chief David Barnea about the alleged call.
A similar warning reached the Prime Minister’s Office from then-Egyptian intelligence chief Gen. Abbas Kamel, according to Perry’s earlier report. Kamel reportedly warned Netanyahu of “something unusual, a terrible operation” being prepared by Hamas. Perry said Netanyahu responded: “In Gaza, we are on top of things, we are in control. Our problem is the West Bank, and that is where we are also moving forces.”
“People in the security establishment said, both in the Shin Bet and the IDF, that if we had known about that conversation, we would essentially have received another assessment reinforcing the information that had already arrived on September 15,” Eldar said. He added: “We have documentation. We are fully backed up on this story. We would not have published it without recordings, documentation and cross-checking.”
The investigation also says that on October 1, during a discussion about unrest along the Gaza border and indications that Hamas was seeking to carry out an attack in the West Bank, Bar again recommended targeting senior Hamas leaders, including Sinwar, who he said was “showing signs of arrogance.”
As on previous occasions when such a proposal was raised, Netanyahu replied: “Prepare plans for me and I’ll consider them,” according to the investigation.
“He never said ‘no,’” one senior security official said. “That was always his way of postponing dealing with the problem.” Another official who attended the meeting recalled Netanyahu concluding: “Keep working on the capability, but for now calm the situation.”
According to the investigation, Netanyahu did not mention during the meeting the warnings that had allegedly reached him from the UAE or Egypt.
“If we had known about the warnings, there is a chance it would have given much greater weight to the first message we received from Sinwar,” a senior Shin Bet official said. “Maybe it would also have clarified what was behind his sudden withdrawal from the talks in early September. We might have put one and one together and reached a completely different conclusion, one that could have changed our entire assessment.”
‘A complete lie’; ‘The report is true’
Netanyahu’s office categorically denied the investigation. “A complete lie. Prime Minister Netanyahu did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and received no warning from him,” it said.
Bar and Halevi also said they had not been informed of any warning conveyed by the UAE president.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who recently met bin Zayed, said the report was true. “The report that Netanyahu was warned 10 days before the October 7 massacre about Sinwar’s intentions is true,” Bennett said. He accused Netanyahu of bearing “personal and direct responsibility” for the failure and said his disregard of warnings amounted to “criminal negligence.”
Gadi Eisenkot, former IDF chief of staff and chairman of the Yashar party, said the report added to evidence that Netanyahu had failed to recognize repeated warning signs ahead of October 7.
“More and more signs indicate that Netanyahu led Israel blindly into the October 7 failure,” Eisenkot said. “Netanyahu received dozens of warnings ahead of October 7 and ignored them all. He is unfit.”
The October Council, a group representing families and activists seeking accountability over the October 7 failures, said the focus should extend beyond whether Netanyahu was awakened on the night of the attack.
“Anyone arguing over whether Netanyahu was woken up on the night of October 7 is ignoring the much bigger question: How many times did people try to wake Israel up before the massacre?” the group said.
It called for answers on who received the warnings, what reached the prime minister, what he did with the information and what was or was not passed on to the security establishment.
“Why, despite all the warning signs published since then, did the State of Israel arrive at the morning of October 7 blind and unprepared?” the council said.

08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Argentina on Monday announced a formal criminal complaint against several international energy companies for drilling for oil and gas under British licenses near the Falkland Islands, which Buenos Aires calls Islas Malvinas.
Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, backed by Treasury Attorney General Sebastian Amerio, filed the complaint in federal court against Israel-based Navitas Petroleum, Canada's JHI Associates and Eco Atlantic Oil and Gas. The government is also targeting individual directors, managers and shareholders, accusing them of carrying out unauthorized hydrocarbon, oil and natural gas exploration in the North Malvinas Basin.
Argentine President Javier Milei's office said the legal action is a "concrete action to protect natural resources and safeguard the sovereignty" of Argentina.
The long-standing sovereignty dispute over the Falkland Islands, a British-controlled archipelago situated about 483 kilometers (300 miles) east of the Argentine coast, has flared recently as offshore drilling projects move toward production. Buenos Aires argues that Britain has illegally occupied the islands since 1833.
As part of a broader defensive policy, Milei also signed a directive instructing Economy Minister Luis Andres Caputo to prioritize funding for an integrated naval base, a strategic military facility designed to support maritime security and territorial defense.
The complaint follows separate sanction proceedings initiated by Argentina on Friday against 45 individuals and entities. Milei previously warned that the Sea Lion oil project, an offshore drilling venture, poses an imminent threat to national resources. While London has dismissed these legal threats as domestic politics, the foreign companies said they plan to proceed with drilling under UK licenses.

Beijing sends record 16 Hong Kong civil servants for UN positions
Officers sent under UN Junior Professional Officer scheme come from 13 grades and departments, topping earlier deployments in 2019 and 2023
Beijing has recommended the largest-ever cohort of civil servants from Hong Kong for roles at United Nations agencies this year, expecting the deployments to broaden their global perspective and strengthen the city’s position as a bridge between the country and the international community.
The 16 officers sent under the UN Junior Professional Officer (JPO) scheme represent 13 grades and departments, including customs, police and the anti-corruption agency.
This marks a steady increase from the five officers sent in 2019, when Hong Kong joined the programme, and the 12 sent in 2023.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Tuesday said previous cohorts had excelled in fields spanning anti-drug operations, climate and resource coordination, trade and transport, and intellectual property protection.
“Previous batches contributed across fields, from drug enforcement to climate coordination. They earned high praise from the UN, with nearly half seeing their tenures extended at the organisation’s request,” he said.
“This affirms [the capabilities of] Hong Kong youth and strengthens our resolve to contribute to the international community.”
Lee said Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, set to be unveiled Wednesday next week, would align with the nation’s 15th five-year blueprint, and that dispatching young civil servants to the UN was part of the city’s effort to serve national diplomacy and meet global commitments by leveraging its professional strengths.

By Monday, the Palestinian Ministry of Health reported that 73,658 people have been killed and 174,622 wounded since October 2023, after 160 additional deaths were certified and added to the casualty figures. Of those, more than 1,340 have been killed since the October 2025 Israeli-Hamas “ceasefire”.
The recovery of bodies has slowly continued alongside the killings.
Families in northern Gaza held funerals on Sunday for around 100 people, including 60 children, whose remains were pulled from the rubble of Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood, many of them members of the extended Malaka family.
Gaza civil defence chief Raed al-Dahshan told Al Jazeera his teams could recover an estimated 8,000 more bodies still under the rubble within 90 days if given proper heavy equipment, but warned that without it, “this work will continue for years”. Between 10,000 and 14,000 people remain missing under Gaza’s rubble.
In the strip, humanitarian conditions continue to deteriorate without sufficient aid getting in. The World Health Organization warned that water contamination in Gaza has nearly tripled since January. The Palestinian Water Authority reported all five of Gaza’s wastewater plants have shut down entirely, with roughly 55,000 cubic metres of untreated sewage discharged daily.
West Bank: Demolitions and villages under siege
Meanwhile, Israeli forces carried out demolitions this week in the West Bank. In the community of Khirbet al-Tabban in Masafer Yatta, those demolitions were absolute – demolishing all 12 homes left 70 people, including 30 children, homeless.
“It’s wiping the village off the face of the earth,” council head Nidal Younis said. Residents, he added, intend to rebuild.
Israeli forces also destroyed four water wells and several greenhouses in nearby Beit Ummar in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, causing an estimated $60,000 in losses, and demolished a home in Nahalin in Bethlehem governorate.
Around Jenin, the bulldozing of hundreds of farmers’ trees continued along the Arraba-Yabad and Jenin-Nablus roads, part of six military orders issued in August to clear vegetation from across four Jenin-area villages, according to to the Palestinian Wafa news agency.
In occupied East Jerusalem’s al-Bustan neighbourhood, community representative Fakhri Abu Diab said municipal bulldozers demolished a four-apartment building – the 60th demolition there since October 2023. On Monday morning another home was demolished in the East Jerusalem neighbourhood of Beit Hanina, according to Wafa, and authorities forced a Palestinian man in the city’s Jabal al-Mukaber area to demolish his home.
Despite all of the land and property destruction, last week’s most sustained violence centred on al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah. Settlers and soldiers raided the village on the evening of Wednesday after accusing residents of stealing livestock.
Snipers took rooftop positions and opened fire as residents tried to stop settlers stealing sheep, killing Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Mohammad Nassan, 19.
The Israeli military told the Times of Israel that troops were “securing the retrieval of livestock belonging to Israeli civilians” when a “violent riot” broke out and soldiers “fired at key instigators”. Eyewitnesses said Nasan was shot in the back.
In the days after, mourners were beaten and pepper-sprayed and their vehicle stolen, with an ambulance also attacked.
Wafa also reported late on Sunday that Israeli settlers killed Omar Tubasi, 20, and injured three people when they raided and opened fire on the village of Hajja, east of Qalqilya governorate in the occupied West Bank.
Elsewhere, settlers stormed Umm al-Khair in the South Hebron Hills on Friday, injuring a child. Soldiers who arrived declared the area a closed military zone that was enforced for Palestinians, not the settlers who remained.
In Turmus Ayya north of Ramallah, a settler wearing a T-shirt bearing the logo of the outlawed Kach movement was filmed atop a Palestinian home declaring “this land is Jewish” after US Ambassador Mike Huckabee visited the town and called settler violence “a form of terrorism”.
In Qusra, south of Nablus, a month-long siege of three homes continued, with the army initially blocking roughly 100 peace activists from delivering food and medicine. Settlers also stole water tanks and livestock in the Jordan Valley and sabotaged water lines serving a Bedouin encampment near Tayasir in the northern West Bank, according to reports and photos from local Palestinian activists.
In East Jerusalem’s Old City, Israeli police shot and killed Ibrahim al-Hendi, 33, from Beit Hanina, near Damascus Gate on Friday, claiming he had tried to stab an officer.

The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) Hindu temple in Paris released a statement apologising for "any pain or inconvenience caused."
The Eiffel Tower reopened on Tuesday after staff staged a walk-out the day before over the removal of women colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group which later apologised.
The operating company that runs the Paris landmark, SETE, acknowledged that the Hindu delegation had requested the visit be organised so as to limit "interactions with women" and said that "these conditions should not have been accepted."
It said the landmark would open its doors again following a meeting between staff and management.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement apologised for "any pain or inconvenience caused" by the incident.
"To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower," the organisation wrote on X.
"Due to the size of our delegation, the visit was arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal operating hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others."
Eiffel Tower staff said in a statement that it condemned "professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex" during the visit by the delegation.
"Instructions were given to female employees of the Eiffel Tower and to female employees of contractors to make themselves invisible in order to welcome this delegation," the staff said in their statement, adding they were shocked to have been put in such a situation.
"Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present."
Paris' Mayor, Emmanuel Grégoire, promised an investigation "as soon as possible."
Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of the National Assembly, condemned the incident on Monday.
"I refuse to accept that women should be told to step aside to meet the demands of foreign visitors," she said.
"Welcoming others never means giving up our values. In France, women are fully present in public life. No one tells them to become invisible there."
The Eiffel Tower's website said the landmark was closed on Monday due to "exceptional circumstances."
It advised visitors with tickets to check their emails and apologised for the inconvenience.

Czech defense contractor: We warned our government against Datasel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:32:00 UTC
14:32:00 KST

Czech defense contractor: We warned our government against Datasel
Czech ammunition manufacturer STV Group told Delfi that Indian company Datasel, with which Estonia signed a contract, is a textbook example of a fraudulent company. STV Group has also been defrauded by Datasel and left without the goods it ordered.
STV Group representative Dominik Drda acknowledged that he is closely following the scandal in Estonia because Datasel advertises STV's products on its website and because STV itself has been defrauded by the same Indian company.
"They lie all the time and use every opportunity, however small, to avoid fulfilling their contractual obligations," Drda told Delfi.
In 2024, STV ordered ammunition from Indian company Datasel, but later discovered that it was an intermediary posing as a manufacturer. Datasel managed to deliver only 10 percent of the goods agreed upon and failed to return an advance payment worth millions of euros to STV. To resolve the situation and recover the money it is owed, STV Group is preparing to take Datasel to court. As the Czech government is procuring weapons for Ukraine as part of an international initiative, STV warned the government that Datasel was unreliable.
"We advised them not to let Datasel defraud them and not to enter into any contracts with the company. Fortunately, they listened to us," the STV Group representative said.
Estonia sought to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine and paid a total of €70 million in advance to the Indian company, which had never previously sold a single shell. Instead of complete military materiel, however, Estonia received a succession of new promises, and the dispute is now in court.
In August 2024, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) signed its first sales contract with Datasel and transferred the first €15 million. The money did not come from Estonia's state budget, however, but from the European Peace Facility.
RKIK's current director general, Elmar Vaher, said he would not have signed the contract and that the decision was made by a very small group of people. He said, for example, that RKIK's head of procurement at the time knew nothing about it.
Magnus-Valdemar Saar, who headed RKIK at the time, disputed this account. He acknowledged that purchasing ammunition from third countries carries risks, but said no major decisions were made without the approval of ministry leaders.

Tokyo tourist hotspot bans short-term rentals amid surge in complaints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:31:26 UTC
14:31:26 KST

A neighbourhood in Tokyo popular with foreign tourists will ban visitors from using thousands of short-term rental accommodations after a slew of complaints about behaviour.
In the latest sign that Japan’s patience with mass tourism is wearing thin, Shinjuku ward – home to the notorious Kabukicho nightlife district and the world’s busiest railway station – will prevent visitors from using private lodgings in residential areas and near schools and important cultural sites, Japanese media reported this week.
The measure, to be introduced through a local ordinance, could encourage other local authorities to follow suit. Shinjuku, with a regular population of more than 350,000, is home to 3,775 private lodgings – or minpaku – the largest number anywhere in Japan.
While tourism has boosted sectors of Japan’s economy and raised the country’s profile overseas, the surge in visitor numbers has created tensions with residents in popular destinations such as Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka.
Shinjuku ward believes the measure will affect as many as 2,000 lodgings in residential areas – almost half the total, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. The number of minpaku residences in Shinjuku has almost tripled since 2022.
Reports said officials had been forced to act after receiving more than 1,300 complaints from residents in the 12 months to March. Many cited disruption caused by visitors who did not dispose of their rubbish properly, made too much noise and smoked in areas where it is banned. There have also been reports of trespassing.
Officials said temporarily revoking the licenses of renters whose tenants misbehaved would not address residents’ concerns. “Even if we crack down on badly behaved operators, the number of complaints remains the same,” a ward official told the Japan Times. “So we decided it’s better to change the ordinance.”
Authorities did not single out particular operators for the ban. But it is likely to affect those using popular companies such as Airbnb.
An Airbnb spokesperson told the Guardian: “Shinjuku has been an important partner to us, and we take residents’ concerns seriously. Home sharing works best when residents, hosts and guests can all live well alongside each other, and that is what we want to help the ward protect.
“We would welcome the chance to work with the ward on measures that target the problem more precisely - a prohibition across residential zones would close thousands of registered homes affecting compliant and responsible hosts, while leaving untouched the unregistered operators behind much of the disruption residents describe.
“We believe there is a version of this ordinance that protects residents’ quality of life without closing responsible, licensed hosts, and we want to help find it.”
The ward will ask for members of the public to give their feedback on the proposal next month, with a view to submitting revisions to the ordinance in February. It also plans to reduce the number of days per year that minpaku in residential areas can be rented out from 180 to 120.
Authorities in Kyoto – where tourists flock to view temples and shrines, rent kimono and photograph traditional geisha entertainers – limit minpaku operations in residential areas to just 60 days a year, during the off-peak season between January and March.
“Residents are concerned that their communities could be falling apart,” Kyoto’s mayor, Koji Matsui, said earlier this year. “We have strengthened the oversight of operators, but that is not enough. We need to go further,” the Asahi Shimbun quoted him as saying.
A record 42 million people visited Japan last year, spending a combined ¥9.5tn ($62bn) – also an all-time high. The government has set a target of 60 million visitors by 2030 – a goal critics say will exacerbate “tourism pollution”.
Authorities near Mount Fuji have introduced climbing fees and imposed a daily visitor cap in an attempt to reduce overcrowding on Japan’s highest mountain. In February, the town of Fujiyoshida, a popular Fuji viewing spot, decided to cancel this spring’s cherry blossom festival, citing a rise in disruptive behaviour by tourists.
The mayor, Shigeru Horiuchi, said the decision had been taken to “protect the dignity and living environment of our citizens”.

Landmark study exposes scale of brain injury crisis in rugby league
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:30:16 UTC
14:30:16 KST

Study on degenerative brain disease finds CTE in 31 former rugby league players
In short:
Of 51 brains of former rugby league players examined, 31 were found to have CTE.
The disease was found in players in their 20s, 30s and 40s, from amateur to professional levels.
The findings were presented at the International Sports Concussion Conference in Melbourne on Tuesday.
A landmark study has found that 31 rugby league players have been diagnosed with the degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).
Rugby league players in their 20s, 30s and 40s have been found to have had the degenerative brain disease, which can only be diagnosed after death.
Among them were decorated league footballer and NRL coach Paul Green, 49, as well as Manly Sea Eagles player Keith Titmuss, who was just 20 when he died.
The ABC has obtained the latest statistics, which are based on the first 150 brain examinations of people who played contact sports completed at the Australian Sports Brain Bank.
Of the 51 rugby league players' brains donated to the brain bank, 31 were found to have CTE. They played at various levels of the game, from amateur to professional.
The paper was presented by molecular biologist and data scientist Jennifer Cropley at the International Sports Concussion Conference in Melbourne on Tuesday.
CTE's sole cause is repetitive hits to the head and body. Symptoms can include memory loss, impulsivity, anxiety and anger.
The disease has been found in several athletes who have died by suicide, but experts say more research needs to be done to establish a "causal" link.
'I feel a massive responsibility'
Former league star Paul Green's widow Amanda Green is calling on all collision sports to do more for the next generation of players.
Experts have repeatedly called for football codes to ban contact until the age of 14.
Loading...
Ms Green has appealed for more people to donate their brains to understand the disease and wants more awareness around the issue.
"Now that we know what we do about this disease I feel a massive responsibility, as we all should, to protect the brain health of the next generation of young athletes," Ms Green said.
"I owe it to my kids and their sports-loving mates. We need to ensure they don't make the same mistakes as our generation did. The key here is to pledge our brains and support the incredible and potentially lifesaving work of the Australian Sports Brain Bank."
Ms Green said she had "no idea" about what CTE was until after her husband died.
"I had been involved in the highest level of professional sport in this country and did not understand this disease we now know as CTE," she said.
"That was not OK. I didn't know what CTE was, and since Paul's diagnosis, I have constantly called for more education on the issue. People needed to understand this disease so no-one else suffered in silence."
Green died by suicide in 2022.
Ms Green said that since learning about the disease, she could see her husband was showing CTE signs prior to his death.
"On receiving Paul's diagnosis from [sports brain bank director] Professor Michael Buckland, he had mentioned that Paul had one of the most severe cases of CTE that he had seen, but due to Paul's intelligence, there was a possibility that he had masked a number of his symptoms, but the symptoms I had seen were symptoms such as anxiety, impatience, he was impulsive in his decision-making, he definitely had lower levels of tolerance and quite elevated emotions," she said.
"These were changes that I had seen over time that I put down to the stress of his job."
Swinburne University professor Alan Pearce, who is an author on the paper which reveals the latest rugby league statistics, said more needed to be done to protect players.
"Given rugby league is a collision-based sport, it is not surprising that we found over 60 per cent of rugby league donors had CTE, but this tells us we need to start implementing modifications," he said.
"Introducing contact limits in rugby league is a good start, but rugby league and all contact and collision-based sports must also start modifying to non-contact versions for children to the age of 14 years of age.
"Keith Titmuss's result, having stage two CTE at 20, tells us that this is not an old person's disease.
"Keith passed in 2020, and his brain results typify that exposure risk for CTE starts at junior sport level.
"Keith played junior rugby league from the age of five years old, then schoolboy rugby union, and his brain results show the effect of that."
Titmuss played as a schoolboy at Newington College in Sydney and had had substantial exposure to repeated head impacts throughout his 15 years playing junior contact sport.
Titmuss died of exertional heat stroke after a 2020 Manly Sea Eagles training session.
His CTE diagnosis was revealed in 2024 and sparked warnings that the major football codes were not doing enough to protect young athletes. His parents Lafo and Paul donated his brain for research.
The latest rugby league statistics follow a Four Corners report in June, which revealed 33 Australian Rules footballers have been diagnosed with CTE and exposed the scale of the AFL's brain trauma crisis.
The Four Corners report triggered enquiries by WorkSafe Victoria and WorkSafe WA into incidents related to footballer safety.
Last month, a Boston University study revealed at least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 was found to have CTE.
The NRL has been contacted for comment.
