Netanyahu's pick Oren Dobronsky drops Likud Knesset bid rather than give up US citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:25:47 UTC
13:25:47 KST

Tech entrepreneur Oren Dobronsky has dropped out of Likud’s Knesset slate rather than give up his U.S. citizenship, abandoning a top-10 spot offered by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opting instead for a potential role as a professional minister responsible for artificial intelligence.
Under Israeli law, Dobronsky would have been required to take steps to relinquish his U.S. citizenship before being sworn in as a member of Knesset. The decision could also have carried a significant financial cost because renouncing U.S. citizenship can trigger an “exit tax” for wealthy Americans with substantial assets. The citizenship issue had emerged in recent weeks as a major obstacle to his candidacy.
Dobronsky announced overnight that he had decided not to run for parliament, saying he and Netanyahu had agreed that he would instead join the Likud team as a professional, non-Knesset minister for AI if Netanyahu forms the next government.
“The prime minister asked me two months ago to join the Likud team in the coming elections, and that is what will happen,” Dobronsky wrote on Facebook.
“The prime minister offered me the position of minister for AI affairs and a reserved spot in the top 10 of the list,” he said. “Nevertheless, I preferred to serve only as a professional minister, where I can contribute the most from my experience, and not to be on the list itself as a member of Knesset, and that is what we agreed.”
“I intend to work hand in hand with Prime Minister Netanyahu, as part of the Likud team, to make sure that the State of Israel becomes an AI superpower,” he added.
Dobronsky’s withdrawal came as Netanyahu continued to hold back the names of his remaining reserved candidates, even after a deadline imposed by Likud’s internal tribunal expired.
The tribunal had warned that the delay could open the way for a secret ballot among members of the Likud Secretariat. Likud officials nevertheless told ynet that Netanyahu “has no intention of allowing such a vote.”
Netanyahu appears determined to leave his remaining decisions until the final hours. A meeting of the Likud Secretariat, which is supposed to approve the reserved slots and was originally scheduled for 11 a.m. Tuesday, was first postponed until 2 p.m. Even that time was not considered final.
The national deadline for political parties to submit their candidate lists to Israel’s Central Elections Committee is 10 p.m. Tuesday.
Netanyahu, through attorney Ilan Bombach, Likud’s legal adviser, criticized the tribunal’s ruling. Bombach said Netanyahu intended to provide the list of reserved candidates Tuesday morning, giving Secretariat members what he described as “several hours of sufficient time” to review it.
“Only 115 minutes were allocated to study a petition consisting of dozens of pages and appendices, receive instructions, establish the facts, formulate a position and submit a legal response,” Bombach wrote. “This was despite the fact that, as far as the respondent knows, the petition itself had already been submitted at around 12 p.m.”
He said the timetable was “unreasonable and disproportionate” and materially impaired the party’s ability to present its case.
“The situation is particularly serious because the decision was issued ex parte, without first requesting the respondent’s position, and even created a new operative outcome regarding the voting mechanism in the Secretariat,” Bombach wrote. “This response is therefore being submitted under protest, solely out of caution, and without exhausting the respondent’s arguments or waiving any procedural or substantive claim.”
The dispute stems from a ruling Monday by the Likud tribunal, signed by attorney Yitzhak Bam. Bombach had informed the tribunal that political circumstances made it impossible to comply fully with an earlier requirement to notify Secretariat members of Netanyahu’s proposed reserved slots 48 hours before the vote.
“Extreme political constraints may justify a deviation from this timetable,” Bam wrote. “But it appears that after some of the parties that created those constraints have already submitted their lists to the Central Elections Committee, the proposal regarding reserved slots, if the movement chairman intends to use them, should be published promptly.”
Bam said the 48-hour notice period was designed to give Secretariat members time to consider the proposed candidates and, if they believed it necessary, demand a secret ballot.
“Publishing a proposed decision shortly before the vote could be interpreted as an improper fait accompli,” he wrote.
The tribunal said that if no formal proposal was delivered to Secretariat members by 9 p.m. Monday, Likud’s legal adviser would have to explain why the failure should not be regarded as implicit consent to a secret ballot without the usual requirement to collect signatures from 10% of Secretariat members.
Netanyahu has nevertheless continued to hold his cards close until the final hours.
He has already spoken with prospective candidates. One has even filmed campaign material, but the video has not been released because Netanyahu has yet to make a final decision.
Senior ministers and members of Netanyahu’s close circle, including his wife, Sara Netanyahu, and son Yair Netanyahu, have also been pressing him to select candidates firmly identified with the political right.
One argument repeatedly raised in the discussions concerns the possibility of a deadlock between Israel’s political blocs. Netanyahu’s allies want to avoid a scenario in which a lawmaker elected with his bloc later crosses sides and provides the rival camp with the 61 seats required for a Knesset majority.
Behind the delay is not only Netanyahu’s tendency to postpone major political decisions until the last moment. He has also so far failed to secure a candidate regarded within Likud as an electoral “game changer.”
Netanyahu has already announced several candidates for reserved positions, including Gideon Sa’ar, Haim Katz and Israel Katz. Likud lawmaker Michel Buskila, a close ally of Sa’ar, is also expected to receive a reserved slot under the agreement with Sa’ar’s New Hope party.
According to senior Likud officials, attorney David Peter is considered one of the most certain candidates for another reserved position. Peter, a lawyer and researcher at the conservative Kohelet Policy Forum, is identified with the political right and has represented the government in several High Court petitions, as well as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Netanyahu is also considering Prof. Keren Assayag, though the prospect has drawn opposition from some members of his inner circle. Some associates view her candidacy as a political gamble with limited electoral value.

Source: Ukrainska Pravda article
Quote: "According to Ukrainska Pravda sources in law enforcement agencies, during searches at the home of Mariia Vdovychenko, Kravchenko's first deputy, who remains in her position for now, materials were found indicating surveillance of the heads of anti-corruption agencies, their families and subordinates."
Details: According to Ukrainska Pravda's sources in the prosecution service, they received an order to collate all available materials concerning the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) on the morning of 7 September.
"This may indicate that, despite the recent events, the prosecutor general intended to launch a counterattack against the anti-corruption agencies," the article noted.
The article also said that the results of last year's attempt to impose Russian influence on the anti-corruption agencies may indicate that "in its actions, the Prosecutor General's Office puts the attack itself before its legality".
Previously: According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Kravchenko and Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, on 7 September.
The decision on whether Kravchenko could continue as prosecutor general was expected to be made following the meeting.
Speaking to journalists on 7 September, Kravchenko said that he had no plans to resign amid the scandal which has arisen following the publication of materials from Operation Carthage, an investigation being conducted by NABU.
On the evening of the same day, Ruslan Kravchenko submitted his resignation as prosecutor general amid the NABU and SAPO investigation into the "protection" of scam call centres.
Background:
- On 4 September, Ukrainska Pravda reported that NABU and SAPO were conducting searches at the premises of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, his deputy Mariia Vdovychenko and Oleh Kiper, Head of Odesa Oblast Military Administration.
- On 5 September, the Prosecutor General's Office confirmed that NABU detectives had conducted searches in official premises "used by Kravchenko".
- According to Ukrainska Pravda sources in business circles, NABU and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) had detained Serhii Kropyva, deputy head of the International Legal Cooperation Department of the Prosecutor General's Office.
- On 5 September, NABU and SAPO announced that they had uncovered a criminal organisation which investigators said is headed by the head of a department at the Prosecutor General's Office. Members of the organisation are suspected of regularly taking bribes from scam call centres and money laundering. Sources told Ukrainska Pravda that the department head in question is Serhii Kropyva.
- On 6 September, Kropyva was remanded in custody with bail set at UAH 120 million (US$2.7 million).
- On 7 September, the High Anti-Corruption Court imposed a pre-trial restriction on 24-year-old Yelyzaveta Ivakhnenko, a suspect in NABU's Operation Carthage investigation into the alleged protection of scam call centres, ordering 60 days' detention with bail set at UAH 20 million (US$450,000).
- Serhii Kropyva's driver, Serhii Kutsyi, has also been remanded in custody with bail set at UAH 3 million (US$67,500).

Anthony Albanese says he's not trying to stop you from doomscrolling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:22:59 UTC
13:22:59 KST

In brief
- Digital duty of care laws will compel social media companies to protect users from harmful content.
- It will also offer Australians the option to opt out of seeing personally recommended content from social media algorithms.
Australian internet users will be given the choice to opt out of algorithmic recommendations under proposed social media reforms.
Draft laws setting up a digital duty of care were introduced by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Tuesday.
As part of the measures, social media companies will need to provide tools for people to choose what they see in their online feeds, under a government initiative called My Feed, My Way.
Social media companies have been accused of creating addictive algorithms that keep people endlessly scrolling through recommended content. Advocates have called for a reversion to chronological feeds that show posts from friends and other accounts a user follows.
"This is not about giving government control. It's about giving people control. It's about putting choice back into the hands of Australians online," Albanese told reporters in Canberra.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"If people want to doom scroll, as you call it, that's fine, that's up to them," he said.
"But if people want to have a change, then this will provide them with the opportunity."
He pointed to global discussion over harms linked to social media, including at the United Nations.
"It's a debate that's taking place in countries all around the world, because of the sort of impact that we're seeing," he added, citing a rise in mental health issues and eating disorders as examples.
The reforms had drawn backlash from both the Coalition and Greens before being formally announced, with Opposition leader Angus Taylor suggesting it could be akin to censorship.
Meanwhile, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young called for the opt-out algorithm to be made the default setting.
'A global reckoning coming for big tech'
Under the draft laws, social media companies will also be required to protect people from harmful content online.
Harmful content will include the promotion of eating disorders, misogynistic content, pornography or content that glorifies crime.
Albanese said the legislation would empower the government to issue removal notices for 'nudify' apps and websites, which typically use artificial intelligence to create fake nude images of people without their consent.
Sharing that type of content — nonconsensual deepfake sexualised images — is already illegal in much of Australia, but developing the tools to do so isn't.
Companies could face fines of $100 million if they don't enact the duty of care.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said the duty of care would build on the world-leading ban on social media for under-16s Australia introduced last year.
"The digital duty of care is not about controlling adults online. It is about giving adults a choice," she said.
"Tech companies can still move fast, but they will no longer be allowed to break things because online harms have real-world consequences.
"There is a global reckoning coming for big tech."
It follows the government looking to pursue stronger penalties for social media companies as part of measures to bolster the under-16s ban.

The flare-up in violence between Saudi Arabia and the militant group came as tensions mounted between the United States and Iran and the wider Middle East conflict sent oil prices soaring with diplomatic negotiations stalling.
Brent crude futures rose $1 to $98 a barrel after the Saudi energy ministry statement, while U.S. crude futures rose over $2 to $93.65 a barrel.
The Houthi military spokesperson announced what he described as a broad offensive against the de facto OPEC leader, targeting Saudi oil giant Aramco facilities in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as an air base in Khamis Mushait, with ballistic missiles and drones.
On Monday, the Financial Times newspaper said Aramco's Jazan oil facilities were hit in new strikes, and the damage was being assessed. Reuters was not immediately able to verify the report and Aramco has not commented.
SAUDI ARABIA CONDEMNS 'DANGEROUS' ESCALATION

The Saudi energy ministry said concerned authorities were dealing with the repercussions of the attacks.
"The needed measures will be taken to ensure the safety of the facilities and workers and the continuation of work according to the approved operational plans," said the ministry.

"The coalition will take all necessary operational measures to deter this terrorist militia and resolutely confront its hostile approach," Colonel Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods take effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:21:56 UTC
13:21:56 KST

Yasin Gungor
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on CAN$27.6 billion ($20 billion) worth of US goods early Tuesday, escalating a trade war between the neighboring countries.
The countermeasures, which took effect at 12.01 a.m. local time (0401GMT), match US Section 338 tariffs "dollar for dollar."
Ottawa is imposing 15%, 25% and 50% tariffs on US imports, targeting key sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.
The escalation follows the collapse of bilateral trade talks in late August, which prompted the administration of US President Donald Trump to impose 50% tariffs on key Canadian goods. The US measures targeted steel, aluminum, lumber and automotive components under Section 338, a US trade provision that empowers the president to impose retaliatory trade barriers.
Canada clarified that the counter tariffs only apply to goods originating from the US and will not affect shipments already in transit on the day of implementation.
The trade dispute has intensified dramatically under the Trump administration, with successive rounds of import taxes and retaliatory measures.
Trump has repeatedly criticized the Canada-US trade gap, pointing to it as a core reason for imposing tariffs and regularly alleging that Ottawa is "ripping off" America.

Taiwan MRT construction subsidies hit record NT$49.9 billion

2026-09-08

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Transportation and Communications' budget for next year includes a record NT$49.9 billion (US$1.58 billion) in subsidies for local MRT construction, about 5.5 times the NT$9 billion allocated for 2026, per a press release.
The ministry said the increase reflects the progress and funding needs of local MRT projects. It said subsidies are allocated based on factors including construction progress, tender results, and previous budget execution.
Despite more funds, not every municipality is content, as New Taipei noted that its request for funding was reduced by NT$5.5 billion. It has requested the ministry reconsider its original request and provide guidance about the reduced allocation.
New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜) said, "New Taipei has seen peak transportation construction in recent years. We have already sent a letter to the transport ministry, hoping that the NT$5.41 billion subsidy for the three MRT lines next year can be prioritized and supplemented," per PTS.
Regarding concerns about a bias in subsidies toward the north or south, the ministry said that it has provided more than NT$716.1 billion in subsidies for local MRT construction over the years, with Taipei, New Taipei, and Keelung receiving about NT$488.2 billion, or 68% of the total, per the press release.
The ministry said the high proportion received by the northern cities is mainly because MRT network construction in northern Taiwan began earlier and requires greater investment. It said funding for central and southern Taiwan has also continued to increase as projects progress.
Deputy Minister of Transportation Wu Sheng-yuan (伍勝園) said, "We don't manage how much money each region has; we only consider the progress of the project and the necessary funding and allocate accordingly. There are certain standards for approving MRT construction; we don't just look at the progress or the so-called north-south orientation," per PTS.
The ministry said its subsidy decisions are based on the actual circumstances and funding needs of individual projects rather than geographic considerations, per CNA. Reviewing the status of MRT projects across Taiwan, the Keelung MRT, which will connect to Taiwan Railways' Badu Station, has completed negotiations for its electromechanical systems and track turnkey projects.
The Taipei Metro Circular Line East Section and the Wanda-Zhonghe-Shulin Line are also under construction. New Taipei's Sanying Line will eventually extend to Bade, connecting with the Taoyuan MRT Green Line. Kaohsiung's Gangshan-Luzhu Extension and Xiaogang-Linyuan Line are also under construction.
The Taichung MRT Orange Line and the Blue Line are in the comprehensive planning stage. The Tainan MRT Blue Line has also been approved by the Cabinet.

KMT Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) argued that Cho was attempting to portray his decision to refuse countersigning as a passive reaction to the legislature, per UDN. TPP Legislative Caucus Convener Chen Ching-lung (陳清龍) argued that if Cho had the power to judge the constitutionality of bills passed by the legislature and ignore legislative decisions on the budget, he would effectively hold the executive and judicial branches in his hands while making the legislature a figurehead.
DPP Legislator Lin Chu-yin (林楚茵) previously defended Cho’s refusal to countersign, arguing that the premier has the authority to take such action to defend the Constitution, per CNA. She urged the legislature to refrain from misconstruing the countersignature mechanism to cover what she described as a track record of destroying the Constitution.
President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) Control Yuan member nominee and Soochow University Professor Hsu Yu-wei (許有為) argued that countersigning laws is a power rather than an obligation for the premier, per Mirror Daily. He stressed that countersigning power has long been among the executive branch’s arsenal, alongside discharging the legislature, requesting reconsideration, and seeking constitutional review.
Hsu emphasized that the legislature could request a no-confidence vote against Cho if it deemed that he had overstepped his authority. He warned that designating countersigning power as a duty could allow the legislature to effectively capture the executive branch and take power away from the president, who received a mandate to govern.
University of Warwick School of Law Reader Kuo Ming-sung (郭銘松) pointed out that countersigning is a legacy mechanism from a system in which the appointment of the premier required legislative consent, per I•CONnect. He argued that reconsideration most closely resembles an executive veto under the Constitution, requiring the premier to accept bills reaffirmed by the legislature.
Kuo said the countersignature mechanism was designed as a check on the president. However, the 1997 constitutional reforms, which gave the president unilateral power to appoint and dismiss premiers, have effectively deprived the mechanism of its significance.
Kuo stressed that the countersignature requirement is now effectively an “ultra-executive veto” that can be wielded against a legislature controlled by the opposition.

Letters Targeting Kashmiri Pandits Surface on Social Media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:12:00 UTC
13:12:00 KST

Letters threatening Kashmiri Pandits that surfaced on social media in August have set off a wave of panic among members of the community living in Jammu and Kashmir (J&K). They have revived memories of the “hit lists” and assassinations that forced around 350,000 Pandits to flee the Kashmir valley over 36 years ago.
Three letters, all issued in the name of the United Liberation Council (ULC), said to be a front organization of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba, have surfaced on social media so far. The most recent letter, dated August 27, was explicitly linked to the Indian government reopening investigations into the massacre of Pandits by Islamist militants at the height of the anti-India militancy in the 1990s.
“If the SIA [State Investigation Agency of J&K] or any other agency is so eager to reopen closed cases involving migrant Pandits, they should also investigate cases like Bijebehara, Gawkadal, Sopore, Handwara, etc., where the so-called Indian mercenary security forces deliberately opened fire on innocent Kashmiris,” the letter said. “We will slaughter all those involved in these crimes no matter how much security they have.”
The first letter, dated August 7, named six Pandits working in the J&K government’s revenue department and included their cell phone numbers. It called on them to “change their ways.” The second letter, dated August 23, named six more Pandits and provided their residential addresses, including house numbers and street names. It described them as “white collar terrorists” and “traitors,” working for their “masters” in Delhi.
The letter’s contents were ominous. “Wherever you are and wherever you go, we are watching your every move,” it said. While the August 7 letter named Pandits working in the valley, the August 23 post listed Pandits in Jammu.
Kashmiri Pandits are Hindus and indigenous to the Muslim-dominated Kashmir valley. At the start of the militancy in 1989-1990, several Pandits, including Tika Lal Taploo, Neelkanth Ganjoo, Sarwanand Koul Premi and Virender Koul were assassinated. Sarla Bhat, a nurse, was abducted, raped and killed. Although militants claimed they were killed for their links to the Indian state – Taploo was a politician and Ganjoo was a high court judge—amid the rising tide of Islamism in Kashmir, it caused immense fear among the Pandits.
In an article I wrote for The Diplomat in 2020, I recounted what Ashok Dhar, a Pandit previously living in Baramulla in the valley, told me about what happened in 1989-90. “It was evident that Kashmiri Muslims wanted us to leave the Valley,” he recalled. Militant groups like the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front and the Hizbul Mujahideen brought out “hit lists” with names of Pandits to be eliminated. People shouted anti-Pandit slogans in mosques and at rallies. “They wanted sharia rule in Kashmir,” Dhar said, adding that Pandits were given a choice to convert to Islam or leave the valley.
Around 70,000 Pandit families comprising over 350,000 women, men, and children fled the valley in 1990. Dhar and his family were among them.
Most of the Pandits who left the Kashmir valley were subsequently housed in migrant camps in Jammu and Delhi. Many settled in other Indian cities. Most of them have never returned home. A few hundred families remained in the valley.
In its letters, the JLC has distinguished between those who remained in the valley and those who left. It is the latter that it is targeting now, the letters say.
While for most part, Pandits in the valley were left unharmed over the decades, Islamist militants have targeted the community periodically. The Lashkar-e-Taiba and the Hizbul Mujahideen massacred 23 Pandits, including four children, at Wandhama in 1997 and another 24 Pandits, including two children, at Nadimarg in 2003.
Memories of the terror they experienced remain deeply etched in the memory of Pandits.
Soon after the second letter emerged, Dhar, who now lives in Bengaluru, spoke to The Diplomat. The JLC’s lists providing names and other identifying details of Pandits “are no different from the hit lists of 1990,” he said.
Since 2008, when former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh announced a rehabilitation package, New Delhi has promised government jobs, cash doles, accommodation and security to Pandits returning to the valley. Yet this has not been enough to convince them to return in large numbers.
Continuing attacks on Pandits in the valley – in October 2021, for example, a pharmacist who stayed back in Srinagar, J&K’s capital, in 1990, was shot dead – have kept the community on tenterhooks. The government may have provided returning Pandits with tight security but since they live in clusters, they fear they are sitting ducks for Islamist militants.
In recent months, New Delhi has reopened investigations into several high-profile murders and massacres by militant groups in Kashmir. Among the cases that have been reopened are the rape and murder of Sarla Bhat, and the massacre at Wandhama.
These investigations could serve to meet the demands of Kashmiri Pandit organizations that have been demanding justice. But also, they will reopen old wounds.
Meanwhile, this is sure to prompt Kashmiri Muslims to demand justice in incidents of mass killings by the Indian security forces. The ULC referred to this in its third letter. “It appears to be positioning itself as a guardian of Kashmiri Muslim interests. But Kashmiris, “even the Muslims, are unlikely to be impressed as they have suffered for decades, even as the militant groups operated from the safety of camps in Pakistan,” Dhar said.
When two non-Kashmiri Indian laborers working at a brick kiln in Kulgam district in the valley were shot dead on July 31, analysts pointed out that militants were hitting “soft targets” as they were not strong enough to take on India’s security forces. The targeting of Pandit civilians is yet another example of militants seeking to assert their presence by intimidating unarmed people.
Should the letters prompt Pandits to leave again, it will deal a blow to New Delhi’s efforts to normalize the situation in J&K.

Breaking: Cricket Australia agrees to bring private investment to Big Bash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:08:01 UTC
13:08:01 KST

Cricket Australia (CA) has agreed to invite private investment into the Big Bash Leagues, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades franchise.
The success of that process will determine whether CA considers taking other franchises to market.
What's next?
CA says it intends to have the Renegades playing under new ownership for the 2027/28 Big Bash season.
Cricket Australia has agreed to bring private investment into the Big Bash League, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.
The Cricket Australia (CA) board made the announcement on Tuesday, with the sale process of the Renegades to be the first venture into bringing private investment into the franchise T20 league.
CA is hoping the Renegades will play under new ownership for the 2027/28 Big Bash season.
Depending on the success of the Renegades sale, CA said in a statement on Tuesday that it would "consider taking other clubs to market under a self-determination model that gives each State member the ability to assess the optimal pathway for its own club and community".
CA chair Mike Baird said the decision was a major moment for cricket in Australia.
"Beginning the sales process for the Renegades allows us to take the first step in a self-determination model for our members and represents a defining moment for the game," he said.
"Importantly, CA and its members will maintain control over the most significant aspects of Australian Cricket operations, including international scheduling, player availability, the Big Bash Leagues' salary caps, branding proposals as well as the reserve price for a licence to operate that must be achieved, and approval of investors."
The move to bring private investment into the Big Bash Leagues has been debated for months.
CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said in May that private investment was "inevitable", and privatisation was thrust into the spotlight when Cricket Victoria made plans to sell the Renegades in June.
Baird said inviting private investment would allow cricket to grow at every level of the game.
"Cricket Australia and its state members are united in our commitment to investing in and growing the BBL and WBBL, and to advancing the interests of cricket at every level," he said.
"By opening the door to private investment in the Big Bash Leagues, Cricket Australia is taking a deliberate step to strengthen and secure the long-term future of the game, accelerate growth and ensuring we can keep investing in community cricket and grassroots participation, domestic and international pathways and the elite level.
"This is a significant decision that has involved an enormous amount of analysis, discussion and collaboration over many months. I'd like to thank all involved as we move to what we believe is the best way to secure cricket's future in this country, strengthen the Big Bash and protect our standing on the global stage."

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs take effect as US trade talks stall
- Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on US goods worth US$20 billion, with duties from 15 per cent to 50 per cent, escalating the 18-month trade war after failed negotiations in August.
- US tariffs target Canadian sectors like wine, furniture, and dairy, affecting 5 per cent of Canadian exports and causing uncertainty over the USMCA trade agreement's future.
- Despite rising tensions, Canada aims to keep trade talks open, with public support for Prime Minister Carney possibly declining as trade war impacts grow.
AI generated
OTTAWA – Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect just after midnight on Sept 8 as Prime Minister Mark Carney increased economic pressure on his country’s biggest trading partner after negotiations collapsed in August, intensifying an 18-month-old trade war.
The counter-tariffs cover US$20 billion (S$25 billion) of US goods, with duties ranging from 15 per cent to 50 per cent across products from steel and furniture to clothing and electronics.
The dollar-for-dollar retaliation marks an escalation in the dispute between the neighbouring countries, and US and Canadian officials have traded blame for scuttling a deal that seemed close to fruition two weeks ago.
The rising tensions create uncertainty about the broader US-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) free trade agreement, which is up for annual review after US President Donald Trump declined to extend it for another decade.
“What we are worried about is an escalatory spiral,” said Michael Harvey, executive director of the Canadian Agri-Food Trade Alliance and a member of Carney’s advisory committee on bilateral US economic relations.
“But at the same time, we totally understand that the prime minister needs to find areas of leverage,” Harvey said.
US tariffs hit Canadian wine, furniture and dairy
Trump’s tariffs implemented in August hit sectors including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment, covering US$20 billion, or 5 per cent, of Canadian exports to the US.
According to Canadian and US government data, Canada has shipped almost 68 per cent of total exports to the US in 2026, out of which roughly 80 per cent moved duty-free due to exemptions under the USMCA pact. Protections under the agreement have provided the domestic economy some resilience.
The new tariffs, imposed under a Depression-era US law, do not allow Ottawa to exercise USMCA exemptions.
Concerns about the USMCA’s future have fuelled uncertainty about investment and growth, as Canada wages a trade war against an economy 13 times its size.
Polls show Carney has broad support from Canadians, but it could disappear within months as the consequences of the trade war sink in, according to political analysts.
Just 20 per cent of Americans approved of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
Carney said last week his government was ready to sign a trade deal that benefits both countries.
Trump threatened in August to raise US tariffs on all cars, trucks and automotive parts from Canada to 50 per cent starting Jan 1, and signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.
A government source said there are currently no talks between the two sides among ministers or government officials.
“The Canadian government needs to keep channels open to the United States and not go overboard in terms of rhetoric and reacting to the rhetoric from the American side, while waiting for the American decision-making process to come back to economics,” Harvey said. REUTERS

Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Saratov Oil Refinery in Russia overnight on Sept. 8, according to footage shared by locals on social media and analyzed by monitoring groups.
Saratov is located approximately 460 kilometers (285 miles) east of the Ukrainian border with Russia, near Luhansk Oblast in eastern Ukraine.
Residents of Saratov reported explosions and a fire at the refinery overnight, posting photos and videos of the attack. Independent Russian outlet Astra analyzed the footage and concluded based on geolocation that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and was burning.
Saratov Oblast Governor Roman Busargin later said that 10 people, including three children, were injured in the attack. Six were hospitalized, though none were in life-threatening condition, according to the governor. Busargin did not specify the target of the strike.
Residents of the Saratov Oblast town of Engels also reported air defense activity near the Engels-2 military airfield, home of Russia's strategic bombers. It is not yet clear whether the base was hit.
Russian regional authorities also reported casualties and damage elsewhere.
In Belgorod Oblast, attacks over the past day killed one person and injured four others, while regional authorities claimed that 130 drones had been downed or suppressed.
In neighboring Kursk Oblast, three settlements lost power after a drone struck a power line in the Belovsky district, according to the Russian Telegram channel Pepel Kursk. The channel also reported damage to homes and a shop, as well as a separate drone strike on an energy facility in the Khomutovsky district.
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that 384 Ukrainian drones were intercepted and destroyed overnight over multiple Russian regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the Black Sea.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports at the time of publication.
The Rosneft-owned Saratov refinery is a major oil-processing facility that has been targeted by Ukrainian forces in multiple previous strikes. The plant has an annual processing capacity of about 4.8 million tons and produces over 20 types of petroleum products, including gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, bitumen.
According to Ukraine's General Staff, the Saratov Oil Refinery helps supply the Russian military.
The General Staff confirmed a successful strike on the facility on Aug. 2. A month before, a July 8 strike forced the plant to halt processing after its only crude distillation unit was reportedly damaged.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have emerged as one of the most economically significant aspects of Kyiv's long-range drone campaign, contributing to fuel shortages and pushing Russian refinery output down sharply over the summer.
The reported Saratov strike came as Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones overnight, bringing the respite afforded by a brief diplomatic pause in attacks on the capital to an abrupt end.

At least 73 civilians were injured following attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group targeting cities and economic infrastructure in southern Saudi Arabia, the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said Tuesday.
At least 73 civilians were injured in Houthi attacks targeting cities and economic infrastructure in southern Saudi Arabia, Saudi authorities said Tuesday, as Riyadh warned against continued attacks on civilians and commercial shipping.
In a statement, the Saudi Foreign Ministry strongly condemned the attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group on civilian and economic facilities in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, saying they injured 73 civilians, including women and children.
The ministry also denounced the group’s continued targeting of commercial vessels in the Red Sea, saying the attacks threaten freedom of international maritime navigation.
It reiterated Saudi Arabia’s rejection of what it called the Houthis’ “hostile approach and criminal behavior,” saying they threaten the security and stability of Yemen and its Arab and Islamic surroundings and undermine peace efforts.
The ministry affirmed the kingdom’s right to take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty and national capabilities and protect the security and safety of its citizens and residents.
It also warned against the Houthis’ continued targeting of civilians and civilian facilities and called for an immediate halt to all forms of escalation and continuing threats to maritime security.
Riyadh called on the international community to shoulder its responsibilities and implement relevant UN Security Council resolutions, particularly resolutions 2216 of 2015 and 2722 of 2024.
In a separate statement, the Saudi Energy Ministry said fires broke out at energy facilities and installations following attacks in the country’s southern region.
The attacks caused a temporary halt to some operations at the targeted sites, the ministry said, adding that specialized teams had begun containing the fires and securing the facilities.
Separately, Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki accused the Houthis of launching “senseless attacks” against civilian and commercial sites in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran.
Al-Maliki characterized the strikes as a “dangerous escalation” and a “blatant violation” of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty.
He accused the group of deliberate “extremist and criminal behavior” that undermines peace and stability in Yemen and neighboring Arab states.
Al-Maliki affirmed that the Joint Forces Command of the coalition would deploy “all necessary operational measures” to deter the attacks and protect Saudi citizens.
The coalition also vowed to take all necessary measures to neutralize the sources of the threat.
In a concurrent statement, the Yemeni army declared its “complete readiness” to stand “steadfastly” alongside Saudi Arabia.
The military leadership backed Riyadh’s “absolute right to take whatever measures it deems appropriate” to defend its security, stability and sovereignty, expressing preparedness to coordinate to “eliminate the sources of threat and chaos.”
The attacks came as Yemeni government forces reported significant battlefield gains on Monday across four separate fronts.
According to Yemen’s official Saba news agency, the military advances took place in the Al-Jawf, Al-Bayda, Taiz and Al-Hudaydah governorates, following a vow by Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi to sustain operations until state authority is fully restored.
The recent fighting has raised fears of a return to full-scale conflict, disrupting a relative lull observed since April 2022.
Yemen has suffered nearly 12 years of war since the Iranian-backed Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014.
The Houthis have also targeted commercial shipping in the Red Sea, while Saudi Arabia, the principal external actor backing Yemen’s internationally recognized government, announced a mission in July to form an international maritime alliance.
Fires broke out at energy facilities in southern Saudi Arabia following attacks targeting the sites, the Saudi Energy Ministry said Tuesday.
The ministry added in a statement that the attacks caused a temporary halt to some operations at the targeted facilities.
“Specialized teams have begun containing the fires and securing the affected sites,” it said.
The statement came after Saudi authorities said early Tuesday that attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group targeted civilian and economic facilities in the southern cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, injuring at least 73 civilians, including women and children.
The Saudi-led coalition called the attacks a “dangerous escalation” and vowed to take necessary operational measures to neutralize the sources of threats.
Two children were killed and 15 people injured in Houthi shelling targeting a gathering of displaced people in Yemen’s central Marib province, local authorities said Tuesday.
The government-run local authority said in a statement that the Houthis fired several projectiles at a gathering of displaced people in the Raghwan district in northern Marib on Monday evening.
The attack killed two children and injured 15 people, including eight children, it said.
The shelling also caused extensive damage to the homes and property of displaced families.
According to the statement, around 16 shelters and their contents were destroyed, leaving 23 families without accommodation and basic belongings, while three vehicles were also damaged.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthi group on the statement.
Yemen’s Houthi group on Tuesday confirmed carrying out large-scale missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia and vowed to continue operations deep inside the kingdom amid a sharp escalation between the two sides.
In a statement, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group carried out a “large-scale” military operation using dozens of ballistic missiles and drones.
He said the attacks targeted Aramco facilities in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as Khamis Mushait Air Base.
Saree claimed the strikes were “precise and direct” and caused extensive damage to the targeted facilities.
The Houthi spokesperson said the operation was in response to Saudi airstrikes in Yemen, claiming that Saudi Arabia had carried out 121 strikes over the past three days in Marib, Al-Bayda, Al-Hudaydah, Taiz and Al-Jawf provinces.
He also accused Saudi Arabia of striking the Central Prison in Al-Hazm, Al-Jawf, causing casualties among inmates and visitors, including women and children.
“We will continue our operations deep inside Saudi territory, target its military buildups, and consolidate the equation of ‘blockade for blockade’ until the aggression stops and the blockade on our dear country is lifted,” Saree said.
The statement came after Saudi authorities said earlier Tuesday that Houthi attacks on Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran injured at least 73 civilians, including women and children.
The Saudi Energy Ministry also reported fires at energy facilities in the kingdom’s southern region and said some operations at the targeted sites were temporarily halted.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki called the attacks a “dangerous escalation” and said the coalition would take all necessary operational measures to deter the Houthis and neutralize sources of threats.
The Yemeni army said Tuesday that it had recaptured the Al-Yatmah area in Al-Jawf province in northern Yemen from the Houthi group.
“Our armed forces managed to liberate the Al-Yatmah area in Khabb wa Al-Shaaf district in Al-Jawf from the grip of the Houthi militias,” the army said in a statement.
It said the development came amid continued field advances against the Houthis, without providing further details.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthi group.
Al-Yatmah is one of the key areas in the strategic Al-Jawf province, which is located near the Saudi border. It shares border with the oil-rich Marib province, one of the most important strongholds of the internationally recognized government.
For days, military confrontations have escalated between government forces and the Houthis on several fronts, particularly in Taiz, Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda provinces, alongside airstrikes on the group’s positions.

Pakistan, he said, stands in "unwavering" solidarity with the Saudi leadership and its people.
"Such dastardly attacks threaten innocent lives as well as regional peace and security. We reaffirm our steadfast support for the Kingdom’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity, and pray for the swift recovery of all those injured," Sharif added.
Russia considers Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure "counterproductive," Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Larov said on Tuesday, backing Riyadh’s efforts to implement an agreed road map.
Speaking at a joint news conference after talks with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan in Moscow, Lavrov such issues should not be resolved militarily, warning that attacks threaten civilians and infrastructure and could disrupt global trade routes and the world economy given the strategic importance of the Arabian Peninsula.
Prince Faisal said the kingdom continues to offer diplomatic solutions aimed at preventing further suffering for Yemen and its people.
He accused the Houthi group of seeking to advance its own interests without regard for Yemen’s interests, saying its recent escalation against Saudi Arabia was part of that approach.

At the time, Carney said the Trump administration's terms were ultimately unacceptable, adding that US negotiators had introduced restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the eleventh hour.
US officials also made unacceptable "threats" to the French language and "Quebec culture", he added, referencing the French-speaking province in eastern Canada.
But Trump's top trade official Jamieson Greer later noted that the US government is aware that French language protections are sensitive and important.
"This is not something where we push hard, or condition, or red-line," he told Canadian public broadcaster CBC last month.
War of words
Ottawa and Washington have not resumed negotiations since, and have continued trading barbs.
Asked if both sides were in a trade war, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC last week (Aug 31) that he did not think one could be in a tit-for-tat fight with a country that is 13 times larger.
"We're not at war with Canada," Bessent said on the sidelines of a G20 finance leaders' meeting. "How are we going to be at war with Canada? They're going to take their two set submarines from the Edmonton Mall and sic them on us?"
He was referring to a former attraction at a shopping center in the Alberta province.
Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth separately appeared to mock the physical appearance of a Canadian soldier on social media.
Read moreHow the French language became a sticking point in the US-Canada trade war
Carney said a day later that the remarks were "beneath their office", adding that this was "not constructive".
He said both sides can have discussions "when the Americans stop doing memes" and start being serious.
Trump also signed an order in August to rename Lake Ontario, on the border with Canada, as "Lake America".
This has sparked anger in Canada, amid a broader wave of patriotism triggered by Trump's hostility.
At the start of his second presidency, Trump also ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed the Gulf of America. He has made claims that Canada should become the 51st US state as well.
Although Carney is backed by Canadian public opinion, his country remains reliant on its neighbour. Nearly 60 percent of Canada's imports come from the United States and about 70 percent of its exports go to the US market.
To help businesses and workers, Canada's government has unveiled an aid package of $7.5 billion (US$5.4 billion).

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of US goods take effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:01:12 UTC
13:01:12 KST

As Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods take effect, tensions soar
Trade tensions soar as Canada matches US tariffs ‘dollar-for-dollar’, impacting 700 products and multiple industries.
Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on imports from the United States have taken effect, as a trade dispute between the two countries continues to escalate.
Tariffs ranging from 15 percent to 50 percent will apply to nearly $20bn worth of US imports from 12:01am ET (04:01 GMT) on Tuesday, matching US-imposed levies on Canadian goods including machinery, textiles and consumer products.
The new retaliatory tariffs apply to products including steel, household appliances, agricultural equipment and dairy.
“We have everything we need to pivot and prosper,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video shared on social media on Tuesday after the tariffs came into effect. “That pivot will come at a cost. There’s always a cost to action. But it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still.”
US President Donald Trump announced 50 percent tariffs against Canada in July, citing “discriminatory treatment” of US products. The announcement prompted the countries to enter trade talks in August, but a final deal failed to materialise before a deadline imposed by Trump as Ottawa walked away from what it said was a bad deal. US tariffs on Canadian goods came into place on August 22.
“Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!” Trump posted on Truth Social in response to Canada’s announcement in August.
On Tuesday, Trump, in a post on Truth Social, directed the General Services Administration, a US government body responsible for providing services for the federal government, to coordinate with the US Trade Representative and “REMOVE Canadian-origin products from GSA’s Multiple Award Schedules unless Canada restores full and fair reciprocity for American Farmers and Companies.”
Also on Tuesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that Carney “needs to stop campaigning and start governing,” adding the US was unsure why Canada pulled out of negotiations.
The Canadian government has said that the counter-tariffs will affect more than 700 products, adding that it would launch a $5.42bn support package for affected small and medium-sized businesses and workers.
On the eve of Ottawa imposing its tariffs, Trump threatened to block Canada-based aircraft manufacturer Bombardier from selling its planes in the US unless it began manufacturing them in the country. Bombardier has said it employs thousands of workers in the US.
Flavio Volpe, president of APMA Canada, a manufacturing trade group, responded on X that Bombardier uses US-made GE and Honeywell jet engines.
Widening dispute
The dispute between the once close allies has also extended beyond tariffs. On Sunday, Trump posted an illustration of himself towering over Carney as they played ice hockey, with Trump saying “Get up, governor” — a reference to Trump’s determination to turn Canada into another US state.
Last month, Trump signed an order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” for US federal use.
The retaliatory tariffs could place a financial burden on US automakers as Canada is the largest buyer of US-manufactured cars.
Americans could soon see increased prices on 550 consumer goods from Canada. According to a report from the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, US importers and consumers absorb 96 percent of the tariff burden.
Analysts have also expressed concern about the impact of greater instability in trade relations between the US, Canada, and Mexico, previously defined by a high level of integration.
“What we are worried about is an escalatory spiral,” Michael Harvey, executive director of the Canadian Agri-Food Trade Alliance and a member of Carney’s advisory committee on bilateral US economic relations, told the news service Reuters.
“But at the same time, we totally understand that the prime minister needs to find areas of leverage,” he added.

World Insights: Far-right AfD's victory in eastern German state rattles political landscape
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:01:11 CST
13:01:11 KST

MAGDEBURG, Germany, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's victory in Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt has sent shockwaves through Germany's political establishment.
The AfD secured a record 43.8 percent of the vote, making it the strongest force in the state parliament. Meanwhile, the ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) suffered a heavy blow, with its share of the vote plummeting to 17.4 percent from 37.1 percent in the last election in 2021.
DEEP-ROOTED ANXIETY
Sunday's election reshaped the eastern German state's political map, making it possible for the AfD to run a German state for the first time.
According to official vote counts, the AfD can secure 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament, just three seats shy of an absolute majority.
According to German public broadcaster ARD, voters mostly endorsed the AfD's hardline stance on migration and approved the party's opposition to weapons deliveries to Ukraine.
Based on such promises, the AfD more than doubled its votes this year compared with the last state parliament election five years ago.
In addition, the party emerged as the strongest force across all age demographics, mobilizing a massive number of former non-voters while drawing significant support away from the CDU.
The AfD's voters told Xinhua that they are worried about their future, as the economic situation worsens and they feel their tax money is being spent in the wrong places.
Bastian, a 40-year-old AfD supporter, voiced his hope to "get the old Germany back."
From the voters' perspective, the CDU has clearly lost ground in terms of economic competence, while the AfD has made massive gains, especially in smaller towns and rural areas, places heavily impacted by ongoing depopulation, according to ARD.
COALITION DEADLOCK
After the election, the AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, said he is open to forming a ruling coalition with other parties in a bid to form a stable government.
But he also stressed that he would not abandon basic policy positions to do so.
Meanwhile, other major parties have repeatedly ruled out the possibility of entering a coalition with the AfD.
If the CDU wishes to keep the AfD out of power, it will be forced to form a highly complicated alliance spanning the political spectrum, potentially including the Social Democratic Party, the Greens, and even the Left party.
It is widely believed that forming stable coalitions will be difficult.
It seems clearer that the AfD is shaking up an increasingly fragmented political landscape in Germany, said economic research institute ING Think.
The institute added that the election results also show that last-moment mobilization against the AfD, as witnessed in other states before, no longer works.
FEDERAL AND EUROPEAN FALLOUT
The political earthquake in Magdeburg is already rattling Berlin.
Head of the Chancellery Nina Warken called the election outcome a "watershed moment" for the CDU, describing it on broadcaster ZDF as a "very, very difficult result."
Warken also insisted that the federal government would resolutely press ahead with its planned reform agenda.
The unprecedented results are expected to intensify internal debates within the federal government over its handling of key voter concerns, particularly regarding economic stagnation and the wealth gap between Germany's eastern and western regions, according to political observers.
ING Think noted a trend in multiple European countries of "an established right-wing party, a crumbling of the political center and a fragmented political landscape."
The potential of the AfD's wider impact depends on how far Siegmund's campaign recipe in Saxony-Anhalt can be replicated and if the AfD can now turn electoral backing into durable governing power, said London-based think tank Chatham House. ■

====================================================================================================

Slovenia, the ideal European destination for active holidays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:00:42 UTC
13:00:42 KST

Alpine lakes, emerald rivers, mountains, waterfalls, forests and an extraordinary underground world make Slovenia one of Europe's top active tourism destinations.
Some countries are places you simply visit; others urge you to travel through them. On foot, by bicycle, paddling across a lake, following a river downstream or heading beneath the surface of the earth. Slovenia clearly belongs to the second group.
This small country of just over 20,000 square kilometres and barely two million inhabitants concentrates an extraordinary variety of landscapes. Around 60% of its area is covered by forest and more than a third of its territory is protected or forms part of the Natura 2000 network.
It is the green lung of the Balkans and also a vast natural stage for anyone who prefers holidays spent on the move.
Hiking, cycling, climbing, kayaking, rafting, canyoning and caving are just some of the options on offer. And distances are short enough that in just a few hours you can go from a Central European capital to an Alpine lake, or from a river of turquoise water to one of the most spectacular underground canyons on the planet.
Over five days we travel around Slovenia in a camper van. It is a particularly appealing way to get to know the country because here the road is part of the journey too.
Ljubljana: The city of the dragon
Our first stop is Ljubljana, the capital and Slovenia's largest city. With fewer than 300,000 inhabitants, it is compact enough to be explored easily on foot. And that is probably the best way to get to know it.
The historic centre stretches out around the Ljubljanica river, which cuts through the city between bridges, terraces and colourful buildings. Bicycles are everywhere and there is a youthful atmosphere that is particularly noticeable in summer. The river is not just part of the urban landscape: its banks become a meeting place and an impromptu venue for sports and games, volleyball included.
Ljubljana is a city made for walking without rushing. A stroll takes you to the Central Market, where stalls piled with fruit, vegetables and local produce offer a snapshot of everyday life in the capital, and then continues along the river to some of its best-known bridges.
One of them immediately reveals the city's great symbol. Dragon Bridge is guarded by four large sculptures of the mythical creature. The dragon features on Ljubljana's coat of arms and appears all over the city. According to legend, its origins are linked to Jason and the Argonauts, who are said to have defeated a monster in the nearby marshes.
Above the old town rises Ljubljana Castle, a fortress with more than 900 years of history that can be reached either on foot or by funicular. From the top you get one of the best views over the city and, on clear days, of the mountains that herald the next stage of the trip.
Bled: Slovenia's picture-postcard view
We leave Ljubljana and head towards the Julian Alps. Our next stop is probably the country's most famous image: Bled. Its lake looks as if it had been made for the front of a postcard. Surrounded by mountains and forest, a tiny island crowned by a church rises out of the water, while a medieval castle commands the landscape from the top of a cliff.
But Bled is not just somewhere to take photos. A route of roughly six kilometres loops all the way around the lake. Cycling it is one of the best ways to discover the area because the scenery is constantly changing and you are forever stopping to admire it from different angles.
In summer it is hard to resist the water. There are designated swimming areas and, after pedalling around the shore, a dip with the Alps as a backdrop becomes one of those small experiences that explain why Slovenia works so well as an active tourism destination.
Bled is spectacular, but it is also one of the most visited places in the country. To find a slightly quieter side of Slovenia, you have to continue on towards Bohinj.
Bohinj: The wildest lake
The change is immediately obvious. Lake Bohinj, the largest permanent natural lake in Slovenia, is just over four kilometres long and lies at the heart of Triglav National Park.
Less touristy than Bled, it feels far more untamed. At certain times of day its waters are like a giant mirror. Mountains and forest are reflected on a surface that seems almost motionless, creating a blend of greens, blues and turquoises that is hard to forget.
There is no iconic island here to photograph. It is not needed. The landscape is the star. One of the best ways to enjoy it is by kayak. Paddling out onto Bohinj takes you away from the shore and lets you admire the mountains from another perspective. You can also swim, go paddleboarding or explore the shores by bike and on foot.
And just venturing into the surrounding mountains multiplies the options. Hundreds of kilometres of trails criss-cross this part of the Julian Alps. There are easy routes along the lakeshore and much more demanding ones that climb up into the peaks. Climbing enthusiasts will also find numerous rock faces and routes of varying levels of difficulty.
Everything unfolds under the watchful presence of Triglav which, at 2,864 metres, is Slovenia's highest peak and one of its great national symbols.
Winding roads
Between Bohinj and our next destination, we discover another of the advantages of travelling across Slovenia. Distances are relatively short and driving is part of the experience.
The roads twist and turn through forest, mountains and small villages. The greenery seems endless. At times, the landscape inevitably calls to mind Switzerland, although here everything is more compact and, in many areas, still less crowded.
A camper van also allows you to stop when you wish, change your route and make the most of a country where a journey of just a few hours can completely transform the landscape. Our next destination is Bovec, in western Slovenia, right in the heart of the Julian Alps.
Bovec and the emerald river
Bovec is small, but it is one of Slovenia's great adventure sports hubs. The reason becomes clear just a few kilometres outside the town.
The Soča river runs through this Alpine valley with water so intensely coloured that in places it barely looks real. Shades of turquoise, blue and emerald green mingle as the river winds its way between white rocks, gorges and forest.
It is one of Slovenia's great natural stages and also one of the best places in the country to go in search of adrenaline.
Rafting, kayaking and canyoning are among the most popular activities. In summer it is common to watch from the bridges as groups of brightly coloured kayaks glide along the Soča's crystal-clear waters.
But you do not have to throw yourself into the river to enjoy the valley. Bovec is an excellent base for hiking, cycling and mountain excursions in the surrounding peaks.
Among its natural attractions are the Boka and Virje waterfalls. Boka is one of the most spectacular falls in Slovenia, while Virje surprises visitors with its more intimate setting and the intense colour of its water.
For keen walkers, another destination is Krnsko Jezero, an Alpine lake at around 1,400 metres above sea level and framed by some of the region's most impressive summits.
And for those travelling through this part of the country by road there is another challenge: the Vršič Pass. At 1,611 metres above sea level it is the highest road pass in Slovenia. Its countless bends cut through the Julian Alps, linking the Soča valley with Kranjska Gora and turning the journey itself into an experience.
Above Bovec rises the Kanin massif, traditionally known for high-mountain skiing and historically connected to Italy's Sella Nevea area. Beyond the winter season, it offers an exceptional setting for hiking and mountaineering.
Bovec perhaps sums up Slovenia's active spirit better than anywhere else: here the landscape is not just something to look at. It is there to be explored.
Škocjan: An expedition underground
Our final major stop takes us into a completely different world. We leave behind the mountains, lakes and rivers and head to south-west Slovenia to delve into the bowels of the earth.
The Škocjan Caves were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986 and are one of the most impressive karst systems on the planet.
The architect of this landscape is the Reka river. Over thousands of years, the water has eroded the limestone rock to create a vast underground universe of galleries, chambers, waterfalls and canyons.
The visit begins on foot, but it soon becomes something very different from a conventional trip to a cave. As you descend and natural light disappears, the size of the caverns increases. The sound of the river begins to rise up from the depths and, at times, visitors have the feeling of having turned into expedition members.
Škocjan is home to one of the largest known underground river canyons in the world. The cave system extends for more than six kilometres of galleries and in places reaches over 200 metres deep. The tourist route covers roughly three kilometres and descends to around 144 metres below the surface.
One of the most impressive moments comes when you cross the Cerkvenik Bridge, suspended about 45 metres above the Reka river. The darkness, the sound of the water and the sheer rock walls surrounding visitors combine to create one of the most spectacular sights of the whole trip.
Visits are guided and the tour lasts around two hours. Even in the height of summer you need to come prepared: inside, the temperature is about 12 °C all year round, so it is advisable to bring warm clothing and, above all, comfortable shoes with good grip.
It is also a good idea to book tickets in advance. In the busiest months, tours can fill up, and turning up without a reservation may mean being unable to get in.
Škocjan or Postojna
Slovenia's underground world offers yet another of the country's major tourist attractions. Not far away are the famous Postojna Caves, although the experience there is very different.
Postojna is more tourist-oriented and more accessible. Part of the visit is made on board a small train that travels several kilometres into the cave system before the tour continues on foot among stalactites and stalagmites.
Škocjan, by contrast, feels much more like an adventure. There is no little train to soften the experience. You walk, you descend and you cross vast chambers while the Reka river keeps slowly carving out the rock beneath your feet.
Postojna impresses with its formations. Škocjan impresses with its scale and with the sensation of exploring an underground world.
Five days after setting off, Slovenia leaves a very clear impression: it feels much bigger than it looks on the map. Not because of its distances, but because of the diversity of experiences it offers.
For those who see active tourism as the best way to travel and discover a destination, this small country is a vast natural playground in the heart of Europe.

‘Why was mum in clothes you could wear in the winter?’: family seeks answers after care home heatstroke death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:00:27 UTC
13:00:27 KST

Anita Bazell had never coped with the heat very well, her family said. So they were worried about her when temperatures across the UK soared to record highs of 35C (95F) in May, and then again in June.
She was living in a nursing home in Southampton near her family, who had struggled to care for her at home due to her declining mobility. Although there were air conditioning units in the communal rooms, there was not one in Anita’s room, which was on the third floor.
“I used to see her every weekend. Heat rises and she was on the top floor, and the windows were open as far as the restrictors would let them go,” said her son, Steve Bazell. “It was hot in there. It was so hot you couldn’t sleep at night around here back then.”
The first phone call came on 25 June – Steve was told his mother was feeling unwell and she was being taken to bed. “I remember it because it was the hottest day on record [for June] that day,” Steve said. It was actually the second of three days that week when the temperature record for June was broken.
The next phone call, just after 9am the following day, was a shock. Paramedics called to say his mother had been found unresponsive and was being taken to Southampton general hospital. The family were urged to get there as soon as possible – medics were not sure she would make it to the hospital.
When they arrived, Anita’s face looked drooped on one side and they thought she had suffered a stroke. Doctors were putting towels soaked in ice water on her, replacing them every few minutes. The family were soon told she had been diagnosed with heatstroke, which had caused a bleed on the brain.
When she arrived in hospital, she had a body temperature of 41.2C – anything above 40C is considered a medical emergency.
“You could see her improving as she was getting cooler but she was still unresponsive,” he said. “We had mixed reactions. I mean, my mum was 88, but she was mentally fine. We couldn’t understand how this had happened – did they check on her?”
Anita was hospitalised on 26 June, which was then the hottest June day on record in the UK with 38C recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk, breaking the previous record of 35.6 degrees set in Southampton 50 years earlier. It was the fifth hottest day in the UK ever.
Steve was told Anita was one of at least seven elderly people taken to Southampton general hospital with heatstroke that day, and some did not make it there before they died.
The day before Anita’s admission, University hospital Southampton NHS foundation trust had declared a critical incident due to the extreme heat, which forced some operations and appointments to be cancelled.
David Higgs, the hospital’s deputy chief medical officer, later said Southampton general came “very close to collapse” during the June heatwave, which was “in many ways almost worse than Covid”.
“There was a huge amount of attendances in our emergency department. Primary care was overflooded. The ambulance service pretty much collapsed,” he told the city’s health and wellbeing board.
Steve said the hospital set up a special “cooling” ward specifically to deal with the influx of patients with heatstroke. Staff ran out of towels to soak in ice water to cool patients down, and resorted to cutting up bed sheets. “I remember I went upstairs to get more towels and help,” said Steve. “The hospital was really good. But they were stretched.”
Anita’s condition improved once her body temperature reduced, but ultimately there was nothing that could be done to save her. Over the next few days, Steve said her eyes would follow family members as they moved around her, and she could gently squeeze a hand when asked, but never regained full consciousness.
Steve and his sister took it in turns maintaining a bedside vigil every day until at least 10pm at night. He said they were a small but close family, and his mother devoted much of her life to supporting them.
As the siblings were growing up, Anita worked as a dinner lady and in their school library, volunteered as a Cub scout leader and supported them in their hobbies of motorbike racing and horse riding. She was married to her late husband, Les, for more than 50 years.
Anita died on 6 July with heatstroke recorded as her cause of death.
She is one of thousands of people believed to have died a heat-related death during the extreme hot weather this year. There were an estimated 2,877 heat-associated deaths in England during the May and June heatwaves, nearly double the 1,504 excess deaths recorded for the entire summer of 2025.
With four more heatwaves recorded across July and August, heat-related deaths this summer are expected to be the highest on record.
On 24 June, the Met Office issued a rare red heat weather warning due to the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke, and predicted increased mortality and hospital admissions due to heat-related illness.
Some deaths may be linked to exertional heatstroke, caused by heavy physical exercise. Sophie Goodyer-Bird, a 35-year-old woman from Birmingham, died of heatstroke after climbing Yr Wyddfa – also known as Snowdon – on 10 July.
But most of the fatalities will be among the elderly population, although heatstroke is rarely recorded on death certificates as extreme heat often acts as an indirect trigger, placing severe strain on pre-existing health conditions that can be fatal.
Care homes for elderly people are on the frontline of dealing with this – during the July 2022 heatwave, nursing home deaths increased by 34.1% and residential care home deaths increased by 13.0%.
This year, many care homes reported using fans, air conditioners, paddling pools, ice lollies and cold fruit to keep residents cool. But research has found many are still underprepared for severe heat caused by the climate crisis.
The Care Quality Commission is investigating a care home in Watford after four residents were taken to hospital during the May heatwave, with one dying and the others “coming to harm”. An inspection report said there were concerns residents were left “at risk of dehydration”.
Anita’s family has written to her nursing home – which they have chosen not to name until investigations are complete – as they have concerns about the care she received in the hours before she collapsed.
After her death they were given the clothes she was wearing when she was brought into hospital, which Steve described as “a short-sleeve woolly jumper and wool trousers”. He said: “Why was mum in clothes you could wear in the winter? And how long had she been wearing them for?”
Steve said he wanted to raise awareness of the risks of heatstroke, particularly among elderly people in care homes, with more extreme heat on its way next year.
“They’re already saying it’s going to be hotter next year,” he said. “What my mum went through, what we went through as a family, it’s really not a very pleasant experience. I’m not saying it wouldn’t have happened anyway, but I do want to know if anything could have been done differently.”
