Why are Bathla and other home builders collapsing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:08:37 UTC
11:08:37 KST

Australia has a housing shortage. So why are Bathla and other home builders collapsing?
Across Australia, thousands of people are waiting to find out if their homes will be built, after several separate construction company collapses.
By far the biggest of those recent collapses has been the Bathla Group, a Sydney developer that's been one of Australia's largest affordable home builders.
Owing about $3.4 billion to private lenders, Bathla's voluntary administration has thrown the construction of more than 2,000 apartments into limbo, while jeopardising a further pipeline of 14,000 homes.
More builders going bust since COVID
Figures released last week show 3,472 Australian construction companies went bust in the financial year to June 30 2026: one in four (24.5 per cent) of all company insolvencies nationally.
The only good news? The number of builder insolvencies was slightly down for the first time since a steep rise began during COVID.
However, our research has found insolvencies in the construction sector remain consistently higher than in other industries. That makes it harder to build the housing we need.
Australia is falling further behind in meeting the federal government's 1.2 million new homes goal by 2029. Official forecasts released last month indicate the target won't be met until December 2030. New South Wales — Australia's largest housing market — may not meet its targets until March 2032, three years late on a five-year target.
There's no shortage of demand for new homes. What we lack is a construction system capable of delivering them reliably, sustainably and at scale.
Loading...
Bathla's financial ripple effects
On Monday, more than 200 of Bathla's 350 staff were stood down as the administrator continues to work on a rescue deal.
While most of its building projects are in Western Sydney, Bathla's collapse is being watched around Australia because of its wider financial impacts.
Like any company collapse, there are specific circumstances involved in Bathla's current woes. Its business model relied on high volumes of low-cost building.
The NSW building regulator has also conducted more than 40 inspections of Bathla sites in recent months, and ordered the builder to fix serious defects in one major development.
Bathla may have taken as many as 1,000 deposits from buyers for homes now stalled. But home buyers aren't the only people affected.
'Troubling developments' in private credit
As well as owing money to subcontractors, Bathla owes money to a long list of non‑bank lenders — also known as private credit firms.
This reflects the construction industry's heavy reliance on alternative finance, because banks have reduced their exposure to riskier lending.
On Friday, Australian Securities and Investments Commission chair Sarah Court said the corporate watchdog was closely following "several troubling developments in the private credit sector, most notably with the recent collapse of Bathla".
Court pointed out that many Australians are exposed to private credit through their superannuation funds — meaning "this is not some peripheral issue".
The perfect storm hitting builders
Bathla is not an isolated case. The wider construction industry is under strain, with higher costs, thinner profit margins and rising risks.
Figures released last month show house construction costs are now 51 per cent higher than before COVID.
For builders with slim profit margins, the rise in costs can make some projects uneconomic.
With costs rising unpredictably, builders locked into fixed-price contracts are absorbing losses they cannot sustain. This was a major driver of the spike in builder insolvencies during COVID.
Falling house prices and poor market sentiment mean some projects no longer stack up financially.
Many investors and buyers are spooked by three interest rate rises this year, higher costs, and recent federal budget changes to housing tax concessions that have made housing less attractive to investors. The prospect of further interest rate increases is also likely to see projects stalled, as the market waits for conditions to improve.
Then there are ongoing shortages of tradespeople. On top of those, home builders are now competing with data centre builders for tradies, which has driven up salaries.
Little wonder construction insolvencies have risen back to pre-COVID levels, despite strong demand for housing.
Structural change is needed
Governments can't fix all the problems we face, such as price hikes driven by the Middle East war.
But federal, state and local governments are increasingly recognising their role in creating structural barriers to building more homes.
A Productivity Commission draft report released in July identified many of the problems we need to address, including restrictive land-use regulation, slow and inconsistent approvals, poor coordination on key infrastructure, and complex regulation. These all increase costs and delays.
Our 2025 report showed over-regulation is particularly hard on small builders, who struggle to comply with overlapping national, state and local requirements. That matters because our research also showed almost two-thirds (63 per cent) of building company collapses were concentrated among small builders.
The National Construction Code is another challenge. Even with some states deferring 2025 code changes, the national rules remain complex and frequently updated — again, making compliance difficult for small builders.
What's safer than houses?
Some builders are responding by pivoting to infrastructure and commercial projects, such as Victoria's Big Housing Build or Queensland's Olympics construction projects. These can offer more manageable terms and less exposure to market volatility.
Good builders can pick and choose their work. Right now, housing is the riskiest option on the table.
Until that changes, we're likely to see more Australian builders moving away from creating the homes we urgently need — along with more headlines about another builder going bust.
Lyndall Bryant is a senior lecturer and Amanda Bull is a lecturer at the Queensland University of Technology. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

AI generated
DUBAI – Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthis attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia’s south on Sept 8, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a major expansion of the six-month-old Middle East war.
The Houthis, who control most of Yemen’s populated areas, including the capital Sanaa, said they launched a broad operation deep into Saudi territory.
They used drones and missiles to strike a Saudi airbase in the southern city of Khamis Mushair and targets belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company in nearby Abha, Najran on the Yemeni border and Jazan, a major Red Sea port.
Saudi authorities described blazes at the sites, with women and children among the 73 people hurt.
The reports of such large numbers of wounded suggested the attacks were among the biggest carried out against Saudi Arabia since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.
Confirmed images of the aftermath of the attacks in the Saudi cities were not immediately available. The Houthis released pictures of an explosion of what they said were trucks from Saudi Arabia that they struck at the border in another area.
Houthi-controlled media reported later on Sept 8 that Saudi warplanes carried out four air strikes in Yemen’s Jubah district east of Sanaa.
After a month of calm in August, fighting in the Gulf has resumed, with Iran and the US exchanging fire, sending global oil prices back up to levels unseen since July. Brent crude prices were up more than 2 per cent on Sept 8, above US$99 a barrel.
Houthi attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia have the potential to worsen the war’s global economic impact by disrupting Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling against the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade. That war calmed in recent years, but a ceasefire there has broken down, with the Houthis threatening shipping at the mouth of the Red Sea.
‘Maritime exclusion zone’
“The coalition will take all necessary operational measures to deter this terrorist militia and resolutely confront its hostile approach,” Colonel Turki al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said in a statement on X.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree accused Riyadh of having escalated the war by launching air strikes on Yemen, adding that the Houthis will respond.
The war in the Gulf has turned into a test of wills between the United States and Iran, with each side hoping that economic pressure from competing blockades will force the other to yield.
Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf, while cutting off Iran’s exports with a blockade just beyond it.
Tehran has announced new measures to seal off the strait, saying it will soon unveil details of a “maritime exclusion zone” that will extend from the perimeter of the US blockade, through the strait and into the Gulf itself.
Washington fired at Iranian tankers over the weekend in retaliation for Iranian fire at US warships.
Iran said it used new, more capable ballistic missiles to attack American ships.
“In recent days, Washington has received a clear warning from Iran’s new missiles,” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said on X.
“Economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to the blockade perimeter,” he added. “The operational posture toward US warships and bases has been fundamentally recalibrated.”
Despite US barrages that have degraded Iran’s conventional forces and punished its already ailing economy, Iran still possesses missiles and drones that can threaten oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and have been used to attack US military bases scattered throughout the region.
About a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments passed through the strait before the war.
The fighting has caused global shortages of crude oil and, even more acutely, the fuels that are produced by refining it.
Diesel fuel in the US is now at a record average retail price of more than US$5.90 a gallon, harming the political prospects of President Donald Trump’s Republicans.
“Oil prices will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping (but more!), when we WIN the war with Iran. Three Dollars a gallon, but ultimately, below Two Dollars a gallon. It will all happen quickly, and Iran will never have a Nuclear Weapon,” Trump said on social media. REUTERS

Gloria Steinem’s revolutionary life – podcast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:00:23 UTC
11:00:23 KST

By the time she died last week at the age of 92, Gloria Steinem had become almost synonymous with the modern feminist movement in the US.
The arc of Steinem’s life – and activism – was a long one. From going undercover as a Playboy bunny to becoming a radical publisher bringing feminism into the mainstream. She was a fearless reproductive rights campaigner. In Ms Magazine she wrote about having an abortion – and encouraged other famous women, and readers, to do the same to break the stigma around it.
Stateside host Carter Sherman tells Annie Kelly that Steinem’s legacy as an icon is secure – but that, at the time she died, many of the rights she fought so hard for are under attack. “Obviously, Roe v Wade was overturned in 2022. Nearly half of US states have some sort of abortion ban in effect at this time, and Gloria Steinem talked about feeling really angry that this was still a fight that was going on in her later years.”

Merz has no good answers as the far right targets his downfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BERLIN — Germany’s far right is moving to turn its landslide election victory into a knockout blow against Friedrich Merz and his beleaguered conservatives — and the chancellor appears at a loss over how to respond.
Merz seemed to have no clear plan for saving himself and his party as his government confronted its biggest political crisis yet, beyond ambiguous promises to become a better, more empathetic politician 16 months into his chancellorship.
“We are all deeply shocked,” Merz said Monday, after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) reached a new high in Saxony-Anhalt’s weekend election while support for his Christian Democratic Union fell by more than half. “This is the worst election defeat the CDU has suffered in years — or even decades,” the chancellor added. “Of course, there will have to be consequences.”
Advertisement
But what those consequences will be remains uncertain. Merz’s dismal approval ratings and the AfD’s convincing win have fueled speculation that his conservatives could seek a Kanzlertausch, or “chancellor swap,” to revive their political fortunes. But Merz said Monday that he would remain in office and stay the course on economic reforms he argues are long overdue and will, with time, solve the country’s economic problems.
The AfD has made little secret of its intent to turn the election loss into a still greater debacle for Merz. The far-right party is openly courting conservative lawmakers in Saxony-Anhalt to defect and join its ranks — a strategy aimed not only at securing the three additional seats it needs to govern alone, but also at fracturing the conservatives and breaking Merz’s control of his party.
“The conservative bloc will never again be able to win a federal election, that is a fact,” AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel said in Berlin on Monday. “The gap between us and them is already at 10 percent, and my stated goal is to significantly widen that gap in the shortest possible time.”
Merz on Monday acknowledged that he is part of the problem. Only 9 percent of people voting in Saxony-Anhalt approved of his performance as chancellor, according to one exit poll for German public television.
“I know that my persona, too, has been a recurring topic in this election campaign,” Merz said. Germans are anxious about their economic wellbeing and security in turbulent times, he went on, adding: “We must try — myself included — to connect more deeply with people, including their full range of emotions.”
Under pressure
The pressure on Merz is likely only to build in the next weeks, particularly as elections loom in two eastern regions on Sept. 20. Merz’s CDU is headed for clear defeat in the state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania, where the AfD is ahead of all other parties. In Berlin, where the CDU is currently governing, the party is likely to fall out of power to a coalition of left-wing parties.
Advertisement
With four more state elections set for next year, conservatives face a clear choice: continue confronting the rising far right under a deeply unpopular chancellor, or fundamentally change course with a new leader at the helm.
Merz appeared to acknowledge the dilemma his party is facing. “This election result is causing major upheaval, not only in our country, but also within my party,” he said Monday. “I take this extremely seriously, and I intend to do my best over the coming days and weeks to personally address the gravity of the situation.”
While most of the talk of replacing Merz is taking place in private, signs of conservative dissatisfaction with Merz’s leadership are beginning to spill out into the open.
Alice Weidel speaks to the media in Berlin on Sept. 7, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
“Anyone who wants to regain trust and credibility must, in the wake of such a result, question everything,” CDU lawmaker Sepp Müller wrote in a social media post.
“After a result like this, we cannot simply carry on as usual,” Gordon Schnieder, the CDU state premier of Rhineland-Palatinate, wrote on X. “If the democratic center wants to regain trust, we must start with ourselves. It is not up to the people to better understand our politics. We must deliver what people expect from politics: less conflict, clear decisions, and concrete results.”
‘Matter of compassion’
The AfD is attacking the chancellor on multiple policy fronts — hitting him on migration, blaming his energy policies for the country’s industrial malaise and pushing for the restoration of cheap energy flows from Russia.
Advertisement
But many of the AfD’s most effective attacks are merely tactical.
Even as the AfD seeks to win power in Saxony-Anhalt by attempting to peel off conservative defectors, the party is presenting itself as willing to work with the CDU, knowing full well that Merz would not sanction a collapse of the “firewall” that keeps centrist parties from cooperating with the far right.
This allows the AfD to simultaneously attack Merz as ignoring the will of the people in the face of the party’s surging popularity, while also depicting conservatives as leftists in disguise for preferring to work with an array of left-wing parties.
The election in Saxony-Anhalt illustrates the strategic dilemma the CDU faces — and one the AfD is benefiting from. To avoid governing with the AfD, the CDU would theoretically have to work with every other party in state parliament, all of them on the political left, including the far left. As conservatives buckle under the strain of governing alongside ideological opposites, the AfD hopes that growing divisions over the firewall will ultimately bring about Merz’s downfall.
“People have lost confidence in the party,” the AfD’s Weidel said Monday. “Before elections, they always promise one thing. And after the elections, they do the exact opposite. And that’s how every party loses the acceptance and trust of its voters. No chancellor before has been as unpopular as Friedrich Merz, who has become a major obstacle to Germany’s prosperous development.”
Tino Chrupalla, the AfD’s other national leader, said that if the CDU does not abandon the firewall, it would mark the party’s end. If the party “continue down this path,” he said, “then in the short term there will no longer be a CDU in eastern Germany.”
Advertisement
While these AfD’s attack lines are proving highly effective, Merz offered no clear plan on Monday for countering them — other than, in effect, becoming a better politician.
“This isn’t just a matter of rational political understanding — it’s also a matter of compassion, empathy, and emotions,” a somber-sounding Merz told reporters in Berlin. “I’m not the type to wear my emotions on my sleeve every day, but the public wants to see different answers.”
He acknowledged he had failed to connect with voters — but suggested there was still time for him to learn.
“It’s certainly true that I have this problem — and you can see it in the polls — that many people don’t follow me in my thinking and in how I assess things,” Merz said. “That’s my responsibility, and I accept it. I’ll try to do things differently — to do better — in the coming weeks and months.”
The question is whether his party will be that patient.

Nigel Farage exploring Ukraine visit, Reform officials say

LONDON — Nigel Farage’s critics have long accused him of having a weakness on Vladimir Putin. Now Reform UK wants to tee up a visit to Ukraine.
Two party officials told POLITICO on Monday that discussions have been held between the party and Ukrainian contacts about the prospect of a trip for the Reform leader.
Farage’s opponents often hurl at him comments he made back in 2014 that he “admired” the Russian president as an “operator.” Then, a decade later, he triggered a mid-general election backlash by claiming it was the West that “provoked” Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
Polling carried out by More in Common last year suggests that while every voting group in Britain overwhelmingly backs Ukraine, only 26 percent believe that Farage feels the same. Some 21 percent reckon he sympathizes more with Russia.

Neither could say at what level the talks have been held. Reform declined to comment, as did the Ukrainian Embassy.

Advertisement
Separate research by Opinium last year suggests that Reform voters are significantly more skeptical about continued British support for Ukraine than backers of other parties.

The most maximalist ambition for a visit to Kyiv would be a meeting with Volodymyr Zelenskyy himself, though officials declined to comment on whether that prospect had been discussed.
Guidance from the Foreign Office, which isn’t facilitating parliamentarian travel to Ukraine, warns against any travel to most of Ukraine because of the assessed risk to British nationals. A Whitehall official pointed out this advice applies to MPs as well as regular Brits.
It would not be unheard of for opposition leaders to visit the Ukrainian president: Keir Starmer did it while Rishi Sunak was prime minister in 2023.
Reform has been arranging a series of visits, due to take place later this year, with international allies, including Marine Le Pen, the president of France’s far-right National Rally party.

Le Pen would be French president if she wins next year’s elections. Jordan Bardella, who played a big role in Reform’s party conference in Birmingham last weekend, would be her pick for prime minister.

The least free place on earth: Occupied Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

People play chess in a park in front of a sculpture reading "Russian Spring" in the Russian-occupied Crimean city of Sevastopol on July 22, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
No political rights. No freedom of expression. No protection from secret detention without access to family, an attorney or a physician. No protection from deportation.
Welcome to Russia-occupied Ukraine.
For the second year running, U.S.-based democracy tracker Freedom House has listed Ukraine’s occupied eastern and southern territories as the most unfree places in the world — outranking South Sudan, North Korea and the Gaza Strip.
Advertisement
Inhabitants here are subject to repressive Russian legislation, including forcibly imposed citizenship and the use of antiterrorism laws against political dissidents and religious minority groups, Freedom House says. And it is this system of surveillance, repression, indoctrination and statetheft that pushes occupied Ukraine to the top of the list.
Discriminatory policies publicly encoded in Russian law permeate every aspect of residents’ lives — measures that appear to be changing the region’s demographics. Russia is “deliberately changing the ethnic composition so as to destroy a culture or tip the political balance in favor of another group,” the report notes.
International humanitarian law forbids any occupying power from introducing permanent changes to territories it occupies, particularly in demographic, social and economic domains. But Moscow claims these areas are not occupied — they are simply a part of Russia, and therefore subject to Russian law.
“This occupation is one of the most well-documented systems of repression, oppression and human rights violations because so much is put on the public record,” said Danielle Bell, head of the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission to Ukraine. “This is a systemic approach to restricting people’s rights and fundamental freedoms.”
The regime has “all the signs of cultural genocide,” said journalist Andrii Dikhtiarenko, a native of now-occupied eastern Ukraine.
Advertisement
From passportization to deportation
Starting from 2014, Russia has occupied about 20 percent of Ukraine in the country’s south and east — land Moscow calls “new historical territories.” And one of the processes aiding the Russification of these areas is passportization.
By officially designating Ukrainians living in Russia-occupied territories as “foreigners,” occupation authorities compel them to obtain Russian citizenship — which they can do through simplified procedures — in order to access essential rights, such as health care, social services, employment or property ownership.
For Liudmila Chub, it all began with her job. Speaking to POLITICO, Chub said that in 2023, she was told by her employer in Melitopol — located in the occupied Kherson region — that she had to obtain a Russian passport to keep working in his shop, or he would be fined. Chub went to the passport office, where she recorded an angry video about being forced to get a “chicken passport” — a dig at the two-headed Russian eagle emblem. The office’s security guard marched her straight to the occupation police.
A man waits for documentation to apply for a new Russian passport at a center in Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region in August 2022. | AFP via Getty Images
Chub spent the next eight months in detention in Kherson, with the courts regularly extending her arrest, alleging she was breaking military curfew. She was eventually given a statement to read out on camera, saying she did not want to live in Russia, then was allowed 15 minutes to collect items from her apartment and transported under armed guard to Russia’s border with Georgia.
Deported from the home she lived in her whole life, Chub still considers herself fortunate. She said others she encountered in prison had gone through the process of obtaining Russian citizenship only to be charged with spying or treason under Russian law, which carries huge sentences.
“They tie this passport to you, and then with it, they make you traitors to their country,” she said. “Everything in me was opposed to getting that passport, and it’s lucky I didn’t get it. That saved me.”
Advertisement
HRMMU has so far documented over 400 such detentions involving treason- and espionage-related charges in Russia-occupied territories, but it’s impossible to track numbers for incommunicado detention.
That is what happened to 59-year-old IT specialist Serhii Gryshchenkov from Sevastopol in occupied Crimea. After Russian security forces took him from his home in May 2025, Gryshchenkov’s family was unable to find out where he was, his daughter Darina told POLITICO. Her father, who did not hide his pro-Ukraine position, was held incommunicado and tortured for a year before eventually being charged with treason in June 2026, she said. The family does not know the details of the charges.
According to Darina, when her father reappeared in pretrial prison, he spoke of fellow prisoners who were still being secretly held after three or four years. “Their relatives don’t even know whether they are alive.”
One strategy encouraging demographic change in Ukraine’s occupied territories is the official confiscation of homes belonging to residents who fled the war, ensuring they cannot return.
Ukrainians who try to comply with this new rule and travel back home have fallen afoul of Russian “filtration,” faced with arrests and entry bans at Moscow’s Sheremetevo airport — the only possible entry point to get to occupied territories, as land borders are closed to them.
Journalist Olena — who was granted anonymity over security concerns regarding her relatives living under occupation — told POLITICO she had fled occupied Donetsk with her family in 2014. Helped by a sympathetic condominium manager, she had paid the utility bills for her own and her parents’ apartments for the next 12 years, hoping one day they could come home.
Later, Olena found out via occupation media that she had been publicly blacklisted as an “enemy.” Meanwhile, an acquaintance of hers was served a 50-year entry ban at Sheremetevo when trying to get back to her home in occupied Ukraine.
People dance at an outdoor bar in Sevastopol on July 22, 2026. | Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images
With this new law, “nothing can help us,” said Olena.
According to HRMMU monitoring, more than 60,000 private properties in occupied Ukraine have been identified as “ownerless” as of July this year. At least 6,500 of those properties have been expropriated, often given to veterans of Russia’s “special military operation” or sold to immigrants from Russia under preferential terms.
The effect of this has heavily impacted education in the region, with the introduction of a militarized Russian curriculum in schools. New textbooks teach the Kremlin’s official narrative that the occupied regions never supported Ukrainian independence and were always Russian. Parents who refuse to enroll their children in these schools, or enroll them in online Ukrainian education, are fined and threatened with losing parental rights.
These educational institutions can sometimes funnel students straight into the Russian armed forces. Once an individual holds a Russian passport — which the enforced system makes almost impossible to survive without — they can be drafted to fight against Ukraine. A practice that, like deportation, is explicitly prohibited by the Geneva Conventions.
The cumulative effect of all these measures has been the eradication of visible expressions of Ukrainian identity and wider dissent, said journalist Dikhtiarenko. “People who want to survive have to accept the rules of the game.”
Over at HRMMU, Bell’s worst fear is that the world will stop hearing about or noticing these violations. “When the climate becomes that coercive and that restrictive, and people are that silenced, that’s when we stop seeing the reports because people stop daring to speak out,” she said.
As more time passes, some inhabitants wonder whether there will be anything Ukrainian left, even if their home ever comes back under Kyiv’s control. However, despite their enforced Russian citizenship, Dikhtiarenko said the majority of residents still hold on to their Ukrainian passports, hiding them under floorboards or buried in the garden.

====================================================================================================

Ceuta crisis forces Europe’s migrant-rights groups to rethink their playbook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Spanish national police officers stand as migrants wait during a distribution of food by volunteers at an industrial site in Ceuta on Sept. 2, 2026. | Antonio Sempere/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The political reaction to the surge of migrants into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta laid bare how sharply Europe’s migration debate has shifted, and how it’s forcing migrant-rights groups to rethink the way they make their case.
Where previous migration crises often divided European leaders between calls for solidarity and demands for tougher controls, the response to Ceuta — where more than 100 people died last month as they tried to enter — was strikingly uniform.
From the far right to the center left, political leaders overwhelmingly called for stronger borders and more effective deterrence.
Advertisement
“The conversation around migration and the language used to refer to migrants has changed in many EU countries, even center-left member states,” said Michele LeVoy, director of the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants, a network of organizations that advocate for unauthorized migrants across Europe.
In response, migrant-rights groups are changing tactics. As humanitarian appeals lose political traction, they are turning more heavily to the courts, building broader alliances and experimenting with new ways to talk about migration.
“We’re trying to be stronger together by working with organizations from across civil society, working with lawyers to challenge litigation, and really showing that these policies are bad for everyone, not just migrants,” LeVoy added.
From rescue to deterrence
In 2013, the death of hundreds of migrants in a shipwreck off the Italian island of Lampedusa shocked the continent.
Top EU officials, including then-Commission President José Manuel Barroso, traveled to the site to declare that “the European Union cannot accept that thousands of people die at its borders.”
The bloc’s then-Home Affairs Commissioner Cecilia Malmström called for a “change of approach towards migration,” adding that “this restrictive approach is not sustainable and that it is now time to move towards more openness and solidarity.”
Advertisement
The 2015 refugee crisis initially generated a similarly humanitarian reaction, with German Chancellor Angela Merkel calling on Europeans to welcome more than 1 million people fleeing war in Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq. The European Commission sought to manage the crisis through measures including the redistribution of asylum seekers among EU countries.
But that approach ran into resistance from figures like then-Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Poland’s Law and Justice party.
Florian Trauner, an expert on EU migration at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel and the College of Europe, said a handful of right-wing politicians succeeded in establishing an “institutional deadlock” that halted EU efforts to integrate migrants and allowed for a “wider shift to a more restrictive, control-oriented approach to migration.”
José Manuel Barroso attends a press conference at Lampedusa Airport on Oct. 9, 2013. | Tullio M. Puglia/Getty Images
That evolution is visible in the EU’s response to Ceuta. Center-left figures like Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen echoed right-wing Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s call for a more robust defense of the bloc’s external borders, and twenty-two EU leaders signed onto a letter demanding a coordinated effort to “deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen likewise stressed that “control of our European borders matters.” Without mentioning the rising death toll, she instead celebrated the fact that “not a single person reached mainland Spain or the rest of the EU.”
The far-right factor
The bloc’s shift on migration has been accelerated by the rise of far-right parties and a scramble by centrist rivals to neutralize them by embracing parts of their agenda.
Advertisement
“The buffer zone that once separated the democratic right from the far right has effectively disappeared,” said Estrella Galán, a European Parliament lawmaker with the far-left Left group who is the shadow rapporteur on the EU’s return regulation.
As hard-line positions have gone mainstream, the far-right has started to push for further measures, including “remigration” — the removal of immigrants from Europe.
“As their policies have become widely accepted, the far-right groups have moved further and further right on other issues,” said Trauner.
Hungarian border police officiers patrol the Hungarian-Serbian border on Dec. 15, 2022. | Attila Kisbenedek/AFP via Getty Images
The Trump administration’s approach to migration — including large-scale deportations — “has given legitimacy to European actors who have been able to reject criticism by pointing out that the world’s major international power is embracing the exact same position,” Trauner said.
Helena Maleno, spokesperson for Caminando Fronteras, an NGO that defends migrants’ rights along the western Euro-African border, said her group was increasingly being targeted by the far right.
“There is a total dehumanization of migrants, especially if they’re Muslims,” she said. “We have had to reinforce protection and security — from digital attacks, but also from threats to our physical safety.”
Advertisement
The far right, however, argues that migrant-rights groups have not lost influence — and still have too much of it.
“I wish we could speak of the failure of pro-immigration NGOs, but what happened in Ceuta proves they have not failed,” said Jorge Buxadé, a European Parliament lawmaker from Spain’s Vox party.
He accused migrants’ rights groups of being “21st-century pirates” who use “hybrid warfare” to undermine Spain’s territorial integrity.
A Polish border guard stands at the Polish-Belarusian border on July 21, 2025. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images
“Billions of euros every year go toward funding the structure and influence of organizations whose sole interest is ensuring that immigration to Europe remains massive and uncontrolled,” he said.
Change in tactics
In the new climate, the humanitarian argument traditionally used by rights groups — that migrants are human beings in need of protection — no longer carries the same political weight, said LeVoy.
Increasingly, NGOs have found themselves on the defensive, fighting criminal sanctions and restrictions on their activities rather than shaping the broader debate.
Advertisement
That pressure is pushing migrant-rights groups to rethink where — and how — they fight.
One response is to take the battle into the courts, investing resources in legal challenges to restrictive legislation, including EU rules governing returns and the criminalization of assistance to undocumented migrants.
Migrant-rights groups are also seeking to broaden their alliances. In Spain, the recent push to grant legal status to hundreds of thousands of unauthorized migrants was backed by support from the country’s conservative employers’ association and the Catholic Church.
Migrants from various detention centers across Italy are escorted by police upon arrival in Shëngjin, Albania on April 11, 2025. | Adnan Beci/AFP via Getty Images
“It’s more important than ever to be in strong coalitions,” LeVoy said. Her group is also reaching out to local authorities, health professionals and housing organizations.
LeVoy advocated for shifting the narrative on migration by focusing less on dangerous sea crossings or dramatic border surges. Instead, she argued, rights groups should highlight the much larger population of unauthorized migrants already living alongside Europeans.
She likened the strategy to that of successful campaigns for marriage equality, which sought to change public perceptions by presenting LGBTQ+ people not as an abstract political constituency but as friends, colleagues and neighbors.
Advertisement
“Borders are really a very small part of this issue, because the overwhelming majority [of Europe’s unauthorized migrants] come in regularly,” LeVoy said.
Caminando Fronteras has likewise reinforced its legal work and security measures and built transnational networks with other rights groups.
But Maleno said her NGO was also staying true to its long-standing commitment to amplify the voices of families whose relatives have died or disappeared at Europe’s borders.
“We will continue to work to make the public administrations listen,” she said. “Europe will one day have to account for all those deaths and disappearances.”

Iranian state media on Sept 6 reported that Iran fired the Qassem Basir missile in its attacks on several US vessels.

About one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments passed through the strait before the war, which enabled Iran to threaten tankers from Gulf neighbours seeking to export oil and gas. That has lifted energy prices at a time when the war, which opinion polls show is unpopular in the US, has increased the risks for President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in November congressional elections.
“Oil prices will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping (but more!), when we win the war with Iran. Three dollars a gallon, but ultimately, below two dollars a gallon. It will all happen quickly, and Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said on social media.

Volkswagen car plant to be converted for Israeli arms production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:54:57 UTC
10:54:57 KST

Volkswagen car plant to be converted for Israeli arms production
German auto giant Volkswagen has agreed on plans to sell one of its factories and convert the site into a military production hub, with Israeli arms manufacturer Rafael Advanced Defense Systems set to become its first major industrial partner.
Volkswagen announced on Monday that it had reached an agreement with the state of Lower Saxony and the Israeli investment company Aurelius Capital on key terms for the sale of its Osnabrück plant. Under the plan, Aurelius would become the majority owner, while Lower Saxony would also take a stake in the facility.
The factory would then be gradually transformed from car manufacturing into what Volkswagen described as a “competence center for security and defense solutions.” Its first anchor project would involve cooperation with Rafael on the manufacture of air-defense systems and components for Germany and other European customers.
Rafael is the Israeli state-owned defense company behind the Iron Dome missile defense system. The Osnabrück factory is expected to manufacture equipment including military vehicles, launchers and generators used by the system, although its Tamir interceptor missiles themselves will not be produced there, according to Israeli media.
The Osnabrück site has a history of military production dating back to Nazi Germany. The factory originally belonged to coachbuilder Karmann, which produced aircraft components for the German war effort and used forced labor during World War II.
Volkswagen took over the company’s Osnabrück operations following Karmann’s insolvency in 2009 and decided in 2024 to end vehicle production by the summer of 2027. The new arrangement is expected to provide employment to more than 1,200 workers, while Volkswagen Group CEO Oliver Blume said the agreement would open up a “new industrial future” for the site.
Lower Saxony Minister-President Olaf Lies meanwhile linked the shift to Germany’s broader military buildup, saying there had been a “fundamental change in our security situation and our need for protection.”
The deal had reportedly faced resistance from Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund, one of Volkswagen’s largest shareholders. The eventual structure keeps Rafael out of the ownership of the plant, with Aurelius and Lower Saxony taking it over instead.
The conversion comes as Volkswagen undertakes one of the biggest restructurings in its history. Last week, the company confirmed plans to eliminate as many as 100,000 jobs worldwide by 2030 as it struggles with weak European demand, high energy costs following the loss of cheap Russian supplies, US tariffs and growing competition from Chinese manufacturers.
Other European carmakers, including Mercedes-Benz, have also been looking increasingly toward the defense sector. The conversion comes amid a broader military buildup across the EU that Moscow sees as preparation for a direct conflict with Russia.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that modern Germany and the rest of the EU are “transforming into a Fourth Reich,” pointing to Berlin’s drive to build the strongest conventional army in Europe.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said in June that NATO countries were no longer concealing their intentions, and had moved beyond supporting Kiev to now “openly saying that they are preparing for war with us.”

EU pledges more than $200m to Greenland amid Trump threats

EU pledges more than $200m to Greenland amid Trump annexation threats
Brussels has proposed doubling direct EU aid to Greenland under the bloc’s next budget as military exercises kick off.
The European Union has signed a declaration with resource-rich Greenland, promising a stronger partnership and announcing a $232m (200 million-euro) investment package to soothe anxiety caused by repeated threats from US President Donald Trump to annex the self-governing Danish territory.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the package, aimed at improving local quality of life over the next two years, during a visit to the Greenlandic capital Nuuk on Monday.
The EU shifted its focus towards Greenland, seeking increased cooperation with the Arctic island, following Trump’s push for greater US control of the semi-autonomous territory. His persistent threats, citing national security concerns, resulted in pushback from Greenland and Denmark and strained relationships with NATO allies.
“Greenland’s future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide. No one else,” von der Leyen said.
The EU-Greenland declaration was signed by von der Leyen, Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen in Nuuk.
The investment package will go to Greenland’s government to strengthen administrative capability and planned programmes promoting sustainable tourism and housing construction.
Von der Leyen said the EU aims to be “more present and more engaged” in the region. Brussels has proposed doubling direct EU aid to Greenland to 530 million euros ($616m) under the bloc’s next budget for the 2028–2034 period.
Her visit coincided with the start of NATO’s Arctic Shield military exercise, bringing together soldiers from 11 countries of the alliance. The exercise will involve about 400 NATO military personnel in Greenland and will run from September 7 to 18.
“Through these challenging times, your support to us is unfailing,” Nielsen said. “You have stood by us and continue to stand by us. We feel it and are deeply grateful.”
“Greenland needs the European Union, and the European Union needs Greenland,” he added.
In January, eight European countries, including Denmark, sent a small group of military personnel to Greenland for public military exercises to show support for the island’s sovereignty and strengthen Arctic security.
Trump responded to the public military display by threatening tariffs on the countries, including Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. The US president backed down in February after NATO agreed to expand its military operations in the Arctic.
At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and NATO.

IAEA warns over Iran nuclear access as Western powers push UN referral
Baghaei warns that Iran will take ‘necessary measures’ if the Western powers pursue the resolution.
France, Germany, the UK and the US are pressing the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to report Iran to the UN Security Council, as the nuclear watchdog warns that it remains unable to verify Tehran’s nuclear material more than a year after losing access to key facilities.
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told the agency’s Board of Governors on Monday that Tehran had provided no information during the latest reporting period on the status of its declared nuclear material or facilities, and inspectors had been unable to conduct on-site verification.

“It is more than a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge” over previously declared stocks of uranium enriched to as much as 60 percent at facilities hit in US and Israeli attacks in June 2025, Grossi said.
He described the lack of information and access as a proliferation concern that “needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency”, calling on Iran to restore effective cooperation with the IAEA.
The nuclear watchdog’s warning comes as the four Western powers seek support for a draft resolution at the 35-member board that would send the Iran issue back to the UN Security Council (UNSC) for the first time in two decades, according to Reuters.
The proposed text asks Grossi to transmit the resolution, previous board decisions and his latest report to the UNSC and General Assembly. It also calls on Iran to provide the information and access required by inspectors.
Iran has rejected the move and maintains that its nuclear programme is peaceful.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Western governments were again turning to the IAEA after failing to achieve their objectives elsewhere.
“Whenever they run out of options, they turn to the agency and Grossi,” Baghaei said at his weekly news conference on Monday.
He argued that restrictions facing inspectors were a consequence of US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities and that it was unreasonable for those governments to blame Tehran for the resulting loss of access.
Baghaei warned that Iran would take “necessary measures” if the Western powers pursued the resolution.
The draft has not yet been formally submitted to the board, and negotiations over its wording are continuing. Even if it is approved, any concrete action at the Security Council could face opposition from Russia and China, two of the five permanent veto powers.

Ukrinform to present Victory Commanders at Lviv Book Forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:40:00 UTC

Ukrinform to present Victory Commanders at Lviv Book Forum
The presentation will take place as part of the Lviv Book Forum.
The book’s subjects include current Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov, Deputy Head of the Office of the President Pavlo Palisa, commander of the “Bakhmut Ghosts” sniper platoon Oleksandr “Ghost,” Head of the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense Oleh Ivashchenko, Commander of the National Guard Oleksandr Pivnenko, and former Commander of the Ukrainian Ground Forces Hennadii Shapovalov.
The book aims to preserve the firsthand accounts of Ukrainian military commanders who are directly involved in the Russo-Ukrainian war, make important decisions on the battlefield, and preserve their stories for future generations.
A distinctive feature of Victory Commanders is that the entire book-production process—from preparing and editing journalistic materials to design, layout, and prepress preparation—was carried out by the Ukrinform team. For the agency, this represents a new direction in working with its own journalistic content and preserving it in book form.
The publication includes original autographs from the project’s subjects, along with handwritten quotations expressing their personal mottos. Another distinctive feature is a bookmark decorated with a spent cartridge case. It was made by Olha Konoval, a volunteer from Ternopil and the wife of fallen Hero of Ukraine Serhii Konoval.
The book is illustrated with unique photographs taken by Ukrinform correspondents, including photographs taken in Donetsk region and on the Zaporizhzhia front. One of the photographs taken by the agency’s photojournalist, Dmytro Smolienko, featuring sunflowers, was included among Time magazine’s 100 best photographs of 2025.
During the presentation, the agency’s team will discuss the book’s creation, from the initial concept and preparation of materials to design and printing. The discussion will also address the role of the media in documenting the Russo-Ukrainian war and preserving the testimonies of those directly involved.
One of the subjects of Victory Commanders, whose name has not yet been disclosed, will also attend the event.
The special guest at the presentation will be Taras Topolya, Honored Artist of Ukraine, serviceman, and frontman of the band Antytila, who will perform an acoustic set.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, the agency is publishing Victory Commanders, which brings together more than 20 stories of Ukrainian commanders and their units. The book is based on interviews published by the agency over the course of a year.

LONDON, September 8. /TASS/. Ukraine’s strategic crisis stems largely from three Western mistakes, the most serious of which is refusing to negotiate with Russia, Owen Matthews, a columnist for The Spectator, argued.
In his view, the West refuses "to countenance seriously engaging the Kremlin in peace talks," instead believing that "encouraging Ukraine to fight and fight forever will somehow magically lead to victory." Matthews described Western leaders’ pledges of unwavering support for Kiev since the start of the conflict as "fundamentally misleading."
The columnist maintained that US President Donald Trump’s administration "has long given up on the idea of backing a full Ukrainian victory," while Europe "continues talking the talk" without a concrete plan to help Kiev.

Matthews identified another Western miscalculation as its purported failure to send offensive weapons to Ukraine out of fear of escalating the conflict and a preference for prioritizing its own defense.

Interview: China coach Ma aims to showcase creativity at FIFA U17 Women's World Cup
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:33:43 CST
10:33:43 KST

by sportswriters Yue Wenwan, Yue Dongxing and Hu Jiefei
BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- China's under-17 women's football team concluded a monthlong training camp on Sunday as coach Ma Xiaoxu prepares her young players for the FIFA U17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, where they are expected to play with confidence and creativity rather than fear.
"We certainly want to win because results are what count in competitive sports," Ma, 38, told Xinhua. "I also hope the players can show their abilities on the World Cup stage without fear or restraint."
China trained from August 5 to September 6 in preparation for the U17 Women's World Cup.
China is in Group E with the United States, Samoa and Kenya. The top two teams from each group and the four best third-placed teams will advance to the knockout stage.
"At this age, I hope they can show their true abilities from training, show creativity, make their own decisions on the field and enjoy the games," Ma said. "The experience of competing is the most important thing for their development. Meanwhile, we will certainly give everything to fight for the best possible results."
Ma knows firsthand how important a youth World Cup can be. As an 18-year-old player in 2006, she helped China finish runner-up at the FIFA U20 Women's World Cup and won both the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player and the Golden Boot as its top scorer.
That same year, she was named AFC Asian Player of the Year.
Twenty years later, Ma is preparing for a global youth tournament from the other side of the touchline.
"When I first took over this team, I felt like I suddenly went back to their age," Ma said. "Seeing their young energy and vitality was exciting for me and gave me motivation."
Ma, however, said she would not simply reproduce the methods that worked for her as a player.
"Every player has a different path of development, and football is constantly evolving," she said. "I am also continuing to learn. I hope to teach them more advanced ideas and, after filtering out some of the problems I experienced before, give them better things."
"I hope every player can have her own personality. As a coach, I need to think more carefully and treat every player individually. The most important thing is to let them maintain their love for football. I think it is very important that they do not lose that love as they get older."
China earned its World Cup berth by reaching the semifinals of the AFC U17 Women's Asian Cup in May. The team came back from two goals down to level the semifinal against defending champion the Democratic People's Republic of Korea at 2-2 before eventually losing 4-2.
Ma said securing a World Cup place was the team's most basic objective.
"We also came through that age group ourselves. Whether you can participate in a world-class tournament makes a completely different impact on a player's development," she said. "Their future development will also help drive the overall development of Chinese women's football."
The semifinal also highlighted both the progress and the weaknesses Ma wants her players to address. Against the DPRK's high press, China tried to build through passing combinations from the back rather than repeatedly resorting to long balls. But mistakes under pressure gave opponents opportunities to shoot.
"I think we have to make some changes and not blindly play long balls," Ma said. "But that does not mean pursuing buildup from the back for its own sake. The most important thing is to get the ball behind the opponent's defense and into the penalty area to create dangerous attacks."
Ma praised her players' execution but said they needed to improve their ability to adjust during matches.
"The players have strong execution, but they still need to improve their ability to adapt during the game," she said. "Under high pressure, they may not even be able to hear some of the reminders we give from the sideline."
"I hope they can bravely face the challenges of high pressing. Results are certainly important, and we will try to win every game. But for 17-year-old players, I think it is more important in this process to develop the habit and awareness of thinking independently."
Ma noted that 18 to 20 years old is an especially important period for young players to develop, and that playing overseas can expose them to higher-level competition.
"I think those few years from 18 to 20 are when players improve the fastest," she said. "If they can experience higher-level leagues and have teammates with stronger technical and tactical abilities, they will gradually adapt to the pace and intensity of matches, learn how to make decisions more quickly under pressure and make better use of their bodies in physical confrontations."
Ma has also used the past several months to develop as a coach.
After completing the Asian Cup campaign, she briefly joined China women's national team coaching staff as an assistant to head coach Ante Milicic during the team's training camp and matches in central China's Wuhan.
"For me, as a coach who has just started out, being able to work with a high-level foreign coach and see their working methods, their thinking and how they organize training camps has been very helpful," Ma said.
"The national team coaching staff is very open. Whenever I have questions, they are willing to help."
Ma said she and the senior coaching staff share similar views on many aspects of modern football, while adding that young Chinese coaches need more opportunities to learn.
"I think we have a consensus on some of the ideas of modern football," she said. ■

Live: Are you struggling to access basic health care? Have your say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:33:00 UTC
10:33:00 KST

Are you struggling to access basic health care? Australians share their stories — as it happened
Whether you are battling high costs, long distances or stretching waitlists, many Australians have told us that accessing health care is becoming harder than ever.
We heard from readers about their experiences, and heard from the Grattan Institute's Peter Breadon and ABC health reporters Stephanie Dalzell and Lauren Roberts.
Look back on the blog below.
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
New: Filters
Choose what information you see below by using filters
Thank you all for sharing
We know health care can be such a personal and sensitive topic to discuss.
Thank you all for sharing with such honesty, and for providing our experts with such interesting questions.
We are wrapping up this blog for today, but here's some further reading on the issues facing Australian healthcare:
Why is it so expensive to see a GP in Canberra?
Why is the GP bulk billing rate so much lower in Canberra than the rest of the country? Until recently we had precisely zero bulk billing GP clinics in the whole city. $100-$110 for a 15 minute consult is typical while the Medicare rebate is $43 - why is the gap so huge, and why can't Canberra GPs make ends meet under the bulk billing incentive while clinics elsewhere can?
- Paul
Hi Paul, as a fellow Canberran I feel your pain. The ACT consistently has the lowest bulk-billing rates in the country and there are a few reasons for this.
Firstly, Canberra has the highest average incomes in Australia, and evidence suggests bulk billing is usually less common in wealthier areas (one argument is that doctors perceive wealthier people have more capacity to pay, so they then don't bulk bill them).
But there are also broader structural issues — Canberra's a small market, and that means it's harder to attract and retain GPs. When there's less supply, there's less incentive to bulk bill as the demand means clinics can still fill appointment slots even when charging higher fees.
Doctors here have also argued that there are high operating costs involved in running a practice in the ACT that mean they need to charge more for consults.
In terms of the gap, that's a broader issue. The rebate has been a long-held gripe of doctors, who argue it doesn't cover the cost of providing care, even with the incentive.
But the Health Minister Mark Butler has said he can't justify increasing rebates without conditions attached, so the incentive is the way the government's currently trying to shift the dial.
Can the National Health Reform Agreement improve public specialist wait times?
I think the national health reform agreement 2012 is partly to blame for long public specialist wait times. This is because public hospitals have addressed inefficiency in in-patient care but still struggle at the 55% share of costs- this was meant to be 50% commonwealth/state. The loser is outpatient care where hospitals use outmoded medicare billing vs NHRA funding. State health services are underfunding outpatient care by underreporting activity and this way they avoid the 55% co pay. For context, i am a metropolitan public hospital specialist of 35 years and have never been less busy!
- DR
Peter has answered this one for us, DR!
Yes, the national reform agreement should do a lot more to reduce specialist wait times.
One part you mentioned is how public specialist care is funded. I agree that public specialist care should be funded through hospital funding, not the Medicare Benefit Schedule (MBS). The MBS is the wrong way to pay for this care.
The MBS is too rigid, requiring care by a named medical specialist. But that doctor might not be working when the patient comes in, or the care might be best delivered by a team member who isn't a medical specialist.
The funding model also creates opportunities for cost-shifting between governments, and in some cases there has been inappropriate MBS billing.
Another area where the national reform deal could help is productivity. It's a big problem if the skills of an experienced specialist like you are going to waste!
Our research found a lot of differences in how public clinics work, even in the same city, ranging from what kind of patients they see, to how they schedule care, to the roles that different health workers play. There is a lot of room to spread best practices and improve efficiency
So, while there should be more funding for public specialist care, it should come with more accountability for productivity. That means the prices governments pay should reflect efficient practices, and there should be public reporting on both wait times and how much care each dollar buys.
The new National Health Reform Agreement, which governments struck earlier this year, creates opportunities for some of these changes. It didn't have the big expansion of public specialist care we proposed. But it does commit to a new national reporting framework, and significant funding to spread new models of care.
Both could be used to help improve the productivity of public specialist clinics.
Shortages may disproportionally affect women
The structural barriers to health care may also have a gendered aspect.
In 2023, the National Women's Health Advisory Council conducted the #EndGenderBias survey to ask Australian women about their experiences of barriers and bias in the health system.
Sixty-two per cent of those women who responded found health care unaffordable, and 45 per cent found it inaccessible.
That included long wait times to consult with healthcare professionals, from the GP level to surgery.
These workforce shortages often left women more disadvantaged than men, the survey noted.
One rural woman who responded said it meant she was left with limited specialist options.
"I have no choice if I want to see a [medical specialist] locally. She is only available every six months and one of those appointments will be by telehealth, which is pointless, except for a prescription renewal that the local doctor can't do."
Are long ED waitlists the 'new normal'?
More of a rant than a question! It worries me that really long wait times in the ED is now so common we're accepting it as the "new normal". EDs will always be busy places, but they're not meant to be places where you stay for long periods of time. The whole point is they're a pitstop to be seen rapidly, stabilised, and sent onwards for the right treatment. But people are stuck there with nowhere to go. The part that worries me the most is it's risky. It's not about frustration or entitlement - it's about safety. These are often people who need to be watched closely or need a specific type of care that the ED was never designed to do. It's not good enough and it should worry us a lot more seeing it get worse and worse every year.
- Alex
Yeah, Alex, you're right.
And a lot of this comes back to the need for better preventative healthcare. If people had more community-based support, including better access to GPs and mental health services, they could avoid a trip to the ED altogether.
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare keeps track of potentially preventable hospitalisations and as the name suggests, these are conditions where hospitalisation may be avoided altogether with better primary health care and early disease management.
We can see the rate of these types of hospitalisations has been slowly trending upwards, from 24.43 hospitalisations for every 1,000 people in 2020-21, to 27.21 hospitalisations for every 1,000 people in 2024-25.
A 19-year wait for tonsil removal
My friend just got booked in for getting her tonsils out in regional Victoria. She's been on the waitlist for 19 years! The last updated referral on the record for her was 10 years ago. They were so surprised by how bad her situation was that they got her straight in. Does this feel like waitlists are being assessed correctly? Maybe people need to be spoken to rather than just being a number on a list.
- Prue
Gee, 19 years is a long time for your friend to wait, Prue!
We know advocating for your health is so important (or having a loved one do it for you if you're unable to).
Loading
A lack of home care services 'not just a rural' issue
Kelley Wright, who has a physical disability as a result of a workplace injury and is studying to re-enter the workforce, is unable to provide all the care her aging mother needs.
So, she recently moved her family from Gatton, about 90 kilometres east of Brisbane, closer to the city in the hope of securing better home care supports.
She says her 83-year-old mum needs support to travel to appointments and recently had a lengthy hospital stay after surgery as Kelley's been unable to look after her at home.
But since they both relocated to Ipswich, Kelley has rung at least a dozen providers, to no avail.
"There's just not the physical bodies to fill the jobs, even if you get the approval and the financial assistance is there," Kelley said.
"It's a systemic thing; it goes across the board. It's not just a rural or just a city issue."
Kelley would like to see better incentives for people to work in the home care industry, as well as more migration to fill the jobs.
"We need them as much as they need us," she said.
"It seems to be getting worse and worse. I'm hearing all my mum's friends not having support.
"We're OK at the moment, but my husband and I are aging. What happens in a few years?"
How to find services for the elderly people in your life
How do you find out what services are available for elderly people or older people who have poor health and limited money/rely on the pension? It is hard to support family ourselves, and knowing if there are any services available might alleviate some of the burden we are starting to feel having to support family who are getting older and sickly
- Aimee
I know this is an annoying answer Aimee, but it really depends on where you live and what health concerns your family members have.
Let me give you a hypothetical example.

Great question Anthony!
Drug pricing schemes like the PBS have certainly been firmly in the sights of US President Donald Trump and US pharmaceutical companies, who argue they undervalue innovation and threaten billions of dollars in lost sales.
The federal government has been adamant that the PBS is "not for sale" nor up for negotiation. But there's a broader issue here which we're seeing play out.
In order for the PBS to be sustainable, the government needs to negotiate lower prices for drugs it's putting on the scheme, otherwise it wouldn't be able to subsidise as many medications as it does.
But big pharmaceutical companies, who have been emboldened by Trump in recent months, have been rejecting those prices in negotiations, threatening to withdraw — or actually withdrawing — medications from the PBS.

How each state compares on subsiding travel for cancer treatment
The Leukaemia Foundation has released new data which shows striking differences between states and territories on subsidies for people who need to travel to access life-saving cancer treatment.

Hi Riley, you're not alone there, and many experts have argued the system has become increasingly difficult to access for those struggling with cost-of-living pressures.
Various studies have told us cost is a major barrier to mental health care, with people like yourself delaying or avoiding getting help because they simply can't afford to.
The divide between those who have money for care and those who don't means people are seeking help later — when their symptoms are harder to treat —and are more likely to present at emergency departments needing more urgent care.

For its part, the federal government has argued it has invested heavily in mental health services — like its Medicare Mental Health centres, which provide free services.

Would there be consequences if the private health insurance rebate was binned?
What if we were to scrap the private health insurance rebate and invest that money into our public hospitals. What would be the consequences, if any?
- Michael
Hi Michael, like many things in the health space the answer depends on who you ask.
Private health insurance has been a contested area of policy for decades, with some experts arguing the billions of dollars spent subsidising private health insurance would be better spent on the public system.
While in the cons column, the private health insurance industry (who of course has a stake in the argument) says reducing the rebate would encourage people to drop or downgrade their cover, pushing demand on to public hospitals already struggling.
There is also a middle ground here with some arguing the subsidies should be reformed rather than binned.
The federal government recently decided to wind back a more generous rebate for those aged 65 and over, which has proved quite controversial, with the Coalition vowing to block it in Parliament and some states demanding the policy be dumped.
So, the reality is a broader move to scrap the rebate entirely is very unlikely. The federal government doesn't want to pick a fight with the industry, and many families with private health insurance rely on the rebate as a cost-of-living measure.
Why are ED wait times so long?

- Nit
Oh, Nit, that sounds like such a horrible experience, hope your mum is OK.
In 2024–25, one in 10 patients spent more than 11 hours in the ED, which is up from seven hours in 2014-15.

One of them is bed-blocking, where there are simply not enough beds for patients.
Another reason is increasing demand, with healthcare workers managing 286,000 additional annual presentations to public EDs over the past five years.
Are you living in a 'pharmacy desert'?
Data recently published by the Australian Journal of Rural Health shows which parts of the country have fewer or even no community pharmacies — and the results might surprise you.
It shows Aboriginal communities in West Arnhem Land and the Tiwi Islands have no community pharmacies at all, as well as rural towns south of the Blue Mountains and the coastal region of Jervis Bay.
But it's not just the bush with fewer community pharmacies, also known as retail pharmacies.
Areas just outside of big city centres, including outer-city Melbourne and outer-city Perth, recorded pharmacy density levels below the national average.
In the graphs below you can see the average number of community pharmacies per 10,000 people in your location.
The study found there was an average of 2.2 community pharmacies for every 10,000 Australians.
This is "well below" the global average of 2.75, according to the study's lead author Michael Leach.
He said overall, community pharmacy density across regional, rural and remote areas was significantly higher than in metropolitan areas.
We know pharmacies might be the first point of contact someone has with the health system when they're unwell, and vital for those who need to regularly take medication.

NEW YORK, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's Zheng Qinwen staged another thrilling comeback from 5-0 down to beat eighth seed Iga Swiatek of Poland 7-5, 6-3 to secure a quarterfinal berth in the women's singles of US Open on Monday.

Hong Kong aviation success today means more than just adding routes
Success was once measured by how far local airlines could fly. Now, it’s about how effectively global networks intersect here to power the wider economy
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Ken Chu (LLD) is the chairman and CEO of Mission Hills Group, with businesses in hospitality, leisure, entertainment, sports, wellness and education in China. 
When Cathay Pacific Airways announced direct flights to Almaty starting next January, the significance went beyond adding another destination. The service will be Cathay Pacific’s first to Central Asia and the only non-stop passenger connection between Hong Kong and Kazakhstan.
Another announcement pointed to Hong Kong’s growing aviation reach from a different direction. Qatar Airways Cargo relocated its regional office to Hong Kong and agreed with the Airport Authority to increase frequencies and develop new routes through the city. The airline already operates around 56 cargo flights a week via Hong Kong.
Taken together, these developments offer an interesting glimpse of how Hong Kong’s aviation map is evolving.
As Cathay celebrates its 80th anniversary this year, Hong Kong also finds itself entering a new era for its airport. The three-runway system and Skytopia development signal ambitions that extend well beyond aviation. Hong Kong International Airport is no longer being positioned simply as one of the world’s best to arrive at or for transit, but as an integrated destination for tourism, business and entertainment.
In this year’s budget, the government reaffirmed the Airport City development as a strategic economic initiative. Hong Kong’s airport handled some 63 million passengers in the year ended March 31, nearly 15 per cent more than in the previous year, while remaining the world’s busiest cargo airport.
Yet these developments also pose an important question. If Hong Kong’s ambitions for its airport have evolved, has our thinking about what makes a successful aviation hub kept pace?
