Hungary: Meta failed to stop anti-LGBTI content on Facebook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

This press release contains information that some readers may find upsetting
Meta failed to address harmful rhetoric on Facebook against the LGBTI community in Hungary by ineffectively applying its own moderation policies, a new Amnesty International briefing shows.
‘It erodes my soul’: Meta’s contribution to anti-LGBTI discourse in Hungary, shows how Meta’s policy decisions, including the weakening of safeguards for high risk groups in January 2025 and the significant reduction in proactive content moderation, have negatively affected the LGBTI community in Hungary.
“Meta contributed to adverse human rights impacts experienced by LGBTI people in Hungary through its policy decisions, and failed to take adequate steps to prevent the resulting harm. Risks to LGBTI people in Hungary were foreseeable and well documented, yet Meta did not adequately act on them,
Daniela Schnidrig, Interim Policy and Advocacy Adviser at Amnesty International’s Big Tech Accountability Team.
One of Meta’s failures was not properly assessing the risks that changes to its global policies posed to the Hungarian LGBTI community. This was despite knowing the hostile political climate and existing legal restrictions on LGBTI-related assemblies, including Pride, and sustained anti-LGBTI rhetoric, including by government and government-aligned actors.
Facebook occupies a uniquely influential position within Hungary’s information environment, reaching over half of the population. LGBTI people interviewed for this research said that sustained exposure to anti-LGBTI content on Facebook caused them anxiety, frustration and feelings of helplessness even in cases where they reported the harmful content.
“Facebook is just another piece in the pile of my anxiety… to them (Meta) users are not people, they are just numbers,” one interviewee told Amnesty International.
Some interviewees temporarily withdrew from the platform and participation in public discussions to protect their mental health. Others self-censored fearing a backlash if they openly expressed their sexual orientation, gender identity, or support for the rights of LGBTI people on the platform. These experiences raise concerns over whether Facebook failed to protect the rights to freedom of expression and non-discrimination, by undermining LGBTI people’s ability to participate in public and civic life on an equal basis with others.
“Over the last decade, members of the Hungarian LGBTI community faced severe smear campaigns and repressive laws from the Orbán government. They also could not express themselves freely on Meta platforms which largely added to their despair” – said Eszter Mihály, LGBTI rights officer at Amnesty Hungary.
Facebook’s central role in debates
As part of the research, Amnesty International also conducted a social listening exercise of public discourse on LGBTI issues across various social media platforms. We found that discussions concerning LGBTI people were characterized by fearmongering, misinformation, and derogatory rhetoric, with Facebook serving as a central forum for these debates.
Representatives of Háttér Society, a Hungarian organization that supports and advocates for the rights of LGBTI people, shared with Amnesty examples of harmful content on Facebook identified between January 2023 and December 2024. They included comments calling for physical violence against LGBTI people, with statements such as “Beat them to death immediately”, “I would shoot this”, “Throw them off the bridge”, and “Death to the extreme genderfluid vermin”.
Other comments used dehumanizing language, referring to LGBTI people as “rats”, “mutants”, “earthworms” or “scum”, while some explicitly advocated the eradication of transgender people. Several other examples pushed narratives portraying LGBTI people as threats to children, public morality, or social order. Some harmful content remained accessible for a period of time after being reported, including content that was still available when checked in March 2026. The continued availability of such content indicates ongoing shortcomings in the consistency and effectiveness of Meta’s enforcement systems.
Interviewees repeatedly encountered anti-LGBTI content despite actively seeking to avoid it by blocking accounts, reporting harmful content, and communicating their disinterest to Facebook.
“Now my feed is really unhealthy. It is not just one or two videos: it’s a series of videos. Now I only can see that. There is rarely any content from friends.
Ádám Kanicsár, an LGBTI activist and journalist, told Amnesty International
Other interviewees also noted that they were shown content they were not interested in.
“Taken together, these findings raise concerns that Facebook’s design may also have increased users’ exposure to harmful anti-LGBTI content. The findings suggest that engagement-driven systems may be contributing to repeated exposure to harmful and divisive content,” said Alia Al Ghussain, the Head of Amnesty International’s Big Tech Accountability Team.
Under the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA), Meta is required to identify and prevent systemic risks related to platform design to ensure that its products are not causing or contributing to human rights abuses. The company must reassess the impact of its January 2025 policy changes in different contexts, and strengthen content moderation and enforcement. This includes an effective complaint mechanism, improve transparency on the enforcements and effectiveness of its policies and the provision of effective remedies to those affected by any harms. The European Commission must robustly enforce the DSA and investigate Meta’s compliance with its obligations. Amnesty International wrote to Meta on 28 July sharing its conclusions. On 11 August, Meta replied stating that, given the scope and detail of the findings presented, it could not share a response within the stipulated timeline.
Background
The research was conducted amid a worsening environment for LGBTI rights in Hungary. Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, the government introduced discriminatory laws and policies with government aligned actors portraying LGBTI people as threats to children, families, and Hungarian values. These trends intensified in 2025 and 2026 with new laws restricting LGBTI related gatherings, including Pride events.

Cambodia Confirms Resumption of Joint Military Exercises With US Next Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:28:00 UTC
10:28:00 KST

Cambodia’s army has confirmed that it will resume joint military exercises with the United States early next year after a decade-long suspension, the latest sign of the improving ties between the two nations.
The Royal Cambodian Army announced on Facebook on Friday that officials from the two nations had concluded an Initial Planning Conference for Exercise Angkor Sentinel 2027, which it said would be held in February of next year.
The exercise has the aim of “strengthening interoperability and disaster-response capabilities, reflecting renewed momentum in Cambodia–U.S. military cooperation and a shared commitment to strengthening defense cooperation.”
The announcement follows several high-level meetings between U.S. and Cambodian officials. These include a meeting last month between Prime Minister Hun Manet and Elbridge A. Colby, undersecretary for policy at the U.S. Department of War, during which the two discussed expanded defense cooperation.
Hun Manet said at the time that he was satisfied with the “positive momentum in Cambodia-U.S. relations” and the ongoing talks about the resumption of Angkor Sentinel, the Associated Press reported. “The joint exercises and training not only build military capability but also serve as a vital bridge to foster close friendship between the armed forces of both countries,” he added.
This was not long after Adm. Steve Koehler, commander of the U.S. Pacific Fleet, traveled to Phnom Penh for meetings with officials including Gen. Vong Pisen, the commander-in-chief of the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces, and Vice Adm. Tea Sokha, the commander of the Royal Cambodian Navy.
The visit “reaffirmed the United States’ long-term commitment to strengthening bilateral relationships and partnerships that advance a shared vision for a free and open Indo-Pacific,” the U.S. Pacific Fleet said in a statement at the time.
Angkor Sentinel was held for the first time in 2010 but was unilaterally canceled by the Cambodian government in early 2017, shortly after Cambodian troops took part for the first time in Golden Dragon, a joint military exercise with the Chinese military. The move reflected the mutually reinforcing deterioration of Phnom Penh’s relations with Washington and its growing proximity to China.
The resumption of the exercise has been anticipated by both sides for some time. It was first publicly discussed in early 2025, just prior to President Trump’s return to the White House, and has been referenced in most high-level diplomatic meetings since then. It reflects the sea change that has taken place in U.S.-Cambodia relations since the midpoint of the Biden administration, as Phnom Penh has sought to diversify its foreign relations and the U.S. has worked to pull the country out of China’s orbit.
However, the rapprochement has gained inexorable momentum since the inauguration of the second Trump administration, whose transactional mode of diplomacy has been much more to Phnom Penh’s liking. In particular, President Donald Trump’s decision to shutter USAID and cut off U.S. funding for democracy promotion efforts and media outlets like Radio Free Asia removed a key impediment to improved relations on the Cambodian side. As I noted in 2025, Cambodia’s government finally has what it has always wanted: “a relationship with the U.S. that strengthens, rather than undermines, the CPP’s hold on power.”
Last June, the U.S. government officially removed Cambodia from its arms sale blacklist, a month after an American ship docked for the first time at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base. The latter was particularly significant, given the extensive Chinese refurbishment of the base, which U.S. and Western officials feared was intended to host a permanent Chinese military presence. Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of the United States Indo-Pacific Command, described the port visit as a sign of the “strong upward trajectory” of relations between Phnom Penh and Washington.
These improvements have come even as branches of the U.S. government have come to officially recognize the extent of the Cambodian elite’s involvement in the country’s gigantic online scamming industry. According to U.S. government agencies, online scamming cost U.S. citizens at least $10 billion in 2024.

Alleged killers of Australian, US surfers go on trial in Mexico
ENSENADA – The suspected murderers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hot spot went on trial on Sept 7, two years after their killings in a suspected robbery.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state.
They had been camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024.
Their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft several days after they went missing. They bore gunshot wounds to their heads.
Three men are on trial over their killings.
The Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the proceedings.
Bereaved mother Debra Robinson stared at the accused before bursting into tears in the courtroom.
“It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” her partner Martin Robinson earlier told reporters.
“We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why,” he said.
The couple did not speak to reporters after the first hearing. Martin told AFP they will do so at the end of the proceedings, which are expected to conclude within a month and a half.
Martin is expected to testify on Sept 8.
‘Good phones’
Authorities say the men were murdered during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was found burnt near their bodies.
Three witnesses appeared before the court on Sept 7, including the stepson of one of the defendants, identified as “Ramon”.
Testifying from an adjoining room with his face concealed, he said he accompanied the accused – known as “El Kekas” – to the crime scene.
Ramon said he was in the vehicle listening to music when the “commotion” began.
“I heard a lot of noise, got out of the pickup and ran as fast as I could to my uncle’s house, where I hid in the bathroom,” he said.
He said he rejoined the group following the crime, after they called to warn him that “the same thing that happened to the gringos” would happen to him if he said anything.
Ramon described his stepfather as violent and said that he had previously attacked his mother. She confirmed the violence in her testimony.
The girlfriend of the witness’ stepfather was sentenced to 20 years in prison in 2025 after admitting she had instigated the robbery in order to steal the pickup’s tyres.
Ary Gisell Silva told a court that she had urged her boyfriend and two other men to rob the surfers, noting they had “good phones and good tyres”.
“El Kekas” previously faced charges for enforced disappearance, but these were eventually dropped.
The other two suspects were initially arrested for possession of methamphetamines. Evidence was later found linking them to the robbery and murder.
The crime sparked outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, where the surfers’ friends and families galvanised a major search on social media for their bodies.
Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the United States. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad played professional football in Guatemala and ran a clothing company in San Diego. He was killed a few months before he was set to marry.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists.
Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while travelling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa in the north-west.
Their bodies were later burnt. AFP

US Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights says antisemitism in America is 'national crisis'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:19:08 UTC
10:19:08 KST

US Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon described the rise in antisemitism in the United States as a "national crisis," pledging that combating antisemitism would remain one of her top priorities at the Justice Department.
Speaking Thursday at a gala for the Israeli-American Council (IAC) in San Diego, Dhillon detailed lawsuits against universities and businesses, criminal proceedings for hate crimes, and settlements totaling nearly half a billion dollars.
"The rise in antisemitism is not a wave of isolated incidents. This is a national crisis that requires national determination," Dhillon said. "Communities are being tested, institutions are being tested, and leaders are being tested."
According to Dhillon, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division is working to ensure that every American, including Israeli-Americans, can "live, learn, pray, and work without fear."
DOJ official details antisemitism enforcement efforts
Dhillon listed a series of institutions that have been the focus of government action.
She cited a lawsuit against Harvard University under civil rights law, claiming that Jewish and Israeli students were harassed and excluded.
Dhillon also mentioned two lawsuits against UCLA following incidents at protest encampments, where, according to her, Jewish students were blocked, assaulted, and sprayed with pepper spray.
She also mentioned agreements with Columbia University, Northwestern University, Cornell University, and Brown University, and added that more than 100 colleges, universities, medical schools, and law schools are under investigation.
Dhillon also noted the use of a law against planning restrictions targeting Orthodox Jewish communities and another law to protect synagogues and religious schools.
According to Dhillon, the Justice Department is simultaneously pursuing indictments in California, New Jersey, New York, and Washington, DC.
"When a Jewish person is attacked because they are Jewish, it's a federal crime," she said.
Oakland café case prompted by community report
Outside university campuses, Dhillon highlighted legal action against an Oakland café accused of refusing service to Jewish customers.
"We are currently pursuing legal action against a café that refused service to Jewish customers – clear antisemitic discrimination in a public place," she said.
Dhillon did not name Jerusalem Café in Oakland, but gave prominent attention to the lawsuit against it.
Jerusalem Café, located on Telegraph Avenue in Oakland and owned by Fathi Abd Al-Rahim Harara and Native Grounds, has closed its doors while facing three lawsuits. The federal case is expected to begin on October 26.
The owners have claimed that the proceedings are part of an effort by "Zionist organizations and the federal government" to use the courts to suppress support for Palestinians, and vowed to continue the "fight for the liberation of Palestine."
The Justice Department filed the lawsuit on June 9, 2025.
According to the lawsuit, Jonathan Hirsch arrived at the café with his five-year-old son. Harara allegedly asked whether he was a Zionist, called the Star of David a "violent hat," demanded that the two leave, and called the police.
In another case, customer Michael Radis was allegedly told, "You're the Jew, you're the Zionist. We don't want you in our café."
Dhillon said a report from the community had prompted the initial investigation.
"In the case of the café, a report from the community led to the opening of our initial investigation," she said.
Dhillon urged Jews and Israeli-Americans to continue documenting incidents and providing testimony, even in the face of fears of retaliation.
"As long as I hold this position, fighting antisemitism will be one of my top priorities," she said.

Panama Canal may cut ship traffic further as El Niño strengthens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:16:10 UTC
10:16:10 KST

Panama Canal may cut ship traffic further as El Niño strengthens
Canal authorities may further reduce ship traffic if a strengthening El Niño worsens the country’s drought.
Panama could impose further cuts on the number of ships sailing through the Panama Canal, an official said, as a strengthening El Niño raises fears of water shortages at one of the world’s busiest maritime trade routes.
The warning from the new administrator of the Panama Canal Authority, Ilya Espino de Marotta, on Monday came after the government declared a nationwide state of emergency over El Niño on August 26.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Strait of Hormuz: What has happened since the US-Iran MoU on June 17?
- list 2 of 4Panama’s Grand Canal
- list 3 of 4Can Iran enforce a restricted zone in the Strait of Hormuz?
- list 4 of 4How much oil is going through Hormuz? Why data doesn’t match US claims
The canal, which handles 5 percent of global maritime trade, has already reduced the maximum number of ships allowed through daily, from 36 last month to 34 starting on September 4.
A further reduction will start on September 15, when the limit will be 32 ships.
Espino, who took over as administrator of the Panama Canal Authority on Monday, told the AFP news agency that restrictions could be tightened again if the drought does not subside.
She said she was not ruling out the possibility that in February or March, the limits “could be reduced to 29 or something similar”.
She said rainfall over the coming months would determine whether further restrictions are needed.
“Depending on how much rain falls in September, October and November – the three critical months – that will determine whether I need to lower any slots further in January, February or March,” she told the Reuters news agency last week.
The restrictions are not expected to become as severe as during the 2023-24 drought, when daily crossings fell as low as 22.
The Panama Canal depends on freshwater to operate the locks that raise and lower vessels travelling between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Water comes mainly from the artificial Gatun and Alajuela lakes, which are replenished by rainfall.
An average transit consumes about 200 million litres (about 53 million gallons) of water.
That dependence makes the 80km (50-mile) canal particularly vulnerable to prolonged dry weather, and levels in both reservoirs have already dropped with the onset of El Niño.
This year’s El Niño – which affects weather patterns and pushes up global temperatures – is expected to be the strongest since record-keeping began four decades ago.
Apart from reducing the number of vessels transiting the Panama Canal, authorities have also reduced their maximum draft, from 15.2 metres to 14.6 metres (50 feet to 48 feet).
Draft is the depth of water a ship needs to float safely. A lower draft limit means vessels may have to carry less cargo to pass through the canal.
The disruption comes at a sensitive time for global shipping.
The Panama Canal’s importance has increased as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East has fallen sharply amid the US-Israel war on Iran. Some vessels have recently paid more than $1m at auction to secure transit slots through the canal.
Panama is betting on a new reservoir at Rio Indio – a river in the country’s centre – as a longer-term solution.
The project is intended to provide water for canal operations and more than half of Panama’s population for the next 50 years, but it is expected to take five to six years to complete.
Espino, the new administrator, told Reuters that the reservoir would “ensure that the canal never again has to resort to lowering the draft or reducing the number of transits”.

Former Israeli army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party would emerge as the largest party in Israel’s parliament with 25 seats compared with 21 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud if elections were held today, according to a poll released Monday.
The survey was conducted by the Israeli market research and public opinion polling institute Midgam for Israel’s Channel 12.
Yashar gained one seat compared with the channel’s previous poll, giving it the largest representation in the 120-member Knesset.
Likud, meanwhile, lost two seats.

The Democrats, led by Yair Golan, a former Israeli army deputy chief of staff, remained unchanged at 11 seats, while Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu party lost one seat, falling to eight.
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party, led by Yaakov Asher, received eight seats, while Aryeh Deri’s ultra-Orthodox Shas party secured seven.
An alliance between the right-wing Religious Zionism and Zehut parties, led by Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin, respectively, was projected to win six seats.
Amcha Yisrael, led by Ofer Winter, received four seats.
Among the Arab parties, the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, secured seven seats, while Mansour Abbas’ United Arab List received four.
Several parties failed to cross the 3.25% electoral threshold, including Benny Gantz’s Blue and White and Avi Maoz’s Noam Yisrael.
In terms of political blocs, the opposition secured 68 seats, including 57 for Jewish parties and 11 for Arab parties.
Netanyahu’s bloc meanwhile received 52 seats, gaining two after the parties led by Smotrich and Winter crossed the electoral threshold.
Forming a government in Israel requires the support of at least 61 members of the 120-seat Knesset.
When respondents were asked who they believed was better suited to be prime minister, 42% chose Eisenkot compared with 35% who favored Netanyahu, giving Eisenkot a seven-point advantage.
The poll results come ahead of Israel’s general election scheduled for Oct. 27.
Earlier Monday, Israeli parties submitted their candidate lists for the elections a day before Tuesday’s deadline.
The submissions came amid divisions over electoral alliances, most notably Eisenkot’s decision not to merge his party with Bennett’s.

Ukraine's chief prosecutor resigns over call centre corruption scandal
- Published
Ukraine's chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko has resigned over corruption allegations related to illegal call centres in the country.
It follows a search of his offices over the weekend by Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators, who said they had identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office.
In his resignation letter, Kravchenko said he did not want his position to be used as a "tool for political confrontation", and referenced an earlier post in which he rejected the claims as "unsubstantiated".
Corruption scandals have plagued Kyiv throughout the war against Russia, with accusations levelled at several members of President Volodymyr Zelensky's inner circle.
According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets".
The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu.
Kravchenko released a statement on Sunday evening dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated", and denied any wrongdoing.
He tendered his resignation a day later, thanking Zelensky and the Ukrainian parliament for their "trust". The Ukrainian president is yet to comment publicly on the resignation.
Despite the creation of two Ukrainian anti-corruption bodies, Nabu and Sap, over a decade ago, corruption continues to be a significant problem in the country.
In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap.
Kyiv's European partners expressed alarm at the announcement, with ambassadors from the G7 group of nations warning it could endanger Ukraine's integration into the European Union.
Ukraine is an EU candidate country, a status it was granted on condition it mounted a credible fight against corruption.
Zelensky reinstated the freedom of the two anti-corruption bodies as a result of the backlash, but questions have persisted over his commitment to anti-corruption reform.
Last month, Nabu said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering.
A senior official in Zelensky's office alleged to be involved was sacked.
In an interview with the BBC last month, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the president needed to be asked about his awareness of potential corruption among his closest team.
"Let him answer this question... I believe that he's ready for such questions. It's his responsibility to tell us all whether he was aware of all that or not... I don't want to make any assumptions," he said.
During his time in office, the 35-year-old was credited with heading a drive against corruption.
Since his dismissal in mid-July, after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces, he has been outspoken against what he has called a "systemic crisis of governance" in Ukraine.
However, he has emphasised that he has no evidence that Zelensky is personally involved in corruption.
"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity," Federov told the BBC.

A mass Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv overnight on Sept. 8 killed at least five people, injured 29 others, and sparked a series of huge fires that filled the morning air across the city with smoke.
Residential buildings, a school, and warehouses were damaged in the attack, signaling a violent end to the brief respite for the capital during a diplomatic visit by U.S. envoys over the weekend.
"It's like The Hunger Games, it's just about survival," Dariia Kolisnyk, a resident of a building damaged by a missile in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, told the Kyiv Independent.
"You just go to bed, wondering whether you'll wake up or not. That's life in Kyiv."
The strike follows Russia and Ukraine's agreement to pause aerial attacks on each other's capitals for three days. While the precise expiration time of the truce was hazy, there is no doubt about its end.
Liudmyla Akhremenko, also a resident in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, said her home has been damaged for the second time in an attack in the area.
"The blast wave blew out the windows, and stones flew into the house. People’s furniture was damaged," Akhremenko told the Kyiv Independent.
According to Akhremenko, no shelter has yet been built nearby, so she was at home when the attack occurred.
"It was very scary," she said. "I was sleeping and woke up to the explosion. I saw that the windows had opened, the glass had shattered, and the flowers had fallen. Everything jumped up to the ceiling."
Explosions rang out in the capital at around 3:30 a.m. local time, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground. Another loud blast occurred about 10 minutes later.
At around 4:14 a.m. local time, Kyiv Independent journalist Yevgeniya Doluda reported a series of up to six explosions in rapid succession.
"There was a very strong bang," Kolisnyk said. "I opened my eyes and saw the window flying, and big flashes. I ran to the second room, where my child and my husband were sleeping and climbed through the broken door and windows."
"I got the child, thank God, sat him up, everything is fine. My husband was cut a little by the glass. But, thank God, everything is fine," she added.
The blasts followed warnings from Ukraine's Air Force that Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered strike drones were bound for Kyiv. Monitoring channels reported that at least 12 ballistic missiles have targeted the city in the span of about an hour.
The Air Force later reported that Russian forces launched 32 cruise missiles, 166 Shahed-type drones of which "more than half" were jet-powered, and an unspecified number of ballistic missiles. Two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles, and 142 drones were intercepted, it said.
It added that missile and drone strikes were recorded at 29 locations.
As of 6:20 p.m. local time, three people had been killed and another 29 injured in Russian attacks, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported.
Meanwhile, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that as of 5 p.m. local time, 23 people had been injured, 14 of whom were hospitalized. Three people are in serious condition.
The death toll had also risen from three to five, the mayor added.
"The Russians tried to deliberately cause as much harm to life as possible — ballistics, cruise and anti-ship missiles, jet-powered 'shaheds,'" President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media.
Speaking to reporters later in the morning, Zelensky described the interception of almost all Russian cruise missiles as "a good result."
"Is it enough? No. We need (interceptor) missiles," he added. "We need a package of ballistic missiles from the Americans. They heard in detail what we need, when we need it."
"I count on meeting with President Trump to raise this topic. And, God willing, we will get a result."
At least two multistory residential buildings in the capital were damaged by drones, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported. Fires also broke out in warehouses, and garages and vehicles were reported damaged.
Rescuers evacuated two people from a 16-story apartment building that was damaged in the attack, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. Another 10 people were rescued after being trapped in a five-story building during the strike.
A drone attacked the building of the We-Ukraine TV channel, which is part of Ukraine's national telethon, which has been broadcasting since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. The attack occurred during a live broadcast, injuring at least five people, Zelensky said.
"‘Shaheds’ against the media is a new chapter in Russia's degradation, and there must certainly be a response from Europe and the world to this," Zelensky said.
The TV channel reported its newsroom and offices were struck during the attack.
Yevhen Panchenko, one of the residents in the Solomianskyi district whose homes were damaged, said he was initially in his apartment on the ninth floor during the attack but ran down to the first floor as the explosions intensified.
"I already call this street a 'training ground' because these attacks are not happening for the first time," he said.
"These attacks destroy people’s lives and livelihoods. They have nowhere to live or work. It’s horrible."
The State Emergency Service reported fires and damage in several neighborhoods, including Kyiv's Holosiivskyi, Solomianskyi, Darnytskyi, Podilskyi, and Dniprovskyi districts.
The attack comes after sustained Russian drone attacks against Kyiv that, before the weekend's truce, targeted the capital around-the-clock for nine consecutive days.
In an apparent sign of their resumption, air raid sirens sounded throughout the morning with the Air Force reporting several jet-powered drones in the airspace above Kyiv. Air defense fire and explosions were heard throughout the day and into the evening as Russian jet-powered drones continued to target the capital.
read also
The assault also affected communities in the surrounding region, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Oblast Administration. Russian forces attacked the area from the evening of Sept. 7 into the morning of Sept. 8, hitting residential areas and civilian infrastructure.
Three people were injured in the region, Tkachenko said. One of those injured was a 2-year-old girl who suffered a shrapnel wound to the eye and was hospitalized, according to Tkachenko.
Two apartment buildings, a house, a warehouse, and a production facility in the town were also damaged in the city of Bila Tserkva. Damage to homes, warehouses, businesses, and vehicles occurred in the Kyiv Oblast districts of Brovary, Boryspil, Fastiv, and Obukhiv, Tkachenko added.
Air raid alarms also sounded overnight in other regions of Ukraine, including Rivne Oblast in the northwest and other areas far from the front lines. The Air Force warned less than an hour earlier that Russia had likely launched cruise missiles from its Tu-95 and Tu-160 strategic bombers.
Moscow on Sept. 6 announced a three-day pause on attacks against Kyiv while U.S. Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the city for peace talks. The Kremlin declared the truce would "begin at midnight today," without specifying if that meant Sept. 5 or 6.
While Witkoff and Kushner's visit passed without an aerial attack against Kyiv, Russia immediately began firing drones at the capital after their departure on Sept. 7.

Chinese woman sues son for US$54,000 in childcare fees after 15 years, sparking debate
‘Grandparenting fees’ disputes are not aimed at commercialising family relationships, but serve to clarify responsibilities, legal experts stress
A woman in eastern China took legal action against her son, seeking more than 360,000 yuan (US$54,000) in compensation for her role in caring for his daughter.
This dramatic case has ignited a nationwide debate concerning evolving perspectives on grandparental childcare responsibilities.
In April, a Shanghai court disclosed details of a case from last year involving Xu, a woman in her 60s, who sued her son, surnamed Liang.
Years after divorcing her husband, Xu had been living with her son. Following Liang’s divorce in 2014, when his daughter was just four years old, Xu assumed most of the responsibility for raising the child. This included covering her living expenses, medical bills, and educational costs, according to a report by Xinmin Evening News.
In the lawsuit, Xu accused her son of lacking a “sense of family responsibility” and failing to fulfil his duties as a father. Liang contended that he had supported his daughter to the best of his ability, given his modest monthly income of only 3,000 yuan (US$450) at that time.
The conflict escalated after Liang remarried and moved out with his new wife, leaving his daughter in Xu’s care. After 15 years of caregiving, Xu expressed that she could no longer continue due to financial pressures and sought compensation from her son.

Should Chinese schools demote English as a core subject?
A teacher’s call to end ‘worshipping foreign things’ reignites debate over the language’s role in schools
The controversy has revived a long-running debate over the role of English in Chinese schools.
The argument came to life again after Tang Jiafeng, a maths teacher known for coaching students through the national postgraduate entrance exam, said on social media that children, parents and schools had devoted disproportionate amounts of time and resources to English, a subject he argued had little relevance to the jobs most people eventually did.
“I publicly call for English to be stripped of its status as a core subject,” Tang wrote on Saturday. “No country in the world places English in such a supreme position as we do.”
He argued that Chinese children were being pushed to cram in English before they had even mastered their own language, despite the country’s thousands of years of civilisation.
“English is just a tool. It is enough to know how to use it,” Tang said. “The history of Chinese people worshipping foreign things and fawning over foreigners should end!”

EU trade chief to meet CEOs over China strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:59:37 UTC
09:59:37 KST

Maroš Šefčovič speaks to the media as he arrives for a meeting of G7 trade ministers in Évian-les-Bains, France on May 6, 2026. | Pool photo by Benoit Tessier via AFP/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič is expected to meet European CEOs on Sept. 18 to get their feedback on the European Commission’s push to diversify critical supply chains away from China, according to four people familiar with the meeting.
The Commission has floated a “diversification tool” to encourage companies to source critical imports, such as raw materials, from at least three different suppliers where alternatives are available.
But before formally proposing such a measure, the EU executive wants to secure industry buy-in — and understand how far companies are willing to go to reduce their dependence on China, given the costs involved.
Advertisement
The push comes as the Commission has stepped up engagement with Chinese officials over the summer as Brussels seeks to reduce the EU’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with the Asian giant. The meeting will happen two days after Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivers her landmark State of the Union speech, in which she is expected to address the EU’s anxiety about the threat China poses to its industrial base.
After technical talks with Beijing, Šefčovič will speak by videoconference with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, in mid-September before heading to Beijing in early October.
Should these talks not yield results, national leaders have urged the EU executive to devise new ways to tackle China’s industrial overcapacity in time for their mid-October summit.
The Sept. 18 meeting is expected to bring together CEOs from the machinery, electrical components, automotive and chemical sectors, two people familiar with the event said.
“I’m glad that I hear more often that even the business leaders themselves — many of them — are realizing that the cost of diversification is smaller than the cost of disruption,” Šefčovič told POLITICO last week.
“That’s the logic which I would like to develop further. I’m inviting the key stakeholders for [a] special forum.”
Šefčovič said such discussions help shape the Commission’s thinking on how such a tool should work.
Among the input sought is “what would be the best design of such an instrument, where we can have the buy-in for the economic leadership of our leading companies,” he said.

The event is scheduled to be held in Dumfries House in Ayrshire, Scotland — the headquarters of The King’s Foundation, a charity founded by Charles in 1990 to advocate on environmental and social issues, the two people said.
According to one of the people, the exclusive gathering's guest list is set to include Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang, British founder of Google DeepMind Demis Hassabis and Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the Vatican on AI.
Advertisement
That person said around 30 high-profile people from the AI industry were invited to attend in total.
A Royal official told POLITICO: “One of the king’s unique abilities as sovereign and global statesmen is his ability to convene top level stakeholders.”
The official stressed King Charles would not issue his own thoughts, but wants to “convene, engage, listen and encourage debate” on one of the biggest issues of the age.
The event is being organized by the Ditchley Foundation — a charity which organizes discussions on global issues, and ministers will also be invited.
Benanti declined to comment. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.
A representative for Google DeepMind said they could not comment on Hassabis’ movements. Hassabis, who is now chair of DeepMind, in July called for the creation of a U.S.-based global standards organization for AI.
Advertisement
King Charles has also shown an interest in the development and regulation of AI.
The king met Nvidia’s Huang and tech executives from Apple, Amazon and Google during a state visit to Washington in April, where he highlighted collaboration on AI between the U.S. and U.K.
He also hosted a banquet at Windsor Castle during President Donald Trump’s state visit to the U.K. last September which was attended by tech industry leaders including Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman.
Trump’s visit coincided with the announcement of significant investment in the U.K. by U.S. tech firms and the signing of a U.S.-U.K. Tech Prosperity Deal, which was later suspended over trade disagreements.
In November, Huang and other pioneers in AI received an award from King Charles, and the Nvidia chief executive said the king gifted him a copy of an address he made at the AI Safety Summit which said: “If we are to realize the untold benefits of AI, then we must work together in combatting its significant risks.”

Qatar seeks to 'phase out' US-Iran crisis through regional dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:57:43 UTC
09:57:43 KST

Qatar has sought to "phase this crisis out" rather than pursue an immediate end to the US-Iran war, aiming to establish conditions for comprehensive regional dialogue and a sustainable political resolution, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari confirmed.
Speaking to CNN, Al-Ansari stated that Doha believes the conflict cannot simply be frozen, cautioning that an abrupt pause without addressing root causes risks paving the way for another round of confrontation.
"We have to phase this crisis out rather than end it immediately," he said.
"What we need to do is make sure the playing field is in a place where we can have the right negotiations for a sustainable solution."
He stressed that Qatar does not want the region to transition between recurring cycles of intense fighting: "We do not want to go from a high-intensity conflict to a high-intensity conflict. We don't want to freeze this conflict and be back here a couple of months later."
Inclusive dialogue
Al-Ansari outlined Doha's two immediate operational priorities: mitigating economic pressure and preventing military escalation across the Gulf and Iran.
"Right now, what we are doing, we have two main priorities. One is make sure that the Strait of Hormuz is open and that the economic pressure on all of us collectively and the peoples in the region, including the people of Iran, has left us," he stated.
The second priority is to halt further military strikes to foster an environment in which regional stakeholders can pursue inclusive engagement.
"When we get to that point, this is the point we need to have a regional push, all of us collectively, to make sure that dialogue happens and it is a comprehensive dialogue that includes all of us, not just outside," he said.
Identifying political will and technical hurdles as the primary barriers to an agreement, Al-Ansari noted that Qatar is actively preparing proposals to address both challenges.
He observed that sanctions have failed to yield expected diplomatic breakthroughs, underscoring that "this issue will only be resolved through a deal. It will only be resolved at the negotiation table."
He also issued a strong warning against normalising maritime disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, which threaten global energy and food security: "We need to kill this in its infancy. It cannot become the new normal in war for countries to basically just close waterways in this way," urging accountability and respect for international law.

Clock ticks down as parties still scrambling over final slates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:50:23 UTC
09:50:23 KST

The first day of filing has ended, and by 10 p.m. Tuesday — or midnight if the chairman of the Central Elections Committee extends the deadline — the final makeup of the party slates competing in the 2026 election should become clear.
Six major parties have yet to submit their candidate lists. Some are waiting for additional candidates, others are still settling internal disputes, and at least one was forced only Monday to announce the replacement of a senior candidate.
With the deadline approaching, here is where each party stands — and where last-minute surprises could still emerge.
Likud
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party has endured several turbulent days over its candidate list, particularly the slots that the party leader is permitted to fill with handpicked candidates rather than primary winners.
Netanyahu has delayed announcing those candidates despite a deadline imposed by Likud’s internal court and appears intent on withholding his decisions until close to the filing deadline.
A meeting of the Likud Secretariat that was expected to approve the reserved slots and was originally scheduled for 11 a.m. Tuesday was postponed to 2 p.m. — and even that time was not considered final.
Netanyahu has also struggled to recruit candidates for the reserved positions, and it remained unclear whom he would ultimately choose.
High-tech entrepreneur Oren Dobronsky, whom Netanyahu had offered a reserved place in the top 10 of Likud’s slate, announced Monday night that he had decided not to run for the Knesset.
United Torah Judaism
United Torah Judaism, the Ashkenazi Haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, alliance made up of the Agudat Yisrael and Degel HaTorah parties, has undergone a dramatic shake-up in recent days, with its new slate expected to look markedly different from the previous one.
Longtime party chairman Moshe Gafni was unexpectedly ousted Sunday, with lawmaker Yaakov Asher named to replace him. Lawmaker Uri Maklev will also not be included on the slate.
On the Agudat Yisrael side of the alliance, veteran lawmaker Yisrael Eichler will give up his place to Elyakim Stark, a senior figure in the Belz Hasidic movement.
Shas
Shas chairman Arye Deri convened the Sephardic Haredi party’s Council of Torah Sages on Sunday to discuss the composition of its Knesset slate.
Several new names are expected to appear, including Yosef Elnatanov, a representative of Israel’s Bukharan Jewish community, and Lt. Col. (res.) Dror Amos, head of Haifa’s religious council, who left career military service about two years ago.
Some incumbent lawmakers have meanwhile been concerned that they could unexpectedly lose their places. Minister Yoav Ben-Tzur and former deputy minister Moshe Abutbul held discussions with several of the party’s rabbis to clarify their status amid concerns they could be dropped, though that now appears unlikely.
Joint List
The slate for the revived Joint List alliance of the predominantly Arab Hadash, Ta’al and Balad parties has yet to be announced.
One candidate who will not be on it is Jaafar Farah, who had been designated for the No. 4 position but withdrew amid allegations of sexual harassment.
Hadash, Farah’s party, said members of its secretariat and central committee would choose his replacement Tuesday. The party appears likely to select a woman for the slot.
Religious Zionist Party
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, which has struggled in polls to cross the electoral threshold, had hoped to unite with former senior military officer Ofer Winter’s Amcha Israel party.
Winter’s party, however, closed the door on an alliance and submitted its slate Monday.
The Religious Zionist Party is instead hoping that a joint run with former lawmaker Moshe Feiglin’s Zehut party will strengthen both factions. The agreement is a technical electoral alliance only, with the parties planning to separate again after the election.
Under the agreement, Feiglin received the No. 2 spot on the joint slate, while Zehut was allocated three places in the top 10.
Blue and White
Another party polling below the electoral threshold is former defense minister Benny Gantz’s Blue and White.
Gantz failed in efforts to forge an alliance with former UN ambassador Gilad Erdan’s Unity party. Erdan has since announced that he is withdrawing from the election entirely.
Reports nevertheless continue of a possible alliance between Blue and White and former lawmaker Yoaz Hendel and his reservists’ movement.
The party has also undergone a last-minute personnel shake-up. Lawmaker Michael Biton informed Gantz that he was leaving the party. Just hours later, former Beit Shemesh Mayor Aliza Bloch announced that she was joining Blue and White.

Durban Conference, 25 years on. Paul Divakar Namala: “Solidarity and resistance work in the long run”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:31:00 UTC
09:31:00 KST

The third UN Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance in 2001 was a watershed moment for millions across the world. Seven thousand people representing governments and civil society from 170 countries gathered in Durban, South Africa. Led by countries in the Global South, the Durban Conference challenged the idea that human rights is a Western concept, recognized the historical roots of contemporary forms of racism and called on States to repair the lasting consequences of colonialism and slavery. While the US and Israel withdrew from the Conference, the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action were adopted, both of which became foundational documents for the global fight against racism. But with racism still very much alive, we spoke with activists about their struggles and hopes.
My name is Paul Divakar Namala. I am the Executive Director of The Inclusivity Project and Convenor of the Global Forum of Communities Discriminated on Work and Descent. My work focuses on communities whose social status, occupations and exclusion are inherited across generations through caste, analogous hierarchies and systems rooted in traditional slavery.
I am a Dalit. Dalits were historically treated as “untouchable” and placed at the bottom of, or outside, the caste hierarchy. This can shape every part of life: access to a common water source, where a child sits at school, where a family may live, what work a person is expected to perform and whether others will eat with or even be seen with them. Poverty is widespread in South Asia, but its burden falls disproportionately on Dalits because caste restricts access to land, education, dignified employment, public services and political power.
Inherited hierarchies remain deeply entrenched
Across South Asia, constitutional guarantees and democratic institutions coexist with caste discrimination and practices of untouchability. These persist in villages and cities, and in public institutions, private workplaces and corporations. Dalits may face threats or violence for asserting land rights, entering places of worship, marrying across caste, accessing common resources, seeking education or standing for elected office.
Dalits in South Asia are not alone. Roma communities in Europe and beyond, Burakumin in Japan, Haratine and other communities affected by traditional slavery in the Sahel, Osu communities in Nigeria, Quilombola communities in Brazil and other communities in Latin America experience distinct histories and realities. They should not be collapsed into a single category. Yet many face structurally connected patterns: inherited stigma and social status, endogamy, segregation in housing and education, exclusion from land and decent work, confinement to dangerous or degrading occupations, trafficking and forced labour, and backlash violence when they resist. We describe these peoples, in all their diversity, as Communities Discriminated on Work and Descent, or CDWD.
Reconnecting with my identity
Where I grew up in India, my family faced repeated attacks as we asserted our rights, including rights over public land. When I was 21, a petrol-bomb attack took the life of my mother.
Only as I grew older did I understand how much of what happened to my family was connected to caste. My father taught me that our purpose should not be limited to seeking justice for ourselves; we had to dismantle the structures that allow such abuses to continue. That teaching guided me away from vengeance and towards challenging the social norms and caste structures that treat some human beings as inferior, exploit their vulnerability and assign them a life of servitude.
Together with my spouse, who came from a different caste, I helped build a community of human rights defenders. For too long, Dalits were portrayed only as victims or survivors. We are also organisers, advocates and defenders of human rights. This work began more than four decades ago, when I was in my twenties.
In 1998, together with leaders from across India, we formed the National Campaign on Dalit Human Rights. We wanted caste-based discrimination and violence to be documented and discussed nationally and internationally. Looking back, I realise how groundbreaking that effort was, especially with so few resources.
Bringing caste to Durban
When we learned that the United Nations was organising a World Conference Against Racism, our immediate response was: “We have to be there.” We were new to these international processes. We contacted people working on caste discrimination and were invited to a preparatory meeting in Bellagio that helped shape the agenda for Durban.
At Bellagio, many participants supported putting caste on the agenda, including Pierre Sané, then Secretary General of Amnesty International. Civil society succeeded in making caste a major issue in the Durban process, but several Asian governments resisted its explicit inclusion in the final Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, arguing that it would target their countries or interfere in internal matters.
Although the final Declaration did not contain the explicit recognition we sought, what the movement achieved was extraordinary. Durban gave unprecedented international visibility to caste discrimination and helped move Dalit rights from the margins towards the centre of international human rights debate.
Dalit activists were present in large numbers, carrying documentation, testimonies, drums and protest across the conference grounds. People approached us and said, sometimes awkwardly but with genuine solidarity, “You are untouchable? Let me hug you.” Those encounters showed both how unfamiliar the issue was internationally and how quickly human connection could challenge the stigma imposed upon us.
Solidarity, resistance and the unfinished agenda
Over the years, we have connected with communities and advocates in Somalia, Ethiopia, Kenya, Niger, Mauritania and Nigeria, with Roma movements across Europe and beyond, and with Quilombola and other communities in Latin America. Their histories are different, but their struggles reveal how inherited status, stigmatised work and exclusion can reinforce one another across generations. Working together makes these structures visible and prevents governments and institutions from excusing them in the name of culture or tradition.
Durban also taught us that affected communities must speak for themselves. They must not be treated merely as victims or sources of testimony, but as human rights defenders and leaders who define the problem and shape the solution. Solidarity does not require us to claim that every oppression is identical. It requires us to respect distinct histories while recognising common structures of dehumanisation and standing together against them.
Amnesty International can make an important contribution by adopting a clear global approach to discrimination based on work and descent; undertaking comparative research across regions; integrating CDWD into its work on racial justice, gender, labour rights, corporate accountability, climate justice and access to justice; and supporting defenders from affected communities to lead this agenda.
The fight is far from over. We are working for stronger international recognition, including comprehensive CERD guidance and, ultimately, a Declaration on the Rights of Communities Discriminated on Work and Descent. Yet the real test is always on the ground. International declarations have meaning only when they change the life of a woman confronting untouchability, a sanitation worker demanding safe and dignified work, a Roma child resisting school segregation, or a Haratine family seeking freedom, land and equality.
This story was originally published by IPS.

At 8:45 p.m. Monday, Ukraine’s Air Force warned of a jet-powered Russian drone over Kyiv, while several others were reported approaching the capital – more than three hours before Moscow’s stated 11:59 p.m. deadline.
The attacks intensified overnight. A series of strong explosions rang out across Kyiv early Tuesday as Russia launched missile and drone strikes on the capital and surrounding region.
The blasts were heard by Kyiv Post reporters across the city at around 3:30 a.m., after authorities declared an air raid alert and warned of a missile attack.
Russian drones also struck the Boryspil and Fastiv districts of Kyiv region. Fires broke out at industrial facilities in Boryspil, seven trucks were destroyed, and a logistics complex was struck twice, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said.

Russian state news agency TASS reported that the three-day suspension ordered by Russian President Vladimir Putin had expired.
However, its precise timing remained disputed. As Kyiv Post reported earlier Monday, Russian accounts said the halt began at midnight between Friday and Saturday, placing its expiration at 11:59 p.m. Monday.
Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Kravchenko Resigns Over Corruption Accusations
Russian drone activity was reported well before that deadline. At 8:45 p.m. Monday, Ukraine’s Air Force warned of a jet-powered drone over Kyiv, while several others were reported approaching the capital – suggesting Moscow breached even the timeline it had publicly set for the truce.
The pause was limited largely to strikes on Kyiv and Moscow rather than a broader ceasefire.
Russian attacks elsewhere in Ukraine continued throughout the weekend. On Saturday, explosions were heard near Boryspil during an air raid alert, while strikes in other regions killed and wounded civilians.
‘Better than Patriot’

But Russia’s failure to abide by even a brief three-day truce underscored a familiar reality for Ukrainians: even high-level diplomacy has failed to stop Moscow from bombarding innocent civilians in Ukrainian cities.

“Following the halt of negotiations resulting from US breaches of commitments and its repeated failures in military engagements, the US has recently conveyed proposals to Tehran through mediators,” the source said.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities were themselves the main obstacle to inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), arguing that Washington was responsible for the resulting lack of access while simultaneously using the issue to increase pressure on Tehran.
“The ball has long been in the US court,” Baqaei said, adding that Washington must end its military attacks, economic sanctions and naval blockade if it wants to resolve the confrontation.
“Diplomacy is a dynamic and continuous process,” the spokesman said, noting that delegations from Oman and Pakistan have visited Iran in recent weeks, while Qatari representatives held talks with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran on Sunday.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari told CNN that Doha had put forward several ideas and was exploring different scenarios aimed at addressing the concerns of both sides.
Tehran and Muscat have meanwhile reported significant progress on a separate arrangement for a temporary safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials have stressed, however, that such an agreement would not amount to the full reopening of the strategic waterway, as Washington has claimed.

Palestinian resistance group Hamas has warned that Israel is attempting to conceal evidence of genocide committed against Palestinians in Gaza by removing, crushing, and transporting rubble under which the bodies of thousands of missing people remain trapped.
In an official statement, the group condemned "attempts by the occupation government and its army to conceal evidence of the brutal crimes committed against our people in Gaza through the removal, crushing and transportation of rubble."

Hamas stated that tampering with sites containing human remains and potential legal evidence "constitutes a violation of international law and the International Court of Justice's order to preserve evidence," describing it as "an assault on the dignity of the martyrs and the right of their families to recover and bury the bodies of their loved ones."
Calls for international forensic teams
Hamas welcomed a warning issued by Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in the Palestinian territories, who cautioned that Israeli debris clearance risks erasing traces of "atrocity crimes."
Calling upon the UN and the International Criminal Court to safeguard these sites, Hamas urged the dispatch of international forensic investigators into Gaza to oversee body recoveries and document forensic material.
While stressing that clearing rubble and rebuilding remains an "urgent humanitarian and national necessity," Hamas maintained the operation must ensure the recovery of missing persons without permitting Israel to evade accountability.
On August 3, the Geneva-based Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor reported that commercial Israeli firms were involved in crushing and clearing debris across military-occupied zones covering roughly 66 percent of the enclave.
The monitor estimated that at least 10 million tonnes of rubble had been displaced or crushed, documenting approximately 100 trucks moving debris out of Gaza daily alongside 400 demolition and crushing machines.
Israel's two-year genocide has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, injured over 174,000, and left over 9,000 missing beneath devastated infrastructure.

Under pressure to explain super policy, Joyce says he is 'not Jesus Christ'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:07:01 UTC
09:07:01 KST

Barnaby Joyce pushes back on need to model impact of One Nation super policy
In short:
Barnaby Joyce has struggled to explain the economic and financial impact of One Nation's early access superannuation policy.
The policy would allow Australians to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years.
What's next?
Mr Joyce has pushed back on warnings the scheme would have an inflationary impact by pumping more money into the economy, which may worsen the cost-of-living crisis.
One Nation Treasury spokesperson Barnaby Joyce has struggled to explain the impact of the party's proposed early superannuation access scheme, saying he is "not Jesus Christ" while being questioned about the policy's financial and economic consequences.
Under the proposal, Australians who pay rent or have a mortgage would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years.
The money would retain the favourable tax concession Australians already receive on super savings under the plan, which One Nation said would provide "breathing room" for people struggling with the cost of living.
On Tuesday, Mr Joyce sidestepped questions about modelling of the proposal after economists warned it could have an inflationary impact.
"The implications that I have to model you getting your own money, I find a little bit perverse. It is actually your money," he said.
He later said one reason One Nation had not modelled their policy was because Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had not awarded the minor party additional staff and resourcing.
When pushed on the loss of people's retirement savings over time, Mr Joyce insisted he was across the detail of the policy.
"I'm the Treasury spokesman, not Jesus Christ. I mean, you have to actually give me the details of these things, if you got to put them forward to me," he told 7.30 on Monday.
Australians 'not stupid', Joyce says
Mr Joyce argued the money in retirement savings was already circulating in the economy because it was being invested via superannuation companies, and therefore would not be inflationary.
Independent economist Saul Eslake said he found the comments "disturbing" because they showed a lack of understanding from Mr Joyce about how the economy works.
Mr Eslake said money that is invested in superannuation is used to buy shares, government bonds and investments in overseas markets, which means it is not circulating in the Australian economy and adding to demand for goods and services.
"If you instead take money out of superannuation so that there is less invested in financial and real investment assets, and instead it is sitting at least initially in a bank account, which history shows [people] are likely to withdraw to fund to use on additional spending, it will then go into the economy," he said.
He warned pumping more cash into the economy would put upward pressure on inflation, and said the Reserve Bank would likely be forced to increase interest rates.
Mr Joyce also said "anyone with a brain" would be able to effectively use the scheme, which would not be means tested.
"People are not stupid,"
"The presumption by the socialists is that everyone's a total moron and is going to take money from a good return and take it to a bad return if they don't need it.
"If there's extra money in the economy and you put it into your bank account and don't spend it, it has no inflationary aspect."
But Mr Eslake said people, especially those on lower incomes, historically did not save additional salary, but spent it.
"What evidence shows us from a wide range of studies over a long period of time is that people on lower incomes, and younger people, are more likely to spend any additional income they get compared to higher income people,"
Pandemic super withdrawals spent quickly
At the height of the COVID pandemic, many Australians found themselves with less work and struggling to make ends meet.
Because of that, some people jumped at the opportunity presented by the Morrison government to access their super savings early.
In total, 2.6 million Australians withdraw money from their retirement nest egg, which was capped at $20,000.
A study written by economist Steven Hamilton, who now works for Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, found a significant portion of the $38 billion accessed by people was spent quickly.
Nearly half the money was spent within eight weeks of it landing in personal accounts, and spending increased by an average of 130 per cent in the first two weeks.
The largest spending category was ATM withdrawals, and the second largest category was gambling expenditure.
Researchers found that overwhelmingly, people who withdrew from their super were not experiencing a reduction in their wage relative to before the pandemic.
The federal opposition's housing spokesman, Andrew Bragg, said the Coalition was looking at ways people could use their superannuation to afford a home.
Senator Bragg said the Coalition was reviewing policy ideas, including letting people use their super to offset their mortgage or as collateral for a loan.
A party spokesperson later denied the options were being considered.
The ideas have previously been discussed as part of Senate committee work Senator Bragg chaired in 2024.
ABC accused of 'socialist' agenda
One Nation announced its policy on Monday, and Mr Joyce has since accused the ABC of being "socialists", pointing to a line of questioning in a number of interviews about the modelling of the proposal.
"I understand the ABC socialist position, that it's not really your money, it's somebody else's money. Therefore, you have to go through a bureaucracy before you get entitled to get your own money," he told ABC Radio Breakfast.
He said it was a "philosophical view" that distorted the reality of the inflationary impacts of the proposal.
"This money is your money," he said.

Poll: Yashar increases lead over Likud; Eisenkot bloc projected to win 57 seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:01:33 UTC
09:01:33 KST

Yashar, led by Gadi Eisenkot, would be the largest party in the next Knesset with 25 seats if elections were held today, according to a Channel 12 News poll published Monday evening.
The party, which won 24 seats in the channel's previous survey, is extending its lead over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud, which is projected to win 21 seats, down from 23.
According to the poll, the bloc led by Eisenkot reaches 57 seats, while the Netanyahu-led bloc captures 52. The Arab parties—the Joint List and the United Arab List—are projected to win a combined 11 seats.
Among the other parties, Naftali Bennett's Beyahad is projected to win 13 seats, followed by the Democrats under Yair Golan with 11. Yisrael Beiteinu and United Torah Judaism are each projected to win eight seats, while the Joint List and Shas take seven seats each.
Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, running alongside Moshe Feiglin's Zehut, are projected to win six seats each. The United Arab List and Ofer Winter's Amkha Yisrael are each credited with four seats.
Several lists failed to cross the 3.25 percent electoral threshold, including a joint ticket of Ofer Winter and Michal Zelekha, which received 2.7 percent support. The Haredi Public party, Blue and White, Makom Lekulanu, Noam and Yisrael Tehila also fell short.
The poll was conducted by the Midgam Institute, headed by Mano Geva, among 503 respondents via telephone and online platforms. The sampling error is plus or minus 4.4 percentage points.

Durban Conference 25 years on. Adnan Barq: “The very fact of existing is a fight in itself”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:01:00 UTC
09:01:00 KST

The third UN Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance in 2001 was a watershed moment for millions across the world. Seven thousand people representing governments and civil society from 170 countries gathered in Durban, South Africa. Led by countries in the Global South, the Durban Conference challenged the idea that human rights is a Western concept, recognized the historical roots of contemporary forms of racism and called on States to repair the lasting consequences of colonialism and slavery. While the US and Israel withdrew from the Conference, the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action were adopted, both of which became foundational documents for the global fight against racism. But with racism still very much alive, we spoke with activists about their struggles and hopes.
My name is Adnan Barq. I’m 25 and I’m a Palestinian from the Old City of Jerusalem. I’m a journalist and also make films.
The Durban Conference was happening when I was one year old. It’s fascinating to see how many people got together back then to try and shape justice in the world but, without being too pessimistic, I see that things are getting worse. This is happening everywhere, not just in Palestine.
Refusing to normalize injustice
I got involved in activism when I was at university, out of a refusal to normalize the occupation. I see how my people survive by being forced to normalize Israeli practices of injustice, apartheid, and colonialism but I just could not do that.
I studied in Bethlehem University, so I always had to cross a checkpoint back and forth to Jerusalem. That was my biggest exposure to the Israeli occupation’s physical system of oppression, even though I also experienced it as a child, when Israeli settlers wanted to take over the Al-Aqsa Mosque.
 
As an adult, I realized that being able to speak English was a privilege and a tool, so I had a responsibility to send a message to the world about Palestine, to expose the occupation. That was in 2020. 
Apartheid, racial profiling and otherness
Israel’s apartheid is sophisticated. The Israeli soldiers on the walls of Jerusalem are trained to racially profile people. Whenever they see a Palestinian, you are dragged from the street out of hundreds of white settlers, and you are taken to the wall and you get fully body inspected while your ID says that your house is in that specific street. 
 
I think the Israeli occupation forces are aiming to create a coercive environment that makes us want to leave because they cannot easily uproot us. But all these practices make us embrace ourselves even more. They reject our existence and this makes us scream louder. 
Systemic racism and resistance
I wish that it was only the government that was the problem so we could fight for change. But the genocide, the call to erase Palestinians is now fully embedded in public discourse.   
 
This is what systemic racism is. It’s coming from everywhere. 
Just the fact of existing is a fight in itself. Me walking from my house to a school, me walking from my house to a café with friends, is in fact resisting the occupation by existing.
I don’t want to accept this but I also don’t want to spend all my life fighting. It’s exhausting.
The power of social media
As Palestinians, we are destined to be like lawyers for our cause.  
 
I felt the need to just show the world how my people are living and social media was a good tool for that. The fact that our cause is universal. The people who are harassing my friends are from Florida, from Norway, London, Germany. The ones who stop me at checkpoints are like some random Spanish Jewish people who just live in Israel.
When the violence escalated in 2021, I had to fully engage in activism. I had the opportunity to travel to Belgium and to other countries and met many parliamentarians to explain what we are going through.
 
I try to keep what I show as real as I can, showing what we are suffering but also that I have a full life. I have family, friends and I also go to parties, we study, we enjoy basic activities and at the same time can talk about why and how we are resisting the occupation. Showing that there are many sides to our lives as Palestinians is very important to me and it is part of the fight.  
Not the end game
It’s difficult to understand the pain that otherness and racial profiling causes unless you experience it. The best thing we can do is unite and keep calling out all these systems that are built to victimize us. We need to organize, meet, plan and seek solutions and not rely on empty slogans that are only good for a sticker. We need more than that.
In this era, we are privileged to have access to each other digitally, but this kind of connection is not enough, we need to turn it into something real. Social media is an important tool, but not the end game.
This story was originally published in ElDiario.es

In Singapore, malls for shopping only are going out of style
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:00:28 UTC
09:00:28 KST

In Singapore, malls for shopping only are going out of style
Marina Square’s future revamp typifies the rise of mixed-use developments incorporating retail, office, residential and other components
Last Monday, property developer Singapore Land Group (SingLand) said in a statement that Marina Square, which was completed in 1986, would close on March 31 for a redevelopment that would include features such as luxury residences, serviced apartments and offices with a gross floor area of more than 360,000 sq m.
The revamp, slated for completion in 2031, will have a 304-key hotel that will place guests close to the Marina Bay area, and Marina Square will be refreshed into a four-storey shopping centre offering a wider variety of food and drink options and pet-friendly environments, according to SingLand.
Three new towers will be integrated into the site, including a 49-storey residential tower hosting 204 luxury homes, while offices will occupy eight floors of a new mixed-use tower, providing around 13,000 sq m of lettable space.
Local media reported that the news of Marina Square’s closure came with disappointment from shoppers and tenants alike. Parents lamented the loss of the shopping centre known for its indoor playgrounds and children’s retail outlets, while tenants said they were shocked by the short notice.
Retail experts point out that consumers today are increasingly seeking experiences, community and connection, and this shift is fuelling the growth of mixed-use developments around the world.

Foreign, mainland students flock to Hong Kong sparking property demand in education sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:00:12 UTC
09:00:12 KST

Foreign, mainland students flock to Hong Kong, sparking property demand in education sector
City to attract around 200,000 extra students, requiring international schools, university campuses to expand, as incentives lure wealthy migrants
Hong Kong’s bid to become a global education hub is likely to transform the sector as a sustainable source of property demand, with the city tipped to see around 200,000 non-local students by 2035, according to CBRE.
The city’s international schools are estimated to require enormous additional real estate to accommodate nearly 30,000 to 40,000 non-local students, as the institutions would need to set up 40 to 50 new school campuses.
This could mean up to an extra 1.11 million square metres (12 million square feet) of gross floor area, a study released by the consultancy on Monday showed.
Moreover, the student accommodation segment would also need more than 70,000 additional beds to provide living space for these students in about a decade.
“Hong Kong’s education sector is undergoing a structural transformation,” said Marcos Chan, executive director and head of research at CBRE Hong Kong.
