Iran Threatens to Target U.S. Energy Assets in Gulf If U.S. Strikes Again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Iran warned on Monday that it could target U.S. oil and gas interests in the Gulf if the U.S. launches any new attacks on its assets.
Responding to U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s warning that “if Iran shoots at U.S. ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers,” Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said: “It’s simple: the oil and gas production chain here is sprawling, accessible, and exposed. American oil and gas companies across these waters and facilities share that exposure. Strike our assets and you get struck."
Ghalibaf’s warning comes as Tehran seeks greater leverage amid Washington’s ongoing economic pressure campaign and stalled efforts to negotiate an end to the war that the U.S. and Israel launched on Feb. 28.
Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary, said Monday that "economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to the blockade perimeter." The "exclusion zone” in the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman would begin at the blockade line, extend through the Strait of Hormuz, and continue into the Persian Gulf, Rezaei said. Vessels entering the zone to transit the Strait would be placed on an Iranian sanctions list.
The latest flare-up began Saturday, when Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attacked U.S. warships in the region. The U.S. responded by striking three Iranian oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub. The U.S. and Iran have for the past week exchanged a flurry of attacks, ending a brief respite in active hostilities. Oil prices reached near six-week highs on Monday as commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway through which a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments flowed before the war, has fallen sharply.
Negotiations remain at a standstill
Diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran have stalled. The two countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on June 17, agreeing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and engage in technical talks to end the war. But the truce was short-lived.
After a commercial vessel was struck in the Strait in late June, the U.S. attacked Iranian missile storage and radar sites, prompting Iran to retaliate against U.S. military installations in the region. Intermittent attacks continued in July, and fighting resumed in late August after a brief, informal pause.
The Trump Administration has said it is investigating a U.S. strike last week on a family compound in southern Iran where a wedding celebration was underway, killing at least five people and wounding more than 60, according to Iranian state media.
No new formal negotiations have been announced since the MOU’s 60-day deadline expired on Aug. 17. Although some of Iran’s top officials, including President Masoud Pezeshkian, have signaled a willingness to return to the MOU and resume talks with the U.S., the two countries’ positions remain far apart. The U.S. wants to significantly restrict or dismantle Iran’s nuclear program and guarantee unrestricted commercial passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has called for broad sanctions relief, access to frozen assets, an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, and a role in managing the Strait.
Hard-liners in Iran have shown little appetite for compromise on those red lines, and analysts previously told TIME that Iranian leaders may believe time is on their side, with Tehran prepared to absorb further economic and military pressure in hopes that rising energy prices will eventually prove too politically costly to U.S. President Donald Trump.
“The Iranian nation accepts neither threats nor coercion, nor negotiations whose outcome would be the weakening of the country’s rights,” Hossein Taeb, head of the IRGC’s Basij paramilitary force, said on Monday. “Negotiations are for securing the nation’s rights, not surrendering them.”
While Trump faces domestic pressure to rein in gas prices and avoid an open-ended war in the Middle East ahead of the November midterms, he has also appeared determined to secure an outcome he can present as a victory.
“I’m not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table,” Trump posted on Truth Social last week. “I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable.”
Iran considers new tactics
Iran is planning to establish a new restricted zone to amp up global economic pressure and force an end to the U.S. blockade. At the same time, Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz and are in talks on its future administration—an arrangement that could formalize Tehran’s role in managing the waterway against U.S. opposition.
But Ghalibaf acknowledged in parliament on Sunday that Iran is struggling with sharp inflation, a collapsing rial, and high unemployment.
Washington’s economic pressure campaign, which includes the naval blockade, sanctions on Iran, and the threat of secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners, has squeezed Tehran. The International Monetary Fund estimates that inflation in Iran is near 70%.
The Strait of Hormuz, which Iran began restricting at the start of the war, has been the country’s most important bargaining chip. But that leverage may be weakening as Gulf states turn to routes that bypass the Strait and the U.S. escorts shipments through the corridor. The conflict has also inflicted mounting costs on Iran’s own economy by trapping tens of millions of barrels of Iranian crude inside the Gulf.
Oil prices near $100 as hostilities flare
Brent Crude oil prices approached the $100 per barrel benchmark on Tuesday, reaching near six-week highs of $98.51, after the Iran-backed Houthis attacked multiple Saudi energy facilities in the early hours.
The strikes represented a significant regional escalation, adding further pressure to crude prices.
Meanwhile, traffic via the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted.
Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm, shared data with TIME that shows only 12 ships crossed the Strait on Monday, significantly lower than the 138 vessels that typically passed through the vital trade waterway during a 24-hour period before the war.
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump on Monday said that “oil prices will drop precipitously" when the U.S. "win[s] the war," but he did not provide a timeline or address the likelihood of energy markets remaining volatile even after the conflict is said to have ended.
Iran faces mounting international pressure
The U.K. is reimposing major economic sanctions against Iran in line with the European Union and the United States, it was announced Tuesday.
The legislation expands trade prohibitions against Iran to additional goods, technology, and services.
Financial measures will "further reduce the government of Iran’s ability to access the U.K. financial system and raise funds in support of its nuclear programme," according to Minister for the Middle East Stephen Doughty.
Additionally, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the U.K. will take action this week to "report Iran to the U.N. Security Council for its nuclear violations, alongside our allies."

The semantics of profane quasi-verbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

The semantics of profane quasi-verbs Social relations in a dynamic framework
Main Article Content
Abstract
Though profane imprecations like F*** you! have received no attention in formal semantics, we might expect our theory of linguistic meaning to have something to say about such common expressions. In this paper, I discuss the nature of the meanings of profane quasi-verbs (Quang 1971) that function syntactically like f*** in the example above, and I provide a formal model that can account for some important aspects of their meaning and conversational use. This analysis throws light on the role of social relations in semantics and pragmatics.

Han double-double helps China seal second place in Women's Basketball World Cup Group D
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:51:01 CST
08:51:01 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Han Xu recorded 19 points and 10 rebounds as China secured second place in Group D with a commanding 71-51 victory over Italy at the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup on Monday.
Having already assured itself of a place in the qualification for quarterfinals, China claimed its second consecutive victory following an overtime win over Czechia. It will face Puerto Rico on Wednesday, with the winner advancing to meet France in the quarterfinals.
China led for all but the opening 21 seconds and seized control with an 11-0 run spanning the first two quarters.
Zhang Ziyu was instrumental in the surge, scoring eight points on perfect shooting from the field as China established an 18-point lead.
Han proved China's most consistent scoring option, converting eight of her 11 attempts from the field, including both shots from beyond the arc, while also controlling the boards.
China took a 40-21 lead into halftime and scored the first six points after the restart, extending the margin to as many as 25 points with 8:02 remaining in the third quarter.
Italy then scored 10 unanswered points to cut the deficit to 46-31. The Italians closed within 12 points later in the period, but China regained control with a 6-0 run early in the fourth quarter and cruised to victory.
Yang Shuyu added 15 points, five rebounds and four assists in a team-high 33 minutes, while Wang Siyu contributed five points, five rebounds, six assists and two steals.
Matilde Villa led Italy with 15 points on six-of-11 shooting. China led for 39 minutes and 39 seconds, while Han posted a game-high efficiency rating of 24 in just over 30 minutes on court.
China completed the group phase with two wins from three games. Third-placed Italy will meet Australia on Wednesday, and the winner will face Spain in the quarterfinals. ■

Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of killing seven in Yemen prison attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:50:53 UTC
08:50:53 KST

Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of killing seven in Yemen prison air strike
Houthi media outlet released footage of destruction and rescue efforts after the Saudi air strike on al-Hazm prison.
Yemen’s Houthi rebels have accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out an air strike on a prison in the northern city of al-Hazm, killing seven people, including a child.
The strike on the Central Corrective Facility in al-Jawf province, on the Yemeni side of the border with Saudi Arabia, also wounded at least seven people, including a woman, Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesperson for the Houthi-run Health Ministry, said on Monday.
The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV channel aired footage it said showed the aftermath of the alleged attack, including a collapsed building and people searching through the rubble.
Saudi Arabia has not commented on the allegations.
Al Masirah TV also released footage it claims shows Houthi forces using ballistic missiles to attack Saudi supply trucks containing military equipment at a border crossing in Yemen’s Hadramout province.
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of “committing massacres” in al-Jawf, flying reconnaissance drones and supplying mercenaries with weaponry.
“The ongoing Saudi aggression against Yemen will not go unpunished, and the Saudi enemy must bear the consequences of its crimes against the Yemeni people,” he said.
Saree also claimed that the Houthis had shot down four Saudi reconnaissance drones over the previous 24 hours, including a CH-4 drone that he said was carrying out “hostile missions” in al-Jawf.
“This aircraft is the second of this type that was shot down during the past 12 hours, and the fourth during the past 24 hours,” he added.
Dually, Riyadh has not commented on Saree’s allegations.
The Houthi claims come as fighting between the group and Yemen’s internationally recognised government has flared up in recent weeks. The Yemeni government said it made significant territorial gains against the Houthis, including in the al-Jawf, Bayda, Dahle, and Marib provinces on Sunday.
Over the past days, government-aligned forces conducted counterattacks in Taiz and Hodeidah after the Houthis launched a major offensive in a struggle to control the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait, with hundreds of people reportedly killed over the past 24 hours.
UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg called Monday on the country’s warring parties to halt hostilities and exercise maximum restraint, warning that the latest escalation could spiral into a full-scale war.
Air strikes on prisons have occurred several times during Yemen’s decade-long war. In 2022, the Saudi-led coalition struck a detention facility in Saada province, killing at least 87 prisoners and wounding about 266 others.
In 2019, the coalition struck a Houthi-run detention facility in Dhamar province, killing more than 100 people and wounding dozens.

Eiffel Tower shut by staff protest after female workers moved for religious visit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:46:44 BST
08:46:44 KST

Investigation after female staff at Eiffel Tower replaced by men for religious visit
- Published
An investigation has been launched in France after female staff at the Eiffel Tower were replaced by male colleagues for the visit of a Hindu religious group.
A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the iconic landmark in Paris on Saturday.
"Women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated", staff union representative Diane Davoine said. The tower closed on Monday as staff went on strike to show their outrage.
BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances.
Ariel Weil, who is the president of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower, blamed its managers for being "a bit overzealous" in complying with the request without considering whether it was "inappropriate".
Weil, who is also mayor of Paris Centre, told French broadcaster Franceinfo on Tuesday that the incident was "totally shocking and unacceptable".
An internal investigation will determine who was responsible for putting the conditions in place, Weil said, and ensure it "never happens again".
In a statement reported by AFP news agency, staff at the monument said that during Saturday's visit, female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present".
"Tensions mounted over the weekend, so [on Monday morning], the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again," Davoine said.
Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), which runs the Eiffel Tower, had previously said the conditions imposed on female staff were not in line with its values "nor with the principles of equality between men and women".
BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in a Parisian suburb.
In a statement on X, BAPS said the trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".
It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".
On its website, the group describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.
It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.
It draws its beliefs from the teachings of Lord Swaminarayan, a late 18th-Century celibate ascetic who is regarded by his followers as an incarnation of Vishnu, the revered Hindu god of preservation.
BAPS says the segregation of men and women was introduced for the benefit of women, but critics say 18th-Century beliefs have no place in today's world, and keeping women out in the name of religious practices is discriminatory.
Politicians in France have condemned Saturday's incident.
Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."
French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."
Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."

What is celebrated on September 8 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:45:42 EEST
08:45:42 KST

What is celebrated on September 8 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On September 8, the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, Literacy Day, Physical Therapy Day, and the International Day of Journalists’ Solidarity are observed. State holidays are also celebrated.
On September 8, one of the greatest Christian holidays — the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary according to the new church calendar, International Literacy Day under the auspices of UNESCO, World Physical Therapy Day and International Journalists’ Solidarity Day — are observed, UNN writes.
International Literacy Day
An official date under the auspices of UNESCO, established at the 14th session of the General Conference in 1966 on the recommendation of the World Conference of Ministers of Education on the Eradication of Illiteracy. The day is intended to remind the global community that literacy is a fundamental human right, the basis for personal development and a key tool for building resilient societies.
Despite global progress, hundreds of millions of adults worldwide still lack basic reading and writing skills, which is why UNESCO dedicates this day each year to a specific theme — from the digitalization of education to expanding the rights and opportunities of linguistic minorities.
World Physical Therapy Day
A professional holiday established in 1996 by the World Confederation for Physical Therapy (World Physiotherapy) to highlight the important contribution of rehabilitation specialists and physiotherapists to restoring people’s health, mobility and quality of life.
This date symbolizes the solidarity of physical rehabilitation specialists around the world and draws public attention to the importance of the comprehensive adaptation of patients after serious injuries, surgeries and strokes, as well as wounded military personnel.
International Journalists’ Solidarity Day
A commemorative date established in 1958 at the 4th Congress of the International Organization of Journalists in Bucharest in memory of Czech journalist, writer and anti-fascist Julius Fučík, who was executed on September 8, 1943, in Berlin’s Plötzensee prison.
On this day, media workers and human rights organizations around the world express support for colleagues who face persecution, censorship and arrest for their professional activities, and also honor the memory of journalists who died while performing their professional duties in hot spots.
Independence Day of North Macedonia
The country’s main state holiday commemorating the referendum of September 8, 1991, during which more than 95% of citizens voted to leave Yugoslavia and establish a sovereign state.
The day is an official public holiday and is marked by a ceremonial flag-raising, speeches by the country’s leadership, award ceremonies for prominent figures and mass festivities.
Victory Day in Malta (Il-Vitorja)
A national holiday that commemorates three important historical events at once: the end of the Great Siege of Malta by Ottoman forces in 1565, the capitulation of Napoleon’s French garrison in 1800, and the lifting of the naval blockade and Italy’s capitulation in World War II in 1943.
The celebrations include a traditional sailing regatta in Valletta’s Grand Harbour, religious processions and ceremonial wreath-laying.
National Day of Andorra (Our Lady of Meritxell Day)
The principality’s main state and religious holiday, dedicated to the country’s patroness — Our Lady of Meritxell.
The tradition of honoring her dates back to the signing of the Act of the Pareage in 1278, which established joint rule over Andorra, and on September 8, a solemn Mass is held at the Meritxell Sanctuary, along with nationwide cultural festivals.
Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary
According to the new calendar, the Orthodox and Greek Catholic churches celebrate the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary — the first of the twelve most important feasts of the new liturgical year. The feast was established in honor of the birth of the Virgin Mary to the righteous Joachim and Anne in Jerusalem, which, according to tradition, came as an answer to their sincere prayers after many years of childlessness.
In folk tradition, the Lesser Feast of the Blessed Virgin was considered a harvest festival, a women’s day and a time to give thanks for the harvested grain, marking the beginning of the wedding season.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the holy martyrs Adrian and Natalia, who suffered for the Christian faith at the beginning of the fourth century in Nicomedia during the reign of Emperor Maximian. Adrian was a pagan official who, struck by the steadfastness of Christians during their torture, himself came to believe and was executed, while his secretly Christian wife, Natalia, supported her husband until the final moments of his life.
People called this day "Natalia the Oat Woman," as it was then that the mass harvesting and threshing of oats began.

OpenAI top scientist urges ‘extreme caution’ with pace of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:44:00 UTC
08:44:00 KST

OpenAI top scientist urges ‘extreme caution’ with pace of AI
- OpenAI's chief scientist warns AI is evolving too fast, urging voluntary slowdowns to ensure safety and better human control.
- AI models now perform complex tasks and soon may self-improve without humans, raising serious concerns about consequences.
- Despite risks, companies and startups invest heavily in advanced AI, including recursive self-improvement, aiming for more human-like intelligence.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – OpenAI’s top scientist has warned that artificial intelligence is evolving so rapidly that it is becoming increasingly difficult for humans to understand and control, saying he expects AI labs to voluntarily slow development for safety reasons.
In a relatively short space of time, AI models can operate computers, collaborate with humans and other AI systems and carry out research projects, chief scientist Jakub Pachocki wrote in a post on Sept 6.
It will not be long before they can also improve themselves without human intervention, a process known as recursive self-improvement, he said.
“This is a time that calls for extreme caution,” Pachocki wrote in the post.
“I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence.”
Developers can either try to steer AI more closely to align with human interests or “slow down future development as needed”, he wrote.
“I expect and hope for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.”
Pachocki’s remarks are consistent with broader doomsaying by AI technology executives.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has warned that AI could replace half of all entry-level jobs.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman once made a similar prediction but told Bloomberg TV in an interview last week that the AI industry had not done enough to communicate the potential benefits to humanity.
At the same time, companies are pushing ahead with ever-more capable models.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang posted on social media platform X that “AGI (artificial general intelligence) has arrived”, in response to the release of OpenAI’s latest model, a reference to AI that is more capable than humans.
The giddy pace of AI releases has coincided with breakthroughs in cybersecurity capabilities, scientific discoveries and apparent formalisation of longstanding mathematical problems.
OpenAI has said the AI models that attacked the research platform Hugging Face coordinated with each other through message boards without being detected.
The company has opted for a limited release of its latest GPT-6 Astra model, citing its advanced cybersecurity capabilities.
Anthropic has not yet released its cutting-edge Mythos model to the public for similar reasons.
A growing number of start-ups are trying to bring about the very thing Pachocki warns about – self-improving AI.
Investors are flooding into recursive self-improvement, betting that this is the route to AI that is truly human-like, or more impressive.
Inherent, founded by former DeepMind researchers, raised US$50 million (S$63.2 million) earlier in 2026.
Recursive Superintelligence, an AI lab founded by renowned scientist Richard Socher pursuing similar research, also landed US$650 million in financing.
Pachocki’s employer, OpenAI, has said it wants to build a “true automated AI researcher” in less than two years. BLOOMBERG

Qatar calls for phased de-escalation for sustainable solution to Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:41:06 UTC
08:41:06 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Qatar is seeking to “phase this crisis out” rather than pursue an immediate end to the US-Iran war, with the broader goal of creating the conditions for comprehensive regional dialogue and a sustainable political solution, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said Monday.
Speaking to CNN, Al-Ansari said Doha believes the current crisis cannot simply be frozen, warning that a temporary halt in hostilities could pave the way for another escalation.
“We have to phase this crisis out rather than end it immediately,” he said. “What we need to do is make sure the playing field is in a place where we can have the right negotiations for a sustainable solution.”
He said Qatar does not want the region to move from one period of intense conflict to another, stressing that any resolution must address the underlying regional issues.
“We do not want to go from a high-intensity conflict to a high-intensity conflict. We don't want to freeze this conflict and be back here a couple of months later,” he said.
Al-Ansari said Qatar’s immediate priorities are to ease economic pressure and prevent further military escalation across the region, including attacks affecting Gulf states and Iran.
“Right now, what we are doing, we have two main priorities. One is make sure that the Strait (of Hormuz) is open and that the economic pressure on all of us collectively and the peoples in the region, including the people of Iran, has left us.”
The second priority, he said, is preventing further military escalation so that regional actors can eventually push for an inclusive dialogue.
“When we get to that point, this is the point we need to have a regional push, all of us collectively, to make sure that dialogue happens and it is a comprehensive dialogue that includes all of us, not just outside.”
Al-Ansari said political will and technical issues remain the two main obstacles to reaching a settlement, adding that Qatar is developing proposals aimed at addressing both.
He also argued that sanctions have failed to deliver the expected diplomatic results, saying the conflict ultimately can only be resolved through negotiations.
“But at the end, this issue will only be resolved through a deal. It will only be resolved at the negotiation table.”
He also warned against allowing the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz to become normalized, saying the consequences could extend beyond the region through energy, food and economic shocks.
“We need to kill this in its infancy. It cannot become the new normal in war for countries to basically just close waterways in this way.”
He called for accountability and international law to prevail, warning that normalization of such tactics could have consequences far beyond the current conflict.

US woman charged with killing son ‘very invested’ in Lindsay Clancy trial, prosecutors say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:41:03 UTC
08:41:03 KST

An Illinois woman charged with killing her two-year-old son had been closely following the murder trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy and was texting friends about the case just hours before her son was found dead, prosecutors said.
Corie Walsh, 40, was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after her son, Barrett, was found dead in the basement of the family’s suburban Chicago home last Tuesday, according to court records obtained by NBC Chicago.
Prosecutors said Walsh had become “very invested” in Clancy’s nationally watched trial and was discussing it with friends until about 12.30pm that day. A neighbor found Barrett less than four hours later.
Walsh was found elsewhere in the home with injuries authorities said were self-inflicted. Prosecutors said she later told investigators that she killed her son because she believed he was the “devil” and the “antichrist”. Her attorney, Andrea Lyon, told reporters Walsh was experiencing a psychotic episode and called the boy’s death a tragedy for the entire family.
Police were called to Walsh’s home in Frankfort, about 35 miles south-west of Chicago, shortly before 4pm after a neighbor discovered Barrett in the basement, according to prosecutors’ petition seeking to keep Walsh jailed before trial.
The neighbor found the boy and began CPR while calling 911, prosecutors said. He was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. An autopsy determined that he died from asphyxia caused by ligature compression of the neck.
Police searching the house found Walsh fully dressed in a bathtub containing bloody water, prosecutors said. She had cuts to her wrists and thighs and was taken to a hospital with injuries authorities described as not life-threatening.
The disclosure that Walsh had been following Clancy’s trial came days after a Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in that case when jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict.
Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, was accused of killing her three young children in 2023. Her lawyers argued that she was legally insane and suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors maintained that Clancy understood what she was doing and knew it was wrong.
Authorities in Illinois have not alleged that Clancy’s trial played a role in the killing of Walsh’s son, and no evidence made public so far establishes a connection beyond her discussion of the case.
Frankfort police and prosecutors in Will county did not respond to calls for comment on Monday.

ISW assesses Putin's new deadline: At current pace, Russian forces would not capture Donetsk region until 2032
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:41:00 UTC
08:41:00 KST

ISW assesses Putin's new deadline: At current pace, Russian forces would not capture Donetsk region until 2032
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said this in a new assessment, according to Ukrinform.
According to the report, Putin has set no fewer than 15 reported deadlines for the seizure of the Donetsk region since February 2022, and Russian forces have failed to meet every one. Russian forces will not meet Putin's new deadline of seizing all of the Donetsk region by December 31, 2026. Russian forces have been fighting for Kostiantynivka since October 2025 and have not seized it in 11 months. Russian forces have not reached, much less entered or seized, the other Fortress Belt cities of Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, and Druzhkivka, and will not be able to seize all three within the remaining four months of 2026, considering that they have failed to complete the seizure of even one in nearly a year.
"Putin's many deadlines to seize all of Donbas reflect in part his need to provide a significant informational victory to the Russian people. Putin has promised Russians victory in exchange for enduring the burdens of war without bringing Russian society to a full wartime footing," the report said.
According to analysts, Russian forces will not seize the Donetsk region until 2032 at their current rate of advance – if they can seize it at all.
The Russian rate of advance across the theater was 2.91 square kilometers per day in August 2026, a slight increase compared to recent months. The average Russian rate of advance for Russian forces' priority effort in the Donetsk region was lower at only 2.36 square kilometers per day in August. Russian forces would take until October 2, 2032, to seize the remaining 19 percent of the Donetsk region at this rate – over a year after the next State Duma elections, which will likely be held in September 2031.
At the same time, ISW is not prepared to assess that Russian forces will be able to take the rest of the Donetsk region on any timeline, however. Russian forces will have to fight attritional urban battles through the cities of Ukraine's Fortress Belt before attempting to advance across fields – terrain that Russian forces have historically struggled to advance through.
"The Russian rate of advance has slowed significantly across the theater since 2025, when Russia's rate of advance had already begun to slow. Ukraine has proven that it can contest the tactical initiative in several areas of the frontline and hinder Russian logistics in 2026, and Russia has struggled to counter these Ukrainian efforts. Neither the trajectory nor any likely dynamics of the current conflict suggest that Russian forces will be able soon to accelerate their rate of advance dramatically as long as Western support for Ukraine continues at roughly current levels," the analysts wrote.
They attributed Putin's ambitions to capture the Donbas to the fact that the Russian military systematically misinforms him about the state of the front line in part due to the pervasive culture of lying within the Russian armed forces that milbloggers refer to as "beautiful reports." Russian high-ranking military commanders also routinely present exaggerated Russian advances as part of Russia's systematic cognitive warfare effort to portray Russian forces as making sweeping advances and Ukrainian defenses as collapsing. The lies and distortions of Russian military commanders at many levels are likely leading Putin to harden his perception that Russian forces can achieve his intended objectives in Donetsk Oblast by the end of 2026 and thus that he need not make any compromises in his aims.
The analysts added that Putin is doubling down on the fictional battlefield situation that he defines as "reality" and insisting that his misrepresentation of the actual state of the war become the basis for any peace negotiations on Ukraine. In particular, on September 6, Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said that Putin provided a comprehensive assessment to Witkoff and Kushner of Russian "significant advances" along the frontline – an exaggerated claim that does not match realities on the ground.

100 Palestinian students expelled from Israeli universities for criticizing Gaza war: Rights group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:28:59 UTC
08:28:59 KST

Abdel Ra'ouf Arnaout and Serdar Dincel
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Israeli universities have permanently or temporarily expelled 100 Palestinian students for criticizing Israel’s war on the Gaza Strip since October 2023, according to a Palestinian-run rights group based in Israel.
A report by Adalah examined changes in how Israeli higher education institutions have treated Palestinian students since the Gaza war began.
It documented cases in which Israeli universities suspended Palestinian students and launched disciplinary proceedings against them, classifying some of their social media posts as “support for terrorism.”
“In more than 80 cases, institutions imposed temporary suspensions before holding any hearing and before even determining whether the alleged violation had occurred,” it said.
“In 20 cases, students were permanently expelled or suspended from their studies for periods ranging from one to five years."
Adalah said the disciplinary measures targeted a wide range of forms of expression, including criticism of government and military policies and the war on Gaza as well as expressions of solidarity with Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
"Simply liking a post, displaying the Palestinian flag or the word Palestine on a personal account, sharing a news report, or praying for the people of Gaza” was enough to prompt a complaint or disciplinary proceedings in some cases, it added.
The group said students were summoned “to appear before disciplinary committees without being informed of the subject of the complaint,” adding that “in other cases, institutions did not verify when the content had been posted or whether the social media account belonged to the accused student.”
Adalah said that institutions “expanded the scope of their disciplinary powers beyond their legal limits, specifically against Palestinian students.”
By contrast, it said, “institutions in many cases maintained the limits of their authority when dealing with Jewish students and refrained from intervening in expressions unrelated to academic matters, even in the face of calls for the extermination of the Palestinian people and racist and inciting posts.”
The report warned that Israeli academic institutions have adopted a “two-track apartheid system” since Oct. 7, 2023, with Palestinian students facing emergency-based disciplinary measures while Jewish students enjoy greater protections for freedom of expression.
It said the policy "creates an atmosphere of intimidation among Palestinian students" and violates international law principles prohibiting racial discrimination and protecting minority rights.
Arab citizens make up roughly 21% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Since the war on Gaza began, Israel has imposed tight restrictions on social media posts and arrested activists who expressed solidarity with Palestinians.
Since October 2023, Israel, with US support, has been committing genocide in Gaza, killing more than 73,000 Palestinians and injuring over 174,000 others while destroying 90% of the infrastructure.

UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg called Monday on the country’s warring parties to halt hostilities and exercise maximum restraint, warning that the latest escalation could spiral into a full-scale war.
In a statement published on the UN’s website, Grundberg said recent attacks by the Houthi group across several fronts had intensified fighting and raised the risk of the conflict expanding further.
He described the developments as “deeply troubling,” citing reports of civilians being killed and injured, families being displaced and civilian infrastructure being damaged.
Yemen has endured conflict for more than a decade, he said, warning that a return to sustained, large-scale fighting would have severe consequences for civilians and further complicate the already difficult path toward a political settlement.
Grundberg said the Yemeni people’s demands for security, functioning institutions and a future beyond conflict require “a credible political path capable of addressing the political, security and economic issues at the core of the conflict.”
He stressed the need to make full use of existing communication channels, including the UN-backed Military Coordination Committee, to prevent further escalation.
He also called on all parties to comply with their obligations under international humanitarian law and protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
Grundberg said he would continue engaging directly with the parties in an effort to contain the current tensions and preserve space for dialogue.
He also urged regional and international actors to use their influence to de-escalate tensions and facilitate a return to political negotiations.
Several fronts across Yemen have witnessed renewed fighting in recent days between government forces and the Houthis, particularly in the governorates of Taiz, Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda, alongside airstrikes on sites belonging to the group.
Since July this year, several fronts have seen a series of mutual attacks that ended the relative calm prevailing in Yemen since a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.
The Houthis have controlled the capital Sanaa and several other cities since September 2014, while the internationally recognized government and allied forces control large parts of southern, eastern and western Yemen.

Greenland’s mineral wealth is of particular interest to the EU. The island holds 25 of the 34 raw materials Brussels classifies as critical, and closer access could help the bloc reduce its dependence on China.
Von der Leyen’s trip came as Trump posted a map on Monday depicting Greenland, Canada and other parts of the Americas under the US flag. The image also included Iceland and was labeled ‘United States of America.’
Washington’s push for control of Greenland has strained relations with Denmark and other European allies. Trump has also repeatedly questioned the alliance’s value to the US.
The visit also coincided with the start of Arctic Shield, military drills involving 11 NATO countries and around 400 troops in Greenland. No US personnel are taking part in the exercises, which run from September 7 to 18.

2026-09-07

08:20:24 KST

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports have come into effect, escalating a trade fight that has been marked by intensifying tensions between the US president, Donald Trump, and the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney.
The tariffs took effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, and range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering $20bn in imports from the US. The measures target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs.
The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $20bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian government said.
Carney said Tuesday that Canada would move faster to reduce its economic reliance on the United States. “In too many areas, they wanted dependency, not a true economic partnership,” said Carney. “We can’t let American goods into Canada tariff-free while they charge our companies to export to them.”
Last month, Trump announced a new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”. The US tariffs hit items such as hockey sticks and cement, affecting about 5.5% of Canadian exports to the US.
Since then, tensions between Canada and the US have intensified, with Carney last week urging the Trump administration to “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions.
Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” – which Canadians have rejected.
On Monday, Trump threatened to block sales of Canada’s Bombardier Aviation in the US, unless the Quebec-based plane maker moves manufacturing to the US.
“No more selling Bombardier in the United States!” Trump posted in all caps on his Truth Social platform, though he did not specify how he would achieve a sales halt.
Thousands of Bombardier aircraft currently operate in US airlines’ domestic fleets.
In a statement on Monday, the aerospace company touted its creation of “tens of thousands of jobs across the United States”, with “direct employment” in more than 20 states including Kansas, Texas, Arizona and California.
The company also noted that it spent more than $2.5bn annually with suppliers, and said its supply chain was “made up of approximately 2,800 American companies across 47 states”.
Negotiations between both sides broke down on 21 August after days of meetings in Washington, with Carney saying at the time that the Trump administration’s terms were ultimately unacceptable and that US negotiators had introduced restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the 11th hour.
US officials also made unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture”, he added, referencing the French-speaking province in eastern Canada, with Carney saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”.
But Trump’s top trade official Jamieson Greer later noted the US government was aware that French language protections were sensitive and important.
“This is not something where we push hard, or condition, or red-line,” he told Canadian public broadcaster CBC last month.
Polls show Carney has broad support from Canadians, but it could disappear within months as the consequences of the trade war sink in, according to political analysts.
Just 20% of Americans approved of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
Carney said last week his government was ready to sign a trade deal that benefited both countries, but US media reports say there are currently no ongoing negotiations between the two sides.

Military propaganda has been incorporated into Moscow’s metro infrastructure — CPD
Kyiv • UNN
War symbols targeting Ukraine were placed at the "General Karbyshev Boulevard" station. The CPD considers this a shift by the Kremlin toward "monumental propaganda."
In Moscow, the General Karbyshev Boulevard metro station was opened, with an inscription dedicated to the war against Ukraine placed in its vestibule alongside World War II symbolism. This was reported by the Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (CCD), UNN reports.
Details
It is noted that bas-reliefs depicting modern Russian sappers, military equipment, and combat drones have appeared on the walls. The facility was opened with putin personally in attendance, indicating support for this step at the highest level.
This is a clear marker of a change in the approach to propaganda: from temporary forms — banners, posters, television segments, and so on — the kremlin is moving to permanent monumentalism. Integrating military symbols into places used daily by millions of people is intended to normalize the war once and for all, turning it into a familiar backdrop
It is noted that, in addition, the attempt to embed war propaganda in infrastructure facilities indicates that the kremlin is not interested in peace scenarios.
"On the contrary, the Russian authorities seek to entrench the cult of war even more deeply in the minds of citizens, preparing society for a prolonged existence under conditions of armed aggression," the CCD concludes.
Reminder
According to the CCD, the visit of Patriarch kirill of the Russian Orthodox Church to the wounded Metropolitan of Horlivka and Sloviansk is a classic example of how the ROC and its head use the religious context and wartime events to promote the kremlin's political and ideological narratives.

A US-Russia deal won’t end the war. It will start the next one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:08:25 UTC
08:08:25 KST

After talks between President Putin and President Trump's representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ended, the White House called them "substantive." Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov called the meeting "substantive, constructive and exceptionally frank," adding that the US representatives "formulated a number of considerations on ways to reach a settlement."
According to Bloomberg, Putin is prepared to end the war only on Moscow's terms, and Russian demands have hardened because the Kremlin believes it holds a military advantage. Putin expects to seize the rest of Donetsk Oblast by the end of 2026, Reuters reported, citing a person close to the Kremlin: "There is no chance of reaching an agreement on the front line until Putin finishes taking the rest of Donetsk Oblast."
Witkoff has made many trips to Moscow. He arrived in Kyiv for the first time only the day after. That speaks volumes about where America's focus lies: Russia, not Ukraine.
The danger, though, is not the deal alone. Two American processes are running at once—a peace negotiated on Moscow's terms and a review that would pull US forces from Europe—and together they lower both the political and the military cost of a Russian attack on NATO. Everything below is why that convergence, not the handshake in Moscow, is the thing to watch.
Negotiating a Russian lie, not its strategic demand
Russia has long used disinformation to create strategic ambiguity, offering the West four different tales—all unpleasant, one designed to look like an "easy way out."
The first—give up Crimea, Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson—is what Trump's plan offers. But Putin's demands transcend Donbas, as both his 2024 speech and Russia's military operations show. His stated prerequisites require Ukrainian withdrawal from territory Russian forces do not even occupy, the "demilitarisation" and "denazification" of the Ukrainian government—meaning its replacement with a pro-Russian one—and Ukrainian neutrality excluding NATO.
The second: Foreign Minister Lavrov said in January that "nothing will work without settling the issue of Novorossiya"—which adds Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa.
The third, "one people, one nation," claims all of Ukraine. And the fourth—"the Russian World," the only one formalised in Russian strategic documents—encompasses the "former territories of Kyivan Rus, the Kingdom of Muscovy, the Russian Empire, the Soviet Union, and the contemporary Russian Federation." Its ultimatum of 17 December 2021 demanded that the US leave the European continent entirely.
This is what Russia is fighting for, and why the Kremlin sees an existential war: Russia becomes a Great Power or remains a pariah state. Trump is negotiating the first lie. If he intended a just and lasting peace, he would be addressing the fourth—Russia's actual strategic aim—not the one designed to look easy.
The so-called peace plan
Six months before Trump took office, I concluded his "peace plan" was a blueprint for Russian victory over Ukraine and the West. The 28-point plan published by Axios in November 2025—which alarmed European leaders, excluded NATO, and imposed demands on the EU beyond America's authority—proved the point.
The transactional logic is explicit. On 2 September, Trump said: "We want to have good relations with Russia, Ukraine, with everybody. Be great for business. Russia's got great land and very valuable land."
Asked whether Washington would pressure Russia if talks stalled, Kushner sidestepped and applied a corporate frame to the war: "In the business world, you think in terms of win-win." Of Putin, he added: "he has certain objectives... but there are different aspirations he has for his country that can also be achieved once this is concluded."
The administration does not care about peace or war, international law or the security architecture—only trade. And it has signalled that the aggressor should be rewarded, implying might makes right. This is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently blamed Ukraine—not Russia—for high fuel prices: "Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets." He said it after a meeting with Russia's finance minister.
The sequence of talks
The US representatives went to Moscow first, Kyiv second—carrying the aggressor's terms to the victim, not the other way around. Since they are effectively negotiating European security, an objective team would have consulted US allies in Europe first. According to the EU Ambassador to Washington, Jovita Neliupšienė, Moscow has not abandoned its military objectives, and "the top priority remains unchanged: to provide Ukraine with everything it needs to defend itself"—implying US and European strategy are no longer aligned. We already know the US is not planning to provide Ukraine any defence aid. French, British and German security advisers were allowed to join only the final Kyiv session—informed, but not allowed to influence their own security.
It is strategically absurd to let Europe's two strategic adversaries negotiate European security—which is what happens when we insist on solving the war from within NATO and the EU rather than through a coalition of like-minded countries able to stand up to both Russia and Washington.
The military half
For Europe, the ongoing US review of its troop levels and basing matters as much as the peace process—and it is equally transactional. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the review at NATO on 18 June, framing it as a transition to "NATO 3.0," with Europeans taking on conventional defence and the US concentrating on strategic and nuclear priorities.
The Pentagon's Terms of Reference reportedly examine troop levels, basing, overflight rights, capability gaps Europeans would have to fill—and, tellingly, "the degree to which individual allies support broader US strategic priorities." The Pentagon expects four options ready by 6 November, with a decision in December. There is no reason for optimism.
There are roughly 80,000 US personnel in Europe. At the June meeting, Washington indicated it would immediately reduce the aircraft, reconnaissance drones and naval assets it would activate for Europe in a crisis. Defenders note that Congress set a floor of 76,000 and that European allies have largely filled earlier gaps. But the floor guards the headcount, not the cavalry. The assets that decide a European war—the aircraft, drones and naval power surged in a crisis—are exactly what Washington signalled it would hold back.
More troubling is a Pentagon questionnaire—sent partly in response to Europe's unwillingness to back Trump's war on Iran—asking whether governments have been "publicly supportive of US foreign policy priorities," whether they restrict US basing and overflight, and whether those restrictions could be removed. It reads as a loyalty test: the US making the size and location of its commitment conditional not on military utility but on political alignment—turning the alliance into a competition for American favour and gutting any European strategic autonomy.
Be afraid
If the USA and Russia reach an agreement, be afraid. It would mean the Kremlin has convinced the White House to give it what it wants—and that Russia is positioned to do what a growing number of European intelligence services warn of: war against NATO by 2029.
The US will want its forces out of Europe before Russia moves. Russia will await the outcome of both processes before it strikes, to reduce the risk of a US response. On my read of both timelines, the assault comes while Trump is still in office—and Russia may attack within three years. Europe will not be ready until 2035.
The two processes are not coordinated. They do not need to be. Both flow from the same transactional instinct, and both land on the same variable: Russia's calculation of whether it can attack NATO and survive the response. A deal on Moscow's terms removes the political cost of aggression—it tells the Kremlin that force sets borders and the West will ratify what the battlefield delivers. The force-posture review removes the military cost, cutting the reinforcement flow that makes an assault on NATO expensive. Lower the political cost through the "peace" and the military cost through the withdrawal, and both sides of Moscow's equation fall at once. That is the link: not a plan, but a convergence—two American processes that together make a Russian war on NATO cheaper to start.

Indonesia reopens major airports as Anak Krakatau ash threat eases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:06:10 UTC
08:06:10 KST

Indonesia's main international airport and several other regional aviation hubs have reopened after days of enforced closures due to volcanic ash from Mount Anak Krakatau, the Transport Ministry confirmed.
The ministry stated that the primary airport serving the capital, Jakarta, alongside four others situated near the metropolis or across Java, are functioning once again as the safety crisis begins to ease.
Mount Anak Krakatau, situated roughly 150 kilometres from Jakarta, erupted on Saturday, spewing a fountain of molten lava and a massive plume of volcanic ash into regional flight paths.
Eight airports suspended flight operations over the weekend after hazardous ash clouds entered their airspace, disrupting nearly 3,000 scheduled flights and leaving upwards of 340,000 passengers stranded.
"Following the current volcanic eruption activity of Mount Anak Krakatau, Soekarno-Hatta International Airport has resumed flight operations," the capital's primary airport announced on Instagram, following repeated extensions of earlier ground stops.
Flight backlogs
Airlines now confront the logistical challenge of clearing vast passenger backlogs and rescheduling aircraft after multiple days of disruption.
The reopened facilities include Halim Perdanakusuma, a smaller Jakarta-area airport catering to civilian and military flights, alongside Hussein Sastranegara in Bandung, the provincial capital of West Java.
With a small airport in southern Sumatra resuming services on Monday morning, six of the initial eight closed hubs have resumed operations, while two remain shut.
On Monday morning alone, more than 240 domestic and international services were cancelled or delayed at Soekarno-Hatta airport, directly impacting nearly 30,000 travellers.
The Transport Ministry had earlier prepared six diversion airports for aircraft scheduled to land in the capital.
Anak Krakatau, meaning "Child of Krakatau", sits in the Sunda Strait separating Java and Sumatra.
It emerged from the sea early last century inside the caldera formed by the catastrophic 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau.
In 2018, a partial collapse of the volcanic island triggered a deadly tsunami that killed 429 people and displaced thousands.

Second-hand smoke causes to nearly 1.7 million deaths globally: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:02:00 UTC
08:02:00 KST

Second-hand smoke causes nearly 1.7 million deaths globally: Study
- More than 2.7 billion people, including 767 million children, were exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023, causing nearly 1.7 million deaths worldwide.
- Second-hand smoke exposure leads to serious illnesses like ischemic heart disease and 5.2 million respiratory infections in children, with no safe level of inhalation.
- Despite declines in smoking rates, exposure remains stable due to population growth; women and children are especially vulnerable, prompting calls for stronger tobacco controls globally.
AI generated
PARIS – More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published on Sept 8 in The Lancet.
Tobacco remains a leading cause of disease globally, the study said, noting many “non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke” were among the estimated total of eight million people who died in 2023 of smoking-related illnesses.
“Exposure to second-hand smoke is a globally recognised health risk, with no safe level of inhalation,” it said.
By reviewing studies published in the US National Institutes of Health database PubMed along with population surveys, the Sept 8 study sought to estimate the prevalence of exposure to second-hand smoke and quantify the burden of disease in 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Among the approximately 2.7 billion people exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023 were 767 million children aged 0 to 14, the study found.
This exposure is estimated to have resulted in 1.66 million premature deaths and causing premature disability and illness, leading with ischemic heart disease, a heart condition caused by insufficient oxygen supply to the heart muscle.
In children, exposure to second-hand smoke is estimated to have caused 5.2 million respiratory tract infections in 2023, it said.
People in proximity to someone lighting up are exposed to both the “sidestream smoke” from the burning tobacco product and smoke exhaled by the active smoker, the study explained.
“The sidestream component, which dominates the air non-smokers breathe, is unfiltered... carrying higher per-unit concentrations of the toxic and carcinogenic compounds” than that being inhaled by the active smoker, it said.
Despite significant declines in smoking prevalence globally since 1990, the absolute number of people exposed has remained stable because of population growth and increased exposure in Africa and the Middle East.
Women are also disproportionately affected by second-hand smoke, particularly in regions where smoking prevalence among women is low, it noted.
“Despite this substantial burden, (second-hand smoke) exposure remains rarely acknowledged as a major risk factor for female health,” it said.
The study called for governments to implement stronger tobacco controls in public places and in homes in order to better protect women and children from second-hand smoke. AFP

Billions for space defence under new national strategy
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:01:53 BST
08:01:53 KST

The government has published a new UK Space Strategy backed by £7.8 billion until 2030, with more than £3 billion of it directed at defence capabilities in orbit, the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade stated.
The strategy brings government space investment and activity under a single plan covering growth, defence and national security, and formally replaces the National Space Strategy published in 2021.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said: “This space strategy recognises that our national security depends on our freedom of action in space and, if necessary, the ability to protect UK and allied space assets. As threats in orbit grow more sophisticated, so must our ability to detect and respond to them, ensuring we protect the interests of the UK and allies while fuelling economic growth along the way.
“Backed by the Defence Investment Plan, we’re investing more than £3 billion to ensure our defence capabilities in space keep pace with the threats we face, supporting reindustrialisation and creating opportunities here in the UK.”
The largest single defence line is £880 million towards space control and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities, funding technologies the department says can track military activity on the ground and potential attacks on satellites.
A further £2.8 billion goes towards connectivity, including the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and SKYNET defence communications programmes, which the department says play a pivotal role in keeping the armed forces connected wherever they are in the world. The same investment is expected to improve rural connectivity and reduce mobile signal dropouts on trains.
Space domain awareness, meaning the monitoring of satellites, rockets and debris in orbit, receives £149 million for the European Space Agency’s Vigil mission and £85 million for the National Space Operations Centre. According to the department, that funding will allow British technology to provide earlier warning of potential satellite collisions, hostile activity and solar storms.
Launch and industry
The strategy commits £148 million to European rocket programmes and £30 million to SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland, which the government says will allow Britain and its partners to launch satellites without relying on countries further afield.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said: “The UK Space Strategy is a huge vote of confidence in Scotland’s Space Sector. Scotland already builds more satellites than anywhere else in Europe, and with a £30 million UK Government investment boost, SaxaVord is now poised to deliver up to three-quarters of the continent’s orbital launch slots.
“This UK Space Strategy has defence, security and economic growth at its heart, creating skilled jobs right across Scotland, showing what we can achieve when government, industry and ambition come together.”
Jonathan Reynolds, the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Secretary, said: “As space becomes a new frontier of economic and military competition, this plan will help keep Britain secure by strengthening our ability to launch satellites, detect threats and protect the services people rely on every day.
“At the same time, this plan will enable our excellent UK industry to seize the boundless opportunities of this new age in space, creating skilled jobs, driving growth and improving connectivity for all of us.”
A further £40 million supports in-orbit servicing, assembly and manufacturing, which the department says will help repair and maintain satellites damaged by debris, solar storms or hostile interference, and clear dangerous objects from orbit. The strategy also allocates £163 million to space science and exploration missions including the Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover built at Stevenage, £190 million from UK Research and Innovation for astronomy and space science research, £57 million from the Department for Transport for rail connectivity and £9 million from the Met Office for space weather forecasting.
For the first time, the department says, government will take a single approach to buying and developing space technology, beginning with satellite communications, which it argues will help British firms win more work and deliver capabilities faster.
Industry response
Kevin Craven, chief executive of the ADS Group, said: “We welcome the publication of the new space strategy, and the sustained effort to bring a cross-government perspective to space capability delivery. It is important that government maintains an open, transparent and ambitious partnership with industry to realise its national security and growth goals.
“Certainty allows the sector to operate at pace and for its industrial base to make long-term strategic and commercial commitments. It is also a vital signal of intent to our international partners for trade and collaboration.”
Doug Liddle, chair of the trade association UKspace, said: “UKspace welcomes the publication of the government’s new UK Space Strategy. It sets out a constructive path towards a refreshed approach to space in the UK, which we hope will result in a stronger emphasis on open, inclusive cross-sector dialogue. The new, focussed strategy offers a valuable opportunity to create a more streamlined framework, strengthen collaboration and deliver greater impact across the UK space sector.”
Professors Anna Hogg and Mark Sims, co-chairs of the Space Academic Network, said: “SPAN welcomes the new cross-Government space strategy and its integrated delivery plan. We look forward to seeing the detail of the strategy and delivery plan, which will be critical in enabling academia and industry to plan, invest and work together to deliver the UK’s ambitions for space. Sustained investment across academia and industry is crucial to creating the cutting-edge technologies, capabilities, talent and growth of the future.”
The department puts the value of the UK space sector at £18.6 billion supporting more than 55,000 skilled jobs. Alongside the strategy, the government is reforming space regulation with the stated aim of reducing costs and rewarding responsible operators.

New space strategy will bolster UK defences against threats from space
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:01:04 BST
08:01:04 KST

New space strategy will bolster UK defences against threats from space
New UK space strategy to bring government's investment and activity under one plan to drive growth, strengthen security and back everyday technologies
- New national space strategy brings together UK’s plans for growth, defence, and national security to help reindustrialise the UK
- Government will design a resilient, integrated national satellite communications system to boost our security and defence
- Strategy also brings everyday benefits to Brits from better connectivity on trains to stronger phone signals
Safeguarding our national security and defence capabilities are the key pillars of a new strategy launched today (Tuesday 8 September) which puts the UK’s space sector to work in reindustrialising the country over the coming years.
Backed by a record £7.8 billion until 2030, the UK Space Strategy brings government’s space investment and activity under one plan to drive growth, strengthen security and back the technologies that underpin modern life.
It also recognises space as an increasingly important domain for keeping our country safe. Work to strengthen Space Domain Awareness – the study and monitoring of objects like satellites, rockets and debris orbiting our planet – is being backed by projects including £149 million for the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Vigil mission and £85 million for the National Space Operations Centre. UK funding will see British tech offer earlier warnings of potential satellite collisions, hostile activity and solar storms, helping protect the power, communications and navigation services people rely on every day.
Meanwhile £880 million will help beef up the UK’s space control and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities, funding technologies that can track military activity on the ground and potential attacks on satellites, meaning we can act quickly and decisively to protect our way of life on Earth and our assets in space.
A further £2.8 billion meanwhile will go towards strengthening connectivity, including the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and SKYNET defence communications programmes, which play a pivotal role in keeping our Armed Forces connected wherever they are in the world.
These benefits will also be felt in everyday life, helping bring faster, more reliable connectivity to rural communities and reducing mobile signal dropouts on trains by using advanced satellite communications.
Together, these investments will help grow a UK space sector worth £18.6 billion and supporting over 55,000 skilled jobs – cementing Britain’s place as a global space leader from satellite services that underpin the economy to landmark missions such as the UK-built Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover.
Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said:
“As space becomes a new frontier of economic and military competition, this plan will help keep Britain secure by strengthening our ability to launch satellites, detect threats and protect the services people rely on every day.
“At the same time, this plan will enable our excellent UK industry to seize the boundless opportunities of this new age in space, creating skilled jobs, driving growth and improving connectivity for all of us.”
Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said:
“This space strategy recognises that our national security depends on our freedom of action in space and, if necessary, the ability to protect UK and allied space assets. As threats in orbit grow more sophisticated, so must our ability to detect and respond to them, ensuring we protect the interests of the UK and allies while fuelling economic growth along the way.
“Backed by the Defence Investment Plan, we’re investing more than £3 billion to ensure our defence capabilities in space keep pace with the threats we face, supporting reindustrialisation and creating opportunities here in the UK.”
The Strategy also offers an opportunity to deliver the jobs and companies of the future, with £40 million to support pioneering in-orbit servicing, assembly and manufacturing technologies (ISAM). These will help repair and maintain satellites damaged by space debris, solar storms or hostile interference, while helping clear dangerous objects from orbit – all while continuing to operate in space.
That support will help bring new products online that are directly developed in the unique environment of space, from new semiconductors that underpin our power grid to pharmaceuticals and drug delivery tools that could transform outcomes for patients.
Additional support for the UK’s wide-ranging space sector includes:
- £148 million for European rocket programmes and £30 million for SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland – helping Britain and our partners to launch satellites without relying on countries further afield while creating new jobs.
- £163 million in space science and exploration missions, including the delivery of the Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover built in Stevenage. These missions power world-leading research while boosting this government’s mission to reindustrialise the UK with high-skilled jobs and new tech in areas like AI and autonomous systems.
- £57 million from the Department for Transport to improve rail connectivity, £190 million from UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) for astronomy and space science research, and £9 million from the Met Office to strengthen space weather forecasting.
For the first time, government will take a single approach to buying and developing space technology, starting with satellite communications, helping British firms win more work, strengthening UK supply chains, supporting skilled jobs and delivering capabilities faster and better value for taxpayers.
The new Strategy formally replaces the previous National Space Strategy, published in 2021, and will play a key role in the delivery of the Modern Industrial Strategy to deliver reindustrialisation and good growth in every postcode.
Alongside the Strategy, we’re reforming space regulations to reduce costs, reward responsible operators and make it easier for UK firms to invest in cutting-edge missions from satellite servicing to lunar exploration.
Supportive comments:
Doug Liddle, Chair of the trade association UKspace, said:
“UKspace welcomes the publication of the government’s new UK Space Strategy. It sets out a constructive path towards a refreshed approach to space in the UK, which we hope will result in a stronger emphasis on open, inclusive cross-sector dialogue. The new, focussed strategy offers a valuable opportunity to create a more streamlined framework, strengthen collaboration and deliver greater impact across the UK space sector.”
Kevin Craven, CEO of the ADS Group, said:
“We welcome the publication of the new space strategy, and the sustained effort to bring a cross-government perspective to space capability delivery. It is important that government maintains an open, transparent and ambitious partnership with industry to realise its national security and growth goals. 
 
“Certainty allows the sector to operate at pace and for its industrial base to make long-term strategic and commercial commitments. It is also a vital signal of intent to our international partners for trade and collaboration. ADS looks forward to supporting government on the crucial next steps for implementation.”
Professor Anna Hogg and Professor Mark Sims, Space Academic Network (SPAN) Co-Chairs said:
“SPAN welcomes the new cross-Government space strategy and its integrated delivery plan. Space technologies and services are integral to modern life, from secure communications to monitoring and responding to environmental change. We look forward to seeing the detail of the strategy and delivery plan, which will be critical in enabling academia and industry to plan, invest and work together to deliver the UK’s ambitions for space. Sustained investment across academia and industry is crucial to creating the cutting-edge technologies, capabilities, talent and growth of the future.”
Joanne Wheeler MBE, Managing Partner at Alden and Director of the Earth & Space Sustainability Initiative, said:
“In addition to enhancing UK security and defence, the UK Space Strategy brings together world-leading innovative regulation and insurance opportunities to enable and drive growth and investment, whilst encouraging responsible and sustainable operations.”
Simon Brown, Met Office Managing Director, said:
“Space based observations are critical for delivering weather forecasts and climate intelligence that people rely on every day to stay safe and grow the economy of the UK. Advancements in space observations are allowing us to improve our weather forecasts and also give us new imagery which helps us show the impacts of other hazards such as wildfires and drought which we have seen this summer.
“Delivering new and innovative space capability is important to enhance our preparedness for extreme weather and exploit the latest advances in our prediction capability using both physics and AI models. We welcome the new UK Space Strategy and its recognition of the vital role space plays in supporting weather and climate services, as well as the Met Office’s role as the UK’s space weather forecasting centre.”
Notes to editors:
The Strategy details how government will go further and faster to develop capability and deliver outcomes in our four priority subsectors:
- Satellite Communications
- In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing
- Space Domain Awareness
- Assured Access to Space
The package of space regulatory financial tools contains measures which have been proposed by government, as well as those received in response to the previous consultation on orbital liabilities, insurance, charging and space sustainability. The package covers the following announcements:
- Adopting a world-first variable liability limits approach for orbital operations to incentivise uptake of government priorities of security and space sustainability, reduce cost burdens on UK companies and stimulate increased commercial investment in the UK’s space sector.
- Waiving operator liability for innovative and novel space missions launched before the end of 2030 (In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly & Manufacturing and lunar missions) to help support development of high potential technologies.
- Adoption of new world-first models for the provision of third-party liability insurance to support innovation in the City of London space insurance market.
- Abolishing decommissioning funds for operators of constellations in favour of a more proportionate approach to monitoring operators’ financial health.
- Further detail on the measures can be found in the government response to the consultation in the link above.
