Le Creuset x Star Trek Collection: Prices, Availability, Release Date
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Logic clearly dictates that the needs of the penne outweigh the needs of the stew, or the bun. While this would have been a gloriously fan-faithful reason for Le Creuset, the French-Belgian maker of colorful cookware for more than a century, to materialize its new limited-edition Star Trek collection, the range is being launched in celebration of 60 years of the cult sci-fi show.
No matter, because when you have such stellar items as Vulcan oven mitts, shuttlecraft baking dishes, and—perhaps best of all—a cheese grater in the shape of the classic Trek communicator (which has somewhat wonderfully been nicknamed the “Communi-grator” by Le Creuset's design team), there's only cause for celebration in the cosmos.
Going on sale today, to coincide with the space series' 60th anniversary, the limited-edition collection has actually been in development for years after Le Creuset approached Paramount to collaborate on the kitchen kit in time for the landmark birthday. Le Creuset is no stranger to fun mashups, with its recent 2024 Pokemon collection being snapped up almost instantly (those looking to get pieces now have to scour the likes of eBay for items way over original retail prices).
As well as the 15-centimeter Communi-grator for $68 (£52), foodies looking for Federation-themed gear might appreciate the $500 (£425) Enterprise round casserole pot complete with Starfleet insignia knob, or the $450 (£385) Klingon shallow casserole dish with trefoil "Heart of Virtue" knob—both in cast iron. Inside the Enterprise NCC-1701 pot is the legend “to boldly go,” while the Klingon dish offers up an encouraging “Qapla!” (“success” in Klingon), handy for experimental cooking.
Carrying culinary adventures into the unknown comes the Le Creuset x Star Trek: Galileo shuttlecraft casserole dish ($150), which has a roomy 1.6 liters of space inside. Vulcan votaries are well catered for with the $35 (£31) Spock ear mug (perfect for Vulcan spice tea), complete with gold detailing along the rim as a nod to the Starfleet uniform; the $55 (£36) Spock hand spoon rest; and the whimsical Vulcan salute “live long and prosper” oven mitt, resplendent in signature Star Trek baby blue for $40 (£36).
Not merely content with digitally launching the collection online, Le Creuset engaged Sent Into Space to boldly send its Enterprise casserole dish where no pan has gone before—more than 111,000 feet above the Earth, atop 99.5 percent of the planet’s atmosphere. While obviously a blatant (albeit fitting) marketing stunt, there's actually some considerable logistics to overcome in sending a cast-iron pot to the edge of space.
Sent Into Space cofounder Chris Rose had the task of launching the pot in the stratosphere via a space-capable balloon taller than the height of the White House, where it stayed for 1 hour, 19 minutes, and 4 seconds, enduring temperatures down to -63.4 degrees Celsius (-82.12 F). “Because of the weight, we had to give some serious consideration to how we were going to hold things, making sure everything was very balanced,” Rose tells WIRED. Rose and his team also have to rely on simulations to take into account considerations such as where the pot would land as it's parachuted back down to Earth, as well as how to avoid bodies of water and built-up areas, for example.
“The legal authorities within the aviation community need to know. We can't have a Le Creuset casserole dish floating past the window of an airborne A380 as it makes its way off to some destination,” Rose says. “So we are in constant communication, both from a flight-clearance perspective before this ever leaves the ground, to onboard systems for telemetry and communication.” Indeed, in the early stages of reentry, Rose says the Enterprise casserole dish reached speeds in excess of 300 mph before slowing and landing safely in Lincolnshire, England.
Back on terra firma, the Le Creuset x Star Trek collection should serve cadets and captains alike, provided you can secure your selections before stock vanishes like a cloaked Bird-of-Prey.

The Renaissance of the Dissident Republican Threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

The Renaissance of the Dissident Republican Threat
The dissident Irish republican terror group threat is changing. Counter-terrorism officials must keep pace to meet the evolving security challenge.
Around 3pm on 22 July the Special Detective Unit of the Garda Síochána, the Irish police and security service, stopped a vehicle travelling on the N2 south of Carrickmacross close to the border between Monaghan and Armagh. A search of the vehicle yielded an ‘extremely sophisticated’ device. One person, a woman in her twenties, was arrested at the scene and subsequently charged. Another man in his forties was simultaneously apprehended by Gardai in Dublin. Both were released on bail, pending court proceedings. The incident catapulted the dissident republican threat back into the spotlight. It has since been reported that the device, which contained 394 grams of Semtex high explosive, a timer, a timing switch and a viable detonator, was linked to the New IRA.
The New IRA has been responsible for a range of violent activities this year, including exploding two crude and unsophisticated car bombs outside Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) stations in Lurgan, County Armagh, and in Dunmurry, on the outskirts of Belfast. Neither of these devices appeared to contain high explosives, which makes the interception of a viable Semtex-based device most concerning.
From Defeat to Containment
For much of the period of the Northern Ireland Troubles between the late 1960s and 1990s the British state’s security services believed it was possible to defeat terrorism. However, by the early 1990s the government had adopted a more pragmatic approach aimed, not at ‘defeating the IRA’ but at ‘containing its activities and limiting their effectiveness’. Regardless of whether defeat was strategically possible, by the time of the Belfast/Good Friday Agreement in 1998, British policy had shifted towards an engagement with the IRA’s political associates Sinn Féin who had by now become vocal advocates for the peace process.
With the Provisional IRA subsequently jettisoning its ‘armed struggle’ in favour of electoral politics, this left a sizable number of influential republicans irreconciled to the idea of power-sharing between nationalists and unionists. Unsurprisingly, they carried on regardless of what some commentators have called a ‘paradox’, with some dissidents maintaining their violent campaign does not require popular support. As Marisa McGlinchey argues, this particular strand of militant republicanism articulates the view that the Provisional IRA failed, not the method. To these militants, it is the means, not the ends, that is vital in their self-declared goal of unifying Ireland by force.
It is unhelpful to see the threat from violent republicans according to the logic underpinning the Northern Ireland peace process: namely that terrorism can be transformed only when those who engage in it see the merits of the ballot box rather than the bomb
For much of the past twenty-five years, law enforcement agencies on both sides of the Irish border have cooperated to contain the threat from dissident republicans. The Continuity IRA, which grew out of a split between the Provisionals and Republican Sinn Féin led by former IRA Chief of Staff Ruairí Ó Brádaigh, was responsible for major bomb attacks on mainly Protestant towns in the 1990s. In 1997 another split occurred inside the Provisionals when the Real IRA appeared, carrying out one of the worst atrocities of the Troubles when it bombed Omagh, a market town in County Tyrone, a year later. 29 people were killed, as well as two unborn children, and many hundreds more were injured.
Despite the revulsion surrounding the Omagh atrocity, dissident republican attacks continued, with several police officers, soldiers, prison officers and civilians killed. In 2012 the New IRA was formed following the amalgamation of several dissident groups, which included the Real IRA and the Republican Action Against Drugs.
The CIRA was dealt a major blow in 2014 when seven men were arrested and charged with a range of terror-related offences following a major MI5 eavesdropping operation in Newry, County Down. At their subsequent trial held in 2020, all the defendants pled guilty, with a range of sentences totally 33 years handed down. Later that year MI5 launched another major surveillance operation, codenamed Arbacia, which targeted suspected leaders of the New IRA. The trials of up to ten people charged are still pending after a judge rejected legal applications to have the case dismissed.
Neither of these high-profile operations have deterred others from becoming involved in similar terrorist activity, with the New IRA blamed for the attempted murder of a PSNI officer, Detective Chief Inspector John Caldwell, on 22 February 2023. In the wake of the shooting of DCI Caldwell, MI5 promptly raised the Northern Ireland Related Terrorism (NIRT) threat level from ‘substantial’ to ‘severe’ on 23 March 2023. The threat level was subsequently returned to ‘substantial’ again on 6 March 2024. Despite the Director General of MI5 reassuring the public in October 2025 that his service would continue to ‘bear down on residual threats and degrade terrorist capabilities’ with respect to NIRT, the New IRA has remained unbowed.
From Containment to Suppression
Irrespective of the New IRA’s resilience in the face of covert intelligence operations, senior police officers remain optimistic about the threat being greatly diminished. In evidence given to the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee in March, PSNI Assistant Chief Constable Davy Beck told MPs his officers ‘continue to work day and night to suppress the dissident republican threat that still exists’. He nevertheless acknowledged they ‘retain that lethal intent, material, munitions and resources’ and are ‘capable of mounting lethal and reckless attacks across Northern Ireland’. ACC Beck remained upbeat in his assessment that the wider nationalist community would reject the ‘narrative around dissident republican threats, and indeed paramilitarism.’ Yet, there remains plenty of evidence to the contrary. Those in the nationalist community where militant republicans hold sway are consistently reluctant to inform on those involved in armed activities.
It is unhelpful to see the threat from violent republicans according to the logic underpinning the Northern Ireland peace process: namely that terrorism can be transformed only when those who engage in it see the merits of the ballot box rather than the bomb. Harbouring such a one-dimensional view greatly underestimates the impact of covert intelligence operations in ensuring the IRA remained on the path mapped out by their political associates in Sinn Féin. Furthermore, the threat posed by violent republicans has adapted over time, with the number of bomb-related incidents doubling in the year to the end of July 2026, compared to the same period the year before.
Rethinking the Security Threat
The perseverance of the authorities on both sides of the Irish border to contain or suppress the New IRA threat is not in doubt. What is questionable is the conceptual framing of terrorism in this context. If we accept that other forms of terrorism can be at once fragmented, complex and less predictable, then it stands to reason the same can be said of republican violence. Scholarly work on ‘Dark Networks’ has greatly aided our understanding of the interplay between organisational attributes and environmental factors in illegal groups that take a network form. One of the key hypotheses in research is that dark networks that survive demonstrate an ‘ability to stay flexible and adapt quickly to changing pressures and circumstances’.
If we accept the proposition that the Semtex-based device is the by-product of the return of technical expertise within the ecosystem of violent republicanism, then this might point towards a renaissance in the New IRA’s campaign not seen since 2016. This would enable us to draw several conclusions. The first is perhaps the most obvious. The attacks in Lurgan and Dunmurry in the Spring of 2026 were relatively unsophisticated and relied on crude IED construction, thereby indicating a capability gap. A second conclusion, based on the interdiction of the Semtex device, reportedly on its way to the north-west city of Derry/Londonderry, is an indication of the New IRA in the city seeking to acquire new means of bolstering its flagging violent campaign. A third conclusion is that dissident republicans are now in the business of collaborating for survival. That means at certain times they may coagulate into a clotted whole, thereby posing a greater networked threat as they did in 2016. The only way to determine whether this is indeed the case is for greater analysis of the Semtex device seized on the Irish border in July. Although it is unlikely the public will be privy to such details until court proceedings are underway, it is likely to drive the law enforcement responses we will continue to see unfold. It might also help us explain why the chair of the Police Federation for Northern Ireland has now called on MI5 to increase in the threat level.
Whatever the true rationale behind the resurgence of violent republican activity, it nonetheless raises serious questions at a time when the British and Irish governments are awaiting the conclusions of a scoping exercise on the prospects of ‘paramilitary group transition towards disbandment’. Leading this scoping exercise is an Independent Expert, Fleur Ravensbergen, who was appointed in September 2025 to engage with all paramilitary groups, including dissident republicans. By their recent actions, militant republicans are clearly determined to derail the process towards greater political normalisation on the island of Ireland. Perhaps they are also seeking to drive a wedge between those seeking less turbulence in the geo-political relationship between Britain and Ireland a decade on from the Brexit referendum? As this article has made clear, to meet this evolving challenge, we require better analytical tools to inform the decision-making process of all those involved in the business of Counter-Terrorism.

Black boxes recovered from Amazon cargo plane that overran Miami runway
NTSB investigators inspect ‘utter devastation’ at crash site where Boeing 767 struck two vehicles, killing five people on the ground
Investigators with the US National Transportation Safety Board said on Monday they had recovered the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder from an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane that overran the runway and crashed while landing in Miami on Sunday, killing five people on the ground.
NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said the two devices, commonly referred to as the black boxes, were being returned to the agency’s headquarters in Washington on Monday night for evaluation.
The 32-year-old Boeing 767-33A, operated by Miami-based 21 Air LLC, overran the runway by some 396 metres (1,300 feet) and crashed into two vehicles on the ground: an Econoline van on the airport grounds carrying seven people from an airline cleaning crew and a Toyota SUV that was driving on a road beyond the perimeter fence.
The two people aboard the plane, the pilot and co-pilot, survived and had yet to be interviewed, Homendy said in a press conference.
Five people were injured, three of them critically, officials said on Sunday.
Homendy, leading a team of 32 investigators at Miami International Airport, briefed reporters on the early stages of the investigation but said a probable cause of the accident would not be determined until the end of the investigation.

Nearly 1.7 million deaths linked to second-hand smoke in 2023, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:53:34 UTC

Nearly 1.7 million deaths linked to second-hand smoke in 2023, study finds
More than 2.7 billion people worldwide, including 767 million children, were exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths, a Lancet study said on Tuesday. Researchers found second-hand smoke remained a major global health risk, with no safe level of exposure.
More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published Tuesday in The Lancet.
Tobacco remains a leading cause of disease globally, the study said, noting many "non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke" were among the estimate total of 8 million people who died in 2023 of smoking-related illnesses.
"Exposure to second-hand smoke is a globally recognised health risk, with no safe level of inhalation," it said.
By reviewing studies published in the US National Institutes of Health database PubMed along with population surveys, Tuesday's study sought to estimate the prevalence of exposure to second-hand smoke and quantify the burden of disease in 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Read moreIn Indonesia, addiction to smoking starts in childhood
Among the approximately 2.7 billion people exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023 were 767 million children aged 0 to 14, the study found.
This exposure is estimated to have resulted in 1.66 million premature deaths and causing premature disability and illness, leading with ischemic heart disease, a heart condition caused by insufficient oxygen supply to the heart muscle.
In children, exposure to second-hand smoke is estimated to have caused 5.2 million respiratory tract infections in 2023, it said.
People in proximity to someone lighting up are exposed to both the "sidestream smoke" from the burning tobacco product and smoke exhaled by the active smoker, the study explained.
"The sidestream component, which dominates the air non-smokers breathe, is unfiltered ... carrying higher per-unit concentrations of the toxic and carcinogenic compounds" than that being inhaled by the active smoker, it said.
Read moreHow French attitudes to cigarettes are changing
Despite significant declines in smoking prevalence globally since 1990, the absolute number of people exposed has remained stable due to population growth and increased exposure in Africa and the Middle East.
Women are also disproportionately affected by second-hand smoke, particularly in regions where smoking prevalence among women is low, it noted.
"Despite this substantial burden, (second-hand smoke) exposure remains rarely acknowledged as a major risk factor for female health," it said.
The study called for governments to implement stronger tobacco controls in public places and in homes in order to better protect women and children from second-hand smoke.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Israeli political parties submitted candidate lists to the Central Elections Committee on Monday amid divisions among alliances, with Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot ruling out a merger with the Together alliance led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Ofer Winter opting to run independently with his People of Israel party.

The alliance also formally submitted its list to the Central Elections Committee.

The general election will be held on Oct. 27 amid a close contest between Netanyahu’s camp and the opposition camp.

Forming a government in Israel requires the confidence of at least 61 of the 120 members of the Knesset.

According to the outlet, Eisenkot's bloc would reach 55 seats and would need the support of the Joint List, a political alliance of Arab-majority political parties, to surpass the 61-seat threshold.
The poll indicates that Arab members of the Knesset would win 13 seats, while most leaders of Jewish opposition parties refuse to accept the support of Arab Knesset members to form a government.

Panama Canal considering more cuts in transits due to El Nino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:50:00 UTC
07:50:00 KST

Panama Canal considering more cuts in transits due to El Nino
PANAMA CITY - The number of ships sailing through the Panama Canal could be cut further due to drought caused by the El Nino weather pattern, the new administrator of the waterway told AFP on Sept 7.
Panama has declared a nationwide emergency over El Nino, a phenomenon developing over the Pacific Ocean that is affecting worldwide weather patterns and pushing up global temperatures.
This year’s El Nino is expected to be the strongest since record-keeping began four decades ago.
Panama’s restrictions come even as use of the canal has risen: Shippers are seeking an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has blocked in retaliation for the war launched by the United States and Israel.
The inter-oceanic Panama Canal – which handles 5 per cent of global maritime trade – has already reduced the maximum number of ships allowed through daily, from 36 last month to 32 by mid-September.
It operates using rainwater that collects in two reservoirs, whose levels have dropped due to the onset of El Nino.
Without water, the locks that lift and lower ships at the start and end of their crossing cannot function.
Ilya Espino de Marotta, who took over as head of the Panama Canal Authority on Sept 7, told AFP that further measures may be implemented if the drought does not subside.
“We do not rule out the possibility that in February or March, we may have to lower the limit – probably not to 24 slots per day, but it could be reduced to 29 or something similar,” she said.
200 million litres per ship
Each ship requires about 200 million litre of water, which is then discharged into the sea.
In 2023, El Nino forced a reduction in daily transits from 38 to 22 due to the dramatic reduction in reservoir levels.
Espino de Marotta, the first woman ever to head the US-built canal authority, stated, however, that she does not expect restrictions to reach the levels seen that year.
Apart from reducing the number of vessels, canal authorities have also reduced their maximum draft, from 15.2 metres to 14.6m.
The draft is the vertical distance between the waterline and the lowest point of a ship’s hull. It is a measure of how much water is needed for a ship to float safely without running aground.
Experts have warned that long-term restrictions on canal crossings could lead to higher shipping costs and longer waiting times for deliveries.
The United States and China are the main users of the canal, which is the fastest maritime route between the east coast of the United States and China.
The canal connecting the Atlantic and Pacific handles around 40 per cent of US container traffic.
The Iran war has pushed up traffic through the channel.
With shipping at a standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, the Panama Canal has become a fallback route for energy shipments. AFP

“On Ukraine, the two leaders agreed on the need to continue working towards a ceasefire that prevented more loss of life,” the British government said in its readout of the call.

The back-to-back meetings marked Washington’s latest effort to revive negotiations that had stalled despite several previous rounds of US-mediated diplomacy.

Monday’s Downing Street statement made clear that London intends to continue supporting both Ukraine and the US-led diplomatic process as Washington seeks to determine whether Moscow is prepared to move beyond talks toward an enforceable ceasefire.

Rubio heads to Ecuador, Colombia, Peru after right-wing victories in region
Rightward shift in Latin America comes as Washington pledges to grow influence, take militaristic approach to cartels.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is travelling to three South American countries whose recently elected leaders have closely aligned with President Donald Trump’s administration.
Rubio will travel to Colombia on Tuesday to meet with newly elected President Abelardo de la Espriella. He will then visit Ecuador to meet with President Daniel Noboa before going to Peru, where he will meet with another newly elected leader, Keiko Fujimori.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 3 of 3‘Winds of change’: How Milei is stirring Falklands claim amid Trump-UK spat
The State Department has not yet released a more in-depth agenda for the trip, saying only that Rubio will discuss “US support for Colombia’s earthquake response; enhanced cooperation in the shared fight against narcoterrorism, which threatens our hemisphere; and the benefits of deeper commercial relationships between our countries”.
The trip comes amid a rightward shift in Latin America that has seen several Trump-aligned leaders take office. Beyond the three countries, Trump also backed Honduran President Nasry Asfura, who won the presidency in November, and Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz, who won in October.
Beyond the new leaders, Trump has also closely aligned with Argentina’s Javier Milei, who took office in 2023, and El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele, who became the leader in 2019.
US influence over Western Hemisphere
Rubio’s visit comes as the Trump administration has pledged to assert more influence over the Western Hemisphere in what Trump has referred to as the “Donroe Doctrine”, a reference to the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that opposed European interference in the Americas.
It has shifted to a militaristic approach to security in Latin American countries, while broadly reframing efforts to combat drug trafficking as a war against “narco-terrorists”.
In August, Colombia’s de la Espriella upped cooperation with the US by joining the Trump administration’s so-called “Shield of the Americas”.
The 19 members of the group have jointly pledged a “commitment to using lethal military force to destroy the sinister cartels and terrorist networks”.
Unlike his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro, de la Espriella has also praised US military strikes on alleged drug smugglers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. At least 227 people have been killed in those strikes, in what rights groups have condemned as extrajudicial killings.
Family members of those killed have charged that the targets were fishermen, not drug smugglers.
The US has proven a major supporter for de la Espriella in the wake of a devastating earthquake in Colombia last month in which at least 330 people were killed and thousands left homeless.
In March, the US military announced it was collaborating with Ecuador, under Noboa’s leadership, to target drug trafficking groups in the country.
Ecuador’s Interior Minister John Reimberg defended the US strikes on vessels allegedly carrying drugs in an interview with broadcaster Teleamazonas last week.
Peru’s Fujimori, the daughter of former leader Alberto Fujimori, who notoriously dissolved the country’s Congress and Supreme Court to consolidate power during his government from 1990 to 2000, has also pledged closer ties with the US and a military crackdown on criminal groups.
Conservative shift
Rubio’s visit comes after the US announced a controversial agreement with Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodriguez. The deal, struck in the wake of the January 3 US abduction of Venezuela’s ex-President Nicolas Maduro, grants US companies access to 65 billion barrels of crude oil reserves over the next 100 years.
It also comes as Washington has continued to up its pressure campaign against Cuba, with Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez on Monday rejecting any talks with the US despite its ongoing fuel blockade of the island.
Brazil and Mexico remain the only regional powers with leftist leaders. Rubio has called the region’s conservative lurch an “extraordinary achievement”.
The shift has accompanied the strengthening of ties between Israel and several Latin American countries since Trump took office.
Brazilians will go to the polls in October, when Flavio Bolsonaro, a son of former right-wing leader Jair Bolsonaro, seeks to unseat Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Trump has remained a staunch ally of the elder Bolsonaro, who has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for leading a conspiracy to hold onto power.
The US president has also shown strong support for the younger Bolsonaro, including inviting him to the White House in May.

Hawaii braces for Hurricane Lowell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:37:25 UTC
07:37:25 KST

Hawaii braces for Hurricane Lowell
Threats of cyclones and deadly surf as the Category 3 storm path approaches Hawaiian islands on Monday night.
Hurricane Lowell, a major Category 3 storm in the Pacific Ocean, has crept closer to the Hawaiian islands with forecasters warning the weather systems could unleash tornadoes on the islands of Kauai and Niihau.
On Sunday, the United States National Hurricane Center issued emergency hurricane and tropical storm warnings for the island chain, advising residents and visitors to brace for severe windstorms and possible mudslides as early as Monday night local time. Lowell is predicted to skirt just west of Hawaii’s most northwest main islands, Niihau and Kauai, as well as portions of the vast Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, tracking from south to north.
Mayor Derek Kawakami of Kauai issued an emergency proclamation in anticipation of the hurricane.
Kauai faces potential coastal flooding of up to 1 metre (3 feet) caused by rolling storm surges and unusually high tides.
The storm has been gradually pivoting toward the more rural islands in the Aloha state, moving north at 9 km/h (6 mph), according to the hurricane center. Lowell started as a tropical depression that formed over the Pacific Ocean on August 27. It was driven by a combination of warm ocean temperatures and an active El Nino pattern.
Lowell has seesawed between Category 3 and Category 5 intensity as its trajectory mushroomed. It first reached Category 5 intensity at 257 km/h (160 mph) on Wednesday morning local time, becoming the second Category 5 hurricane of the season. Only two other Pacific hurricanes in recorded history have regrouped to a Category 5 after losing strength mid-path: Emilia (1994) and Ioke (2006).
Ioke was the strongest ever recorded in the central Pacific, while the island of Kauai sustained billions in damage during Hurricane Inike, a 1992 Category 4 storm and the largest recorded in Hawaii’s history. Six people were killed.
Forecasters said Lowell could bring rainfall of 150mm to 250mm (6 to 10 inches), with maximum totals of 360mm (14 inches).
Lowell had maximum sustained winds of 195km/h (120 mph) and was pinpointed about 895km (about 555 miles) southwest of the state capital, Honolulu.
Local officials have been urging residents and visitors to prepare for a downpour of rain and fierce winds which could cause major flash flooding and hazardous mudslides.
According to the National Weather Service, tornadoes could accompany tropical cyclones. They typically occur in rain bands well away from the center of the storm.
Hawaii’s Big Island can expect as much as 100mm to 200mm (4 inches to 8 inches) of rain, with localized peaks reaching up to 305mm (12 inches).
Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 85km (50 miles) from the centre while tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 280km (175 miles).
Residents prepare for the worst
Kauai’s Emergency Management Agency urged residents to fill gas tanks, charge devices, refill prescriptions and store water and food ahead of the storm. The agency also said residents should be prepared to stay home for several days.
Swells generated from Lowell are expected to produce “life-threatening surf and rip current conditions”, according to a statement by the Kauai County government on Sunday evening. It urged visitors to stay out of the ocean and steer clear of the shoreline as coastal conditions rapidly worsen.
“Residents should not assume conditions will be limited to areas near the storm’s center,” the government said.
As panic-buying emptied supermarket shelves in Lihue on Kauai, residents of the 8,000-person airport town scrambled to stock up on food and water.
Real estate agent Lori Benkert bought an extra 4.5kg (10 pound) container of propane so that she could cook on the barbecue if power shut off. Benkert manages dozens of properties on Kauai and has boarded up two houses on the western side of the island.
“We’ll lose some power, probably have some trees, a bunch of tree limbs coming down,” Benkert told The Associated Press. “Everybody is probably going just to hunker down”.
Meanwhile, Category 1 Hurricane Marie churned 1,120km (695 miles) south-southwest of San Diego in southern California, bringing dangerous surf to the area and Mexico’s Baja coast. Packing 120km/h (75mph) sustained winds, the storm tracked northwest at 11km/h (7mph).
Even without coastal watches or warnings, updrafts from Marie will hit southwest Mexico, Baja California and Southern California over the next few days, creating pounding surf and dangerous rip currents.
The islands of Hawaii rarely experience tornadoes, averaging about one per year. Just 42 tornadoes were reported in the state between 1950 to 2018, according to Stephen Parker, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Honolulu.

Europe’s biggest nuclear power plant back to normal after weeks in emergency mode
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:32:21 UTC
07:32:21 KST

Europe’s biggest nuclear power plant back to normal after weeks in emergency mode
Power has been restored to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) after more than two weeks in emergency mode, the CEO of the Russian state nuclear energy corporation Rosatom, Aleksey Likhachev, has said.
The main external power line to the plant was cut off in March following what the Ukrainian authorities described as “damage” to transmission towers. It has never been restored, with no explanations from Kiev.
Since then, the ZNPP has had to rely solely on the backup line – until August 20, when it was shut down by automatic control systems following an unspecified “incident” in territory controlled by Ukraine. That forced the power plant to fall back on emergency diesel-powered generators.
On Monday, Likhachev told journalists that the external power supply to the ZNPP had finally been restored, and the facility was now “operating as normal.” The Rosatom chief thanked all the parties involved in establishing a temporary local truce needed for the repair work, including the Russian defense and foreign ministries. He also praised the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for its “mediation efforts.”
The ZNPP operator also confirmed that external power had been restored. No violations of safety limits were reported, and the radiation situation at the plant and in the surrounding area remained stable and did not exceed natural background levels, it said in a statement. The operator added that the second power supply line has yet to be restored and regular fuel supplies to the station need to be facilitated.
Diesel fuel deliveries to the station were “problematic” because of Ukrainian shelling targeting the roads in the area, ZNPP communications director Evgenia Yashina told Interfax earlier.
Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and the adjacent city of Energodar have been targeted by Ukraine on multiple occasions with artillery and drones since Russia took control of the facility in March 2022.
In July, a Ukrainian drone hit a ZNPP service vehicle on the edge of the plant’s industrial site, killing its chief engineer, Aleksandr Yakovlev, and his driver. At the time, Likhachev called the strike a “deliberate terrorist act.”
According to the Rosatom CEO, more than a dozen employees of the plant have been killed and many others wounded in Ukrainian attacks over the past three months. Kiev’s actions pose the “real danger of a massive nuclear incident” affecting parts of Russia, Ukraine, and the EU, he warned.
Several months ago, the Ukrainian military also started remotely mining the area near the ZNPP and Energodar, where plant employees reside, according to the nuclear chief. In early August, four ZNPP employees were injured by Ukrainian landmines dropped by drones.
Moscow has repeatedly criticized the IAEA, which has experts deployed at the ZNPP, for acknowledging the attacks on the facility but stopping short of blaming Ukraine for them.

Israel sees 58% drop in returning citizens amid rising emigration: Knesset panel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:27:30 UTC
07:27:30 KST

The number of Israelis returning to the country fell by 58% in 2025 compared with 2009, an Israeli parliamentary committee revealed Monday, amid estimates that nearly 1 million Israelis are living abroad.
The figures were presented during a meeting of the Knesset’s Committee for Immigration, Absorption and Diaspora Affairs convened to examine the growing emigration of Israelis, according to the parliament’s official website.
Data from the Knesset Research and Information Center showed that 4,483 Israelis returned to the country in 2025, down from 10,903 in 2009.
Between 2005 and 2024, approximately 141,000 Israelis returned after living abroad, an annual average of roughly 7,000, the center said.
Estimates presented to the committee indicated that around 1 million Israelis currently live outside the country.
- Where are Israelis returning from?
According to the center’s analysis, 45% of returning Israelis came from the US, followed by 6% from the UK, 5% from Canada and 4% from France.
Germany, Russia, Romania and Ukraine each accounted for 3% of returnees, while Australia, Italy and Moldova each accounted for 2%.
More than a quarter of those returning were minors, while 47% were aged between 28 and 60.
Around 70% returned after living abroad for at least five years, the data showed.
- Government accused of inaction
Gilad Kariv, chairman of the Immigration, Absorption and Diaspora Affairs Committee, accused the Israeli government of failing to take steps to encourage Israelis living abroad to return.
“Since our last discussion on this issue, additional data have been published indicating a decline in the number of Israelis returning to Israel,” Kariv said.
He said the committee had called on the government to formulate a five-year plan aimed at bringing Israelis living abroad back to the country.
A similar plan was introduced in 2010 but has not been renewed since, he added.
“We presented a wide range of measures that could be taken to encourage Israelis to return to their homeland, but unfortunately, the government chose to ignore our recommendations,” Kariv said.
He added that the government had also failed to establish a roundtable to examine ways to encourage Israelis to return.
“There is no body in Israel responsible for addressing emigration,” he said, accusing the government of refusing to take responsibility for the issue.
The meeting also highlighted a growing exodus of medical professionals.
“We are seeing an increase in the number of doctors leaving Israel and a decline in the number of those choosing to return,” said Itai Ater, a professor at Tel Aviv University.
Highly experienced senior doctors account for around 20% of those leaving, he said, noting that other countries offer incentives to attract medical professionals.
The Israeli daily Haaretz reported Sunday on a study by Tel Aviv University showing that at least 1,370 doctors left Israel between 2023 and 2025.
One in five doctors who left during the period was over the age of 45, a trend the study described as “worrying.”
A previous report by the Israeli Finance Ministry found that around 24% of specialist doctors at public hospitals are expected to reach retirement age in the coming years.
Nearly 25% of doctors currently working have already passed retirement age but remain in their positions because of staff shortages, according to the report.
Another Tel Aviv University study published in early August found that 268,509 Israelis left the country for at least three months between 2023 and 2025, a figure the Israeli public broadcaster KAN described as a record.
Israeli reports have attributed the rising emigration to the repercussions of the Gaza war, soaring living costs and the political crisis surrounding the government’s efforts to weaken the judiciary.
A Kantar poll conducted for KAN and published on Aug. 9 found that nearly one-fifth of Israelis had considered emigrating during the previous two years.
Around 12% said the outcome of the upcoming general election could affect their decision to remain in or leave the country.
The Israel Hayom newspaper also reported on Aug. 7, citing an internal Tax Authority document, that the emigration rate among wealthy Israelis doubled between 2019 and 2024.
Annual tax losses resulting from their departure rose from around 500 million shekels ($166 million) to 1.2 billion shekels ($400 million) in 2023 and 2024, according to the document.
The figures come as Israel continues its genocidal war in the Gaza Strip, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000, most of them women and children, while destroying around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure.
They also coincide with Israel’s continuing attacks on Lebanon and its ongoing threats against Iran.

Resolution doesn't endorse any specific map: MEA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:23:42 UTC
07:23:42 KST

India was among the 164 countries that voted in favour of UN General Assembly's Sept 4 resolution, "Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World's Regions, Particularly Africa".MEA said the resolution's purpose is to encourage the use of equal-area map projections that preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses, and it neither adopts nor authenticates any particular world map, nor does it address political cartography, including international boundaries, disputed territories or place names.
"India voted in favour of the resolution and also made an explanation, stressing the underlying principle of promoting equal-area cartographic representation. We also highlighted that the resolution does not constitute endorsement of any specific map, projection or depiction of national boundaries," said Randhir Jaiswal.The resolution received abstentions from Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine, and a lone vote against it from US.
The resolution noted that the Mercator projection remains widely used in educational, media, digital and official materials, despite the considerable distortion of landmasses to the North and South, far from the equator.
It expressed concern that this distortion contributed to minimising the perceived sizes of Africa, Latin America and South Asia, and perpetuating an unbalanced view of the world. India welcomed the intention behind the resolution to promote more accurate and representative cartographic practices.

Burnham, Trump Agree to Keep Working Toward Ukraine-Russia Ceasefire

The resignation comes amid the fallout from a major investigation by Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) into an alleged criminal organization operating within the Prosecutor General’s Office.

Kravchenko said Monday that security personnel initially prevented NABU detectives from entering because investigators had not shown which offices they intended to search. He said he later spoke with the heads of NABU and SAPO and ordered that investigators be given access to his office, other rooms and safes.
NABU and SAPO say their Operation Carthage investigation uncovered a criminal organization allegedly headed by an official at the Prosecutor General’s Office. Investigators accuse members of taking bribes in exchange for shielding fraudulent call centers and laundering proceeds from the scheme.
Ukrainska Pravda identified the suspected official as Serhii Kropyva, deputy head of the Prosecutor General’s Office’s International Legal Cooperation Department. Kropyva was detained and on Sept. 6 remanded in custody with bail set at Hr.120 million, about $2.7 million.
Kravchenko has denied involvement in protecting illegal call centers.
His submission does not immediately end his tenure. Under Ukraine’s Constitution, the prosecutor general is appointed and dismissed by the president with the consent of the Verkhovna Rada. Ukrainian law states that the prosecutor general’s powers end when the relevant parliamentary resolution takes effect.
Kravchenko has served as prosecutor general since June 21, 2025, after parliament approved his appointment and Zelensky formally appointed him by presidential decree.

Eiffel Tower employees strike after female workers removal
Unknown

Eiffel Tower employees strike after female staff removed
September 8, 2026
The Eiffel Tower in Paris, France, was closed on Monday after staff went on strike to protest the exclusion of female workers during a visit by a Hindu religious group.
Visitors to the tower on Monday saw a message that says its opening is "delayed for operational reasons."
The staff released a statement in which they condemned "professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex" during the religious group's visit.
Around 100 men from the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement were visiting the landmark.
The company that operates the Tower, SETE, said that the group had requested a visit as part of which the "interactions with women" would be limited.
Emmanuel Gregoire, Paris' Socialist mayor, called the incident "unacceptable."
"Equality between women and men will never end at the foot of our historic monuments, nor anywhere else in this city," Gregoire said.
Eiffel Tower operator regrets incident
SETE accepted that the decision was a mistake.
"These conditions should not have been accepted," SETE said.
Company head Ariel Weil told the AFP news agency that SETE will "draw the necessary conclusions" from the case. Weil himself is an elected official in Paris.
"No motive of a religious order could justify a distinction based on gender or any other discriminatory consideration in welcoming the public," Weil wrote on his X account.
The Eiffel Tower sees some seven million visitors a year. It was closed all day due to the strike, but will open again on Tuesday, a staff representative said.

North Korea slams joint drills by US, South Korea and Japan, warns of consequences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:17:57 UTC
07:17:57 KST

North Korea has denounced a five-day military exercise by the US, South Korea, and Japan, warning of consequences from what it called Washington's increasingly provocative military activities on the Korean Peninsula.
The fourth iteration of the Freedom Edge exercise began with an opening ceremony at Yokota Air Base in Japan and will run through Friday, according to the US Pacific Command.
The drills are being conducted in international waters and airspace south of South Korea, as well as at military installations and command posts in Japan.
Freedom Edge focuses on interoperability across air, maritime and cyber domains, along with integrated air and missile defence.
South Korea has described the exercise as defensive and aimed at strengthening deterrence and response capabilities against North Korea's nuclear and missile threats.
'Military provocations'
North Korea, however, condemned the trilateral drills as a threat to itself and other countries in the region.
In a Defence Ministry statement carried by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), North Korea accused Washington of pursuing "military provocations" and vowed to take "response measures."
North Korean Defence Minister Kim Song-ji issued "a note of warning against the reckless military moves of the US and its satellite countries to create a serious military confrontation and possibility of conflict on the Korean Peninsula" in the statement.
He also "solemnly" warned of "the consequences to be entailed by them," according to KCNA.
The statements said there would be no change in Pyongyang's policy of responding to US hostility with the "toughest stand to the last."
The drills come weeks after US President Donald Trump said that he had instructed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to "substantially reduce" separate planned bilateral military exercises between the US and South Korea, citing their cost and his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
Trump said those exercises sent an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to Pyongyang.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 8, 2026
Jakarta airport and four others near Indonesia’s capital reopen after volcanic ash disruption
Indonesia’s main airport and several other air travel hubs reopened early on Sept 8 after days of closure due to ash from a volcanic eruption, the Transport Ministry said.
The ministry wrote on Instagram that the airport serving the capital Jakarta and four others near the city or around the island of Java are now operating again, as the air safety crisis that left hundreds of thousands of travellers stranded subsides.
Mount Anak Krakatau, about 150km from Jakarta, erupted on Sept 5, spewing a fountain of lava and a plume of volcanic ash.
Eight airports halted operations over the weekend after ash was detected in their airspace, disrupting nearly 3,000 flights and leaving more than 340,000 passengers stranded, the Transport Ministry reported on Sept 7.
Britain set to impose trade ban on Israeli West Bank settlements
Britain is set to announce wide-ranging economic restrictions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank as soon as Sept 8, according to seven officials briefed on the measures, in what experts say would be a significant censure of Israeli policy toward Palestinians.
The measures are expected to include a trade ban on goods produced in the settlements, the officials said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Three of the officials said the measures could also include sanctions on companies helping to build settlements.
Israel has become increasingly isolated on the world stage in the aftermath of the devastating war in the Gaza Strip, and international attention has focused on Israel’s tightening grip over the West Bank.
Paris probes claim that women were hidden from Hindu delegation at Eiffel Tower
Female employees at the Eiffel Tower were asked to step out of sight during a visit by a Hindu religious delegation at the weekend, according to union representatives, prompting a staff protest and an investigation by the Paris city authorities.
The monument was closed late on Sept 7 as employees held a meeting over the incident, which has angered staff and drawn criticism from French politicians.
The dispute stems from a private visit on Sept 5 by a delegation of about 100 people linked to BAPS (Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha), a Hindu group whose representatives were in France for festivities related to the inauguration of a Hindu temple in the Paris suburbs.
Europe’s biggest mobile operators in talks for satellite-to-mobile venture
A group of Europe’s biggest mobile operators are in early talks to create a consortium to bid on satellite spectrum and offer direct-to-mobile service, which would rival Elon Musk’s Starlink service on the continent, people familiar with the matter said.
Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone Group and Telefonica would jointly bid for a share of airwaves that the European Union has proposed reserving for a local operator, a plan aimed at increasing sovereign satellite capabilities, the people said, asking not to be identified because the plans are private. No final decisions on the consortium or plans to bid have been made, they said.
To comply with the EU’s proposal, any satellite operator would need to be majority controlled by a European business.
Elena Rybakina tops Naomi Osaka, sets US Open quarter-final clash with China’s Zheng Qinwen
World number two Elena Rybakina swept past four-time Grand Slam champion Naomi Osaka 6-1, 6-4 on Sept 7 to line up a US Open quarter-final against China’s Zheng Qinwen.
Kazakhstan’s Rybakina, who added the French Open title to her 2022 Wimbledon crown this year, is into the US Open last eight for the first time in her career.
The meeting with 2024 Olympic gold medallist Zheng will carry extra weight. If Rybakina reaches the semi-finals she is assured of supplanting Aryna Sabalenka atop the world rankings, even if the Belarusian wins her third straight US Open title.

SANAA, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Seven people, including a child, were killed and seven others injured in an airstrike on a prison in Al-Jawf province in northern Yemen on Monday, Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported, attributing the strike to Saudi Arabia.

Iran retaliates after US strikes on oil tankers (VIDEOS)
Iran has begun retaliating after US forces struck Iranian oil tankers near Kharg Island, with ballistic missiles launched toward American military facilities in the region and the IRGC warning tanker crews near Bahrain and Kuwait to leave their vessels “immediately.”
The IRGC Navy issued what it called an “urgent warning” late Tuesday, telling tanker crews around the docks and anchorages of both Gulf states to immediately abandon their ships.
“We warn all crew members of the tankers in the vicinity of the docks of Kuwait and Bahrain [...] to immediately leave their vessels, whether at anchor or at the docks, as they will be targeted,” the IRGC Navy Command said.
The statement accused Bahrain and Kuwait of hosting US forces and being “partners” in Washington’s attacks on Iranian shipping.
Additional footage of a PATRIOT battery conducting a massive ballistic missile engagement over Jordan tonight. 
Well over a dozen interceptors can be seen engaging incoming Iranian ballistic missiles. pic.twitter.com/u69lJKtFJ7
Iranian retaliation began shortly afterward, with numerous videos circulating online showing ballistic missiles being launched from multiple locations across Iran toward US military facilities in the region.
Videos from Jordan appeared to show intense air-defense activity, with multiple Patriot interceptors engaging incoming projectiles, including what some OSINT accounts identified as medium-range ballistic missiles equipped with cluster warheads.
Multiple OSINT accounts identified Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, a major facility used by US forces east of Amman, as one of the principal targets. Some reported missile impacts near the base, but neither the alleged impacts nor the type of warheads used had been officially confirmed.
Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported that two Iranian oil tankers were targeted near Kharg Island and Jask earlier in the day. The crews of both vessels were safely evacuated and were being transferred toward the coast aboard lifeboats.
The latest attacks follow another round on Saturday, when US Central Command said it struck three Iranian crude carriers after ballistic missiles were fired toward an American aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. Two tankers were disabled and a third, which was carrying no oil, was destroyed after its crew was ordered to abandon ship.
Iran subsequently claimed to have struck three tankers traveling along what it described as an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as three US-linked vessels elsewhere.
The maritime confrontation has become an increasingly prominent front in the six-month conflict. Washington maintains a naval blockade restricting traffic to and from Iranian ports, while Tehran has imposed its own controls over passage through Hormuz and recently announced plans for an additional restricted maritime zone in the Persian Gulf.
About one-fifth of global oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war, making threats to commercial shipping particularly sensitive for energy markets. Oil prices have continued climbing, with Brent trading near $100 a barrel and US benchmark WTI over $93 on Tuesday as markets priced in growing risks to global energy supplies.

Yes, the AfD victory signals a danger to democracy, but not the way they tell you

Unknown Publisher

Yes, the AfD victory signals a danger to democracy, but not the way they tell you
Say what you will about ex-BlackRock bigwig German Chancellor and uber-grinch Friedrich Merz, but he has his moments of unexpected alertness.
Currently, he is shocked, shocked! He has noticed that his party, the mainstream conservatives of the CDU are “in serious danger” after suffering their worst defeat in decades.
Germany’s dark star of unpopularity was, of course, talking about the results of the regional elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. They have produced a landslide victory for the new-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, under its shooting star Ulrich ‘Uli’ Siegmund.
They delivered a colossal, devastating fiasco to the CDU and, of course, Merz personally: The AfD has scored 43.8 percent of the vote, the CDU 17.2 percent. When compared with the last state election, the AfD gained 23 percent, while the CDU lost 19.9 percent.
Polls show that the AfD has massively siphoned off former CDU voters and also mobilized previous non-voters with unprecedented success. In terms of age cohorts, the AfD is dominating almost the entire spectrum except among the very old.
The CDU, which had been in charge in Saxony-Anhalt’s capital of Magdeburg for over two decades, has suffered no ordinary defeat but a catastrophic wipe-out shaking the party, to quote Merz again, “to its very foundations.” The former default ruling party of first West and then post-1990 Germany is in tatters. It is a sign of even worse things to come. In Saxony-Anhalt it has no future, quite literally: among the youngest voters the CDU achieved a pitiful 5 percent, far below its already horrific overall result.
The man who has pro-actively led the party of Helmut Kohl and Angela Merkel into this total debacle may still be in office for now. True to form, he shows no signs of accepting responsibility, that is, resigning. But rumors about a CDU rebellion against Merz were circulating even before the disaster. Calls for ending his ruinous tenure have only become louder now. And if not now, then soon: Having suffered – and produced – one catastrophic defeat, Merz will soon face more regional elections that are likely to go badly for the CDU as well.
It is true that Saxony-Anhalt is small. One of Germany’s 16 federal states, it has a population of 2.1 million, of whom about 1.7 million can vote. That is less than the electorate of, for instance, the city of Hamburg. Yet no one in Germany even tries to pretend that what has happened in Saxony-Anhalt will stay in Saxony-Anhalt. On the contrary, everyone – across the entire mediascape and political spectrum – takes it as self-evident that these elections are bound to have massive national effects. Likewise, it did not even take US President Donald Trump’s unusual social media post to rub in that the Magdeburg quake is reverberating internationally, too.
If Merz falls – and perhaps even if he sticks to his seat for a long time before doing so – the radical-Centrist coalition currently in charge in Berlin will be under enormous pressure. Witness the fact that its frontman from the Social-Democrats (SPD), Finance Minister and austerity-imposer-in-chief Lars Klingbeil is already making terrified noises about rethinking some Berlin’s mean cuts to pensions, healthcare, and social security. How a little pain can concentrate the mind.
One thing seems to finally have sunk in with Germany’s slow, lazy, and complacent establishment: Neither the so-called ‘firewall’ – that is, deliberate discrimination against not merely the AfD but its millions of voters – has failed and offers no hope for the future. Clinging to that moronic, deeply undemocratic and simply indecently unfair strategy will only make the AfD stronger. Exactly as it has up until now.
Yet make no mistake: Germany’s radical Centrists are obstinate. Even with the ‘firewall’ demolished, they might still try to cling to its ruins for a while. That, however, will not make a difference in the end. What could have more substantial and very disruptive consequences is something else. What if they radicalize their strategy against the AfD, its electoral surge (in free and fair votes), and its supporters further?
Among the sane, such a doubling down might appear absurd: Where would it be supposed to lead? Severe unrest? Secession? But you only have to look at the current establishment’s policy toward Russia, Ukraine, and the Ukraine conflict to realize that Berlin, as it is now, does not shy away from anything just because it’s entirely mad and highly damaging to Germany.
And that, notwithstanding the ceaseless and ever less effective mainstream media propaganda smearing the AfD as Nazism redux, is where the real threat to democracy lies. Merz has already struck a tone that is, in effect, threatening: “Reassuring” German citizens, who mostly cannot stand him, that the German Basic Law, the de facto constitution, “prevails in Saxony-Anhalt as well.”
Since, in reality, no one has challenged that fact, Merz’s statement is suspect. It can easily be read as a crude hint that Berlin is looking for pretexts to engage in dirty lawfare against the AfD in general, the AfD specifically in Saxony-Anhalt, or a state government led by the AfD in Magdeburg. This may become even more likely if the AfD there is joined by CDU renegades, as seems probable.
In that case, the CDU leadership in Berlin – if Merz continues to dominate it – would also want to make an example of these local rebels and punish the AfD for the CDU’s own failure to keep its troops together. Finally, never forget that Merz is also ‘Mr. Firewall’: there is no politician in Germany more associated with that failed policy. His personal frustration must be boundless; his good faith and fairness are infamously limited.
And then there is – drumroll, fanfare blast, and an endless, tormented yawn – Russia, Russia, Russia. Yes, you have guessed right: after tanking the German economy as never before since World War Two, maneuvering the country as close to World War Three as also never before since World War Two, and throwing German taxpayers’ earnings into the Kiev money burner to the tune of, at least, a hundred billion euro and counting, Merz and his motley crew are seriously trying to tell us that the real reason why no one wants them anymore is Moscow or, why not, President Vladimir Putin personally.
The usual “civil society” cut-outs have already started pointing fingers. Merz himself has found time to reaffirm that “especially now” he won’t “budge a millimeter” from, in effect, trying to drive Germany into an open shooting war with Russia because the current proxy war is just not good enough for him.
And, of course, the public is subjected to an ongoing propaganda barrage smearing the AfD as a whole and in Saxony-Anhalt in particular Moscow’s fifth column. In reality, its crime is to have articulated many ordinary Germans’ perfectly reasonable resistance to the establishment’s out-of-control warmongering.
In sum, take these two lines of CDU defense – or attack – together and it is obvious that the real threat to German democracy comes, as before, from the radical Center: Accusing the AfD of being a Russian Trojan Horse and, at the same time, hinting that its success is somehow incompatible with the constitution – those are the key ingredients for justifying repression. Let’s hope that neither Merz nor his CDU nor the establishment as a whole dare try, because if they do, there will be resistance. Berlin has already ruined peace abroad. Domestic peace should not follow.

Merz ‘shocked’ by AfD win but refuses to change course (VIDEO)
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has blamed his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party’s crushing defeat by the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt on poor communication with voters, while refusing to change course.
Merz, who has been described as Germany’s least popular head of government in some 30 years, maintained he would not budge an inch on his “reform” agenda following what he called his party’s “most serious electoral defeat in decades.”
The AfD took 43.8% of the vote in the eastern German state over the weekend, coming close to securing an absolute majority in the regional legislature. The conservative CDU, which has dominated Saxony-Anhalt’s political landscape for much of the period since German reunification, finished a distant second with 17.5%.
Ahead of the vote, a regional party official told Euractiv that the CDU branch in Saxony-Anhalt was being forced to pay the price for the deeply unpopular policies of the federal government.
Speaking at a press conference following the election, Merz said he and other senior party officials were “deeply shocked” by the result. “We did not expect this, certainly not in this form,” he said, adding that the outcome would likely have implications far beyond Germany.
Merz also said his party could not accept a situation in which “almost 60% of voters in a federal state, with a very high turnout, vote for political parties that fundamentally call into question our country’s democratic institutions and rules.”
Apart from the AfD, the Left Party – descended from the former East German Communists – and the recently formed left-wing Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) were also condemned by the chancellor for supposedly challenging Germany’s “democratic” order, according to state broadcaster DW.
Merz maintained that certain things are “not up for a vote” in Germany, including the principle that “power is granted, not seized.” He vowed to “strengthen our political order and our firm anchoring in Europe.”
The chancellor acknowledged that he himself had been “a constant topic in this election campaign,” but insisted the federal government would not change course. “My determination to continue on the path of reform remains unbroken,” he said, adding that the government apparently just needed to explain the measures better.
Merz came to power following snap elections in February 2025, promising to revive Germany’s struggling economy, but has since poured more money into the military while blaming some of the country’s economic problems on Germans themselves. He has told citizens to work more and claimed that the “welfare state as we have it today can no longer be financed.” In May, his government announced plans for social spending cuts and unveiled an unpopular pension reform.
The chancellor also doubled down on his support for Kiev, while acknowledging that “exactly 57.7% of voters” had backed parties critical of Berlin’s anti-Russian policies and unwavering support for Ukraine.
“I will not deviate by a single millimeter from my fundamental conviction that, especially now, we must defend our freedom against Russia,” he stated, advocating for increased military spending and continued aid to Kiev. Berlin has repeatedly justified the policy by citing an alleged “Russian threat,” which Moscow has consistently dismissed as “nonsense.”

‘Pack your suitcases’: Israel’s far right unveils its blueprint for emptying Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:49:54 UTC
03:49:54 KST

‘Pack your suitcases’: Israel’s far right unveils its blueprint for emptying Gaza
Israel’s far-right national security minister has put a seven-year timetable on emptying Gaza of most of its people, and dressed it up as choice. Gazans RT spoke to call it what international law already names it: forced displacement.
Last week, Jewish Power chairman and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir unveiled ‘Disengagement 710’, a policy blueprint for what he calls the voluntary migration of Gaza residents to countries willing to take them. Destinations floated by his party include Türkiye, unspecified Arab states, Ethiopia, and Congo.
The numbers are not modest. The plan foresees the departure of about 250,000 people in the first year, 1.11 million within three years, and some 1.86 million within seven, encompassing the bulk of the Strip’s population.
To run it, Jewish Power wants the next government to create a dedicated ministry for “voluntary migration,” complete with a minister, a director-general, its own budget, an international negotiating team, and an implementation apparatus.
Ben-Gvir vows to make the ministry a coalition demand after Israel’s October 27 election. “Instead of illusions of peace now, we need actions of emigration now,” he said. “Instead of them digging tunnels, it’s time to pack suitcases.”
This idea is not new for the Jewish state.
A Zionist through-line
In 1937, David Ben-Gurion, then a leading Zionist figure, promoted the transfer of Palestinians and argued they should be moved to Transjordan. In the 1980s, the same ‘voluntary’ formula was championed by far-right politicians Rehavam Ze’evi – nicknamed ‘Gandhi’– and Meir Kahane. Their schemes never left the drawing board.
Ben-Gvir now presents his version as newly realistic, citing earlier public backing from US President Donald Trump. Trump floated mass relocation from Gaza in early 2025, then walked the idea back under Arab and international pressure.
His later 20-point framework stated that no one would be forced to leave and that residents should be encouraged to stay. Ben-Gvir treats the first Trump remark as political cover and the second as an inconvenience.
Gazans RT interviewed rejected the initiative as illegal under international law and a crime against humanity.
”People in Gaza and across Palestine know Ben-Gvir’s plans go far beyond our existence in the Strip,” said Abdallah Ali, a resident of central Gaza.
“He wants people out of Gaza, then out of West Bank villages, then out of West Bank cities toward Jordan. He believes in transfer and an ‘alternative homeland’.”
Ali said that is why Gazans, himself included, intend to stay put.
Rami Al Meghari, from Al-Maghazi camp in central Gaza, reached the same conclusion for a different reason: memory of exile.
“Many Palestinians found life in other countries, especially Arab states, awkward and humiliating,” he said. “They will not leave Gaza for a destination that cannot guarantee dignity, whether an Arab capital or some African country Israel has long suggested, like Somalia.”
Polls, rubble, and the meaning of ‘voluntary’
A PCPSR poll last year found 56% of Gazans interviewed unwilling to emigrate. A substantial minority, some 43%, said they would.
Ali and Al Meghari were not surprised. Despair is real, and the findings of various UN reports show it clearly.
As of June 16, 2026, satellite analysis by the UN Satellite Centre found 201,290 structures damaged, an estimated 82% of all buildings in Gaza. Of those, 134,422 were assessed as destroyed, 13,848 severely damaged, 28,096 moderately damaged and 24,924 possibly damaged.
Most of Gaza’s 2.1 million people remain displaced. The Shelter Cluster, surveying in June 2026, said 1.98 million people, 94% of the population, need shelter and household items.
Food and water continue to be an issue. Between mid-April and June 30, 2026, more than 1.2 million people (59%) were still in dire need of assistance.
Assessments in 2026 found 43% of households below the 15-liter humanitarian minimum per person per day, and 62% below the 6-liter drinking-water floor.
But Ali and Al Meghari insist the pull of the land is much stronger.
“Whatever the suffering, even with around 97 percent of cropland destroyed and most of the built environment gone, people are putting up tents and staying in displacement camps. They are not packing to leave,” Ali said.
“They lived through the 1948 catastrophe and the 1967 Nakba. They will pull through again.”
Al Meghari still hopes the political weather will change. “Life can move forward in Gaza if there is serious international and Arab pressure to implement the second phase of the ceasefire. The United States has a particular responsibility to make that happen. Russia also needs to play a pivotal role to bring the suffering of the Palestinians to an end.”
Reconstruction as leverage
There is little movement on reconstruction. Israel is blocking construction materials, demanding that Hamas disarm and demilitarize first. The Board of Peace has pushed for weapons to be collected and placed under international supervision, a formula Israel rejects.
Ali sees the stalled effort as a policy, not an accident. “This is taking a very long time. I do not think Israel will accept Gaza’s reconstruction anytime soon. It will keep complicating reality until leaving becomes the only realistic option.”
Ahmed Al-Masri, a lawyer in Gaza, argues Israel has played this hand before and lost. “We lived this in 2014 [Operation Protective Edge – ed.]. Israel said Gaza should not be rebuilt. Then, under international pressure and with UN supervision, it was forced to comply.”
And he also pins some hope on Israel’s October 27 parliamentary vote. “If the far-right government is removed, there might be a beginning, a glimmer on the horizon, and a better political reality for people here, if Palestinians also insist on rebuilding political, social and economic life.”
That is the wager Gaza is making: that endurance outlasts a plan that needs other countries to open their doors, Washington to revive an idea it already shelved, and two million people to accept that ‘voluntary’ means leaving home because the alternative has been made unlivable.
Ben-Gvir is betting the opposite – that the wreckage, a ministry, and a slogan about suitcases can finish what earlier transfer schemes could not. Gazans say they have heard that speech before.

Netanyahu knew about Oct. 7 Hamas attack days in advance – report

Netanyahu knew about Oct. 7 Hamas attack days in advance – report
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally warned that Hamas was preparing a major attack days before October 7, 2023, but did not relay the information to Israel’s top security chiefs, Haaretz reported on Tuesday.
According to the newspaper, Emirati President Mohammed bin Zayed called Netanyahu roughly ten days before the assault and told him that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major operation that could cause bloodshed and destabilize the region.
Netanyahu reportedly played down the threat, saying he believed Hamas was more likely to act in the West Bank and that Israel was prepared.
His office has rejected the report as an “absolute lie,” insisting no such call took place.
The alleged advance notice has added to scrutiny over what Israeli leaders knew ahead of the Hamas-led assault and whether warning signs were ignored.
Haaretz previously reported that Sinwar had sent messages through Palestinian intermediaries warning that he was preparing an “earthquake.” The message reportedly reached Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security service, whose then-chief Ronen Bar briefed Netanyahu. Egyptian intelligence was also reported to have warned Israel shortly before the attack.
Israeli intelligence had separately obtained a Hamas battle plan known as ‘Jericho Wall’, outlining a cross-border assault, attacks on military positions and hostage-taking. The New York Times later reported that the document closely resembled the October 7 operation. Israeli officials have disputed how seriously the plan was taken and whether it was considered an imminent threat.
Netanyahu’s government has also faced criticism for allowing Qatari funds to flow into Hamas-run Gaza for years. Critics argue the policy ultimately strengthened the group Israel later went to war to destroy.
Questions have also been raised over Israel’s military response on October 7. Investigations have suggested that the so-called ‘Hannibal Directive’, which permits extreme measures to prevent the capture of soldiers, may have contributed to Israeli civilian deaths as forces struck vehicles and other locations where hostages or civilians may have been present.
Around 1,200 people were killed in the Hamas-led attack and 251 were taken hostage. Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza has killed more than 73,600 Palestinians, according to the enclave’s Health Ministry.
